16498-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Dated December 23, 1897, this number of The Great Round World explains Austria's troubles to young readers. Count Badeni's fall and Baron von Gautsch's rise did not end the unrest; serious rioting broke out in Bohemia. The paper counts Austria-Hungary's peoples: Germans near ten and a half millions, Slavs near twenty millions in nine races, and Magyars near seven and a half.

The Czechs, or Bohemians, lead the Slavs at five and a half millions. The issue teaches the news as a story, with figures a school reader can grasp. It shows the children's paper at its didactic best, turning a tangled empire into clear, lively current events.
21091-the-life-of-william-ewart-gladston:
John Morley, himself a leading Liberal politician, wrote this three-volume life of William Ewart Gladstone, published in 1903. Volume One covers the years 1809 to 1859, from Gladstone's birth to the middle of his career. Morley worked from the vast Gladstone papers kept at Hawarden.

He also drew on thousands of letters from Gladstone's many correspondents and on journals from other sources. The volume traces a young Tory who became a Peelite and then a rising Liberal leader. Speeches, budgets, church questions, and party fights fill the story. Morley's access made this the standard life of Gladstone for years.
4804-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
In this fourth volume of The Rise of the Dutch Republic, dated 1855, John Lothrop Motley covers Philip the Second in the Netherlands from 1555 to 1559. Chapter two sketches Philip the Second and Mary Tudor, with his council and the rivalry of Ruy Gomez and Alva. Ruy Gomez, Queen Mary of Hungary, and Philibert of Savoy follow.

The truce of Vaucelles and a secret treaty between the Pope and Henry II lead to Philip's purposes and a re-enactment of the edict of 1550. The king's dissimulation, a request to the provinces, and an infraction of the truce in Italy follow, with Pope Paul IV and Cardinal Caraffa. France resolves on war against Spain, with a campaign in Italy, a siege of Rome, and peace with the pontiff. Hostilities on the Flemish border, where Coligny was foiled at Douai, carry the narrative on. Readers get Motley's account of Philip's early reign.
6419-copyright-renewals-1959: The hosted file for this title holds no renewal data itself, only a short placeholder note explaining that the 1959 renewals were placed in two other files instead. Readers looking for the 1959 entries are directed to two files: January to June, and July to December. The note marks this file as an unused empty reserve from the series. No lists, names, or renewal records appear in the sample.
agassiz-essay-on-classification-1859:
Louis Agassiz published his Essay on Classification in 1859, in the English edition of his 1857 work. Agassiz, the Swiss-born Harvard naturalist, was then America's most famous scientist. The essay states his system: species are fixed forms in the mind of a Creator, classed by a divine plan.

Agassiz sorted animals by body plans he called branches, and he argued that classification reveals thought, not descent. The book appeared the same year as Darwin's Origin of Species, and it became the great anti-Darwinian statement of special creation. Agassiz's students filled American museums and universities. Modern readers meet in the essay the strongest case the losing side made, by its most gifted champion.
andronomy-or-magneto-physiognomico-crani:
Andronomy, or Magneto-Physiognomico-Craniology, published in 1859 by J D L Zender, offers a new system on the magnetic constitution of man. In Zender's scheme, that makeup is shown by physiognomy blended with craniology, the reading of face and skull together. The system claims to be maintained by moral and physical hygiene, according to the rules of physiology, therapeutics, metaphysics, and present practice.

The book is enlarged from the author's Physiognomony and Craniology of 1843, and it carries a little treatise of phrenology at its back. The copy preserved here rests in the Harry Houdini Collection at the Library of Congress, a fitting home for a work of magnetic character science. It shows the nineteenth century blending body, mind, and magnetism into one system.
antarctic-treaty-1959:
Twelve nations signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington in 1959, setting the whole southern continent aside for peace and science. The signers included rival Cold War powers and states that claimed slices of Antarctic land. They agreed to freeze the quarrel over ownership and keep soldiers and weapons off the ice.

The articles ban military bases, weapons tests, and nuclear explosions on the continent. They guarantee free scientific research and open inspection of all stations by other parties. No new land claims may be made while the treaty lasts. Many more nations have joined since, and the system remains one of the most successful arms control agreements ever written.
appreciation-phrenologique-de-monsieur-t: Appréciation Phrénologique de Monsieur Triat, published in 1859 by A Castle, is a French phrenological assessment of a named man. In thirty pages with a plate, a practitioner applies the science of head reading to Monsieur Triat as an individual case. His faculties are weighed, and his character is pronounced from the form of his skull. Such published readings were part advertisement and part demonstration for phrenology. This slight volume preserves the French practice of the art at mid-century, in a single worked example.
arxiv-2412-00559:
Łukasz Grzybowski, Jakub Pokrywka, Michał Ciesiółka, Jeremi Kaczmarek, and Marek Kubis turn Poland's real medical exams into a benchmark for language models, in a 2024 paper. The hosted title frames the work as a test of Polish-English medical knowledge transfer. The exams are the licensing and specialization tests that Polish doctors must pass. Scraped from public sources, the set holds more than 24,000 questions, including a matched Polish-English portion translated professionally for foreign candidates.

The team ran leading language models, general, medical, and Polish-tuned, through the questions and compared them with human medical students. The strongest model, GPT-4o, came close to human performance. Yet scores sagged across languages and specialties, exposing weak spots in cross-lingual transfer and deep domain knowledge. The authors flag the limits this sets, and the ethical questions it raises, for using such models in real clinical work.
arxiv-2412-01359:
Cordieri, Bordin, and Mishra study small solar plants that make power from heat for local trade, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The plants use sun heat to spin a cycle that works well at low heat. That makes them a good fit for small grids. In these grids, homes both use and make power and trade with each other.

The team builds a plan to run the plant and its battery in the best way. They test how plant traits change the gains. Pairing the plant with storage makes output more steady and easier to trade. Across test cases, running costs fell by sixteen percent on average. The work shows clear value for local peer-to-peer trade.
arxiv-2412-03259:
Event cameras, which report only changes in a scene, are fast and frugal but hard to study, because real recordings rarely say exactly how the view moved. Jens Egholm Pedersen, Dimitris Korakovounis, and Jörg Conradt built a simulator, GERD, to fill that gap in a 2024 paper. It renders objects under precisely controlled shifts, stretches, and timing changes, and records the true motion at every step.

The tool adds three kinds of sensor noise and allows motion finer than one pixel. The authors show it can train and test models that claim geometric guarantees, and they release it openly as a companion to real sensor data.
arxiv-2412-03759:
Valery Zhdanov studies still, ball-shaped solutions in a modified theory of gravity, in a paper from 2024. The theory swaps the curvature term of general relativity for a function of it. A change of frame turns it into a scalar-tensor theory with a field called the scalaron. He weighs three known shapes for that field's energy hill.

His study centers on heavy setups whose centers hide a naked flaw. Across masses, field weights, and zone sizes, parts of the solutions look strikingly alike. The scalaron field keeps a universal shape far from the center. Some metric traits near the center also match across all three models. He works out the far-field values of the metric for each case. The sameness hints at deep rules in this gravity family.
arxiv-2412-04359:
Lira-Barria and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-four about shrinking chemical networks used to model exoplanet atmospheres. Detailed models track many species and reactions, but three-dimensional versions cost enormous computing time. Cutting networks down helps, yet past cuts lacked clear, cheap methods. Their algorithm, DARWEN, picks reduced networks using data from a standard one-dimensional model. Sensitivity analysis and a genetic search do the heavy lifting.

The method can tune networks for several similar planets at once. Users can weight accuracy against speed as they wish. It also handles light-driven chemistry, a first for genetic network cuts in this field. Three schemes target accuracy, speed, or photochemistry. All cut costs while keeping results close to the full network.
arxiv-2412-05059:
Benjamin von der Heyde and six co-authors watch the outer matrix of a green alga grow, cell by cell. Their 2025 paper studies Volvox carteri, a ball of cells in a self-built gel. Multicellular life began when plain walls became complex matrices. Volvox shows that transition in a living, simple form.

A glowing tag fused to one matrix protein lit up key structures. Confocal images tracked the compartments around each cell over the life cycle. Compartment sizes followed sturdy gamma-shaped spreads. Packing loosened from tight polygons toward rounder shapes with age. The pattern echoes wet foams yet keeps its own rules. Growth geometry can be measured, not just admired.
arxiv-2412-05859:
Dan and co-authors present a 2024 study of a fast wind of warm gas blowing out of a bright, dusty galaxy. The Webb telescope's mid-infrared eye mapped the galaxy, named F08572+3915 NW, in fine detail. Four glow lines of hydrogen molecules trace a spinning disk and a twin-cone outflow. The outflow holds a mid speed near 1,100 kilometers per second out to a wide radius, with peaks near 3,000.

The outflowing gas runs warmer than the disk gas, a sign of shock heating in the churn. The new wind shares its aim and motion with a smaller warm wind seen before from the ground. It outruns the cold winds mapped by other telescopes. Galaxy winds of this speed can starve a galaxy of star-making fuel.
arxiv-2412-06059:
Coriasco, Fatibene, Garruto, and Orizzonte published lecture notes in 2024 on the Cauchy problem inside loop quantum gravity, the question of whether starting data determine a spacetime's future. The notes study how the analytic behavior of solutions to covariant equations mirrors algebraic features of the equations themselves, especially a key object called the principal symbol.

Relativistic models can be at once under-determined and over-determined, the notes show, yet a well-posed evolution problem can still be carved out of them. That carving leads to pre-quantum configurations and Cauchy bubbles, devices for setting up evolution inside a compact patch of spacetime. General relativity is sketched as the working example. The notes serve readers building the quantum theory's foundations.
arxiv-2412-07959:
Vianello and team wrote in twenty twenty-four on leg exoskeleton control. Therapists guide the control with simple input. Such frames help patients relearn walking by taking part, not just being moved. Usual layered controls need long tuning for each user. Stairs and ramps make that tuning even harder. Their three-step method reads walking traits from sensor data.

Therapists can then tweak those traits on a simple screen. The tweaked traits set joint pose and spring stiffness. How unsure the forecast is shapes the stiffness of help. Two healthy people tested the system on treadmills and stairs. Speeds changed, and therapists tweaked traits live. Walking patterns followed the tweaked traits as planned. Power readings showed the frame truly helped motion. The team aims to cut tuning burden in rehab clinics.
arxiv-2412-08259:
Zhiqiang Yuan and co-authors build, in a 2024 paper, the largest data set yet for teaching machines to make animated chat stickers. Stickers are a daily language on social apps, short and expressive, but good ones are slow to craft by hand. Video generators exist, yet stickers run at low frame rates with looser, more playful meaning, and training data for them were missing.

Their VSD2M set holds two million stickers, still and animated, paired with text. On top of it they add a model layer that mixes meaning across time while guarding fine detail, aimed at the gaps they saw in plain video methods. Several known generators were trained on the set as baselines, with a full analysis of where each stands. The authors offer the set as shared ground for a young field.
arxiv-2412-09959:
Xinhao Zhong and colleagues distill huge image collections into tiny training sets by selecting patches with the help of a diffusion model, rather than generating new pictures. Dataset distillation promises models trained on a handful of synthetic examples, but generation-based versions drift away from the real data distribution and need repeated runs under different settings. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team's method scores each real image patch by the diffusion model's prediction loss, flagging the most distinctive regions. Clustering and ranking inside each class then enforce variety among the chosen patches.

The whole distillation finishes in one pass, and the selected real patches carry no generator bias. Extensive experiments showed consistent gains over previous approaches, by the authors report. The framework is designed to combine with, not replace, diffusion-based distillation methods. It suits teams that must retrain often on a budget.
arxiv-2412-10059:
Kam and co-authors design a neural network accelerator called Panacea in this 2024 paper. Large networks run faster when numbers are stored at low precision and split into slices. Skipping zero slices saves energy, but only with symmetric quantization, which loses accuracy.

Asymmetric quantization keeps accuracy yet produces many nonzero slices that older accelerators cannot skip. Their AQS-GEMM design instead compresses the frequent nonzero slices and skips their operations. Two joint algorithm-hardware tricks raise slice sparsity in the activations further. The result aims to give large-scale inference both high accuracy and low energy use. The work targets the matrix multiplications that dominate neural network cost.
arxiv-2412-10459:
Aoming Liang and co-authors bring conformal prediction to uncertainty scoring for learned models of moving physical systems, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Models that read physics from video need trust scores with real guarantees. Physical data uncertainty had lacked a systematic treatment.

The method wraps benchmark operator learners and returns ranges with stated coverage. Two rivals, dropout sampling and ensembles, were compared on equation data sets. Scores came from straight roll-outs of the forecast, suiting time-series work well. The authors frame the approach as a reliability layer for spatial intelligence systems.
arxiv-2412-10659:
Kaichen Xu and seven co-authors detect anomalous tissue regions by fusing microscope images with spatial transcriptomics in MEATRD. Their paper from twenty twenty-four notes that image-only detectors fail when diseased and healthy tissue look near alike. Gene expression maps add a molecular view of each spot. The method trains on normal tissue alone, learning to rebuild its image patches and expression profiles.

A masked graph dual-attention transformer shares information across modalities and neighboring spots while fighting over-generalization. Bottleneck codes carry the task-relevant signal, a claim the team backs with theory. Reconstruction errors then feed a one-class classifier that flags the odd regions. Across eight real datasets, MEATRD beats rival anomaly detectors, even where visual differences are slight.
arxiv-2412-11459:
Shuo Wang and Issei Sato wrote a 2024 paper on how large language models learn from examples placed inside a prompt. They focus on the induction head, a part of the model linked to this in-context learning. Their question is how the model mixes fresh prompt facts with word links it learned during training.

Working with a two-layer transformer, the authors study the weights in the attention layers as a form of linked memory. They work out what the model should output when prompts come from a simple word-pair model. They then build test prompts to check whether a trained model matches the theory. The study helps explain how models balance new context against stored knowledge.
arxiv-2412-11659:
Gabriele Bressanini, Farhan Hanif, Hyukjoon Kwon, and Kim introduce a new tool for quantum theory in this 2024 paper. They define what they call quantum observables over time, an operator that joins what is measured at two different moments. The idea mirrors an older notion of a quantum state spread over time.

The authors prove a no-go result that sets out when such an operator can be defined at all. They then use it to build a form of time reversal for quantum channels, tied to a chosen reference observable. From that they construct recovery maps that undo noise on the values a user cares about. Worked examples show the method can match the best known sampling cost and beat probabilistic error cancellation.
arxiv-2412-12559:
Taeho Hwang, Sukmin Cho, Soyeong Jeong, Hoyun Song, SeungYoon Han, and Jong Park present EXIT, a method that trims reading material handed to a question-answering system, in a 2024 paper. Such systems fetch documents, then answer from them. But weak fetching forces them to swallow long, noisy context, which slows answers and hurts accuracy. Rewriting context into a summary costs time, while older trimming methods pick sentences one by one without seeing the picture.

EXIT instead classifies whole sentences at once, keeping their links to the surrounding context. It adjusts how much it keeps to the question's difficulty and the fetch quality. On single-fact and multi-step question sets, EXIT beat other trimming methods and systems given the full untrimmed text. It cut answer time and the number of words processed, which the authors offer as a path to cheaper, sharper question answering at scale.
arxiv-2412-13859:
Anna Scius-Bertrand and four co-authors test whether large language models can sort document images with little or no training data, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Sorting scanned documents needs reading of image, layout, and text together. Top systems on the standard benchmark now score near perfect, but they train on hundreds of thousands of labeled pages.

Language models learn well from few examples, which raises a sharp question. How far can prompting with no examples, or fine-tuning with a handful, go on this task? The paper sets up that test in detail. Its aim is to cut the human labeling burden that document sorting usually demands, while keeping accuracy honest.
arxiv-2412-14159:
Johan Samsing and nine co-authors show how bent gravitational waves can reveal the side drift of their source, in a 2024 arXiv paper. A heavy galaxy can bend waves from a merging pair of black holes into two or more copies. Each copy reaches us along a unlike line of sight.

If the source drifts side on as it merges, one copy looks a touch blue shifted and the other red, like sound from a passing car. That split leaves a phase gap between the copies that detectors can read. The team shows the next fleet of ground detectors, set to catch hundreds of bent events a year, can catch such gaps. The trick opens a rare view of how sources move in their homes across deep time.
arxiv-2412-14759:
Jing-Juan Qi and four co-authors study rare decays of B mesons in a 2024 particle physics paper. B mesons are particles containing a heavy bottom quark, and their decays test the standard model. The authors focus on decays that pass through a light scalar particle, where a soft rescattering step adds hard to compute parameters.

Using a factorization method, they fit those parameters from measured event counts in two decay channels. They then predict branching rates and charge asymmetries for decays involving other scalar particles. Predicted patterns for forward backward and local asymmetries matched experimental findings. The work supports extending the same interference picture to other beauty and charm decays.
arxiv-2412-15259:
Fatima AlGhamdi, Reem Mohammed, Hend Al-Khalifa, and Areeb Alowisheq wrote this data paper, published in two thousand twenty-four, to present GLARE, a giant set of Arabic app reviews. The reviews come from the Saudi store of Google Play.

The set holds seventy-six million reviews in all, sixty-nine million of them in Arabic, spread over nearly ten thousand Android apps. The paper walks through how the reviews were gathered and cleaned. A detailed exploratory analysis maps the set's shape: ratings, lengths, app classes, and time spans. Feature engineering steps are also reported. The authors point to uses in sentiment analysis, dialect studies, and app market research. Arabic text data at this scale is rare, they note, and the set is meant to serve language technology for the region.
arxiv-2412-15459:
Alejandro Saavedra and four co-authors test whether neutron stars stay stable in a modified gravity theory. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. The theory adds a Gauss-Bonnet term to Einstein's gravity in four dimensions. Its compact stars can be smaller than general relativity allows. Doubts about their stability have lingered. The authors settle the question with radial perturbation analysis.

They solve the perturbation equations for several realistic equations of state. Skyrme-based and Müller-Serot models both enter the tests. Stability ends exactly at the maximum mass point, as in standard theory. A fresh twist appears near the black hole limit, where stability returns. Modified gravity survives this neutron star check. Dense matter still constrains how gravity may bend.
arxiv-2412-15659:
Yuebei Xiong, Zhirui Gong, and Hao Jin tune the nonlinear anomalous Hall effect in MoS2 in two thousand twenty-four. Time reversal symmetry kills the linear Hall effect in this monolayer. The nonlinear form needs a Berry curvature dipole to appear. Uniaxial strain breaks the crystal symmetry and creates that dipole.

Strain tunes both the size of the effect and its Hall angle. The angle acts like birefringence in optics, they show. That likeness stems from the pseudotensor nature of the dipole moment. Two extra cases mirror an imaginary refraction ratio in optics. Strain controlled devices on such materials are the aim.
arxiv-2412-16359:
Nilanjana Das, Edward Raff, Aman Chadha, and Manas Gaur show, in a 2024 paper, that the most dangerous prompts for a language model may read like ordinary conversation. Classic jailbreaks hide in gibberish strings that filters catch easily. These authors instead wrap harmful requests in rich situational context, such as movie scripts, so the full prompt looks natural while the payload slips through.

They also built a way to launder gibberish attack text into readable, innocent-looking prose that keeps its bite inside a full prompt. Extending an existing attack framework with a sampling tweak produced varied readable attacks that worked well against both open and commercial models. The authors argue that safety checks tuned for weird strings will miss this class entirely. Their aim is to push defenses toward reading meaning and context, the way the attacks do.
arxiv-2412-17059:
Zsolt Gyongyosi, Timothy Hollowood, and Prem Kumar study teleportation after a local jolt in a two-dimensional field theory in two thousand twenty-four. New black hole ideas use maps that shrink space and post-picked outcomes to recover lost information. The authors build a lab-like test of that idea inside conformal field theory.

A local operator jolt is paired with a projection of part of space onto a special boundary state. Math maps turn the setup into a theory with a boundary, where entropies can be computed two ways. The two systems act in distinct ways. Entropy results show a surprise pattern in the replica count: teleportation does occur, but not at the best rate, since the projector is not tuned for it.
arxiv-2412-17559:
Amr Salem and Anirban Mondal tested a deep learning method to guess a person's risk of kidney stones from their genes. Their twenty twenty-four paper uses data from a large gene scan that found many small gene marks tied to stone risk. Stones are common and painful, and genes play a real part.

The pair fed the gene marks into a type of network called a CNN, which can catch links that simple scores miss. They trained it on five hundred sixty people and split the data for training and tests. The CNN beat three standard methods, with a test score the authors call a good sign. They frame it as a step toward care shaped by each person's genes.
arxiv-2412-17759:
Priyaranjan Pattnayak and co-authors survey data sets for large multimodal models in a 2024 paper. Multimodal learning combines text, images, audio, and video, echoing how people use many senses. Progress depends on large, well organized data sets for training and testing.

The survey reviews data sets for training, domain specific tasks, and real world applications, and organizes them into application categories and a taxonomy. Benchmark data sets receive special attention for how they test performance, scale, and practical use. The authors argue that solving data set gaps and quality problems is key to the next advances in the field.
arxiv-2412-18259:
Tianyu Zhao and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on a neural network that can count and separate overlapping gravitational wave signals. Next-generation detectors will hear many cosmic mergers at once, tangled into one stream. Standard searches and earlier networks handle at most two at a time.

Their attention-based model, UnMixFormer, first counts how many signals hide in the stream, even up to five. Separate decoder heads then pull each waveform apart. On synthetic data it counted with near-perfect accuracy and rebuilt waveforms that matched the originals closely. It also held up on spinning, off-round, and higher-mode signals. The method readies analysis for a crowded gravitational sky.
arxiv-2412-18659:
Marco de Paula and co-authors report, in a 2024 paper, a role reversal hiding in theories where electromagnetism goes nonlinear. In Einstein's mechanics, a particle's velocity and momentum need not point the same way, and either can flip its causal character. Coupling gravity to nonlinear electrodynamics, a family that includes models built to tame singularities, makes that abstract possibility concrete for light itself.

For a wide class of these models with the right weak-field limit, the photons that travel causally, at or under light speed, carry spacelike momentum: good tachyons, in the authors' phrase. The well-behaved timelike momentum instead rides with acausal propagation, the bad bradyons. Which way the split falls is decided by the curvature of the theory's Lagrangian, matching an energy-condition analysis. As a corollary, two famous regular black holes, Bardeen's and Hayward's, come out acausal in this light.
arxiv-2412-19159:
Muhammad Muttaqien, Ayanori Yorozu, and Akihisa Ohya teach robots through staged lessons in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Mobile robots must follow task-based human instructions indoors. Environments shift and instructions can be complex. Training a robot on the full task at once is inefficient.

Their approach mixes incremental curriculum learning with deep reinforcement learning. The curriculum mirrors how human learning builds in complexity. Robots first master simpler instructions, then progress to harder ones. That structure improves training efficiency in their experiments. It also gives the generalization needed for dynamic indoor spaces. Robots trained this way beat those trained without a curriculum. Readers get evidence that lesson order matters for machines as it does for people.
arxiv-2501-00559:
Mustapha and seven co-authors build a test set of Arabic science questions for language models in this twenty twenty-four paper. Most known test sets use English, so skill in other tongues stays poorly gauged. Their set is born in Arabic, not flipped from English, and spans school to high levels.

Inside, the set holds choice questions across a range of science and tech themes. Scoring high takes a true grasp of science Arabic. Public models of all sizes scored poorly when the team ran them. The authors say the gap shows a need for models tuned to one place and tongue. The set is free for all to use online.
arxiv-2501-00659:
Kazuki Irie wrote a paper, published in 2024, revisiting an old and half-forgotten result about how language models know word order. Transformers are often given explicit positional encodings, tags that mark each word's place. Irie shows that deep models which generate text one word at a time do not need them: depth alone lets the network tell apart shuffled word sequences.

The reason is that stacked layers of set-style processing can jointly act in an order-sensitive way during generation. The fact was known around the first GPT models but faded as the field exploded, leading to recent rediscoveries. The paper restates the explanation plainly, with its history, so the record is clear.
arxiv-2501-01359:
Stop-and-go waves ripple through traffic jams, wasting fuel and time, and a few well-driven automated cars might calm them. Shian Wang, Jose Carlos Acedo Aguilar, and Miguel Velez-Reyes design a controller that lets an automated car do exactly that. Their controller needs only what the car's own sensors see: the gap to the car ahead and the relative speed.

The car follows a softened version of the leader's speed changes instead of copying every jerk. The authors also give a method for picking the controller's settings for the best smoothing. In simulations, a ten-car platoon with their controller cut fuel use sharply and shrank traffic swings. The effect grew as more cars were automated. They trade a touch of peak performance for a design that is far easier to deploy.
arxiv-2501-01559:
Mike Qin and colleagues coordinate fleets of moving robots with an algorithm that plans in segments and only mediates conflicts when they arise. Kinodynamic planning respects each robot's physics, not just its geometry. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's method alternates two toolkits. Optimization-based planners draft smooth initial paths. Sampling-based planners then repair the spots where robots would collide. The design inherits a parent framework's thrift: coordination effort is spent only where robots actually interfere.

Simulations ran fleets of up to dozens of planar robots. Against earlier methods, the new algorithm was up to ten times faster in some scenarios. Harder scenes and more complex dynamics widened its lead. Warehouse and traffic applications, where many simple robots share tight space, are the natural home.
arxiv-2501-01659:
Deepak Patel, Praveen Srivastava, Noritaka Shimizu, and Yutaka Utsuno model atomic nuclei in a 2025 arXiv paper. They use large-scale shell-model calculations on odd indium isotopes. The focus is on states that look like a single hole in a closed shell.

They compute energy levels, electromagnetic moments, and spectroscopic factors for four states across the isotope chain. The results match measured data well. The match depends on strong mixing of configurations away from closed shells. Mixing with two proton orbitals proved key to placing one state's energy correctly. Simpler single-particle trends alone could not do it.
arxiv-2501-02459:
Boroun wrote a solo study in twenty twenty-five on how atomic cores act when hit by fast electrons. At very low share of the hit, the parts inside a core start to shade each other. That shade effect needs terms that go past a straight-line model.

He works out how those extra terms change the size of the hit that a planned collider would see. The extra terms matter most for heavy cores at low share and low hit strength. His results fit the trend in a known data set used in the field. The work may help plan tests at two planned colliders.
arxiv-2501-02859:
Meng-Yuan Li, Wen-Tao Lyu, Li-Juan Liu, and En Wang calculate how two fleeting particles shape a charm baryon decay in a 2025 physics paper. The decay sends a lambda-c baryon into a pion, an eta meson, and a neutron. Two guests may appear mid-decay: the nucleon resonance N(1535) and the scalar meson a0(980), each possibly born from the swirl of lighter particles interacting. The authors fold both into their calculation of the decay's mass spectra.

The eta-neutron spectrum shows a strong near-threshold bump tied to the resonance, while the pion-eta spectrum carries the scalar's sharp cusp. A predicted branching ratio near 0.313 gives running experiments, and a planned charm factory, a number to shoot at.
arxiv-2501-03259:
Abdullah Mushtaq and co-authors audit frontier language models for cultural bias in a 2025 arXiv paper. Models such as GPT-4 and Llama 3 are entering classrooms worldwide. Their values often mirror Western, educated, rich, and democratic settings, sidelining other views.

The authors propose judging and fixing bias through multiplexity, an idea that holds many cultural viewpoints at once. Their analysis finds cultural polarization in both plain answers and subtle cues. They suggest two fixes: building multiplex rules into the system prompt, and using a team of agents that each carry a distinct viewpoint. The aim is educational AI that serves diverse learners fairly.
arxiv-2501-04159:
Peñuñuri, Cantún-Avila, and Peón-Escalante build DNAOAD, in a 2025 preprint, a Fortran tool that computes derivatives of any order without the usual memory blowup. Dual numbers, a classic trick, extend arithmetic so derivatives fall out of plain evaluation. Stacking them for higher orders works in theory. In practice, nested implementations balloon in memory and crawl. The authors store the dual parts directly, in one flat representation. No recursive nesting is used at any order. Memory use drops sharply as a result.

Very high-order derivatives become practical on ordinary hardware. The framework targets high-performance scientific computing, where Fortran still rules. Problems like sensitivity analysis and series solutions need such derivatives in bulk. The authors present DNAOAD as the scalable base those jobs lacked. Its design keeps the elegance of dual numbers while shedding the cost that kept them a low-order tool.
arxiv-2501-04859:
Lars Rohwedder, in a solo paper from twenty twenty-five, gave a near best algorithm for job scheduling on machines of mixed speed. The task is to split jobs across machines to cut the worst finish time. Past tools had a squared term in the run time's exponent. His runs in time set by the top job length and the count of distinct lengths. A bound from a famed hypothesis says this is near the best one can hope.

The method leans on integer programming plus fresh tricks with modular math. It also fits the compact code form for jobs with many repeats. The result shuts an open question in the field. Readers in algorithms get a tight tool for a base scheduling task.
arxiv-2501-06059:
Sarath Sivaprasad, Dmitry Kangin, Plamen Angelov, and Mario Fritz show how an image sorter reaches its call, in a human way. They point to parts of shots one knows. Their tool, COMIX, splits the test shot into zones tied to learned themes. Each zone is matched to like bits in shots from the training set. The sort is the sum of those traced bits, and the tale it tells is the call itself, not a tale spun next.

The truth claim is both proved on paper and shown in tests. Rivals span late add-on aids and tools built to be read at once. On a big test set, the truth score rose by near 49% past the best past mark. Tales got short too, a gain of its own. Part-based thought gives checks a thing to hold: this patch, from that known shot, cast a vote for this class.
arxiv-2501-06259:
Farina Riaz and four co-authors add quantum computing to an image generating model in a 2025 paper. Variational autoencoders compress images into compact codes and rebuild them, but reconstructions often lose fidelity. Their hybrid model puts a quantum encoding step inside the encoder while keeping classical layers around it, with a standard convolutional decoder rebuilding the picture.

On two handwriting datasets, the quantum version beat both a plain classical model and a classical variant with windowed pooling filters. Its image quality scores were consistently lower in the good direction, meaning rebuilt images sat closer to real ones. The authors pitch quantum encoding as a route to higher quality synthetic data and reconstruction.
arxiv-2501-06559:
Jianbin Chen, Dennis Lin, Nicholas Rios, and Xueru Zhang design tests where the order of steps matters. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with limits on which orders are allowed. In surveys and job plans, parts come in groups with a fixed group order. That fixes the order of any two parts from different groups.

The team builds models for these grouped limits, plus a mixed form with one set pair per group. They prove that using every allowed order once gives the best design. They also give ways to build smaller designs that stay near best. A survey data set shows how question order can be judged with the new tools.
arxiv-2501-08259:
Chen and three co-authors fine-tune bot spread plans by folk taste picks in this twenty twenty-five paper. Bots learn hand acts from folk shows, yet tastes shift with new rooms. A full re-drill for each taste shift costs time and drill files.

Inside, taste picks first teach a prize law for what folks want. Prize-led drill then bends the stock plan to that law's pull. A keep-close term bars the bent plan from straying too far. Bot task tests show taste fit with core skill kept whole. The route fits new tastes with no fresh show files at all.
arxiv-2501-08759:
Takashi Higuchi and Hiroyuki Fujioka propose an X-ray experiment on atoms where an antiproton replaces an electron, aiming to sharpen knowledge of how antinucleons grip nuclei at low energy. The standard model of that grip is an optical potential fitted globally across the periodic table. Its isovector part stays poorly pinned because nucleon distributions inside nuclei carry their own uncertainty. The proposal removes that fog.

Calcium isotopes, whose nucleon layouts are well charted, become the targets. A superconducting microcalorimeter promises resolution of fifty to seventy electron volts in the band of interest. Isotope-by-isotope shifts and widths of the X-ray lines can then be measured precisely. Refined potentials follow. The data would also serve searches for neutron-antineutron oscillations, a process that would rewrite baryon number's rules.
arxiv-2501-10359:
Amedeo Chiefa and co-authors compare theory with collider data in a 2025 particle physics paper. Their subject is parton distribution functions, which describe how a proton's momentum is shared among its inner parts. Every prediction for collider events rests on these functions, so testing them against precise data is vital.

The team confronts several function sets with high-precision measurements from the LHC's second run and from an earlier electron-proton machine. Processes include boson, top-quark, and jet production, computed at very high accuracy. Errors from the functions, from coupling strength, and from missing higher terms are all counted. The paper weighs which set predicts best and where the limits come from. Careful error control, the authors stress, is the heart of precision work.
arxiv-2501-11159:
Self-driving hardware in cheap vehicles cannot carry a data-center chip, so object detection must shrink to fit an FPGA. Konrad Lis, Tomasz Kryjak, and Marek Gorgoń designed LiFT around the chip's hard limits from the start. The limits were strict: an operations budget, eight-bit arithmetic throughout, flat cell-based processing instead of 3D voxels, and few skip connections.

Novel pillar features and a careful input quantization scheme clawed back accuracy within that budget. The finished detector ran at about twenty-one billion operations, among the leanest in its class. On the nuScenes benchmark it ranked first among comparable minimal methods. The authors will release the code.
arxiv-2501-11759:
Fatemeh Nazary, Yashar Deldjoo, and Tommaso di Noia wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It shows how a poison attack can bend a recommender system that uses retrieval-augmented generation, where a language model draws on stored item data.

Their frame, Poison-RAG, tweaks item metadata such as tags and blurbs to push fringe items up and knock hits down. One plan tailors tags per item, the other stamps the same tags on all. Tests on the MovieLens data set, run blind, show the tailored plan boosts the sway by up to half, while the uniform plan can backfire and boost hits. Hit items prove easier to sway than fringe ones. Sound metadata care is the defense the authors urge.
arxiv-2501-12059:
Atanu Paul, Nagaprasad Reddy Samala, and Ilya Grinberg present a 2025 paper on a faster way to compute Raman spectra. Raman scattering reveals a material's vibrations, and simulations can predict its spectrum if they can track how electrons polarize as atoms move. Exact calculations are too costly for long simulations. The classic bond model is cheap but misses angle effects, skewing spectra. The team generalizes it to include pairs of atoms not directly bonded.

The generalized model matched exact polarizability and spectra closely for a range of test molecules. It also improved results for a complex ferroelectric crystal. For liquid water, its simulated spectrum agreed far better with experiment than the old model's. The authors present the model as a base for large-scale spectral simulation and for future, richer polarizability models.
arxiv-2501-13059:
Aman Sharma, Mithilesh Nayak, Henrik Rønnow, and Frédéric Mila study excitations in a chain of spin-1 atoms. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, varies the tug between near and next-near neighbors. At weak second-neighbor pull, waves called magnons carry the action. As the pull grows, the magnon pattern slides off the regular grid.

At a sharp point, the chain snaps into a new phase. There, domain walls free fractional particles called spinons. Near that point the spinons bind into pairs, visible in the spectrum. A single-mode formula tracks the magnon far from the switch. The team extends it to map a spinon right at the switch.
arxiv-2501-13159:
José Benavides and co-authors ask, in twenty twenty-five, why some small galaxies in open space have stopped forming stars. Such quiet field dwarfs are rare nearby, but appear in a major simulation called TNG50. The team used that simulation to trace their origin. All quiet field dwarfs, they find, lost gas due to their surroundings. Some were flung out of a massive host galaxy after passing through it. Others lost gas while crossing dense cosmic web strands, a process they call cosmic web stripping.

The quiet share rises steeply as galaxy mass falls. With a strict isolation rule, the share drops to about one percent. Flung-out dwarfs lost more dark matter and gas, and stopped forming stars earlier, than web-stripped ones.
arxiv-2501-13559:
Paul Eastham, Conor Murphy, and Luisa Toledo Tude propose a way to laser-cool solids below the temperature floor of existing methods. Standard laser cooling relies on anti-Stokes fluorescence from impurities, and the impurity's level spacing sets a minimum reachable temperature. Their alternative uses strong laser driving to form dressed states.

Dressed states create a spectrum whose gaps can be tuned to optimize heat absorption. The resulting cycle could in principle operate at any temperature with power near the thermodynamic maximum. Non-radiative decay and other heating will compete, the authors note. Still, the scheme could reach temperatures impossible for fluorescence-based cooling, with diamond vacancies as the test platform.
arxiv-2501-13659:
Vishnupriya Anupindi and Peter Kritzer study reduced digital nets, point sets used in fast numeric integration. Their paper from twenty twenty-five builds on recent work where trimmed nets speed up matrix-vector products. Quasi-Monte Carlo rules use such point sets as sample nodes. Trimming rows or columns of the net's matrices cuts the cost.

The authors bound the quality score of row-reduced and column-row-reduced nets. These bounds feed the error study of rules built on the trimmed sets. They also compare the three trims: row, column, and both at once. Notes on further angles round out the piece. The results help users know what accuracy they trade for speed. The work serves fields where such products recur, from finance to physics sims.
arxiv-2501-13759:
Empty space itself pulls nearby metal plates together, a quantum effect named for Casimir, and measuring it in superconductors could settle a long argument about its low-frequency part. De Jong and co-authors report such a measurement in a 2025 paper using a superconducting drum inside a microwave cavity. The force bends the drum's motion into a nonlinear pattern that betrays its strength.

The inferred force matched the expected size for the gap in their device and clashed with estimates of rival effects. The strength surprised them: a redesigned drum should reach a regime where single sound quanta matter, a long-sought playground for quantum mechanics of moving parts.
arxiv-2501-16059:
Tânia Tomé and Mário de Oliveira derive the core laws of irreversible thermodynamics from the statistics of small fluctuating systems, in a physics paper from 2025. Their subject is a system held under temperature gradients and outside forces. Such gradients drive flows of heat and matter and create entropy, the disorder measure of thermodynamics.

The authors show the rate of entropy creation is a curved, bowl-shaped function of the flows. From that shape it follows that the excess part of entropy creation can never be negative. That fact is the Glansdorff-Prigogine principle, a classic rule of the field. They also link the principle's stability function to a thermodynamic potential when temperature is uniform. The paper grounds a macroscopic theory in microscopic statistics.
arxiv-2501-16559:
Farzad Farhadzadeh, Debasmit Das, Shubhankar Borse, and Fatih Porikli solve a costly problem when base models get replaced. Their twenty twenty-five paper introduces LoRA-X for cross-model adaptation. Small adapter modules tune large foundation models cheaply. When a base model is retired, every adapter normally needs retraining.

Original training data is often locked away by privacy or licensing rules. Synthetic data may fail to match the real data well. LoRA-X instead moves adapter settings between models with no training at all. It forces the adapter to work inside the source model subspace. Tests support the transfer approach. Teams can keep useful tuning work when platforms upgrade their base models.
arxiv-2501-16659:
Yuling Max Chen, Bin Li, and David Saunders wrote this finance paper in 2025. It studies how to split wealth across assets when the market flips between states, such as calm and stormy spells. The classic mean-variance aim trades gain against risk. The trio let a learning agent explore choices inside that aim, rather than solving it in one closed pass.

They state and prove a rule for when a new plan truly beats an old one. The usual temporal difference way of learning, they show, fits this task poorly. In its place they use a method built on a martingale trait of the best value path. In fake markets, the method found the true market traits, and on real data it earned the best mean yearly gains with fair calm. The work ties control theory to market learning.
arxiv-2501-17259:
Nuzhat Nuari Khan Rivu, Md Kamrujjaman, and Shohel Ahmed model the HIV epidemic with an eye on gender. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that most models treat men and women alike. Yet the chance of spread and the uptake of treatment can differ by gender, and those gaps can steer the whole epidemic.

The team builds two linked models, one for each gender, and runs them in two ways: fixed, with set rates, and random, with chance built in. One case treats only one gender, to see the spillover. Random models, above all a Runge-Kutta version, tracked the real ups and downs best. The work urges care with such models in health planning.
arxiv-2501-17759:
Keshav Bhandari, Geraint Wiggins, and Simon Colton address a weak spot in computer-made music: keeping a motif developing in a planned way across a whole piece. Transformer models write note by note, so once they drift from the motif they cannot correct themselves. Their framework, Yin-Yang, splits the job among three models. One generates phrases, one refines them, and one selects among the results. The refiner is trained by corrupting good phrases and learning to repair them, so at generation time it can turn a stray phrase back into a variation of the motif.

The authors also add a score that measures how smoothly the motif shows itself through the piece. In tests, Yin-Yang beat leading transformer models while giving the user more control over the outcome. Its choices stay partly readable, which helps musical analysis. Code and a demo page are released with the paper.
arxiv-2501-17859:
Fabrício Olivetti de França and Gabriel Kronberger wrote this computer science paper, published in 2025. It introduces rEGGression, an interactive tool for browsing the forest of formulas that symbolic regression produces, instead of staring at a single best answer.

Symbolic regression searches for formulas that fit data while staying readable. Standard tools hand back a frontier of trade-offs, hiding near-tied alternatives. The new tool stores every candidate expression ever visited in equality graphs, a compact structure that shares repeated pieces across formulas. Users can query, filter, and pattern-match inside that huge store. The real prize, the authors say, is seeing the building blocks the search kept reusing, which hints at the phenomenon's true structure. The tool works with any symbolic regression engine, making exploration a dialogue rather than a verdict.
arxiv-2501-18259:
Sanjay Mukherjee, Kamal Patra, and Binod Sahoo wrote a math paper from 2025 on how hard it is to split a network built from a group of numbers. The network links each member of a cyclic group to its powers. A cut-set is a set of points whose removal breaks the network apart. The smallest such sets show where the network is weakest.

Past work had settled the smallest cut-sets when the group's size is a product of at most three prime powers. A later paper narrowed the field of candidates for all larger cases. This paper finishes the job for several of the open cases with four or more prime factors. It names the exact smallest cut-sets and the network's link strength in each case it covers. The result completes a long chain of work on this family's networks.
arxiv-2501-18359:
Haichen Hu and co-authors build one decision algorithm that learns whole outcome distributions instead of single summary numbers, in a 2025 theory paper. Online decision problems, from medical dose choices to risk controls, need different statistics at different times: sometimes the average, sometimes the spread, sometimes a quantile. Learning each separately wastes data. Learning the full distribution is far harder, since a distribution is an infinite-dimensional object, and naive methods would accumulate endless regret.

Their framework models each outcome distribution as a mix of basis distributions whose weights depend on context. The key quantity is how fast the eigenvalues of a certain operator decay, which governs how hard the regression is. Under the right decay, the algorithm's regret stays controlled. The authors present this as a universal engine: plug in whichever statistic the application needs, after the learning is done.
arxiv-2501-18759:
Meirav Amram, Michael Chitayat, and Yaacov Kopeliovich rebuild a classic description of the loops on a closed curved surface from the view of a branched cover. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A compact Riemann surface is a smooth closed surface with a rich geometric structure. Its fundamental group captures all the ways a loop can wind around it.

The classic answer uses twice as many generators as the surface has handles. One relation ties them: a product of twists in pairs equals the identity. Textbooks often state this without a clean path to it. The authors start instead from the surface as a cover of the sphere, branched at set points. From that picture they derive the generators and the single relation step by step. The route gives students a concrete way into a core fact of surface theory.
arxiv-2501-19059:
Casti, Baggio, Zampieri, and Pasqualetti wrote in twenty twenty-five about one neural controller that can regulate many different linear systems. Multi-task control asks a single controller to handle varied plants. Their controller is a neural network with smooth ReLU activations. Its wiring matrix stays fixed once designed. A bias vector, which can change, adapts it from task to task. The bias sets the equilibrium and thus the local linear behavior.

Proper bias choice can make the network mimic any single linear controller locally. The team designs gradient algorithms to train both parameters. Upper and lower performance bounds accompany the training method. Numerical examples validate the theory across tasks. Brain-inspired architecture motivates the fixed-wiring, shifting-bias split. The results suggest flexible control from a compact learned structure.
arxiv-2502-00359:
Diffusion models generate images by working in a compressed latent space. Wanghan Xu and co-authors argue that space is the bottleneck. Standard autoencoder latents squeeze pixels but carry little meaning. Their ReaLS approach aligns the latent space with semantic representations. Generators trained on it should know what they are drawing, not just where the edges go. Two transformer generators were retrained on the new space.

Both improved their image quality score by about 15 percent. The meaning-rich latents also helped other tasks, like segmentation and depth estimation. The authors present representation alignment as a general upgrade for latent generation.
arxiv-2502-00959: Greenlees constructs explicit, calculable algebraic models for rational U(2)-spectra, objects in algebraic topology tied to the symmetry group U(2). The models are assembled from seven blocks taken from earlier work, including the toral part and previous results on small toral groups. Joining the blocks is the hard step: it demands detailed input about fusion and about Weyl groups. The abstract is only two sentences, so the paper's substance lies in the construction itself and in the care needed to fit the blocks together.
arxiv-2502-01259:
Rajat Hazra, Nikolai Kriukov, and Michel Mandjes present a 2025 probability paper on random graphs that change over time. In a dynamic Erdos-Renyi graph, each edge switches on its own random schedule. The team tracks counts of small subgraphs as the graph evolves. All counts are packed into one vector. The aim is to describe how that whole vector moves together, not just one count at a time.

Their main result is a functional central limit theorem. After centering and scaling, the count vector converges to a named multi-dimensional Gaussian process. The result needs only mild rules on the edge schedules, chiefly a smoothness bound. Probabilists get a joint limit law for network motif counts over time. Such laws let analysts judge whether a real network's motif swings are normal noise or a real shift.
arxiv-2502-01459:
Sahana Rayan and Ambuj Tewari extend a learning framework in a 2025 paper. In learning to defer, a model may answer a task itself or hand it to a human expert. Older methods force one choice for a whole output. That all-or-nothing rule fits poorly when the output is a long sequence, such as a summary or a route plan.

The authors let the system defer only parts of a sequence, mixing machine and expert work step by step. One rejector hands off single tokens to an expert who can predict the next token. Another hands off the whole rest of the sequence from a chosen point, for experts who cannot work token by token. Tests on route solving, news summaries, and weather forecasts showed better trade-offs between cost and accuracy than whole-output deferral.
arxiv-2502-01759:
Zeus Moreira, Carlos Herdeiro, and Luís Crispino explored light round a pair of spinning black holes. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a fresh multi hole space time that grows the classic Majumdar-Papapetrou form. The holes are charged, spinning, and held in balance. The team read null paths, the tracks light takes, with care for the two hole case. A charge based count sorts the light rings that form.

By spin picks, rings of opposed charge can meet and wipe out, to leave four, six, or eight rings. Back ray traces then drew the holes' shadows and lens bends. The shadow looks much like the known double Kerr case. Readers in gravity get a new twin hole toy with rich light play.
arxiv-2502-02459:
Zeyu Wang led a large team reviewing smart ring research in a 2025 paper. Rings packed with sensors can catch subtle finger movements and sit on blood-rich, nerve-rich skin all day. The team gathered just over two hundred publications and sorted them with a taxonomy of sensing and feedback types. Four areas organize the field: interaction input, interaction output, passive sensing of body signals, and passive sensing of outside activity.

They map what each area has achieved and where the gaps are. Health monitoring and gesture control dominate so far. The authors offer the review as a guide for designers of future ring devices.
arxiv-2502-02559:
Every drone flight into controlled airspace needs a safety case, and writing each one from scratch does not scale. Michael Hunter and co-authors borrow an idea from software families in a 2025 paper: build one parameterized safety case with the variation points marked, then generate each flight's case from it. The work starts from a hazard analysis.

A feature model captures what can differ between drones and missions, and a template case is tied to those features. A case study shows the generator producing flight-specific arguments. The aim is automated, customized safety evidence that keeps pace with growing small-drone traffic.
arxiv-2502-02859:
Haochen Zhang, Zhong Zheng, and Lingzhou Xue present a 2025 theory study of federated Q-learning, a method where many agents learn together without pooling their raw experience. The setting is a set of short, repeating decision tasks. Older analyses gave worst-case bounds that grow with the square root of time, plus messaging costs that grow with the number of agents, states, and actions.

The new analysis uses a kinder feature of many tasks: the best action beats the rest by a clear margin, called a gap. With that feature, the learning loss grows only with the log of time. The messaging bound also drops its heaviest term, and the speedup from adding agents follows a clear pattern. Even with one agent, the switching cost improves on earlier results.
arxiv-2502-03359:
Ryan Rabinowitz, Steve Cruz, Manuel Günther, and Terrance Boult tackle fairness in open-set recognition. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Such systems must sort known classes and flag ones never seen before. Scores are usually reported as one overall number. The authors show that per-class results can swing wildly behind that average. Hidden weak classes raise fairness and trust problems.

Their method, GHOST, needs no tuned settings. It models each class's deep features as a Gaussian spread with a simple shape. Scores are normalized so odd feature sizes do not inflate them. That lowers the chance an unknown sample scores high by accident. Tests compare the method against rivals on large-scale recognition. The paper pushes evaluation toward class-by-class honesty.
arxiv-2502-03559:
Yassine El Kheir and four co-authors pull apart how self-supervised models spot fake audio. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses models that learn from raw sound with no labels, then flags deepfake speech. They test across many settings: three languages, plus partial fakes, songs, and scene-based fakes.

The team checks each layer of these transformer models, one by one, to see which layers carry the clues. Lower layers, they find, hold the most telling traits, while upper layers add little. In fact, a few low layers alone match the full model's scores. That means fake-spotting can run faster and cheaper. The team shares its code and trained models for others to use.
arxiv-2502-03759:
Emily Kuhn and co-authors (2025) fly a drone to map the beams of a radio telescope array, a calibration step that 21-centimeter cosmology cannot skip. Knowing each dish's true beam pattern decides whether faint cosmic signals survive analysis. Their system works across 400 to 800 megahertz and carries a switchable calibration source, a first for drone payloads. That source allows background subtraction and direct measurement of interference from the drone itself. The test target was the TONE array.

The flights produced full two-dimensional beam maps in both polarizations over a wide grid, capturing the main beam and first two sidelobes. Main beam measurements carried errors of only seven to nine percent. Above 600 megahertz the antennas leaked polarization significantly, and the polarization axis rotated with frequency. The authors report the first drone-based maps of cross-polar structure for an array.
arxiv-2502-03959:
Edwin Bedolla-Montiel, Ramón Castañeda-Cerdán, and Ramón Castañeda-Priego test a soft stand-in for the classic hard-sphere fluid in a 2025 paper. Hard spheres are theory's favorite simple fluid, but their instant-contact force breaks ordinary simulation. A continuous pseudo-hard-sphere potential mimics their thermodynamics while staying smooth.

The stand-in had been checked only in the fluid region, in two and three dimensions. The authors run Brownian dynamics with it across the fluid-solid boundary in three and four dimensions, comparing against exact event-driven hard-sphere results and against theory. The question is whether a soft imitation can reproduce freezing, not just flowing. Their comparison judges the potential's equation of state across the whole diagram.
arxiv-2502-05059:
Foivos Fioravantes and co-authors study how far a graph sits from having exactly one smallest vertex cover, in a 2025 paper. A vertex cover is a set of points that touches every edge in a graph, and earlier work fixed some points in or out while keeping the cover size fixed. The new work drops that size demand and asks only that the best cover stay unique.

Dropping the demand makes the problem much harder than expected, the authors show. It sits at a high level of hardness even for flat graphs with few edges per point. Still, they give a fast method for tree-shaped graphs, and they map when the problem stays tractable under width and degree limits.
arxiv-2502-05859:
Qingsong Yan and co-authors present SphereFusion, a fast method for estimating depth from panoramic images, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Each way of flattening a panorama warps something: the standard wide format stretches and tears, while a pure spherical view loses fine texture. Their system reads the image in both formats at once.

Features from the two views are lifted onto the sphere, where a gating module picks the most trustworthy ones to merge. A caching scheme keeps the mesh work cheap. On three public panorama datasets the method matched leading rivals on accuracy while running far faster, about seventeen milliseconds for a full frame. The authors target robot sensing and self-driving cars.
arxiv-2502-05959:
Vincent Tan and Hamdi Joudeh refine the theory of decoders that guess codewords in ranked order and give up after a set count, in a paper from 2025. Such decoders suit channels where testing each guess is cheap. They stop when a guess hits the codebook or the guess budget runs out. The team ask how fast such a scheme can send data with few errors.

They pin down tight first-order rates for both the data and the give-up share. Guessing beats classic testing when the channel is roomy enough. The heart of the paper is finer: second-order rates and error exponents. Those results map how the error odds fall as blocks grow. A linked result covers near-lossless source coding as a special case. The work gives decoder design a firm math base.
arxiv-2502-06259:
Biao Shan and six co-authors show a new way to link spin and motion in very cold atomic gases. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Light from two lasers can tie an atom's spin to how it moves, an effect called spin-orbit coupling. The team's twist is that the link runs one way only, set by the handedness of the light.

They build the scheme with two lasers crossing at a right angle, with the light polarised in a set way. Along one sense of the field axis the coupling shows up, and along the other it fades away. They then stretch the setup into a square grid of light, giving two one-way couplings at once. The result gives labs a fresh tool for faking the band structures seen in quantum matter.
arxiv-2502-06659:
Somin Wadhwa, Chantal Shaib, Silvio Amir, and Byron Wallace published a 2025 paper asking whether a small AI model reveals which large model taught it. Distillation trains a small student model on the answers of a large teacher model. If the teacher can be identified from the student’s output, companies could detect misuse of their models.

The team tested summarization, question answering, and instruction tasks, treating each candidate teacher as a black box. Simple word overlap proved unreliable for naming the teacher. But patterns in parts of speech, the grammatical shapes a student prefers, did mirror its teacher’s habits. The work suggests teaching leaves traces that survive in a student’s style.
arxiv-2502-07759:
Dori Blakely and colleagues re-examine telescope data on a young star's disk. They report a tentative point of light inside the disk's cleared gap, where a forming planet might sit. The disk belongs to the star HD 100546. Sparse aperture masking interferometry sharpened the view in two infrared bands across two observing years. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team fits three model families to the data. One is a plain forward-scattering disk. The others add either an arbitrary lopsided feature or an unresolved point source in the gap.

The point source model wins. Its position shifted between the two epochs, consistent with orbital motion inside the gap. Allowed orbits are either disk-aligned and highly eccentric, or tilted steeply at any eccentricity. The authors stress the detection is tentative and call for follow-up before claiming a protoplanet.
arxiv-2502-07959:
Bratsberg, Thoresen, and Goeman showed in twenty twenty-five that a sparse-fit tool can predict well even when the true pattern is dense, not sparse. The tool, the Lasso, is a stock pick for vast gene data sets. They test it under a shared hidden-factor model that fits such data better.

Under that model the tool still gives sparse rules with sound error bounds. Its error bound even shrinks as more inputs are added. Sims back the proof in full. Strong scores from a sparse rule thus do not prove the named inputs drive the outcome, they warn.
arxiv-2502-10059:
Teng Li and colleagues made camera-directed video generation usable on ordinary photos in 2025. Image-to-video models can animate a still picture along a specified camera path, giving creators sweeping pans and zooms. The catch is usability: for an arbitrary real-world photo, users rarely know the scene's depth or scale, so they cannot supply precise camera parameters. The team's framework, RealCam-I2V, fixes the missing geometry first.

A preprocessing step estimates metric depth from the single image and reconstructs the scene in three dimensions. During training, that reconstruction lets camera parameters scale correctly to each scene. The diffusion model then generates video following complex, interactive camera moves in real-world units. Grounding the controls in recovered geometry means a user's intuitive instruction, move two meters left, means the same thing across photos. That brings cinematic camera work closer to casual use.
arxiv-2502-10159:
Alessandro Conigli and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 sharpening a key input to tests of the standard model of particle physics. Two electroweak quantities drift with energy, and their values at the Z boson mass need a hadronic piece that theory alone cannot give. Lattice simulations supply it by computing how the vacuum responds to light and to mixed probes. The team updated their calculation with finer grids and new control tricks.

They simulated with three quark flavors on several lattice spacings, down to the true pion mass. Two ways of building the current cross-checked each other. A careful subtraction tamed short-distance errors, with textbook theory repaying what was removed. Extrapolations to the real world used many fit forms to bound the uncertainty. The authors report excellent prospects for a high-precision value at the Z pole.
arxiv-2502-10459:
Yang Gao and five co-authors present a toolkit that uses large language models to design graph neural networks automatically. Their toolkit appeared in twenty twenty-five. Graph networks learn from linked data, but each new task usually demands hand-tuned redesign by experts.

Search methods exist, yet adapting them to new search spaces takes heavy code work. The toolkit instead steers the search by editing prompts to the language model. It bundles three parts: feature building for graphs, the architecture search itself, and tuning of settings. Users can extend it without deep rewrites. In tests on both uniform and mixed graph types, the toolkit beat existing search methods. The authors pitch it as a lower-effort path to tailored graph models.
arxiv-2502-12759:
Luca Lanzendörfer and three co-authors build a neural vocoder that turns spectrograms back into high fidelity music, in this 2025 paper. Vocoders shine at speech, but polyphonic music, with many notes at once, has been far less explored. Their system, DisCoder, borrows the compact code of a trained audio codec to guide the rebuild.

First the spectrogram is mapped into the codec's low dimensional space. A tuned decoder then renders full 44.1 kilohertz audio from that code. On objective measures and on a listening study with human raters, DisCoder reached state of the art quality for music. It also held up well on speech, which hints at one vocoder for both jobs. The design pairs an adversarial encoder decoder with the codec's learned sense of sound.
arxiv-2502-14259:
Lab tests guide diagnosis and monitoring, but frequent testing burdens patients and results are not always at hand. The three authors propose LabTOP, a single model that predicts lab test outcomes from electronic health records by treating the task as language modeling. Older methods covered only a subset of tests or sorted results into coarse ranges. LabTOP instead predicts continuous values for a wide range of lab items.

The team tested the model on three public health record data sets. It beat existing methods, including classic machine learning models and leading large language models. Ablation studies confirmed that the design choices mattered. The authors present LabTOP as an accurate and general framework for predicting lab outcomes, with possible uses in clinical decision support and in early spotting of critical conditions.
arxiv-2502-14659:
Robert Graf and co-authors build MAGO-SP, a pipeline that catches and fixes water-fat swaps in MRI scans. A breath-hold scan type splits tissue signal into water and fat images. Mix-ups during rebuilding can swap the two, wrecking fat fraction measures. Their three-step system first learns to label volumes as fat-like or water-like.

Fake swaps, made by blending volumes with cloud-like noise, train that sorter. A diffusion model then predicts a clean water image as a guide. A physics-based solver folds the guide in and recovers true signals. Swap detection error fell under one percent on the six-point scan. Swaps hit underweight and very obese patients most often.
arxiv-2502-15359:
Kai Li and co-authors present a 2025 paper on delivery routing. Real routing tasks carry many practical limits, such as time windows and load rules. Hand-building a solver for each variant takes deep skill and time. Past auto-design work covered only a few variants. The team builds a test set of 1,000 routing variants from 24 traits. That set can judge how well auto solvers handle hard limits.

Their solver uses language model agents to write limit-aware code. The agents extend a base solver frame from task text and sample cases. Logistics teams get a path to custom solvers without months of hand work. The test set also gives the field a shared yardstick. Auto design can now be checked on hard, messy variants, not just textbook ones. The paper pairs the solver with the test set, so others can rerun and compare fairly.
arxiv-2502-16659:
Song and Kim tune data hunts for pick-the-best tasks with shared fact frames. All picks share one set of fact frames, fed by more than one source. Data comes in step by step, on a fixed spend cap. The best pick is read by the most apt best rule. That rule's chance of right pick nears one as spend grows. Its pace of growth is a fast curve in their proof.

With fact traits in a finite set, best split shares get worked out. Those shares span both fact hunts and sim runs for the picks. Their plan, OSAR, hits those shares in the long run. A ridge step lifts sim mean reads in a fresh twist. The twist boosts small-spend scores and spans smooth fact sets too. Tests show OSAR beats a top peer plan in runs.
arxiv-2502-18459:
Ceccotti and co-authors built a sharper radio model of the bright galaxy Cygnus A in a 2025 paper. Astronomers hunting the faint 21-centimeter signal from the early universe must first remove bright foreground sources. Cygnus A is one of the brightest, so any error in its model leaves residue behind.

Using LOFAR telescope data between 110 and 250 megahertz, the team made a high-resolution model that builds in how the source's brightness changes with frequency. Their method captures the turnover in the brightest hot spots, which older models missed. A cleaner Cygnus A model means cleaner subtraction, and a better chance of seeing the faint cosmic signal underneath.
arxiv-2502-18559:
Zhang and co-authors analyze the atmosphere of 2MASS 1207 b, the first planet-mass companion ever imaged directly. The object has taught astronomers much about young planets and brown dwarfs over 20 years. The team fit models to its spectrum from the JWST space telescope. A new framework allowed patchy clouds, clear hot spots, or both. They ran 24 model fits under varied assumptions.

A patchy cloud model fit best. It gave a temperature near 1,174 K and a radius about 1.4 times Jupiter's. The air's metal content sat near the Sun's, with a carbon-to-oxygen ratio of 0.44. Clouds seem to cover only part of the globe. The results sharpen the portrait of this landmark world.
arxiv-2502-19559:
Jonas Becker and co-authors study how groups of language models, debating a problem in turns, slowly wander away from the question they were asked, in a 2025 paper. Such debates often solve hard problems well, but their edge fades on problems that need long chains of thought. The authors name the wandering 'problem drift' and measure it across ten tasks of several kinds.

Open-ended writing tasks drifted most, in up to nine cases out of ten, while hard knowledge and reasoning tasks drifted far less. Eight human experts then read 170 drifting debates. The top causes were stalled progress, poor-quality replies, and unclear statements, in roughly a third, a quarter, and a quarter of cases. The team built a judge tool that spots drift and a policy that repairs about a third of the cases. The work explains one reason longer debates can hurt rather than help.
arxiv-2502-19659:
Economists read economic shocks from data using structural vector autoregressions. Which shocks are which depends on exclusion rules, and those rules may change over time. Annika Camehl and Tomasz Woźniak build a model that lets the data choose. Their Bayesian model switches between regimes and between patterns of restrictions. Shocks also vary in volatility within each regime. That time-varying volatility itself helps pin down the shocks.

With volatility doing part of the work, the exclusion rules become testable rather than assumed. Applied to United States data, the method supports changing identification for the monetary policy shock. The authors verify that volatility identifies the shock inside regimes too.
arxiv-2502-20159:
Andrei Buciulea, Elvin Isufi, Geert Leus, and Antonio Marques learn the structure of a simplicial complex from observed signals. Graphs only capture pairwise relations, while simplicial complexes also encode triangles and higher interactions. Their setting assumes signals on all nodes and on a subset of edges, with the remaining edges and filled triangles unknown.

Assuming signals are smooth on the true complex and higher-order relations are sparse, the authors cast topology learning as a nonconvex optimization problem. They develop an efficient block-coordinate algorithm to solve it. The work is a first step enabling simplicial signal processing in domains where the higher-order structure itself must be inferred from data.
arxiv-2502-20659:
Anthony Christiana and six co-authors compute homology of Yang-Baxter operators in two thousand twenty five. The operators in view yield the HOMFLYPT polynomial in knot theory. Homology of such operators is costly to compute directly. Their reduction cuts the work to a finite set of cases.

The nth homology for any parameter reduces to n plus one initial conditions. That turns an infinite family into a finite checklist. Explicit formulas follow for the third homology groups. The fourth homology gets closed form expressions as well. The scheme systematizes a knot theory computation.
arxiv-2502-20759:
When two particles bind at the edge of falling apart, a strange tower of three-body states can appear, each a fixed multiple larger than the last. Ning Sun, Lei Feng, and Pengfei Zhang show that tower inside a quantum spin chain in a 2025 paper. Their chain lets each spin talk to far neighbors, which reshapes the waves that run through it.
