Two wave packets on the chain can hover at a matching state with an unbroken scaling rule. Adding short-range walls then breaks that rule into steps, and the tower appears. The team works out how the step size depends on the coupling range, and computer checks agree. The same math stretches to other dimensions, with the classic case as one instance. Trapped-ion setups could test the effect in the lab.
arxiv-2502-20959:
Zhaorui Wu and six co-authors sped up serverless deep learning with a split management design. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with serverless computing for model serving. Such rigs scale on their own and bill by use. Their weak point is the cold start: loading a model eats time. Pipelined loading helps but stalls on layer by layer builds and one block weight loads.

Their frame, Cicada, splits those jobs apart. One part trims layer build cost by smart starts of the weights. A second part splits weight loads so the pipe keeps flow. A third lines up compute, storage, and schedule as one. Readers who serve models get a fix for the cold start tax.
arxiv-2503-00559:
Small, Ballatore, Giverso, and Balbi model how brain tissue twists and relaxes over time, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Brain tissue bends in curved ways and its stress fades with time. That fading, called relaxation, is one of its clearest traits. The team twisted fresh sheep brain samples and held the twist fixed.

They varied twist speed across three rates and tracked torque and push force. A modified viscoelastic model fit both signals at once with high accuracy. The fitted constants matched past torsion studies on brain tissue. Computer simulations confirmed the fits. The constants could improve models of head injury. They may also help design safer helmets for sports and racing.
arxiv-2503-00959:
David Loeffler and Michael Stoll report a 2025 project that rebuilds a core part of number theory inside the Lean proof assistant and its Mathlib library. Their objects are the Riemann zeta function and the wider family of L-functions, central tools for studying how prime numbers are spread. Formalizing means every step is checked by computer, with no gaps.

The project includes a full formal proof of Dirichlet's theorem, which says each valid arithmetic progression holds infinitely many primes. It also states the Riemann hypothesis formally, setting a precise target for future work. The authors present the effort as groundwork for verified number theory.
arxiv-2503-01259:
Sang-In Shim, Yoshiki Chazono, Kazuki Yoshida, Tomohiro Uesaka, and Kazuyuki Ogata compare two theories of nuclear transfer reactions in this two thousand twenty-five paper. At intermediate energies, transfer reactions are suppressed because momentum matching is hard to satisfy. The standard distorted wave Born approximation describes them as neutron pickup. An alternative, the distorted wave impulse approximation, treats the reaction as quasi-elastic scattering from a preformed deuteron cluster, and it has worked well for knockout reactions.

Both formalisms were applied to the same reaction, oxygen-sixteen with a proton producing oxygen-fifteen and a deuteron, at two hundred mega-electronvolts. The standard approximation matched the measured angular distribution and cross section well. The impulse approximation reproduced the shape but underestimated the cross section by about a hundredfold. The authors conclude the standard approach suits this reaction better, raising questions about the alternative's reach.
arxiv-2503-02059:
Setton and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about the missing dust glow in compact red galaxies called Little Red Dots. These distant objects look red and shine brightly in visible light. That redness suggested heavy dust around furious star birth or a hidden black hole. Yet far-infrared glow from such dust had not been seen. The team gathered deep images from space and ground telescopes. They targeted two of the brightest known examples.

Near-infrared data ruled out a strong hot dust component. Far-infrared non-detections ruled out much cold dust as well. A carbon gas signal expected from dusty starbursts was also absent. The limits clash with fits that assume heavy dust reddening. The authors favor models where these galaxies are naturally red instead. That shift eases the need for extreme dust in the early universe.
arxiv-2503-02859:
Emma Ceccherini, Ian Gallagher, Andrew Jones, and Daniel Lawson embed changing networks into vectors while they pledge the embedding will not drift in arbitrary ways. Dynamic network embeddings often break the match over time. The same behavior at two times should earn the same position. Their method also uses node attributes that themselves vary with time.

The attributed unfolded adjacency spectral embedding builds on spectral techniques. Its stability guarantee is proved through uniform convergence to a latent position model. On four real attributed networks it beat top learning methods at link prediction and node classification. The team note theirs is the sole attributed dynamic embedding with such guarantees that needs no ground-truth labels. Stability, they argue, is what makes downstream checks count.
arxiv-2503-03359:
Andrea Lepori, Alexandru Calotoiu, and Torsten Hoefler present a 2025 paper on making pointer-heavy C code easier for compilers to optimize. Pointers give programmers direct control over memory, but their targets are hard to track. Optimizers, and often programmers, cannot tell which data a pointer will touch.

Their method splits a loop-based pointer into a data container plus an offset. That split exposes the access pattern to static analysis. With it, they analyzed and sped up code from the OpenSSL library, a benchmark suite, and a compression algorithm. On one benchmark they found every parallel opportunity the developers knew of and beat the reference code by up to eighteen percent. A password hashing routine ran up to eleven times faster.
arxiv-2503-05359:
Sijme-Jan Paardekooper and Hossam Aly wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It asks whether a fast drag instability of dust in gas survives when the grains come in many sizes, not just one.

Drifting dust can lock onto a passing gas wave and swell fast, even when dust is scarce. This acoustic form may stir AGB star winds and supernova wreckage. The team solves the flow laws for a spread of grain sizes at low dust loads. The growth then slows from a square-root pace to a plain one. The fastest short waves of the one-size case are damped out. The instability still grows, but at a gentler rate, and the math turns from singular to regular.
arxiv-2503-07459:
Yanjun Shao leads a team benchmarking two styles of machine reasoning on hard medical questions. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. One style reasons inside a single model. The other scaffolds several models as cooperating agents. Which route wins, or whether they blend, was unclear. The team built MedicalAgentsBench to decide.

The bench holds eight hundred sixty-two complex clinical questions. Eight source datasets were filtered by difficulty and screened for contamination. Three reasoning models, seven base models, and nine agent frameworks face the set. Internal and external approaches are compared head to head. The findings test whether the routes compete or complete each other. Clinical AI design gains hard comparative evidence.
arxiv-2503-08259:
Yu Tang Liu and four co-authors teach a drone to handle two flying tasks with one brain. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, covers quadcopter attitude control. One task is smooth tracking of a target tilt. The other is fast recovery from any odd start pose. The two tasks want quite different moves, which makes one reward rule hard to write.

Their learning system trains both tasks side by side in simulation. A graph-based network forms the control policy. It learns faster and more surely than single-task training. The tiny final network runs on a real flight controller at high speed. A live drone test shows the method works off the screen.
arxiv-2503-08359:
Stefano De Angelis and co-authors design, in twenty twenty-five, a way for blockchain users to trust query answers without running a full node. Full nodes keep a local copy of the ledger and can verify everything themselves. Most users instead rely on servers, which reintroduces a single point of failure. Some queries can be answered by very few servers, sometimes all from one organization. Their architecture lets superlight clients outsource a query to a possibly untrusted server and still get a trustworthy answer.

The design relies on SNARKs, compact proofs that a computation was done right. It makes the proofs cheaper by using data from full nodes and blockchain explorers, and by leveraging smart contracts where present. Experiments on concrete scenarios confirm the approach works.
arxiv-2503-08759:
Siddhant Dutta and four co-authors sharpen low-resolution images with a hybrid quantum model in a 2025 paper. Classic upscaling networks work well but carry heavy parameter counts. Quantum methods promise compact power, yet scaling them to real images remains difficult on today's noisy hardware.

Their framework extends a shifted-window transformer with a quantum attention step. The quantum part runs on small circuits suited to current devices. It helps the model learn the mapping from blurry inputs to crisp outputs. Tests on handwritten digits, fashion images, and medical sets report strong quality scores. The authors frame the design as a practical bridge between quantum methods and everyday image repair tasks.
arxiv-2503-09159:
Andrej Tschalzev and five co-authors warn that careless use of shared data tables can warp machine learning research, in a 2025 paper. Big public archives host thousands of tables for testing new methods. The archives also advise how each table should be used, and that advice shapes whole fields. The team shows, with cases from recent high-profile work on one large archive, how traps in that advice have cut rigor.

Three traps recur: weak rules for picking the best model, missing strong rival methods, and sloppy data cleanup steps. Each trap can make a new method look better than it is. The authors then sketch fixes the archives could adopt to block misuse. They argue that archives should act as guards of research quality, not just hosts of files.
arxiv-2503-09559:
Shijie Chen and six co-authors build a learning system that rebuilds MRI images from spiral-style scans while fixing its own calibration maps. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Fast MRI samples the signal space along curves, not grids. Rebuilding images from such data with neural nets is hard to scale to many coils or higher dimensions.

Their design, iR2D2, stacks small networks that each clean the leftover error of the last. Two such stacks alternate: one forms the image, the other refines the coil sensitivity maps. Bad maps from sparse data can poison the rebuild, so the self-fixing matters. An error check decides when to stop updating. Tests in simulation and on real scans back the design. The method borrows its core idea from radio astronomy imaging.
arxiv-2503-10459:
David Couto, Arash Samani, and Alec Yonika present a cheaper way to hide radio signals from eavesdroppers in a paper from 2025. Directional modulation scrambles a beam so only the intended receiver reads it cleanly. Classic versions waste much power and repeat patterns on small arrays. Their phasor-pursuit method rotates element weights by real-valued phase steps, building a random walk to each symbol.

The scheme supports many modulation types in phase, amplitude, or both. Power loss versus plain beamforming can be as small as one decibel, far better than the usual six. The set of possible weights is also much larger, resisting pattern analysis. Tests used a standard noise injection setup. The authors target small arrays like home routers.
arxiv-2503-10559:
Georg Jäger and co-authors design a robot steering method that pairs a learning driver with a trusted backup, in a 2025 paper. Robots must follow paths safely in messy settings. Classic steering methods are steady but adapt poorly when conditions change. Learning-based drivers adapt well, yet they rarely come with firm safety promises. The authors use a design called the Simplex architecture to get both at once.

In that design, a learning controller drives when things look safe, and a proven high-assurance controller takes over when risk grows. The paper first sets out the safety and stability points any such pairing must handle. It then presents the team's path-tracking version. Tests in simulation, backed by early field trials, showed the controller working as intended. The setup also serves as a safe testbed for trying new planning methods.
arxiv-2503-10759:
Joseph and Peleg identify people across videos by their moving skeleton alone in this 2025 paper. Re-identification usually leans on appearance, which collapses when a person changes clothes. Their clothes-changing task removes that crutch entirely.

The method feeds joint positions into a spatio-temporal graph network, which learns a descriptor of how each body moves. No color, texture, or clothing features enter at all. At test time, predictions from several clip segments are pooled to firm up the match. On the CCVID benchmark, with several pose estimators tried, the method reached state-of-the-art accuracy. Skeleton dynamics offer a privacy-friendlier route to tracking identity across cameras.
arxiv-2503-11359:
Mallick and four co-authors wrote a twenty twenty-five study on how self-driving cars can save fuel. The cars must pick both a speed and a gear as they drive. Doing both at once in a smart control plan can cost too much time to run live.

The team trains a learned rule to pick and lock the gears for the plan ahead. The main control task then solves a much simpler task based on speed alone. In tests run in a computer, the new plan cuts the work by a large amount. Its fuel use stays close to the full joint plan.
arxiv-2503-11459:
Wang, Bi, Liang, Yang, and Gong studied tiny solar flares in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Microflares are small bursts in the sun's outer air, the corona, and their cause is still debated. The team used sharp images from the Solar Orbiter probe. They watched four flares that followed one another in the same region.

In three of the flares, about a dozen small ejections of hot plasma shot out from the center. They moved across the flare loops rather than along them. Each began as a dot about one thousand kilometers wide, then stretched into a loop shape. The authors argue the ejections come from small-angle reconnections inside braided magnetic fields. That would make microflares cousins of a proposed nanoflare process.
arxiv-2503-11759:
Adrian Ka-Wai Chung, Kelvin Ka-Ho Lam, and Nicolás Yunes compute the ringing tones of spinning black holes in a modified gravity theory. Their 2025 paper uses a spectral framework to get precise quasinormal mode frequencies, the damped tones a disturbed black hole emits. The theory tested adds a Chern-Simons term to general relativity.

They compute tones for both families of metric disturbance across several modes, for spins up to a set limit. The results carry tiny numerical uncertainties, reached without simplifying the field equations. They also supply fitting formulas so others can evaluate frequency shifts fast. Such tone tables are what gravitational wave observatories need to test modified gravity in the ringdown after a merger. This is the first precise set for spinning holes in this theory.
arxiv-2503-14059:
Zhonghao Tu and Ang Li study, in a 2025 astrophysics paper, why some neutron stars cool with a long delay before their surface temperature drops. For most, the drop comes within ten to one hundred years, a span set by heat escaping the star's crust.

The team adds two twists: neutrons pairing up into a superfluid state, and exotic particles called hyperons in the core. Under the right conditions, each twist can hold back the cooling wave. Rapid cooling driven by a fast core process can also arrive late if only a small core region allows it. Matching the young remnant Cassiopeia A pins down how cold the neutron pairing can be.
arxiv-2503-14259:
Ziyad Sheebaelhamd, Michael Tschannen, Michael Muehlebach, and Claire Vernade published a paper in 2025 on teaching robots by imitation without chopping actions into a fixed codebook. Most transformer policies first quantize smooth movements into discrete tokens, which breaks the natural continuity of motion. Their method plugs a generative transformer that speaks in continuous values directly into the policy.

The change simplifies the training pipeline while keeping the step-by-step prediction style that makes transformers strong. On a range of standard simulated robot tasks the method matched the best published results. The authors also study how the way actions are sampled at run time changes performance, and tune it for further gains. Smooth actions, represented smoothly, seem to imitate better.
arxiv-2503-14959:
Justin Iurman and co-authors fix, in a 2025 systems paper, a slowdown in how the Linux kernel handles lightweight tunnels for the modern internet protocol. Such tunnels serve in-band monitoring, segment routing, and low-power networks. Under some hardware mixes, the kernel copies packet buffers twice, which wastes effort on every packet.

The team traces the fault to how buffer room is reserved when a tunnel header is added. Their patch reserves the room once, in the right place. Tests showed forwarding rates up to about twenty-nine percent higher on the affected setups. The fix lands in the shared path, so all three tunnel users gain at once.
arxiv-2503-15759:
Anup Pradhan Sakhya and a large team of co-authors mapped the electronic structure of a new kagome metal, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Kagome metals, named for their woven lattice pattern, mix unusual magnetism with rich electron behavior. The compound studied pairs lanthanum and titanium with bismuth, and theory predicted special points in its electron bands.

Using a light-based probe alongside computer calculations, the team found several van Hove singularities, points where electrons pile up, with one sitting right near the key energy level. They also saw two flat bands born from wave interference inside the titanium lattice. The electron pattern proved strongly directional, since the crystal breaks sixfold rotation. The authors offer the material family as a fresh playground for quantum phenomena.
arxiv-2503-15859:
Wave equations with a strong damping term model everything from vibrating structures to the membrane of a nerve cell. Ali Raza and co-authors sort and solve a broad family of these nonlinear equations in this 2025 paper, giving the nerve membrane model special attention with and without the damping.

They list the equations' symmetries in full, find the changes of variables that leave the family intact, and reduce the equations to simpler ones whose solutions can be written down. Conservation laws are built by a direct method. Some solutions, including solitary waves, are shown as graphs to make their shapes plain.
arxiv-2503-16359:
McCann and co-authors wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five computing atomic data for zirconium in support of neutron star merger studies. When two neutron stars collide, the blast, called a kilonova, glows with light from heavy elements. Reading that light needs accurate data on how atoms absorb and emit energy.

The team modeled the first three ion stages of zirconium, an element expected to be common in the debris. They built precise atomic structures, then computed how electrons striking the ions excite them across a wide range of temperatures. The resulting rates feed models that produce synthetic spectra. Those spectra can be compared with telescope observations to reveal what the merger debris contains.
arxiv-2503-17159:
Deakin and Shillito rebuilt in twenty twenty-five the number-side base for a pair of two-way logics. Such logics track both proof and dis-proof in one frame. Past work in the line held grave flaws, and its number side had not been fixed.

They treat the two logics as links that must hold, not as sets of true lines. Tools fit for link-based logic are used for the main read. They also give a grade-of-truth read for each logic in turn. All claims are checked in a proof tool that talks back, for full trust.
arxiv-2503-17359:
Jiwen Yu and co-authors present a 2025 position paper arguing that interactive generated video should become the next game engine. Classic engines ship fixed content, which makes games costly and caps their novelty. Modern video models can synthesize vivid, playable worlds on the fly.

The authors name the concept Interactive Generative Video and build the case for Generative Game Engines on it. They cite five strengths: endless fresh content, world models that respect physics, direct user control, long-term memory, and causal reasoning. A framework lays out the core modules such a engine would need. A five-stage maturity roadmap, from L0 to L4, charts the climb. The paper is a call to reshape how games are built and played.
arxiv-2503-17859:
Khirk and co-authors wrote this nuclear physics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on the fleeting nucleus helium-7. This nucleus falls apart at once, so its excited states show up only in the debris of reactions that briefly create it.

The team reanalyzed data from a reaction that knocked a proton off helium-6 in flight. Their fresh look uses improved analysis plus detailed reaction calculations. A claimed state near two units of excitation energy does not survive the scrutiny, they find. Another state is pinned to a range a bit higher, with a favored value in the middle. Signs also point to a further state at still higher energy. The authors stress that angle patterns in the decay debris carry rich clues. Fuller studies of such patterns should sharpen the map of this unstable nucleus.
arxiv-2503-18259:
Yingli Wang, Zhenyu Cui, and Lingjiong Zhu connect a discrete-time order-flow process to the rough Heston model used in option pricing. They study nearly unstable, heavy-tailed integer-valued autoregressive processes in two dimensions. Under a one-factor parameterization and suitable scaling, these processes converge to the rough Heston dynamics for prices and variance.

The limit yields explicit formulas tying the discrete asymmetry parameters to the leverage correlation and volatility scale. For pricing, they derive an exact transform recursion at finite step size and reduce it to a discrete Volterra equation comparable to the continuous fractional Riccati equation. Weak-error bounds follow, and a fast simulator prices European and path-dependent options. The work gives rough volatility a microstructural foundation.
arxiv-2503-18959:
Two authors, Rejmund and Lemasson, built a seven dimensional path rebuild for a magnetic spectrometer. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with VAMOS++, a large accept tool for ion beams. Its optics bend in a strong nonlinear way, so soft math must rebuild each ion's track to read its stiffness and path length. Old reads take the hit spot as a point. That fails for wide beam spots or gas targets with depth.

Their method adds the reaction spot's three coordinates to the rebuild. Deep neural nets, trained on a built data set, do the math. Readers in nuclear physics get track reads that hold when the source is a cloud, not a point.
arxiv-2503-20959:
Joss Moorkens, Andy Way, and Seamus Lankford discuss side effects of machine translation in a 2025 book chapter. Translation tools help in many settings, but neural and large model systems carry costs. Training huge corporate models uses much electricity and produces large carbon emissions, while smaller or tuned models can cut that footprint.

The chapter also covers harm to translators and other users, copyright and data ownership, and ethics of data use. It closes on a positive case. Used properly, machine translation in crisis settings can save lives, and the authors give a method for doing so.
arxiv-2503-21159:
Kanishka Ranaweera and co-authors present a 2025 method for training AI across many sites without pooling raw data, while keeping a formal privacy shield. Such federated learning trims each site's updates before merging, a step called clipping. Clip too hard and the model dulls; clip too soft and privacy leaks. Set clip levels fit poorly as training runs on.

Their method adjusts the clip level live, driven by a joint score that weighs privacy and accuracy as twin goals. Theory checks show the method still settles toward a good model. Tests on three image sets beat fixed-clip rivals at the same privacy budget. Live tuning could help hospitals and banks train shared models under tight privacy law.
arxiv-2503-21559: Chomicz computes the fourth power level of p-adic completions for biquadratic number fields. The work fixes a prime ideal above two in a number field. It treats the case where the ramification index is four. The inertial degree is taken as trivial in that case. That result unlocks the fourth level for any quartic field completion. Applied to biquadratic fields, it gives lower bounds for their fourth level.
arxiv-2503-22959:
Ulrich Horst and Huilin Zhang published this probability paper in 2025. It develops control theory for systems driven by rough, jagged noise, where the driving signal is too irregular for classical calculus. The Pontryagin maximum principle is the classic tool that characterizes optimal controls through necessary conditions. Extending it to rough stochastic systems, including controls that may anticipate the future, is the paper's goal.

The authors first show that a class of controlled rough equations is well-posed, with solutions that depend continuously on the driving path. That foundation lets them define pathwise control problems precisely. A flow transformation argument then yields a maximum principle that is both necessary and sufficient for optimality. They prove the rough problem and its pathwise twin share the same value. For the benchmark linear-quadratic case with bounded controls, they establish the matching result for the controls themselves.
arxiv-2503-24259:
Deprez and co-authors sweep step-learn ways for graph tools in wash hunts. Banks must flag wash trades by law and watch vast trade flows. Wash hands shift their tricks fast to dodge the hunt tools. Tools thus need fresh tune on a near-live pace in banks. Stock learn tools lose old facts when tuned on new facts. That loss, called vast forget, caps their use in fast zones.

Step-learn ways aim to add new facts and keep old ones. Work on step graph learn for wash hunts still runs thin. The sweep grades top step ways for wash use in banks. Ways split in three camps: play-back, rule, and build forms. All sit in the graph net frame in the sweep text. Tests run on made and real wash sets for the grades.
arxiv-2504-00259:
Bock, Futorny, Neklyudov, and Zhang built new forms in twenty twenty-five for a math frame called a Yangian, from sets of curve-fit rules. Each set of such rules, called orthogonal polynomials, gives a new form of that frame. Most of the new forms break a known link rule that old forms kept.

They get a like of a known cross rule for sums of those fits. The build works for any set that meets a step rule, like a class of symbols and wave forms. A map trick then gives a three-way form of the frame as a flat bend of a current frame.
arxiv-2504-03459:
Anna-Lee Jessop and co-authors report, in 2025, how the shimmering green scales of a butterfly actually build their color crystals. The wing scales hold a gyroid, a labyrinth-like nanostructure that acts as a photonic crystal. Textbooks assumed the structure grows as a smooth solid.

Microscopy of developing pupal tissue tells a different story: the gyroid is woven from fibers, helically threaded along its geometry. No crystalline order exists inside the fibers. Scales from pupae whose development was surgically altered, turning the color blue, showed the same woven construction. The finding rewrites the assumed growth mechanism and may guide bioinspired optical materials.
arxiv-2504-03859:
Van Eijk and Ghosh bring modal regression into forecast combination, in a statistics paper from 2025. Combining forecasts is a standard way to improve predictions, and equal weights are often defended as a safe choice. That defense rests on symmetric loss, yet real forecast errors are often lopsided and heavy-tailed.

Modal regression aims at the most likely value rather than the average, which suits skewed errors better. The authors build a Bayesian layered model with weights that shift over time and fade past data. They try three skewed error forms, led by the asymmetric Laplace. Tests on made-up data checked the fitting, and a real set of analyst forecasts came next. The modal method beat mean regression on hit rate and win rate for revenue surprise calls.
arxiv-2504-04559:
Mohammed El Baraka and Siham Ezzouak present faster algorithms in two thousand twenty-five for a hard math operation behind a candidate post-quantum code system. The operation links pairs of hyperelliptic curves, a richer cousin of the elliptic curves used today. Quantum computers threaten current codes, so new foundations are being explored.

Their algorithms cut the work for genus two curves from a fourth-power cost to a third-power cost in the genus. They give full step-by-step procedures and complexity counts, checked in theory and in practice. A security analysis argues the scheme resists known quantum attacks, including the famous factoring and search algorithms. The authors present hyperelliptic isogeny codes as a promising path to secure, efficient post-quantum systems.
arxiv-2504-05259:
Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, Buck Shlegeris, and Geoffrey Irving ask how to test safety controls on language model agents fairly as the agents grow stronger. Control evaluations pit a red team, playing a misaligned agent, against the safeguards meant to contain it. If the red team is granted superhuman attack skills, the test misprices the real risk.

Their framework scales the red team's affordances to the actual capability profile of the model being deployed. Five fictional models of rising ability anchor five AI control levels. For each level the authors sketch fitting evaluation rules, control measures, and safety cases. The aim is evaluations that stay practical and affordable without going soft.
arxiv-2504-05659:
Ruijie Xu wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five on when equations from counting lattice walks can be solved cleanly. Walks confined to three quadrants of the grid produce functional equations that resist standard methods. Xu frames the problem as a matrix version of a classic boundary value problem from complex analysis.

A problem counts as integrable when it reduces to enough polynomial equations in one helper variable. Xu shows integrability hinges on the eigenspaces of an associated matrix. For three-quadrant walks, the obstinate kernel method turns the counting equation into a three-by-three matrix problem. One special eigenvalue yields two independent equations and another yields a third. The framework widens earlier results from walks with full symmetry to walks meeting only orbit-sum conditions, and explains known counterexamples.
arxiv-2504-06859:
Athira S and three co-authors study exotic matter inside neutron stars in a 2025 physics paper. The cores of these stars squeeze matter far past normal density. Under such pressure, particles called antikaons may condense into a new phase. How antikaons grip other particles is still poorly known.

The team uses a symmetry of particle physics to fix those grips. Three key settings come out of that symmetry based approach. One mixing angle and one coupling ratio are pinned down. A third weight is left free to test its influence. With stiffer settings, the star's matter resists squeezing more strongly. The work is a first use of this symmetry for antikaon condensation.
arxiv-2504-07659:
Suprovo Ghosh and co-authors study in 2025 tidal heating during the inspiral of strange quark stars. As two such stars spiral together, tides heat them and change the gravitational wave signal. For normal neutron stars this heating is small, but quark matter may behave very differently.

They compute viscosity from weak processes among quarks and find it orders of magnitude above nuclear matter values. Equal-mass binaries reach high temperatures by the end of inspiral. The extra heating shifts the wave phase by a detectable amount, they estimate. Spotting that shift in low-mass systems could signal strange quark stars.
arxiv-2504-07859:
Jan Heisig reviews a route by which dark matter may have formed in the early universe, in this 2025 paper. The classic picture needs dark matter to interact strongly enough to freeze out of the hot early cosmos, and searches built on that picture have found nothing. Conversion-driven freeze-out offers an escape: a partner particle keeps dark matter in balance even when its own couplings are feeble.

Because the standard searches go blind here, the scenario predicts something else to hunt: long-lived particles that decay inside detectors at the Large Hadron Collider. Heisig surveys the model variants built on this mechanism. He stresses its links to other open problems, above all the origin of ordinary matter. In some variants the same conversions that set the dark matter amount also tip the balance between matter and antimatter. The review frames one framework for two of cosmology's biggest gaps.
arxiv-2504-09359:
Sebastián Mendizabal and five co-authors published a paper in 2025 refining a classic formula for how particle showers grow in the air. When a cosmic ray or gamma ray hits the atmosphere, its cascade swells and fades in a pattern first captured by the Greisen formula. That old form fits poorly near and past the shower's peak, which is exactly where detectors do their reading.

The team introduces a new slope profile that matches the original within three quarters of a percent across the heart of the shower's life. They also complete the formula for particle count and add the effect of the shower's tilt. High-altitude observatories, which sit close to the action, stand to gain the most from the sharper fit.
arxiv-2504-09659:
Hayk Soghomonyan and seven colleagues build a laser measuring system into a laser cutting station, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Parts can then be profiled in three dimensions without being moved. Developing a micromachining process is slow largely because checking the result usually means carrying the piece to a separate instrument.

Their system uses dual-comb LiDAR, which ranges with two interfering laser frequency combs, mounted coaxially with the machining beam. It profiles in place, non-destructively, while the workpiece stays in the station. The raw depth precision is below a micron. There is no mechanical scanning delay, and the working range is large. That mix suits the variety of tiny structures micromachining produces, from channels to molds. In-situ feedback should compress the trial-and-error loop of process development. The authors present the integration as a practical upgrade for precision laser manufacturing.
arxiv-2504-10359:
Aryan Shrivastava and Paula Akemi Aoyagui propose a 2025 frame for judging language models by the setting in which they will be used. Models now sit inside many tools, yet standard tests often miss how people use them in real work. A score on a fixed test may say little about worth to a team with its own needs and limits.

The frame scores models on fine, split traits rather than one mark. Some traits apply in any setting, such as staying sound under odd inputs, keeping sense, and being frank about doubt. Other traits must be shaped to each setting and to the people who must trust the tool. The paper lays out ways to put the frame to work and the gains and hard parts it brings.
arxiv-2504-11959:
Joachim Deutscher and Tarik Enderes set out a way to steer a class of heat-like systems from data in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The systems are semilinear parabolic partial differential equations with control at the edge. Their true rules are not known. The team lifts the curved dynamics with a small set of Koopman operator eigenfunctionals. That gives a model with a set size that standard design tools can make stable.

A bilinear form of the lifted model links how eigenfunctionals are set to feedback linearization. The paper checks that the closed loop stays stable in an exponential way. That holds even with errors from the data-based sums for the eigenfunctionals. The controller comes from generalized eDMD used on state data. A test case is an unstable reaction-diffusion system that would blow up in finite time. It shows the method at work.
arxiv-2504-12559:
Emil Ryd and Grey Nearing tune a world flood model on local stream data to lift its calls at home. World models learn from wide datasets, yet home crews cannot bend them to their own streams, which blocks field use. Their 2025 method pre-trains on the world dataset, then fine-tunes basin by basin on local readings. Gains test the worth of local facts.

Calls rose after tuning, which proves local datasets hold news the world dataset missed. Gains ran biggest where the world model had run worst. A road map for home crews closes the work: how to take a world model in hand with their own data. The aim is field-ready flood warning rigs in more lands.
arxiv-2504-12659:
Agnese Barbensi, Alexander R Klotz, and Dimos Gkountaroulis give a way to steer a filament toward a knot, or away from one, in simulation. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Past runs rely on chance moves to find a knot path. Their method seeks the best path under a set physics, in a guided way.

They project the curve onto many surfaces and read a knot spectrum from each. A mean unravelling count then sets a slope to climb or drop. On a plain chain, the best paths make torus knots, much like long DNA. With protein-like bend and twist rules, twist knots grow common, as in real proteins.
arxiv-2504-13659:
Andrea Govoni and three co-authors test how a spring-based model mimics bendy objects in robot simulators. Their 2025 study covers cables, wires, and strings, known as deformable linear objects. Such items are hard to simulate because they flex and twist freely. Good simulation matters for training robots to handle wires and assembly tasks.

The model treats the object as masses linked by springs and dampers. The team varied its settings and watched how the object's motion changed. Two simulators, Isaac Sim and Gazebo, hosted the tests. The goal was to gather force data with randomized settings for later robot training. The study checks whether such randomization works in these simulation setups.
arxiv-2504-14659:
Domanovitz and Khina ask when the best possible estimate changes smoothly as data change slightly. Minimum mean square error estimation is used across signal work and information theory. In practice it behaves sturdily, yet it can jump under standard forms of convergence. The team reviews classic counterexamples to its smoothness. Two culprits stand out: second moments that fail to settle, and data that know more than the limit they approach.

Under two natural guards, smoothness returns. The guards are a settling second moment and a Markov limit on informativeness. The estimate and the estimator both become continuous. Related settings get matching one-sided results. The work explains why the estimator rarely breaks in practice.
arxiv-2504-14959:
Qianye Wang, Yuejie Wang, Yongting Chen, and Guyue Liu present NetCloak in two thousand twenty-five. NetCloak hides the true shape of a network when its settings are shared. Shared device settings can leak group size and resource spread. Fake routers and hosts are added to blur the real scale.

The frame embeds the true graph in a larger reference graph. Link rules make each real node hard to tell from peers. A generator copies command style from real devices for the fake ones. A repair step then restores sound routing. Tests on campus and data center graphs show strong gains in hiding scale and in fidelity.
arxiv-2504-15659:
Language models can write chip design code at register transfer level. But training sets usually check only that the code compiles, not that it behaves as specified. The eight authors present VeriCoder, a model fine-tuned on functionally validated data. Their recipe starts with a specification and a draft design. A teacher model writes unit tests, then revises the design against simulation results. It also fixes the tests when they stray from the spec.

The resulting set holds 125,777 examples, each a description, an implementation, and passing tests. Fine-tuned on it, VeriCoder tops functional correctness scores on VerilogEval and RTLLM, with relative gains up to 71.7 and 27.4 percent. Ablations confirm that validated data, not just more data, drives the win. Code, data, and models are public.
arxiv-2504-16959:
Zhang and six co-authors presented a method in twenty twenty-five for testing models of the stochastic gravitational-wave background. That background is a faint sea of ripples in spacetime from many distant sources. Scientists summarize its sky pattern with an angular power spectrum, a measure of variation by scale.

The authors show common estimators for this spectrum lack a simple likelihood formula, and a bell-curve approximation often fails. They develop a robust analysis that avoids assuming a distribution shape. They also derive a new, consistent estimator for the spectrum's uncertainty. Details of the method are set out step by step. They apply it to data from the third observing run of the LIGO and Virgo detectors.
arxiv-2504-17159: Victor G Kac and Minoru Wakimoto present a 2025 arXiv paper in pure mathematics. It studies characters of modules over an affine Lie algebra. The work sits at a special class of levels called subprincipal admissible levels. The authors prove that the span of these normalized characters stays fixed under the modular group. They also give the explicit formula for how the characters transform. Such results anchor representation theory and its links to conformal field theory.
arxiv-2504-17659:
Kaustav Mukherjee, Grant Biedermann, and Robert Lewis-Swan offer one framework for the slow, sticky relaxation seen in disordered quantum systems, in a 2025 paper. Arrays of atoms held by laser tweezers can now place each atom at will, making them ideal sandboxes for such physics. The framework says the relaxation pattern of a whole ensemble follows from simple statistics of its disorder, chiefly the average and the spread of the random placements.

Exact computer calculations back the claim across many settings. With it, the authors separate how much the number of dimensions and the reach of interactions each matter for glassy, slower-than-exponential decay. They also give a recipe, called J-mapping, that lets a one-dimensional array imitate the relaxation of a disordered system of any dimension and interaction range. The work points to programmable experiments on today's atom-array machines.
arxiv-2504-17759:
Surya Teja Avirneni wrote this security paper in 2025, a theory piece on zero trust infrastructure. Zero trust systems grant no access by default, and every request must prove itself. Avirneni proposes an Identity Control Plane, a single layer that speaks for all comers: people, workloads, and automation. It blends three ID kinds: workload IDs from SPIFFE, user IDs from web standards, and scoped robot credentials.

Brokers issue short transaction tokens under rules set by policy engines such as OPA and Cedar. The paper lays out the parts, join patterns, and use cases, then weighs the design against current models. It also maps the plan onto FedRAMP and SLSA compliance needs. No build is reported; the aim is a blueprint for researchers and platform architects.
arxiv-2504-19759:
Huichi Zhou and five co-authors built a test of moral sense for big language models that runs across five tongues. Moral calls shift with tongue and with how much text wraps the case. Their test, the MMRB, grades cases at three depths: a lone line, a full passage, and a whole file. Tongues with thin web lore, such as Vietnamese, sit at the weak end of model skill.

Scores fell as depth grew, and fell most for the thin-lore tongues. The team then tuned an open model on one-tongue data, both clean and spiked. In a turn that caught them off guard, thin-lore tongues swayed the mixed-tongue scores more than rich ones did. Weak tongues are thus not a side case: they steer how fair a model can be for all.
arxiv-2504-21359:
Kondo, Nakajima, and Sasada studied links between Yang-Baxter maps and a property of random variables in twenty twenty-five. Yang-Baxter maps are transformations that obey a famous equation. They come from integrable systems, models that can be solved exactly. The independence preserving property means that, after a map acts, random variables stay independent. That trait is prized in probability.

Recent work began to connect these two ideas, which seem unrelated. The authors use ultra-discretization, a limiting process. It turns smooth formulas into piecewise linear ones, made of straight parts. They extend that process to probability distributions, and that step is new. They prove that both the Yang-Baxter property and independence preservation survive the limit. Used on a known family of maps, this gives fresh examples of piecewise linear maps with the independence property. Open questions close the paper.
arxiv-2504-21759:
Mohamed Moursi, Norbert Wehn, and Bilal Hammoud put an oil spill detector on a drone in this 2025 paper. Spills at sea demand fast mapping of where the oil is and how thick it lies, since thick patches are skimmed first. Neural networks can read that from radar, but they are usually too heavy for small aircraft.

The team shrank a standard segmentation network hard, cutting blocks and channels until it was about two hundred seventy times smaller. Trained on synthetic radar scenes, the small model still scored about seventy-nine percent overlap on spill outlines and judged slicks up to ten millimeters thick. It runs on a programmable chip aboard the drone at about two watts, close to real time. The authors present the system as proof that sharp environmental sensing can live at the edge, on the device itself.
arxiv-2505-00859:
Anthony Forbes and Carrie Rutherford settle a question in graph theory in a short paper from two thousand twenty-five. The design spectrum of a graph is the set of sizes for which a complete graph can be split, edge by edge, into copies of it. They study the Shrikhande graph, a well known strongly regular graph.

They prove that the Shrikhande graph and the line graph of a related complete bipartite graph share the same spectrum. The valid sizes form a simple arithmetic pattern, starting at ninety-seven and stepping by ninety-six. The result completes the classification for these two graphs. Short papers of this kind close off cases in the broader theory of graph decompositions.
arxiv-2505-01459:
Abdoul Majid Thiombiano and colleagues proposed a new language model design in 2025 called MoxE. Large models are costly to run because every part of the network fires for every word piece. Their design mixes a memory-based block type with a team of expert blocks, so only a few experts handle each piece.

A routing step sends each piece to the right experts by watching how spread out the choices are. Rare pieces tend to go to the memory-style blocks, while common pieces use other experts. Extra training losses keep the workload balanced across experts. Tests and theory in the work report better speed and quality than rival designs.
arxiv-2505-01659:
The Gini index is the standard yardstick for inequality, but it comes in one fixed form. Roberto Vila and Helton Saulo introduce a more flexible version, the extended Gini index. It is built from the gaps between ranked values inside small subsamples of the data, which lets the user tune which part of the spread matters. They study the case where the data follow a gamma distribution, a common model for income like quantities.

The authors derive a closed form formula for the expected value of the sample estimator under this distribution. They prove the estimator is unbiased, meaning it hits the true value on average. That extends earlier results by other researchers. A computer simulation confirms the unbiasedness on finite samples. They also apply the new measure to data on GDP per capita to show how it works in practice.
arxiv-2505-02259:
Stanislav Semenov hides whole numbers inside smooth curves in this 2025 paper. Instead of writing an integer as a symbol, he builds a wavy function from soft bumps with alternating, shrinking weights. The area under the curve carries the number's fingerprint.

As the target integer grows, the total area shrinks toward zero, and the integer can be read back as the point where the balance nearly cancels. The recovery works through curve fitting or direct inversion formulas. The scheme stretches to lists of numbers at once, not just single values. The author studies how the construction settles as terms accumulate and shows the numeric build of the area map. He pitches the method as a bridge: discrete logic written in a continuous language that optimizers and learning systems can move through smoothly.
arxiv-2505-03859:
Will Hawkins, Chris Russell, and Brent Mittelstadt count how easy it has become to fetch deepfake image models from the open web, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Text to image tools now let anyone forge a real person's likeness. Such non consensual forges are the harm at stake.

The team mined two big model hubs for shared variants. They found near thirty-five thousand deepfake variants free to pull, most on one hub. The set had been pulled near fifteen million times since late 2022. Most target women, and many flag an aim to make fake intimate shots. A cheap trick needs as few as twenty photos and a home grade machine. The authors say hosts and law lag far behind the spread.
arxiv-2505-04459:
Muriel Bonetto and three co-authors modeled trapped-ion thermometry in twenty twenty-five. Trapped ions serve as simulators of heat transport and quantum thermodynamics, but reading their temperature is delicate. One tool fits dark resonances — dips in the ion's fluorescence spectrum — yet that fit needs simulations of coupled electronic and motion dynamics that trade speed against accuracy.

The authors compare simplified simulation techniques, starting from a three-level model and moving to the realistic eight-level calcium ion. A cheap shortcut, mimicking thermal motion with extra dephasing, proves convenient but can bias the temperature estimate significantly. Proper calibration can counteract the bias. The study maps when each shortcut is safe, supporting dark resonances as a practical ion thermometer.
arxiv-2505-04759:
Mohit Chaudhary, Chirag Jain, and Preethu Rose Anish wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tests whether ChatGPT can sort app reviews into requirement types with no training examples given, a mode called zero-shot.

App reviews guide how apps grow, and sorting them into what a feature must do versus broader quality traits helps teams plan. The team had ChatGPT sort close to two thousand hand-marked reviews from ten apps into four bins. The model scored well overall, though some kinds of review trip it up. The authors also check how the ease and length of a review sway the result, and mark which bins draw the most errors.
arxiv-2505-05659:
Vieira Neto and Valle present a paper from twenty twenty-five on a new kind of image sorting network. The base model family balances width, depth, and image size to use its parts well. Standard networks learn links between image channels as they train. The pair instead build channels into the data as one unit from the start. Their models can take vector data of any length as input.

They test the models on a medical image task, sorting blood cell images for a type of leukemia. The models scored very high on that test set. They also used far fewer parts than rival models and beat the base model. The authors post their code in public for others to use.
arxiv-2505-06459:
Pablo Flores, Olga Graf, Pavlos Protopapas, and Karim Pichara improve how physics-informed neural networks report their own doubt, in a paper from 2025. These networks solve equations of motion and change, but they give no sense of error by default. A user cannot tell where the answer is firm and where it is a guess. The team add a two-step Bayesian layer on top.

Known error bounds for the networks shape a variance that shifts across the domain. That richer doubt model sharpens the uncertainty bands. They then solve forward problems and feed the doubt into inverse ones. A cosmology case shows the payoff: unknown parameters come with honest error bars. The method makes such networks safer for science use. It also helps flag where more data would count most.
arxiv-2505-06759:
Xavier Martínez-Luaña and three co-authors present a 2025 paper on adding privacy to federated learning with coded computing. In federated learning, many parties train a shared model without pooling raw data. Coded computing can shield the math, but most schemes demand exact arithmetic and special function types. The team adapts a private approximate scheme, shortened to PBACC, to three learning setups of rising spread.

Their versions cover central gathering, central data with spread training, and fully spread data and training. Tests on image networks, generative models, and a medical survival model showed quality barely changed. Measured privacy leakage stayed under a fraction of one bit per participant. Encoding cost grows only with how spread the data are. The authors present the scheme as a general privacy tool for distributed learning.
arxiv-2505-07059:
Sanchita Nandi and Santanu Maiti proposed heat as a probe of a localization shift in a 2025 paper. The Aubry-Andre-Harper model is a clean test bed where a wavy pattern traps electrons as its depth grows. Past a sharp depth, equal to twice the hop strength, electrons stop roaming and the material turns insulator-like.

Past probes read that shift through charge or wave traits. Nandi and Maiti show that the electronic specific heat carries its own clear mark of the crossing. The mark tracks how the state density warps as disorder grows. A heat read is a bench-friendly test that many labs can run.
arxiv-2505-07459:
Heydar Soudani, Evangelos Kanoulas, and Faegheh Hasibi analyze confidence estimates in twenty twenty-five. Retrieval-augmented generation feeds outside documents into a language model's prompt. Uncertainty estimation should tell users how much to trust each answer. In the RAG setting, the authors show, current methods cannot reliably judge correctness.

They build an axiomatic framework to say exactly what goes wrong. Five constraints define what a good uncertainty method must do once documents join the prompt. Experiments reveal that no existing method satisfies all five axioms. That failure explains their weak performance in retrieval settings. Readers get design rules for the next generation of uncertainty tools, grounded in logic rather than trial and error.
arxiv-2505-08259:
Amangeldi and three co-authors compared convolutional networks with vision transformers for image classification in twenty twenty-five. Convolutional networks are the established workhorse; transformers, borrowed from language models, are challengers. The practical question is efficiency: which gives acceptable accuracy with lower latency and fewer parameters on modest hardware?

Using ResNet-18 as the baseline, the team fine-tuned four sizes of vision transformer, from tiny to large, on a skin image dataset and on Tiny ImageNet. Systematic tuning of training settings showed the transformers could match or beat the baseline while running faster and carrying fewer parameters. The authors conclude that properly fine-tuned vision transformers are viable for deployment in resource-constrained settings like clinics and edge devices.
arxiv-2505-08559:
Fochesato, Wang, Papachristodoulou, and Goulart worked in twenty twenty-five on proofs of safety for step-time systems that face noise. They pair a safety proof sheet with a plain rule that steers the system by its state. For noise with a capped size, they give a math task whose pass means a safe rule exists.

For noise with no cap, chance math gives a task that yields chance-based safety for a set span. They add ways to fold in caps on inputs and doubt on the chance spread. Safe screens and dodging blocks are also fit in the frame. The tools aim at sound, check-able safety claims.
arxiv-2505-08759:
Bagaev and four co-authors tame the jagged loss landscapes that stall quantum machine learning, by deliberately injecting noise, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Variational quantum algorithms train by descending a landscape riddled with poor local minima, making training provably hard in general. Practical heuristics, though, may still work on typical cases.

Their protocol adds targeted noise that exponentially damps the high-frequency ripples in the loss function's wave expansion, smoothing the terrain. It runs efficiently both on real hardware and in simulation. Across problem types, solution quality improved significantly and robustly. The method pairs with existing tricks such as the quantum natural gradient, adding a fresh tool to the quantum optimization kit.
arxiv-2505-10059:
MirSaleh Bahavarnia, Muhammad Nadeem, and Ahmad Taha work on controlling power grids in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Power networks run in sync, and small upsets can cascade into blackouts. Knowing which lines matter most is key to keeping control. Older rankings of network parts look only at the wiring map and ignore how the grid actually swings. The authors build a control-based measure for edges, the lines themselves.

Their edge centrality matrix scores each line by its effect on controllability. From the scores, they pick the most vital lines. They also compute small changes to line traits that near-optimally boost control. Tests run on standard IEEE grid models. Grid operators and control engineers are the audience.
arxiv-2505-10759:
Achmad Ginanjar, Xue Li, Priyanka Singh, and Wen Hua wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tests random client selection as a shield for contrastive federated learning on tabular data.

In vertical federated learning, parties train one model while each holds part of the data, but shared mid-steps can leak private facts. Contrastive methods cut that leak, yet gradient-based attacks still pry. The team ran broad tests of such attacks in this setting. Picking clients at random for each round blunted the attacks well. The findings give a plain, strong step for safer joint learning.
arxiv-2505-11259:
Gabriele Iommazzo and co-authors prove fast convergence for the Frank-Wolfe algorithm on product polytopes in this 2025 paper. Frank-Wolfe solves smooth optimization problems using only linear steps. Its speed depends on the shape of the feasible region. Product polytopes arise when several simple regions are combined into one larger problem.

Two shape measures are analyzed for products, the pyramidal width and the vertex facet distance. Both are bounded from the measures of the parts. For objectives with a Polyak-Lojasiewicz property, linear convergence rates follow from those bounds. A test problem asks for a feasible point in a high dimensional polytope intersection. Experiments confirm the theory runs efficiently in practice. The work extends known fast rates to combined domains.
arxiv-2505-11959:
Wajdi Zaghouani and Md. Rafiul Biswas put out a bilingual data set of emotion and hope speech in a 2025 paper. Texts expressing hope, encouragement toward a goal despite hardship, are understudied next to hate or sentiment. Resources covering both emotions and hope in Arabic barely exist. Their EmoHopeSpeech corpus pairs a large Arabic collection with a smaller English one. Each entry labeled for emotion type, intensity, complexity, and cause, plus a detailed hope sorting with subcategories.

Trained annotators agreed strongly under a standard reliability measure in both languages. A usual test learning model reached a respectable score, validating the labels as learnable. The resource targets cross-linguistic study of how hope and emotion intertwine online.
arxiv-2505-12059:
Saikat Roy, writing solo in 2025, takes up a plain question: given a target and a tidy set of stand-ins, how near can one come, and which comes nearest? His stage is the space of operators, the math objects that stretch and turn spaces, under two ways of measuring size. For each way he derives the gap outright.

Finite cases drawn from quantum-style algebras get the same treatment. Worked examples show the formulas earning their keep: where a search would grind, the closed forms answer at once. Best-fit problems of this kind sit under signal work, control, and quantum theory, so a clean gap formula has reach beyond its own page.
arxiv-2505-12159:
Doctors who plan a sequence of treatments need methods that learn from records where follow-up often ends early. Jeongjin Lee and Jong-Min Kim build such a method in a 2025 paper, joining reinforcement learning with a classic survival statistics trick.

Their framework learns, step by step, which action would have led to the best long-term outcome, a counterfactual question. The Buckley-James method fills in the missing survival times that early censoring hides. A linear form of that method keeps the learning fast and stable. The setting is longitudinal survival data, where each patient's story unfolds over time and may be cut short. Better tools here can sharpen treatment rules for chronic and life-threatening disease.
arxiv-2505-12459:
Ni, Claussen, and Ho design a scheduler that keeps quantum network links pure enough without wasting scarce resources. Quantum networks trade in entanglement, whose quality fades and must be restored by purification rounds. Each round costs time and consumes paired particles.

Their scheduler picks routes and purification depth together, aiming at a target quality at the lowest cost. Two hop-level estimators, a neural classifier and a Bayesian optimizer, guess the fewest rounds each hop needs. Simulations showed latency down by up to 8 percent and success rates up 14 percent against fixed-round scheduling. The approach flexes the final quality to fit each request.
arxiv-2505-12859:
Lucas Charpentier and Pierre Lison attacked de-identified documents to test how safe redaction really is in a 2025 paper. Privacy practice masks names and identifiers in records before release, assuming the person stays hidden. Their re-identification method works like lookup-augmented making run in reverse: a retriever pulls background documents that might describe the masked person. Then a text model fills each blank with its best guessing, repeating until no masks remain.

Across biographies, court rulings, and health notes, up to four fifths of masked spans were recovered correctly. More background knowledge meant more recovery. Masking alone, the results warn, is a weaker shield than custodians of sensitive archives assume.
arxiv-2505-13559:
Sathya Suresh and three co-authors built a test for how well models summarize talks that swap languages mid-stream, in a paper published in 2025. Such swaps are the norm in much of the world, yet models are built for one language at a time. Their set, CS-Sum, holds hand-labeled talks in three pairs: Mandarin with English, Tamil with English, and Malay with English, each near a thousand strong.

Ten models took the test in three modes: few-shot, translate then summarize, and light tuning. Scores on standard scales ran high. Human readings told a worse tale: small slips that flip the whole sense of a talk. Three slip types recurred, at rates that swung by pair and model. The authors call for training on true code-switched data.
arxiv-2505-14259:
Petr Sedlák and four colleagues measured how the elasticity of nickel-titanium wire evolves as its crystal structure transforms under stress. Using a laser-ultrasonic method, they tracked the Young's modulus of stress-induced martensite across stress and temperature. The values, ranging from thirty to fifty gigapascals, fall on one smooth surface in stress-temperature space.

Monitoring the modulus during shape setting revealed further softening, down to nearly ten gigapascals at high temperature and stress. The elasticity data also pinpointed where shape setting starts and ends. That temperature interval proved the same for martensite induced by tension and by torsion, a useful check for shape-memory alloy processing.
arxiv-2505-14859:
Akash Patel and co-authors guide a ground robot and a drone as one team through layered maps that judge terrain by risk and reward, in work from twenty twenty-five. Unknown spaces strain solo robots: wheels stall where wings would pass. Teamwork needs a shared sense of where each partner belongs.

Their framework stacks graphs at several resolutions, holding shape and meaning about passable ground. A confidence score weighs likely new volume, path safety, and collision risk. The ground robot uses it to decide when to send the drone ahead. In a real cave like trial, the ground robot flagged dead ends fit for flight. Shared frontier targets let the drone push past obstacles.
arxiv-2505-15259:
Lee and nine co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on teaching agents to find screen elements with far less training data. Agents that use computers must locate buttons and fields exactly. Prior work leans on huge web datasets to raise that accuracy. Their framework learns through self-made reasoning steps, tuned by online reinforcement learning. A spatial critic checks guesses against flipped or shifted views of the screen. At test time, a spatial search plus vote step boosts results further.

The method tops grounding benchmarks while using a sliver of rival training data. One comparison uses only a tiny fraction of the best open baseline's samples. The authors stress data thrift over data scale. Their frame suits web agents where labeled data are costly.
arxiv-2505-15359:
Anatole Dahan published a research paper in 2025 introducing a logic that can count the size of a group built from definable permutations. Logicians hunt for a logic that captures exactly the queries a computer can answer in reasonable time. Adding a rank operator got close but failed on a known hard case.

The new operator extends rank by counting the groups it forms. Checking formulas in the new logic stays fast. The counterexample that defeated the rank version becomes expressible here, because the logic can standardize structures with abelian color classes. The result makes the new logic a fresh candidate for capturing efficient computation.
arxiv-2505-15559:
Zixun Guo and Simon Dixon brought in Moonbeam in 2025, a base model for music in MIDI form. It was pre-taught on a large, diverse collection of symbolic music, tens of thousands of hours and billions of tokens. Most language-style models treat musical notes as plain symbols. Moonbeam instead encodes both absolute traits, like a note's actual pitch, and relative ones, like intervals between notes, through a specially built tokenization.

A process called Multidimensional Relative Focus captures those relationships without extra trainable settings. On top of the pre-taught model, the authors build two fine-tuning setups covering music understanding and conditional generation, including filling in missing passages. They report Moonbeam outperforming other large pre-taught music models in most contrasts. A single model that both understands and composes symbolically could serve study, education, and creative tools alike.
arxiv-2505-16459:
Guiyao Tie, Xueyang Zhou, Tianhe Gu, Ruihang Zhang, Chaoran Hu, Sizhe Zhang, Mengqu Sun, Yan Zhang, Pan Zhou, and Lichao Sun wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents MMLU-Reason, a benchmark for how well multimodal large language models reason, not just what they answer.

The set holds over a thousand hard questions across six kinds of reasoning, each needing steps that hop between text, image, and form. A scoring pipeline grades the thought traces themselves for fit, coherence, and kinds of error. Models that show their thought beat those that do not, yet even the best, named in the paper, show flaws such as drift and overthinking. The gap between right answers and sound thought is the point.
arxiv-2505-16959:
Alessandro Favero, Antonio Sclocchi, and Matthieu Wyart studied in twenty twenty-five when overparameterized diffusion models memorize their training data versus generalize. Perfect training would reproduce the training set; empirically, huge models do memorize eventually. The authors show the story has a timing structure: generalization arrives first, progressively, before memorization begins.

Across image and language diffusion models, memorization time scaled in proportion to data set size. In a toy grammar-learning model they watched generalization unfold as the stepwise acquisition of deeper rules, and priced what early stopping costs. The resulting phase diagram suggests a principled stopping rule — halt training on a schedule growing with data set size — to capture generalization, dodge memorization, and transfer hyperparameters across scales.
arxiv-2505-17459:
Jingwen Cheng, Ruikun Li, Huandong Wang, and Yong Li wrote a 2025 paper on forecasting how complex systems change over time. Such systems, from weather to fluids, follow hidden rules that are hard to learn from raw data. Most models squeeze data into a compact code, then predict step by step from that code.

Their method, SparseDiff, fixes a flaw in that plan: flat codes lose where things sit in space. It updates its coding scheme at test time, while forecasts are running. This lets the model catch new patterns that emerge late in a run. The design aims for sharper long-range forecasts. Better forecasts help in fields like climate study and engineering design.
arxiv-2505-17759:
Chris Pearson and six co-authors present the deepest far-infrared field image in a 2025 paper. A patch of sky near the north ecliptic pole was observed again and again to check an instrument's stability during a space mission. Stacking well over a hundred observations made it one of the deepest views of the submillimetre universe. Two extraction methods, one map-based and one guided by a prior catalog, pulled out the galaxy sources.

Both methods found the expected turnover in galaxy numbers and agreed with earlier surveys. The guided method reached about twice as deep. Modern galaxy evolution models matched the counts well overall.
arxiv-2505-17959:
Nguyen Duc and seven co-authors measure the gap between real and fake sensor data in a 2025 paper. Self-driving car makers train systems on simulated street scenes, yet fake data never matches the road perfectly. For safety, that gap needs a credible measure rather than guesswork.

Their approach compares real scans and simulated scans of the very same place. Pairing the two removes confusion from scene differences. A new metric scores gaps in shape and other traits of the point clouds. The analysis can separate gaps caused by the network from gaps in class labels or object models. Such clarity helps teams fix training data before cars meet the road.
arxiv-2505-18159:
Jesus Alvarez and a team of co-authors bring language technology to Comanche, an endangered Uto-Aztecan language. Their twenty twenty-five paper calls this the first computational study of Comanche, a language near extinction. Without digital tools, such languages are shut out of research and revival work.

The team hand-built a set of four hundred twelve phrases and a pipeline to make more data. They tested two GPT-4o models on language identification. With no examples, the models did poorly on Comanche. With just five examples in the prompt, accuracy rose to near perfect. The moral is that small, community-led steps can put a language on the digital map.
arxiv-2505-18359:
Seda Dogan-Tusha and co-authors carried out the first thorough reading campaign in 2025 for outdoor Wi-Fi in the new 6 gigahertz band. In the United States, standard power Wi-Fi 6E may operate outdoors under a machine-run rate coordination system that protects incumbent users of the band. While low-power indoor use has spread freely for two years. How the two modes coexist around real buildings, and whether incumbents stay safe, was unmeasured until this study.

The testbed was a major university football stadium fitted with about nine hundred access points serving tens of thousands of seats, ringed by indoor deployments in nearby buildings. The team measured during and after games, inside and out. Among their headline findings: within roughly two months, Wi-Fi 6E already carried a substantial share of client links, evidence of rapid adoption that makes the sharing rules more than theoretical.
arxiv-2505-18459:
Viacheslav Tsaran and co-authors link nuclear reaction theory with nuclear structure in a 2025 paper on pion scattering from calcium. Pions hitting a nucleus bounce and rescatter, and charge can swap along the way. Modeling that well needs detailed maps of where protons and neutrons sit.

The team extend a multiple scattering framework with second order rescattering for nuclei with uneven proton and neutron counts. Densities come from advanced many body methods and modern nuclear forces. Second order effects proved sizable and were needed to match measured scattering patterns near a known resonance energy.
arxiv-2505-18759:
Ruichen Zhang and five co-authors build a benchmark for judging how the choice of teaching data shapes small reasoning models, in this 2025 paper. Big models can be distilled into small ones by training them on written chains of thought. Teams tweak that data by growing it, filtering it, or mixing sources, but no shared yardstick existed for comparing the tweaks.

Their benchmark, DC-CoT, tests data recipes across methods, teacher models, and student sizes. Teachers include several leading commercial systems, and students run at three and seven billion parameters. The tests check reasoning on familiar material, on unseen material, and across topics. The goal is a set of best practices so smaller models stay capable and cheap to run. Code is shared openly.
arxiv-2505-19459:
Kaichao Jiang and co-authors try to give one image model three talents at once: sharp labelling of images, toughness against attacks meant to fool it, and the power to make new images. Two existing kinds each miss part of the trio. Energy-based joint models label and generate well but break easily under attack. Models hardened by attack training resist well yet lose accuracy and cannot generate.

The team compares how each kind scores clean, attacked, and made-up samples on an energy scale. Each kind closes a different gap on that scale, which hints that lining up all three sample types could close the whole triangle. Their method, EB-JDAT, trains with an energy objective that pulls the three groups together. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet subsets it reached top toughness while keeping near-original accuracy and image quality rivalling the generative models.
arxiv-2505-20259:
Haoyu Wang and six co-authors propose lifelong safety training for chatbots in a 2025 paper. Jailbreak attacks keep evolving to slip past a model's guardrails. Defenses trained on known attacks fail on fresh ones. The team builds a sparring system that invents new attacks forever.

One component, a meta attacker, learns to craft novel jailbreaks. It warms up by mining insights from a pile of jailbreak papers via a top commercial model. A defender model trains against the attacker's latest tricks each round. Early rounds saw the attacker win often, even across models. After repeated rounds, its success fell to single digits. The authors release their code for the safety community.
arxiv-2505-20759:
Ansel Blume and nine co-authors built Partonomy, a test set that checks if large image and text models can find the parts of things at pixel level. Real things are made of distinct parts, and fine thought needs those parts named right. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The set holds hundreds of part labels and object labels, drawn from past part sets and a new hand marked set. Tests use niche terms, ask models to compare parts across things, weigh part and whole links, and back text claims with drawn masks. Top models scored very low, the authors found. They also flag two design flaws in models that draw masks, which Partonomy helps expose.
arxiv-2505-20859:
David Ceddia and co-authors test classic training models with math optimization in a 2025 sports science paper. Coaches use tapering and periodized plans, easing load before a big race. Two famous models, from Banister in 1975 and Busso in 2003, turn training impulses into predicted performance. The team solved for the training plan each model calls best.

Under the Banister model the proof is stark: the best plan is always maximal training, then total rest before the target date. No gentle taper or cycle appears. That clashes with both lab evidence and coaching practice. The authors read the gap as a model flaw, not a coaching error. They propose nonlinear tweaks to the model's dose response that let true tapering emerge.
arxiv-2505-20959:
Bertram Højer, Terne Jakobsen, Anna Rogers, and Stefan Heinrich survey researchers on what intelligence means. The word frames much language tech work, yet its sense stays vague. Their survey drew full replies from 303 researchers across five fields. Fields spanned language tech, machine learning, mind science, linguistics, and brain science.

Three marks of intelligence won broad assent: generalization, adaptability, and reasoning. Only twenty-nine percent called current language systems intelligent, a minority view. A still smaller share, about sixteen percent, named building intelligent systems as a goal. Those who did hold that goal were more apt to call current systems intelligent. The authors map a field split on its core term.
arxiv-2505-21159:
Matheus Brito and Adriano Moura study special building blocks in the representation theory of quantum loop algebras. Their paper from twenty twenty-five deals with modules, structured spaces on which the algebra acts. Some modules are called imaginary, and cluster algebra tools miss them. The authors widen a frame built with Chari to find more of them.

Their work starts from tensor products of snake modules. The first main result describes the socle, the simple base layer, of such products when the snakes form a covering pair. A broader covering link yields a chain of nested submodules. The authors guess that each step's quotient is simple and imaginary, save the socle. They prove the first quotient is simple, and imaginary under a mild extra term. New classes of imaginary modules result.
arxiv-2505-22759:
