Nine researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five presenting an open speech model for English and Italian. Famous speech systems are closed: their training data and code are secret, which blocks checking and fair comparison. Open-science models lag behind in speech, unlike in other fields.

Their model family, FAMA, was trained on over one hundred fifty thousand hours of openly licensed speech. The team also released a cleaned, labeled set of sixteen thousand hours for both languages. FAMA matches existing systems on quality while running up to eight times faster. Code, data, and models are all openly released.
arxiv-2505-23559:
Kunlun Zhu and eight co-authors bring in SafeScientist, a frame to make AI research bots more safe and more fair in their work. Language model bots now do parts of search work on their own, but they can take on high risk or wrong tasks. SafeScientist is built to say no to such tasks. It stresses care through the whole search path.

Its shields are checks on prompts, checks on work with peers, checks on tool use, and a part that checks if acts are right or wrong. The team also built SciSafetyBench. It holds 240 high risk tasks in six fields, plus tasks on risks of tool use. Tests show a gain in safe acts of thirty-five per cent next to old frames. Scores for work did not drop. The team also tests how well it stands up to tricks aimed at its shields.
arxiv-2505-24059:
Sean Foley, Hong Nguyen, and colleagues separate the contributions of mouth movement and sound in recognizing phonemes in a 2025 speech science study. Real-time magnetic resonance imaging films the vocal tract while a person speaks, giving audio and articulation together. Earlier multimodal work pooled many speakers, and the large differences between speakers' anatomy drowned the fine link between movement and sound.

Single-speaker depth lets the authors train separate audio-only and video-only models and compare them cleanly. Knowing which channel carries which phoneme distinctions guides hearing technology and speech therapy tools that teach articulation.
arxiv-2506-00459:
Elinor Ginzburg, Itay Segev, Yoash Levron, and Sarah Keren compared classic and learning-based control of energy storage in twenty twenty-five. Batteries and other storage units need a policy that says when to charge and when to discharge. Classic methods compute the best policy for a set case, while reinforcement learning trains a general policy from trial and error.

Their test bed is a simple micro-grid with a load, a solar panel source, and one storage unit. Three cases grow harder in turn: perfect storage, storage with losses, and storage with losses on the lines too. The authors spell out each case and its math hurdles, then compare both methods head to head. They map where each method wins and suggest open questions for careful use of learning in power systems.
arxiv-2506-01459:
Prem Kumar led a team testing how measurement errors warp orbit reconstructions in a 2025 paper. Several galaxies host thin, coherent planes of satellite galaxies, structures the standard cosmology model finds improbable. Judging whether such planes last needs accurate motions and distances, which are poorly known. The team simulated satellite systems, added mock observing errors, and ran the orbits backward.

Errors in sideways motion made a truly stable plane look wider in the past, with width growing in step with the error size. Even the systematic errors of a current space observatory had strong effects. Wrong distance and a too-light host halo also distorted the picture. The authors warn that apparent instability may be an artifact.
arxiv-2506-01659:
Daniel Szelogowski published this theory paper in 2025 on how memories are stored and recalled. The engram idea holds that each memory lives in a small set of neurons changed in lasting ways by experience. Evidence for engrams has grown, yet no single model ties the biology to computation. This paper gathers findings from cell neuroscience and from computing to close that gap.

It asks three questions. How are engram neurons found and manipulated, how do synaptic changes keep memory traces stable, and why does sparse activity help memory stay sharp? The paper reviews computing tools that mirror these ideas, including sparse coding and spiking networks. Its claim is that memory works well because plasticity and sparsity act together. The synthesis ends with a roadmap for future work, including better diagnosis and treatment of memory disorders.
arxiv-2506-04059:
Mir Faizal and Arshid Shabir present, in a 2025 string theory paper, a new way to build a universe like ours, with positive vacuum energy, inside heterotic string theory. Such states, called de Sitter vacua, are hard to get in a controlled way from string theory. Their build rests on three parts of the theory working together.

First, a flux in the setup yields a special algebra for phase-space brackets. Second, a wider form of that algebra keeps the gauge structure sound. Third, a small correction to the action adds strictly positive energy and lifts the whole setup. The result is a stable state with positive energy, helped by a standard hidden-sector effect.
arxiv-2506-05059:
Shijian Xu, Marcello Massimo Negri, and Volker Roth wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It introduces NIMO, a model that keeps the clear, readable feature effects of simple linear regression while borrowing the flexibility of neural networks.

Plain linear models show exactly how each input moves the answer, but they often predict worse than black-box networks. Methods that explain a network after the fact can mislead and wobble with settings. NIMO instead builds interpretation in from the start. Its training scheme solves for the network parts and the linear weights together, by eliminating one set of variables, and a self-tuning penalty keeps the model sparse. In tests, NIMO's feature effects stayed faithful and readable while scores matched strong rivals. The authors pitch it for fields that must justify each prediction.
arxiv-2506-05359:
Qiangqiang Liu, Qian Huang, Frank Fan, Haishan Wu, and Xueyan Tang wrote a 2025 paper on hidden risks in meme token markets. The catalog creator field adds rank numbers to their names, but the head gives them plainly. Meme tokens are joke-born crypto coins that trade wildly and can be rigged by small groups acting through many wallets.

Their method links wallets that likely belong to one owner. It combines money flows, alike behavior, and odd trades to spot those links. With the links known, they build risk scores for how thin or fake a token's liquidity is. Tests on three named tokens showed real liquidity was far weaker than it looked. The work gives traders and regulators a way to see through the show.
arxiv-2506-05459:
Raphael E Hviding and co-authors present a spectroscopic census of little red dots, a puzzling class of early galaxies. Their 2025 paper draws on a large survey with a space telescope. These compact red objects were found in images, but photos alone could not show what they are.

The team analyzed spectra for a large galaxy sample at early cosmic times. They found dozens of sources with broad emission lines, a sign of fast gas near a black hole or dense core. A sub-group with a V-shaped spectrum and a point-like core forms the largest confirmed sample of these dots so far. All such V-shaped point sources showed broad lines, a striking pattern. The census gives theorists a firmer base for explaining these objects.
arxiv-2506-05559:
David Gribble, Christian Iliadis, Robert Janssens, and a team refine a nuclear reaction rate that counts for stars, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The reaction is silicon-thirty taking a proton and giving off a gamma ray to make phosphorus-thirty-one, helping set elemental abundances in stellar settings. Its rate rests on phosphorus-thirty-one energy levels near the proton threshold. The team probed those levels with nuclear resonance fluorescence.

They set excitation energies and spin-parities for a set of states, two of them resonances at low energies not seen before. Angular correlation work gave the first orbital angular momentum calls for those states. The new rate is much lower than calls below two hundred million kelvin, shifting calls of silicon isotope abundances in models of globular clusters and other astrophysical sites. The work also shows off resonance fluorescence as a tool for such reaction studies.
arxiv-2506-05959:
Jeong Bae and Jae-Hoon Kwon write a pure math paper from two thousand twenty-five on a deformed form of Howe duality. Duality here links the actions of two linked math structures on one shared space. Their version uses a deformed number system and deals with superalgebras that mix two symmetry types.

The authors define both actions in full and show they do not clash with each other. They then break the shared space into simple parts. When the deformation is removed, the old known duality comes back. Special cases cover the classic pairs tied to symmetric and exterior forms.
arxiv-2506-06159:
Parham Dehghani, Mariana Frank, and Benjamin Fuks published this particle physics paper in 2025. It asks how well future muon colliders could find superheavy Majorana neutrinos, a proposed kind of particle that is its own antiparticle. The team studies machines where muons collide head-on or where two beams of like-charged muons meet, at energies from 1 to 10 TeV, plus a proposed 2 TeV facility.

At such energies, the main way to make these heavy neutrinos is through vector boson fusion, where force-carrying particles from each beam merge. The authors test both simple selection cuts and trained decision trees that exploit the odd patterns these events leave. They find mixing angles as small as 0.001 could be probed for masses up to 100 TeV. That region lies far beyond what current machines can reach.
arxiv-2506-06959:
Alena Makarova and Houssam Abbas teach reinforcement learning agents to follow duties while they pursue a goal. Their twenty twenty-five paper models choices as a Markov decision process, the standard frame for decisions under chance. The agent maximizes a utility, its mission, like reaching a target fast.

On top of that sits a constraint written in deontic logic, the logic of duty and prohibition. It bans classes of behavior, on ethical or social grounds. The team uses a probabilistic logic of action and gives a policy improvement method that climbs to a constrained local best of the mission. Tests on sample problems show the agent can serve both masters at once.
arxiv-2506-07459:
Wang and co-authors let a protein-design model improve itself through online trial and reward, in this 2025 paper. Design models trained on fixed data often miss real goals like stability. Checking designs with physics is too slow to steer learning live.

Their system, ProteinZero, scores its own output with a fast structure predictor plus a self-taught stability estimator. A diversity guard at the embedding level stops the model from collapsing onto a few safe sequences. On a standard benchmark it beat three leading design tools, cutting failure rates by roughly forty percent and pushing success above ninety percent.
arxiv-2506-08359:
Li-Ming Zhan and four co-authors present a framework in two thousand twenty-five for steering large language models from the inside. Steering at inference time changes a model's answers without retraining it. The hard part is finding which internal modules drive the target behavior.

Their framework, REAL, trains a small autoencoder on each attention head or layer's activity. A shared codebook splits that activity into behavior-relevant and irrelevant parts. A classification score then rates how well each module separates aligned from violating responses, guiding both module choice and steering strength. Across eight models and nine data sets, REAL beat a leading steering method by about twenty percent on average. Its chosen modules also transferred to new domains.
arxiv-2506-08459:
Juanran Wang, Marc Schlichting, Harrison Delecki, and Mykel Kochenderfer train a diffusion model to imagine the ways a self-driving car can fail. Testing on real roads is dangerous and expensive, and failures are rare and varied. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team conditions the generator on any starting traffic state. It then produces plausible failure scenarios for the vehicle under test. Experiments center on a four-way intersection, a classic conflict zone. The generated samples looked realistic while covering a wide spread of failure types.

No external training data set is required. Training and inference run on modest hardware. The method assumes nothing about the driving system's internals, so it can audit black-box stacks. The authors pitch it as a general safety validation tool for intersections and beyond.
arxiv-2506-08559:
Sen and Yuce study loss that piles up at a system's edges in a 2025 paper. In certain non-Hermitian lattices, particles leak away mostly at the boundaries, an effect called the edge burst, and it was tied to the skin effect, where states crowd to one side. Their test system is a lossy lattice whose skin effect points both ways at once.

By weakly coupling two such lattices, they produce a scale-free form of localization that grows with system size rather than sitting at a fixed depth. Maps of where decay happens, and how they shift with the settings, confirm the edge burst still occurs. The message: the skin effect is not required for the burst, widening where engineers might find or use it.
arxiv-2506-08959:
Arnaudo, Bonelli, and Tanzini compute in 2025 one loop corrections to the heat physics of near extremal rotating black holes in de Sitter type spaces. Their route runs through connection coefficients of the Heun equation, which governs black hole perturbations in the standard formalism. Euclidean path integrals supply the thermodynamic frame.

Unlike near extremal limits lead to unlike physics, since distinct limiting equations describe them. Light modes in each limit set how one loop terms scale with temperature. The cold case shows universal log temperature corrections to entropy, even in the ultracold regime. Those terms vanish when the event and cosmic horizons merge. One check matches a known formula for a simpler case.
arxiv-2506-09059:
The CRESST Collaboration, with Angloher and co-authors, reported a study from 2025 on a new way to set the energy scale of dark matter detectors. Such detectors sit deep in cold and watch for tiny kicks when a particle strikes a crystal core. Their gauges must be trusted at very low energy, near a few hundred units. A known method gives kicks of one set size in that range.

The team fired neutrons at a crystal of aluminum oxide and saw a sharp peak at a set energy. They trace the peak to neutrons caught by aluminum atoms, which then shed the extra energy as a single ray. Computer models of the setup matched the result. The team asks whether wear to the crystal from the hits could shift the peak. If the peak is steady, it could serve as a built-in ruler for this kind of detector.
arxiv-2506-09359:
Qingyun Zeng, Simin Ma, Arash Niknafs, Ashish Basran, and Carol Szabo use language models to judge whether two SQL queries mean the same thing. Their paper from twenty twenty-five serves text-to-SQL systems, which turn plain questions into database code. Grading their output is tricky: user asks are vague, and many queries can be equally valid. String match alone misjudges such cases.

The authors test model judges on two bars: strict semantic sameness, and a looser weak form fit for practice. Common patterns of sameness and difference in SQL are cataloged. Where model judges stumble gets close study. The work is a methods probe rather than a new system launch. It maps how far LLM grading can be trusted for database tasks, and where human checks must stay.
arxiv-2506-10659:
Amnon Leviatan and Nahum Gavrielov give a geometric reading of a model for nuclei that mix boson and fermion parts, in a paper from 2025. The model is algebraic, built from symmetry rules, and it allows several shapes to mix in one nucleus. A picture in geometric terms can make that mixing easier to grasp.

Their frame rests on matrix coherent states extended to the mixed Bose-Fermi setting. They apply it to odd-mass niobium nuclei, where shape changes and shape coexistence intertwine. The picture clarifies how the nucleus can sit near a tipping point between shapes while holding two shapes at once. The authors offer the frame as a tool for reading other mixed nuclei.
arxiv-2506-11459:
Rahul Mistry and Ramesh Sreekantan study when the Jacobian of a genus two curve carries real multiplication, in this 2025 mathematics paper. A Jacobian is a geometric object built from the curve, and real multiplication means it has extra symmetries given by a square root number system. Over a century ago Humbert settled two special cases of this question.

The curve family here has a simple equation with three free parameters. The authors use modern work by Birkenhake and Wilhelm, plus classical counting results from geometry, to answer the question in principle for every discriminant, not just Humbert's two. They also carry out the answer fully for a few more cases. The result turns a case by case curiosity into a general method.
arxiv-2506-11759:
Sebastian Deffner and Steve Campbell used nonlinearity as a resource in a 2025 quantum control paper. The Landau-Zener problem, a system swept through an avoided crossing, is a basic test of whether a quantum state can follow a changing landscape without jumping. Nonlinear versions arise in many real systems, yet they resist analysis because quantum theory is built on linear machinery, including the adiabatic theorem itself.

The authors define a generalized energy spectrum from the stationary states of the nonlinear model. They then show the nonlinear term acts like a built-in shortcut, suppressing the jumps and coherences the linear sweep would suffer. Turning a complication into a control knob is the paper's appeal for quantum device design.
arxiv-2506-12659:
Chihiro Nakajima wrote this 2025 paper on a fast test for when an origami crease pattern cannot fold flat. Deciding flat foldability in general is a known hard problem. Even patterns that pass every local angle check at their corners may still fail as a whole, because sheets would have to pass through each other.

Nakajima turns the pattern into a graph that records which folded pieces would overlap. Each cycle in the graph is sorted by the kinds of nodes along it. A parity rule on those cycles then proves some patterns impossible to fold flat. The test runs in polynomial time, giving a quick screen before harder methods are tried.
arxiv-2506-12959:
Kenneth Odoh presents a book on distributed computing, the craft of making many machines act as one system, in this 2025 text. The work addresses a wide readership, from new engineers to seasoned researchers and working professionals. Its stated aim is to open up the core ideas of the field to readers of any background.

Rather than stop at theory, the book implements several foundational algorithms of the field in full. Readers can follow how a typical distributed system works under the hood, step by step. Odoh frames the book as a teaching guide for both the principles and the practice of distributed systems. It suits readers who learn best by seeing complete, working constructions rather than sketches.
arxiv-2506-13759:
Runpeng Yu, Qi Li, and Xinchao Wang survey discrete diffusion models for language and multimodal generation. Their paper from twenty twenty-five contrasts these models with the autoregressive standard. Diffusion models build many tokens at once by denoising, with full attention across the sequence. That style buys parallel speed, fine output control, and flexible perception. Word-by-word models struggle to match those traits.

Industry and open models in this family now rival their autoregressive kin. Speed gains can run large in the team's telling. The survey traces the family's history and lays out its math. Model classes, training and inference tricks, and quantization are sorted. Trust issues get a section of their own. Uses span language, vision-language, and biology. A linked paper list is kept for the field.
arxiv-2506-15859:
Petrov, Ploetz, and Schartner assess in 2025 how well radio telescope networks pin down the tilt and spin of the Earth. Several networks ran at the same time in split programs, which let the team compare their results head to head. The spread between matching runs serves as a fair gauge of true error.

Standard error bars, they find, give a poor guide to real error. Fancy plans for short sessions brought no clear gain, which points to air delay above the sites as a hard limit. Errors grew in summer and shrank in winter, and that yearly swing far outweighed noise from the radio sources themselves.
arxiv-2506-16959:
Shu-Tong Guan and Jin An study a topological Josephson junction with mixed pairing types, in two thousand twenty-five. A Josephson junction joins two superconductors, and mixed s-wave and p-wave pairing can drive a topological phase change as their ratio shifts. Bound states inside the junction can sit at exactly zero energy.

Two such zero-energy crossings appear at symmetric spots, and outside fields can move them. A magnetic field or unevenness can destroy or recreate them in pairs, giving a band-like pattern. Near the phase change, junctions ruled by the topological pairing show a strong diode effect, passing current one way far better than the other. Trivial junctions show a much weaker effect.
arxiv-2506-17259:
Sebastian Barros argues that phone and internet carriers should build one shared AI operating system rather than a pile of separate tools, in a 2025 paper. Carriers run sprawling operations, from customer care to network control, and each corner has bought its own AI. The pieces do not talk to each other, and vendor platforms lock carriers in. Barros proposes a horizontal layer that any operator can run agents on.

The system would keep data where it legally belongs, let operators train models together without pooling raw records, and plug into the industry's existing support software. It must follow telecom standards for networks and management, he writes. He also wants the platform governed by a neutral body so no single vendor controls it. The goal is ecosystem-wide intelligence instead of silos.
arxiv-2506-17759:
Fadi Abdeladhim Zidi, Djamel Eddine Boukhari, and colleagues present a lightweight transformer for classifying hyperspectral images in a 2025 study. Each pixel in such an image carries hundreds of spectral bands, many of them redundant. Labeled examples are scarce, and large transformer models adapt poorly under that limit.

Their design uses local attention, an efficient feed-forward block, and low-rank adaptation to cut trainable size. The architecture targets spectral and spatial patterns together while staying small. That balance matters for remote sensing, where new scenes arrive with few labels and modest hardware must still deliver useful maps.
arxiv-2506-18359:
Juanita Gomez and co-authors present a 2025 paper on finding all the open source software a university system produces. Academic coding is scattered across personal accounts and labs, so institutions cannot see their own footprint. The authors built a pipeline that sweeps GitHub, pulls project metadata, and guesses each project's home institution and type.

Across ten universities the pipeline found over 200,000 repositories. It also scored how each project handles licensing, documentation, and community care. Many strong tools stay invisible because they skip those basic practices. The framework turns the harvest into action items for open source program offices. It can track whether support programs actually raise the quality and lifespan of campus software.
arxiv-2506-18659:
Tomonori Ikeda and three co-authors warn gamma-ray astronomers in twenty twenty-five. Compton cameras use the angular resolution measure, ARM, to state angular uncertainty. Event selections are often built on ARM values. But the ARM distribution is not the point spread function, which is the camera's true imaging response.

Treating ARM resolution as if it were PSF resolution skews results. Simulations of gamma rays showed the mismatch plainly. An ARM-based selection with a stated resolution matched the background rejection of a far worse PSF resolution. Signal-to-noise ratios are then badly overestimated. Readers who build or use Compton cameras get a systematic bias named and measured, with imaging consequences spelled out.
arxiv-2506-19359:
Bhaumik and three co-authors fix broken game levels with search. Their 2025 paper tackles levels that look right but cannot be played. A fix may mean making spots reachable or the goal reachable at all. The repair should also change as little as it can.

The team tests evolution-based search, plus methods that keep varied fixes. Their test levels come from a learning-based generator that makes stylish but often broken stages. The search then patches them into working shape. Results were strong across the trials. Pairing a maker with a fixer, the authors argue, is a strong path for game building tools.
arxiv-2506-19959:
Jordan Cioni and Fabio Semperlotti present a 2025 quantum method to work out slopes and areas from a series of sampled values. Such calculus from data, not from a closed formula, sits at the core of much science computing. Past quantum methods took a formula as input, yet real field data most often comes as samples.

Their method uses a spectral tack built on the quantum Fourier transform, a fast quantum tool. Superposition lets it score all points of the domain at once, in parallel. The slope method extends to gradients in more than one direction, and post steps recover the sign of each result. Outputs come as quantum states in direct scale to the true slope or area. Those states can feed later quantum steps in image work, data study, and learning.
arxiv-2506-20459:
Sebastián Donoso and colleagues settled an open problem in pure math in 2025, in a field that studies how systems change over time. The question asks when several number patterns, watched along the same moving system, settle into joint regular behavior. Two simpler checks, based on differences and products, seem like they should be enough to guarantee that behavior.

For a broad family of patterns that grow like polynomials, the team proves the hard direction: passing both checks does force joint regular behavior. They also show, to their own surprise, that the reverse can fail for some strange families. New tools on factor structures and joining results support the proof and may help elsewhere.
arxiv-2506-20659:
Agterberg and Vidal compared two ways to recover a low-rank matrix in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Sensors often record only linear mixtures of a matrix's entries, plus noise. One recovery method relaxes the problem into a convex one with a nuclear-norm penalty. The other factors the matrix directly and optimizes without convexity.

In a high-dimensional regime, the authors prove the two behave like simple thresholding rules. Every local minimum of the factored method mimics hard thresholding of a denoised matrix. The convex method instead mimics soft thresholding of the same target. Hard thresholding keeps more signal, so the nonconvex method wins on squared error across the board. The proof extends a Gaussian comparison theorem to matrix operators.
arxiv-2506-21459:
Mounzer and a large team use the ESPRESSO tool to read the air of the hot giant planet HD 189733 b as it crosses its star. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Star light that grazes the planet can show what gases sit high in its air. But the star's own bright and dark patches can bend those reads and fake or hide true signs.

Two full crossings were taped at very fine detail. Once star effects were cut out, the sodium sign was less deep but more blue-shifted than past reads had claimed. The team also found a faint lithium sign from the planet. They warn that past sodium reads of this system all need a fresh look.
arxiv-2506-21659:
Abhishek Banerjee, Csaba Csáki, Michael Geller, Zamir Heller-Algazi, and Ameen Ismail look at a candidate in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The dilaton is tied to broken scale invariance, which keeps its mass safe and makes it a draw as ultralight dark matter for tabletop tests. A catch sets it off from pseudo-Goldstone bosons: a non-derivative self-coupling that would swell its mass through radiation if naught kept the scale gap safe.

The team asks if supersymmetry can keep that gap safe against symmetry breaks. To do so calls for a way to keep the dilaton stable. The misalignment route can make the dark matter share, for a mass range. But gravity-mediated corrections can not be cut out: they shrink how the dilaton couples to matter, past any test's reach. The paper ends that it can be built, but is hard to build.
arxiv-2506-21959:
Umberto D'Alesio, Carlo Flore, and Marco Zaccheddu test a basic assumption of particle physics using pions born inside jets, in a 2025 paper. The Collins effect links a quark's spin to the sideways pattern of the hadrons it spawns. If the effect is truly universal, one measured function should describe it in every setting. The team took fresh values for that function from other experiments and carried them to proton-proton collisions.

Their estimates matched data from the STAR experiment at two energies across several momentum ranges. The agreement held within a simplified treatment that keeps sideways motion only in the fragmentation step. The authors read the match as support for both the universality of the Collins function and the factorization picture behind it. They also offer predictions that fold in single-spin data through a Bayesian update.
arxiv-2506-22159:
Ivica Turkalj and co-authors wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on quantum methods for tasks with more than one goal. Such tasks require trade-offs, not a single best score. The authors work with variational quantum algorithms, which mix quantum circuits with classic computer search.

First, they recast the tuning of the circuit as a task with more than one goal, so classic search tools can be used at once. That mix beat the single-goal form on test tasks. Second, they add measures of spread to the cost score, which lets users control how wide the set of trade-off answers is. Spread rose by up to forty percent.
arxiv-2506-22759:
Xing Wang, Xiangjin Xu, and Cheng Zhang characterize special sets on curved spaces in a 2025 paper. Logvinenko-Sereda sets are regions thick enough that a function's size there controls its size everywhere, a principle used in control and signal theory. Earlier work settled the geometry of such sets on the sphere and, for the square-integrable case, on closed manifolds.

The authors extend the characterization to all power ranges on compact manifolds, with or without boundary, and do the same for the companion notion of Carleson measures. For eigenfunctions they complete the picture on the standard sphere above a threshold power. Below it, they conjecture that a tube-like thickness condition decides the matter and offer partial evidence, advancing a standing open problem.
arxiv-2506-23759:
Zheng Fang and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a way for hospitals to train one surgical video model together without pooling their footage. The model outlines instruments in operation videos. Privacy rules block centralizing the data, so training must be federated. Surgery adds two twists: operating scenes differ widely between sites, yet the instruments look and move alike everywhere, and simulators can mint unlimited practice footage.

Their scheme splits the representation in two. Each site privately keeps the part that encodes its own background. The shared part, including motion across frames, trains globally. Text guidance helps the model adapt its channels to each site. At the server, synthetic simulator data supplies a common yardstick that pulls the merged model into line. The authors report stronger outlining than generic federated methods on surgical data.
arxiv-2506-24059:
Milan Jovanovic and Jinmin Wang prove a comparison result in geometry for spaces with cone-like rough points. Their paper from twenty twenty-five treats spin manifolds that carry layers of conical singularities. One layer of cones can itself bear smaller cones, and so on. The theorem compares scalar and mean curvature on such spaces.

The proof uses the Dirac operator, a tool from quantum-style math. The authors study the index theory of a twisted form of this operator. A two-case argument lets them finish without knowing the exact index. The same frame yields more results. One says flat domains of a plain type must be rigid. Another gives a positive mass theorem for near-flat spaces with layered cone points. The work extends smooth-space tools to a rough class.
arxiv-2507-00059:
Naik uses computer search to test a graph path conjecture for small cases and to build paths for larger ones, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The conjecture gives a neat rule for when a path can use a prescribed multiset of edge lengths. Past checks covered all primes up to twenty-three. Naik extends the check with a Python program.

The program lists length patterns and searches with backtracking. It verifies all patterns for values below thirty-two. Some single cases took many hours on modest hardware. Two growing strategies build paths step by step up to forty. One raises the count of a length in use. The other adds a new length. Results give strong support for the conjecture in the tested range.
arxiv-2507-01059:
Xiangbo Gao and colleagues argued in 2025 that self-driving cars cooperating with each other should talk in plain language. Fleets of automated vehicles could improve safety and traffic flow by sharing perception and decisions. Existing communication channels send raw sensor data, neural features, or finished perception results. Each has flaws: too much bandwidth, incomplete information, or poor compatibility between different manufacturers' systems. Decision-level reasoning is usually not shared at all.

Natural language, the authors contend, hits a practical balance. It packs dense meaning into few bytes, adapts to changing conditions, and any agent can interpret it. Vehicles could exchange intent and reasoning, not just observations: I am yielding because a cyclist is hidden behind the truck. Language would not replace sensor sharing everywhere, but the paper makes the case it belongs in the protocol stack.
arxiv-2507-01259:
Michał Matak and Jarosław Chudziak build a legal assistant that answers from the Polish Civil Code. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents GAIus. Big language models often bluff on law, above all outside English. Their agent must ground each answer in retrieved clauses and cite them properly.

Their search method beats embedding-based rivals and reads clearly to humans. Test questions come from real entrance exams for Polish law apprentices. A mid-tier model leapt in score once grounded by the system. A stronger small model rose from about a third correct to near nine in ten. The design shows retrieval craft matters more than raw model size here.
arxiv-2507-01659:
Govert Nijs and Wilke van der Schee estimate a subtle risk in planned light-ion runs at the Large Hadron Collider in a 2025 paper. In July 2025 the machine was set to collide oxygen and neon nuclei to study how matter behaves in such small, hot systems. Many lighter isotopes share the exact charge-to-mass ratio of the beam ions, so they could be made in flight and quietly mix into the beam.

Using a collision framework joined with a decay code, the authors estimate how much of that contamination to expect and what it would do to the data. They also note a possible bonus: mixed collisions between oxygen and helium could give a measurement worth having in its own right.
arxiv-2507-03359:
Handing out goods by a shared eating rule, where everyone consumes favorites at a steady pace, is a classic fair mechanism, yet under real-valued tastes it can waste value. Jugal Garg and co-authors settle how much in a 2025 paper. The loss against the best possible split is at most a logarithmic factor, and they prove that factor cannot be improved.

The proof runs through a welfare measure that the eating rule approximates far better than it approximates total happiness. The results extend to a broader class of valuations. A fast algorithm in the paper also delivers envy-free splits with a small constant loss, closing a standing question.
arxiv-2507-04059:
Chenyang Ren, Yifan Jia, Huanyi Xie, and a wider team wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It develops ways to judge which training examples help or harm a model trained with sharpness-aware minimization, a method that seeks flat, forgiving spots in the loss landscape.

Rating data matters when labels are noisy or privacy is tight. Classic influence tools break under this training method, whose two-step structure doubles the computation and tangles how data steer the weights. The authors build two adapted influence measures. One uses only the finished model's curvature, in closed form. The other follows the path of gradients during training for a sharper, cheaper read. Tests showed both can spot mislabeled data, guide model edits, and tune settings. The work brings data bookkeeping to a popular training style.
arxiv-2507-04159:
Dykman and Pollanen study single electrons floating on liquid helium as building blocks for quantum machines, in a 2025 physics paper. An electron held above helium stays clean of the defects that trouble solid materials. Trapped in a tiny electric well called a quantum dot, the electron's energy levels become separate steps. Its two lowest steps can serve as the states of a quantum bit, or qubit.

The catch is the helium surface itself, which ripples with tiny waves. The authors show the electron couples to those ripples strongly, and that link narrows where such qubits can work. They compare the setup to color centers, flaw sites in crystals that trap electrons, except here the coupling can be tuned from weak to strong. That tuning opens a fresh way to study color center behaviour in the lab.
arxiv-2507-04259:
Saeed Jamshidiha and four co-authors train an AI that spots Alzheimer disease from images of the back wall of the eye. The eye is a clear pane to the small vessels and nerves of the brain, so its images may hold early marks of the disease. Their 2025 model, Retformer, uses a web that weighs all parts of an image at once. It trains on images of many kinds from patients and healthy peers of like age.

The model beat a set of known rivals on score after score, by up to about 11 points. A heat map tool then shows which zones of an image drove each call. Those zones were set next to marks that clinics have named in past work. The team reads the match as a sign the model keys on true marks, not noise. Clear sight into its calls is the pitch for clinic trust.
arxiv-2507-04859:
Siddharth Gavhale compares two monthly timing plans for index investing in India in a paper from 2025. Many Indians invest a fixed sum each month through a systematic plan. Most invest on the first trading day, but futures contracts expire on a set day each month, which may move prices. Gavhale tests investing on expiry day instead, using twenty-two years of Nifty 50 data.

Expiry-day plans beat first-day plans by a small margin over one to five years. The edge faded over ten to twenty years, where steady participation mattered more. The study also challenges a popular claim of twelve percent yearly returns. It finds the twenty-year yearly gain closer to seven percent before tax.
arxiv-2507-05159:
Soumyadeep Chaudhuri computes scalar determinants on curved disks with Neumann edge rules in two thousand twenty-five. A determinant here is a single number that sums how a wave field behaves across the whole disk. The disks are round, of fixed size, with flat, sphere-like, or saddle-like bend.

Working in the zeta-function scheme, he finds endless series for the log of the determinant at any mass. The route links the Neumann case to the known Dirichlet case through a map on the rim. An appendix checks the series by a second path. On bent disks, the series collapse to exact closed forms at special mass values. The work extends a past study of the Dirichlet case by the same scheme.
arxiv-2507-05359:
Maryum Sayeed and co-authors test whether having a companion star explains why some red giants hold too much lithium. Their 2025 paper starts from a puzzle: a star's first deep mixing should drain surface lithium, yet about one in a hundred red giants is rich in it.

The team matched survey data on lithium-rich giants with a code that evolves millions of binary star systems. The best match was mass transfer from a medium-mass aging star to a normal star, which later became the rich giant. That path explains mild cases but not the most enriched giants. Models of the donor stars showed which masses hold the most lithium to give away. The work narrows the hunt for the true origin of these odd stars.
arxiv-2507-05459:
Christian Bär and Rudolf Zeidler wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on Llarull's theorem, a famous result about curved spaces and the maps between them. The theorem says a space with a set floor on its scalar curvature must match the sphere it maps to exactly. That holds when the map wraps around the sphere a counted number of times. That wrapping count, the degree, is the key condition of the theorem.

The pair asks whether that condition can be weakened. Is it enough that the map simply reaches every point of the sphere? In dimensions of three or more, they show the answer is no. In dimension two, the answer is yes. They then replace the scalar curvature with its stricter relative, Ricci curvature. With that replacement, the weakened form holds in every dimension. The work probes where the teeth of the famous theorem truly sit.
arxiv-2507-05959:
Roberto Castorrini and Kasun Fernando prove limit theorems in a 2025 mathematics paper. Their setting is a class of maps on a two-dimensional torus, a surface shaped like a doughnut. The maps are partly hyperbolic, which means they stretch in some directions and shrink in others. The authors ask how sums of measured values behave over many steps.

They prove a central limit theorem, a Berry-Esseen bound, and a local limit theorem for these maps. The results hold even when the system has more than one steady statistical state. The class covered is broad and includes skew products and small changes to them. Such theorems help predict long-run averages in chaotic systems.
arxiv-2507-06059:
Kumar and co-authors, with the WEST Team, studied tungsten loss at a radio frequency antenna in the WEST tokamak in two thousand twenty-five. A tokamak holds hot plasma for fusion research. Strong electric fields near the antenna can knock tungsten atoms off its limiters, the parts that guard the wall.

The team used a new combined model that links plasma, sheath fields, sputtering, and impurity travel. The model found very high sheath voltages and strong wear at the upper limiter. Oxygen ions with high charge did most of the damage. Wear rose about thirty-fold when heating was on, close to what light measurements showed in the machine.
arxiv-2507-06459:
Riadul Islam and co-authors build an autoencoder for event cameras, sensors that report brightness changes pixel by pixel. Their 2025 paper targets high-speed vision for robots, vehicles, and factory automation. Frame cameras blur and lag in fast scenes, while event streams are sparse and noisy, which complicates detection.

Their model compresses event data and rebuilds it while keeping the spatial and timing features that matter. An adaptive threshold and a light classifier raise recognition accuracy at low cost. On a face data set, accuracy matched a popular detector while using far fewer parameters. On small embedded boards the system ran at usable frame rates, much faster than prior art. Compact event vision could put fast perception on cheap hardware.
arxiv-2507-06859:
Wang Chi Cheung and Zitian Li study online choices under tight resource budgets across episodes. Each episode starts with a fresh stock of resources, and the spread of requests shifts within an episode. A hidden conversion model, shared by all episodes, links each request and choice to a random outcome. Uses range from pricing goods that spoil to bids in repeated auctions.

Their algorithm keeps total regret growing slower than the count of episodes. It leans on an oracle that gives confidence bounds with like guarantees. The hard part is the endless range of request types, which blows up the state space. Extra unlabeled feature data can sharpen the bounds in some settings. The frame adds a fresh case to budget bandit theory.
arxiv-2507-07659:
Victor Dachet, Antoine Dubois, Bardhyl Miftari, Raphaël Fonteneau, and Damien Ernst bring order to a sprawling idea: build energy hubs where the renewables are, not where the people are. Sunshine in deserts and wind in far northern coasts outstrip anything near load centers. A remote renewable energy hub harvests that abundance and synthesizes energy molecules for export. Each hub design picks its own chain of technologies and its own way of fitting the local environment.

The design space has grown too diverse to navigate by anecdote. Their taxonomy characterizes hubs precisely, so designs can be described and compared on shared terms. Gaps in the taxonomy point to hub types nobody has designed yet. Policymakers and engineers get a common language for cost and local integration trade-offs. Classification here is a design tool, not bookkeeping.
arxiv-2507-07859:
Sagnik Jana and Yulan Qing prove a result about random paths on graphs in this two thousand twenty-five math paper. Take an endless graph and give each edge a random length. The shortest routes through this warped graph are called geodesics. An earlier result showed that, under certain shape conditions, a two-way endless geodesic exists. That result leaned on a notion called Morse geodesics, which stay stable under detours.

Jana and Qing loosen the shape demand. They only require a geodesic that is Morse in a sublinear sense, a weaker grip. With edges of bounded degree, positive lengths, and finite mean, they prove the endless geodesic still almost surely exists. The setting is called first passage percolation. The work extends the theory of random metrics on graphs.
arxiv-2507-09159:
Cong-Bang Trang and Hoang-Hung Vo present a 2025 math paper on how a sickness spreads in space and over age. Their model tracks people of different ages as the sickness moves from place to place. It uses a boundary rule where nothing flows out at the edge. A death rate in the model can grow very large, which makes the math hard.

The authors first show that the model has a time-based answer that makes sense. They then work out a threshold number that tells whether the sickness can take hold. When the number is below one, they show the sickness-free state holds and stays stable. The paper is formal theory, with proofs and links to past work. It suits readers who study spread models with age and space together.
arxiv-2507-09759:
Manaf and Mughal built a computer system in twenty twenty-five to spot pneumonia in young children's chest X-rays. Pneumonia kills more small children than almost any other illness, and reading the scans takes scarce expert time.

Their learning model trained on five thousand eight hundred sixty-three labeled scans of children up to age five from a hospital in Guangzhou, China. To stretch the limited data, they rotated and flipped images and used a second network to invent extra realistic scans, balancing the healthy and sick classes. The blend of real, altered, and invented images gave the best scores on accuracy and balance measures. The finished system runs inside a simple web app that returns a diagnosis with a confidence level. The authors aim it at clinics with few specialists, where a fast second opinion matters most.
arxiv-2507-09859:
Guntur Dharma Putra and Bagus Rakadyanto Oktavianto Putra design a blockchain identity system for the Internet of Things that lets trust spread by endorsement, in a 2025 paper. Connected devices need identities they can prove without a central office. Existing self-sovereign identity systems let only approved issuers, usually the device maker, hand out credentials. That bottleneck chokes fast-changing networks of devices.

In the proposed design, anyone with a verifiable chain of trust can issue credentials. Trust scores are computed from endorsements and kept alive through a hierarchy of trust links. The blockchain acts as the public registry, and smart contracts automate issuing, checking, and cancelling credentials. A working prototype showed the system is feasible with minimal overhead, the authors report. The goal is identity that scales with the swarm.
arxiv-2507-10359:
Bastien Laville and Théo Bertrand present a study from twenty twenty-five on tracking point sources that cross and tangle over time in a stack of frames. Grid free methods can follow such points, but tangled paths break them in theory and in practice. The pair lift the task into a higher space: the group of shifts and turns in the plane.

In that space, paths can be teased apart and rebuilt. A new penalty, based on a soft form of the Reeds-Shepp metric, caps how sharply each path may curve. They prove traits of the grid form and a limit result that backs its use. Tests on a place finding task match the best known grid free method.
arxiv-2507-10659:
Xiaojing Lin and a large team found nearby twins of a puzzling distant galaxy class in a 2025 paper. James Webb observations revealed little red dots in the early universe, compact red sources that defy standard black hole models. Mining a ground-based survey database, the team picked out three candidates at low redshift and confirmed them with follow-up spectroscopy and imaging across optical and near-infrared bands.

The local trio matches the distant dots on every checked trait: broad hydrogen and helium lines, compact shape, a V-shaped spectrum, fading near-infrared output, and steady brightness. Blue-shifted helium absorption appears in all three, alongside rich iron emission in two. Nearby examples let astronomers study the class with far sharper tools.
arxiv-2507-10859:
Ramaneswaran Selvakumar, Ashish Seth, and Nishit Anand brought in MultiVox in 2025, a benchmark for voice assistants that can also see. Modern omni models listen and look at once, but current tests barely check whether an assistant picks up the fine print of speech, pitch, emotion, timbre. And volume, or the sounds of the room, let alone whether it combines those cues with what it sees. MultiVox was built to close that gap.

The benchmark contains one thousand human-annotated, human-logged spoken dialogues spanning a wide range of paralinguistic traits and acoustic settings. Tasks need the assistant to align what is heard in the voice with complementary visual signals before answering. The authors present it as the first benchmark of its kind, giving builders a way to measure truly multimodal understanding rather than transcription plus captioning.
arxiv-2507-11759:
Lena Nehane Ezzine, Alexandra Volokhova, and co-authors present a computing paper from 2025 on drug shapes. A small molecule can twist into many shapes, and which shapes it favors affects how it binds a target. Older physics-based sampling of shapes is slow and costly.

The team's model learns to suggest shapes at rates that match the true physics odds. It works from the molecule graph plus fixed bond lengths and angles. It then samples twists of the bonds that can rotate. One trained model can handle many molecules at once. It can also cope with bond facts it never saw in training. The authors say the method could scale to larger systems in time.
arxiv-2507-12759:
Yunxiang Zhang and co-authors elicit long reasoning from language models without training in a 2025 paper. Large reasoning models think through long chains with backtracking and self correction. Some evidence suggests base models already hold those abilities latently, locked behind decoding choices rather than missing skill.

Their method, ThinkLogit, uses arithmetic on output scores to steer a large target model with a much smaller reasoning model as guide. Correct answers rose sharply across four math data sets. Training the guider with preference pairs improved results further, and skills learned by reinforcement could transfer through the same route.
arxiv-2507-12959:
Charlie Freeman and a team of co-authors switch tiny magnetic patterns in a layered magnet with laser pulses, in two thousand twenty-five. The magnet is a van der Waals material, a stack of weakly bound sheets. Its spin textures include round skyrmion bubbles and winding labyrinth patterns, both prized for memory ideas.

Working at room temperature, the team used laser heating and cooling to reach the bubble state at low fields. Pulses then toggled the material between the bubble and labyrinth textures. Computer models of the magnetism traced the switching to that heat and cool cycle. The authors highlight the result as a step toward laser-controlled, lasting memory storage.
arxiv-2507-13859:
Aleksandr Gashkov and co-authors study how well large language models turn plain questions into SPARQL queries, the language used to search knowledge graphs. Their paper appeared in 2025. A worry hangs over such tests: the models may have memorized the test data during training, which would inflate their scores. The team designed a way to measure that effect directly.

They ran models under three setups: no help, added knowledge from the graph, and added knowledge with names hidden. Hiding the names strips out what memorization could supply. Comparing the three scores shows how much of the success comes from memory and how much from real query skill. The authors say this check helps judge whether a question-answering method will travel to new graphs or only shines on familiar ones.
arxiv-2507-14059:
Tianyuan Wang and co-authors design a mobile robot that inspects and services hardware inside a planned orbital warehouse, in this 2025 paper. The STARFAB hub would store and reuse space parts in orbit. Something must check both the stored goods and the station itself.

Their module rides on walking manipulators through standard connectors, so several units can be parked and fetched as needed. It carries sharp cameras, a 3D surface scanner, and a heat camera, with room for more sensors. A gripper and torque wrench ride inside for repair jobs by an attached arm. The paper lays out operations plus the mechanical and electronic design.
arxiv-2507-14559:
Zixuan Hu and five co-authors pick the best pretrained vision model by watching its outputs evolve. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Pretrain-then-finetune practice has flooded the field with candidate models. Choosing well for a new task is costly trial and error. Transferability scores try to predict the winner cheaply. Older scores track features, not the fine-tuning goal itself.

Their method, LEAD, works in logit space, the model's raw output scores. It models fine-tuning as a nonlinear path toward a final state. An ordinary differential equation describes that path. The score derives from where the path leads, not from static features. That keeps the estimate aligned with the true objective. Vision teams can shortlist models with more confidence.
arxiv-2507-15759:
Deep research by chat model runs like a sealed pipe: ask, wait, take what comes. A team of twenty-six authors call that pipe a flaw in 2025 and name their fix Interaction as Intelligence. The catalog record is garbled here, giving an author's name as the title and a stray digit as the author; the head carries the true title and byline. Their claim is that the talk between human and model is not a wire to the smarts, but part of the smarts.

Their system lets a person watch the model's thought, halt it, and steer at the forks, while the model learns the person's habits on its own. In user tests the shared-oversight way beat the best sealed pipe on six counts, from openness to worth of the yield. The team frame oversight as the human's new desk in research work.
arxiv-2507-16259:
Yineng Sun, Armin Fügenschuh, and Vikrant Vaze present a 2025 arXiv paper on planning joint truck and drone deliveries with real flight physics. Drones save time and emissions but planning their flights inside truck routes is a hard puzzle. Plans that ignore flight physics can waste the drone's edge, so the team folds energy and motion equations into the planning itself.

Neural networks trained on solved flight problems estimate drone flight times inside a route-building heuristic. Tests on synthetic and real cases showed shorter tours and lower drone energy use than physics-blind benchmarks. The authors estimate the framework could save operators millions of dollars a year.
arxiv-2507-17159:
Hong-Suk Choi and co-authors identify hidden altermagnetism in a distorted perovskite magnet, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The compound, a sodium osmium oxide, orders antiferromagnetically yet insulates in an unusual in-between way. Calculations find it altermagnetic under all three typical spin orders.

A gap opens even without correlation terms, and a modest repulsion matches the measured gap. Weak magnetism comes from a spin-orbit driven canting of about three degrees, backed by the altermagnetic order. Spin-split bands reach about a hundred milli-electron-volts. Chiral magnon splitting and a doping-induced Hall effect round out the predictions.
arxiv-2507-17959:
Ali Abedi and co-authors release OPEN, a dataset for recognizing engagement of older adults in virtual rehab, in this 2025 paper. Engagement predicts satisfaction and adherence, but automated measures were built on young students. Older adults in telehealth settings lacked data entirely. Their data come from weekly group learning sessions in cardiac rehabilitation.

Eleven older adults took part over six weeks, giving more than 35 hours of recordings. Raw video stays private for safety. Released features cover face, hand, and body joint movements per frame. Session context and time course are preserved, since engagement drifts within a meeting. A baseline model shows the data can train recognizers. Telehealth programs could flag fading attention and intervene kindly.
arxiv-2507-18959:
Bishal Deb and Alan Sokal study two new families of number triangles that generalize the classic Stirling cycle and subset triangles. Each family is indexed by a positive integer order. The paper asks four total positivity questions about these arrays, covering the triangle itself, its row reversal, and generating polynomials.

Positivity questions of this kind connect to continued fractions and whether polynomials have only real roots. The authors state several conjectures arising from the four questions across both families. They then prove some of those conjectures for the second-order case. The work sits in enumerative combinatorics, where such triangles often encode counting sequences with hidden structure.
arxiv-2507-19159:
Steven Bramwell explained in twenty twenty-five a long-standing puzzle in how materials relax. Many systems respond to a push with a power-law tail whose exponent sits oddly below two, a pattern seen for decades without a settled cause. Bramwell studies the phonon bottleneck, a classic model where spins in a material can only shed energy through a limited channel of lattice vibrations.

When that channel is strongly choked, the vibrations settle into a near-steady state held up by slow spin relaxation. Bramwell computes the response to an applied field exactly in this setting. A spectral density with exponent three halves emerges, holding over a widening range of frequencies as the bottleneck tightens. He discusses which real systems might show this effect and compares it with other cases of anomalous relaxation.
arxiv-2507-19359:
Liu and co-authors build an avatar that gestures in line with what it says. Past systems made beat gestures that matched rhythm but not meaning. SemGes adds meaning at both the word level and the whole-speech level. It first learns a motion code with a vector-quantized autoencoder. A second stage then makes gestures from speech, text meaning, and speaker identity.

Two modules keep the gestures tied to the speech content. One checks local fit, and one checks broad sense across the clip. Tests and user studies beat prior methods on two benchmarks. Gains showed in both hard scores and viewer ratings. Code, data, and trained models are posted on the project site.
arxiv-2507-20359: Grigorii Konovalov, a solo author, proves a version of adelic descent for continuous localizing invariants in a 2025 math paper. The work builds on a known result about solid quasi-coherent sheaves on schemes of finite type over the integers. Those sheaves satisfy adelic descent, a gluing rule that rebuilds global data from local pieces at each prime. Konovalov extends that descent picture from sheaves to the stated class of invariants.
arxiv-2507-20659:
Akita, Hamaguchi, and Ovchynnikov map the full span for ghost-grain dark stuff. Ghost grains are spare grains that could fill the dark stuff role. Big trait gaps twixt grain kinds join the play in this work. Those gaps have net sum zero, so dawn bounds still hold. Grain flips wash the gaps out at MeV heat in the tale. The team builds a half-stock heat sum for the spare grains.

That sum is checked next to full quantum sums for faith. For spare masses up to 60 keV, the live mix span grows wide. It swells by up to two ranks of size in their runs. Broad test odds come with that span in next-wave hunts. X-ray, dawn, and growth probes may all catch the spare grains. A free code frame ships with the work for peer use.
arxiv-2507-20959:
Giovanna Citti, Mattia Galeotti, and Andrea Pinamonti prove two classic views of optimal transport agree in a curved, constrained geometry in a 2025 mathematics study. The Kantorovich view plans transport as a coupling between distributions, while the Benamou-Brenier view watches mass flow over time. On sub-Riemannian manifolds, where motion is allowed only in certain directions, their equivalence was not known in general.

With no boundary, completeness, and no abnormal shortest paths, the authors prove the two problems match for measures with finite second moments. They also prove a flowing minimizer exists and ties to the optimal plan.
arxiv-2507-21259:
Van Chung Nguyen and four co-authors bring advanced flight control onto tiny chips, in a 2025 paper. Model predictive control steers robots by constantly planning a few steps ahead. Its nonlinear form suits fast, agile machines but demands heavy computing, far beyond small microcontrollers.

Their system, NMPCM, generates lean code that runs the full nonlinear method on a small chip. The test craft is a quadrotor drone, a machine that punishes slow or sloppy control. Simulations in a standard robot testbed and real flights both confirm the method works at high update rates. The team released the code openly. Putting smart control on cheap chips could widen the use of agile drones outside big labs.
arxiv-2507-21459:
Galaxy clusters, the largest bound structures in the universe, announce themselves by the shadow they cast on the cosmic microwave background. A 2025 catalog paper from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope team lists the clusters found that way in the telescope's sixth data release.

The search swept more than sixteen thousand square degrees of sky at three microwave frequencies, using data gathered from 2008 to 2022. Clusters were picked out by the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, the distortion their hot gas imprints on the background glow. The catalog reports positions with redshift and mass estimates for each system. Three survey collaborations joined the effort, cross-checking the microwave finds against optical data. Such catalogs anchor studies of how structure and dark energy shape the cosmos.
arxiv-2507-22759:
Black holes deform under the tidal pull of their surroundings, and that response is captured by numbers called Love numbers. Yusmantoro, Freddy Permana Zen, and Hadyan Luthfan Prihadi compute the scalar-field version of that response in a 2025 paper. They study four kinds of black holes sitting in a universe with a negative cosmological constant. Still and spinning holes are tested with a neutral field, and charged holes with a charged one.

Unlike in flat space, the Love numbers never vanish here; the cosmological constant sees to that. Energy loss, by contrast, can vanish for certain field frequencies and hole settings. The authors map when each behavior occurs.
arxiv-2507-23159:
Guan-Ting Lin and co-authors release a benchmark for speech systems that talk and listen at once in a 2025 paper. Natural conversation includes interruptions and overlapping voices. Most dialogue software still takes strict turns, and overlap handling is rarely tested in a systematic way.

Their benchmark, now in version 1.5, simulates four overlap scenes. A user may interrupt, add a brief backchannel, talk to someone else, or speak over background voices. Scores cover response choices, stop and reply delays, and voice adaptation. Tests of five leading agents reveal two styles: quick responders and floor holders that filter overlaps. The open framework lets builders compare systems and improve overlap behavior.
arxiv-2508-02159:
Dongchi Huang and co-authors wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on safe reinforcement learning when the agent cannot see the whole world. Hidden dangers are hard to dodge, so agents often train with extra facts that real use will not give them.

The team first builds a formal frame for this setup, naming it an asymmetric constrained decision process. On that frame they build PIGDreamer, an agent that learns a world model and aligns its inner view with the extra training facts. A split actor-critic design keeps safety in view while it learns. Tests show the agent beats other safe learning methods on score and safety. It also held up better than other methods that use the same extra facts. The team has posted its code in public.
arxiv-2508-02859: Hannah Knight computes the essential two-dimension, at odd defining prime, for several families of linear groups. The computation covers the general linear groups and the projective general linear groups. It also covers the special linear groups when the dimension is odd or equals two. Quotients such as the projective special linear groups are included under stated conditions. Those conditions concern the field size and a trivial Galois group attached to roots of unity.
arxiv-2508-02959:
Chia-Tung Ho and five co-authors present Polymath, a self optimizing agent in two thousand twenty-five. Language models solve hard tasks through workflows of steps and rules. Hand built workflows scale poorly and waste skill. Code based auto methods lean on tagged data, which real tasks often lack.

Polymath shapes its workflow as a task flow graph in code. A multi grid style graph search tunes the shape. A self reflection guided evolutionary loop refines it further, with no tags needed. Tests span coding, math, and multi turn question tasks. Mean gains over the best past baselines were clear. The agent adapts its own plan as it works.
arxiv-2508-06259:
Zhangquan Chen and six co-authors teach a vision-language model to look where it matters, in a 2025 paper. Such models still fumble tasks needing fine spatial sense, like locating a small object or judging distances. People cope by shifting their gaze and zooming attention step by step.

Their framework interleaves depth-marked boxes with words, so the model reasons while visibly refocusing on prompt-relevant regions. A three-stage strategy first builds training chains of this mixed text and image thinking, yielding a fifty-thousand-example dataset. A reinforced training stage then rewards good focusing directly. Across spatial and fine-grained tests the method beat current leaders. The authors present looking as a skill to train, not a fixed input.
arxiv-2508-06759:
Farshad Kamalinejad and Zachary Slepian work out how the mass of neutrinos changes the math used to map the cosmos. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. They give a formula for the spread of matter and galaxies that adds these effects at one level of detail. A fast method speeds up the heavy sums the work needs.

The pair fit their model to a large set of simulated universes. The new math gave the same answers for the main cosmic values as the standard math. Only the values tied to galaxy bias, read from a three-point measure, shifted. Forecasts show that adding that three-point measure shrinks the error bars a lot. For neutrino mass, the doubt drops by about a fifth.
arxiv-2508-07959:
Changhao Song and co-authors wrote this survey, published in two thousand twenty-five, on how large language models handle subjective language. Such language carries feelings, opinions, and figures of speech rather than plain facts, and it is full of ambiguity and context traps.

The survey covers eight tasks: sentiment, emotion, sarcasm, humor, stance, metaphor, intent, and beauty judgment. For each, it lays out the task's terms, the main data sets, the best model-based methods, and what still fails. It also traces how model designs evolved in ways that help with subtle human judgment. Shared threads across the tasks suggest one unified model of subjectivity may be within reach. Open problems include thin data, bias, and ethics. The authors aim the survey at both affective computing and language model researchers.
arxiv-2508-08159:
Cem Ata Baykara, Mete Akgün, and three co-authors predict epileptic seizures across hospitals without moving patient data. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses federated learning on brain wave records. Privacy law and wide data variety block the usual pooled training. Four public data sets span adults, children, and newborns.

Local models fail badly when moved to a new site. Standard federated averaging skews toward the biggest data set. One site hit near ninety percent while others sat near chance. Their fix trains each site on a same-size random slice per round. That balances the merge and lifts weak sites a lot. One recording channel is all the models need.
arxiv-2508-08359:
Priyesh Chakraborty, Timothy Cohen, Daniel Green, and Yiwen Huang revisit positivity rules for de Sitter space, in a 2025 physics paper. De Sitter space models a universe that expands at a steady rate. Loop corrections there can make operator dimensions come out not real, unlike in its better-known cousin space. That oddity clouds the rules that correlators, the basic measures of the theory, must obey.

The paper compares two ways of computing: a spectral method and an effective theory built for soft physics. The focus falls on vertex operators for compact scalar fields, a case with fresh complications. The authors resolve clashes between the methods and give new proofs that certain dimension shifts stay positive. They also show the flow of those shifts matches a diagram sum in the rival method.
arxiv-2508-08559:
Alexandrine Fortier, Sonal Joshi, Thomas Thebaud, Jesus Villalba, Najim Dehak, and Patrick Cardinal test an attack on speaker recognition in a 2025 study. Backdoor attacks hide a trigger in training so a system behaves normally until the trigger appears. Earlier work of this kind usually aimed at one target speaker at a time.

Their attack uses short clicking sounds that do not depend on position, and it can aim at many speakers at once. The authors report high success rates and vary background noise to show a trade between stealth and strength. They also extend the idea to speaker verification using a similar sounding stand-in target.
arxiv-2508-09859:
Érico Goulart and Eduardo Bittencourt wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It recasts nonlinear electrodynamics, the study of very strong electromagnetic fields, in geometric terms, so the field's waves behave as if they travel through a curved space built by the field itself.

The key object is the principal symbol, which governs how small ripples in the field evolve. Assuming the field does not split light into two speeds, the authors show this symbol comes from an optical metric, a field-dependent geometry. Ripple evolution then takes the form of a covariant divergence on that curved background. That is the same shape as Maxwell's theory on curved spacetime, so the tools of quantum field theory in curved space can be borrowed. The authors note the reformulation could guide lab analogues built from tailored materials.
arxiv-2508-10759:
Katarzyna Dutkowska and co-authors build, in 2025, chemical templates for the Milky Way's Central Molecular Zone, the dense gas region around the galactic center. Conditions there are extreme: thick gas, high temperatures, and intense cosmic rays. Surveys keep finding rich chemistry, and reading it needs models tuned to those conditions.

Running a time-dependent gas-grain chemistry code over grids of shocks and young stellar objects, the team tracked twenty-four species, including complex organics. Shocked and protostellar gas evolved on different timescales, and three hundred kelvin emerged as a dividing temperature. Cosmic rays and temperature proved the main drivers of the chemical signatures.
arxiv-2508-11659:
Zhuo Liu and Tao Chen make a brain-like learning method practical by rebuilding the network it trains. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. The method, equilibrium propagation, learns in a way brains plausibly could, but past versions were unstable and slow.

Their network adds feedback control that reins in runaway signals, so training settles fast. That speed cuts computing cost by orders of magnitude. Residual shortcuts, arranged in brain-inspired patterns, stop signals from fading in deep networks. On standard benchmark tasks the method now matches backpropagation, the industry workhorse that brains cannot use. The authors say the design also guides learning built directly into physical hardware.
arxiv-2508-12459:
Alham Fikri Aji and Trevor Cohn introduce a benchmark for twenty Indonesian languages in this 2025 paper. Indonesia is one of the most populous nations, with about seven hundred languages spoken. Its local languages lag behind in language technology. Their suite, LoraxBench, covers six tasks, from reading and question answering to translation. It also tests causal reasoning and questions about culture. Three languages appear in two formality registers as well.

The team ran many multilingual and region-focused AI models on the suite. Scores lagged far behind those for standard Indonesian. That gap was worst for the lowest-resource languages. Region-specific models held no clear lead over general ones. Changing the formality register also shifted scores in real ways. The authors offer the suite as a yardstick for fairer language tools.
arxiv-2508-12759:
Ihara and co-authors probe a magnetic crystal under fields far beyond ordinary magnets in this 2025 physics paper. The material arranges copper atoms in square cupola shapes, and past 15 tesla its magnetic pattern flips through unusual states that also shift electric behavior. Superconducting magnets cannot reach the fields where later states live.

Using pulsed fields up to 32 tesla, the team recorded nuclear magnetic resonance spectra along one crystal direction. Above 29 tesla the spectrum split into two peaks, marking fresh transitions. Comparing shapes with cluster mean-field theory let them propose concrete magnetic structures for the high-field states. The work maps territory earlier instruments could not enter.
arxiv-2508-13759:
Max-Niklas Steffen and Christoph Schweigert characterize a major family of three-dimensional topological field theories through conditions on their boundaries. Their paper came out in 2025. Such theories assign algebraic data to shapes and underlie parts of quantum computing and condensed matter physics.

They formulate explicit boundary locality conditions for theories defined on spaces with boundary defects. Any theory satisfying those conditions, they prove, can be rebuilt by a state sum, a recipe that assembles the theory from local pieces. As a check, the known Turaev-Viro state sum models obey the conditions. So do the Dijkgraaf-Witten theories with defects, thanks to recent progress they build on. The result tells researchers exactly which theories admit a fully local construction.
arxiv-2508-13959:
Maryam Aliakbarpour and co-authors published a 2025 paper on learning the state of a quantum system when some readings have been tampered with. Quantum devices are fragile, and their measurement results can be wrong. Errors may come from sloppy human reading, or even from an attacker who alters results on purpose. The authors design methods that still work in that worst case.

They study a model where a foe can freely change a fixed share of the measurement outcomes. Each quantum copy is measured only once, matching what near-term devices can do. Their method learns an unknown state of low complexity to an error that grows in a set way with the tampered share. They also prove no method using such measurements can do better, so their result is the best possible. The same bounds hold for the simpler job of testing whether a state matches a known one.
arxiv-2508-14459:
Hidetaka Kuniyoshi, Shinsuke Imada, and Takaaki Yokoyama test swirls as solar heaters in a 2025 paper. Why the Sun's outer atmosphere is so hot remains a core puzzle. Small swirls crowd the visible surface and may ferry magnetic energy upward. Using a three-dimensional simulation running from the churning depths to the corona, they counted the swirls' share of the energy flow statistically.

Swirls carried about half of the total magnetic energy supply. The analysis also suggests swirls spark heating events by snapping magnetic fields together. Those events follow the same size pattern as observed nanoflare heating signatures, making swirls strong driver candidates.
arxiv-2508-14759:
Winter Allen, Anand Shanker, and Sanjay Rebello study student views of AI feedback in a 2025 paper. Physics students often chase final answers instead of principles. Writing scientific arguments can build deeper skill, but large classes make timely personal feedback hard. Their study gave students delayed AI feedback and scores on argument essays in an introductory physics course, then surveyed the students.

The survey asked how useful and how accurate students found the model's comments. The findings inform whether AI feedback can realistically support problem solving and self-monitoring in big classes. The authors frame the work as a viability check for real-time AI feedback in such settings.
arxiv-2508-15159:
Aditya Ramabadran and Johannes van Vliet present a 2025 math paper on spectral sets. A set is spectral when its square-integrable functions admit a basis of exponential waves.
