Products of spectral sets are known to be spectral. The reverse claim fails in general: a spectral product need not come from spectral parts. The authors settle the reverse claim for one special case.

The special factor is a set close to an interval, sitting inside a bounded range. Both factors have measure one. For such pairs, the product is spectral exactly when both parts are spectral. The proof gives a clean if-and-only-if result where the general case stays open. Harmonic analysts get a sharp boundary for a classic question. The result also shows how a near-interval shape restores order that wilder shapes can break.
arxiv-2508-15359:
Qian Huang and Christian Rohde build ranked equations for the statistics of a scalar conservation law with random starts. Their paper from twenty twenty-five takes a model problem with a known link to fluid theory. For the Navier-Stokes case, solution statistics obey a ranked chain of linear equations. The authors seek the same kind of chain for their scalar law.

Two frames are built. One tracks density functions at many points at once, which keeps cross-point links in view. The other tracks one point but adds higher-order slopes there. Each chain lays bare how stats at one rank feed the next. The chains also guide closure plans, ways to cut the chain at a set rank. The work gives a clean test bed for stat methods aimed at harder flows.
arxiv-2508-15959:
Mahmoud Khalil, Ahmad Khalil, and Alioune Ngom rethink how vision models chop up images in this 2025 paper. Standard models slice pictures into fixed square patches, whatever the picture shows. Their model instead groups pixels into adaptive regions that follow the image content, then encodes those regions with a transformer.

The method, called Adaptive Superpixel Coding, learns without labels in a self-supervised setup. The authors analyze why the approach works, pointing to regions that respect object boundaries better than rigid grids. On standard image benchmarks, their model beat widely used alternatives. The work suggests vision systems need not assume the grid structure that nearly all current models depend on.
arxiv-2508-17259:
Sumedha Arya and Nirmal Gaud present ResLink, a deep network that sorts brain tumors on CT scans. Their paper from twenty twenty-five stresses early, accurate calls, since tumors threaten core brain function. ResLink mixes area attention with residual connections in a staged convolutional pipeline. Dropout, regularization, and downsampling steps shape the feature flow. A final attention pass refines the verdict.

Training used a balanced data set of scans. Reported accuracy lands high, and the model holds up on fresh cases. Attention helps the net weigh the right regions of a scan. Residual links keep deep features trainable. The authors pitch the design for spatially rich medical images beyond this one task. The work is a compact classifier study, not a clinical trial.
arxiv-2508-18159:
Sara Ghazanfari, Wei-An Lin, Haitong Tian, and Ersin Yumer present SpotEdit in two thousand twenty-five. SpotEdit benchmarks image editing guided by both sight and text. Such edits promise fine, steerable control of generated content. Past tests were too simple to mirror real editing demands.

The benchmark spans diffusion, autoregressive, and hybrid generators. Scores split widely across those model families. A special part probes hallucination in the editing step. Top models often invent a visual cue that is not there. They then edit as if the cue were real. Code and data are shared in public.
arxiv-2508-18559:
Katalin Berlow and Edward Hou wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five about coloring infinite grids under measurability rules. A polychromatic coloring paints grid points so that every unit cube contains every color. In the ordinary setting, grids always admit a coloring using all two-to-the-d colors, where d is the dimension.

The Borel setting, where colorings must follow definable rules arising from free group actions, is stricter. The authors prove every free action of the integer lattice admits a Borel coloring with one fewer color than the classical count. The bound is sharp: for actions with ergodic generators, the full color count is impossible. The paper closes with open questions about extending the theory beyond cube tilings and about how the number depends on the action.
arxiv-2508-19159:
Das and six co-authors adapt robust safety barriers online for a tracked vehicle navigating under state uncertainty, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Safety guarantees rely on accurate state estimates, which practice rarely supplies. Prior robust barrier methods impose strict input limits that can be infeasible or costly. Their method tunes barrier parameters online through optimization.

Multiple safety constraints merge into one numerical barrier via Poisson's equation. That merger keeps parameter tuning tractable in real time. A dual relative degree issue in vehicle tracking is also addressed. Trials among multiple obstacles show clear gains over prior formulations. Control effort falls while safety holds under estimation error.
arxiv-2508-20059:
Thomas Le Corre, Julien Cardinal, and Ana Bušić present a control framework for thermostat loads in a 2025 arXiv paper. Water heaters and similar loads must be steered as a group without breaking comfort or device limits. Their method recasts the task as optimal transport with moment constraints.

The transport framing folds grid-level limits and physical feasibility into one design. A huge problem collapses to a small finite one. Gradients come from Monte Carlo runs of load trajectories, and the sampling law can be chosen freely, speeding the math. Tests on water heaters show clean coordination. An online version runs on simulated data.
arxiv-2509-00359:
Alexie Leauthaud and Adam Riess argue in 2025 that cosmology must prepare to move beyond the standard Lambda-CDM model. That model pairs cold dark matter with a cosmological constant, lambda, as dark energy. It now struggles to fit the full expansion history drawn from the cosmic microwave background, baryon acoustic oscillations, and local Type Ia supernovae at once.

Taken at face value, recent results hint at a dark sector more complex than assumed. Testing one dark energy value will no longer suffice, in their view. The authors urge deeper pursuit of the physics of dark matter, dark energy, and gravity on cosmic scales, guided by robust new data. Settling for the simplest account risks missing real structure.
arxiv-2509-00559:
Xuhui Zhou leads five authors in total, with Jiarui Liu, Akhila Yerukola, Hyunwoo Kim, and Maarten Sap, in proposing social world models. People navigate talk by guessing hidden beliefs and intentions, but AI systems lack clear records of such unspoken states.

Zhou and his co-authors define a structured form, S3AP, that tracks evolving states, actions, and mental states of agents instead of loose free text. Across five social reasoning benchmarks, the form lifts language model scores sharply, with gains the authors trace to explicit modeling of hidden mental states. An added algorithm lets agents model partners and predict their next actions, improving multi-turn social interaction test scores as well.
arxiv-2509-00659:
Jie Feng leads fourteen authors in total, with thirteen co-authors, in diagnosing laser-heated deuterium ions in dense plasma. Measuring ion behavior over ultrashort times is vital in high energy density physics, research on matter under extreme pressure and heat, but it is extremely hard in experiments.

Feng and his co-authors fire intense femtosecond laser pulses, pulses lasting quadrillionths of a second, at a heavy water stream at a high repetition rate. Neutrons from a deuterium fusion reaction are gathered by a single time-of-flight detector into a fine spectrum. From that spectrum they calculate ion temperature and angular distribution, and particle-in-cell simulations confirm the results, opening a way to track picosecond ion transport.
arxiv-2509-00759:
Xinyue Liu leads a team of six authors on Janus monolayers. These atom-thin layers may serve as piezoelectric materials. They may also work as photocatalysts for water splitting. A Janus layer has unlike atoms on its two faces. That asymmetry builds in a vertical polarization.

The team uses first-principles calculations on nine indium-based layers. Eight of the nine prove stable. Those eight show very high in-plane piezoelectric response. Their band edges straddle the water redox potentials. Exciton binding energies are low, which helps free charges form. Carrier mobility is high and varies with direction. A junction of two layers shows still better traits. It has strong visible-light absorption and a direct Z-scheme charge path.
arxiv-2509-01159:
Feng Guo proves new results about polynomials that stay positive on sets defined by matrix inequalities. Such results, called Positivstellensatze in German, give certificates that prove a polynomial is positive without checking every point. Guo extends two classic scalar theorems, by Handelman and by Krivine and Stengle, into the matrix setting.

The certificates Guo derives avoid sums of squares and instead use Kronecker powers of the defining matrix with positive semidefinite coefficient matrices. Under a sparsity pattern, leaner certificates also exist, cutting computation cost. Guo then applies the theory to polynomial optimization, building a ladder of relaxations whose size depends on the matrix dimension, not the number of variables. That trait could keep large problems within reach.
arxiv-2509-01459:
A smarter power grid must coordinate millions of devices and software agents. Demand response, shifting power use to match supply, is a key part of that vision. Ozan Baris Mulayim, with seven co-authors, examines semantic tools for demand response. Such tools use ontologies, formal word lists for concepts. Systems can then read shared data in the same way.

Current ontologies for buildings and demand response face two gaps. They are often built without a formal frame tied to real needs. Plans to join general with specific ones also stay untested in practice. The team applies a formal evaluation method to start closing those gaps. Their roadmap is organized by real data needs. The aim is shared understanding without costly custom work for each new device.
arxiv-2509-01659:
Jiahao Qiu and eight co-authors describe Physics Supernova, an AI agent built to solve hard physics problems. The test bed is the International Physics Olympiad, a contest for top school students from many countries. Strong scores there need both the right laws and careful steps to apply them. The agent pairs language model reasoning with tools chosen for physics work.

On the 2025 theory problems, the system scored well enough to rank near the top of hundreds of entrants. Its score passed the middle score earned by human gold medal winners. The authors also probe where the agent stays flexible and where it fails. Their case is that careful tool use can lift AI skill on tough science tasks.
arxiv-2509-01859:
Zachary Buckley and Shayne Waldron link reflection groups to special basis sets in quaternionic space. Their groups come from classic collineation groups, sets that map lines to lines, in complex four space. Those groups turn out to guard a maximal set of five mutually unbiased bases, meaning bases that overlap as evenly as possible. In quaternionic settings such basis sets are rare and prized.

From the symmetries, the pair build other fixed line sets with neat traits. One new set holds sixteen lines with only two overlap values and meets a special design bound. Side findings include groups with several splitting systems at once. A reducible subgroup with a continuous family of special vectors also emerges.
arxiv-2509-02259:
Guillem Bonafos leads six co-authors in testing pretrained speech transformers on baby cry classification. Transfer learning from speech models excels when labeled data are scarce. Whether those representations suit non-speech audio, and what acoustic traits they encode, stayed largely unexplored. Five pretrained speech models face eight baby cry datasets totaling many hours from hundreds of babies.

Latent representations from each model are assessed across all classification tasks in every dataset. The representations classify cries effectively and encode vocal source instability plus infant identity. Architecture and training strategy comparisons yield design lessons for similar tasks. Emotion detection and related health audio problems stand to benefit. Pretrained speech knowledge transfers further than expected.
arxiv-2509-02359:
Wanyue Zhang and seven co-authors present a 2025 analysis of why multimodal language models, AI systems that read images and text, still handle space poorly. Earlier checks looked at narrow settings, so the full picture stayed unclear.

The team built a benchmark called MulSeT covering single images, multiple views, and video. Experiments show performance levels off quickly as training data grows, with a low ceiling on tasks needing spatial imagination. That pattern means more data alone will not fix the gap. Tests also locate the weakness mainly in the visual encoder's position coding, not the language part. The authors sketch fixes through better architecture and reasoning training.
arxiv-2509-02559:
Aguinaldo Fraddosio and three co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on reinforcing old masonry. The work aims to keep historic walls safe without changing how they act. Strong modern fixes can fight the old structure. They can also harm heritage value.

Their weak reinforcement concept comes from limit analysis. That method estimates collapse loads. A new computational framework measures how tensile reinforcements raise capacity. Cracks can still open, as they did before. Rocking motion and settlement adaptation stay possible. Forces passed to supporting parts stay limited. Example designs cover a trilithon facing seismic loads and an arch under a point load. Settlement behaviour is checked by minimising total potential energy. The strategy pairs safety with conservation.
arxiv-2509-02659:
Zilong Guo and six co-authors present a 2025 autonomous driving paper reporting their second-place entry to the CVPR 2024 end-to-end driving challenge. Their system drives from camera input using a vision-language model, which reads images and reasons in words.

Most end-to-end designs stack specialised neural modules. This team instead pairs the end-to-end layout with a knowledgeable multimodal model, betting that broad scene understanding transfers to driving decisions. The entry used only a single camera. It finished as the best camera-only solution on the leaderboard. The authors present the result as evidence that vision-based driving, guided by large pretrained models, can rival sensor-heavy setups. Full technical detail stays brief in this challenge report, which focuses on the approach and its standing.
arxiv-2509-02859:
Sandipana Dowerah and nine co-authors wrote a 2025 speech technology paper. It introduces Speech DF Arena. The arena is a shared benchmark and leaderboard for detecting audio deepfakes. Synthetic speech keeps improving. Detectors need one standard yardstick, not scattered tests.

The arena supplies a toolkit. It scores detection systems uniformly across fourteen datasets and attack scenarios. Standard metrics and protocols support reproducibility. Its leaderboard ranks systems to guide development. The study covers twelve open-source detectors and three proprietary ones. Many systems posted high error rates on out-of-domain material. That underlines the need for cross-domain testing. Tools and data live on public hubs. The aim is comparable, transparent progress in deepfake detection.
arxiv-2509-02959:
Jacob Paltrowitz wrote a 2025 combinatorics paper on a two-player game played on partially ordered sets, or posets. A move in the Ungar game removes some largest elements from the set. Players alternate, and whoever cannot move loses. Earlier work by Defant, Kravitz, and Williams defined these games and studied one classic lattice.

Paltrowitz focuses on graded posets, where elements sit in even ranks or levels. He first gives recursive rules, meaning each case reduces to smaller ones, for deciding when the second player wins. He then restates those wins in the language of boolean circuits, which are networks of simple logic gates. He also extends the earlier lattice results from two dimensions to any number of dimensions.
arxiv-2509-03159:
M. Papoutsis and 4 co-authors tested in 2025 whether X-ray light bouncing off accretion discs explains how quasars flicker. Quasars are brilliant galactic centers fed by black holes, and their ultraviolet and optical brightness varies over time. The reverberation idea says X-rays from a hot corona above the disc strike the disc, which then re-emits at longer wavelengths after a delay.

The team computed disc responses across model settings, including whether the corona draws power from the disc itself or from outside. They built predicted power spectra, measures of how much flicker occurs at each timescale, and fit them to real quasar light curves from a major survey. Fits worked well across a wide wavelength range. Best fits favored disc-powered coronas, moderate black hole spin, and corona heights in a stated band.
arxiv-2509-03259:
Konstantinos Boutivas and 3 co-authors computed special functions of a quantum field theory from entanglement in 2025. In renormalization group flow, a theory's description changes with the energy scale viewed, from ultraviolet to infrared. Functions called c and a measure something like the number of active degrees of freedom, and they should only shrink along that flow.

The authors test that link with entanglement entropy, a measure of how strongly two regions of a system are quantum-linked. For a free massive scalar field, a case computable from first principles, they track the entropy of a spherical region as its radius grows. From it they extract a c-function in two space-time dimensions and an a-function in four. Both slid smoothly and monotonically from one to zero, as theory expects.
arxiv-2509-03359:
A. Anand, R. Egger, and A. De Martino studied two-dimensional Dirac fermions in a magnetic field in a 2025 physics paper. Dirac fermions mimic electrons whose energy grows in a cone-like way, as in graphene. Here their mass varies in a repeating one-dimensional pattern, a mass superlattice, while a perpendicular magnetic field is applied.

Exact solutions for single and finite arrays of domain walls, the borders between mass regions, show special Jackiw-Rebbi modes surviving with a field-tuned speed. For the endless periodic case, a gauge-invariant projection onto magnetic Bloch states yields the full miniband spectrum, checked against the finite arrays. From those spectra the authors predict altered quantum Hall plateaus, steps in electrical response. They also predict Weiss-like oscillations in magnetoconductivity with much smaller amplitude and a shifted phase than in electrostatic versions.
arxiv-2509-03559:
H. Abele and 59 co-authors report a 2025 research paper on expected particle backgrounds for the NUCLEUS reactor experiment in France. NUCLEUS uses cryogenic detectors, cooled to extreme temperatures, to catch coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering. In that process a neutrino bumps a whole atomic nucleus at once. Most signal is expected at very low energies, below one kiloelectronvolt.

The team measured radiation around the Chooz power plant site and ran extensive Geant4 simulations of the setup. Sources studied include cosmic-ray products, environmental gamma rays, and radioactivity in detector materials. The design should reject backgrounds by more than a factor of one hundred. Cosmic-ray neutrons still dominate what remains. In the key energy window, predicted background leaves a signal-to-background ratio above one, meeting the experiment's needs.
arxiv-2509-03659:
A 2025 theoretical physics paper by Oscar Castillo-Felisola and three co-authors focuses on splitting the connection of an affine gravity model into its basic parts. A connection is the geometric rule that lets physicists compare directions at neighbouring points in space. Affine models of gravity build their laws from such a connection without assuming a metric, the usual distance rule, in advance.

Working on an affine manifold's tangent bundle, they decompose the most general linear connection into irreducible tensor pieces. Those pieces relate to conformal transformations, which rescale shapes while keeping angles, and to projective transformations, which preserve straight lines. The setup supports gravity models that are invariant under coordinate changes without depending on a metric. The guiding question is whether the connection alone can reveal something about the metric that emerges from it.
arxiv-2509-03859:
Haichao Zhang and six co-authors' 2025 research paper is about teaching a legged mobile manipulator to pick and place objects through many stages, entirely in simulation. Their robot is a quadruped carrying an arm, whose skills must range widely over long horizons with partial views of the world. Pick-and-place, with searching, approaching, grasping, transporting, and dropping, captures those demands.

Their trained visuo-motor policy learns the whole sequence in simulation and transfers to the real robot. It reaches nearly eighty percent success in real-world trials. Behaviours like re-grasping after a failed grip and chaining subtasks together emerge without being programmed. Real experiments include ablation studies isolating which training and transfer techniques matter most. Deployment spans varied indoor and outdoor environments, showing the policy is not tied to one laboratory setup. The authors present simulation-only training as a route to capable legged manipulation.
arxiv-2509-04259:
Idan Shenfeld and two co-authors explain why reinforcement learning forgets old skills less than ordinary fine-tuning in a 2025 research paper. Both methods can teach a model a new task equally well, yet supervised fine-tuning erodes earlier abilities far more. The gap tracks how far the tuned model's behavior drifts from the original, measured by KL-divergence, a standard distance between probability patterns.

Learning from its own live attempts biases reinforcement learning toward the closest working solution, the authors show. Supervised training faces no such pull and can land far away. Experiments span large language models and robot foundation models, with theory backing the pattern. They name the principle RL's Razor, after the preference for the nearest adequate answer.
arxiv-2509-04559:
L Ighina and twenty-one co-authors examine an extraordinarily luminous quasar from the universe's first billion years in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The radio-powerful quasar sits at redshift 6.13, meaning its light left when the cosmos was young. Radio telescopes in India, Australia, and beyond measured properties typical of distant radio quasars. The Chandra X-ray observatory, though, caught a faint flux that implies enormous intrinsic X-ray power once distance and spectrum are accounted for.

Its X-ray glow is remarkably soft, meaning weighted toward lower energies. Jets cannot explain that softness even with relativistic boosting, the authors find. A black hole swallowing matter faster than the usual Eddington limit fits instead. Confirmation would make the object a unique laboratory for early black hole growth.
arxiv-2509-04959:
A confusion matrix mixes two effects: how similar classes look, and how skewed the data are. Johan Erbani, lead author with four co-authors, study how normalising that matrix can separate the effects in a 2025 paper. Standard row and column normalisations leave the two factors entangled, which hampers diagnosis of classifier errors.

They introduce bistochastic normalisation using iterative proportional fitting, a generalisation of row and column scaling. The method recovers the underlying structure of class similarity in their analysis. They also show normalisations correspond to geometric views of the model's internal class representations, deepening what a normalised matrix can reveal.
arxiv-2509-05059:
Deeply virtual Compton scattering probes the internal structure of targets, and its dispersion relations need corrections at higher twist. Víctor Martínez-Fernández and one co-author add kinematic power corrections up to twist four in a 2025 particle physics paper. They treat scalar, pseudoscalar, and spin-half targets.

The formal shape of the subtracted dispersion relations survives, but the subtracted constants change. One relation, previously thought to depend only on a single term, now also depends on two double distributions. The authors note this mixing is not suppressed in the Jefferson Lab range. That could strongly affect attempts to extract pressure forces inside hadrons from scattering data.
arxiv-2509-05159:
Spherical magnets with perpendicular anisotropy can settle into saddle point configurations that are not simple energy minima. Stephen Gustafson, lead author with two co-authors, investigate those configurations in a 2025 mathematical physics paper. A micromagnetic energy functional on the unit sphere produces a curvature-induced interaction between spins.

The authors prove two distinct types of saddle points with zero mapping degree exist. Their proof uses a parabolic flow modelled on the harmonic map heat flow, ruling out blow-up for highly symmetric starting data. Solutions of the governing equation appear as the long-time limit, contrasting with harmonic maps between spheres.
arxiv-2509-05359:
Turning speech into discrete units, like words for sound, is examined by Yanis Labrak, Richard Dufour, and Mickaël Rouvier in a 2025 paper on speech language models. These models adapt text-trained systems to spoken language, and the pre-training stage is where the sound units matter most.

The authors vary model design, unit representation, and training robustness to see what drives results. Encoder choice and cluster size, which sets how many distinct sound units exist, matter differently at different model scales. They also study how the units line up with speech sounds and carry tone and speaker traits. Matching the clustering data to the target domain proved important for robustness.
arxiv-2509-05759:
Worldwide database transactions could commit in one wide-area trip, Jinkun Geng and three co-authors propose in a 2025 distributed systems paper. Geo-replicated databases like Spanner must agree on order and copies across continents, and each extra round trip adds delay users feel.

Their system, Tiga, merges concurrency control and consensus into a single round. Synchronised clocks let it stamp each transaction with a future time at submission, so most arrive before their stamp and serialise in that order within one round trip. Late transactions fall back to a slower path. Evaluations beat all baselines on throughput and latency by wide margins. The system is open-sourced.
arxiv-2509-05859:
How the molecular ion NeH+ breaks apart after capturing a slow electron is calculated in a 2025 paper led by Riyad Hassaine with four co-authors. The process, dissociative recombination, matters where cold plasmas and interstellar gas are modeled. Here it proceeds without the direct curve crossings that simpler theories rely on.

The team applies multichannel quantum defect theory, adding couplings between electronic states in fuller form than an earlier helium hydride study, including second-order terms and a density-of-states factor for the ionization continuum. Their potential curves and couplings for NeH feed the calculation. Resulting cross sections agree well with measurements and fill a gap at low energies, where no detailed quantum results existed before.
arxiv-2509-06859:
Small satellite galaxies can lose much of their mass and still sit on a famous scaling relation, show Alexander H. Riley and eight co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. The mass-metallicity relation links a galaxy's stellar mass to its chemical enrichment, and its tightness in the Local Group had been used to argue satellites suffer little tidal stripping.

Using the Auriga simulations, the authors tracked every accreted system twice: counting all its stars, and counting only the surviving progenitor. The total-mass relation is tight, with scatter driven by age. The progenitor-only relation has scatter about as large as observed, so the data cannot rule out heavy mass loss. Satellites above the relation have typically lost much mass, while even some exactly on it have lost over half their stars. Only satellites well below it are reliably intact.
arxiv-2509-06959:
That solutions exist, and are unique, for fractional differential equations in a sequence space is shown by Khurshida Parvin and two co-authors in a 2025 analysis paper. The equations use Caputo fractional derivatives and carry three-point integral boundary terms. The setting is the generalized Hahn sequence space, a space of endless sequences with a tailored notion of size.

The main tool is the Hausdorff measure of noncompactness, which gauges how far a set is from being compact and powers fixed-point arguments in endless dimensions. With it, the authors prove solutions exist inside that space. A Banach fixed-point argument then gives enough conditions for uniqueness, and Hyers-Ulam stability is discussed, asking whether near-solutions stay near true ones. Worked examples close the paper, showing the conditions at work. The setup extends fractional equation theory into a less-studied sequence space.
arxiv-2509-07059:
Swati Ravi and 3 co-authors study the shape of the corona around the X-ray burster GX 13+1 in a 2025 paper. Data from the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer show the polarization angle turning in several neutron star systems in low-mass binaries, this source among them.

The team built QUEEN-BEE, a Bayesian nested sampling tool that works on unbinned Stokes parameters, the numbers that describe polarization, and finds the best rotation rates. They ran it on three earlier looks at GX 13+1. In the first, the rate it found matched earlier binned work. Splitting that look by energy pointed to a flat, slab-like corona, the first time slab and shell shapes could be told apart for this source. The second look showed no turning, and the third only brief, passing behaviour.
arxiv-2509-07659:
Fernando Ballesta-Yagüe and 1 co-author survey sparse domination in harmonic analysis in a 2025 expository article. Sparse domination bounds a complicated operator by a simpler sparse sum, and it has become a central proof strategy for weighted estimates. Several schemes of proof exist, and the article briefly reviews the main known ones for Calderón-Zygmund operators, the singular integrals at the field's core.

The authors then use the scheme based on the Calderón-Zygmund decomposition to prove a dual sparse domination estimate for such operators with Dini-smooth kernels, a mild smoothness class. They keep an eye on the difficulties that arise when moving the argument to spaces with nondoubling measures, where balls can grow irregularly. As an exposition with a new result attached, the article serves both newcomers learning the technique and specialists tracking its frontier.
arxiv-2509-07859:
Sebastian Kalhöfer argues in a solo 2025 physics paper that vibrating atoms help explain puzzling measurements in electron spin resonance. That technique probes how electrons respond to magnetic fields, and the response is summed up in a number called the g-factor. Textbook accounts often treat the g-factor as fixed for a given material.

Including spin-dependent links between electrons and phonons, the quantised vibrations of a crystal, Kalhöfer shows the g-factor changes with temperature in line with experiments. At low temperatures it should also shift with magnetic field strength, an effect not previously considered. The prediction gives experimenters a concrete target: measure carefully at low temperature and look for the field dependence the theory expects.
arxiv-2509-07959:
Helical microrobots, tiny corkscrews steered by rotating magnetic fields, could one day swim through the body delivering medicine. Joost Wijnmalen, Leon Abelmann, and Iulian Apachitei compare two magnetic materials for them in a 2025 research paper. Hard-magnetic versions keep their magnetization. Soft-magnetic versions magnetize only in a field, and suit the body better.

Hard-magnetic robots reached spin rates and top speeds several times higher than soft ones. Below saturation, soft-magnetic performance barely depended on the material's susceptibility. Torque in those robots comes from shape alone. A tapered ribbon design tripled speed compared with regular helices. The numbers give designers a clear trade-off: raw propulsion from hard magnets, against the biocompatibility of soft ones, with shape improvements available either way.
arxiv-2509-08059:
Copying an unknown quantum process, not just a state, is the problem framed by Pavel Sekatski and 3 co-authors in a 2025 quantum information paper. Cloning a quantum channel means reproducing what a device does to any input, at the best rate and quality possible. Surprisingly, state cloning turns out to be one special case, equivalent to cloning a simple trash-and-replace channel.

Using higher-order quantum operations, the authors build one framework for general cloning tasks. They derive necessary conditions for super-replication, a regime where copies multiply quadratically while errors vanish. Noisy channels are among the cases examined. Limits on process copying govern quantum networks and repeaters, where unknown operations may need duplicating faithfully.
arxiv-2509-08259:
Dipankar Jana and 11 co-authors review sheets of material one atom thick as sensors for many signals at once, in a 2025 paper. Such sheets can be stacked without matching their crystal patterns. Designers can thus mix layers with very different traits and build new devices by choice. The sheets bend easily, grip light strongly, and some hold magnetism at room warmth.

One sheet can react to light, strain, heat, and stray chemicals at the same time. It can even emit single photons from point defects. The review maps this range as one sensing platform. A single soft patch that reads several body or field signals could shrink wearables and field kits that now need a box of separate probes.
arxiv-2509-08359:
Predict first, optimise second is the usual pipeline for decisions under uncertainty, and Haeun Jeon with 4 co-authors blend its two rival training styles in a 2025 machine learning paper. Prediction-focused learning is stable but ignores whether predictions lead to good decisions. Decision-focused learning trains on decision quality directly, yet its loss landscapes mix flat and sharp regions, so convergence wobbles even with good gradients.

Prediction loss is brought in as a guide to steady the decision-focused training. The hybrid aims at decisions that are both well-aimed and reliably reached. Portfolio choices, inventory orders, and energy dispatch all share this predict-then-decide shape, and all suffer when a forecaster optimises the wrong scoreboard.
arxiv-2509-08759:
Mominul Rubel and 2 co-authors introduce the Fourier Learning Machine in a 2025 paper on neural networks for science. The design represents a Fourier series, a sum of waves, in many dimensions. Unlike older Fourier models, it keeps a complete separable basis.

A simple feedforward network with cosine activation learns frequencies, amplitudes, and phase shifts as trainable values. Those values map directly to Fourier coefficients, giving a clear link between the two forms. Tests cover benchmark differential equations and a family of optimal control problems. Performance matches or beats established models such as SIREN. The basis adapts to both periodic and nonperiodic functions.
arxiv-2509-08859:
Robot teams that can barely communicate must still divide tasks without two robots chasing the same job. Vincenzo Suriani and 3 co-authors present a coordination method for exactly that bind in a 2025 research paper. Their setting is harsh: active obstacles, partial visibility, and a communication channel with tiny messages sent rarely. The method adapts market-based task assignment, where agents bid for work.

A key twist is treating obstacles as asymmetric, as most real obstacles are. Existing methods usually pretend obstacles look the same from every side. The team validated the approach in simulation and with real NAO robots at official RoboCup competitions. Task overlaps, the costliest coordination failure, fell sharply in the limited-communication settings. The architecture targets any distributed robot team working where bandwidth is scarce and the world will not sit still.
arxiv-2509-08959:
Vision transformers see the whole image at once but can miss fine local texture, especially when training data is scarce. Puskal Khadka and 3 co-authors present CoSwin in a 2025 research paper. CoSwin fuses convolutional feature learning into a hierarchical shifted-window transformer. Convolutions supply the locality biases that pure attention lacks.

A learnable enhancement module inside each attention block strengthens local features. Global semantic structure still comes from the attention windows. The team tested CoSwin on five classification benchmarks, from handwritten digits to tiny natural images. It beat strong convolutional and transformer rivals consistently. Gains were largest on the harder hundred-class and tiny-image sets. The message is architectural humility. For small-scale vision, convolutional local processing and the transformer's global view work better married than apart.
arxiv-2509-09059:
Paulette Koronkevich and 1 co-author develop dependent-type-preserving memory allocation in a 2025 paper. Dependently typed languages let programmers write detailed specs and prove programs meet them. Those specs are erased after checking, so linked external code can break them during compilation.

A C program linked to a Coq program, for example, could return uninitialized memory and violate a safety spec. The authors build a typed middle language in which memory allocation carries dependent types. A compiler pass preserves those types through allocation. Linking with ill-typed programs could then be blocked at check time. The work is ongoing and aims at safer linking.
arxiv-2509-09359:
Gait rehabilitation works better when patients feel their mistakes the moment they make them. Stefan Resch and 7 co-authors built a wearable system for that feedback in a 2025 research paper. The modular setup combines a smart foot orthosis with an instrumented forearm crutch. Sensors track plantar pressure and motion, and vibration delivers the feedback.

A smartphone application ties the devices together wirelessly. Eight participants tested the system's mobile gait detection and the app's usability. They compared vibration patterns across the two devices. Pattern-based feedback was rated more useful and more suitable for daily use than simple vibration alerts. Where the buzz lands also matters: the orthosis and crutch felt clearly different. The findings argue that feedback design deserves as much care as the hardware in assistive technology.
arxiv-2509-09759:
Chiang-Mei Chen and 3 co-authors study an unevenly expanding universe in 2025 under a version of gravity where the constants themselves drift with scale. Their Bianchi-I cosmos stretches at different rates along different axes. Quantum corrections enter through a running Newton coupling and cosmological term, fixed by the flow of the effective action in asymptotically safe gravity.

With no classical cosmological constant, they derive corrected series solutions for a wide family of matter types, expanded in both time and unevenness. A general rule predicts when such a universe smooths itself out, which happens in most cases studied. Numerical checks show quantum effects make that smoothing start sooner. With a positive constant, smoothing always wins, in line with the cosmic no-hair idea.
arxiv-2509-09859:
Razvan Stefanescu and 5 co-authors present WAVE-DETR in a 2025 paper, a drone detector that listens as well as looks. Small drones are hard to spot in real settings, and a camera alone can miss them. Their system fuses ordinary color images with sound, joining a deformable detection transformer with a speech-trained audio model that turns sound into rich feature vectors.

Along with an existing drone-versus-bird set, the team built a new data set with thousands of matched image and audio clips. Four ways of merging the two signals were trained and compared. The gated fusion version worked best. It lifted detection scores for small drones by a wide margin on familiar and unseen test data. Medium and large drones gained less.
arxiv-2509-10059:
Yue Zhou and 7 co-authors build the first benchmark for mathematical reasoning over drone imagery in a 2025 vision-language paper. Remote sensing from small aircraft constantly needs distances, areas, and trajectory estimates, yet today's image-aware models had never been seriously examined on maths grounded in aerial vehicle views. Their AVI-Math collection holds nearly four thousand questions tied to vehicle scenes shot from varied heights and angles.

Questions span six school subjects and twenty topics, from geometry through logic and algebra, well past simple counting. Fourteen prominent vision-language models were run through the set, and even systems that shine on older benchmarks stumbled here. Careful error analysis maps exactly where the reasoning breaks, and the authors point to the gaps as the most useful agenda for the next round of model building.
arxiv-2509-10259:
Removing an object from a photo sounds simple, but Hua Yuan and five co-authors show how image-filling models go wrong in this 2025 computer vision paper. Models often invent unwanted content inside the blanked region, called mask hallucination, or they fill the hole with something shaped like the hole itself, a mask-shape bias.

Their fix, Mask Consistency Regularization, works during training. The mask is perturbed in two ways, stretched larger and reshaped, and the model must keep its filled output consistent with the original mask's result. The stretched masks pull the fill toward the surrounding scene, while reshaped masks break the habit of copying the hole's outline. Experiments show fewer invented objects and cleaner, more believable removals.
arxiv-2509-10559:
Shaba Shaon and 5 co-authors survey how quantum methods could strengthen federated learning in future 6G networks in this 2025 article. Sixth-generation networks aim to embed AI everywhere, with devices training shared models without sending raw data home. Classical federated learning strains under weak devices, flaky links, and privacy attacks in such messy settings.

Quantum federated learning applies quantum computing, communication, and cryptography inside that training loop. The authors organize the possible gains under edge intelligence, network optimization, and security and privacy. A case study shows a quantum optimization approach converging better than classical methods. They close with the hard parts: fragile quantum states, clashes with classical protocols, and hardware limits.
arxiv-2509-10659:
Bo Lei, Victor M. Castillo, and Yeping Hu speed up physics simulations with a hierarchical graph network in this 2025 computational engineering paper. Mesh-based graph networks can stand in for partial differential equation solvers, but on big meshes their message passing is slow and blurs fine detail. Hierarchy helps, yet building coarse graphs that respect the mesh's physics is tricky.

Their network, M4GN, works in three tiers. A segmentation step pairs a fast graph partitioner with superpixel-style refinement guided by vibration modes, grouping nodes that move consistently. Segments are summarized by an order-blind aggregator, then a small graph network handles local dynamics while a transformer reasons between segments. On benchmark datasets the design improved prediction accuracy by up to about half while running up to a fifth faster than leading baselines.
arxiv-2509-10959: Shai Haran explores structures growing out of the Farey fractal in this solo-authored 2025 paper. The work mixes operadic constructions, Farey-type graphs, and Fibonacci expansions. Its central new objects are Fibonadic numbers. They are built as an inverse limit from the Zeckendorf shift. The Zeckendorf system writes numbers with Fibonacci numbers. Haran equips the Fibonadic numbers with three things. A metric comes first. An order comes next. A commutative rig structure completes the picture. In a rig, addition and multiplication behave, but subtraction need not exist.
arxiv-2509-11159:
Dat-Thinh Nguyen, Kim-Hung Le, and Nhien-An Le-Khac wrote this 2025 machine learning security paper. It concerns model extraction. An attacker copies a paid prediction service with a substitute model. The substitute trains on made-up data. The real training set is never seen.

Earlier data-free attacks share a practical flaw. The substitute's accuracy swings up and down during the attack. The attacker cannot tell when to stop. The new method is called MetaDFME. It uses meta-learning while training the data generator. Each batch of synthetic data stays closer to the target's knowledge. The swings calm down as a result. On four standard image datasets, MetaDFME beat the best previous attack. Its substitute accuracy also stayed steadier.
arxiv-2509-11259:
David Schiff, Ofir Lindenbaum, and Yonathan Efroni ask a sideways question in this 2025 machine learning paper. Can a model trained only for regression solve control problems? No control-task training would be involved. The model would drop straight into reinforcement learning.

Their method is called ICR-RL. It needs no extra training at all. At each step, the regression model reads past experience in its context. It then predicts good actions. Decision-making becomes a prediction problem. The authors used a recent regression foundation model. They tested on classic control benchmarks from the Gymnasium suite. The model held its own against standard methods. Those included DQN, PPO, and TRPO. Regression pre-training alone may ground future reinforcement learning systems.
arxiv-2509-11359:
J. Cepila and three co-authors predict a measurement for the Large Hadron Collider in this 2025 nuclear physics paper. Oxygen or neon nuclei can pass close without touching. One nucleus can flash light on the other. The photon can create a vector meson. The meson is a light rho or a heavy J/psi.

The authors use an energy-dependent hotspot model. They compute cross sections for this photonuclear production. Two pictures of nuclear shape are tested. One uses standard Woods-Saxon profiles. The other uses clustered shapes, an alpha-cluster oxygen and a bowling-pin neon. Predictions cover energy, momentum transfer, and rapidity. Coherent and incoherent production are both included. The incoherent channel should reveal gluon saturation approaching.
arxiv-2509-11859:
Carlos E. Budde, working with four co-authors, asks whether statistical model checking can answer richer questions than averages alone, in a 2025 paper on quantitative verification. The method tests a probabilistic model by running many random samples and reporting estimates with firm error bounds.

Their tool is a classic inequality that bounds a whole distribution curve at once, not just its center. With that guarantee, the authors compute quantiles, conditional value-at-risk, and entropic risk for sampled systems, covering worst-case and tail behavior that plain means hide. They built the new quantities into the modes simulator of the Modest Toolset. Benchmarks from the verification literature show them off, stressing how much more a single distribution-wide bound lets an analyst ask.
arxiv-2509-11959:
Turning a plain-language request into a full moving LiDAR scene is the aim of LiDARCrafter, presented in 2025 by Ao Liang and seven co-authors. Video and occupancy generators have advanced quickly, yet synthetic LiDAR, the laser sensing that self-driving stacks rely on for precise 3D perception, has lagged behind.

Instructions are first parsed into scene graphs centered on the moving vehicle, and a three-branch diffusion model turns those into object layouts, paths, and shapes. A second diffusion model draws the opening scan as a range image, and an autoregressive step stretches it into a smooth sequence over time. Because layouts stay explicit, users can insert or move objects directly. The team also releases an evaluation suite and reports leading scores on the nuScenes benchmark.
arxiv-2509-12059:
Carson G. Valdez and 6 co-authors demonstrate a programmable optical filter in a 2025 paper. The device is an integrated photonic circuit, a chip that guides light instead of electricity. Its feed-forward photonic mesh can be reconfigured to perform different spectral filter functions, selecting which wavelengths of light pass or are blocked.

In experiments, a triangular mesh with four inputs and three layers used self-configuration algorithms to filter three chosen wavelengths from an incoming spectrum. Pre-set filters could be swept continuously across the device's range, so the design does not lock in one center wavelength at manufacture. The team showed wavelength rejection as deep as forty decibels and channel separation for dense wavelength division multiplexing, a method that sends many signals at once, with low crosstalk.
arxiv-2509-12259:
Kenneth G. Young presents a diabetes risk prediction model in a 2025 paper with a long name: the Quantum-Inspired Stacked Integrated Concept Graph Model. The model borrows ideas from quantum computing without using quantum hardware. Its goal is accurate prediction that still runs efficiently on ordinary processors.

Young trained the system on the PIMA Indians Diabetes dataset, expanded with synthetic samples to balance its classes. A self-improving concept graph feeds a stacked ensemble combining random forests, extra trees, transformers, and neural networks. Reported out-of-fold scores were strong on standard measures, beating traditional methods in the paper's comparison. Inference ran on CPU at a modest rate. The paper also describes the architecture, theory, code, and performance visualizations in detail.
arxiv-2509-12359:
Perfect secrecy is sometimes out of reach on a fading wireless link, and settling for partial secrecy is the honest fallback. Henry Carvajal Mora and five co-authors analyze that regime in 2025 under a broad fading model that contains many classic channel models as special cases.

Both the legitimate receiver and the eavesdropper carry antenna arrays using maximal ratio combining, which stacks the signal across branches. The authors derive exact and approximate formulas for outage probability, leaked information rate, and the average fraction of the message an eavesdropper can decode. Simulations confirm the formulas, and more branches at the receiver improve secrecy.
arxiv-2509-12459:
Suvojit Acharjee, Utathya Aich, and Asfak Ali ask whether language models truly understand language in a 2025 paper. Models generate and interpret text well overall, yet they struggle with fine-grained features such as tense, negation, voice, and modality. Those features are central to clear human communication.

The authors evaluate leading models in English and Bengali, motivated by educational uses such as tutoring, automated grading, and translation, where misreading can harm learning. They introduce evaluation guidelines and a dataset called LUCID, built from carefully crafted sentence pairs in both languages. The pairs challenge models on negation, tense, and voice variations. Their structured assessment aims to show where model interpretation aligns with human reading and where it breaks down.
arxiv-2509-12859:
Etienne Buehrle and Christoph Stiller propose a black-box approach to reducing large semidefinite programs in a 2025 paper. Semidefinite programs are optimization problems that arise, among other places, in polynomial optimization, where the goal is to minimize a polynomial under constraints. Large instances can be very hard to solve directly.

Their method projects a large program onto random linear subspaces, breaking it into a set of smaller semidefinite programs that are easier to handle. Consensus among those smaller problems then informs the overall solution, as reflected in the paper's title. The authors evaluate the approach on a set of polynomial optimization problems. They report improved scalability, suggesting the reduction can make previously oversized problems tractable without opening up the solver's internal workings.
arxiv-2509-13259:
Matthew Goeckner, Donovan Harcey and three co-authors generalize particle reduction in 2025 for the stochastic weighted particle method. The method tracks velocity spreads for rarefied gases and plasmas. Particle counts grow over time, so grouping and cuts must save cost without losing moments.

A general frame builds cuts that keep a chosen moment set exact. Weights solve a linear system set by speeds and target moments. The frame is used to keep all moments through third order. Tests check higher moments and tail traits too. A trade-off between high moments and tails emerges, to guide cut design.
arxiv-2509-13459:
Arna Ghosh and 3 co-authors study representation geometry across the human visual cortex in a 2025 paper whose title warns that not all roads lead to Rome. Any system that encodes the world, living or built, faces a trade. It must pack in many features of its input, and stay steady when noise hits.

The authors use a population geometry framework, a way of describing how whole groups of neurons represent things. With it they examined the visual cortex, and set artificial neural networks beside the brain data. Along the ventral visual stream, most areas held broad, general-purpose representations. Their spectra fell off like a power law, the mark of scale-free geometry. Scale-free geometry, in other words, is not found everywhere in the brain. Networks trained without supervision showed a similar geometry.
arxiv-2509-13659:
En-Jui Chang, writing alone in 2025, proposes a flaw in quantum communication. He calls it quantum keystroke logging. Superdense coding sends two classical bits by transmitting one qubit of a shared entangled pair. The protocol has long been regarded as secure. Adding error-correcting logical states seems an obvious safety upgrade.

Chang argues the upgrade opens a side door in systems based on GKP encoding. That scheme protects quantum states inside oscillators. An organization that prepares and sends the logical Bell pairs could still extract the sender's input. It could do so without detection, he claims. This holds even if it never assembles the full encoded state. The claim reframes who must be trusted in such networks.
arxiv-2509-13759:
The ATLAS Collaboration measures W boson production with unusual precision in a 2025 particle physics paper. It uses proton-proton collision data from the Large Hadron Collider. The data come from special low pile-up runs in 2017 and 2018. The angular patterns of the lepton pairs from boson decays probe quantum chromodynamics. That is the theory of the strong force.

For the first time, the team measure the full set of angular coefficients. They pair that with the differential cross-section across the W boson's transverse momentum. The coverage spans the full phase space of the decay leptons. Negative and positive W bosons are measured separately. Few overlapping collisions per crossing kept the data exceptionally clean. Every result agrees with predictions that include quantum chromodynamics corrections up to second order.
arxiv-2509-13959:
Pragya Belwal and Mahender Singh connect three algebraic structures in a 2025 mathematics paper. The three are Rota-Baxter groups, skew left braces, and the semi-direct products naturally attached to them. Skew braces are sets carrying two compatible group operations. Each one manufactures a well-behaved solution to the Yang-Baxter equation. That equation is a cornerstone of integrable systems and knot theory.

Given a skew left brace, the authors define its square. The square is a new brace living on the semi-direct product of its additive and multiplicative groups. They show the construction differs from the older double construction from matched pairs. The square produces fresh Yang-Baxter solutions from old ones. It behaves functorially and fits the field's cohomological and extension-theoretic machinery. They also give a condition under which two isoclinic braces yield isoclinic squares.
arxiv-2509-14259:
Lynna Jirpongopas and four co-authors ran a live trial in 2025 on how the tone of a travel chatbot shapes what users do. An online travel agency let them vary the assistant freely. One version sounded warm and keen, one stayed neutral, and one got no tone guidance at all.

Users facing the warm version wrote longer prompts than the other groups. Users in both the warm and neutral groups bought subscriptions to the service more often than the control group. The team also studied word cues in the chats to explain purchases and clicks on partner links. Results suggest tone is not mere polish. How an assistant sounds can shift effort, trust and buying, which matters for any firm designing customer facing AI.
arxiv-2509-14359:
Hakop Hakopian and Anush Khachatryan extend a result in 2025 on Hermite multivariate interpolation, fitting a polynomial to values and derivatives at set points. The core question is which point and derivative patterns can be solved at all. Degree and total multiplicity decide the border.

The authors characterise solvable sets when total multiplicity reaches at most twice the degree plus two. That step extends a theorem from 2000 by one of the authors, which stopped one lower. The older result itself extended a classical theorem by Severi from 1921. Knowing the exact border matters for computer aided design and numerical methods. Near the border, small changes in the data pattern decide whether a unique fitting polynomial exists.
arxiv-2509-14559:
Paolo Torrado and four co-authors present Radiolunadiff in 2025, a physics informed deep learning system for predicting radio signal strength on the Moon. Lunar terrain blocks and reflects signals in complex ways. Mission planners need radio maps before placing relays or rovers.

A terrain generator built from public NASA data creates realistic lunar topography. Ray tracing over that terrain produces a high fidelity data set of propagation cases. A triplet network of two U-Net models plus a diffusion model then learns the propagation patterns. Tests on their terrain set beat existing deep learning approaches across several metrics. Physics built data may generalise better than purely synthetic radio maps for off world planning.
arxiv-2509-14659:
Kartik Hegde and three co-authors align audio captioning with human preferences in 2025, instead of training only on paired audio and caption data. Paired supervision is costly to curate, and reference captions may not match what listeners actually prefer. Preference learning offers a directer signal.

A reward model based on contrastive language audio pretraining is trained on human pairwise preference labels. That reward then fine tunes any baseline captioning system through reinforcement learning, with no ground truth captions needed at that stage. Human evaluations across several data sets preferred the tuned captions, especially where baselines were wrong or unnatural. Preference aligned captioning supports accessibility tools whose descriptions must please human listeners, not metrics.
arxiv-2509-14959:
Anton Selitskiy, Shaikh Akib Shahriyar, and Jishnuraj Prakasan turn discrete optimal transport into an attack on voice security systems in a 2025 speech security paper. Speaker verification confirms who is speaking, and countermeasure systems try to catch synthetic speech. Their attack needs no access to model internals, gradients, or training data.

Working after generation, the method takes frame-level embeddings from a strong speech model and aligns them toward a pool of genuine speech using entropic optimal transport. A barycentric projection and neural vocoding then rebuild the audio. Across two standard spoofing benchmarks, the attack sharply raises error rates for countermeasures and degrades verification for many spoof types. It transfers across datasets and survives fine-tuning of the defenses. Embedding analysis suggests the shift moves fake speech into regions the systems treat as genuine.
arxiv-2509-15159:
Saket Chaturvedi, Gaurav Bagwe, Lan Zhang, and Xiaoyong Yuan attack retrieval-based AI through its standing prompts, in a 2025 paper. Such systems fetch documents to ground a model's answers. That fetch step opens new attack paths. Past attacks mostly bent the user's own query, a path that is often fixed or guarded in real use.

Standing prompts are the softer path: they are reused, shared in public, and rarely checked. The team's attack plants crafted prompts that quietly shift what gets fetched, while the user's question stays the same. Since the trick rides on trusted scaffolding, it stays hard to spot. The work warns that guarding the model and the query is not enough when the standing prompts can be turned.
arxiv-2509-15459:
Yiyi Liu leads a team of nine that rebuilds floor plans from point cloud maps. Old methods mark wall corners first, which breaks when data is noisy or parts are missing. Newer methods group lines, but fine detail still gets lost. The team wanted plans that stay whole and true to shape, with walls that meet cleanly.

Their network, CAGE, treats each wall piece as a directed edge with a clear path. A two query decoder joins noisy and hidden queries to steady training and speed it up. On two known data sets, the method tops past work on rooms, corners, and angles. It also transfers well to a data set it was not trained on.
arxiv-2509-15659:
Shan Cheng leads a team that probes the makeup of a light particle called f0(980). Their probe is a rare decay of a charm meson into two pions. Long standing tension pits simple cascade views against quark based reads of this particle's guts. The team bring a new tool: shape functions for the two pion system as a whole.

Their study is the first of its kind at this twist level for these decays. They find a lopsided term in the two pion shape functions that single particle functions lack. That term drives a large canceling between two parts of the rate. The predicted rate then falls well below the measured one. The pair system, they argue, is not mainly a simple quark pair.
arxiv-2509-15759:
Mohit Sharma leads a team that steers data toward fairness with proof attached. Biased data in, biased results out is a known flaw in fair learning. Past work steered data or model signals toward ideal forms, but without proof that the output would be fair. The team define an ideal spread strictly: any cost aware best fit on it must give exact group fair outcomes.

They cast the search for the nearest ideal spread as an optimization over a known distance. Fast solvers handle common spread families, like bell curves. On fake and real data, their steering lifts fairness without hurting accuracy, and sometimes helps both. They also steer a language model's inner signals to cut bias.
arxiv-2509-16359:
Underwater listening posts must measure background noise, but loud passing sounds corrupt those measures. David Campos Anchieta and John R. Buck blend several ranked-data filters into one noise estimator that adapts on its own. Older filters each pick a cutoff rank to dodge loud bursts, a choice that fails when burst rates shift without warning.

The blended version weights its parts by recent performance, favoring whichever has the least spread lately. Theory says it nears the best fixed choice, and tests on simulated and real data agree. It cleans spectrograms without anyone setting a threshold rank by hand.
arxiv-2509-16459:
Stars spend parts of their lives hidden in dust, and a new catalog catches them in the act across nineteen nearby galaxies. Hamid Hassani and thirty co-authors combine Webb, Hubble, and radio data to list tens of thousands of compact mid-infrared sources. Fake star tests set the depth each list reaches.

The sources sort into kinds from bright young clusters and red supergiants to aging stars rich in oxygen or carbon. Sources bright at the longer band supply a fair share of each galaxy's glow there. Dusty young clusters that stay faint in visible tracers are rare, which hints their hidden phase is brief.
arxiv-2509-16559:
Tsuyoshi Miyatsu, Myung-Ki Cheoun, Kyungsik Kim, and Koichi Saito model the dense hearts of neutron stars in a 2025 paper. At such high density, heavy particles called hyperons may appear. Their presence tends to soften the matter, which clashes with the great mass of some observed stars. This clash is known as the hyperon puzzle.

The team use a mean-field model tuned to lab data on nuclei. They work within a flavor scheme that links the particle types. Added terms help keep heavy stars possible. One coupling choice does most of that work. Their setup fits both lab and space data, and offers a plausible way past the puzzle.
arxiv-2509-16759:
Alexander Dranishnikov, working alone, compares two ways to measure motion planning in a 2025 math paper. One measure counts how hard it is to plan paths for points in a space. A newer, distributional version allows plans that work in a looser sense. Dranishnikov asks when the two measures agree for groups and shapes.

For two large classes of groups, he proves the measures are equal. One class is hyperbolic, the other nilpotent, both without torsion. For lens spaces, he gives upper bounds on the new measure. In prime cases, those bounds become exact. The work clarifies a modern tool in topology.
arxiv-2509-17159:
Sergei Kuksin, writing alone, compares two ways to study a class of tidy physical systems when small random shocks disturb them. The systems are integrable Hamiltonian systems, whose motion can be described in full when left alone. His 2025 arXiv paper focuses on what happens over long times, and in the limit of endless time.

One approach follows the motion of single solutions as the shocks average out. The other tracks how the whole spread of possible states evolves. Kuksin sets out both lines of work and weighs what each one proves. He then compares the random-shock results with the known results for steady, non-random pushes on the same systems. The paper serves as a guided map of a field he helped build.
arxiv-2509-17259:
Ilham Wicaksono and five co-authors probe the safety of AI agents in a 2025 arXiv paper. A lone model and the same model wired into tools and live surroundings may fail in distinct ways. Past work hints that model-level flaws do not capture the risks that appear once a model can act.

The team red-teamed GPT-OSS-20B, an open model, at both levels with harmful goals drawn from HarmBench. Their AgentSeer frame breaks agent runs into single actions and parts, so attacks can be watched step by step. Some attacks worked only inside the agent loop and stayed inert on the bare model. Repeated agent-level attacks cracked goals that fully failed at model level, and tool use raised the risk further. A few model-only tricks, in turn, died when moved into the agent setting.
arxiv-2509-17759:
Chengbo Yuan and eight co-authors let robot policies learn motions straight from human VR data. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a bottleneck: real robot data are scarce, and while images and language can be borrowed from the web, motion knowledge cannot. Human demonstrations hold a rich stock of manipulation moves, if a robot can absorb them.

Their framework, MotionTrans, joins a data collection rig, a pipeline that transforms human data for robot use, and a weighted cotraining strategy. Thirty human-robot tasks train together at once. Motions for a good share of the tasks moved from human data into deployable robot policies. Several tasks reached real success rates with no robot demonstrations at all, in zero-shot fashion. The authors frame the result as proof that human motion, properly translated, can teach robots new skills rather than just polish old ones.
arxiv-2509-17859:
Kai Schenck and Gasper Begus test if a speech model can learn Mandarin tones with no labels at all. Their 2025 paper uses a generative net that makes speech from hidden choice codes. Tones are a hard test, since pitch alone sets word sense apart.

All three trained models tied their choice codes to pitch gaps that mark tones. A model trained on male voices only coded tone in a steady way. The learnt steps look like a stage in how kids pick up tones. The team also maps where tone facts sit inside the net's layers.
arxiv-2509-18259:
Bibek Pokharel leads a large team that tames quantum chaos with measured feedback on a real quantum chip. Their 2025 paper runs adaptive circuits, where mid-run measures and resets steer the state as it evolves. The test bed is a quantum form of a classic chaotic map that scrambles facts fast.

Feedback fights to hold the state at a fixed point of that map. That fight drives a phase shift between quantum and classic behaviour, which the team sees on the chip. Runs used up to a hundred qubits and thousands of gates. Maths twins of the run, from noisy sims to product states, back the read.
arxiv-2509-18459:
Drug dose trials need a sound read on how response rises with dose. Jiangshan Zhang, Vivek Pradhan, and Yuxi Zhao study the Binary Emax model, a standard curve for such trials, in this 2025 paper. Trials in phase II are often small, and the usual estimation method leans on large-sample theory. That can bias the dose picked for later trials.

The team compares three bias-reduction methods: a classic correction, the Firth score tweak, and a penalized likelihood method using the Jeffreys prior. Wide simulations test bias and spread, including cases where the model form is wrong. The Firth and penalized methods both proved robust. The penalized method was most stable, with lower variance. A case study on a real phase II trial shows the methods at work. The authors recommend the penalized route when response may not rise smoothly.
arxiv-2509-18559:
Ultraviolet light from a star can help or harm life on its planets, and that light fades as the star ages. Xue Li and five co-authors trace that fading for nearly four hundred thousand dwarf stars in this 2025 paper. Their sample spans types from hot A stars to cool M dwarfs, with ages from a few million to ten billion years. Data come from the GALEX space telescope's near-ultraviolet views.

After correcting for how complete the sample is at each distance, clear paths emerge. Hot stars fade weakly on the main sequence. Sun-like stars fade steadily as spin-down weakens their magnetic activity. The coolest dwarfs drop fast as they settle onto the main sequence. The team also maps how the ultraviolet habitable zone moves with age. Sun-like and K-type stars keep the best overlap between warm and ultraviolet-safe zones over time.
arxiv-2509-18859:
Undergraduates rarely touch real data from a major particle physics experiment. John Waiton and eight co-authors built a teaching lab that does exactly that in this 2025 paper. Students work with data from MicroBooNE, a liquid-argon detector at Fermilab. Their quarry is the sterile neutrino, a proposed fourth kind of neutrino.

The search matters beyond the classroom: sterile neutrinos could bear on dark matter and the origin of neutrino mass. Past experiments have hinted at them without proof. In the lab, students learn oscillation theory, then analyze a real MicroBooNE sample. Statistical methods drive the search, and machine learning sharpens event sorting. Students are urged to try their own improvements. The paper presents the lab design and its physics payoff. It shows research-grade data can teach, not just publish.
arxiv-2509-18959:
Carles Batlle and Joaquim Gomis build a general action for a single particle moving in anti-de Sitter space with two space dimensions and one time dimension. Such curved spaces are a standard arena for testing ideas about gravity and symmetry. Their tool is the nonlinear realization framework, a method that builds actions from broken symmetries. The work appeared in a special issue honoring the memory of a colleague, Miguel Carlos Muñoz-Lecanda.

The authors find special sectors of the theory, called critical, and describe them through the parameters in the action. They also study how the particle moves and what the new terms in the action mean geometrically. By joining two chiral copies of a lower-dimensional action, they recover the same theory in new variables. That route exposes extra gauge symmetries hiding in the critical sectors, and they solve a key equation to first order.
arxiv-2509-19059:
Photosynthetic bacteria move energy from a ring of light-harvesting molecules toward a reaction center, and engineers copy that layout in quantum devices. Stephon Alexander and three co-authors model such a system: a donor ring of sites linked evenly to a central acceptor, driven by a single photon mode in a cavity. They track losses from spontaneous emission and from dephasing, the fading of quantum phase. In the clean, symmetric case the whole system collapses to three effective parts, giving exact formulas.

Near-perfect transfer arises when the photon mixes the parts into a dark channel that barely touches the ring, dodging loss. Disorder in the photon-ring coupling spoils this by waking lossy ring modes. Stronger coupling inside the ring can rescue efficiency by moving the lossy channels out of the way. The authors read the model as a tunable quantum-optical transport device with clear design rules.
arxiv-2509-19159:
Reinforcement learning agents that learn task after task often forget the old tasks, a failure called catastrophic forgetting. Qingfeng Lan and two co-authors study what inside the neural network makes forgetting worse. Recent fixes mostly change the learning algorithm. This team instead examines the activation functions, the small nonlinear switches inside the network, and how their gradients behave during training.

Besides sparse activity, they find that sparse gradients also protect old knowledge. They design a new family, elephant activation functions, that produce both sparse outputs and sparse gradients. Swapping them into standard value-based learning methods, with no other change, made networks far more resilient to forgetting. Learning became more sample-efficient and memory-efficient as a result. The finding gives designers an architectural lever against forgetting, not just an algorithmic one.
arxiv-2509-19459:
Some memory keeps its data after a crash, but only if the code forces each save to reach storage. Programmers must add flush and fence steps by hand, and missed steps are a common bug source. Yutong Guo, Weiyu Luo, and Brian Demsky built PMRobust, a compiler that adds those steps on its own. Past tools could flag a missed step only when a test happened to expose it.

PMRobust studies the code as a whole and guards newly made objects with extra care. The team tried it on known memory libraries and data structures. Added cost stayed well under one percent on average next to hand-tuned code. The result is a stronger promise: programs built with it should not lose saved data to a missed flush.
arxiv-2509-19659:
Vision-language models answer questions about images, but social cues in a photo can bend their answers. Aravind Narayanan, Vahid Reza Khazaie, and Shaina Raza built a benchmark of news images to measure that bending. The set holds over thirteen hundred image-question pairs from varied outlets. Each pair carries checked answers plus tags for age, gender, race, occupation, and sport.

A large language model served as judge, with humans verifying its calls. Visual context shifted open-ended answers in systematic ways. Bias risk ran highest for gender and occupation cues, and varied by model. More faithful answers did not guarantee less bias. The team released prompts, rubric, and code for repeat use. News images are a stern test because their social cues are real, not staged.
arxiv-2509-19959:
Rowhammer attacks flip bits in memory by hammering neighboring rows, and Antoine Plin with two co-authors move the hammer onto the graphics card. Their work-in-progress report uses OpenGL compute shaders to drive rapid, patterned memory access. Statistical targeting spreads the hits to dodge existing mitigations. Known patterns are planted first, then victim rows are hammered while errors are watched.

Parameters adjust on the fly to raise the flip rate within a tight time budget. Graphics processors bring massive parallelism to the attack, which is exactly the worry. Defenders study such routes to close them before abuse spreads. The authors frame the work as an exploration of feasibility. GPU paths to system memory are a growing surface that memory defenses must cover.
arxiv-2509-20259:
How many small integer matrices share the same determinant? Jonathan Chapman and Akshat Mudgal answer that counting question in a 2025 arXiv paper in analytic number theory. They count two-by-two matrices whose entries lie in a fixed range and whose determinant equals a chosen positive value. Earlier work had estimated the count with weaker error control.

Their main result gives an exact main term plus a sharply bounded error. The main term involves a sum over the divisors of the chosen determinant. For small determinants, the error shows square-root cancellation, a strong form of randomness in the count. For large determinants, they show the error is close to the best possible size. The paper quantitatively improves the earlier estimates of Afifurrahman and of Ganguly and Guria.
arxiv-2509-20359:
UGCA 320, a small gas-rich galaxy near our own, is profiled by Adebusola Alabi and three co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. It belongs to a loose, isolated group of dwarf galaxies. The team combined space telescope images with deep spectra from two ground instruments. Their goal was to read both its stars and its ionized gas.

The galaxy's disc is dominated by young, metal-poor stars about one hundred twenty million years old. Abundant ionized gas glows mostly from recent star formation. Stars and gas rotate in the same sense, though the stars spin faster and perhaps in a slightly different plane. A sharp change in motion appears partway out, and the outer disc looks distorted. The authors read those signs as scars of a recent tidal encounter with the neighboring galaxy UGCA 319.
arxiv-2509-20459:
The universe holds more matter than antimatter, and Debasish Borah and four co-authors want to hunt the cause at colliders, as a 2025 arXiv paper sets out. Their model adds new colored particles and singlets to the known set, guided by an idea called Dirac leptogenesis. Heavy colored fermions fall apart out of balance, making opposed gaps between matter and antimatter in two hidden sectors. A resonant boost makes the gap large at collider energies.

That same boost makes the decays open to direct tests.
