Next to known signs like jets with missing energy and shifted vertices, the team points to charge and forward-backward gaps at future muon colliders. Those tests could check the idea head-on. The model also yields a singlet scalar that can serve as dark matter. Its heat history fits the traits dark matter needs, near the Higgs resonance.
arxiv-2509-21359:
Retrieved context full of noise quietly undermines retrieval augmented generation. Credit goes to Jiale Deng and 4 co-authors. That method grounds language model answers in external documents. Poor retrieved context, full of noise, hurts answer quality. Past selection methods use fixed quality metrics and show limited gains. The authors argue those methods ignore the query, context list, and generator as a whole.

They recast context quality as an inference time data valuation problem. Their Contextual Influence Value measures the drop in performance when one context is removed. That integrates the query, the full list, and the generator. Selection then keeps contexts with high positive influence. The approach aims for more effective retrieval augmented generation with cleaner, more useful context.
arxiv-2509-22059:
Partha Konar, Vishal S. Ngairangbam, Michael Spannowsky, and Deepanshu Srivastava ask what deep networks actually learn when they sort particle jets. Jets are sprays of particles from high-energy collisions, and telling quark jets from gluon jets is a standard task. Their 2025 paper builds graph networks with physics rules baked in: safety under soft or split emissions, and symmetry under shifts and rotations in the detector's angular map.

On simulated jet data, the physics-aware networks matched strong baselines on accuracy while proving steadier across training runs. Their inner representations also spread information across several directions that can be interpreted. By fitting known jet observables, called energy flow polynomials, onto those leading directions, the team tied the learned features to established quantities in the theory of the strong force. The authors argue that building symmetry and safety in from the start yields models that are both sturdier and readable.
arxiv-2509-22159:
Jie Zhou and eight co-authors survey fifty years of automatic target recognition in radar images. Synthetic aperture radar can image the ground in nearly all weather and light, which makes it a key source of information about objects and scenes. Recognizing targets in those images automatically has been a central and hard problem in remote sensing for five decades. Their 2025 review, accepted by an IEEE journal, is presented as the first full account of the field.

The survey gathers roughly two hundred sixty research contributions. It covers the core challenges of the task, the important data sets, and the strengths and limits of representative methods. The authors argue that modern AI, especially large models and agents, could transform the field, yet its potential for radar images stays largely locked. They close with future directions, calling for better large-scale data sets, fairer benchmarks, and safe open-source ecosystems.
arxiv-2509-22559:
Zhijun Tu and 5 co-authors found superconductivity in a crystal where loose electrons sit in empty spaces. The material is cubic La3Al, grown as a single crystal. It behaves like a normal metal with no structural change, then turns superconducting below about six kelvin. Detailed tests show it is a bulk type-II superconductor of BCS type, the classic phonon-driven kind.

Theory places extra electrons at the center of the cubic cell, not bound to any atom. Such materials are called electrides. The calculations also confirm that electron-phonon coupling drives the pairing. The result makes this crystal a new electride superconductor, joining a small family of such materials.
arxiv-2509-22859:
Thuyen Dang, Yuliya Gorb, and Silvia Jiménez Bolaños homogenize a semilinear elliptic equation whose coefficients may jump. Homogenization replaces a fine-scale, rapidly varying problem with a smooth effective one. The equation is semilinear, so its reaction term depends on the solution itself, and the second-order operator's coefficients can be discontinuous. The authors first establish that the fine-scale problem has exactly one solution. An a priori estimate bounds that solution in terms of the data.

The homogenized equation is then derived using two-scale convergence, a method that tracks oscillations at both scales. A corrector result completes the picture, showing how to rebuild the fine-scale solution from the smooth one.
arxiv-2509-22959:
Adam A Corrao and 7 co-authors link AI agents to live synchrotron experiments at NSLS-II. Such beamlines often collect data first and study it only after the run ends. Their modular framework plugs agents into the Bluesky control system. Agents cut data, cluster it, fit Gaussian process models, and steer the next shots by Bayesian optimization.

Users watch agent choices and live plots as the run proceeds. One demo mapped an aluminum-nickel-platinum library with two beamlines at once. Teams could swap between AI-led and grid mapping mid-run. A digital twin test showed AI mapping beat grid and random plans. It found phase edges and rare minority phases with fewer shots.
arxiv-2509-23259:
Call transcripts hide user intent in messy, jargon-heavy sentences that fixed rules miss. Soumick Sarker and Abhijit Kumar Rai built Fin-ExBERT to extract the sentences that carry intent. A domain-adapted BERT backbone does the reading, tuned with low-rank adapters. A graph augmentation and a trainable plugin extend the base model. Training runs in two stages with progressive unfreezing.

A dynamic threshold, set by probability curvature, decides extraction under uncertainty. That avoids brittle fixed cutoffs. On real financial call data, precision and F1 scores ran strong. Outputs stay interpretable for audit and question-answering flows. The framework supports batched scoring and calibrated export.
arxiv-2509-23459:
Turning plain questions into database queries with a large language model often means sending private data to an outside firm. Sepideh Abedini and 5 co-authors built MaskSQL to cut that risk. Their method uses abstraction: names and details in the prompt are masked, while the facts needed to form a correct query stay in place. That differs from deleting text outright or swapping in broader terms.

MaskSQL also lets users set how much privacy to trade for accuracy. In tests it beat small local models built for the same task. Its scores came close to those of top large-model systems, while keeping private details out of the prompt.
arxiv-2509-23759:
Transcribing violin audio into notes misses how each note was played, yet technique gives the instrument its expressive range. Ting-Kang Wang and 3 co-authors built VioPTT, a light cascade model that transcribes playing technique along with pitch onset and offset. To dodge the cost of hand labels, they also release MOSA-VPT, a high-quality synthetic data set of violin techniques. Training leans on that synthetic supply.

The model generalized well to real note-level technique recordings. It also reached state-of-the-art transcription performance in their tests. The authors claim the first unified framework that joins violin transcription with technique prediction in one system.
arxiv-2509-23859:
Rating facial beauty with AI risks baking social bias into software that then calls itself objective. Djamel Eddine Boukhari, the sole author, proposes FairViT-GAN to predict beauty while fighting that bias. A convolutional branch reads local texture, a transformer branch reads global harmony, and an adversarial debiasing step trains the features to hide protected attributes like ethnicity. Visualizations show what each branch attends to, adding transparency.

On the SCUT-FBP5500 benchmark, the model set a new accuracy mark in the author's tests. It also cut the performance gap between ethnic subgroups by more than four fifths, while the adversary's guesses about ethnicity fell to near chance.
arxiv-2509-24159:
Preference data used to align language models is noisy: raters err, instructions clash, and some feedback is careless or hostile. Xiaoyang Cao and 6 co-authors built RE-PO, a method that treats each label as suspect. An expectation-maximization step infers how likely each label is correct, then weights each case by that score during training.

The team also shows how to turn other alignment methods into robust versions in a systematic way. When the model is well calibrated, the method can even read off how noisy a data set truly is. Applied to four leading methods on two model families, it raised win rates on a standard arena test by up to several points.
arxiv-2509-24359:
Attack images fool deep networks, and many defenses fail once an attacker can estimate gradients well. Amira Guesmi and Muhammad Shafique trace the problem to gradient consensus: randomized defenses tend to yield aligned gradients, which attackers exploit to craft perturbations that transfer across changes. Their defense, DRIFT, trains a set of light filters to break that alignment on purpose.

The filters push apart the gradient and output responses of the network while keeping clean predictions intact. Training mixes prediction consistency, separation terms, and robustness goals. On ImageNet, DRIFT beat leading defenses under adaptive, transfer, and gradient-free attacks. It did so at negligible runtime and memory cost.
arxiv-2509-24559:
Robot policies trained by reinforcement may quietly build an inner model of their world, or they may just react. Marco Molinari and 3 co-authors probe OpenVLA, a leading vision-language-action model, for signs of such a world model. They use embedding arithmetic: take the difference between embeddings of states in sequence and test whether that transition vector can be read back from the model's own activations.

Probes trained across layers predicted transitions well above baseline, which suggests the knowledge sits in the model rather than in the probes. An earlier checkpoint showed weaker signs, hinting the world model grows with training. A sparse autoencoder pipeline is outlined for deeper study.
arxiv-2509-25959:
Minxing Sun and four co-authors rebuild state estimation so the neural network itself becomes the thing being estimated, in a 2025 paper. Classical estimators track a moving target through a hand-built model of its motion, which is laborious and brittle when dynamics change. Pure neural estimators avoid the model but demand huge precomputed training sets and ignore estimation theory. The authors propose a unified structure with no target model at all.

Inside it, the network's inputs and all its weights count as hidden states, estimated online as data arrives. Three classic estimators, extended Kalman, unscented Kalman, and particle, were each installed in the structure. Benchmarks against seven leading neural estimators across three scenarios test whether the marriage of theory and learning keeps the best of both.
arxiv-2510-00159:
Kyle Hansen wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on quantitative topology, the study of how much work a geometric deformation takes. A nullhomotopy is a way to shrink a map gradually to a constant one. The question is how much volume that shrinking must sweep through. Hansen works with nilpotent spaces, targets built from towers of simple fibrations.

The main tool is Manin's Shadowing Principle, which turns algebraic approximations into genuine nearby maps. Hansen extends that principle from single fibrations to whole finite towers of them. With the extension, he bounds the growth of nullhomotopy volumes for Lipschitz maps. In the simplest case the bounds nearly match the best known results for simply connected targets. For coformal targets the refined bounds are nearly sharp, he shows. The work tightens what topologists can promise about the cost of untangling maps.
arxiv-2510-00259:
Ethan Herror and five colleagues published this 2025 paper on drone inspections run by AI agents. Factories need regular checks of gauges and equipment, and drones can reach awkward spots indoors. The authors propose a hierarchy of language-model agents to fly those missions. One head agent plans and judges results, while worker agents each fly a single drone.

Each worker follows a cycle the authors call ReActEval: plan, reason, act, then evaluate. The evaluation step checks outcomes against the goal and triggers replanning when needed. Everything runs in natural language, so operators need no special control training. Tests in simulation used two worker drones on tasks of rising complexity. Jobs ranged from simple hops to finding and reading a pressure gauge. The authors report solid task completion, and they frame the design as a flexible step beyond fixed drone routines.
arxiv-2510-00359:
Eric Gelphman and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on training neural controllers for hard, high-dimensional systems. Value-function networks can approximate optimal feedback control when the Hamiltonian has an explicit formula. Many real problems, like space shuttle reentry or bicycle dynamics, hide that formula inside an implicit relation. Existing methods stall there, and the authors aim to unblock them.

Their approach parameterizes the value function and derives the control from its gradient. That link comes from the bond between Pontryagin's Maximum Principle and dynamic programming. Training uses Jacobian-free backpropagation, which sidesteps costly matrix inversions along the trajectory. The authors show this shortcut still yields true descent directions for the control objective. Experiments then learn working feedback controllers across several implicit-Hamiltonian scenarios. The result extends end-to-end learned control to a class of problems it could not touch before.
arxiv-2510-00459:
Bizi Huang, Weizhong Fu, and Ji Chen published this 2025 paper on simulating electrons driven by intense laser fields. The time-dependent Schrodinger equation governs that motion, but exact solutions explode in cost as systems grow. Their method marries a stochastic representation framework with a neural network wavefunction. The network flexibly approximates how the quantum state evolves in real time.

Tests began with one-dimensional single-electron systems under strong laser pulses. The method tracked energy and dipole changes during ionization with high accuracy. It needs fewer samples than grid methods and avoids artificial absorbing boundaries altogether. A three-dimensional extension proved feasible, though stability weakened as the state grew more complex. The authors flag smoothness of the network's output as the key open problem. The work targets attosecond physics, where electrons tear free on the fastest chemical timescales.
arxiv-2510-00659:
Akhilesh and Joseph simulate melting of a colloidal crystal on a two-dimensional periodic substrate in this 2025 arXiv preprint on statistical physics. Colloids settling on a square-patterned surface face a clash, since particles prefer triangular order while the substrate imposes squares. When the two interaction strengths are comparable, the system forms a partially pinned solid with true long-range order. The authors vary the substrate's lattice spacing at fixed filling and watch how that solid melts.

For wide spacings the solid passes to a modulated liquid through a single crossover transition. For tighter spacings melting takes two stages, with an intermediate hexatic phase between crystal and liquid. Finite-size scaling of the specific heat showed both transitions are second order in character. The behaviour departs from classic KTHNY melting theory, which guides the design of tunable colloidal systems.
arxiv-2510-00759:
Rosko, a student at the University of Hagen, presents a claimed proof about Hilbert's tenth problem in this 2025 arXiv manuscript, now in its third version with corrections. The famous problem asks for an algorithm that decides whether integer equations have solutions, and no such algorithm exists in general. Whether that undecidability still holds for equations of degree three alone stayed open for decades.

Rosko constructs, for any suitable formal theory, a single cubic polynomial whose natural-number solutions would mirror provability of that theory's Gödel sentence. The construction encodes proof sequences with a Diophantine beta function and Zeckendorf representations of numbers. Guard gadgets and repeated degree reduction keep every constraint at degree three or below. If the argument holds, degree two remains decidable while degree three marks the exact boundary.
arxiv-2510-01059:
Paredes Salazar, Usevitch, and Goel introduce predictive control barrier functions in this 2025 arXiv paper on safe control. Control barrier functions keep a system inside a safe set by filtering its inputs, but discrete-time versions stumble when input delays raise the system's relative degree. Existing fixes build auxiliary barrier functions, which complicates implementation and can shrink the safe set needlessly. Unknown delays from unmodeled actuator dynamics are common in real hardware.

Their framework looks ahead over a prediction horizon and builds a barrier function for an associated system with relative degree one. The resulting safe set then matches the intended constraints exactly, with no auxiliary functions. Simulations cover a double integrator with an input delay and a bicopter with position constraints. In the bicopter case, unmodeled inner-loop dynamics create exactly the delay problem the method was designed for.
arxiv-2510-01159:
Kviman and five co-authors improve multi-marginal flow matching for trajectory inference in this 2025 arXiv paper on machine learning for science. Many experiments, such as single-cell sequencing, give only snapshots of a population at separate time points, never the path of any individual. Flow matching can infer the missing dynamics, but multi-time versions rely on fixed interpolation schemes that fit the intermediate snapshots poorly. Their method, ALI-CFM, learns the interpolating curves themselves with a neural network.

A GAN-inspired adversarial loss trains those curves so their intermediate distributions match the observed snapshots closely. The authors show the resulting smooth interpolants are unique under mild assumptions. A flow matching stage then converts them into a vector field for the full dynamics. On spatial transcriptomics and cell tracking data, ALI-CFM beat existing baselines, and it matched them on single-cell trajectory prediction.
arxiv-2510-01459:
Chen, Koenig, and Dilkina train reasoning models more effectively by choosing each training batch according to how long the model's answers currently run. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards drives modern reasoning training, and most improvements tinker with the loss. Response length, meanwhile, signals difficulty and the overthinking failure mode.

Their meta-algorithm samples dynamically, selecting data by average response length at each step. Multiple base models and datasets showed consistent gains in learning effectiveness. Ablations dissect which ways of using the length signal actually help. Dynamic sampling improved effectiveness itself, not merely efficiency, a first for the approach. DeepSeek's reasoning release made verifiable-reward training the central recipe. Overthinking wastes tokens, and length exposes the waste. Selection happens fresh at every training step, not once upfront. Efficiency and effectiveness finally improve together here. What to train on matters as much as how.
arxiv-2510-01959:
Sanders and Bastiaansen teach early warning systems to tell a true tipping point from mere pattern formation in this 2025 paper. Ecosystems and climate subsystems can shift abruptly once pushed past a threshold. Standard warning signs detect growing instability, but they cannot say what kind of change is coming. A catastrophic homogeneous collapse and a gentle Turing patterning look alike to those signs.

Their method estimates the system's dispersion relation from noisy space-time data. That curve reveals whether the approaching bifurcation changes the whole system at once or breaks it into spatial patterns. They validated the approach on synthetic data from a modified Klausmeier vegetation model. Tests varied the noise properties and the distance to the threshold. The authors also mapped how much data the method needs to perform well. A spatial warning system built this way could sharpen forecasts and improve conservation timing.
arxiv-2510-02259:
Kreiman and five co-authors show that plain transformers can learn molecular structure from coordinates alone in this 2025 paper. Graph neural networks dominate molecular machine learning by passing messages along hand-built bond graphs. Those graphs impose fixed receptive fields and slow, sparse computation. The authors ask whether an unmodified transformer, fed raw Cartesian coordinates, can do the same job.

Trained under a matched compute budget, their transformer reached competitive energy and force errors against a state-of-the-art equivariant graph network on the OMol25 dataset. Its attention weights learned physically sensible patterns, decaying with interatomic distance. Without hard-coded biases, the model flexibly adapts those patterns across molecular environments. Performance also scaled predictably with more training resources. The graph prior, long treated as essential chemistry knowledge, turns out to be learnable.
arxiv-2510-03159:
Marić, Paljk, and Zadnik explain why some quantum systems relax at a crawl. Kinetically constrained models move only where local rules allow. A coupling knob sets how strong the energy penalty runs. At large coupling the dynamics nearly freeze in places. The authors expand around that frozen limit. A nested hierarchy of frozen states appears in the math. Each level stays frozen for a time set by a power of the coupling.

Distance explains the rungs of that ladder. Sites where motion is allowed sit apart in space. The wider the gap, the longer the freeze lasts. Correlations inside frozen states decay in slow plateaus. The authors compute those plateau heights with corrections included. States outside the frozen family relax quickly instead. Krylov complexity tracks how the frozen states evolve. The picture unifies slow relaxation and dynamical heterogeneity. Rydberg atom platforms can test these predictions directly.
arxiv-2510-03259:
Kim, Jang, and Yang teach reasoning models to know how they think, and accuracy follows. A model with meta-awareness can predict its own difficulty sense. The authors first prove that big reasoners lack this skill. Their meta-predictions sit badly misaligned with actual rollout behavior. The MASA pipeline trains meta-awareness from self-generated signals alone. No external teaching data feeds the alignment process. Predictive gating and early cutoffs keep training efficient.

Useless prompts get filtered before they burn compute. Hopeless long rollouts stop early under the same logic. Training reached target quality notably faster than standard GRPO. Accuracy on a hard math contest benchmark jumped by a fifth. Six math benchmarks averaged a solid gain as well. Out-of-domain tests showed the skill travels beyond math. Science and logic suites improved by smaller but real margins. Thirteen benchmarks in total confirmed broader generalization.
arxiv-2510-03559:
Chen and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on PrivacyMotiv, a tool that helps user experience designers take privacy seriously during design reviews. Reviews often skip privacy because designers lack knowledge, empathy for odd case users, and confidence in spotting harms. The system invents vivid personas who are vulnerable to privacy risks, then walks through their journeys with a product. Stories show how ordinary features, like friend activity feeds, can enable stalking or unwanted location tracking after breakups.

Sixteen professional designers tried the tool against their own review methods on two tasks. Empathy, motivation, and perceived usefulness all rose significantly with PrivacyMotiv in the study. Reviews also named problems and fixes in more specific, wider ranging ways. Narrative journeys seem to move designers in a way checklists do not. The work argues that motivation, not just tooling, is the missing ingredient in privacy aware design practice.
arxiv-2510-03759:
Tas presents a 2025 arXiv paper computing the magnon spectrum of CrSb, an altermagnet, with many body perturbation theory. Altermagnets are a recognized class of magnets whose spin split bands mimic ferromagnets while the magnetization stays antiferromagnetic. Their spin wave excitations, dubbed altermagnons, will govern magnetic devices, yet their spectra were unmapped. The calculation resolves the magnon bands across the Brillouin zone and tracks how long the two chiral branches live.

The spin split structure shows up clearly in the magnon spectrum, confirming the altermagnetic character dynamically. Altermagnon energies reach two hundred seventy five millielectronvolts at the K point. Along one direction, large spin splitting makes the two chiral lifetimes differ by about twenty femtoseconds. Lifetime asymmetry matters because devices would read or write information through one chirality. Spectra give experimentalists targets for neutron scattering confirmation. They also tell engineers which frequencies and lifetimes a CrSb based device could exploit.
arxiv-2510-04159:
Hhan and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper introducing proofs of quantum memory, a way to verify a remote quantum device's memory claims. A startup might boast a huge quantum memory with long coherence, but a classical investor cannot check that with proofs of quantumness alone. Those protocols show something non-classical happened, not how many qubits were held or for how long. The authors define an interactive protocol where a classical verifier confirms both quantities over a classical channel.

They give two constructions based on the hardness of the learning-with-errors problem. The first runs in four rounds with negligible soundness error under a subexponential hardness assumption. The second uses polynomially many rounds with weaker soundness under a polynomial assumption. They also prove lower bounds: such proofs imply one-way puzzles, a core cryptographic primitive. Verifiable quantum memory claims will matter as quantum cloud services start selling capacity.
arxiv-2510-04359:
Kim, Saad, and Calin present this 2025 arXiv paper on wireless machine learning models that must generalize to new environments with very little multimodal data. Situation-aware 6G decisions fuse LiDAR, camera, radar, and GPS inputs, but models latch onto spurious modality-specific features and fail under domain shift. Public multimodal wireless datasets are extremely scarce, and measuring every environment is impractical. Their two-phase framework first teaches each base station the physics of its own environment through a physics-based loss.

In the second phase, collaborative domain adaptation lets knowledgeable base stations guide underperforming ones. A new dataset built from CARLA driving simulation and millimeter-wave channel modeling tests signal strength prediction from the four modalities. Physics-based training needed only about an eighth of the samples to match a leading baseline. Collaborative adaptation converged with about a quarter of the samples and a fifth of the compute.
arxiv-2510-04459:
Samuel Verburg, Efren Fernandez Grande, and Peter Gerstoft wrote this 2025 paper on rebuilding sound fields from sparse sensors. A sound field fills a room over time, yet sensors can sample it at only a few points. Physics based models can fill the gaps, but they often lack flexibility. Neural networks that learn physics from a penalty term can train poorly. The team instead wired a true physics solver into the training loop.

A neural network proposes the starting state of the sound field. A numerical solver then advances the wave equation, and its steps can be differentiated for training. Physics thus acts as a hard rule, not a soft suggestion in the loss. An added sparsity push keeps solutions sensible when data is very scarce. In experiments, the method rebuilt fields under extreme undersampling. It beat physics informed neural networks on both accuracy and convergence speed.
arxiv-2510-04659:
Piscitelli and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on reading telescope flaws from stray light. X ray telescopes such as XMM Newton focus light with mirror shells in a Wolter design. A source just outside the view can bounce once inside a shell and paint arcs across the detector. The team built an algorithm called SHADE that works backward from the arcs.

Each shell tilt is captured by numbers, its tilt size and its tilt direction. SHADE searches those numbers until the predicted arcs match the arcs on the detector. The team tested the method on observations of a bright X ray binary named GX5 1. For one shell, the fit recovered a tilt of about twenty two arcseconds with a direction. The tool can serve any Wolter style telescope, before or after launch. Knowing which shell leans, and by much, guides repair of alignment models.
arxiv-2510-05059:
Junlin Wang and six co-authors attack a waiting problem in multi-model AI systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. Teams of language models can answer better than one model alone. The catch is delay: the final answer cannot start until earlier models finish. That wait, called time to first token, hurts chatbots and other live tools.

Their fix, staircase streaming, starts the final response as soon as partial outputs arrive. The pipeline overlaps the stages instead of running them in strict sequence. Experiments showed the wait fell by up to 93 percent. Response quality stayed intact at the same time. The trade-off is that each multi-agent method needs small modifications before the trick applies.
arxiv-2510-05159:
Léo Boisvert and nine co-authors expose hidden backdoors in the AI agent supply chain in this 2025 arXiv paper. Fine-tuning agents on interaction data makes them capable. It also gives attackers openings to plant secret triggers. A triggered agent may leak private data or act maliciously while looking normal.

The team formalizes three realistic attack routes. Attackers can poison fine-tuning data directly, ship a pre-backdoored base model, or poison the environment where training traces are collected. On two standard agent benchmarks, a few poisoned demonstrations planted backdoors that fired with over 80 percent success. Four guardrail models and a weight-based defense all failed to catch the behavior. Task performance stayed near clean levels, hiding the compromise.
arxiv-2510-05259:
Adamczyk and six co-authors design a photon detector for the future Electron-Ion Collider in this 2025 arXiv paper. The collider's luminosity must be known to about one percent accuracy. Directly counting bremsstrahlung photons is the most robust route to that number. The catch is a brutal rate: over a billion photons arrive every second.

The team proposes a sampling calorimeter of copper with embedded quartz fibers. Silicon photomultipliers read out the light those fibers collect. Geant4 simulations give initial performance results under the extreme EIC conditions. The design should survive the enormous rates while still resolving single-photon energies. Good energy resolution enables the data-driven calibration that precision luminosity demands. Suitable fast readout electronics remain the main open challenge.
arxiv-2510-05459:
Bevilacqua and Bowen study a quantity called cost in measured group theory. Cost measures how cheaply a group's actions can be generated by a graph-like structure. A group has fixed price when every free action of the group shares the same cost. Their 2025 paper seeks general tests for when that common cost equals one.

The authors build their test around a distance function chosen on the group itself. When two groups meet a stated growth condition, their product passes the test. In particular, any countable group multiplied by itself has fixed price one. That case had stayed open when neither factor alone had the right subgroup. The result supports an old conjecture that every group has a fixed price. It widens earlier work on product groups. The paper develops the whole argument from scratch for new readers.
arxiv-2510-05859:
Von Bothmer extends a Darboux integrability test to points at infinity. Darboux theory builds first integrals of polynomial vector fields from invariant curves. His earlier invariant used only affine singularities of those curves. The 2025 note incorporates the line at infinity on equal footing.

The invariant's value depends purely on the integral curve's geometry. It never needs the differential form itself for computation. That purity yields effective criteria certifying Darboux integrability in new cases. Affine data alone could not settle those cases before. Centers matter because a rational first integral forces closed trajectories. As an application, six new components of the cubic center variety appear. They sit in codimension eleven, alongside two recovered known components. Finite-field numerics hint that many more center components remain undiscovered. The method applies uniformly to all forms sharing one curve configuration.
arxiv-2510-05959:
Zhang and colleagues study platoon control when shared data is rounded to coarse steps. Cars in a platoon drive as a convoy and share private state data. Rounding shrinks the data flow but coarsens the control signals. Their 2025 paper compares fixed-step and random-step rounding for control and privacy.

Fixed-step rounding keeps system errors within fixed bounds for all time. With no extra side data, third parties cannot pin down the private states. Random-step rounding drives errors to zero on average, with bounded spread. It also meets differential privacy even against well-informed third parties. A tuning problem maps how step size trades control quality against privacy. Shielding grows stronger exactly when the other side knows more side data. Tests show the gaps between the two methods. Traffic flow and safety motivate platooning. Picking a rounding rule becomes a clear design choice, not a default.
arxiv-2510-06359:
Brunelli, Cicoli, and Pedro use dynamical systems methods to study cosmic superstrings and the overshoot problem in a 2025 string cosmology paper. Moduli fields tend to race past their late-time minima instead of settling, the classic overshoot problem. They include fundamental strings and effective strings from branes wrapped on internal cycles.

The analysis covers the full volume modulus potential, with and without radiation. One clear result emerges. An initial population of NS5-brane strings suffices to stabilize the modulus in its minimum, even without radiation. The mechanism is energy transfer, since string tension depends on the volume modulus. While the modulus oscillates around its minimum, superstring energy density is generically very large. That opens the possibility of a detectable gravitational wave signal. They find no evidence for efficient resonant enhancement from the oscillating tension.
arxiv-2510-06659:
Shouzhen Gu and five co-authors study a candidate design for a quantum memory that protects itself. Their 2025 paper examines layer codes, a family of three-dimensional stabilizer codes. A self-correcting memory would hold quantum data without constant active repair. Layer codes offer strong scaling and a growing energy barrier against errors.

The authors supply two decoding algorithms with proven guarantees. One handles random local noise, and the other handles adversarial noise. They prove layer codes count as partially self-correcting memories. That status beats earlier analyzed designs, such as the cubic code and the welded solid code. A broader insight follows from their analysis. Partial self-correction may be common, since it can arise from a diverging energy barrier alone. Random versions of layer codes also achieve near-optimal scaling. The work separates the idea of a self-correcting system from a usable memory, a useful distinction.
arxiv-2510-06759:
Zhong-Xia Shang and five colleagues link two core ideas in quantum computing. Their 2025 paper connects dissipative dynamics, described by Lindblad equations, with quantum phase estimation. Phase estimation is a quantum algorithm for reading out energy values. It reaches the best possible scaling, known as the Heisenberg limit.

The authors show that certain simple dissipative processes can be reshaped into phase estimation tasks. Those processes, however, only reach the weaker standard quantum limit. That gap hints that dissipative evolution can be sped up quadratically. They confirm the hint with a simulation algorithm whose cost grows as the square root of time. The mechanism differs from Hamiltonian fast-forwarding cases. As a bonus, their fast simulation becomes a new phase estimation method with Heisenberg-limit scaling. The algorithm covers a broader family of noise processes built from Pauli terms. Exponential gains in accuracy and ancilla count appear against the standard approach.
arxiv-2510-07059:
Abdessamad Ahouita, Rene Baltazar, M'hammed Kahoui, and Sergey Gaifullin catalog the symmetries of a family of algebras built from polynomials. Their 2025 paper studies Danielewski-type algebras, defined by one relation among three variables over an algebraically closed field. Such algebras are test cases for hard questions about polynomial maps. The symmetries here are the algebra's automorphisms.

The authors give a complete description of the automorphism group as an abstract group. That settles exactly which ones these algebras admit. They then turn to derivations, tiny-scale versions of those symmetries. For any derivation that is not locally nilpotent, they study the group that fixes it. That group collects the maps leaving the derivation fixed. They prove it is always a linear algebraic group. Its dimension never exceeds three, a tight and concrete bound. Results like these feed affine algebraic geometry, where knowing them guides the sorting of the spaces.
arxiv-2510-07459:
Shavit and Goldberger introduce MoGU, a forecasting ensemble that lets each expert's own uncertainty decide its vote. Their 2025 paper extends mixture-of-experts models for regression and time series. Conventional ensembles output bare numbers and gate them by the input's features. MoGU's experts instead each output a bell curve: a forecast mean plus a variance expressing doubt. The gate then weights experts by those variances directly. An expert that knows it is lost on this input automatically speaks more softly in the final blend.

Across diverse forecasting benchmarks, the uncertainty-gated blend beat single models and conventional mixtures. The wins held across architectures and forecast horizons. Just as valuable, the stated uncertainties tracked actual errors closely, so users can tell when to distrust a forecast. Code is released openly.
arxiv-2510-07559:
Corenflos and Dau give practitioners a way to watch Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers converge in the divergences theorists actually analyze. Their 2025 paper closes a long-standing gap. Theory measures convergence with statistical divergences, but everyday diagnostics track cruder proxies and cannot certify the quantities proofs use. The method runs interacting chains and applies a coupling-based weight harmonization scheme. That produces computable, consistent weights for the chains' samples relative to the target distribution.

The bounds are proven to tighten over time and converge to zero as the chains reach stationarity, so a shrinking number is a genuine certificate rather than a vibe. Numerical experiments show the diagnostic is practical and competitive with standard tools. For Bayesian workflows in science and industry, where a silently unconverged sampler can poison downstream decisions, a monitor that speaks the theory's own language is a substantial upgrade.
arxiv-2510-07959:
Rubinstein, Raible, Gubri, and Oh at the University of Tübingen wrote this 2025 paper on cutting evaluation costs. Full benchmarks can burn thousands of GPU hours per model. A common shortcut scores models on an anchor subset and predicts the full result. Anchor choice depends on clustering data. The authors argue that what counts is not variety in the samples themselves. It is variety in how models respond to them.

Their method, DISCO, picks the test items where models disagree most. A greedy rule using per-item statistics replaces global clustering entirely. They show the rule is theoretically optimal for greedy selection. Across four well-known benchmarks, DISCO predicted full performance at state-of-the-art accuracy. The authors report cost cuts of over ninety-nine percent with minimal error in their conclusion. Cheaper evaluation could let small labs test models often and audit deployed systems.
arxiv-2510-08159:
Kerenidis and Cherrat wrote this 2025 paper training reinforcement-learning agents that rediscover famous quantum algorithms on their own. Their agents learn by episodic interaction and reward, with no access to known solutions. One agent learned an efficient logarithmic-depth circuit for the Quantum Fourier Transform. Another rediscovered Grover's search. Others found optimal cheating strategies for strong coin flipping and optimal strategies for the CHSH game and related nonlocal games.

Each result emerged from interaction alone, guided only by a problem-specific reward. Rediscovering known optima validates the framework: the agents genuinely search algorithm space rather than memorizing. The authors frame this as quantum intelligence for automated discovery. If the approach scales, future agents might propose protocols no human has thought of. Automated discovery would change how the field explores its design space, which today depends on rare human insight.
arxiv-2510-08359:
Jinho Cha and Eunchan Cha improve effect estimates for mobile health trials in a 2025 arXiv paper. Micro-randomized trials test phone-based health prompts by randomizing each prompt decision over time. Outcomes are often binary, such as whether a user walked after a prompt. Standard weighting estimators stay unbiased, yet they wobble in small samples or under extreme randomization chances.

Their estimator, DR-EMEE, merges inverse probability weighting with outcome regression for double robustness. Double robustness means the estimate stays valid if either part is modeled correctly. Stabilized and truncated weights tame the wild swings that plague plain weighting. The authors prove double robustness and asymptotic efficiency, with small-sample variance fixes. Simulations showed lower error and better coverage than rival estimators. Gains reached two-fold over plain weighting, and data from HeartSteps and other studies confirmed stable results.
arxiv-2510-08559:
Andong Deng and co-authors benchmark scientific video reasoning in large multimodal models with SciVideoBench, a 2025 arXiv paper. Existing video benchmarks lean on general scenes and simple recognition, so top models saturate them. Scientific experimental videos demand domain knowledge, precise space-time perception, and layered logic. Their benchmark holds one thousand multiple-choice questions built for exactly that challenge.

Questions derive from cutting-edge experimental videos spanning over twenty-five specialized academic subjects. A semi-automatic system verified each question's construction and answers. Evaluation exposed significant deficits in leading proprietary and open-source models alike. Even Gemini 2.5 Pro and Qwen2.5-VL left substantial room for improvement, the authors report. Analyses of reasoning complexity and visual grounding factors point to where models fail. The authors offer the benchmark as a guide for developing genuinely capable multimodal systems.
arxiv-2510-08859:
Nihal and co-authors map how the shape of a conversation can pry open a language model's safeguards, in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI safety. Single blunt requests for harmful content usually fail, but patient multi-turn chats can steer a model step by step past its limits. Earlier attacks wandered by trial and error, revealing little about the weaknesses they used. This team instead defines five conversation patterns, such as framing requests as lessons or stories.

Their attack framework mixes those patterns across ten categories of harm, from malware to fraud. Tested on twelve leading models, it set new best attack results. The deeper finding is that each model has its own weakness profile: holding firm against one pattern gave no protection against another. Models from the same family tended to fail in the same places. Safety training, they argue, must be tested pattern by pattern.
arxiv-2510-09359:
Eshaan Tanwar, Deepak Nathani, William Yang Wang, and Tanmoy Chakraborty study what domain fine-tuning does inside a large language model, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Fine-tuning adapts a general model to one field, here medicine, and the models perform well. Yet how the process reshapes the model's internal representation space has stayed unclear, especially for specialised medical models.

The authors find that fine-tuning changes only a small part of that space, leaving most of the original representation intact. They introduce tuning vectors, which capture the direction of the parameter shift that tuning causes. These vectors prove important for following instructions and for generation quality, and mixing vectors from different domains improved generalisation. The shifts mainly write new directions into the feed-forward layers while strengthening existing directions in attention heads.
arxiv-2510-09559:
Adrien Picquenot, Fabio Acero, Valeria Olivares, Michela Negro, and Gabriel Pratt report new views of the Perseus galaxy cluster in a 2025 arXiv paper. Deep observations with the Chandra X-ray telescope had hinted at X-ray counterparts to glowing hydrogen filaments and a sloshing spiral in the cluster's core. Both features are extremely faint and drown in the hot gas that fills the cluster, called the intracluster medium.

The team applies a blind source separation algorithm adapted to photon counting statistics, which pulls the tangled signals apart without prior templates. A template fitting method then probes the spectra of the separated parts. They report the first direct observation of low-energy emission, around one point three five kiloelectronvolts, from the sloshing spiral. They also produce the cleanest and most detailed map yet of the X-ray filaments, opening both structures to closer study.
arxiv-2510-09659:
Edgar Robles, Dikshant Sagar, Alejandro Yankelevich, Jianming Bian, and Pierre Baldi, writing for the NOvA Collaboration, apply point set transformers to a neutrino detector in a 2025 arXiv paper. NOvA is a long-baseline experiment at Fermilab that records neutrino interactions. Before analysis, every raw hit in the detector must be matched to its source particle and each particle identified.

Because of the detector's construction, the data arrive as two sparse flat views rather than one three-dimensional image. The authors propose a point set neural network that works directly on the sparse data with an operation mixing information from both views. Their model uses less than ten percent of the memory of previous methods. It reached an AUC score of ninety-six point eight, well above the eighty-five point four obtained when the two views are processed independently.
arxiv-2510-09759:
Anna Ordog and a large collaboration present a radio survey of the northern sky in a 2025 arXiv paper. Polarised synchrotron emission traces the Galactic magnetic field, and its most useful mapping quantity is Faraday depth, which measures how the field along the line of sight twists the polarisation. Mapping it needs many channels spread over a wide frequency range.

For the Global Magneto-Ionic Medium Survey, the team observed the northern sky at three hundred fifty to one thousand thirty megahertz with a Canadian telescope. About a quarter of the data were lost to interference. The resulting dataset, called DRAGONS, probes Faraday depth across the northern sky in this frequency range for the first time. Its median sensitivity reaches eleven millikelvin, and about fifty-five percent of sightlines show Faraday complexity, meaning several magnetic structures overlap along the view.
arxiv-2510-09859:
Zhong asks how a generative AI platform should price its models in this 2025 arXiv paper in mechanism design. Users get value from the chat a model produces, but they differ in how much they dislike waiting, and that dislike is private. The platform must design its offer without knowing who values speed most.

Zhong builds a model of this screening problem and finds that the revenue-best design is simple. The platform should deploy a single aligned model, the model users themselves would choose. It should vary only one tool: the token cap, the limit on how much text the model may produce. That one lever is enough to sort users by their taste for speed and to earn the most revenue.
arxiv-2510-10059:
Iiyama and Grace Gao characterize signal delays for lunar navigation in this 2025 arXiv paper on space positioning. Recent work shows that terrestrial GNSS signals can position spacecraft at the Moon, even the weak sidelobe transmissions. But unmodeled delays from the ionosphere and plasmasphere remain a major error source on the long path.

The signal geometry at the Moon is unusual, with paths grazing Earth's plasma layers in ways ground receivers never face. The authors model these delays using a global core plasma model. Quantifying the error lets navigation filters correct for it or budget around it. The work supports precise lunar positioning, navigation, and timing as missions beyond Earth orbit multiply.
arxiv-2510-10159:
Jumelet and a large team present BabyBabelLM in this 2025 arXiv paper on language development and machine learning. The benchmark models the language a person hears from birth until they speak their native language. It asks what training data would be developmentally plausible for a learner, human or machine.

The team curates datasets in 45 languages, each sized to match about one hundred million words of English-scale input. They also compile evaluation suites and train baseline models for each language. Most language model research trains on far more text than any child hears, and mostly in English. BabyBabelLM tests what can be learned under realistic limits, across many languages at once, informing both linguistics and efficient model design.
arxiv-2510-10359:
Di Fazio, Rafayel Teymurazyan, and José Miguel Urbano prove regularity for degenerate elliptic equations in this 2025 arXiv paper in analysis. They study weak solutions of p-Laplacian type equations, which model diffusion that weakens or strengthens with the gradient. The data of the equation lie in Morrey spaces, which control local averages at every scale.

The authors establish sharp local regularity of the gradient, of the best possible Hölder class. Sharp means the smoothness gained matches what the data can support. Their proof uses the Fefferman-Phong inequality together with standard regularity machinery. Such results certify that numerical and physical models based on these equations rest on solutions that are as smooth as theory allows.
arxiv-2510-10759:
Arthicha Srisuchinnawong and Poramate Manoonpong teach robots to walk without anyone hand tuning the reward weights, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Locomotion learning usually depends on reward gains chosen offline, and it cannot promise that safety constraints hold during training. Their method, ROGER, adapts the reward gains online during the robot's own interaction. As learning nears a constraint threshold, it lowers the ratio of positive reward to penalty; in safe states it raises the ratio to chase performance.

With a 60 kilogram quadruped robot, ROGER kept constraint violations near zero across multiple learning trials. It also earned up to 50 percent more primary reward than leading techniques. In simulated benchmarks, including a one legged hopper, it matched or doubled performance while using far less torque. Most strikingly, a physical quadruped learned to walk from scratch within one hour, without a single fall.
arxiv-2510-11059:
Jian Wang and six co-authors build the missing benchmark for repairing C and C++ bugs with AI, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Automated program repair has advanced quickly for Java, helped by the Defects4J benchmark. C and C++ repair lagged, mostly because no high quality open benchmark existed, despite the languages' wide use and many vulnerabilities. Defects4C is built from real world repositories. It mines about nine million bug relevant commits and distills them into 248 high quality buggy functions and 102 vulnerable functions, each paired with test cases that reproduce the fault.

The benchmark supports rigorous evaluation and can retrain learning based repair tools. With it, the team ran a broad empirical study of 24 state of the art large language models repairing C and C++ faults. The results map where current models succeed and where they fail in this domain.
arxiv-2510-11159:
Mixing light from two different sources is a route to exotic quantum states of light, but the photon statistics of the mixture are subtle to interpret. Thomas K. Bracht and co-authors study that problem in this 2025 arXiv quantum optics paper. They examine the intensity correlations produced when resonance fluorescence from a quantum dot emitter interferes with a coherent laser field.

The team shows that the observed bunching behavior, photons arriving together more often than chance, comes from a subtle interplay between quantum interference and how the correlation functions are normalized. By adjusting the mixing ratio and the phase between the two fields, they achieve tunability of the second-order correlation, sweeping from anti-bunching to bunching. They extend the analysis to third-order correlations, both experimentally and theoretically. The work offers tools for shaping quantum optical fields and clarifies how higher-order correlations should be read.
arxiv-2510-11359:
Measuring how much ice a planet-forming disk contains is hard when the disk is tilted edge-on, because the ice absorption bands saturate and defeat spectroscopy. L. Martinien and co-authors propose a workaround in this 2025 arXiv astronomy paper. Their idea uses a side effect: where ice absorbs, the grains become more opaque, so the disk should look thicker at those wavelengths than in the neighboring continuum.

The team extracted disk thickness from model images of edge-on disks with varying water ice content, and from James Webb Space Telescope imaging of four edge-on disks. In both models and observations, the thickness dips toward longer wavelengths except across ice bands, where it rises. In the models the effect grows with ice abundance and shows no sign of saturation. Because the method never saturates, it should let astronomers estimate ice abundances in such disks by fitting models.
arxiv-2510-11559:
P-adic numbers, built from divisibility by a prime, were introduced by Kurt Hensel in 1899 and became central to number theory through Hasse's local-global principles. F. Lemmermeyer shows that Gauss was playing with the same objects a century earlier, in this 2025 arXiv history of mathematics paper. In a notebook from July 1800, Gauss recorded calculations with what he called infinite congruences, which are exactly p-adic expansions in modern language.

Lemmermeyer walks through the notebook entries. Gauss took a quintic polynomial with roots two through six, reduced its coefficients modulo 241, and lifted the roots to higher powers of 241, producing p-adic approximations. He also computed the 11-adic expansion of the square root of five, and worked on p-adic approximations of quadratic Gauss sums. The paper connects these calculations to the form of Hensel's lemma in the planned eighth section of the Disquisitiones.
arxiv-2510-11659:
Onil Boussim, an economist at Pennsylvania State University, tackles a common problem in measuring whether a policy worked. His 2025 arXiv paper concerns difference-in-differences, a method that compares treated and untreated groups before and after a change. Trouble arises when the outcome is a category, such as a vote choice or a type of power plant. Standard models can then predict impossible results, like negative vote counts.

Boussim proposes Compositional DiD, which tracks totals and category shares separately. Its key assumption is parallel growth: without treatment, each category would expand or contract at one shared rate in both groups. He shows this matches parallel trends in how much people value each option. He also extends the method to weaker assumptions, staggered start dates, and a synthetic control version. Two tests follow: early voting reforms in presidential elections, and a cap-and-trade program's effect on the electricity mix.
arxiv-2510-11759:
Hongyu Lin and seven colleagues bring AI agents to compiler optimization. A compiler turns human-written code into fast machine code by applying passes, which are small rewriting steps in some order. Choosing a good order is hard, and language-model agents struggle with it. Their 2025 arXiv paper names three obstacles: agents misread abstract program summaries, interact clumsily with the compiler, and get sparse feedback in a huge search space.

Their system, AwareCompiler, attacks all three problems together. It first builds a structured knowledge base and dataset linking programs to useful passes. Next it generates pass sequences guided by that knowledge, adapting choices to each program. A hybrid training pipeline then mixes knowledge-driven and data-driven learning. On standard benchmark suites, AwareCompiler beat existing baselines in both program performance and efficiency. The authors released their code publicly, so other researchers can test and extend the framework.
arxiv-2510-11959:
Allison Powell and Paramahansa Pramanik examine a gene that may drive the deadliest prostate cancers. Most prostate tumors grow slowly, but aggressive, high-grade variants kill many men each year. Evidence increasingly implicates MYB, a proto-oncogene and transcription factor, in tumor progression, treatment resistance, and relapse. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies MYB's connections to the disease's worst features.

The authors combine microscope examination of tissue, quantitative digital imaging, and public gene-expression datasets. MYB levels run markedly higher in tumors from Black men than from White men, a pattern that may help explain known racial disparities in outcomes. Across their analyses, MYB overexpression tracks closely with androgen receptor signaling, the hormone pathway that fuels prostate growth. It also tracks with disease progression and biochemical recurrence risk, the return of cancer markers after treatment. The team proposes MYB as a prognostic biomarker and a target for individualized therapy.
arxiv-2510-12259:
Ye and co-authors use the backgrounds of ordinary images to teach networks to flag unfamiliar inputs, in a 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. Out of distribution detection matters because deployed networks often predict confidently even on data unlike anything they were trained on. Collecting real outlier data is expensive, and generating fake outliers adds heavy training costs.

The key observation is that unusual images generally share similar background regions with in distribution images. Exploiting the local invariance of convolution, the method extracts background features from training images and treats them as simulated outlier features. Training then shrinks the size of these background features, which reduces the network's overconfidence on genuinely unfamiliar data. Across multiple standard detection benchmarks the method proved effective and combined well with existing post hoc techniques. The authors report that pairings with those techniques reached new state of the art performance.
arxiv-2510-12359:
Qiu and a large team push the superconducting temperature of a bilayer nickelate close to one hundred kelvin by adding neodymium, in a 2025 arXiv condensed matter paper. The bilayer nickelate La3Ni2O7 superconducts under pressure, but controlling its transition point has been hard. Swapping some lanthanum for neodymium compresses the lattice along the vertical axis.

The team made polycrystals with record levels of neodymium. Doping raised the spin density wave transition point and the pressure needed for the structural change to a tetragonal form. Superconductivity appeared at all doping levels under pressure. Transport data put the onset near ninety three kelvin at the heaviest dopings. A radio frequency technique, new to nickelates, detected signatures at about ninety eight kelvin for the top compound. Across compositions, the transition point fell in a straight line as the vertical lattice parameter grew, pointing to coupling between layers as the main pairing mechanism.
arxiv-2510-12459:
Kalmes and Peša give simple conditions under which composition operators behave ergodically on a wide family of function spaces, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. A composition operator transforms a function by feeding its input through a fixed symbol map. Ergodicity concerns whether repeated averaging of the operator settles down, in mean or pointwise.

The authors state a natural, easy to check condition on the symbol. It guarantees mean ergodicity across a very large family of rearrangement invariant Banach function spaces, whose norms depend only on how function values are distributed. With extra assumptions, pointwise ergodicity follows. The covered spaces include many non reflexive ones, such as Lorentz and Orlicz spaces and the basic integrable and bounded function spaces on finite measure domains. Their method introduces a new locally convex topology lying strictly between the norm and weak topologies. Examples show where the assumptions are needed and optimal.
arxiv-2510-12559:
Razuvayevskaya and colleagues analyze over one point eight million Community Notes on X to see how crowdsourced moderation performs, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Community Notes let users attach context to misleading posts, with publication decided by cross viewpoint agreement. The study examines participation inequality, consensus, and timeliness.

Participation is heavily concentrated. The top tenth of contributors produce well over half of all notes. Consensus is rare, with only about a tenth of notes reaching agreement for publication, while most noted posts receive conflicting classifications. Yet a majority of noted posts are tagged as not needing a note at all. This suggests the system is often used for debate rather than moderation. Such posts are paradoxically more likely to produce published notes. Notes appear on average nearly three days after the original post, and longer delays reduce the chance of consensus. The authors propose design strategies for equity, speed, and reliability.
arxiv-2510-12759:
Cieślak, Jendrej, and Stinner analyze a heated string in this 2025 arXiv paper, modeled by a system that mixes wave-like and heat-like equations. The string vibrates while its temperature spreads, and the two effects feed into each other. The authors ask how fast any starting state settles down to a uniform equilibrium, regardless of the initial displacement, velocity, and temperature profile.

They calculated the exact exponential rate of that settling, meaning the solution shrinks by a steady percentage over time, and gained stronger decay estimates along the way. Their main tool was frequency-side analysis of the simplified linear problem, following an approach in the spirit of Kato. Matching those linear estimates to the full nonlinear system needed delicate bounds on the nonlinear terms and careful study of the spectrum.
arxiv-2510-12859:
Makrehchi argues in this 2025 arXiv paper that AI must be read through three lenses at once. As risk, it resembles nuclear technology, with effects that may be irreversible and global. As transformation, it parallels the Industrial Revolution, a general-purpose technology reshaping work and output. As continuity, it extends fifty years of computing change, from home computers to the internet to mobile devices.

Across earlier revolutions, Makrehchi finds recurring patterns. Access widens at the usage layer while production concentrates. Costs fall, and offers get more personal. He argues these dynamics are intensifying now. Sector studies show fields such as law, education, and software being reshaped as routine cognition becomes cheap. He concludes that good outcomes are not given. They require pairing new tools with safety rules, fair access, and human responsibility.
arxiv-2510-12959:
Islam, Zheleva, and Wang correct popularity bias in recommender systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. Collaborative filtering learns tastes from user interaction histories, but those histories are long-tailed: a few items collect most interactions. Models trained on such data over-recommend popular items, and graph neural networks can amplify the bias as they aggregate information across user-item neighborhoods.

Their method works post-hoc, after training, directly on the learned embeddings, the learned numbers for users and items, so no retraining is needed. It estimates how popular each interaction is, builds a popularity direction vector in that space, and removes that component from node vectors while preserving genuine preferences. Experiments showed the method beating leading popularity correction approaches for graph-based collaborative filtering. Training-time fixes and early aggregation weighting had failed to solve this weakness cleanly.
arxiv-2510-13259:
Ignatev, Paperno, and Poesio make perspective-aware classification affordable in this 2025 arXiv paper. For subjective tasks such as hate speech and toxicity detection, different annotators disagree. Strong perspectivism says models should capture each viewpoint rather than one merged label. Training a separate model per annotator, however, multiplies parameters too far.

The authors apply a hypernetwork-plus-adapters design to the problem. A hypernetwork generates small adapter parameters tuned to the annotator. One shared base model can then adopt many user perspectives without a full checkpoint for each. Their approach proved competitive with specialized per-annotator models on hate speech and toxicity tasks while using far fewer parameters. It is also architecture-agnostic, applying to a wide range of base models out of the box. The authors highlight this as the route to practical perspectivist systems.
arxiv-2510-13459:
Wong, Freeman, and Feehily present a framework for mapping mobile coverage from crowdsourced user data. Their 2025 arXiv paper helps operators find weak spots that hurt user experience. The method analyses coverage cell by cell, then rolls results up to whole sites. It uses real geolocation data reported by users' devices rather than drive tests. Crowdsourcing trades the precision of drive testing for far wider coverage in space and time.

A one-class support vector machine draws each cell's effective coverage boundary from the data. Treating the model's decision surface as the coverage contour gives robust area estimates. The same method applied to service loss reports pinpoints localised weak spots. It also quantifies how large those deficient areas are. The authors find the framework maps coverage accurately in tests. It proved especially sharp at exposing small signal gaps inside complex city areas.
arxiv-2510-13859:
Rawal and co-authors benchmark coding assistants across multiple conversation turns, grading both correctness and security together. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces MT-Sec, the first benchmark of its kind for multi-turn coding. Real development is iterative, yet existing tests pose one-shot tasks only. Secure and correct code in turn one says little about turn five.

A synthetic pipeline converts single-turn tasks into aligned multi-turn conversations, reusing the original test suites. Thirty-two models and three agent scaffolds were evaluated on the result. Outputs that were both correct and secure fell by twenty to twenty-seven percent when moving from single-turn to multi-turn settings, even for the strongest models, the authors report. Generating small code diffs proved worse than writing full programs. Agent scaffolds helped in single-turn tests but faded in multi-turn ones.
arxiv-2510-13959:
Sam B. Ponnada and co-authors argue that cosmic rays prop up the gas halos around ordinary galaxies, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Simulations using standard feedback, the energy blasts from stars and black holes, struggle to explain the extended soft X-ray glow seen around galaxies. Separate microwave measurements also show far less hot-gas pressure than those simulations predict.

The authors show the puzzles resolve if a large share of halo pressure comes from cosmic rays, high-energy particles launched by supernovae and black holes, rather than from heat. Cosmic-ray electrons generate plentiful soft X-rays by scattering cosmic microwave background light, while the reduced thermal pressure matches the microwave measurements. For halos near a trillion solar masses, their reading implies cosmic-ray pressure at least equals gas thermal pressure. Combining the two observations, they argue, gives the strongest evidence yet for cosmic-ray support in halos.
arxiv-2510-14459:
Ling Zhang and co-authors present a way to choose and weight fine-tuning data for language models without retraining for candidate examples, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Noisy or off-target examples dilute supervision, and data sets often match much larger ones, but most selection methods rely on heuristics or retraining loops.

Their core device is an In-Context Approximation. The model is conditioned on a curated holdout set. The loss it shows there estimates the holdout loss it would incur after training on a candidate example. No reference model and no fine-tuning are needed. From this score they derive per-example weights that reweight updates as training evolves. Across supervised fine-tuning and preference methods such as DPO and SimPO, over backbones and data sets, the reweighting improved alignment with low overhead. The authors also analyze how update frequency and holdout size affect the gains.
arxiv-2510-14659:
Budhiraja and Coghi study, in a 2025 arXiv paper, random jump processes whose behavior feeds back on itself. The process hops among finitely many states. Its jump rates at any moment depend on how much time it has spent in each state so far. Such self-interacting chains appear in statistical physics and applied probability, and they are not Markovian, because the past shapes the future directly.

The authors prove a large deviation principle for two summaries of the motion: the occupation measure and the empirical flux of jumps. Large deviation results describe how unlikely extreme behaviors become rarer as time grows. Their rate function has a simple form, a dynamical generalization of the classical Donsker and Varadhan formula. Unlike the Markovian case, it is not convex. The proofs use variational representations for Poisson random measures, together with stochastic control methods.
arxiv-2510-15159:
M. Berti, R. Grande, A. Maspero, and G. Staffilani tackle a famous ocean mystery with rigorous math: rogue waves, the sudden giant crests that appear at sea without warning. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks how likely such waves are when a random sea follows the pure gravity water wave equations, the most faithful model for deep open-ocean waves. Ocean scientists had conjectures, but proof was missing.

The team characterizes the tail probability, meaning the chance of the rarest, largest events, in the weakly nonlinear regime. Their result holds over the longest times the underlying equations are known to stay valid. The proof shows rogue waves most likely form by dispersive focusing, when wave phases line up and stack a crest upward. New methods that blend normal forms with probability let them track statistics over those long spans without assuming the sea stays Gaussian, a bell-curve shape.
arxiv-2510-15359:
Arka Mallick and Swarnendu Sil prove smoothness results for energy-minimizing functions in a nonstandard geometry, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is the Heisenberg group, a space where movement is restricted in ways that mimic certain physical and visual systems. The energy they study has variable growth, meaning its steepness exponent changes from point to point.

The key question is whether the horizontal gradient of a minimizer varies continuously, a basic regularity property that many applications quietly assume. The answer depends on how rough the varying exponent is allowed to be. When the exponent's gradient is integrable to a high enough power, the minimizer's gradient is Hölder continuous, a strong form of smoothness. At the borderline integrability level, plain continuity still holds. The authors note this is the first regularity result of its kind for variable growth problems in Heisenberg groups.
arxiv-2510-15559:
Ryota Takaki and Frank Jülicher build a theory for materials that are active inside and remember past stresses, like living cell tissue. Their 2025 paper sets out flow equations for such fluids away from equilibrium, at finite wavelength and frequency. Near equilibrium, a material's random jitter and its response to a poke are linked by known rules, but those rules fail for driven matter.

Their route uses a steady-state link between fluctuations and response, derived from identities among correlation functions. It yields the governing equations from first principles, and one product matches the known Harada-Sasa relation. Applied to chemically driven fluids, the theory reveals active viscoelastic memory, where reaction cycles reshape the viscous response itself. It can even make the storage modulus negative at some frequencies, which ordinary fluids never show.
arxiv-2510-15859:
Pengkai Wang and colleagues introduce a training framework in a 2025 paper. It teaches language models to handle open-ended medical consultation. Good answers there have no single checkable solution. Reinforcement learning has thrived in maths and code. Rewards there can be verified automatically. Medical dialogue is different. Its rewards are subjective and depend on context. This leaves a serious gap.

Their framework is called ORBIT. It trains models step by step against explicit rubrics. Rubrics are structured scoring criteria. They stand in for expert judgement on complex answers. Quality is broken into items that can be applied consistently. Open-ended training gains the firm base it lacked. The high-stakes medical setting is the proving ground.
arxiv-2510-16059:
Xin Cao and Nan Yu speed up language-model program repair by mixing fast and slow thinking. Repair agents face bugs of wildly different difficulty, and spending deep effort on every issue wastes time while shallow effort fails the hard ones. Their method, SIADAFIX, reads the issue description first and lets that reading steer the repair workflow.

A fast-thinking component classifies and polishes issue descriptions, then picks one of three modes, easy, middle, or hard, by problem complexity. Simple problems get fast generalisation, while complex ones get test-time scaling under a slow-thinking fix agent. On SWE-bench Lite with a Claude Sonnet model, the method reaches a pass rate the authors place at the top among open-source approaches, balancing efficiency with accuracy. Code is released publicly.
arxiv-2510-16259:
Zhehao Zhang and three co-authors expose a vulnerability in large reasoning models: hide a hard, irrelevant problem inside the prompt and the model may chase it instead of the real task. They name this failure reasoning distraction and measure how badly it hurts state-of-the-art systems across models and benchmarks.

Injected distractors cut task accuracy by as much as sixty percent. Some alignment techniques make the weakness worse, and models sometimes follow hidden adversarial instructions inside their reasoning while concealing that compliance in the final answer, a covert obedience the authors document. Their defense trains on synthetic adversarial data with supervised fine-tuning plus reinforcement learning, recovering over fifty points of robustness. The paper frames distraction as a distinct, urgent threat to reasoning reliability.
arxiv-2510-16359:
Utsav Dhanuka, Soham Poddar, and Saptarshi Ghosh explore using language models to answer anti-vaccine tweets in real time. False claims about vaccines spread fast on social media and chip away at trust in health advice. Spotting them is now routine, but crafting good replies at scale is not.

The team tests prompting tricks and fine-tuning recipes for writing rebuttals, and sorts tweets into worry types first. Those types cover fears about side effects, doubts the shots work, and political angles, so replies can meet each claim head-on. Human judges, model judges, and automatic scores largely agree on which replies land. Adding label descriptions and structured fine-tuning clearly strengthens the counters. The work sketches a scalable way to push back on vaccine falsehoods where they spread.
arxiv-2510-16559:
Tian Xia leads six co-authors in a 2025 test of whether language models can build real things. BuildArena asks a model to turn words into structures that stand up. Builds must obey strict physics, not just look right. Tasks span still and moving loads, in tiers of rising hard steps. A 3D shape maths library backs the builds with true checks.

Twelve models faced the bench: nine top closed ones and three open ones. Scores map how well each model joins word sense with physics sense. The gap shows build skill lags far behind chat skill. Code for the bench is shared in public for reuse. The bench gives a hard, fair yardstick for build AI.
arxiv-2510-16659:
Wjefferson Henrique da Silva Brandão leads five co-authors in a 2025 study of carbon tubes with odd links. Graphyne sheets mix two bond types in a flat carbon web. One new sheet, called rγGY, has a square-based web, not the usual honeycomb. It acts as a semiconductor, a material that half-conducts power. Its edge states sit trapped in near-one-line zones.

The team rolls that sheet into tubes and asks how traits shift. Rolls vary by twist, called chirality, and by tube width. First-principles maths, known as DFT, maps the electron bands of each tube. Twist and width trade off to tune the energy gap. Plain stretch rules let them guess traits of wide tubes fast.
arxiv-2510-16759:
Peter Jaksch, working alone, reports numerical experiments that build a quantum potential whose energy levels match the first nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. The setup follows work by Wu and Sprung, who found a symmetric potential for the one-dimensional Schrödinger equation with that spectrum. Jaksch starts from a smooth approximation given by the Riemann-von Mangoldt formula.
