He then adds a series of correction functions to the starting potential. The corrections show a clear pattern. Jaksch argues the pattern can be explained in simple terms, almost fully by the error in the smooth approximation. That explanation also accounts for the fractal pattern Wu and Sprung had noticed in their potential.
arxiv-2510-16959:
Surendra Ghentiyala cuts the randomness cost of private counting in a 2025 paper. Differential privacy hides individuals while answering counting questions about data. The 2020 census privacy system needed an estimated ninety terabytes of randomness. Generating that much randomness can be costly or impossible.

Earlier work showed many counting questions need surprisingly little randomness. Roughly, the cost grows only with the logarithm of the question count. That earlier method, however, was too slow to run in practice. Ghentiyala gives a fast method with nearly the same tradeoff. The trick starts by randomly shifting each answer before rounding. Many shifted answers then coincide, so fewer random choices matter. The result makes private counting cheaper to deploy at census scale.
arxiv-2510-17059:
Kathryn Wantlin, Chongyi Zheng, and Benjamin Eysenbach teach agents to copy demonstrations in a 2025 paper. Zero-shot imitation means copying an expert from one demonstration. The agent gets no practice runs or updates at test time. Success hinges on guessing what goal the expert pursued.

Their framework, CIRL, turns imitation into goal inference. Many useful tasks, they note, reduce to reaching one goal state. During pretraining, no rewards or demonstrations are used at all. A contrastive method learns goal-reaching policies for many goals. A goal proposal tool drives exploration toward interesting states. A probabilistic model then infers goals from observed trajectories. Proofs show the method recovers the demonstrator's intent consistently. Earlier similar methods can pick the wrong goal, they show.
arxiv-2510-17459:
Working out the orbit of a planet photographed directly, far from its star, usually relies on slow sampling methods that test millions of guesses. Bo Liang, leading a team with eleven co-authors, pairs a modern generative method with the classic sampling approach to speed that work up. Their combined method first narrows the plausible range of orbital values, then samples carefully within that range to pin down the final estimates.

On the well studied planet beta Pictoris b, the combined method ran many tens of times faster than the standard samplers it was compared with, while keeping similar accuracy. Liang and his co-authors also record the best average fit score among the methods tried. They argue the same pairing could serve other fields that face hard inference problems, from cosmology to medical imaging.
arxiv-2510-17759:
Qilin Liao, Anamika Lochab, and Ruqi Zhang probe hidden weaknesses in vision-language models. These models read both images and text to answer questions. Their combined design opens attack paths that text-only safety checks miss. Older attack tests used brittle templates and single attack settings.

Their framework, VERA-V, treats attack design as learning a probability distribution. It samples paired text and image prompts that slip past guardrails together. Three tricks help: harmful cues hidden in styled text, crafted images, and distractors. Distractors are extra content meant to split the model's attention. Tests beat prior methods on two standard safety benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-17959:
Jeff Shen, with twenty-seven co-authors, trains one model to read star and galaxy spectra from many surveys in a shared form. Spectra arrive at varied resolutions and wavelength ranges, and studies stay split by range and object type. Their tokenizer works on each spectrum's own wavelength grid and learns without labels.

The shared codes line up across data sets and carry clear physical meaning. Small added training then reaches strong results on many later tasks. For astronomy, the work is a step toward foundation models that pool millions of spectra instead of treating each survey as its own island.
arxiv-2510-18059:
Jesenko Vukadinovic, as sole author, studies a crowd of weakly linked oscillators that carry a phase offset from time delays. The classic Kuramoto model syncs such crowds with pure sine coupling, but large networks lag, and the Sakaguchi-Kuramoto extension adds a frustration term for that delay. The paper works at the mean-field level for the whole crowd.

A sharp global shift is proved: the crowd jumps from disorder to one traveling-wave state. That state has a new skewed bell form on the circle, built by filtering the classic shape. Synchronization theory gains a fully described pattern for delayed crowds.
arxiv-2510-18359:
David Eppstein, writing alone, studies a construction in graph theory called the subdivided double. A graph is a network of points joined by lines, and here each graph under study has four lines at every point. Earlier researchers used subdivided doubles to build and study semi-symmetric graphs, which look the same along their edges but not at their points.

Eppstein proves that these graphs have a further property that does not depend on symmetry at all. Each one contains a very large number of Hamiltonian cycles, meaning closed routes that visit every point exactly once before returning to the start. Better still, every such cycle can be paired with a second cycle that complements it, so the two routes together cover the graph in a balanced way.
arxiv-2510-18659:
Dong Yun, joined by Marco Schouten and Dim Papadopoulos, teaches a retrieval system to ask good clarifying questions. A single user query is often ambiguous, and dialogue-based search can narrow the target down, but many systems ask questions with no real strategy, wasting turns. Their framework, SherlockLLM, learns a questioning policy through reinforcement learning, without needing large collections of annotated dialogues.

The agent asks a sequence of yes-or-no questions, each chosen to shrink the search space efficiently. The authors built a benchmark with both structured tasks, where items have clear attributes, and unstructured ones, where they do not. On structured tasks the agent matched strong baselines and came close to the theoretical optimum set by binary search. On the unstructured task it clearly beat those baselines, showing it had learned a genuinely effective information-seeking style.
arxiv-2510-18859:
Shuwei Wang, writing alone, proves a surprising result about ordinals in intuitionistic set theory, where the logic does not assume every statement is true or false. Classically, ordinals form one thin linear chain. Intuitionistically, two ordinals can be incomparable, neither below the other, and Wang starts from exactly such a pair.

From two incomparable ordinals, he constructs canonical one-to-one correspondences between any arbitrary set and a family of mutually incomparable ordinals, an antichain. Consequently, any subset of the given set can be defined using ordinals as parameters. The headline consequence is an equivalence: in the theory with two incomparable ordinals assumed, the statement that every ordinal lies in the constructible universe holds exactly when the whole universe is constructible. A small change in logic, the result shows, reshapes a pillar of set theory.
arxiv-2510-18959:
Nicholas Earley and eleven co-authors present a near-infrared census of large-amplitude variable stars from the Palomar Gattini-IR survey. Over three years the survey watched the northern sky, detecting tens of millions of stars, and a small set stood out by changing brightness by large amounts many times.

For the strongest cases the team gathered spectra with telescopes at Palomar and in Hawaii, building both a spectral library and light records. The catalog gives researchers a clean starting sample for studying pulsating and erupting stars that are hard to spot in visible light but clear in infrared.
arxiv-2510-19159:
Sam McKeown studies the Busemann process in directed first passage percolation, a model where travel times grow along paths on a grid and the fastest routes matter. The Busemann process tracks long-run differences in travel time between starting points, and it connects to several interacting particle systems used in probability theory.

McKeown extends existing methods to build the process in this planar setting and finds its exact distribution in several solvable models. Those formulas measure how often near-optimal routes pass through thin rectangles and how competition boundaries cluster. Distributional results also yield the invariant laws for multi-class versions of a classic traffic particle model.
arxiv-2510-19559:
Nidham Tekaya, Manuela Waldner, and Matthias Zeppelzauer ask whether vision-language models like CLIP know where images belong in time. They built TIME10k, a benchmark of more than ten thousand images with known dates, and tested thirty-seven models with a new evaluation method. The question matters because these models are used to organize and search visual collections.

Time turns out to be encoded along a low-dimensional, curved surface inside the models' representation space. Building on that structure, the authors extract an explicit timeline representation that supports chronological reasoning. Their timeline methods matched or beat a prompt-based baseline at lower computing cost, showing that temporal knowledge is present in the models even when it is not obvious.
arxiv-2510-19959:
Gauri Kotiwale and nineteen co-authors measure how metal content scales with galaxy mass when the universe was under a billion years old. They use about eight hundred galaxies picked by their oxygen emission in James Webb Space Telescope grism data. Direct temperature-based metallicities from stacked spectra land between a tenth and a fifth of the Sun's metal content. That holds across the mass range studied, and it agrees with other recent Webb results.

The surprise is the relation's flatness. Low-mass galaxies are more enriched than leading simulations predict, and selection effects cannot explain the difference. Simple modeling suggests metallicity at fixed mass barely depends on star formation rate. That implies enrichment runs out of equilibrium at these epochs, with metals building up rapidly in small galaxies. Larger samples with single-galaxy measurements are needed to confirm the picture.
arxiv-2510-20459:
Rajasmita Sahoo and three co-authors model quark stars with strong fields that squash them to a flat ball shape. Their state law comes from the MIT Bag model. It adds fields that grow with mass per space and the push split that breaks round form. Two kinds of quark stuff are checked: plain magnetized strange stuff and a color-flavor locked kind.

The team works out mass-size curves, flatness, light shift, quad traits, and tide bend for two bag rates. Quad traits then give the steady wave strain from a lone spun quark star. Strong fields and color locks can shift how tight the star is by a lot. Next wave tools may spot the signs.
arxiv-2510-20859:
Craig Sanders and four co-authors ask how vision language models see. Their question is old in both mind science and AI. Do machines build inner pictures that match human ones? Or is any match only shallow and surface level? Models may look aligned while using very different inner dimensions.

The team asks models to judge how alike pairs of objects are. From those judgments they rebuild low dimensional maps of objects. The map axes line up well with axes of human perceptual space. Perceptual space means the mental map of how things seem alike. When their map feeds a classic model of sorting, it works well. It predicts human sorting choices better than human built maps. That hints models can learn a cleaned form of human structure. The method also gives mind science a larger way to measure.
arxiv-2510-20959:
Sam Hughes and one co-author develop the theory of L2 torsion for self maps of groups and compute it across a wide range of examples. Torsion values distill symbolic shape study data into numbers that distinguish spaces and mirror rules.

Computations cover every automorphism of groups that are curved and one ended relative to virtually polycyclic pieces. A combination formula expresses the torsion of a group through the torsions of stabilizers for a nice action on a contractible space. Applications reach CAT(0) lattices, relatively curved groups, higher dimensional graph manifolds, and handlebody groups, showing the invariant is broadly computable.
arxiv-2510-21059:
Mahmud Wasif Nafee leads three co-authors on DR-IKE, a dynamic retriever for editing knowledge inside language models through in context examples, with no gradient updates. Models keep repeating stale facts, and black box services rule out weight editing, so example based editing is attractive.

Static example sets chosen by surface similarity face a quantity quality trade off and cannot adapt to edit difficulty. DR-IKE trains a small BERT retriever with policy optimization to pick demonstrations by their actual utility for each edit. Lightweight and adaptive selection aims at edits that stick without flooding the prompt with weak examples.
arxiv-2510-21559:
The CMS Collaboration measures a delicate ratio in particle decays at the Large Hadron Collider. The ratio compares two decays of a special meson. One ends with a heavy tau lepton, and the other with a light muon. If nature treats lepton flavors even-handedly, the ratio should match a precise Standard Model prediction. Any excess would signal new physics.

The data come from proton collisions recorded between 2016 and 2018. The tau is caught through its decay into three charged prongs. That is a harder channel than the muon decay used earlier. This channel alone gives a ratio near one, with wide error bars. Combined with the previous channel, the result sits near forty-nine hundredths. That stays consistent with the predicted value near twenty-six hundredths, within uncertainties. The collaboration reports no sign of flavor rules being broken.
arxiv-2510-21659:
Yongyi Zang and eleven co-authors restore battered vocal recordings with one compact model built for phones. Singing and speech captured on consumer devices often arrive with several faults at once. Background noise, room echo, missing high frequencies, and clipped peaks from loud moments, and fixing them usually takes a chain of separate tools.

Their model, Smule Renaissance Small, repairs the recording end to end in the frequency domain, using phase-aware training goals that let it analyze sound in large windows for finer frequency detail. It runs more than ten times faster than real time on an iPhone 12 processor. On a blind challenge set it beats a strong adversarial baseline and nearly matches a far costlier flow system, despite never training on speech. On the team's new extreme degradation benchmark it leads open models on singing.
arxiv-2510-21759:
Rubik Khachatryan and Georgy Lukyanov study how a reputation for toughness can reshape market entry. A newcomer must choose whether to enter neither, one, or both of two markets served by an incumbent. Fighting back in one market drains resources the incumbent could spend in the other, so the entry choices interact in a way single-market thinking misses.

The entrant learns the incumbent's capability by watching its response to an earlier rival. Publishing such conduct more often tempts a weak incumbent to imitate a strong one's response, which blurs the record's information and, paradoxically, expands later entry. Comparing conduct publication against a direct public audit of capability, the authors find full publication can maximize total surplus when publishing is cheap. While the audit never wins in either version of their economy.
arxiv-2510-21959:
Eduard Brüll, Samuel Mäurer, and Davud Rostam-Afschar survey German tax advisors to learn how employers really expect artificial intelligence to reshape white-collar work. Through a randomized information experiment, some firms were given evidence about which tasks machines can automate, and the team watched how beliefs and plans moved.

Firms began by underestimating how automatable their work is, and the information raised perceived risk, most for routine-heavy roles. Yet near-term hiring plans barely budged. Instead, updated firms expected higher productivity and revenue with only small wage changes, a pattern pointing to gains captured inside the firm rather than shared broadly. Employers also foresaw new work in legal technology, compliance, and handling AI tools, and reported stronger intentions to train staff and adopt the technology.
arxiv-2510-22259:
Hao Chen, Conghui Xie, and Cunsheng Ding announce a claimed solution to a seventy-five-year-old open problem. The problem sits in coding theory. Codes are judged partly by the sphere packing bound. That bound caps how good a code with a given minimum distance can be. Codes meeting it are called distance-optimal.

Since Hamming's founding work in nineteen fifty, such families were known only for small distances. Whether the distance could grow without bound stayed open. The authors state that they settle the question. They present infinitely many families of distance-optimal binary linear codes. Some families have arbitrarily large minimum distance. By-products include families with small distances. Two families of binary codes use exactly five distinct weights. Further open problems close the paper.
arxiv-2510-22859:
Exploration can conflict with safety in reinforcement learning. Kaitong Cai, Jusheng Zhang, Jing Yang, and Keze Wang split those roles in 2025. Their frame is called RLPD-GX. A reward seeking learner explores freely. A projection based guardian enforces rules at execution.

The guardian also guards value backups for safety. This design avoids overly conservative policies. Dynamic curricula extend time horizons gradually. They also anneal the mix of offline and online data. The team proves convergence by a contraction property. On Atari-100k, scores beat prior hybrid methods by a lot. Ablations show gains on safety critical tasks too.
arxiv-2510-23759:
Marlon Estanislau generalizes two theorems that characterize permutation modules over group rings of cyclic p-groups. The setting mixes a prime p, a cyclic group built from it, and a complete discrete valuation ring in mixed characteristic. Earlier results by Torrecillas and Weigel described these modules but required p to be unramified in the ring, a real restriction in number-theoretic settings.

Estanislau removes that restriction, allowing p to ramify. The new proofs lean only on basic facts from group cohomology and a version of Weiss's theorem, deliberately avoiding the heavier categorical machinery of earlier approaches. That lighter toolkit makes the characterization easier to check and to teach. The extension widens the class of rings where permutation modules over cyclic p-groups are fully understood, a useful step for representation theory over arithmetic bases.
arxiv-2510-24159:
Keiya Hirashima and two co-authors tackle a hard measurement in astronomy: the mass of young stars still buried in dense gas. Mass sets how a star lives and evolves, but clouds hide young stars and make simple motion based estimates unreliable. Supervised learning could help, yet it needs large labeled sets from costly high resolution simulations.

The team pretrains a vision transformer on one million synthetic fractal images with a self supervised method, then freezes it and applies it to a small set of detailed simulations. This transfer lets the model read complex gas structure and infer the stellar mass inside. The approach cuts the need for expensive labeled simulation data.
arxiv-2510-24259:
Ziqi Ma and two co-authors test whether large language models can translate human instructions into the internal symbols of a learning robot agent. Developmental agents that learn in a hierarchy form emergent symbolic representations, which help them plan and generalize. The question is whether a language model can map plain instructions onto those agent specific symbols.

The team evaluates well known models including GPT, Claude, DeepSeek, and Grok with a structured framework. They use symbolic partitions from a hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithm in two ant robot environments, Ant Maze and Ant Fall. Results show the models can partly perform the translation, though performance varies with the partition and environment.
arxiv-2510-24459:
Habtom Kahsay Gidey and three co-authors address how autonomous software agents build an actionable model of their digital environment. Agents read structured data such as a web page's document object model and service descriptions, but raw HTML is too verbose for foundation models to use directly. Hardcoded integrations, meanwhile, cannot adapt when services evolve.

The authors introduce a pattern language for world modeling from structured data, presenting two complementary architectural patterns. The patterns focus on affordances: what actions the environment offers the agent and how to recognize them. The goal is a compact, adaptable internal model that lets agents act reliably across changing web services.
arxiv-2510-24659:
Krishnadas Mohandas, Piotr J Gorski, Krzysztof Suchecki, Georges Andres, Giacomo Vaccario, and Janusz A Holyst study a signed net that grows under strict balance rules. New members meet a random old member and join one of two camps, with a bias toward the camp they met. Over time the camp sizes act like a classic urn draw with a twist.

When bias is low, the two camps tend toward the same size no matter how they start. When bias is high, the first gap can last, and at a key point the size spread splits into two humps. The team gives ways to gauge that key point.
arxiv-2510-24959:
Andrea C Burgess, Nancy E Clarke, Shannon L Fitzpatrick, and Melissa A Huggan stretch a hunt game on graphs where each hunter moves once at most. In the base game, hunters seek a hid robber on a graph, but hunters on far points can not talk to plan. Their new form lets each hunter make up to a set count of moves.

They weigh the new hunt count for a few graph kinds: paths, loops, full graphs, and two part full graphs. Linked forms built as grid and strong blends of paths are also worked out. The count tells how many hunters a graph needs when moves are capped. More moves per hunter change the count in ways that shift by graph type.
arxiv-2510-25159:
Anchang Bao, Enya Shen, and Jianmin Wang speed up point in or out tests on trimmed faces, a base task in CAD work. Past ways such as ray casts and broad wind counts can be slow or frail. Their way rests on a loop form of the wind count for a trimmed face.

In place of costly curve cuts, an oval bound on each curve span lets the count run in line time. For faces that wrap in a loop, trim curves are lifted to a cover space so counts stay true for loops that can not shrink. Tests show large speed gains over past wind tools, with strong hold in noise, open edges, and wrap cases.
arxiv-2510-25259:
Yehjin Shin, Jeongwhan Choi, Seojin Kim, and Noseong Park built TV-Rec. Their 2025 paper deals with sequential recommendation. Such systems learn from the order of past user actions. They then suggest what a user may want next. Most models pair fixed filters with self-attention. Self-attention lets a model weigh links across a whole sequence.

TV-Rec drops both fixed filters and self-attention. It uses filters that change over time instead. Those filters come from graph signal processing. They catch how a pattern shifts with position. The authors report faster inference and less computation. Across six public test sets, TV-Rec beat top rivals. The average gain they report is about seven and a half percent. That matters for services needing quick, sharp suggestions.
arxiv-2510-25659:
N Roldan-Levchenko led five co-authors on optical gain. D J P de Sousa, C O Ascencio, and J D S Forte helped. L Martin-Moreno and T Low complete six authors. Their 2025 theoretical paper studies metallic electro-optical effects. Optical gain is critical in semiconductor technology today. It is most often achieved via stimulated emission. They find a possible gain route without it.

A resonant transverse electric mode appears in biased systems. Low-symmetry two-dimensional metallic systems host that mode. Optical conductivity is modeled with Boltzmann transport theory. A scattered-wave formalism simulates the scattering problem. Systems may possess a Berry curvature dipole. A nonzero magnetoelectric tensor may also be present. Conductivity depends nontrivially on applied bias direction. That dependence allows probing the resonant mode. The resonant mode is accessible only with both effects. Further studies must find suitable materials.
arxiv-2510-25959:
Gabriel Meyniel and Fei Zhou propose a practical route to lattice models that yield a single Weyl fermion at low energy. A Weyl fermion is a massless particle like excitation with a definite handedness. A classic no go result says a lone Weyl cone cannot appear in a normal three dimensional lattice, so a workaround is needed.

Meyniel and Zhou use spontaneous breaking of charge symmetry to evade that theorem. They explore three paths that start from gapped topological states protected by symmetry. They then either push the system to a critical point, peel off extra degrees with symmetry breaking fields, or combine both moves. In the low energy limit, the models reduce to known gapless superconducting, superfluid, or chiral fermion phases.
arxiv-2510-26059:
Qiuye Jia, Junyong Zhang, and Jiqiang Zheng prove a sharp bound for a smoothing operator on a cone shaped space. Bochner Riesz means are a family of operators that cut off frequencies in a rounded way, used to rebuild a function from its frequency content. Their space is a flat cone, built from a half line times a circle with a scaled metric, which has a singular tip.

Jia and the team give an if and only if condition for the operator to be bounded on L p spaces for all p except two. These are function spaces that measure size by a power p. The threshold depends in a simple way on p. The result also covers an infinite wedge with either fixed or free boundary values, settling the critical exponent there.
arxiv-2510-26459:
Andres Stump and Jeremy R Green speed up a key step in lattice quantum chromodynamics, the grid-based study of the strong force. Spectroscopy there means computing how particles pass signals between two points, which needs repeated costly solving. A method called distillation trims the work by using a few key patterns of the grid, but local operators with four or more quarks get very costly in it.

Stump and Green add position-space sampling: they project momentum only over sparse grids of points instead of the whole lattice. The estimator stays unbiased, and they show it works for single mesons, single baryons, and local four-quark operators. Applied to a known particle state, adding local four-quark operators shifted several energy levels a lot. Those shifts in turn moved the scattering results drawn from them.
arxiv-2510-26559:
Francesco De Roma, Luca Maffioli, Edward R Smith, and Antonio Buffo improve a simulation method for fluids under very gentle shear. The method, dissipative particle dynamics, models a fluid as soft particles. Its weakness is noise: at low shear rates, the signal drowns unless runs use unrealistically strong deformation.

De Roma and his three co-authors apply a transient time correlation function technique to a simple Newtonian fluid in this framework. They sort out what changes the particle force field demands. Across all tested shear rates, their viscosity values had lower standard error than the classic averaging route. Error shrank in step with shear rate, so the signal-to-noise ratio stayed flat instead of collapsing. They also settle a version of the method that needs no trajectory mapping, with no loss of precision.
arxiv-2510-27059:
Momo Ellwarth leads eight co-authors in testing a new marker of magnetic activity on the Sun. Stellar activity can shift measured star velocities and hide or fake planet signals, so reliable activity markers matter for finding small planets. The team studies the helium D3 line, a feature in sunlight tied to the chromosphere, in high-resolution solar spectra from the EXPRES instrument.

Changes in the line strength track the Sun unsigned magnetic flux from a space observatory closely, and they also track solar velocity shifts. The authors argue the line offers a simple, promising activity proxy to complement existing markers. Adding it to analyses could help separate true planet signals from stellar noise and improve searches for Earth-like worlds.
arxiv-2510-27359:
Kenneth Yang, Wen-Li Wei, and Jen-Chun Lin speed up a cheap way to tune big AI models in this 2025 paper. The cheap way tunes only a chosen subset of the model's weights. Picking the subset by gradients, the usual slope signals, costs a full backward pass and lots of memory. The pick also shifts with random batch luck.

Their method, GD-FPS, makes the pick with forward passes only, so no gradients at all. It scales each weight by how much its activity grew since pretraining, measured against a fixed anchor. Across twenty-six vision tasks, the picks matched or beat rival methods. Next to the gradient method, it used about eighteen times less memory and ran over twice as fast at the picking stage. The pick is also fixed and repeatable.
arxiv-2510-27459:
N. A. Makda, S. L. Blyth, and R. E. Skelton survey ultra-diffuse galaxy analogues across a large sample of galaxy clusters in the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam wide-field survey. Ultra-diffuse galaxies are faint, spread-out systems whose abundance in clusters tests formation theories. The team finds thousands of analogues above background counts in most of the clusters studied, spanning a nearby redshift slice and a wide halo mass range.

Analogue properties resemble previously studied ultra-diffuse galaxies, reaffirming they extend a continuous galaxy distribution. Their counts per cluster follow a power law in halo mass consistent with earlier studies and with simulations of galaxies in cored dark matter halos formed by tidal stripping. Red analogues thin out toward cluster outskirts more clearly than blue ones, hinting environment affects red systems more strongly.
arxiv-2510-27559:
Raffaele D'Avino, Gabriel Senno, Mir Alimuddin, and Antonio Acín study a quantum setup in 2025 where trust in the tools is kept low. In a prepare-and-measure test, one side makes states and the other side checks them. The sole rule here is a cap on the energy of each state that is made. Links called entanglement, where states affect each other at a distance, are allowed.

Allowing such links widens the set of results that can occur. That change cuts the amount of provable random bits, in some cases to zero. It also breaks a known bound for telling one quantum channel from a plain, unchanged path. Low-trust tests must hence account for linked tricks.
arxiv-2511-00059:
Aditya Singh, Zihang Wen, and Srujananjali Medicherla automatically find neurons in OthelloGPT that encode rule-based game logic. The transformer, trained to predict valid Othello moves, is complex enough for rich computation yet grounded in clear rules, making it an ideal interpretability testbed. Regression decision trees map board states to neuron activations in the feed-forward layers.

Decision paths where neurons fire strongly are extracted and converted into human-readable logical forms. Interpretability readers get an automated alternative to hand-inspecting neurons. Turning activation patterns into stated rules lets researchers check whether a model's internal logic matches the game's actual rules.
arxiv-2511-00659:
Wang Chen and six co-authors hunt for one law behind erratic driving, human and machine alike. Certifying self-driving cars demands realistic rates of rare, dangerous behavior, yet models calibrated on real data often miss collision rates because behavior has long statistical tails. Mining large micro-level trajectory datasets from global human and autonomous fleets, the team uncovers a shifted power law that fits both.

The law needs only one or two parameters, so it calibrates even when data is sparse. It matches frequent behavior and rare safety-critical deviations in one form, with a nearly identical tail for humans and machines, clearly beating Gaussian baselines. Plugged into an agent-based traffic simulator, it reproduces real-world crash patterns for both driver types without after-the-fact correction, a data-efficient foundation for simulation-based certification.
arxiv-2511-01059:
Hailong Yin, Bin Zhu, Jingjing Chen, and Chong-Wah Ngo propose ET2RAG, a cheaper way to combine retrieval with language model generation. Retrieval can drag in irrelevant documents, while methods that sample many answers and vote among them are accurate but expensive.

Their framework needs no training. It retrieves the most relevant documents, then has the model draft several candidate answers with controlled lengths. Similarity among the candidates feeds a majority vote that picks the final answer. A key finding is that partial drafts already carry enough signal for the vote, so generation can stop early. That shortcut is how the method balances computing cost against answer quality.
arxiv-2511-01159:
Slawomir Kolodziej and Ngoc Cuong Nguyen work in complex analysis on compact Hermitian manifolds, studying m-subharmonic functions, a family of generalized plurisubharmonic functions tied to a background form. Their focus is the size of the sets where such functions dive toward negative infinity.

They prove a sharp decay estimate for the capacity of the sublevel sets of these functions. The result generalizes both the top degree case and the earlier range of cases known on compact Kahler manifolds. They also fully characterize the polar sets of such functions, the exceptional sets where the functions are not locally integrable, in terms of local and global capacities and of extremal functions. Such characterizations anchor the potential theory used across complex geometry.
arxiv-2511-01259:
Zhiqi Li and colleagues make fluid simulation differentiable on flow maps, so that gradients can flow through a simulation for tasks like identifying, predicting, and controlling vortices. The key observation is that the forward simulation and its backward adjoint twin share the same flow map, which transports fluid quantities from the first frame to the current one.

Their adjoint solver runs directly on that map, propagating gradient information backward without differentiating every intermediate numerical step or storing intermediate states, the twin costs of conventional adjoint methods. A sparse representation mixing long and short maps keeps the cost down. The method uses modest memory even at high resolution while tracking vorticity accurately, opening differentiable tasks that need precise vortex control.
arxiv-2511-01959:
Eleonora Villa and six colleagues continue a program to free pulsar timing array results from the analyst's prior choices. Array analyses must model each pulsar's noise before any gravitational wave background can be inferred, and fixing a uniform noise prior per pulsar can bias the combined inference. Their hierarchical Bayesian strategy instead parametrizes the noise priors by higher-level hyperparameters shared across the array.

The remaining danger is sensitivity to the hyperprior itself. The authors recast the model. They project the hyperparameters at right angles onto the physical parameter subspace. The projection runs through normalizing flows. The flows keep the transformation reversible. They also preserve shrinkage and information pooling between pulsars. Sampling uses the flow-guided i-nessai sampler. Applied to a minimal three-pulsar case, the method simultaneously inferred noise and background parameters, with the reparametrized treatment constraining the noise more stably.
arxiv-2511-02159:
Stefano Falletta and six co-authors resolve a standing confusion in materials modelling about how to correct a known error in modelling polarons, electrons or holes that distort the crystal around them. Density functional theory suffers a self-interaction error that misplaces these states and misprices their formation energy. Two kinds of fixes, one adding charge to the simulated cell and one staying neutral, grew up side by side with no clear map between them.

The authors prove the formulations are equivalent: several named methods all produce the same corrected energy, fully fixed by the neutral state of the distorted structure. Remaining differences come only from how each method handles screening and finite-size effects. Tests on five prototype polarons, in materials from magnesium oxide to titanium dioxide, showed very close agreement between the approaches.
arxiv-2511-02359:
Davor Dragičević, Yeor Hafouta, and Juho Leppänen study how quickly a chaotic system forgets, when the system itself is chosen at random at every step. Their objects are random intermittent maps of LSV type, which linger near a neutral point and produce polynomial, rather than exponential, loss of memory. The randomness comes from a parameter drawn from a fast-mixing environment, and the question is what survives of the classical limit theorems in this quenched, random setting.

When the parameter stays essentially below one fifth, the authors obtain polynomial decay of correlations, central limit theorems with explicit rates, moment bounds, and almost sure invariance principles, which describe path-by-path fluctuations. Their threshold, stated through the parameter's essential infimum, is more natural for this problem than an earlier result phrased through its supremum. The abstract machinery is built to be reusable for other random dynamical systems.
arxiv-2511-02459:
Mark Bell and Saul Schleimer, mathematicians in geometric topology, settle the running time of a basic decision problem about surfaces. The mapping class group of a compact surface collects all the ways the surface can be deformed and twisted onto itself, up to continuous deformation. Its word problem asks: given a word written in the group's generators, does it represent the identity, the deformation that does nothing overall?

The authors give an algorithm that answers the question in quasi-linear time, on the order of n times the cube of the logarithm of n for an input of length n. That is essentially as fast as reading the input a few times over. Word problems are the most basic algorithmic question one can ask about a group. For mapping class groups, which encode the symmetries of surfaces, an efficient solution anchors a wider theory of computation with curves and surfaces.
arxiv-2511-02759:
Julius Fiedler, Carsten Knoll, and Klaus Robenack describe a way to turn control engineering knowledge into formal, machine-readable form with help from language models. Their 2025 paper builds on a framework called PyIRK, which stores knowledge in a graph that people can read and software can process. The raw material is plain text and math definitions in LaTeX.

The models assist in converting those sources into structured graph entries, rather than doing the job alone. As a first use, the team generated an interactive semantic layer that enriches the source documents themselves. Readers can then follow linked concepts while they study. The authors see the approach as a step toward shared, checkable knowledge bases that a whole field can build together.
arxiv-2511-03359:
Hans De Raedt and colleagues simulate a full fifty-qubit quantum computer on JUPITER, Europe's first exascale machine. Tracking every state of fifty qubits strains memory past what graphics chips hold alone. Their new simulator stretches memory through fast links to processor memory, packs data adaptively to save space, and tunes network traffic on the fly.

Those moves lift speed many times over the prior forty-eight-qubit record held elsewhere. Full simulation matters because it lets researchers test quantum programs exactly before hardware can run them. Running on a mixed processor and graphics design also shows how exascale machines can serve quantum science directly. The team frames the run as a first for this machine class.
arxiv-2511-03659:
Aurora Wilde and colleagues check whether the giant black holes in six early quasars sit at the centers of their host galaxies. Images from a millimeter array pin each host through glowing carbon and dust at fine detail. A space telescope's infrared camera pins each quasar, with star positions from a sky survey anchoring the alignment.

All six black holes fall within the central few hundred parsecs of their hosts, with no real offset found. Centered black holes fit a picture where early growth happens deep in the galaxy's core, fed by its densest gas. A wandering-hole story would have predicted measurable shifts. Tight early centering also steadies models that grow billion-sun black holes within the universe's first billion years.
arxiv-2511-03859:
Tammy Mackenzie, Sukriti Punj, Natalie Perez, Sreyoshi Bhaduri, and Branislav Radeljic examine how senior decision makers handle power when AI enters their institutions. Respondents came from schools, government, business, and civic groups in North America and Europe, answering tailored surveys built on a governance framework.

Answers are reported through twelve fictional personas that hide names while keeping real facts. The personas show how personal agency, workplace logics, and formal structures meet in AI governance. Discussion covers field-level power, keeping bodies stable during change, and pushing change itself. A table of power dynamics and five testable claims close the study for later work.
arxiv-2511-04259:
Poulami Bag, Tanwi Debnath, Shubhadip Nayak, and Pulak K Ghosh show how wall alignment can steer active Janus particles into directed motion inside a narrow channel. Rectifying the random-looking swimming of active particles is a route to controlled transport and sorting of artificial and natural swimmers.

Simulations find that a slight difference in alignment strength between the two walls, or a small gravitational drag, breaks up-down symmetry. Chiral particles then rectify with efficiency above sixty percent in its runs. Achiral swimmers need an added unbiased flow that induces orbiting before the same trick works. Effects stayed robust across propulsion, chirality, and preferred orientation changes.
arxiv-2511-04359:
Sinchan Snigdha Rej and Bimalendu Deb propose multi-qubit geometric phase gates for neutral-atom quantum computers based on double stimulated Raman adiabatic passage. Adiabatic geometric gates resist fluctuations better than Rydberg blockade gates that rely on dynamical phase, and every atom stays individually addressable in their design.

A controllable geometric phase is imprinted without extra lasers on target atoms as the gate scales from two qubits to many. Numerical fidelity reaches ninety-eight to ninety-nine percent at gate times near six tenths of a microsecond in their analysis. Error analysis shows resilience to Rabi frequency swings, finite blockade strength, and atom position variation. Grover search simulations complete the feasibility case.
arxiv-2511-04759:
Hala Lamdouar leads eleven authors with HiSAXy, a fast way to find solar wind structures in huge data sets. The interplanetary magnetic field carries small discontinuities that scientists now hunt by hand. Millions of time series make manual hunting hopeless.

Their hybrid method joins indexable symbolic approximation with density-based hierarchical clustering. The first step compresses series into searchable symbols, the second groups real patterns and rejects noise. Applied to magnetic field records, it finds the embedded discontinuities automatically. The authors report large savings in human analysis time while keeping detection quality high.
arxiv-2511-04859:
Yik Lun Kei leads six authors clustering nodes in attributed graphs with a decoder-only design. Each node carries several measured attributes alongside its graph links. Low-dimensional node representations get node-specific priors in their framework.

A neural decoder bridges those latent variables back to the observed attributes. A graph-fused LASSO penalty on the prior means pulls linked nodes toward shared clusters. Alternating direction optimization fits the model, with Langevin dynamics for posterior sampling. Tests on grid graphs and messy real data show the clustering works, using structure and attributes together rather than either alone.
arxiv-2511-05159:
Shubhayan Pan and co-authors extend convex clustering into kernel spaces, so it can group data whose clusters bend or cannot be split by a straight line. Convex clustering starts with each point as its own center and merges them step by step, with no set cluster count.

Their version lifts points into a rich feature space first, where bent shapes turn simpler. They give finite-sample bounds and prove the method settles to the right answer as data grow. Tests and theory together show where the kernel lift beats the plain method and where it costs more.
arxiv-2511-05459:
Jingxuan Xu and co-authors introduce SWE-Compass, a broad benchmark for the coding skills of agentic language models. Past software tests leaned hard on Python bug fixes or puzzle tasks, which miss much of real developer work and favor one tongue.

SWE-Compass spans eight task types, eight work scenes, and ten programming languages in one structured frame. It aims to match how code is built in production, from fixes to features. A unified score lets buyers and builders compare models on the full spread of software work, not a narrow slice.
arxiv-2511-05759:
Marcelo Arenas and co-authors ask whether generating a language from examples is merely possible or actually feasible. A known result says generation in the limit is always possible in principle: with enough positive examples, a learner can eventually mimic a target language. That says nothing about how many examples it takes.

The team studies sample complexity for several classic families of formal languages. Infeasibility shows up early, already for regular and context-free languages. It persists for simpler subclasses and for pattern languages, a family long studied in language identification. Their results draw a clear line between what theory permits in the limit and what any learner could do with realistic amounts of data.
arxiv-2511-05959:
Ali Eghbali, Meysam Hosseinpour-Sadid, and Adel Rezaei-Aghdam build WZW models on low-sized Lie supergroups, exotic symmetry objects that mix two kinds of directions. In the smallest such size only three non-Abelian superalgebras carry a suitable metric. The authors review models on two of them and build the model on the third.

That third model lacks a wanted Poisson-Lie symmetry, so they gauge a subgroup to create three new exact field theories of WZW type. One gauged model's dual keeps its key invariance at one loop, a first for this setting. They then sort all Yang-Baxter deformations of the third model by solving a graded form of the classic equation. Such sortings are rare for supergroups and took heavy technical work.
arxiv-2511-06159:
Rasman Mubtasim Swargo and Md Arifuzzaman tackle a practical problem in science computing: moving petabytes of data between distant computing clusters. Older tools force users to tune transfer settings by hand or adjust only one setting at a time. Their method adjusts several transfer parameters together to keep data moving fast.

Their system combines heuristic parallelism, continuous pipelining, and a deep reinforcement learning optimizer that sets concurrency. A lightweight network simulator cuts agent training to under four minutes, far faster than training online. In tests across varied datasets, the method beat existing tools, reaching up to nine and a half times higher throughput.
arxiv-2511-06259:
Yiwen Zhang and co-authors improve how chemists identify unknown compounds from tandem mass spectra. Matching a spectrum against a library fails when the compound is missing from that library, and newer cross-modal methods often misalign spectra with structures. Their framework, GLMR, uses generative modeling to close that gap.

First, a contrastive model shortlists candidate molecules for the measured spectrum. Then a generative language model uses those candidates plus the spectrum to draft refined structures, which re-rank the shortlist by similarity. On the MassSpecGym benchmark and a new twenty-thousand-entry dataset, GLMR improved top-one accuracy by over forty percent relative to prior methods and generalized well.
arxiv-2511-06359:
Jiacheng Wang and co-authors defend low-altitude drone networks that combine sensing and communication in one system. Air taxis and similar services depend on these integrated systems, yet channel-access attacks can degrade them and threaten safety. The defense is framed as a Stackelberg game, a contest where one side commits to a move first.

The attacker plays leader, while the legitimate drone and ground base station respond as followers. Metrics for communication and sensing quality measure the damage under attack. Solving the game by backward induction gives an equilibrium where defenders adjust their strategies as conditions change. Simulations showed the method settling to a stable outcome and beating existing baselines.
arxiv-2511-06459:
Huanbo Lyu and co-authors improve offline optimization, where candidate designs are judged only by surrogate models trained on fixed data. Surrogate errors can flip which candidates look best, misleading the whole search. Earlier fixes leaned on Gaussian process uncertainty, which ties the method to one model family and heavy computation.

Their dual-ranking strategy ranks candidates twice: once by predicted quality and once by an uncertainty-aware score, using whatever surrogate supplies both numbers. Candidates that are strong and reliable on both rankings rise to the front. Wide experiments, including ablations and sensitivity checks, showed the strategy stays effective and robust across different surrogate types.
arxiv-2511-06559:
Rui Ai, David Simchi-Levi, and Haifeng Xu design markets where platforms buy content from human creators and generative models side by side. Content is not an ordinary good here, because material from one domain can train and improve generation in another. Video models, for instance, lean heavily on image data to gain quality.

The authors build optimal nonlinear procurement mechanisms that maximize platform revenue or social welfare, and isolate which traits of generative systems keep the high-dimensional design solvable. Some domains face fiercer competition and others overproduction. Adding data intermediaries as a third market layer can leave everyone worse off, a finding the authors use to argue for regulation, backed by simulations.
arxiv-2511-06759:
Alexey Rosaev, Eva Plavalova, and Pavel Nesterov model the restricted three-body problem just outside an orbital resonance. A light test particle with small eccentricity moves near, but not exactly in, resonance with a larger body. When the resonant argument circles the resonance instead of locking, the dynamics need their own treatment for small perturbations.

A linearization method handles the motion in that near-resonant zone. Keeping only the strongest single-frequency perturbation reduces the problem to the Mathieu equation, the classic parametric oscillator. The model describes how the perturbation acts near resonance and can estimate where one resonance sits and where the borders between neighboring ones fall.
arxiv-2511-06959:
B Jia, Q Zhong, Y Li, and Y Xiao build a reduced theory of the ion temperature gradient instability, a major source of turbulence that leaks heat from tokamak fusion plasmas. Starting from an averaged magnetic drift model with a first-order finite Larmor radius expansion, they reduce the mode's eigenvalue equation to a Schrödinger-type differential equation. Generalized translational invariance then extends the model to reversed magnetic shear configurations.

Benchmarks against global gyrokinetic runs from the GTC code show good quantitative accord. In reversed shear the model reveals a double-well potential, which makes the lowest even mode and the first odd mode degenerate when the wells sit far apart. Growth peaks when two rational surfaces are slightly separated, and the instability resonates with the magnetic drift frequency.
arxiv-2511-07159:
Mehmet Turker Takci, James Day, and Meysam Qadrdan quantify how much flexibility data centres can offer the power grid. Data centres are growing fast and strain systems rich in variable renewables, yet they are usually run as passive loads. The authors build a whole-facility optimization model that schedules IT workloads, uninterruptible power supply storage, and cooling together to find the least-cost baseline operation of a facility.

On top of that baseline, their duration-aware assessment computes, for any start time and requested power change, how long the deviation can be sustained within operational, thermal, and recovery limits. Flexibility turns out asymmetric: reducing load works mainly by deferring IT work, which also cuts cooling, while increasing load leans on cooling, thermal storage, and charging the UPS. The envelope could serve reserve and frequency response markets.
arxiv-2511-07559:
Md Motaleb Hossen Manik and co-authors fix a quiet failure inside neural networks: dead neurons. The standard ReLU activation cuts all negative values to zero, so some units stop learning entirely. Their replacement keeps the same average behavior while staying alive.

Noise-ReLU swaps negative outputs for zero-mean Gaussian noise instead of silence. Gradients keep flowing through quiet regions, and the noise acts like a gentle regularizer during training. Tests on handwritten digits with two network styles check whether accuracy holds or improves. If the trick scales, a one-line activation change could reduce wasted capacity across many models.
arxiv-2511-07659:
Sai Shridhar Balamurali and Lu Cheng revive an old tool for judging language model answers. Lexical scores miss meaning, while using a giant model as judge costs heavily. Natural language inference, which checks whether one text entails another, offers a cheap middle path.

Adding a simple lexical-match flag lifts inference scoring to match a top commercial judge on long-form questions, with far fewer parameters. A new benchmark of three thousand human-rated samples across five datasets and five models tests alignment rigorously. Cheap metrics that track human judgment let teams evaluate more answers, more often, without renting a giant judge for every check.
arxiv-2511-07859:
Jason Li settles a classic algorithms problem: shortest paths when some road lengths are negative. Negative weights break the fast greedy methods used for ordinary graphs, and deterministic near-linear algorithms were missing. Randomization had carried the field, leaving a determinism gap.

A deterministic padded decomposition for directed graphs supplies the key ingredient. Built on that decomposition, the shortest path algorithm runs in near-linear time without dice rolls. The decomposition itself may serve other directed graph problems. Deterministic guarantees matter when software must behave identically on every run, from routing engines to program analysis tools.
arxiv-2511-07959:
Pulong Ma builds space-time covariance functions through hierarchical mixtures, aiming at data that vary across place and time together. Covariance functions describe how strongly values at two points relate, and real patterns are often asymmetric in space versus time. A flexible construction should still give formulas simple enough to use.

The mixture approach breaks model building into layers, where simple mixing choices yield closed forms and matching process descriptions. A characterization theorem links mixing measures to statistical properties. New models outperform older ones on Irish wind data and United States air temperature data, and the method extends to nonstationary and multivariate cases.
arxiv-2511-08059:
Stefan Albert Horstmann and colleagues studied how software developers search for help on privacy law during design work. Rules such as the European GDPR and California CCPA force developers to make legal choices they are rarely trained for. Thirty developers worked through a privacy sensitive scenario using their own knowledge, web sources, and an AI assistant.

Think aloud sessions and interviews showed trouble with every source. Personal knowledge fell short, web pages were often too complex, and AI answers were clear but missed case specific issues. The authors call for privacy resources that developers can understand quickly and turn into concrete action.
arxiv-2511-08159:
Ludwik Dabrowski, Sugato Mukhopadhyay, and Filip Pozar compute the spectral torsion of the internal noncommutative geometry behind the Standard Model of particle physics. Noncommutative geometry rebuilds the model from spectral data, and torsion is one geometric quantity that can be extracted from that data. With a suitable change to the usual differential calculus, the spectral torsion matches a functional built from the connection.

The authors also trace how torsion affects other spectral quantities tied to volume, metric, Einstein tensors, and scalar curvature. Standard Model Yukawa couplings and the Majorana mass matrix shape the outcomes. The work clarifies which parts of the internal geometry torsion actually controls.
arxiv-2511-08359:
Arun Atwal, Jessica Burridge, Antonio Jacques Costa, and Christoph Englert survey how future colliders could reveal CP violation in Higgs effects, a possible source of the cosmic matter mirror matter gap. Their analysis centers on new CP breaking effects in the gauge Higgs sector, described through dimension six effective field theory terms. Several planned electron positron and proton proton facilities are compared against the high luminosity LHC program.

Future machines promise roughly an order of magnitude better sensitivity to these anomalous effects. That reach could both reveal beyond Standard Model physics and spot its character. The authors aim their comprehensive comparison at the community now choosing a future collider roadmap.
arxiv-2511-08759:
Haoxiang Wan, Linhan Fang, and Xingpeng Li ask whether data centers can help the power grid simply by moving their computing around. Data center demand is set to double globally by 2026 under AI growth. Big fixed loads congest transmission lines, while solar and wind farms lose output whenever the grid cannot absorb it.

An optimal power flow model coordinates generation, security reserves, and movable data center load together. On a modified IEEE seventy-three bus test system, rigid placement causes severe violations, with some lines overloaded by about thirty percent. Allowing workloads to migrate restores feasibility in the studied scenarios. Solar curtailment falls by up to sixty-one percent when load shifts toward sunny regions. The authors argue spatial flexibility could defer costly transmission upgrades.
arxiv-2511-08959:
Adriana Gavidia and thirteen co-authors refine the physics models behind a new detector material for the NEW-MUSIC submillimeter camera. The camera will observe from eighty to four hundred twenty gigahertz in six bands with polarimetry, chasing galaxy evolution, the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect, and dusty sources across cosmic time.

Its ninety GHz band needs aluminum-manganese kinetic inductance detectors, because pure aluminum's pair-breaking energy is too high, yet the alloy is barely explored as a device material. The team first improves the standard BCS model fitting for aluminum devices by dropping analytic shortcuts for the complex conductivity, which reduces overlap among fit values when analyzing the alloy. A gap smearing parameter, a standard extension for high kinetic inductance materials, is then tested and found not to improve the fits. Optical readings of the devices anchor the work.
arxiv-2511-09159:
Thomas Lamby revisits Rademacher's theorem, a classic result saying that a Lipschitz function has a total differential at almost every point. He reads the theorem as an improvement principle: rough pointwise control should sharpen into vanishing control nearly everywhere. His paper asks whether the same sharpening holds in finer spaces built from polynomial approximation.

Working in pointwise Calderón-Zygmund spaces with a flexible growth function, Lamby allows fractional smoothness and logarithmic corrections. He proves that uniform membership on a measurable set improves almost everywhere to a vanishing approximation rate. The proof uses measurability arguments, a generalized Whitney extension theorem, and fine Sobolev properties. Counterexamples show the gain cannot generally be pushed one step further.
arxiv-2511-09259:
Evgeny Andronov studies special fluctuation gauges used in nuclear collisions to probe the phase diagram of strongly interacting matter. Event-by-event fluctuations mix trivial volume effects with real dynamics, and strongly intensive quantities are built to cancel the volume part. His focus is forward-backward rapidity correlations of particle multiplicities.

Within the color string model, the second-order quantity is fixed by single-string correlations and the string fusion process. Andronov extends the analysis to a third-order strongly intensive measure for the same correlations. He then tests how that observable behaves inside the PYTHIA8 event generator, a standard simulation tool for particle physics. The work shows what such gauges can reveal about collision dynamics.
arxiv-2511-09359:
Dany Davesne and two co-authors compute the surface energy of nuclear matter. They solve Hartree-Fock equations with the Lagrange mesh method. Surface energy governs how nuclear matter in a slab resists creating new surface, a key input for nuclear models. Earlier calculations mostly relied on the slower Numerov algorithm.

The mesh method proves faster and more accurate, letting the authors use boxes large enough to tame Friedel oscillations. They reach precision on the surface energy within a few dozen kiloelectronvolts. Results are reported for several Gogny interactions not discussed before in this context. Including the spin-orbit term lowers the surface energy by roughly one to two megaelectronvolts, they find.
arxiv-2511-09659:
William G. Lamb and seven co-authors show that the gravitational wave background pulsar timing arrays have found should not be perfectly Gaussian. The background should come from a finite set of supermassive black hole binaries, not an idealized endless ensemble. Current analyses also assume idealized emission frequencies and ignore interference between binaries' signals.

The team builds analytic and numeric models of the background from circular, inspiralling, inclined binaries without those shortcuts. Finite set size and observation windowing introduce measurable non-Gaussian traits into the timing signal. Those traits are currently unmodeled in pulsar timing analyses, they warn. Accounting for them could matter as data sets grow more sensitive and readings of the cosmos sharpen.
arxiv-2511-09759:
Borna Bateni, Yubai Yuan, Qi Xu, and Annie Qu address a common trial problem: a target site has control patients but no treated ones, while a source site has both. Rather than estimate only an average effect, they aim to rebuild the full distribution of treated outcomes at the target site. Sites may differ in measurements, features, reporting, and patient mix, which the method must absorb.

Their approach learns a transformation between sites by comparing the control groups, using an optimal transport criterion. Applying that map to the source treated sample creates a synthetic target treated sample, and they prove it converges to the true distribution. Simulations and a real test on patient-derived xenograft data show the framework recovering the target treated distribution well.
arxiv-2511-09859:
Shreya Shukla, Abhijith Jayakumar, and Andrey Y. Lokhov attack the inverse problem for statistical field theories: recovering the small-scale couplings of a system straight from data. The forward route, predicting observables from an action, is often computationally intractable. Their approach handles discrete, continuous, and hybrid variables in a single approach, and it learns from whatever data is available, including correlation measurements when full configurations are missing.

Benchmarks include Wegner's Ising gauge theory, the phi-four theory, Schwinger and sine-Gordon models, and mixed spin-gauge systems, with accurate parameter recovery throughout. Repeating the procedure under coarse-graining reconstructs full renormalization-group flows, exposing phase boundaries and fixed points without perturbation theory. The authors expect wide use in strongly coupled regimes where analytic tools fail.
arxiv-2511-09959:
Ayumu Fukushi, Yoshinori Nakanishi-Ohno, and Takeru Matsuda examine the geometry of a family of probability laws under the Wasserstein metric, which measures distance between laws by transport cost. One-dimensional location-scale models are known to be flat in this geometry. They are flat in themselves, and they sit flat in the larger space too. The authors present a location-scale-shape model that adds a shape parameter controlling tail heaviness, generalizing several laws used in extreme-value theory.

For this richer family, they show the geometry splits. The model is intrinsically flat, meaning its internal curvature vanishes. Yet it is extrinsically curved, meaning it bends inside the ambient space of laws. The contrast separates two notions of flatness that coincide for the simpler location-scale case and clarifies the shape family's structure.
arxiv-2511-10059:
Qilang Ye and six co-authors test whether multimodal language models can notice when a video's sound does not match its picture. They built AV-ConfuseBench, which alters an object's sound, for example muting a sounding object, then asks whether that sound is present. Leading models, including Qwen2.5-Omni and Gemini 2.5, largely failed, reasoning from what they saw rather than what they heard.

Their remedy, RL-CoMM, adds a large audio language model that reasons from sound alone as a reference. A step-wise reward then teaches the main model to improve its audio-visual reasoning against that reference, and a confidence optimization stage steadies the final answer. Across audio-visual question answering and hallucination tests, accuracy rose by roughly ten to thirty points over the baseline with limited training data.
arxiv-2511-10359:
Oleksiy Klurman and Vlad Matei revisit a question in random polynomials: how often is a polynomial with random multiplicative coefficients irreducible, meaning it cannot be factored into smaller polynomials? Their coefficients come from a random completely multiplicative function taking values plus or minus one, so each coefficient is forced by the values at primes. The polynomial's degree grows with a cutoff parameter.

The authors prove that the probability of irreducibility has limsup equal to one as the degree grows. In plain terms, along a suitable sequence of degrees, almost all such random polynomials are irreducible, even though the coefficients are far from independent. The result sharpens earlier understanding of factorization behavior in this rigid random model.
arxiv-2511-10659:
Vikram Aggarwal and six co-authors show how large language models can unlock government fiscal documents, using the annual publications of the Indian state of Karnataka as their test case. These documents run past 200 pages of complex, hierarchical tables, and traditional optical character recognition cannot verify that the numbers it extracts are right.

Their multi-stage pipeline combines domain knowledge, sequential context across pages, and algorithmic validation. The key trick uses the documents' own structure: because fiscal tables carry totals at every level of the hierarchy, extracted figures can be checked against those totals at several levels. The result is high-accuracy extraction that turns PDF disclosures into research-ready databases, an approach the authors say should transfer to other developing country contexts.
arxiv-2511-10759:
Joseph Paul MacManus proves a rigidity theorem about infinite graphs that look the same from every vertex. His setting is a connected, locally finite, quasi-transitive graph in which every bi-infinite quasi-geodesic that uniformly separates the graph splits it into exactly two deep pieces.

MacManus shows any such graph must be quasi-isometric to one of only two shapes: the Euclidean plane or the hyperbolic plane. When the graph is a Cayley graph, the group is therefore a virtual surface group, extending the classic fact that a hyperbolic group with circular boundary is virtually Fuchsian. The result settles a problem posed by Churkin in the Kourovka Notebook in 1999. The proof runs through an isoperimetric inequality that forces the graph to be either hyperbolic or of quadratic growth.
arxiv-2511-10859:
Xuchen Gong and Tian Li look for a cheaper way to train machine learning models without leaking private data. Standard private training is safe but slow and memory hungry. A lighter route guesses slopes from function values alone, yet on its own it often learns worse than the standard method.

Their PAZO methods use public data to guide those guesses and come with theory for when public and private data are alike. On picture and text tasks, in both first training and fine-tuning, PAZO gave a better balance of privacy and skill than strong baselines. It also ran much faster, with speeds up to sixteen times higher in their tests.
arxiv-2511-11059:
Yoshiki Fukusumi and Taishi Kawamoto use modern symmetry theory to classify a broad class of quantum systems that bend the usual rules of energy and balance. Their frame views symmetries as algebraic data inside a higher symmetry theory. From that data they build a general form of quantum dimension, a number that measures how a charge-like object counts states, for these nonstandard systems.

The general data sort both gapless and gapped flows between phases, which describe phase change in the systems at hand. The discussion also links standard constructions and dualities to wall problems between topological theories. The work gives a tidy, algebra-based sorting of symmetries for this class.
arxiv-2511-11259:
Anish Kumar, Vivek Semwal, and Shradha Mishra study a polar flock, a group of self-driven particles that tend to align, moving through a patchy two-dimensional setting. Random patches carry higher noise, so particles that enter lose their alignment, though the patches do not block motion the way solid disorder does. The question is how order in the flock changes as those patches fill more of the space.

As patch coverage grows, the flock passes from long-range order to a weaker quasi-long-range order and then to full disorder. The jump from order to disorder also softens from abrupt to gradual. Overall, the pattern matches what solid disorder produces in flocks.
arxiv-2511-11359:
Matthew Burns and Jiaming Liang propose LAMP, a linear-space method for large-scale optimal transport, the problem of moving mass between two spreads at least cost. Primal-dual methods for transport store a full matrix, which explodes memory at scale. LAMP instead tracks an averaged dual sequence, cutting storage from the product of the two sizes to their sum while keeping dense, graphics-friendly arithmetic.

The method keeps the arithmetic cost of classic mirror prox schemes and adds a computable certificate for how far the last iterate sits from optimal, plus a checkable condition for best-iterate convergence. A tuned graphics implementation beat first-order baselines on high-accuracy problems and scaled to sizes beyond prior reach.
arxiv-2511-11559:
Alex Kasman and Robert Milson share two practical facts about generating functions, the formal power series that encode number sequences in a single expression. Facts of this kind let mathematicians read properties of a sequence straight off its generating function.

First, when a differential operator has the generating function as an eigenfunction, recursion relations for the sequence can be built directly from it. Second, taking the inner product of the generating function with itself reveals whether the sequence is orthogonal under some inner product. Examples include a number sequence, exceptional Hermite polynomials, and a non-commutative case, showing the tricks work well beyond textbook settings.
arxiv-2511-11759:
Fred Heiding and Simon Lermen demonstrate, end to end, how AI chatbots can be turned into phishing machines aimed at elderly people. Their pipeline runs from jailbreaking language models, through generating deceptive messages, to testing them on real volunteers.

Six frontier models were probed across four attack categories, and several showed near-complete susceptibility to some approaches. In a human study with one hundred eight senior volunteers, AI-generated phishing emails compromised eleven percent of participants. The authors present the work as a warning: safety guardrails currently fail the people most vulnerable to fraud, and defenses must be judged by complete attack chains, not single prompts.
arxiv-2511-11959:
Leonardi Melo and four co-authors compare three U-Net networks on ancient rock art. The task is to outline petroglyphs at Brazilian sites. Carved figures fade into weathered stone there. Automatic tracing would speed documentation a lot. All three networks share a border-enhanced Gaussian loss, built to sharpen edges.

The variants add distinct attention designs. One adds residual blocks with gated attention. Another uses spatial-channel attention modules. All are tested with five-fold cross-validation. The images come from the Poço da Bebidinha Archaeological Complex in Piauí. The attention-residual design ranks among the strongest performers. Carved art cannot be replaced, so automated readings must earn trust.
arxiv-2511-12359:
Yifan Zhu, Sammie Katt and Samuel Kaski argue that people who act in seemingly irrational ways may instead be acting rationally under biased beliefs and limited memory. Predicting such behavior in users and human collaborators is a key challenge for AI. A bounded memory process can make beliefs drift in a dynamically inconsistent way over time.

The authors define a family of computational-rational user models where agents act optimally given those biased beliefs. The open problem is to infer, from passive observations alone, both the user's hidden belief state and their specific cognitive bound. They propose an online method based on nested particle filtering that tracks both at once, and argue the task is tractable for their model family.
arxiv-2511-12459:
Marco Pollanen argues that large-scale surveillance screening has a built-in probabilistic limit that intuition misses. Forensic statisticians have long debated whether searching huge DNA databases weakens a match. Modern systems face a harder version: they screen people across thousands of attributes with threshold rules instead of exact matches.

Pollanen shows with a worked example that flagging anyone who matches any small subset of many attributes turns a seemingly impossible coincidence into hundreds of expected false alerts in a city-sized population. The failure is structural, not a coding flaw. Systems pass through sharp transitions from reliable to unreliable as data scale grows, which sets fundamental limits on screening reliability.
arxiv-2511-12759:
James Moore asks whether hunting through memory works like an animal foraging for food. In semantic fluency tasks, people name words in bursts from one cluster of related ideas, then jump to a fresh cluster, much as foragers leave a depleted patch. Optimal foraging theory, through the marginal value theorem, predicts when to leave. Moore tested whether modern embedding spaces with simple search can reproduce the human pattern.

Plain random walks on the embedding space matched optimal foraging behavior. Surprisingly, a fancier sampler, Metropolis-Hastings, which accepts or rejects new clusters strategically and was expected to model human choices better, did not match human behavior. The conclusion favors the view that the structure of the embedding does the heavy lifting: with a well-organized semantic space, even simple sampling produces near-optimal foraging. It is a caution against assuming that more complex cognitive machinery explains a pattern better.
arxiv-2511-13059:
Johannes Wehrstein and seven co-authors argue that database benchmarks test a workload nobody runs. Traces released by cloud data warehouse providers show real workloads full of repeated queries and string-heavy operations, traits the standard TPC-H and TPC-DS benchmarks lack. Redbench generates workloads that reproduce those real traits. It combines several techniques to reshape existing benchmarks into realistic query streams. The streams are tuned to specific objectives while preserving the intrinsic signals found in the traces rather than run-specific artifacts.

Evaluating it, the authors show Redbench produces more realistic and repeatable workloads for cloud warehouses, and that it exposes the true impact of system tuning across four commercial platforms. Benchmarks steer an industry: vendors optimize what benchmarks measure. A generator that makes benchmarks resemble production traffic pushes tuning effort toward what users run, which is the point of the exercise.
arxiv-2511-13259:
Yushuo Zheng and 7 co-authors release GeoX-Bench, a benchmark for finding where a ground photo was taken by matching it to satellite views. Large multimodal models do well on many tasks, yet their skill at cross-view location and pose had not been tested. Such skill matters for navigation, self-driving, and outdoor robots.

GeoX-Bench pairs panoramic and satellite images from many cities and countries, with a large set of questions for training and testing. The authors test twenty-five leading models on location and pose tasks. Models handled location fairly well but dropped sharply on pose, and extra training on the bench data lifted their cross-view skill a great deal.
arxiv-2511-13459:
Bingkun Huang and 4 co-authors build a contact-safe reinforcement learning framework for robots that must touch varied surfaces. Most learning methods work in joint space with little sense of the 3D scene or of contact forces, so safety suffers. Their approach works in task space and plans whole episodes for steadier motion.

Movement primitives reparameterized through Proximal Policy Optimization generate reliable, safe paths, while an energy-aware impedance control goal guards each interaction. The energy check keeps contact forces within safe bounds as the robot works. In tests across surface types in 3D settings, the method beat rivals on success rate while keeping paths smooth and interactions energy-safe.
arxiv-2511-13659:
Koen de Boer and 3 co-authors prove average-case hardness for finding short independent vectors in module lattices of fixed rank.
