Short vector problems anchor the security of post-quantum standards such as ML-DSA and ML-KEM, and module lattices are their working ground. Average hardness was known only for rank one, where the lattice space forms a compact group.

In higher rank that space is neither compact nor a group, so the old proof collapses. Their main tool is automorphic form theory, used to prove rapid equidistribution of random walks over the lattice space. Assuming the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, they obtain a worst-case to average-case reduction with polynomial loss, for every fixed rank.
arxiv-2511-13959:
Jan Maelger develops a framework for pricing the hidden cost of rules inside an insurance company. Insurers must hold assets under solvency rules such as Solvency II and the Swiss Solvency Test, which limit how freely they can invest. Maelger sets up a profit optimization for existing business under those regulatory and risk policy constraints.

From that setup he derives the asset allocation that maximizes profit within a chosen risk appetite. The gap between that best return and what the constraints allow defines an annual opportunity cost faced by the firm. The formalism applies across life, property and casualty, and reinsurance lines and across regulatory frameworks built on a solvency ratio.
arxiv-2511-14359:
Sebastian Lubos, Alexander Felfernig, Damian Garber, and two co-authors test if large mixed-media models can judge how easy a recommender screen is to use. Hand checks of screens are slow and need skill, so a fast machine check is a draw. The team took shots of screens from a set of public recommender sites. The shots cover both the screens that ask what a user likes and the screens that show the picks.

A mixed-media model was told to rate each screen by known ease-of-use rules and to state its grounds. The runs show such models can do rule-style checks at scale and give notes that builders can act on. The team frames the tool as help for user studies, not a stand-in for them.
arxiv-2511-14459:
Alberto Domínguez Corella and Vladimir Veliov revisit a key stability question in optimal control. They study systems where the control enters in a simple linear way. In such problems the best control often switches sharply between extremes. The authors ask how stable the full set of optimality conditions is under small changes.

They define a new distance in the control space that respects that sharp switching form. With it they prove stability under weaker and broader conditions than before. The result also covers some cases that are not linear in the state. The work matters for predictive control methods used in practice.
arxiv-2511-14659:
Chia-Yu Hung, Navonil Majumder, and eight co-authors introduce NORA-1.5, a robot model that links vision, language, and action. Models of this kind can follow instructions and act in the world, but they often fail on new robots or new settings. NORA-1.5 adds a flow-matching action expert to the earlier NORA design.

That change alone lifts scores past the prior model and several leading rivals in both simulated and real tests. The team then trains reward models that judge whether planned actions move toward the goal and how far they stray from shown examples. Post-training with those rewards makes the robot more robust and more likely to finish its tasks.
arxiv-2511-14859:
A. Plati, G. Petrillo, and five co-authors study how dense granular material flows when it is shaken from below. Sand-like flows under vibration matter for handling powders and grains, yet their effective thickness has resisted simple rules. The team simulates a stress-driven vane turning inside a vibrated grain bed.

The flow thickens as the confining pressure rises and thins as shaking grows stronger. Frequency behaves in a trickier way: mid-range shaking weakens the flow most, while very fast shaking loses that benefit. The pattern is explained by a balance between the jiggle energy fed to the grains and the squeeze that holds them down. That balance unifies older, conflicting reports on vibrated grains.
arxiv-2511-15059:
Keito Sasagawa, Shuhei Kurita, and Daisuke Kawahara test how well multimodal language models read Japanese text written vertically. Many Japanese documents run top to bottom, and any serious document tool for Japanese must handle that layout. Yet model testing has mostly used horizontal text, leaving vertical skill unmeasured.

The authors render Japanese passages into images in both directions, building a synthetic reading data set for training and testing. Existing models are then graded on the vertical cases, and fine-tuning effects are checked. The study gives the first focused picture of a gap that matters for real archives, books, and forms in Japan.
arxiv-2511-15159:
Firdavs Nasriddinov, Rafal Kocielnik, and two co-authors teach machines to give surgical trainees feedback in the voice of a human trainer. Good in-the-moment coaching is central to surgical skill, but expert trainers cannot watch every practice case. The team mines real trainer-to-trainee transcripts from dozens of surgeries to learn what useful feedback is built from.

From the transcripts they extract instrument-action-target triplets and cluster them into a clean ontology of surgical moves. A video model then reads new footage and predicts those triplets, using the procedure type and fine instrument motion as context. Feedback text is generated from that structured reading, and the paper also tackles how to grade such feedback fairly.
arxiv-2511-15659:
Fredrick Olness connects atomic nuclei to their quark and gluon foundations with a factorized nuclear structure model. Nuclear physics describes matter through protons and neutrons, while particle physics uses quarks and gluons. Bridging those levels has long been a central challenge. The model explicitly includes both single nucleons and correlated nucleon pairs.

High energy data from lepton scattering, Drell-Yan, and boson production are analyzed together. The fit extracts a universal distribution for quarks and gluons inside correlated pairs. It also finds each nucleus's fraction of such pairs. Successful extraction marks a significant advance, Olness argues. Universal pair distributions let nucleon level and parton level quantities be linked quantitatively across nuclei.
arxiv-2511-15859:
Hina Saeeda, Mazen Mohamad, and three co-authors study how annotation rules are written for AI perception in self-driving cars. Annotation labels the images a system learns from. Poor rules can bake in bias, mixed labels, and safety risk. Yet how such rules are set and used in practice had not been closely examined before this study.

The team interviewed nineteen people from six firms and four research groups. Five main problems stood out: vague rules, hard edge cases, rules that keep changing, mixed practice, and scarce staff and time. Good practice fell into three groups: ethics checks, clearer rule guides, and built-in quality checks. Rule flaws were shown to flow through labels into data quality and system behavior.
arxiv-2511-16059:
Qi-Jun Hong and eight co-authors extend the SLUSCHI run package to automate diffusion runs from first principles molecular motion. The original workflow estimated melting points through solid liquid coexistence runs. Diffusion work instead needs a clean production path at a chosen volume. The extension adapts input and output handling to isolate that stage automatically.

Post processing parses run outputs and computes mean square displacements. Tracer diffusivities follow from the Einstein relation with block averaged error figures. Diagnostic plots show displacement curves, running slopes, and velocity correlations to find true diffusive regimes. Case studies cover liquid alloy diffusion and sublattice melting. Automation reduces manual error in a workflow solids scientists run repeatedly for alloy and energy solids.
arxiv-2511-16159:
Preeti Kharb, Anderson Caproni, and five co-authors report second-epoch radio observations of eight Seyfert and LINER galaxies, classes of active galactic nuclei with relatively quiet radio emission. Sources were chosen for double-peaked or asymmetric emission lines in survey spectra, hints of jets or dual black holes. Using very long baseline interferometry, which links antennas for parsec-scale sharpness, they revisit each galaxy years after a first epoch.

Parsec-scale radio emission appears in seven of eight sources, and jet-like features persist over roughly four to nine years. One source changed structure markedly over nine years, and two show tentative faster-than-light jet motion, including a candidate binary black hole system. Larger-scale images reveal core-lobe and core-halo structures supporting jet interpretations.
arxiv-2511-16259:
Chiara Rubaltelli and three co-authors experimentally realize mobile base stations in 5G through wireless access backhaul across multiple bands. Vehicles and other mobile uses need stable connectivity that fixed networks struggle to give. A recent standard lets base stations relay wirelessly with native mobility support. Their testbed is the first multi band experimental realization described.

A millimeter wave backhaul link pairs with a lower band access link. Open source software and commercial off the shelf parts build the system. End to end operation under mobility is validated in practice. Millimeter wave coverage extends through the mobile relay as intended. Flexible relay networks could densify coverage cost effectively for transport corridors and temporary deployments.
arxiv-2511-16659:
Zhaoning Wang and five co-authors introduce PartUV, a pipeline for UV unwrapping, the flattening of a 3D surface into a 2D map that textures are painted on. AI-generated meshes are noisy and poorly conditioned, and existing unwrappers shred them into many tiny charts with messy seams.

PartUV starts from a learned part decomposition, so charts follow the object's semantic parts, and a top-down recursive scheme keeps each chart's distortion below a user-set threshold while minimizing the chart count. The pipeline extends parameterization and packing algorithms, handles non-manifold and degenerate meshes, and is heavily parallelized. Across man-made, CAD, AI-generated, and common shape datasets it beat existing tools and neural methods on chart count and seam length at comparable distortion.
arxiv-2511-16759:
Isiah M. Holt, M. Coleman Miller, Alexander J. Dittmann, and Frederick K. Lamb test whether a mishandled background can bias neutron star radius measurements, a key input for the physics of ultra-dense matter. Pulse waveform modeling with NICER data has proven robust to several systematics, but the unmodulated background component had not been stress-tested.

The authors jointly analyze synthetic NICER and XMM-Newton data modeled on the heavy pulsar PSR J0740+6620. Even when the assumed background underestimates the true one by more than a factor of five, the inferred radius shifts by only about one standard deviation. In every case the Bayesian evidence favored the correct background model. The results add confidence that careful waveform analyses measure neutron star radii accurately, thorough sampling and good fits being the main requirements.
arxiv-2511-16859:
Vincent Savignac and Eve J. Lee reconstruct how Earth began, using neon isotopes locked in the deep mantle as a fossil record. Neon in mantle plumes carries a nebular signature, implying Earth's embryos swallowed primordial gas, some of which dissolved into magma oceans before the solar nebula dispersed.

The authors simulate envelope growth with modern gas accretion schemes and compute how nebular neon dissolves at chemical equilibrium. They find the embryo mass matching today's deep mantle neon is tightly pinned near three tenths of an Earth mass, inside a nebula depleted at least a hundredfold in gas. Smaller embryos never melt enough; larger ones drown the mantle in neon. The picture has Earth starting as such embryos during nebula dispersal, finishing through at least two giant impacts afterward, with light and heavy noble gases recording different chapters.
arxiv-2511-16959:
Saúl A. Blanco and four co-authors attack an open problem about generating the full symmetric group with three prefix reversals, the pancake flips that reverse the front of a stack. The Cayley graphs of these generating sets are the cubic pancake graphs, and nobody knows exactly which triples of flip lengths generate everything.

The largest flip, of the whole stack, is always in the triple. The authors completely solve the problem whenever the triple includes the two smallest lengths, or the two largest apart from the full flip. They also give conditions under which a triple provably fails to generate the group. Computational results on diameter and girth for several cubic pancake graphs round out the paper, with conjectures pointing at the remaining cases.
arxiv-2511-17259:
Chinonso Onah and Kristel Michielsen examine a basic weakness of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm on problems with tight constraints. In permutation problems like the traveling salesman problem, valid answers occupy an exponentially tiny fraction of all bit strings, so a generic quantum search mostly samples nonsense. Using random traveling salesman ensembles, the authors prove that optimized generic QAOA keeps an exponentially small chance of landing on any feasible answer, across wide ranges of its parameters.

They then test a constraint-enhanced variant that starts inside the feasible subspace and mixes only within it. That variant's feasible probability is vastly larger, an exponential separation that persists to linear circuit depths under linked parameter schedules. The bounds also imply that adaptive sampling schemes face exponential raw-sample costs. The paper draws a clear design lesson: build constraints into the algorithm's structure.
arxiv-2511-17559:
Gyubok Lee, Woosog Chay, and Edward Choi introduce SCARE, a benchmark for the safety layer of hospital question-answering systems. Language models can translate a clinician's question into a database query over electronic health records, but a wrong query, from model error or a flawed question, can mislead care. Before any query runs, a checker should judge whether the question is answerable, ambiguous, or unanswerable, and verify or correct the generated query. No unified benchmark existed for that post-hoc role.

SCARE holds 4,200 triples of questions, candidate queries, and expected outputs, drawn from three major intensive care databases, with candidate queries produced by seven different text-to-SQL models. Benchmarking methods from two-stage pipelines to agentic frameworks exposed a real trade-off between classifying questions well and correcting queries well. The authors map that tension as the key challenge for safe clinical deployment.
arxiv-2511-17759:
Artyom Hovhannisyan and Ulrich Nierste work on a precise particle physics calculation tied to how B mesons mix with their antimatter partners. Measuring a small width difference in that system needs a decay matrix computed to a demanding order, including corrections for strong force effects.

The hard part involves operators of higher dimension mixing into lower ones under renormalization, where no general method existed. The authors show that terms breaking the expected counting are finite and can be absorbed into added terms. They compute all those terms and check them against a limiting case, clarifying rules for related calculations.
arxiv-2511-17959:
Yuhao Wu, Ke Yang, Franziska Roesner, Tadayoshi Kohno, Ning Zhang, and Umar Iqbal argue that artificial agents acting for users need permission systems, but classic permission models do not fit automated action. They propose letting a learned assistant predict the permissions a user would grant.

A user study shows that choices depend on communication context, yet each person's choices stay consistent within a context and resemble other people's. A prediction model built on those factors is accurate overall and very accurate when confident. Even a few examples of a person's past choices raise accuracy a lot, suggesting practical automated permission help.
arxiv-2511-18259:
Xiaochen Zheng, Alvaro Serra, Ilya Schneider Chernov, Maddalena Marchesi, Eunice Musvasva, and Tatyana Y Doktorova introduce DiscoVerse, a multi-agent AI assistant for drug research at Roche. Pharma archives hold decades of work, much of it from programmes that were stopped. And reusing that knowledge could guide new projects in reverse translation, working back from human data to the lab. In practice the archives are vast and scattered, so reuse rarely happens.

DiscoVerse answers staff questions with evidence-linked replies: it retrieves data, joins documents, summarises findings, and keeps institutional memory intact. Experts judged its source-linked outputs on a slice of one hundred and eighty molecules drawn from more than four decades of Roche research. The team presents it as a human-in-the-loop co-scientist whose every claim can be traced to its source.
arxiv-2511-18359:
Alexandros Stergiou asks how video models reach their answers, and builds a way to watch the process. Vision and language models read rich scenes with ease, yet the rules inside their choices stay opaque. New text to video tools, which make clips from words with high visual truth, hint at a probe.

Stergiou sets a new task: turn a model's score list back into video. His method, TRANSPORTER, learns a match map to the model's high sense space, so score shifts steer the clip build. The clips shift as object traits, action words, and scene context shift in the text. Tests across models show the probe gives a rich, new view of what drives a model's call.
arxiv-2511-18559:
Kuan Wei Huang, Brandon Li, Bharath Hariharan, and Noah Snavely match ground level photos to floor plans of the same place. Geometry models can read scene shape from photo pairs, yet they fail when views differ wildly, like air versus ground, or when one input is a drawing, not a photo. Photo to plan matching is a hard case of that kind.

Past data sets lack either varied input types or known matches. The team build C3: scenes are rebuilt in 3D from internet photo sets, then hand aligned to floor plans from the web, which yields true matches. Their model predicts a point map that links photo pixels to plan spots. The set and method open joint photo plan reasoning.
arxiv-2511-18659:
Jie He and five co-authors fuse search and writing in one shared latent space for question answering. Retrieval augmented generation feeds a model with found texts, but long contexts slow it and the search and write steps train apart, so they pull in unlike ways. Their frame, CLaRa, compresses each text into rich vectors that stay findable.

A synthesis scheme builds the training data by question and paraphrase checks that guard key facts. Reranker and generator then train end to end on one language loss, with gradients that flow through a smooth top pick step. Theory says the joint fit aligns search relevance with answer quality. Tests across question sets back the design. Shorter inputs and one goal are the gains.
arxiv-2511-18759:
Xiyong Yan classifies the multisigns of Hamiltonian circles in a complete graph whose edges carry vector signs. Each edge holds a sign in a binary vector space of set dimension. The multisign of a circle is the sum of its edge signs. A Hamiltonian circle visits every vertex once and returns.

For a fixed sign dimension and a large enough vertex count, Yan shows the set of such sums takes a rigid form. It is a subspace, an affine subspace, or the whole space, apart from set exceptional cases. The result tames a sum that could in principle scatter widely. Rigid structure of this kind aids the algebra of signed graphs.
arxiv-2511-18959:
Qingyuan Jiang, Wei-Ping Li, and Yu Zhao answer a long open question from Vafa and Witten that links instanton counts to conformal field theory. The question tied a blow up formula for instantons to the WZW model at level one. That formula is due to Yoshioka. The model is a bridge between geometry and quantum field theory.

For the moduli space of instantons of a set rank on a blown up algebraic surface, the team build an affine Lie algebra action. It acts on a spread of cohomology theories. These include sheaf groups, Hochschild homology, Chow groups, and Hodge cohomology. The module is the basic representation. A key step recasts perfect complex Grassmannians. It uses a finite Clifford spin representation.
arxiv-2511-19059:
Pei Liu and nine co-authors build LLMAID, a tool that finds and names AI features inside Android apps with a language model's help. AI now sits in much mobile software, and users and regulators ask plain questions: does this app use AI, and what kind? Past checks leaned on hand inspection and fixed rules, which cost much and age fast as methods change.

LLMAID reads app artifacts and reasons over them to flag AI capabilities and their types. The language model base lets it adapt to new AI forms that rule sets miss. Clear answers feed store labels and audits. Knowing what runs inside an app is a base step for trust.
arxiv-2511-19659:
Peter Brearley and Philipp Pfeffer extend high-order operator splitting to the dissipative dynamics that quantum computers find hardest. Splitting breaks a simulation into steps, but at high orders the classic formulas demand negative time steps, which are ill-posed when the dynamics lose energy irreversibly, as open systems do. Their construction encodes product formulas with complex coefficients through a sequence of ordinary Hamiltonian evolutions in real and imaginary time, keeping high-order accuracy throughout.

The unitary substeps use positive real coefficients, while the dissipative substeps use complex coefficients whose real parts preserve the shrinking character of the evolution. Alongside known formulas of orders four and six, they give a new symmetric formula of order eight in this class. The approach targets simulations of open quantum systems on near-term hardware.
arxiv-2511-19859:
A robot action system called VITA is presented by Xiangkai Ma, Lekai Xing, Han Zhang, Wenzhong Li, and Sanglu Lu. Vision-language-action models teach robots from images and words, but text-only reasoning misses fine scene detail. Visual guidance helps, yet a gap remains between what a robot sees and the low-level moves it must make.

VITA learns one shared discrete code for vision and action, so seeing and moving are modeled together. Its tokens decode at once into predicted future frames and robot actions, letting visual dynamics guide motion planning. Tests in simulated and real settings show clear gains over earlier systems on standard robot benchmarks, with strong success across six real-world tasks.
arxiv-2511-19959:
Yujia Wang, Yuanpu Cao, and Jinghui Chen present ParaBlock, a federated learning method for large language models. In block coordinate federated training, each client trains only part of the model, which saves local work. Even one block can hold so many parameters, though, that sending it dominates the time, above all for weak clients.

ParaBlock runs communication and computation in two parallel threads, so sending and training overlap instead of taking turns. The authors prove it keeps the same convergence rate as standard federated block coordinate methods. Fine-tuning tests on instruction following and math reasoning show strong performance with clearly better communication efficiency. The method suits federated settings where bandwidth, not computing, is the bottleneck.
arxiv-2511-20459:
Rezaei and colleagues teach language models to imitate classic novelists, then grade the fakes. Their 2025 paper works on stylometry, the measurement of writing style. Five nineteenth-century authors anchor the study. They are Dickens, Austen, Twain, Alcott, and Melville. Models were fine-tuned using only single-token prompts as style signals.

Two training routes were compared head to head. Full fine-tuning beat the lighter LoRA method on fidelity. LoRA still offered big efficiency gains in trainable parameters. A DeBERTa classifier graded generated sentences as an automatic judge. At high confidence it agreed with the intended author eighty-two percent of the time. Twain and Melville proved the hardest voices to capture. Syntax comparisons checked parse shapes and sentence lengths. Alcott fakes grew longer parse paths than the real thing. Attention and gradient analyses revealed which cues drive imitation. Human judges confirmed the thematic and linguistic match.
arxiv-2511-20759:
Sijia Wang and colleagues propose in 2025 a way to give quantum spacetime a working clock. Many quantum gravity theories describe nearly classical geometries with coherent states, quantum states that mimic classical shapes. The trouble is time: the standard Wheeler-DeWitt equation freezes evolution entirely, the famous problem of time. Wang's team builds an evolution rule in the coherent-state basis, timed by a clock at infinity.

Because coherent states overlap instead of sitting cleanly apart, a starting geometry is driven into a blend of neighbouring geometries. That blending supplies a mechanism for tunnelling between geometries, an effect other approaches assume but rarely derive. Applied to black hole evaporation, the framework recovers the semiclassical law, mass falling with the cube root of time, as the most probable path. The authors read this as a hint that unitarity, the rule that information is never truly lost, survives with quantum corrections included.
arxiv-2511-21259:
Susanna Terron connects two distant corners of mathematics in 2025: the Brown-Thompson group F3, a group of piecewise-linear symmetries, and the theory of links, which studies knotted loops in space. Vaughan Jones had shown that every link can be built from a group element, inspired by questions from conformal field theory. Terron extends his construction to pointed links, where each loop carries a marked base point, and proves the extended map is surjective.

Terron then defines a new operation on the group, creating a structure she calls the central monoid. Under her extended construction, this monoid maps onto pointed links combined by connected sum, the operation that splices two links into one. That correspondence yields a standard form for the group elements representing a connected sum. She extends the machinery further with disjoint union and linking moves for a wider family of links.
arxiv-2511-21459:
Lorenzo De Rebotti, Emanuele Giacomini, Giorgio Grisetti, and Luca Di Giammarino rebuild 3D scenes at the resolution each corner deserves, in 2025. Reconstructing surfaces from depth data usually means a voxel grid, tiny cubes tiling space, at one fixed resolution: fine grids waste memory on empty walls, coarse grids blur detail. Their variance-adaptive grid sizes each block by the local variance of signed distance observations, spending detail only where the surface is complicated.

De Rebotti and his coauthors store all blocks in one flat spatial hash table instead of a recursive octree, giving constant-time access and full graphics-card parallelism. The grid also feeds a parallel quad-tree that controls Gaussian Splatting density for rendering. Their open-source CUDA implementation ran up to 13 times faster than fixed-resolution baselines while using 4 times less memory, with reconstruction accuracy on par. It accepts both RGB-D cameras and LiDAR input.
arxiv-2511-21559:
Balasubramanian, Matthew Hague, Rupak Majumdar, Ramanathan Thinniyam, and Georg Zetzsche show that softening counters makes hard verification problems decidable, in 2025. Programs are often modeled with counters tracking resources or threads, but whole-number counters make reachability questions brutally hard. Continuous counters relax the values to non-negative rationals, letting transitions fire at fractional strength, a safe over-estimate used to prove safety.

The surprise is how tame the relaxed systems are. Despite being infinite-state, the instruction sequences that can drive such a system into a target state form a regular language. A finite automaton recognizing that language can be computed effectively. Reachability therefore stays decidable when continuous counters are added to many systems, including higher-order recursion schemes and well-structured transition systems. One caveat tempers the triumph: the automaton can outgrow any fixed tower of exponentials, so decidability here maps the terrain rather than giving a practical algorithm.
arxiv-2511-21659:
Guy Goldberg, Tom Gur, and Sidhant Saraogi prove that error-correcting codes with a relaxed local decoder cannot be much shorter than known constructions, in 2025. A relaxed locally decodable code lets a decoder recover any message bit by querying only a few codeword positions. It tolerates nearby corruption under a relaxed success rule. The best construction, from 2004, achieved length slightly superlinear in the message, and whether that overhead was necessary stayed open.

Goldberg and his coauthors show it is. Any linear code with a q-query relaxed decoder must stretch k message bits to length at least k raised to the power one plus a constant over q. That nearly matches the 2004 upper bound. Their proof introduces robust daisies, flower-like set families with pseudorandom structure. A new spread lemma extracts dense robust daisies from arbitrary distributions. The result essentially closes the length question for linear relaxed codes.
arxiv-2511-22159:
Kranz, an economist at Ulm, dusts off Warren Buffett's 2003 proposal for tradeable import certificates as an answer to today's strategic-sector anxiety. Governments want domestic capacity in chips, medicines, and green technology, but subsidies invite waste and tariffs invite retaliation. Under Buffett's scheme, importers must hold certificates earned by exporting. So the certificate price acts as a self-adjusting blend of tariff and export subsidy whose strength tracks the net import balance in the strategic sector automatically.

In a two-country model with competitive markets, Kranz finds the certificates transparent and efficient. They are notably good at removing other countries' incentives to cheat agreements through hidden subsidies or non-tariff barriers, since the mechanism responds to outcomes rather than policies. The warning is domestic market power: if local producers can corner the certificate market itself, the instrument turns adverse, a caveat policymakers would need to design around.
arxiv-2511-22259:
Weissenborn and Wendzel, security researchers, hide messages in what a network did, not in what it says. Covert channels smuggle data past monitors, usually by tweaking packet contents or timings, which watchdogs can spot. History covert channels instead point at past network events: the covert message is a small pointer to historical timing patterns both sides already observed. So the embedded data is tiny while the referenced information is large, an amplification that keeps the channel's footprint minimal.

Their method uses relative pointers to timing patterns, dropping centralized timekeeping. The synchronization scheme tolerates timing noise and variability, and experiments reach a better covert bitrate than previous work. The authors also tailor the design for robustness and undetectability, and their agenda includes wider input sources, adaptive pointer strategies, and, on the defensive side, countermeasures against history channels.
arxiv-2511-22359:
Safronov, Bostan, Allott, and Martin, Oxford researchers, build one tool that inventories the software inside routers and IoT devices and flags what is vulnerable. A Software Bill of Materials lists a product's components. Existing generators lean on package metadata and miss code that arrives as binaries or unmanaged C and C++, exactly where most IoT software lives. UniBOM analyzes binaries, filesystems, and source code together, tracks historical product identifiers, and classifies vulnerabilities by severity and memory-safety relevance.

The validation is comparative: across 258 wireless router firmware images and the source code of four popular IoT operating systems. UniBOM's finer-grained inventories detect vulnerabilities that widely used SBOM tools miss. An interactive web dashboard visualizes the dependency risks and their history. Released for open-source distribution, the tool targets security accountability for networked systems whose hidden dependency webs otherwise surface only after incidents like the Mirai botnet.
arxiv-2511-22459:
Nazarenus and colleagues reconstruct real flames in three dimensions from as few as three camera views. Fire is a hard capture target: transparent, fast-moving, and full of fine flickering detail, so sparse views badly underdetermine its geometry. Their method separates the static background, recovered with multi-view stereo plus single-image depth estimates, from the dynamic fire, and represents the flame with 3D Gaussians each carrying a lifetime and a velocity.

The fire's motion starts from a 3D flow field fused from dense optical flow in each view. A custom hardware synchronisation pattern keeps the cameras aligned below one frame, using affordable commodity hardware. Across many real fire scenarios, the reconstructions held up in quantitative scores and visual quality. They captured high-frequency flame structure that earlier methods could not attempt from so few views. Those earlier methods assume dense camera coverage.
arxiv-2511-22559:
Aboubrahim, Giman, and Nath model dark energy as an ultralight axion field whose potential is a sum of cosine terms, a shape motivated by supergravity and string theory. Their dark energy also exchanges energy with dark matter via an interaction derived from a Lagrangian, keeping the treatment self-consistent. They study the two-cosine case and fit it against cosmological data, including DESI's second data release.

The two-term potential fits better than the standard single-cosine version. The fits pin the axion decay constant below the Planck scale, matching string theory's preference. The fits force the dark matter-dark energy interaction to be feeble, below about four millionths in the units used. With three or four cosine terms, the field can transmute alone. It starts out thawing, its equation of state drifting from the cosmological-constant value, then freezing back. That twist is relevant to the Hubble tension.
arxiv-2511-23259:
Banerjee and colleagues construct a dark matter model in which the dark matter is a spin-1 particle below a giga-electronvolt. Charged under a dark SU(2) force broken by two dark Higgs fields. A dimension-five portal interaction, a non-Abelian cousin of kinetic mixing, then gives the dark matter magnetic dipole couplings to the photon and the Z boson. And the spectrum puts the mediator lighter than twice the dark matter mass.

That reversed hierarchy forbids the on-shell invisible mediator production at fixed-target experiments. So the team catalogues replacement signatures for LDMX and NA64, off-shell dark bremsstrahlung, dark Higgs-strahlung, invisible vector meson decays, and visible mediator decays. Computing the thermal relic abundance across the sub-giga-electronvolt range and applying bounds from direct detection, the cosmic microwave background, colliders. And nucleosynthesis, they find a viable region survives, with dark coupling near a hundredth still open.
arxiv-2511-23359:
Caldevilla-Asenjo and colleagues report the first observation of coherent subgap transport through a spin-split superconductor. In vertical junctions where a europium sulfide layer magnetically splits the energy states of an aluminum film. Theory had predicted an even-odd effect for multiple Andreev reflection, the process where charge carriers bounce repeatedly across a junction. But testing it beyond the weak tunneling regime had never been done experimentally in this work.

Their conductance measurements show exactly the predicted pattern, with odd-order reflection peaks split by the induced spin-splitting while even-order peaks remain untouched. And a measurable Josephson current confirms strong coupling through the barrier. Fitting quasiclassical transport models, they find about 23 percent of the transmission channels are highly transparent and dominate conduction. And they show a single spin-split superconductor suffices for the effect, simplifying future superconducting spintronic devices based on these junctions.
arxiv-2511-23459:
Crespi and colleagues present a new cleaner way to measure the cosmic baryon fraction. The share of ordinary matter in the total matter budget, from the amplitude of baryon acoustic oscillations in galaxy clustering. The signal comes from how baryons and dark matter were distributed before recombination. But earlier template-based methods split the two components with approximate transfer functions that threw away information and risked inconsistencies for cosmology.

Their method adds one extra parameter inside the CAMB Boltzmann solver controlling the balance between baryons and dark matter in the growth terms of the perturbation equations. Capturing the baryonic suppression of dark matter growth before recombination. Validated on noiseless standard and early-dark-energy cosmologies with DESI-like errors, the scheme matches earlier precision while reducing systematic biases. Strengthening baryon-fraction routes to the Hubble constant expected from future DESI and Euclid data.
arxiv-2512-00459:
Hybrid mesons mix quarks with excited glue, and some carry quantum numbers no ordinary meson can have. Christian Farina and Eric Swanson compute strong decays of two light exotic hybrid mesons in 2025. The states studied have exotic quantum numbers forbidden to simple quark-antiquark pairs.

Their model builds hybrid structure from the QCD Hamiltonian in Coulomb gauge with a single constituent quasigluon. Decay patterns are the fingerprints experiments use to identify new particles. Predictions like these tell collider and spectroscopy experiments which channels to watch for the first confirmed exotic hybrids. Exotic quantum numbers are a guarantee that any confirmed state is genuinely new physics. Hadronic decays are how such short-lived states announce themselves to detectors.
arxiv-2512-00659:
Aligning two sets of rotations sounds simple until time alignment is missing and axes are unknown. Anik Sarker and Alan Asbeck present a fast, robust method for rotation pattern alignment in 2025. Their approach is invariant to permutation and sign, the two ambiguities that plague the task.

Calibration and registration in robotics and sensing often hit exactly these obstacles, along with outliers. A correspondence-free method skips the fragile step of matching individual rotations first. Reliable alignment underpins camera calibration, motion capture, and spacecraft attitude estimation, where a wrong rotation quietly corrupts everything downstream. SO(3) is the group of three-dimensional rotations, the native space of the problem. For folks who tune rigs in the field, the gain is time. Two sets of spins can be lined up fast, with no need to pair them off one by one.
arxiv-2512-01059:
Anantha Padmanaban Krishna Kumar tests whether smaller vision transformers can work better in a 2025 paper. Scaling laws suggest bigger models usually win, but accuracy and training behavior do not always rise with size. Kumar studies one standard model, ViT-B/16, trained on the ImageNet-1K image dataset.

Two simple parameter-reduction strategies are applied to its MLP blocks: sharing weights and reducing width. Each removes about a third of the baseline parameters. The comparative study measures how performance changes as rank and size shrink. If leaner models match or beat the original, training and deployment costs fall for everyone.
arxiv-2512-02059:
Grand unified theories try to merge the forces of nature into one scheme, and hints of them may hide in unexpected algebra. M. Adeel Ajaib's 2025 paper studies nilpotent matrices, matrices that vanish when raised to some power, that produce the Schrödinger equation when written in first-order form.

Ajaib carries out a rigorous search for all such matrices and finds they fall naturally into group-theoretic patterns reminiscent of grand unification. No unified structure was assumed at the start; the organization emerges from the algebra itself. Whether coincidence or clue, the fingerprints suggest the quantum equation carries more symmetry history than its usual form reveals.
arxiv-2512-02259:
The Apache Software Foundation's libraries run much of the world's software, from Log4j to Tomcat and Struts, which also makes them prime targets for attackers. Derek Garcia and four co-authors present CVE Breadcrumbs in 2025, a way to track known vulnerabilities through the versioned history of Apache libraries.

Incidents like Log4Shell showed how a flaw in one ubiquitous component can endanger thousands of downstream systems. Following a vulnerability across versions shows which releases carry it and where fixes landed. That trail helps security teams decide what to patch first in a sprawling dependency tree.
arxiv-2512-02559:
Bárbara Muniz, David Plaza, and Claudia Rojas-Andías prove a structural fact about a small but rich algebra. The algebra is the spherical Hecke algebra of type G2, tied to an affine Weyl group. Its Kazhdan-Lusztig basis is a special basis used to study symmetry and representation theory.

The authors show each basis element splits into atomic pieces, an atomic decomposition. As a side benefit, they give a new algorithm for generalized Kostka-Foulkes polynomials in this type. Concrete decompositions like this make hard algebraic objects easier to compute with and compare, both by hand and by machine. Small cases done with care often crack the big ones open in time, and this one is no odd case out.
arxiv-2512-02759:
Aref Farhadipour, Teodora Vukovic, and Volker Dellwo match faces to voices in languages the system never saw. Cross modal verification asks whether a face and a voice belong to the same person. The FAME2026 Challenge tests this under multilingual strain, with unseen and unheard languages.

The Zurich team compares two designs. One is a dual encoder trained from scratch with contrastive and orthogonal losses. The other adapts the ImageBind foundation model with small LoRA updates. Knowing which approach travels across languages helps build media tools that work worldwide. Tongues the tool has not heard are the true test, since real world use will not stay in two or three tongues.
arxiv-2512-02959:
Dmitry E. Pelinovsky and Rudi Weikard construct breathers, wave packets that ride on a periodic wave without spreading. On an elliptic wave background, a breather superposes a soliton and a periodic wave traveling at different speeds. The two interact periodically in space and time.

For the defocusing modified Korteweg-de Vries equation, building general breathers stayed open for years. The elliptic background ties to genus two hyperelliptic solutions at a degenerate edge. Bright and dark breathers both appear in their construction, enriching the known wave families for this classic nonlinear equation. Wave forms that hold their shape on a wavy sea are the gems of this field. Each new one found by proof adds a gem that tests can chase in tanks.
arxiv-2512-03059:
Electric buses paired with solar power could clean up city travel. Jiaju Qi, Lei Lei, Thorsteinn Jonsson, and Dusit Niyato study bus charging in this 2025 work. The hard part is to keep costs low while no bus runs out of charge.

Real life adds shifting solar output, changing power prices, varied trip times, and few charge points. The authors use a layered form of deep learning that learns charging plans under set limits. Safe plans matter for transit fleets that want low carbon trips. Good timing can also cut bills for bus firms. Transit planners reading it gain a view of the trade-offs behind each charging choice.
arxiv-2512-04059:
Scientists who hunt signals in noisy fields, from brain scans to sky maps, first find peaks, then ask which peaks are real and where they sit. Alden Green and Jonathan Taylor build inference for that two-step reality in a 2025 statistics preprint. The catch is selection: confidence statements made after choosing significant peaks must account for the choosing.

Their method first tests each peak against a null hypothesis of no signal. Peaks declared significant then receive confidence regions locating the nearby true peak and bounding its height, valid post-selectively. Their assumptions pair a smooth signal with noise of constant variance, in a high-curvature asymptotic regime. There they prove control of both false discoveries and of regions missing their true peak. An intermediate result uses the Kac-Rice formula to approximate the intensity of the peak process, second-order accurate near true peaks.
arxiv-2512-04159:
New particles at the tera-electronvolt scale should, by rights, have shown up already in flavour-changing processes, unless something shields them. Admir Greljo, Ajdin Palavrić, and Ben A. Stefanek ask how little shielding is actually needed, in a 2025 particle physics preprint. Full flavour universality is stronger than the data demand.

The authors identify the minimal continuous symmetry that must survive approximately: a product of an SU(2) acting on quarks and a U(1) factor. With only a few symmetry-breaking spurions, each around a percent in size, the framework still reproduces the observed fermion mass hierarchies. That gives the Standard Model flavour puzzle a fresh angle. Within effective field theory, the setup structurally protects generic TeV-scale new physics from flavour bounds. The allowed space of collider scenarios grows beyond minimal flavour violation and U(2) frameworks, with richer patterns of flavour violation.
arxiv-2512-04259:
People ask ChatGPT for code every day and ship much of what it returns. But studies of its security usually test code generated on demand for the study itself. Kobra Khanmohammadi and colleagues revisit the question with real-world material in a 2025 preprint on software security. Their dataset is code that actual users requested, in the wild.

The study evaluates that code for both correctness and security, and examines what users were trying to do when they asked. A further experiment tests whether common prompt engineering strategies improve matters, using real-life prompts. The findings back the earlier synthetic studies: the generated code is frequently insufficient on security. The authors also observe that users rarely ask how secure the code they request actually is. That pairing, weak code and unasked questions, is the paper's real warning.
arxiv-2512-04359:
Hongye Cao and five co-authors aim to fix a flaw in how large language models learn to reason: their training drive can collapse too soon. When rewards check only final answers, models stop exploring and settle into narrow habits. That entropy collapse caps how far their reasoning can grow. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses entropy, a measure of spread and surprise, at two levels to keep learning open.

On the data side, lessons are ordered by semantic entropy, from plain tasks to rich, varied ones. That order guides the model from easy wins toward harder problems. On the rule side, tokens with low entropy get gentle pressure to stay flexible. High-variance spots inside those tokens face firmer limits to keep training stable. The mix raised reasoning scores while using training compute well, which matters for labs that fine-tune models on tight budgets.
arxiv-2512-04559:
Hyeongyu Kang, Jaewoo Lee, Woocheol Shin, and co-authors present SQDF, a gentler way to fine-tune diffusion image models toward a reward. Tuning often overfits the reward: pictures score high yet look odd and lose variety. Their 2025 arXiv paper frames the fix as reinforcement learning with a soft value function that grades each denoising path. A reworked policy gradient lets that value guide updates while a leash on drift keeps outputs natural.

Three add-ons sharpen the method. A discount factor assigns credit across denoising steps. Consistency models refine the value estimates cheaply. A replay buffer of past samples widens coverage of modes. In tests, SQDF raised reward scores without the usual collapse in diversity. The balance matters for art tools and product imagery, where a model must please a metric yet keep surprising its users.
arxiv-2512-04759:
Malvina Nissim, Danilo Croce, Viviana Patti, and co-authors present CALAMITA, a joint effort that tests large language models in Italian. Most model grading centers on English, leaving other languages poorly served. CALAMITA brings together more than eighty people from schools, firms, and the public sector under the Italian group for language computing. Their 2025 arXiv paper sets out the effort and what it values: sound method over leaderboards.

The group designed and documented a wide task set together. Tasks cover language skill, common-sense reasoning, factual care, fairness, briefing, translation, and code writing. Each task carries shared write-up rules, so results can be trusted and reused. The aim is a living test culture for Italian, not a one-off ranking. Its shared model could guide other language groups building their own strict benches.
arxiv-2512-04859:
Matthias Jasny, Muhammad El-Hindi, Tobias Ziegler, and co-authors study when and how database systems should adopt io_uring, Linux's modern interface for batching input and output calls. Databases live and die by storage and network speed. io_uring promises low-overhead, asynchronous operations that unify both. Yet swapping it in naively does not guarantee gains. Their 2025 arXiv paper measures two real use cases to find where the wins hide.

The first case wires io_uring into a storage-bound buffer manager. The second uses it to shuffle data at high throughput in network-bound analytics. Advanced features, such as registered buffers and passthrough access, are graded for their end-to-end effect. The study shows which low-level tricks turn into real speed and which do not. Database builders gain a field guide instead of folklore.
arxiv-2512-04959:
Alan Price and Frank Krauss present a route toward a fully automated generator of high-order electroweak corrections for lepton colliders. Proposed electron-positron machines will measure with unmatched precision. Theory must match that precision, or the data's power is wasted. One bottleneck is adding second-order corrections in a steady, process-free way, well joined with resummation of soft radiation. Their 2025 arXiv paper offers a solution built on the Yennie-Frautschi-Suura theorem.

The method uses local subtraction to remove divergences where they arise, point by point. It then matches the result to an all-orders resummation of soft logarithms. Hand-built work cannot cover the many processes a collider program needs, so automation is the point. A working tool would let theorists supply precise predictions on demand. That would help future lepton collider teams plan searches and read their data with care.
arxiv-2512-05059:
A. V. Bednyakov, M. V. Kompaniets, and A. V. Trenogin compute hard numbers for a classic model of magnetism-like behavior, the three-dimensional O(N) model. Their targets are the scaling dimensions of a family of operators built from powers of the field squared — quantities that govern how the system behaves near a phase change. Earlier semiclassical work had produced an all-orders formula for the largest contributions at high powers, leaving the next tier untested.

Working through six loops of perturbation theory, the authors obtain expressions for both the leading contributions and the next ones down. The leading part matches the semiclassical prediction, a reassuring cross-check, while the subleading part is new and gives future all-orders formulas something concrete to answer to. As a by-product, they supply the full dependence on the power for the four-loop answer, a result practitioners can use directly.
arxiv-2512-05259:
Georgios Chatzichristodoulou and four co-authors fix a blind spot in three-dimensional human modelling: systems that recover shape and pose from images work well for adults and fail for children and infants. Their framework, AionHMR, extends a top-performing model with a body model that spans ages, fitting adults, children, and infants within one optimization-based approach. Child data is scarce, so the method manufactures its own supervision.

The team used the extended model to generate pseudo-ground-truth annotations for child and infant image databases, then trained a transformer model on that data for real-time, age-inclusive reconstruction. Accuracy improves for the young without costing anything on adults. The recovered meshes double as privacy-preserving stand-ins for the original photos. They keep action, pose, and geometry while hiding identity, enabling anonymized dataset releases. A new collection of children interacting with robots demonstrates the idea.
arxiv-2512-05659:
Andrew Ledingham and seven co-authors study what generative AI will do to jobs inside the UK Civil Service. Rather than guessing role by role, they scored exposure task by task. A language model read nearly two hundred thousand job adverts posted over six years. From them it rated more than one and a half million tasks for how exposed each is to AI.

Rolled up, the scores show wide differences even between jobs with the same title. The team then asked a model to redesign the jobs, automating some tasks, improving others, and moving work between people and machines. After redesign, the tasks left with humans leaned on human strengths: strategic leadership, hard problem solving, and managing stakeholders. The authors conclude that most value will come from higher productivity, not from cutting roles. So redesign beats simple automation as a plan.
arxiv-2512-05759:
Johannes Meyer and seven co-authors cut the labeling cost of teaching machines to segment three dimensional point clouds. Labeling such data is slow, so active learning picks the most useful pieces to annotate next. Older methods use elaborate tricks to carve clouds into regions and choose among them. Their 2025 strategy is deliberately simple: lay a two dimensional grid over the cloud and cut it into columns.

To choose which columns to label, an ensemble of networks votes, and disagreement among them signals uncertainty worth resolving. The method was tested on two public benchmarks, for indoor rooms and for city streets, and on a large urban scan of Freiburg. It matched or beat far more complex state of the art methods on all three. The authors argue labeled area, not point count, is the fairer measure of effort. Simpler pipelines make 3D mapping cheaper to keep current.
arxiv-2512-05959:
David Anugraha and four co-authors build a proving ground for retrieval augmented question answering that speaks the world's languages and respects its cultures. Vision language models answer questions about images from fixed training data. Retrieval can refresh them, but multilingual retrieval is barely tested. Their benchmark, M4-RAG, spans forty two languages, fifty six regional dialects and registers, and one hundred eighty nine countries, with over eighty thousand image question pairs rooted in local culture.

Questions run against a controlled library of curated documents. The systematic results are uncomfortable. Retrieval reliably helps smaller models. For larger ones it fails to scale and often drags performance down, exposing a mismatch between model size and today's retrieval quality. When prompts or retrieved passages arrive in languages other than English, scores drop sharply, however strong the model. M4-RAG measures the gap between slogan and fact.
arxiv-2512-06359:
Di Hou, Tianyun Tang, and Kim-Chuan Toh speed up a workhorse method for hard planning problems written with polynomials. Such problems can be eased into relaxed forms that give safe lower bounds on the best answer. One strong family of relaxations mixes flat sided shapes with the cone of well behaved matrices, but its cost balloons as the problem and the relaxation order grow.

Their solver, RiNNAL-POP, uses a low rank approach, storing lean factors instead of full matrices. A custom projection step handles the huge set of sign and matching rules at a cost that grows only in a straight line with problem size. They also find hidden flat faces in the relaxation that let them drop many rules outright by confining the matrix to a smaller flat subspace. The result is a solver that can take on large relaxed problems that once stalled standard tools.
arxiv-2512-06559:
Ivor van der Hoog, Eva Rotenberg, and Daniel Rutschmann settle an open question about algorithms that exploit order already present in their input. Sorting is the classic case: if data arrives in long rising runs, clever merging is fast, and a matching lower bound proves no one can do better for those run sizes. For geometric tasks like drawing the convex hull of a point set, or listing its Pareto front, newer algorithms gain similar speedups from ordered input, measured by a range partition entropy.

Whether those gains were the best possible was unknown. The authors prove matching lower bounds for building a convex hull or a Pareto front, adaptive to the same entropy measure. Any algorithm must spend at least that much on such inputs. The result certifies the adaptive algorithms as optimal, in the same strong sense as the classic sorting ones.
arxiv-2512-06959:
Marco Bernardo, Andrea Esposito, and Claudio A Mezzina work on a fine question in the theory of concurrent systems: when do two processes count as behaving the same? Their target notion, hereditary history-preserving bisimilarity, is a strict equivalence that respects not just actions but the causal history behind them, even when steps are undone. Earlier accounts leaned on naming each event uniquely, which is heavy machinery.

The authors give two matching characterizations of the notion. One is denotational, built from stable structures that record configurations of events. The other is operational, set inside a calculus of reversible processes. Both rest on a simpler device: comparing, for each label, how many incoming events carry it, rather than tracking identities. The new equivalence still separates two subtle cases, self-concurrency and self-causation, though it holds only when conflicts stay local. Companion logics are developed to match each style of characterization.
arxiv-2512-07059:
Richard Young stress-tests the safety training of the largest language models by replaying a known attack method at full scale. The method, TEMPEST, works over many turns of conversation, patiently steering a model toward harmful outputs that a single prompt could never extract. Young applied it to ten frontier models from eight vendors, across a thousand harmful behaviors, piling up tens of thousands of attack conversations graded by independent safety classifiers.

The spread of results was wide. Six models fell almost every time, with attack success near total. Four resisted meaningfully, though still often. Turning on an extended reasoning mode in one model cut its failure rate by more than half, the single biggest defense observed. Bigger models were not safer models: scale did not predict robustness at all.
arxiv-2512-07159:
The MicroBooNE collaboration reports a decisive test of a long-standing neutrino puzzle. Odd results from two earlier studies hinted that muon neutrinos were turning into electron neutrinos over distances the standard three-flavor picture cannot explain. The favored patch was a fourth, sterile neutrino that feels no ordinary forces. MicroBooNE, a liquid-argon detector, watched for the same effect using two different accelerator beams at once, a first for this kind of search.

Using two beams breaks a confusion between new electron neutrinos appearing and existing ones disappearing, which had weakened earlier tests. The data show neither effect. With that, the single light sterile neutrino answer for the old anomalies is excluded at the standard ninety-five percent confidence level. And much of the room for explaining a separate gallium anomaly is also closed.
arxiv-2512-07259:
Tharindu Wickremasinghe and Marco F Duarte clean noisy images patch by patch, with a model that respects how image patches actually sit in space. Patch methods group similar tiles from across a picture, fit a simple model to each group, and let the models vote on the clean image. Linear subspaces are the usual model, but they pass through the origin, while real patches, built from non-negative brightness, never do. Flat, offset planes, affine subspaces, match that geometry better.

The authors study affine subspace clustering for patch groups and build a denoiser on top: each patch is projected by least squares onto its group's affine model. Several algorithmic routes to the clustering problem are reviewed and compared. Experiments show the offset-aware models cluster patches more faithfully and denoise better than their through-the-origin counterparts.
arxiv-2512-07359:
Bin Zhao and co-authors build a digital twin of a human hand that a physics simulator can actually move. Hand simulation serves medicine, robotics, and virtual worlds, but faithful anatomy is computationally heavy. Their pipeline starts with optical motion capture of one person's hand and fits a personalized version of a standard parametric hand model. That model is then converted into a robot-style description of rigid segments and joints, with axes placed to match anatomy.

The hard step is translation of motion: the parametric model's joints rotate freely in ways rigid hardware joints cannot. The authors derive closed-form answers for one-axis joints and an iterative, correction-based method for two-axis joints that respects how rotations refuse to commute. Validation closes the loop: reinforcement learning policies drive the rigid twin to replay the captured demonstrations.
arxiv-2512-07459:
Xiangjun Tang, Biao Zhang, and Peter Wonka wrote this 2025 computer graphics paper. Animating a digital human is hard because cloth must move in a natural way. Fine surface detail matters too, and training data for such motion is scarce.

The team offers two linked designs in a two-stage system. First, a compact latent code, built on distributions, stores human shape in a tidy form. A more even mapping between a standard body model and avatar shapes improves that code. Second, a generative model learns to animate inside that coded space. It focuses on short motion steps while an identity condition keeps long sequences coherent. Tests show shapes with finer detail than earlier methods produced. The animations also look more varied and natural to human judges. Both stages, the authors say, get more out of limited motion data.
arxiv-2512-07659:
Beau Leighton-Trudel wrote this 2025 physics paper on measuring direction-dependent patterns in quantum systems. Correlations in such systems can stretch unevenly along different directions. A fair description should not depend on the coordinates a researcher happens to pick.

Leighton-Trudel builds a geometric map from mutual information between nearby points. A line element, calibrated against a vacuum benchmark scale, turns information into distance. He proves the map forms a smooth geometry only under one condition. Short-range mutual information must follow an anisotropic inverse-square law. If the pattern is the same in all directions, the geometry collapses to a flat, conformal form. Directional richness is therefore what switches the tensor geometry on. A split of the metric separates density changes from pure directional shape. His MI Tomography protocol rebuilds both parts from finitely many directional readings. A test on a quantum harmonic lattice recovers the true coupling pattern.
arxiv-2512-07759:
Jiayi Shen wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on symmetries of free groups. The automorphism group of a free group collects all its reversible reshufflings. Take a small finite subgroup there, and ask what its normal closure generates.

The normal closure is the smallest normal subgroup containing the given one. Shen's answer is sweeping: the closure is usually everything it could be. For rank at least three, a nontrivial finite subgroup with odd factors does the trick. If it sits inside the special automorphism group, the closure is exactly that group. Otherwise the closure fills the full automorphism group. Powers of two get a partial theorem. The same story repeats one level up, for outer automorphism groups. There, closures land on the special or the full outer group. Two-primary cases resist a complete answer in both settings.
arxiv-2512-08059:
Jesse Balgley, Jinho Park, Xuanjing Chu, and colleagues, physicists and engineers who build quantum devices, posted an experimental study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is the superconducting qubit, the basic unit of many quantum computers. Standard qubits rely on a narrow set of thin film materials, which limits how new material combinations can be tried.

The team demonstrates merged element transmon qubits built entirely from van der Waals Josephson junctions, layered crystals stacked together. These first generation devices stayed quantum coherent, with microsecond lifetimes in a very compact footprint and no external shunt capacitors. Measurements point to dielectric loss as the main relaxation channel, even at temperatures of hundreds of millikelvin. The results establish layered van der Waals materials as a workable platform for compact superconducting quantum devices, with room to tune them by gate voltage.
arxiv-2512-08959:
Ard Kastrati and coauthors introduce EEG Bench, a unified benchmark for testing EEG foundation models in clinical use. Brain wave recordings, known as EEG, support diagnosis across many conditions, but model tests have lacked a common standard. The benchmark covers eleven tasks across fourteen public data sets.

Conditions included span epilepsy, schizophrenia, Parkinson disease, OCD, and mild traumatic brain injury. The method uses minimal preprocessing and shared evaluation protocols, so classic baselines and modern foundation models can be compared side by side. Results show foundation models perform strongly in some settings, yet simpler models often stay competitive. That gap is clearest under clinical distribution shifts, where patient groups differ from training data. All prepared data and code are released in an accessible, open format. The authors aim to support repeatable research and wider use of rigorous evaluation in this field.
arxiv-2512-09059:
Marina Vicens Miquel and coauthors present a diffusion based deep learning method for high resolution rainfall forecasting over the continental United States. Accurate rainfall forecasts are essential for managing flood risk and protecting infrastructure. Their study compares three residual prediction strategies that differ only in their input sources, under one unified setup.

One model uses only past radar based observations. One corrects forecasts from a leading numerical weather system. One hybrid model joins both sources. Forecasts are made at fine spatial resolution, starting at one hour and extending to twelve hours by rolling the model forward. Across all lead times, the learning method beats the numerical baseline on pixel and spatial measures. The hybrid model is best at the shortest lead, while the corrective model leads at longer leads. Calibrated uncertainty estimates are included for reliability. Gains at long leads matter most for emergency preparation and decisions.
arxiv-2512-09459:
Rafael Abreu and colleagues present the Complex-Step Integral Transform, a tool for finding derivatives and studying signals. The method grows out of the link between the Hilbert transform and derivative tools, together with complex-step derivatives, a trick that gets precise derivatives from imaginary steps. Their transform unifies analytic continuation, derivative estimates, and smoothing at several scales in one framework.

A spectral analysis shows the transform preserves phase while suppressing high-wavenumber noise, an advantage over Fourier derivatives. The authors explain the roles of the real and imaginary step parameters and compare versions built on fast Fourier transforms and on interpolation. Demonstrations cover the advection equation and instantaneous-frequency computation, where the method gives smoother results than Hilbert-based approaches and adds built-in stabilization for solvers. They suggest uses in spectral analysis and seismic signal processing, with several directions for future work.
arxiv-2512-09559:
Chengdong Liu, Yimin Wei, and Guofeng Zhang start a phase theory for tensors, extending an idea used for matrices in control work. For matrices, phase information complements magnitude and underlies stability tests for feedback systems. Tensors, multiway arrays, arise in multilinear control, but they had no phase theory.

Working under the Einstein product, the tensor analogue of matrix multiplication, the authors derive a sectorial decomposition for sectorial tensors. That lets them define tensor phases, and give a procedure to compute them. They prove maximin and minimax expressions for these phases under compression. They then define compound spectra and numerical ranges for pairs of tensors and characterize them. They show that the angles of eigenvalues of a product of two sectorial tensors are bounded by the sum of their phases. They finish with a tensor version of the small phase theorem for stability analysis of multilinear feedback systems.
arxiv-2512-09659:
Ritabrata Karmakar and colleagues build a hypothesis test for comparing where two populations sit that works no matter how many variables each observation carries. Standard theory splits awkwardly: high-dimensional methods need the dimension to grow under relations with sample size, while multivariate tests assume fixed dimension and samples large compared with it. In practice, researchers often cannot tell which regime they are in.

The authors introduce uniform-over-dimension convergence, a strengthening of the usual limit theory that holds across all dimensions, and prove a central limit theorem of that kind. From it they develop a two-sample test for equal locations whose validity holds uniformly over the dimension. In simulated data, the new test outperformed high-dimensional tests and the scaled two-sample tests for multivariate data, including Hotelling's T-squared test for Gaussian data. The paper replaces the authors' earlier work on the subject.
arxiv-2512-10359:
Sunqi Fan and co-authors at Tsinghua University tackle video question answering, where a model must watch a video and answer questions about it. Their 2025 paper notes that large multimodal models still struggle to track where things are in each frame and how events unfold over time in complex scenes.

The team built a video toolkit that a model can call on while it reasons, plus a framework called STAR that schedules the spatial and temporal tools in a planned order. That order helps the model narrow in on the key part of a video step by step, instead of guessing. Added to GPT-4o, the setup raised scores on two public video benchmarks, and the code is freely available.
arxiv-2512-10559:
Tommaso Favalli, Žan Kokalj, and Andrea Trombettoni probe the limits of atom interferometers, devices that read tiny phase shifts to measure the world with extreme precision. Real interferometers leak into their environment, so the authors model a linear two-mode device under Lindblad noise of two kinds, one that conserves particle number and one that does not.

They find points in time where the sensitivity blows up and phase estimation becomes impossible, which they call insensitivity points. These points move with the input state, the particle count, and the noise type, but notably not with the noise strength. Their fixed measurement scheme favours number-conserving noise for few particles. Yet the Cramér-Rao bound tells a stricter story: non-conserving noise sets a worse best-possible sensitivity at every particle number they tested.
arxiv-2512-10659:
Tommaso Amico and co-authors explain outliers found by one of the most popular detectors, Local Outlier Factor. That method flags points whose local density is low compared with their neighbours, but it cannot say why a point was flagged or what would have to change to clear it. Counterfactual explanations answer exactly that, yet generic counterfactual tools ignore the quirks of outlier detection.

Their method, DCFO, is built for this detector. It partitions the data space into regions where the detector's score varies smoothly, which makes gradient-based search for the smallest change efficient and reliable. On fifty public datasets from OpenML, DCFO beat competing explainers on both closeness, how little the counterfactual changes, and validity, how often the changed point really stops being an outlier. The paper appears as additional material, extending the main study.
arxiv-2512-11359:
Yifan Niu and colleagues turn community detection in networks into a battleground, with methods both to attack it and to defend it. Finding communities in social or transaction networks can expose individuals who would rather stay hidden, and small, hard to notice changes to a graph can mislead detection models. The authors design an attack that hides targeted people and a defence that hardens the detector.

Their CD-GAME framework lets attacker and defender adapt to each other repeatedly, following game theory until neither can improve, a Nash equilibrium. The defender builds on a classic spectral quantity called the Rayleigh quotient. Experiments showed both their attack and defence beating existing baselines by wide margins. An interactive lesson emerged: one shot attackers use obvious moves that defenders easily counter, while equilibrium attackers choose subtler strategies that still work after the defence adapts.
arxiv-2512-11659:
Abhay Ashtekar, Daniel E Paraizo, and Jonathan Shu extend the laws of black hole heat physics to holes that are far from calm. The classic first law links tiny changes between near calm states. It says nothing about the wild process that drives a hole from one state to another.

Working with dynamical horizon segments, pieces of a hole edge that grow as matter falls in, the team proves a first law for finite changes from real processes. With the matching second law, the area of these segments earns the role of entropy, even mid chaos. The result firms up how we count disorder in merging and feeding black holes.
arxiv-2512-11859:
Michael Chertkov introduces Guided Harmonic Path-Integral Diffusion, a method for steering random paths to a set end point at low cost. The task, called stochastic optimal transport, asks for the best way to move a cloud of possibilities from start to a fixed final spread while paying path costs.

A low dimensional guidance protocol steers the cloud while keeping the math linear and solvable. The best score has an explicit Green function form, and mixture shaped targets give closed forms. Three 2D navigation cases show crafted guidance, learned guidance for one task, and a fusion of rival expert paths. The method yields shaped paths that hit the target while cutting total cost.
arxiv-2512-12059:
Luke Bhan and co-authors test whether language models can police forecast quality at retail scale. Bad forecasts hurt stock, profit, and customer trust, yet human review cannot cover millions of series. Their Forecast Critic uses model world knowledge to flag forecasts that look plainly wrong.

Across synthetic and real tests, models reliably caught time shifts, broken trends, and spike errors. The best model reached an F1 of 0.88, near the human mark of 0.97. With past promotion context, multimodal models spotted missing or fake promo spikes at F1 0.84. On the real M5 data set, flagged forecasts scored at least 10 percent worse by sCRPS. No fine tuning was needed.
arxiv-2512-12159:
Thomas A Trainor reworks a key measure in heavy ion physics in a 2025 paper. The measure, called v2, tracks how particles spread in angle after lead nuclei collide at 2.76 TeV. It is often read as elliptic flow, a sign of a dense form of matter made in the crash.

Trainor notes that v2 is a ratio, with a single particle spectrum at the bottom. Using the Cooper-Frye method for emission from a moving source, he shows the top part hides an extra factor. From the data he pulls out a clean quadrupole spectrum and a radial flow value. Several new results follow from that split.
arxiv-2512-12359:
Antton Goicoechea and five co-authors show how one antenna plus a smart surface can image scenes beyond line of sight in a 2025 paper. Imaging hidden scenes needs the full reflection matrix, which normally takes large antenna arrays. Such arrays are costly, bulky, and hard to build at microwave frequencies.

A reconfigurable intelligent surface is a wall of elements whose reflection can be tuned. Paired with a single sending and receiving antenna, it acts like a programmable synthetic array. The team rebuilt the full reflection matrix from far field measures. They then imaged complex scenes, focused through clutter, and tracked moving targets in real time.
arxiv-2512-12459:
Jiachen Tao and fifteen co-authors turn photon mapping into a continuous field for faster rendering in a 2025 paper. Photon mapping simulates light transport for effects like caustics, the bright patterns from focused light. Standard methods retrace photons for each new viewpoint, wasting work when many views of one scene are needed.

Their Gaussian Photon Field stores photon distributions as 3D Gaussian blobs with position, rotation, scale, and spectrum. Training starts from physically traced photons, then refines the field against multi-view radiance targets. Once trained, the field answers radiance queries along camera rays directly. Tests kept photon level accuracy while cutting computation by orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2512-12759:
Biman Bagchi connects fictive temperature to frequency dependent specific heat in a glassy liquid in a 2025 paper. When a glass forming liquid is cooled fast, it falls out of equilibrium because its relaxation time is finite, and relaxation slows as time passes. A fictive temperature describes that frozen in state: during cooling it sits above the actual temperature, then drifts toward it once cooling stops.

Using linear response theory, Bagchi ties the fictive temperature's time course to a memory function linked to the frequency dependent specific heat, which itself depends on the fictive temperature. A self consistent calculation is therefore required. He applies the relations to silica, modeling relaxation as a stretched exponential and relaxation time by the Vogel-Fulcher-Tammann law.
arxiv-2512-12859:
Marina Echeverria Ferrero, Nicolas Moreno, and Marco Ellero model how blood clots begin inside tiny vessels. Clotting is run by reaction networks that act while blood flows through uneven spaces. Simpler models of the two main pathways have had little testing in lab settings.
