Drawing on not-knowing thought and eager-conduct research, the team argues these theories offer key advice for building safe agents.
arxiv-2602-15559:
Saco works alone on a knot in adaptive experiments: treatment odds keep shifting as data arrive, so the usual variance target for an effect estimate may never settle. A Wald interval scaled by one long-run variance can then mislead, since it ignores which variance regime actually played out. The paper asks how to give an honest interval at a fixed horizon for the average treatment effect.

Two auditable pipeline rules do the work: the platform must log the executed randomisation chance for each unit, and the nuisance fits used to score each unit must use past data only. Under those rules plus standard assumptions, the centred score increments form an exact martingale difference sequence. A self-normalised statistic, scaled by realised variation, then tends to a standard normal law, and simulations show where fixed-variance Wald reporting fails.
arxiv-2602-15859:
Pachtrachai and colleagues build a full setup for chat AI aides directly from past call transcripts. Incoming calls are first graded using a simple version of the PIPA setup, focusing on watching match and fitting response acts. Only high-quality chats with clear flow and strong human agent responses are retained.

Structured knowledge is then pulled from picked calls using large language models as the sole grounding source. Assistant acts are governed through prompt tuning, moving from single prompts to lean, parted, ruled designs ensuring calm, safety, and steered running. Testing uses a call-based fake user, letting counted measure of call reach, true scores, and human hand-off acts. Tests in real estate and expert hiring fields show the assistant alone taking about 30 percent of calls, hitting near-full true scores and refusal acts, with strong toughness under hostile testing.
arxiv-2602-16259:
Yilong Hou and coauthors study flexible maximum likelihood estimation of densities under a TV-type penalty, known as sectional variation norm. TV regularization has a long history in regression and density work. Revisiting the task through the Highly Adaptive Lasso framework, they formulate a HAL-based estimator using a log-spline link function. In the univariate setting, the bounded section assumption underlying HAL coincides with the classical bounded TV rule.

That equivalence directly connects HAL-MLE to existing TV penalized approaches. Three new theoretical results follow. The univariate HAL-MLE is linear in the limit. It admits pointwise limit normality. It achieves uniform convergence at a stated rate up to logarithmic factors for smoothness order at least one. Those results extend prior work that guaranteed only uniform consistency without rates. The paper aims to unify TV density methods.
arxiv-2602-16359:
Paweł Wajer, Małgorzata Królikowska, and Jakub Suchecki compute Lyapunov times for trans-Neptunian objects and main-belt asteroids. They use three approaches: the variational method and two implementations of the renormalization technique. For each object, a time comes from the nominal orbit and from one thousand and one clones, allowing comparison of single-orbit and ensemble-based estimates.

Across the sample, the methods mostly agree, though some main-belt bodies differ more. Those distant objects agree more consistently, likely from fewer overlapping resonances. Clone ensembles give more robust stability indicators than nominal-orbit computations. Median clone values reduce method-dependent biases and reveal behavior hidden in single-orbit analyses, especially for poorly constrained or resonant-region objects. The study covers a limited but diverse set of objects, and its method extends to larger populations for exploring how orbits evolve over the long term across the Solar System.
arxiv-2602-16559:
A team led by S. Belkin reports the discovery and broadband follow-up of gamma-ray burst GRB 250818B, caught by the Space Variable Objects Monitor and pinned down in optical light by the GOTO survey. The authors gather X-ray, optical, near-infrared, and radio data into unified light curves and spectral energy distributions, with MeerKAT detecting the source and ALMA setting deep higher-frequency limits.

The afterglow is unusually bright for a nominal short burst, among the most luminous high-redshift short-burst afterglows in radio, and Keck spectroscopy gives a redshift above one from metal absorption lines. Synchrotron forward-shock modeling favors a constant-density medium with refreshed energy injection in a two-component jet, while the host galaxy link stays ambiguous. Astronomers get a showcase of rapid multi-wavelength burst science.
arxiv-2602-16659:
Ujjwal Upadhyay, Yashi Tiwari, and Tarun Souradeep revisit infrared cutoff models for the primordial power spectrum. The near scale-invariant spectrum sets standard early conditions, but the largest scales stay weakly pinned by cosmic microwave background data. That leaves room for a cutoff, a prospect spurred by large-scale anomalies such as low quadrupole power.

The authors test broad classes of cutoff forms against the latest microwave background, baryon acoustic oscillation, and supernova data. Cutoff models do damp low-multipole power, but fit gains are marginal and do not beat the cost of extra values. No strong evidence favors cutoffs over the standard power-law spectrum. The paper also probes how cutoff traits interplay with a higher reionisation optical depth tied to recent data tension.
arxiv-2602-16959:
Kourosh Shahnazari and co-authors present Eigenmood Space, a doubt-aware spectral graph analysis of mental patterns in old Persian poetry. Old Persian poetry is a historically sustained archive where affective life is expressed through metaphor, intertextual convention, and indirect phrasing. Those traits make close reading essential while limiting repeatable comparison at scale.

The frame uses large-scale automatic multi-label annotation. Each verse is linked to mental concepts with per-label trust scores and an abstention flag signaling thin evidence. Trust-weighted evidence aggregates into a Poet Concept matrix. Each poet is read as a probability distribution over concepts, with individuality gauged as divergence from a corpus baseline. A trust-weighted co-occurrence graph over concepts yields an Eigenmood embedding via Laplacian spectral decomposition. On a corpus of over sixty-one thousand verses across ten poets, over a fifth of verses are abstained, underscoring the importance of doubt.
arxiv-2602-17059:
Yan Guo led a two-author mathematical study of steady, symmetric fluid flow in a channel with a viscous inflow boundary condition. The paper works with the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. A Navier slip condition holds on the channel walls. The authors build an exact steady solution close to a broad class of symmetric shear profiles that vanish at the walls.

A new weighted vorticity energy method then proves uniform linear stability with exponential decay of perturbations in a weighted norm. In short channels the method gives nonlinear asymptotic stability. In long channels, under concavity and a spectral condition, a new Rayleigh vorticity quantity tames the hard terms and yields nonlinear stability. The work gives sharp decay rates and stability thresholds for this inflow setup.
arxiv-2602-17159: Levent Ali Mengütürk, writing alone, proposes a new way to gauge how far apart two Gaussian distributions sit. The paper sets out a duality linking the spherical squared-Hellinger distance with a hyperbolic invariant of the Poincare disc under the general Mobius group. That link motivates using the L2-embedded hyperbolic invariant as another gauge of divergence for Gaussian measures. The idea speaks to information theory and machine learning alike, offering a geometry-flavored yardstick for statistical difference where standard measures now rule.
arxiv-2602-17359:
Artur Dróżdż led a three-author experimental study of wavy-wall control for turbulent boundary layer separation on a convex plate. The wavy-wall method, first proposed for a flat plate, is tested here at high Reynolds number on the suction side shape of an airfoil. Applying the method raises the friction coefficient by more than forty percent, substantially delaying turbulent separation from the convex wall while maintaining total momentum, as tracked by momentum-loss thickness.

Other efficiency signs include a steady friction Reynolds number and a thinner boundary layer. Together the signs promise aerodynamic gains for airfoils, similar to active suction on the suction side. New insight into the mechanism suggests small-scale turbulent activity drives the benefit, enhancing streamwise convection and sweeping motion for superior momentum transport. Poorly chosen geometry, however, can induce large-scale motions like trough separation that counteract the mechanism and harm efficiency.
arxiv-2602-17459:
Ting-Wei Chao led a three-author team on set systems with uniform witnesses. Frankl, Pach, and Erdos conjectured a size bound for uniform families with VC-dimension at most d, for large n. Ahlswede and Khachatrian disproved it with a larger counterexample. For such a family, the VC-dimension condition restates in terms of witness sets. For any set F in the family, some witness set B_F governs how F relates to the sets.

The lead author and colleagues conjectured the bound holds if every witness set has size s, with s between zero and d. The case s equals zero is the Erdos-Ko-Rado theorem. Here the team shows the claim holds when s is at most half of d. The maximal constructions are stars. They build non-star families of the bound's size for s between half of d and d minus one.
arxiv-2602-17659:
Yu Fang and team study a failure mode of vision-language-action models for robots: language gets overridden by vision. Such models promise to ground language in robot control, yet they often act on vision shortcuts from dataset biases, repeating well-learned acts and picking familiar objects no matter what the words say.

To study this systematically, the team built LIBERO-CF, the first counterfactual benchmark for these models, which assigns alternative instructions under visually plausible layouts. Tests show counterfactual failures are common yet underexplored across leading models. Their fix, Counterfactual Action Guidance, pairs a standard policy with a language-free vision-action module for counterfactual comparison at action choice. It cuts vision-shortcut failures and lifts task success, with no extra demos or architecture changes.
arxiv-2602-17759:
Isabelle John and team analyze cosmic-ray travel using time-varying AMS-02 measures spanning a full solar cycle. They fit two Galactic travel scenarios, convection models and re-accel models, combined with three solar modulation recipes. These are the standard force-field take, an extended force-field model with a stiffness break, and the heliospheric code HelMod.

Time-varying antiproton data offer a unique probe of charge-sign effects and low-energy errors. The force-field take describes plus-charged nuclei fairly well outside solar maximum in convection models, but fails during high solar activity and for antiprotons at all times. In re-accel scenarios, strong mix-ups between modulation and low-energy travel yield unreal results under simple modulation models. Across all models, doubts of about ten to fifteen percent in rebuilt between-star spectra and numbers limit precision, far above the percent-level error of current measures.
arxiv-2602-18759:
Recommender systems learn mostly from clicks. So they must invent negatives, items a user presumably did not want. A bad choice of negatives teaches bad taste. Chen Chen, with two co-authors, proposes ICPNS in 2026. It is a negative sampling method grounded in the communities users actually belong to.

The insight is that exposure runs through latent communities. An item that is popular inside a user's own community yet still unclicked is a far more trustworthy negative than a random unseen item. By estimating exposure from in-community popularity, the method picks negatives that are real, hard, and interpretable. Tests on four benchmarks improve graph-based recommenders and stay competitive on matrix-factorisation models.
arxiv-2602-18959:
In trauma surgery, knowing where hands are, and whether each is left or right, supports rapid, precise choices. Kedi Sun, with one co-author, proposes a YOLOv10-based framework in 2026 that localises hands and classifies laterality at once in complex surgical scenes.

Training uses first-person surgical videos from a trauma challenge dataset, with marked hand bounding boxes. Heavy augmentation and a multi-task design improve robustness against motion blur, lighting variation, and diverse hand appearances. Evaluation shows moderate left-hand and right-hand classification accuracy, while separating hands from background remains challenging. Mean average precision is modest, yet inference stays real-time. The work lays a foundation for hand-instrument interaction analysis in emergency surgery. Real time matters in theatre. This model keeps pace.
arxiv-2602-19259:
Quantum computers raise a tempting hope: squeeze a large nearest-neighbor search structure into very few qubits, using quantum states as a kind of hash. Sajjad Hashemian tests that hope in a broad model where a dataset is stored as a quantum state and each question is answered by measuring a fresh copy. The question is whether a handful of qubits, growing only slowly with dataset size, could ever suffice.

The answer is no. For any approximation quality and any success chance above one half, the paper builds hard examples that no such sketch can handle. In these examples, points are bit strings and distance counts differing bits. The result closes off a whole family of quantum shortcuts for nearest-neighbor search. It shows the hoped-for compression would need a fundamentally different model, not just a cleverer encoding.
arxiv-2602-19359:
Matching a robot simulator to real hardware often relies on hand tuning or black-box optimizers that cannot say which physical mismatch drives the error. Kevin Qiu and three co-authors present Vid2Sid, a pipeline that identifies systems from video. It couples foundation-model perception with a vision-language model optimizer. That optimizer studies paired simulation and real videos, diagnoses concrete mismatches, and suggests physics parameter updates, each with a written rationale.

Tests cover a tendon-actuated finger in MuJoCo and a deformable continuum tentacle in PyElastica. On held-out real controls, Vid2Sid ranks best on average, matching or beating black-box optimizers while explaining each step. Simulation-to-simulation checks show it recovering true parameters most accurately, with mean relative error under 13 percent versus 28 to 98 percent for rivals.
arxiv-2602-19759:
A geometric view of heat and energy assigns curvature to a system's state space. The sign of that curvature has long hinted at whether particles effectively attract or repel. A 2026 arXiv paper by Hosein Mohammadzadeh and three co-authors extends that geometric view to fast-moving ideal gases.

Using a metric drawn from the partition function, the team studies curvature for classical, boson, and fermion cases. Exact results cover two dimensions; the three-dimensional case is numerical. The usual signs survive fast motion: positive for bosons, negative for fermions. One effect of fast motion shifts curvature singular points to a mass-set threshold. The condensation temperature for fast-moving gases also gains mass-based corrections. The paper unifies geometry, particle statistics, and fast motion in one picture.
arxiv-2602-20359:
Rayan Mazouz and three co-authors present StochasticBarrier.jl, an open-source Julia toolbox for building stochastic barrier functions. Such functions certify the safety of discrete-time stochastic systems with additive Gaussian noise. The toolbox covers linear, polynomial, and piecewise affine systems, with the last class opening verification to a wide range of dynamics, including general nonlinear types.

Two optimization routes are offered: a sum-of-squares route using semi-definite programming solvers, and a piecewise-constant route with three engines, two based on linear programming and one on gradient descent. Benchmarks against the state of the art show the tool beats rivals on computation time, safety probability bounds, and scalability across more than thirty case studies. Against its closest rival, it runs faster by orders of magnitude, gives better safety bounds, and supports higher-dimensional systems.
arxiv-2602-20459:
Can AI trained on the science record foresee the gains that follow? Anirudh Ajith and nine co-authors offer PreScience, a dataset and benchmark for science forecasting. It builds from ninety-eight thousand recent AI research papers, plus linked papers on author records and links for five hundred two thousand papers. Records include titles, abstracts, named authors, key sources, topic labels, cite paths, and details frozen at time cutoffs.

Seven sample tasks cover work generation, partner forecast, prior work choice, cite-count forecast, future mix forecast, and two topic trend outlooks. Starting points range from simple rules to frontier models and agentic systems, with a new LACER metric judging made contributions more like humans do. Building task models into a twelve-month made-up corpus yields papers clearly less diverse and less novel than human research from the same period.
arxiv-2602-20759:
Human values rarely speak with one voice, yet most chat models answer as if they do. Yu Fu and two co-authors train a single language model to give varied, fair views on one query, with no extra prompts and no separate parts bolted on.

Their method first tunes a text-similarity tool to judge how well replies cover real views. Then a two-part reward trains the model to cover many views while keeping each one distinct. A small 3-billion-parameter model trained this way beat a much larger 20-billion baseline on a test of inference, gaining 37.4 percent, and also beat a modular rival system.
arxiv-2602-20859:
Financial prediction from long documents is noisy work: useful signals are sparse, and the best embedding model shifts with task and time. Zirui He and four co-authors propose FinAnchor in this 2026 arXiv paper, a light framework that merges embeddings from several language models without fine-tuning any of them. One anchor embedding space is chosen, and linear maps align the other models into it.

The aligned features then combine into a single representation for prediction. Across several financial language tasks, FinAnchor beats strong single-model baselines and standard ensembles. Readers get a practical recipe for robust prediction: anchor heterogeneous representations instead of betting on one model or averaging blindly.
arxiv-2602-20959:
Reading atomic structure out of spectra is central to materials science, yet it works only for a narrow set of methods and materials. Ian Slagle, Faisal Alamgir, and Victor Fung widen that reach in this 2026 arXiv paper using ActiveStructOpt. The framework pairs graph neural network surrogates with active learning to find candidate structures that reproduce target spectra at low computational cost.

Tests on X-ray pair distribution data, and on the heavier simulations of X-ray absorption near-edge spectra and extended fine structure, show the method reliably matching spectra across diverse material classes. Under equal budgets it beats existing structure-determination methods. Readers get a flexible, data-efficient route to structural refinement across many computable spectroscopic techniques.
arxiv-2602-21059:
Automated metrics for language-model reliability miss how scientists actually judge answers. Anna Martin-Boyle, William Humphreys, Martha Brown, Cara Leckey, and Harmanpreet Kaur build an expert-grounded alternative in this 2026 arXiv paper: a schema for evaluating errors in scholarly question-answering systems. Working with domain experts, they identified twenty error patterns across seven categories from thematic analysis of sixty-eight question-answer pairs.

Validation through contextual inquiries with ten additional scientists showed which errors experts spot naturally and how structured schemas help them catch issues they had missed. Experts work through orderly routines when they judge: they test fine technical detail, weigh results against their own values, and turn back to review their own judging. The paper points toward tools built on the schema and tuned to each expert's habits and skill.
arxiv-2602-21159:
Global hypoellipticity can fail for perturbed vector fields, and the set of bad constants has a curious size. Maria Bartmeyer, Paulo Dattori da Silva, and Rafael Gonzalez measure that set topologically in this 2026 arXiv paper, using Kronecker's approximation theorem. In some situations the set is discrete and enumerable, hence meager, within the real line.

In other situations the set is a dense G-delta subset of the complex numbers, hence nonmeager, contrasting with a known result that the set has null Lebesgue measure. Readers get a topological refinement of size: measure-zero sets can still be topologically large. The contrast clarifies what different notions of smallness actually capture.
arxiv-2602-21259:
Vehicles that fly and dive could monitor coasts, infrastructure, and disaster zones, but air and water demand very different control. Ricardo Grando and five co-authors tackle persistent monitoring for hybrid aerial-underwater vehicles in this 2026 arXiv paper, combining deep reinforcement learning with transfer learning for cross-domain adaptability. A shared architecture trains on lidar data in air and sonar data underwater.

That unified policy proves feasible across both environments, handling environmental uncertainty and multiple moving targets. The framework lays groundwork for scalable autonomous monitoring with hybrid vehicles. Readers get evidence that one policy can span two domains, rather than requiring separate controllers for sky and sea.
arxiv-2602-22159:
Upscaling an image far beyond its training range usually falls apart: noise, blur, and artifacts pile up as the scale grows. Wenhao Guo and five co-authors reframe extreme magnification as a chain of small, in-distribution scale steps, in a framework called CASR. One single model walks the image up through those steps, keeping inference stable at arbitrary scales.

Two modules handle the hard parts: one aligns structural distributions across steps to stop error buildup, the other restores fine textures while preserving self-similarity. The design tackles distribution drift and patch inconsistencies together. Despite using only one model, CASR cuts distribution shift sharply, giving super-resolution a steadier ladder to climb.
arxiv-2602-22259:
Backpropagation is powerful but costly, and alternatives that skip it have struggled to scale. Guoqing Ma and Shan Yu propose LOCO, a perturbation-based weight-modification method inspired by brain-like representations and dynamics. Its key insight is that low rank is inherent to perturbation methods, and an orthogonality constraint then tames the variance of gradient estimates.

That taming pays off in depth: LOCO locally trains spiking networks deeper than ten layers, the deepest such training reported, with strong continual-learning ability and better task performance than rival non-backpropagation methods. For neuromorphic hardware, where backpropagation fits poorly, the method offers a scalable learning rule that learns locally and keeps improving.
arxiv-2602-22559:
S. Jalalzadeh and one co-author build a unified semiclassical picture of a charged Reissner-Nordstrom black hole. They treat the quasi-local horizon energies as the true thermodynamic variables. From that base they write a first law and Smarr relation horizon by horizon. Then they quantize a reduced phase space to get a discrete mass spectrum for both horizons, matching the smallest allowed entropy step.

Jumps between adjacent levels shift the Hawking temperatures by Planck-scale amounts and add a universal logarithmic term to the entropy, in line with independent quantum gravity work. The authors pack these corrections into a deformed geometry that keeps horizon positions fixed while matching the corrected surface gravities. The result slightly cools both horizons, weakens inner-horizon instability, and nudges photon-sphere and shadow features for large black holes.
arxiv-2602-22959:
Zihao Zhao and four co-authors test whether agents can tell apart sicknesses that look alike. Medical imaging agents usually handle routine workflows, but telling apart lookalike sicknesses zero-shot matters for clinics and stays underexplored. The team benchmarks sample agents on two imaging-only proxy tasks: melanoma versus odd nevus, and lung edema versus pneumonia.

A multi-agent setup based on side-by-side judging lifts test scores by eleven points on skin scans and cuts unbacked claims on descriptive samples. Overall scores still fall short of clinic use, and the team admits tagging doubt plus missing clinic context as limits. Within its tight setting, the pilot study offers early guidance on zero-shot agent scores where vision alone fools.
arxiv-2602-23059:
Stefano Cipolla and three co-authors find the nearest time-symmetric Markov chains under thinness constraints. Time-symmetry is central to Metropolis-Hastings and other MCMC methods, yet many applications yield non-reversible chains, prompting approximation by time-symmetric ones with minimal change.

The team frames the task as a matrix nearness problem for sparse step tables. The ensuing problem is a quadratic tuning task, and number tests show the value of the approach. The setup gives a ruled way to impose time-symmetry and thinness patterns in Markov chains, with uses in MCMC, computer chemistry, and data-driven models.
arxiv-2602-23159:
Oshani Seneviratne and four co-authors use the FinSurvival 2025 challenge as a case study in how to benchmark temporal Web3 intelligence, the study of how decentralized platforms change over time. Web3 systems leave rich, time-stamped event trails, but the field has lacked shared tests that capture real-world quirks such as censored data and shifting behavior over long spans.

The challenge drew on 21.8 million transaction records from the Aave v3 lending protocol and posed 16 survival-prediction tasks about user behavior. The winning entries showed that features built with domain knowledge about time beat generic modeling by a clear margin. The authors draw lessons for future benchmarks, arguing that Web3 data offers a high-fidelity test bed for churn, risk, and change across the wider Web.
arxiv-2602-23359:
Vaibhav Agrawal and four co-authors tackle occlusion reasoning in 3D layout-based image making. Occlusion reasoning is basic yet missed: partly hidden objects need depth-steady shapes and scale. Older methods make lifelike scenes that follow input layouts but often fail to model precisely which objects hide which.

The key is OSCR, an occlusion-aware 3D scene representation in which objects appear as see-through 3D boxes in a virtual setting, rendered from the desired camera viewpoint. See-through sides reveal hidden object regions, letting the model reason about what hides what, while the viewpoint gives camera control. Visual tokens from that picture condition a ready flow-based text-to-image model, and masked self-attention binds each object box to its caption, avoiding trait mixing. Trained on made-up multi-object scenes with much hiding, SeeThrough3D extends to unseen kinds with precise layout and camera control.
arxiv-2602-23559:
Cho-Ying Wu and three co-authors present the first study of cross-sensor view synthesis across different modalities. Aligned RGB-X data are hard to obtain: most prior RGB-X work assumes such pairs exist and focuses on modality fusion, yet collecting them takes huge calibration effort.

Their match-densify-consolidate method first matches RGB-X images, then densifies points with guidance, using confidence-aware densification and self-matching filtering for better view synthesis. Results are then consolidated in 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method uses no 3D priors for the X-sensor and assumes only nearly no-cost COLMAP for RGB. By removing cumbersome calibration for various RGB-X sensors, it aims to advance cross-sensor learning and break the bottleneck in large-scale real-world RGB-X data collection.
arxiv-2602-23659:
Jeff Nijsse and one co-author study privacy, tech, and anonymity in central bank digital money. As money goes digital, central bank digital currencies have become a focal point for tech progress. Privacy compliance now shapes CBDC design beyond tech needs, affecting legal needs, trust, and security.

Building privacy-lifting tools demands a cross-field approach, yet no common grasp of privacy or key tech traits slows progress. The work asks how privacy can be defined within CBDCs, what that meaning implies for design, and which tools can lift CBDC privacy. It offers a full privacy meaning mapped to the crypto landscape, tested on 20 current CBDCs. Full privacy can be planned at the proposal stage, but it does not reach launched versions. Failure study of dropped privacy pilots finds four root causes of the research-to-launch gap: rule watch, compute cost, blame sharing, and bank rewards.
arxiv-2602-23859:
Lorenzo Liverani and Enrique Zuazua present HYCO, a hybrid framework that joins physics-based and data-driven models for partial differential equations. The 2026 paper rejects forcing physical rules directly onto a synthetic model; instead it trains both parts as cooperating agents, nudged toward agreement by mutual regularization.

The cooperative scheme runs naturally in parallel and stays robust when data are sparse and noisy. Tests on static and time-dependent benchmarks show that HYCO recovers accurate solutions and model parameters even under ill-posed conditions, where data alone cannot pin down an answer. The framework also admits a game-theoretic reading as a Nash equilibrium, which supports alternating optimization. It offers a principled way to blend known physics with learned flexibility.
arxiv-2602-23959:
Kesen Zhao and five co-authors present Numerical Visual Chain-of-Thought, a framework that lets multimodal language models reason over images with continuous coordinates. The 2026 paper notes that current visual reasoning grounds regions either as textified coordinates, which fragment meaning across modalities, or as fixed patches. Fixed patches limit precise selection and demand nontrivial architecture changes.

The new framework widens the model's action space from discrete tokens to continuous Euclidean space. In short, the model can point at places in a picture with smooth steps, using coordinates as actions. It supports both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, replacing categorical token policies with Gaussian or Laplace policies over coordinates and sampling through reparameterization for compatibility with group-relative policy optimization. Tests on three benchmarks against many baselines show better localization precision, answer accuracy, and faster training convergence.
arxiv-2602-24159:
Martial Guidez and two co-authors present RAViT, a resolution-adaptive vision transformer for image classification that cuts compute cost while preserving accuracy. The 2026 paper notes that vision transformers perform excellently but cost far more compute than convolutional networks, a barrier to wider deployment.

RAViT uses a multi-branch network that processes several copies of the same image at different resolutions. In a two-branch design, a first transformer predicts from a downscaled image. Then that prediction is reused alongside the full-resolution image by a second transformer, using less total compute than a classical vision transformer. An early-exit mechanism lets the model stop at intermediate branches, letting users choose the accuracy-cost trade-off at run time. Tests on three image classification benchmarks show accuracy equivalent to a classical vision transformer at roughly seven-tenths of the floating-point cost.
arxiv-2603-00359: Manna, Snyder, and Tabor train Meta's OPT model on the BabyLM set of one hundred million words and test its grasp of grammar rules. In close to a third of the test groups, the model keeps ranking wrong sentences above right ones even after long training. The team finds these wrong calls often lock in early and then persist. They propose that early word-pair habits may drive this stubborn mislearning, and sketch a test for that idea.
arxiv-2603-00859: Olukola and Rahimi propose AMDS, an attack-aware multistage defence for network intrusion detection, learning attack specific strategies. The system combines ensemble disagreement, predictive uncertainty, and anomaly signals, with two stage learning tuning detection per attack. Across seven adversarial attack types, the analysis finds each attack leaves a distinct detection signature. Evaluation on a benchmark intrusion dataset shows 94.2% area under the curve, beating trained ensembles on accuracy and F1. Under white box attacks, the system holds up well, though only two variants were tested and no formal guarantee is claimed.
arxiv-2603-01259: Mohanta, Paul, and Basak map the spectrum of the doubly charmed tetraquark Tcc, a four-quark particle with quantum numbers 0(1+), on MILC gauge ensembles at two lattice spacings. They include diquark-antidiquark, molecular, and scattering operators, varying heavy and light quark masses. Heavy quarks use the anisotropic Clover action and light quarks an O(a)-improved Wilson-Clover action, with a modified Lüschers method handling the non-analyticity near the Left Hand Cut.
arxiv-2603-01359: Dessena, Civera, and Bonilla-Manrique study working modal analysis of aircraft frames via sideways filling, coupling the Loewner Framework with NExT to yield the NExT-LF method. The method exploits Loewner speed from sideways filling plus impulse response recovery enabled by NExT, easing Stochastic Subspace Identification burden on large systems and NExT-ERA noise struggles. NExT-LF is tested on lab benchmarks including the eXperimental BeaRDS 2 high-aspect-ratio wing main spar.
arxiv-2603-01759:
Zichen Tian, Yaoyao Liu, and Qianru Sun tune the fine-tuning knobs of large models automatically in this 2026 work. Their test bed is remote sensing, where training a model from scratch fails for lack of data. Parameter-efficient methods update few weights, yet their fixed settings can badly cap results on new image types.

Their method, MetaPEFT, adds adaptive scalers that adjust module influence while fine-tuning runs. Three levers move together: where modules insert, which layers they touch, and how fast each learns. Tests span three transfer settings and five data sets in satellite and normal images. The method sets new top scores for cross-spectral adaptation with few trainable weights. Tail-class accuracy, often the weak spot on skewed sets, improves a lot as well.
arxiv-2603-01859:
J. Pawlowski, P. Lydzba, and M. Mierzejewski extract conserved quantities of a quantum system from just a few of its states. Their 2026 work focuses on the XXZ model, a standard chain of interacting quantum spins. Local integrals of motion, quantities that never change, define whether such a system counts as integrable.

A single energy state can already reveal if a system is integrable or chaotic, past work showed. The team shows those integrals can also be estimated from a small set of states. As system size grows, the needed share of states shrinks toward zero. A cousin model with fragmented Hilbert space breaks the pattern, since most states are needed there. That split marks a rare deep difference between true integrability and mere fragmentation of the state space.
arxiv-2603-01959:
Mehran Shakerinava, Behnoush Khavari, Siamak Ravanbakhsh, and Sarath Chandar map exactly what diagonal state-space models can and cannot track. Their 2026 work studies sequential state-tracking, where a model must follow a changing state step by step. Diagonal state-space models are fast and parallel, yet their expressive limits were unclear.

For a single layer with complex diagonal dynamics, non-Abelian group tracking proves impossible at finite precision. Non-Abelian means step order matters, a trait of many real state systems. With more layers, the reachable groups are exactly those with a layered series of Abelian factors. That places the model family precisely inside the solvable groups of algebra. Experiments add a warning: multi-layer models often fail to learn even the tracking they can express.
arxiv-2603-02459:
F Dai, E Kosov, and V Temlyakov survey sampling discretization in this 2026 mathematics paper. Discretization replaces continuous norms of functions with sums over sample points. Classic inequalities for polynomials, tied to Marcinkiewicz and Zygmund, anchor the field. The survey generalizes those results to functions in arbitrary finite-dimensional spaces.

Norms come from general probability measures, not just uniform ones. Discrete sums must approximate them faithfully for every function in the space. The authors emphasize recent advances, especially their own research line. Main proof ideas and techniques are highlighted, not just final statements. The survey complements three recent surveys on the same topic. Readers gain a map of where sampling theory stands now.
arxiv-2603-02859:
Zuzana Haniková tests whether an alternative logic of sets can capture the idea of feasible numbers. Her 2026 paper works inside Vopěnka's Alternative Set Theory, a framework often used to model vague notions. The target is Yessenin-Volpin's view that only numbers small enough to handle in practice fully count as numbers.

She tries to model Dummett's weakly infinite totalities, collections that behave as finite from some angles and endless from others. Dummett treated their coherence as the test case for the whole feasible-number idea. The verdict here is negative: the set theory captures some features of feasible numbers, but not all. Haniková stresses that one failed route does not settle the broader debate over ultrafinitism.
arxiv-2603-02959:
Julio Silva-Rodríguez and Ender Konukoglu stretch a handful of labeled medical images much further with unlabeled ones. Vision-language models adapt well to new tasks from few examples, but rare disease classes often get too few labels and drag accuracy down. Their 2026 method targets exactly that low-shot squeeze in medical imaging.

A fast semi-supervised solver spreads pseudo-labels, guided by the model's text side, from labeled to unlabeled images during adaptation. The unlabeled pool helps cover classes that annotation budgets miss. The authors report labeling effort cut by at least half in low-shot settings while keeping adaptation efficient. For hospitals, where expert annotation is the bottleneck, cheaper adaptation could decide whether these models get used at all.
arxiv-2603-03059:
Alex Binh Vinh Duc Nguyen examines a paradox in teaching architecture with generative AI. Design schools are adding these tools to the curriculum, yet learning to judge them critically means using them more, with little way to count the environmental cost. His 2026 paper views the problem through human-computer interaction research.

Three directions follow. Contextual eco-feedback would show students the footprint of their AI use as they work. Participatory scoping would let affected stakeholders help set the terms of adoption. Treating data centers as a shared study topic would tie the tool back to the built world architects shape. The paper argues generative AI is a socio-technical process, not just a new drawing tool, and education must engage it critically.
arxiv-2603-03159:
Friederike Ihssen, Renzo Kapust, and Jan Pawlowski sample probability distributions whose weights can be complex numbers. Such sign problems plague quantum field theory and real-time quantum dynamics, because negative or complex weights break standard sampling. Their 2026 paper builds a generative architecture around physics-informed kernels designed for exactly this obstacle.

The architecture preserves total probability weight while mapping the hard sampling task onto a simpler, sign-free landscape where sampling is efficient. Both burdens, the sign problem and slow sampling, are addressed by the same construction. Demonstrations cover zero-dimensional field theories with complex couplings and the real-time evolution of a quantum harmonic oscillator. Success there would point toward broader use in lattice field theory.
arxiv-2603-03359:
Swapnil Parekh audits speech recognition for accent bias, asking whether accuracy gaps across accents run deep or sit on the surface. His 2026 audit, ACES, works in three stages on a model's internal representations. It first finds the directions in representation space that carry accent information, then aims adversarial attacks along those directions, and finally tests whether deleting them would help fairness.

On a standard wav2vec model covering seven accents, tiny inaudible perturbations along the accent directions widened the error-rate gap by nearly half, far beyond random-direction controls. A label-shuffling check confirmed the effect tracks real accent structure. Surprisingly, partly removing the accent directions made both accuracy and disparity worse. Accent information is deeply entangled with recognition itself, so Parekh positions the subspaces as auditing tools, not simple erasure levers.
arxiv-2603-03459:
Peter Balogh asks how much of a transformer's heavy nonlinear machinery is actually needed. Every layer's feed-forward network transforms every token elaborately, yet many of those computations may be nearly linear. His 2026 study tests six models across two architectures and three text collections. A tiny learned gate, a single logistic classifier, decides token by token whether the full nonlinear path is required.

The gate works, but its logic resists simple rules. Whether a token needs nonlinearity cannot be predicted from the token itself: routing lists built on one corpus fail completely on another. The decision is fully contextual, best predicted by a token's contribution to the passing residual stream. Still, the gate routed a large share of computations through cheap linear paths at tiny accuracy cost in one architecture, while another family resisted more. Frozen linear layers even improved one fully retrained model.
arxiv-2603-03659:
Julia B Kieserman and four others expose a privacy leak hiding inside social media ads. TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram let advertisers aim campaigns at touchy traits. Those ads are interactive by default: anyone can comment or react. Their 2026 paper shows that this design choice lets advertisers view the profiles of all who interact, in effect naming the people who match the touchy targeting tests.

That behavior flatly contradicts the platforms' promises to keep user data hidden from advertisers. A reaction meant as a casual tap becomes an unintentional disclosure of exactly the trait the ad targeted. The authors close with design changes that would warn users about the consequences of interacting and give them a clear view before the tap. That would restore the promised protection without banning aimed ads outright.
arxiv-2603-03759: Emile Anand and Ishani Karmarkar study approximate Nash equilibria in multi-agent reinforcement learning via mean-field subsampling. The setting is a Markov game of cooperation with a global agent and local agents under communication constraints. The global agent observes a subset of local states each step. The authors propose a framework: the global agent performs learning against a local policy, while local agents optimize in an induced Markov decision process. They prove approximate best-response dynamics converge to an approximate Nash equilibrium, separating state and action sample complexities.
arxiv-2603-03859:
Bart De Bruyn and Thijs van Veluw classify Hoffman colorability for connected graphs whose smallest eigenvalue is at least minus two. A graph is Hoffman colorable when the spectral Hoffman bound on its chromatic number is tight. Building on the Cameron-Goethals-Seidel-Shult classification theorem, the authors extend an earlier characterization that covered only line graphs to this whole class of graphs.

They characterize Hoffman colorability for generalized line graphs. They also completely classify the exceptional graphs that are Hoffman colorable, finding several hundred of them arranged in a natural partial order, with a small set of maximal ones. As a byproduct they also determine all graphs maximal with respect to being representable in one of the classical root systems. The results complete a chapter of spectral graph theory linking eigenvalues, colorings, and root system geometry.
arxiv-2603-04159: Daniel Linford asks whether we can infer that all of real reality began to exist, offering results suggesting a negative verdict. He offers two necessary but not sufficient terms for a cosmic beginning. Three theorems then show observers cannot infer global spacetime structure across a wide range of spacetimes. One theorem makes beginning-satisfying spacetimes indistinguishable from failing ones, while two extensions bar enough data to judge singularity terms or the necessary terms.
arxiv-2603-04259: Popchanovska and colleagues sort real world AI failures into a guide for stopping harm before it spreads. From thousands of news reports on AI incidents, they extract the concrete steps organizations took afterward. Those steps extend an MIT taxonomy with four new groups covering fixes, legal action, market controls, and denial. Their labels span dozens of response types, many previously unseen, and support steadier monitoring after deployment.
arxiv-2603-04359: Federici and colleagues explain why rotation style transforms help quantized models. Quantization boosts efficiency but usually costs accuracy, for unclear reasons. The quantization noise ratio splits into concentration plus alignment of main directions. Prior transforms target concentration alone, but better alignment can cut error further. Block CAT transforms use a small calibration set to lift both factors at once. At 4-bit precision CAT matches or beats prior transform methods on several large language models.
arxiv-2603-04459: Chu and colleagues audit code quality and adoption in safety benchmarks. Benchmarks guide safety work, yet runnability and adoption drivers lacked systematic study. The team measures 31 benchmarks against 382 other papers with static analysis, human tests over 220 hours, and bibliometrics. Only 39 percent run unmodified, 16 percent give flawless install guides, and 6 percent address ethics despite harmful content. Adoption tracks prominence and runnability, not code quality, and some repos expose jailbreak outputs without warnings.
arxiv-2603-04559: Bandopadhyay and colleagues model repeat nuclear transients as partial tidal disruptions. Repeat outbursts from galaxy nuclei arise when bound stars meet huge black holes again and again. A subset with month to year repeat rate fits infall flares from tidal stripping. Model runs and math forecasts track how stars hold up under repeat mass loss and how flares change by type and orbit. High mass, dense stars survive many passes, while low mass, less evolved stars die within a few orbits, pinning down sources like ASASSN-14ko and AT2020vdq.
arxiv-2603-04659: Sejersen and colleagues plan multi-agent trajectories with GIANT. The approach joins global path planning with local navigation for multi-robot collision avoidance. Attentive graph neural networks manage dynamic interactions among agents. A local model follows pre-planned global paths while adjusting to changes. Training noise boosts robustness in complex, dynamic settings. Tests against three baselines, NH-ORCA, DRL-NAV, and GA3C-CADRL, in diverse simulated scenarios show better success, fewer collisions, and faster navigation, especially where baselines struggle.
arxiv-2603-04759: Han and colleagues propose SharedLLM, a framework extending LLM context windows via multi-grained compression. Continual pre-training on long-context data is straightforward but costly. SharedLLM stacks two short-context LLMs from the same underlying layers: a lower compressor and an upper reader. The lower model squeezes long inputs into compact multi-grained codes for context-aware processing above. Information transfer happens only at the lowest layers, skipping lengthy forward passes and cross-attention. A tree-based data structure supports fast encoding and query-aware lookup of contextual information.
arxiv-2603-04859: Shi and colleagues reveal a model hijack threat in transfer learning with fake distilled sets. Dataset boiling cooks a compact set keeping key facts from a large original set. A foe can hijack a model with just a few poisoned samples in the fake set. Osmosis Boiling, the proposed attack, hits deep learning models using the fewest samples. Tests show high attack success on hidden tasks while keeping high utility on original tasks. The distilled osmosis set enables hijack across diverse model designs.
arxiv-2603-05259: Garreth Kemp and Sanjaye Ramgoolam study projectors in semisimple subalgebra chains, motivated by AdS/CFT and quantum information. Degeneracy graphs are finite layered projector trees in chains built one piece at a time. From these graphs comes a simple monomial-basis formula for the algebra, tagging nodes by generator eigenvalue variables. The build matches counting, and they give one- and two-layer constructions. Machine evidence backs determinant invertibility between bases, and the same build shows up for symmetric group centers and Jucys-Murphy subalgebras.
arxiv-2603-05459: Souza and team present DEBISS, a set of spoken debates, each with one speaker at a time and a semi-structured form, made to fill the gap in debate sets. Debate runs through study, work, day to day talk, TV politics, and posts made online. Yet the wide range of forms makes a fair set hard to build. The set has wide labels for language tool tasks, such as debater quality assessment, argument mining, speaker diarization, and speech-to-text conversion.
arxiv-2603-05559: Yamagami and team analyze a stochastic-process model for the two-armed bandit problem, where a threshold and a Markov signal evolve jointly. Test results show a setting-based pattern, with negative autocorrelation best when rewards are rich and positive autocorrelation best when rewards are poor. Negative autocorrelation wins when the winning chances sum to more than one, and positive when the sum is less than one. Results do not depend on autocorrelation when the sum equals one. The findings point toward bandit solving for reinforcement learning in wireless comms.
arxiv-2603-05659: Ikezogwo and colleagues identify a reference-free gap in post-training methods, where many tasks admit multiple valid outputs and lack a single ideal answer. They propose Implicit Error Counting, which enumerates what a response gets wrong instead of what it gets right. As a case study, they validate Implicit Error Counting on virtual try-on. They introduce Cascaded Error Counting and curate Mismatch-DressCode, a benchmark with maximal attribute mismatch. On that benchmark, Implicit Error Counting outperforms Rubrics as Rewards across all metrics.
arxiv-2603-06259: Gaudillot-Estrada classifies irreducible covariant representations for any pair of a group acting on a variety in the algebraic affine setting, by using the Mackey machine. Applications follow for motion group representations on Banach spaces and other related examples, showing the classification's reach beyond the algebraic case. The paper thus gives a full classification in the algebraic case with real uses. The main result stays in the algebraic case, and the uses look past it.
arxiv-2603-06459: Shkolnikov shows vision-language models encode geometry text fails to say, with a probe reading hand joint angles at 6.1 degrees error from frozen parts. Text output performs worse, and fine-tuning narrows the gap, suggesting a pathway-training deficit, not a stored one. Training objective matters more than architecture: five nets meet at same accuracy despite little shared overlap. Stepwise making damages geometric truth through making, not language fit. A network peak appears, with layers 18 to 22 carrying signal, letting a backbone serve as a shape sensor.
arxiv-2603-06559: Yue and team propose a sampling-based tuning framework for making messenger RNA sequences for a protein, searching a large synonymous space while lifting stability and performance. Design has multiple coupled objectives beyond folding criteria, with uses preferring varied trade-offs. It samples matching ones, tests them against black-box metrics, then updates a sampling spread. Across a UniProt protein set and the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, the method improves the chosen goal. Strong gains appear on unpaired probability and accessible uridine share over LinearDesign and EnsembleDesign.
arxiv-2603-06759: Cadirci and Singull study how to estimate Kullback-Leibler divergence and test fit for multivariate continuous distributions. From the maximum entropy rule, moment-matched Gaussians give the highest Shannon entropy. KL divergence from such a Gaussian thus becomes an entropy difference. They estimate it with k-nearest-neighbor estimators from the Kozachenko-Leonenko line, with proofs that the estimators converge. Their test statistic tends to zero under normality and to a positive bound otherwise.
arxiv-2603-06859: Chen and colleagues present C3, counterfactual credit assignment for LLM agent teams that share context. Credit for a message is guessed by a learned critic, a run score, or an agent ablation standing in for a rarely run counterfactual. When all agents read is written into the trace, trace is state, and the counterfactual can be run. C3 swaps a message at a choice point and continues the run to reward, giving credit unbiased and right up to sampling error. Its variance follows a law with no agent term.
arxiv-2603-07059: Sadhukhan and colleagues pair a stats tool with a waveguide filter to steady laser beams warped by air turbulence. Their method splits the beam shape into a smooth core plus skew and peak corrections. That gives clear scores for how far it strays from a clean Gaussian form. They then show a dielectric waveguide strips out higher spatial modes, which carry most of the warp. The beam that comes out is thus closer to the ideal shape.
arxiv-2603-07159: Legrand and colleagues improve language model reasoning at inference time by minimizing uncertainty thought by thought. Instead of heavy sampling or outside evaluators, their method picks, at each reasoning step, the continuation with the highest self-certainty from the model's own predictive distribution. It needs only a small number of samples, uses model-internal signals alone, and works on open-ended questions, unlike majority voting. On MATH500 and GSM8K, it beats greedy decoding and equals or tops self-consistency at similar token budgets.
arxiv-2603-07259: Podobryaev studies a one-parameter family of symmetric Lorentzian shapes on the universal cover of a classic matrix group. These shapes bend the anti-de Sitter geometry while keeping a fixed symmetry, and the paper tracks their longest paths. A sub-Lorentzian shape appears as a limit of the family, and the author traces how its traits shift as that limit is approached.
arxiv-2603-07459: Hwang and colleagues study how freelance workers and clients handle disclosure of AI use. Workers often disclose only when asked, assuming clients can already spot AI-assisted work. Clients, however, feel far less able to recognize such work and prefer upfront disclosure. Unclear or missing client AI policies leave workers guessing at expectations. The authors call for clearer guidelines, with lessons for trust and accountability in AI-mediated work beyond freelancing.
arxiv-2603-07759: Zhou and colleagues propose DECADE, an unsupervised diffusion model for Rb-82 cardiac PET denoising. Rb-82 cardiac PET diagnoses coronary artery disease, but short half-life noise degrades frames, and no paired clean-noisy data exists. DECADE keeps temporal consistency in training and sampling, with noisy frames as guides preserving quantitative accuracy. Trained on Siemens Vision 450 and Quadra data, it produces high-quality dynamic and parametric images with less noise while preserving flow. On Quadra 15 percent-count inputs, it beats UNet-based and other diffusion models in quality and flow measures.
arxiv-2603-07959: Xu and colleagues build WeldAR, an augmented reality system that guides novice welders live through a headset built into a welding helmet. A torch attachment plus five learning modules overlay real-time guidance during live welding. In a study with 24 novices, AR guidance beat video instruction in assisted practice and unassisted tests. Gains came mainly from travel speed and work angle, and novices carried skill into independent work.
arxiv-2603-08059: Zhao and colleagues propose ImageEdit-R1, a multi-agent framework for image editing that uses reinforcement learning to coordinate high-level decisions. Commercial multimodal models edit images well in simple cases. But they often falter on complex, indirect, or multi-step instructions that demand nuanced, context-aware changes aligned with user intent. ImageEdit-R1 spreads the work across specialized agents and trains their coordination with reinforcement learning. It aims for edits that follow indirect requests more faithfully than single-model systems manage.
arxiv-2603-08459: Lechuga and colleagues build MedCertAIn, which lets clinical models say how sure they are about forecasts of patient deterioration. Such trust matters for decision support, yet most models give no measure of doubt. MedCertAIn draws on clinical time series and chest X-rays from MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-CXR. It sets priors over parameters from cross-modal similarity in self-supervised latent spaces plus corruptions of each data type. Tests on in-hospital mortality risk claim strong prediction scores and big gains in selective prediction over rival baselines.
arxiv-2603-08859: John Cooper and colleagues probe where hybrid sequence models beat their pure parents. Pure attention or state-space models need either many parameters or much working memory on a broad task family. Small hybrids provably solve selective copying and associative recall, and learned hybrids beat pure models with up to six times the parameters while generalizing better in length and distribution.
arxiv-2603-09059: Jason Brown and Isaac McMullin prove that nearly all graphs carry a nonreal reliability root. In a connected graph where each edge fails alone with chance q, the reliability polynomial gives the chance the live edges stay linked. They also show reliability roots lie dense on an interval from about negative 0.5707202942 to zero.
arxiv-2603-09559: Edward Troccoli and Christoph Federrath study how kinetic energy is lost as heat in subsonic and supersonic turbulence, and what pattern that loss takes. The heating matters for interstellar clouds, yet it stays poorly understood. In high-resolution simulations with set viscosity, this loss lags big energy injection events by part of a turnover time. When flow is subsonic it tracks vorticity squared; when supersonic it tracks density, and full spectral convergence proves hard to reach.
arxiv-2603-09759: Mingyu Kang and colleagues tackle logo design with text in many languages, a task where image models often warp letters. LogoDiffuser needs no training and feeds the target characters in as pictures, holding their shape steady. It finds the attention tokens that carry letter form and injects the best of those maps across layers. User studies place its multilingual logos at the top.
arxiv-2603-09959: Bols and coauthors complete a classification for a class of two dimensional symmetry protected topological states. Such states, for a finite symmetry group, were conjectured to be sorted by a third cohomology group, but completeness stayed open. The team looks only at states built from a product state using a symmetric entangler. For that class, they prove the cohomology classification leaves nothing out at all.
arxiv-2603-10059: Yingjun Tian and coauthors jointly design flexible sensor layouts and the network that reads them, for tracking soft body deformation. Sensor count, length and placement are normally set by guesswork, yet they strongly shape prediction accuracy. Their model free pipeline learns from data sets of deformed shapes alone, with no physics simulation needed. Differentiable losses balance accuracy against whether the layout can actually be built, beating unoptimised layouts in tests.
arxiv-2603-10659: Adel Abbout investigates a gauge transformation built by removing time-dependent onsite potentials at single sites, in finite or infinite systems. The trick works site by site, one site at a time. The change resets the inward hoppings by one phase factor and the outward hoppings by its inverse. That reshaping pays off in two places. It eases simulating how pulses propagate in scattering systems. It also greatly simplifies the time-ordered integrals in the evolution operator for the time-dependent Schrödinger equation.
arxiv-2603-10859: S. W. Huang and a large international team report the first direct measurement of three-neutron emission from excited helium-7, produced by knocking a neutron out of a helium-8 beam. The reconstructed spectrum points to sequential decay through an excited state of helium-6, matching simulations that include neutron-neutron correlations. No sign appeared of extra three-neutron correlations or of a trineutron resonance beyond known two-body effects.
arxiv-2603-11259: S. Rostami and coauthors predict the masses of fully heavy baryons and exotic pentaquarks two independent ways, aiming at states experiments have not yet observed. A data-driven route trains deep networks and a particle transformer on Particle Data Group hadron data, reading masses off quantum numbers. A second route extends the Gürsey-Radicati mass formula to charm and bottom quarks, covering ground and radially excited states. The two approaches agree strongly with experiment where data exist and together predict many unobserved states to guide future searches.
arxiv-2603-11359: Dylan Müller works out the special values of the spectral zeta function of a regular tree. This function is built from the eigenvalues of the tree's combinatorial Laplacian. At positive integers, the values take explicit formulas through certain polynomials. These turn out palindromic, with non-negative integer coefficients carrying a meaning in counting. Symmetries link the two signs' values through their generating functions. From these, he gets a functional equation of s-to-one-minus-s type, for a natural full form of the function.
arxiv-2603-11459: Jiang and Liu dive deeper into the booklet wormhole, a geometry proposed as the holographic dual of the GHZ state. Their focus is the junction conditions that matter fields must meet at its multi-way interface. The GHZ state's symmetry, they show, forces bulk Killing vector fields that standard manifolds cannot realize. The junction rules turn out to be quantum and non-local in a new way. Observers who enter from different horizons then see different states inside. Boundary deformations, they note, could make such wormholes traversable.
arxiv-2603-12259: Zhao, Mandal, Liu, and Yan resolve clashing reports on the anomalous Hall effect in MnTe films. Transport tests on this altermagnet had shown opposite signs and odd thickness behavior. The team splits bulk and surface contributions for distinct crystal terminations. Bulk states host a g-wave Fermi surface, yet surface states carry ferromagnet-like spin polarization. Those surface states dominate the Hall response at the Fermi energies experiments reach. A tellurium cap can even flip the surface sign, which points to interface design as a control knob.
arxiv-2603-12459: Garbarz finds ready-to-use bases of steerable kernels for equivariant convolutional networks. The steerable kernel constraint sits at the heart of such network design tasks. His bases come in real and complex forms, for varied symmetry groups and tensor types. The route skips Clebsch-Gordan coefficients entirely, a major practical simplification. It builds kernels that meet a simpler invariance at one point, then steers them to arbitrary points. Coverage runs from 2D rotations to the Lorentz group, with minimal technical tools for a broad audience.
arxiv-2603-12559: Chengbo Zhang and co-authors build a simulation test bed for on-demand delivery work. In their system, riders are large language model agents with profiles drawn from real data. Each agent can reject an offer, take one order, or bundle several at once. The system then resolves clashes, builds pickup and drop-off routes, and runs them on road networks. A one-day test with 60 agents and 8,656 orders kept key gaps between rider types seen in real data.
arxiv-2603-13059: Sebastian Frey and co-authors forecast cost-per-click in paid search with competition in the model, not just past bids. A single advertiser sees only part of the auction landscape that sets prices. From 1.66 billion Google Ads records, they built weekly series for a car-rental market. Semantic and behavioral neighborhoods plus geographic traits proxy the rival field. Graph models won at one week, while covariate-fed foundation models won at longer horizons. Gains clustered on pricey, volatile keywords where errors cost most.
arxiv-2603-13159: Alessio Catanzaro and co-authors prove that sparse random graphs with independent edges can cluster, with no geometry at all. Real networks are both sparse and rich in triangles, a pairing once thought to need latent distances. Their model, invariant under node aggregation, yields finite clustering by proof and by numerics. What drives it is a node fitness with infinite mean, which also gives a power-law degree spread. Self-averaging of network traits also breaks down in this model, a new effect they pin down.
arxiv-2603-13259: Javier Marín studies how decoder-only transformers process correct and incorrect factual continuations. When forced to carry a wrong token, a model's hidden states rotate away from the correct path. Angular separation grows through mid-depth, then late layers settle on an asymmetric outcome. Marín reads this pattern as geometric, and stresses that the evidence is observational, not causal. The pattern held across six models from four architecture families, with one flat exception. Probes and patching tests suggest the effect is spread across the trajectory, not one layer.
arxiv-2603-13559: Adrien Corenflos tackles robust automatic differentiation of square-root Kalman filters. These filters propagate covariances in Cholesky-factor form for numerical stability and suit gradient-based parameter learning. Differentiating through triangularization fails when the semi-orthogonal factor is non-unique or the input is rank-deficient. His key observation is that filter outputs depend on the input only through its Gramian. That makes the composite loss smooth even where triangularization is not. He derives a closed-form chain rule from the Gramian differential and extends it to rank-deficient inputs.
arxiv-2603-13759: Tajamul Ashraf and co-authors introduce QTrack, a query-driven method for multi-modal multi-object tracking. Some applications need only user-specified targets tracked, not every detected instance in a clip. Their offline task gives a video clip, a natural-language query, and reference-frame boxes for the targets. QTrack is a vision-language policy trained with structured trajectory rewards and Temporal Perception-Aware Policy Optimization. That training contrasts outputs under the observed clip versus a repeated reference frame to force use of visual evidence.
arxiv-2603-14359: Hayes and Kunnawalkam Elayavalli prove a result about inner amenable groups and the factors they generate. The setting is finitely presented groups that are icc and inner amenable. Such groups arise in the theory of von Neumann algebras. The authors show that these groups yield strongly 1-bounded II_1 factors. That boundedness is a strong finiteness trait for the factor. The theorem ties a group property to a sharp limit on the algebra it builds.
arxiv-2603-14459: Newell and Nejad derive a reduced one-fluid model for relativistic magnetized plasma. They start from the relativistic Vlasov-Boltzmann-Maxwell system. A moment hierarchy cut plus strong-guide-field ordering shrinks the model. Unresolved moments collapse onto one slow thermodynamic mode. A single scalar then tracks charge imbalance, pressure anisotropy and kinetic losses. The reduced state fits the GENERIC framework for mixed reversible and irreversible dynamics. Fast modes match known cold-plasma waves, while the slow mode drifts the spectrum over time.
arxiv-2603-14559: Ghatwary and co-authors release a dataset for scoring ulcerative colitis in endoscopy images. The disease inflames the colon lining and raises cancer risk. Doctors grade activity with the Mayo Endoscopic Score or the UCEIS index. Automated scoring lacks open, expert-labeled data and firm benchmarks. Their set spans many centres and image resolutions. Expert labels cover both scoring systems, plus written clinical descriptions. The release aims to make UC scoring tools more robust across hospitals and devices.
arxiv-2603-14759: Sotolongo-Costa, Mora-Rodríguez and Mora-Ramos test entropy scaling in a fragment-asperity earthquake model. Stress-bearing contacts carry energy tied to their contact surface. A linear energy-surface law is put forward as the sole workable choice. Only it yields a closed, clean total Tsallis entropy in the parameter q. Scanning q marks a critical band from about 1.4 to 1.8. Entropy swings hardest inside that band. Reported main-shock q values from recent decades mostly land there. The band casts q as a criticality gauge, they argue.
arxiv-2603-15059: Iiduka proves that the Muon optimizer still converges when training noise has heavy tails. Muon keeps updates orthogonal by projecting gradients onto the Stiefel manifold, which steadies large network training. Real noise can break the bounded-variance assumption that older proofs need. He studies nonconvex Holder-smooth empirical risk under a bound that allows heavy-tailed noise. Muon reaches a stationary point under that bound. He also shows it converges faster than mini-batch stochastic gradient descent.
arxiv-2603-15359: Hu and co-authors present NavThinker, a framework that couples prediction and planning for robots moving among people. Safe navigation among people needs foresight about how paths interact. An action-conditioned world model predicts future scene depth and human motion for each candidate action. Those forecasts feed the policy as extra features and shape its social rewards. The system set state-of-the-art success on Social-HM3D tests. It transferred to a new benchmark with no retraining and ran on a real Unitree Go2 robot.
arxiv-2603-15459: Sakhno and co-authors present FinTRACE, a retrieval-first system that turns raw bank transactions into evidence for downstream reasoning. General language models cope poorly with time-spread tabular records. FinTRACE converts transactions into reusable features, runs rule-based detectors, and stores the signals in a behavioral knowledge base. On public and industry tests, zero-shot churn scores doubled, and few-shot scores rose as well. Instruction tuning on the retrieved patterns then gave language models state-of-the-art results on transaction analytics tasks.
arxiv-2603-15759: Levy and co-authors pretrain robot world models inside physics simulators. Real-world training data for action-aware world models is scarce and mixed in quality. Their Simulation Distillation method distills simulator structure into the model first. The world model then plans from raw real sensor input. At adaptation time, encoder, reward model, and value function transfer as-is. Only the latent dynamics model updates, from real prediction errors. Tests cover contact-rich manipulation and quadruped locomotion. Gains came fast, while rival methods stalled or degraded.
arxiv-2603-16159: Chen surveys how journals rule on AI-generated figures in papers. Generative tools now draft publication-grade figures and graphical abstracts. Publisher policies on such images stay scattered and vague. Nature, Science, Cell Press, Elsevier, and PLOS stances face review. Reproducibility, authorship credit, and visual misinformation drive the worries. SciDraw examples show a science-focused drawing tool in use. Best-practice rules cover disclosure and quality checks for authors. Careful use can speed science communication, he argues. Integrity holds when the checks stay in place.
arxiv-2603-16259: Zhou and co-authors extract structured facts from web text paired with images. The hard case mixes known and brand-new entity types. Prior zero-shot tools handle only the unseen set. Their HMGRL framework works in hyperbolic space, not flat Euclidean space. That shape fits the layered links between samples and category prototypes. A similarity alignment loss aids generalization. Tests on two benchmarks beat prior baselines.
arxiv-2603-16359: Wang, Jiang, and Lyu present One Kiss, a comic maker steered by emojis. Prompt-based tools force a trade-off between control and creative flow. In One Kiss, users sketch panel frames to set the pacing. They pair keywords with emojis to set the mood. Feelings build across panels and slowly shift the story's genre. A small study with six users hints at a new role. Creators act more like directors than prompt writers.
arxiv-2603-16459: Qian and co-authors detect hallucinations in diffusion language models. These models write whole sequences at once, unlike step-by-step rivals. Token uncertainty is a common error signal. But most tokens carry little signal here. Averaging over all tokens dilutes the clue. Their DynHD builds evidence from the informative tokens only. It learns the normal path of uncertainty during denoising. Deviations from that path flag likely hallucinations. Tests beat strong baselines with better efficiency.
arxiv-2603-16759: Graf and co-authors study how well language models handle long, multi-turn chats. Most training and test data cover single turns only. They build TurnWiseEval, a benchmark that compares multi-turn skill against matched single-turn tasks. They also build TurnWiseData, a pipeline that makes synthetic multi-turn training data at scale. In tests with Olmo 3, multi-turn training data proved vital for strong chat results. The authors report that just 10,000 such chats in post-training lifted scores by 12 percent.
arxiv-2603-17759: Sharshar and co-authors build a benchmark for harmful humor in text, image, and video. Dark jokes hide harm in cultural cues that static toxicity sets miss. Their hand-curated set holds 3,000 texts and 6,000 images in English and Arabic, plus 1,200 videos. Labels split safe jokes from harmful ones, and harmful ones into overt and covert kinds. Closed models beat open ones by a wide margin, they find. Arabic trails English across both groups.
arxiv-2603-17859: Dowling and co-authors test which human saliency cues best guard iris scans from fake attacks. Iris presentation attack detectors must generalize to attack types never seen in training. Mouse-click notes, eye-gaze heatmaps, masks, and model embeddings compete as training guides. Denoised eye-tracking heatmaps won the contest, they report. That cue cut attack error most at a strict bona fide threshold. Code, models, and maps ship with the study for reuse.
arxiv-2603-18159: Alsallom and Limmer trace the origin of edge currents in chiral active liquids. Such liquids show one-way edge flow in confinement, with no agreed universal cause. Starting from microscopic equations for a simple 2D model, they derive currents from global angular momentum balance. A conductance law gives mean current from density, active torque, and substrate drag alone. Molecular dynamics tests confirm the law, which extends to other chiral models.
arxiv-2603-18359: Wang and co-authors use sparse autoencoders to interpret neural audio codec representations, with accent as the test case. Codecs are core to modern speech systems, but their encoding of accent is unclear. Sparse autoencoders split dense codec features into sparse, readable activations. Across four codecs and 16 settings, DAC and SpeechTokenizer score highest on their index. Acoustic codecs store accent in activation sizes; phonetic codecs store it in activation positions.
arxiv-2603-18959: Filippi and co-authors grow tiny crystal stacks on flat perovskite sheets in a controlled way. The flat sheets move energy well along their plane. The small crystals emit light well and can stack into ordered arrays. Past blends were hard due to clashing solvents and transfer steps. Their growth can stay on side faces, forming crown shapes, or cover the top as a shell. The joined forms pass energy from sheet to stack. They work as strong light harvesters in tests.
arxiv-2603-19259: Lan and co-authors build open tools for Taiwanese Hokkien speech tech. Their Breeze Taigi sets a shared benchmark for speech recognition and synthesis in Taigi. It uses 30 paired Mandarin and Taigi clips from public service notices, with cleaned transcripts. Character error rate is set as the shared score, with fixed text cleanup rules. A Whisper model tuned on about 10,000 hours of synthetic Taigi speech leads the test. It posts a 30.13 percent error rate, ahead of prior systems.
arxiv-2603-19559: Ang and co-authors study scalar quantization of two matrices before they are multiplied. Each entry is rounded with its own quantizer, and the product uses the rounded values. They seek the rounding that minimises mean-squared error of the product. In the high-resolution limit, they derive a sharp error expansion and the best centre densities. For correlated Gaussian pairs, the best density has a closed form. A phase transition appears: the density is one-peaked, then two-peaked as correlation grows.
arxiv-2603-19659: Zheng and co-authors present CS-MUNet, a Mamba network for segmenting many abdominal organs. Prior Mamba methods miss cross-channel anatomy links and lack boundary-aware fusion. One new module makes pixel-level boundary maps with a Bayesian attention step. Those maps feed the core scan parameters, so boundaries shape the state flow. A second module treats channels as the scan sequence itself. That models how channels share anatomical meaning in a data-driven way. On two public benchmarks, it beats prior methods.
arxiv-2603-19759: De Lambilly and Duffner introduce networks that grow and prune themselves while they train. Most image classifiers keep a fixed size from start to finish. Their GNAP models start small and add capacity when progress stalls. Between growth steps, gradient descent prunes weights with no outside control.
