When no anchor items exist, background traits bridge forms, but those traits may be measured on different forms, biasing results. Their method adjusts the trait first within the kernel framework, then adjusts scores. Tests show adjusting the trait cuts bias, above all when trait spreads differ and trait-score links are strong, and a national school-leaving exam example shows practical use.
arxiv-2605-28659: Manuel Dileo and Andrea Sottoriva explore temporal graph learning for predicting living-system motion. Static foundation models apply transformers to gene tables but miss how growth programs change over time. Their approach infers pseudotime paths from single-cell data, splits cells into growth snapshots, rebuilds one gene control network per snapshot, and predicts states with time-based graph neural networks. On two mouse growth sets, graph models beat scGPT and scFoundation, and time-based learning captures control motion including key gene hubs.
arxiv-2605-28859: Yannick Mvondo-She proves analytic traits of the Jost functions via Poincaré-Picard. From the radial Schrödinger rule for a short-range central field, he derives a differential system for factor functions tied to Riccati-Bessel and Riccati-Neumann. The many-valued pattern on energy comes from the square-root link to momentum. Factoring out branching terms turns the scatter problem into a system with single-valued analytic coefficients. Classical parameter theory shows the new Jost functions stay single-valued and analytic in energy.
arxiv-2605-28959: Sabine Thater and colleagues measure six supermassive black hole masses in early-type galaxies from stellar motions in SINFONI and MUSE observations. With Hubble photometry, they build triaxial Schwarzschild orbit-superposition models that recover the galaxies' complex 3D shapes. Strong triaxial features can bias mass estimates, and the authors correct for that effect. The six masses range from under half a billion to about three and a half billion solar masses. They agree with earlier axisymmetric models and Jeans models, and fit local black hole scaling relations.
arxiv-2605-29059: Kaihua Qin, Dawn Song, and Arthur Gervais present SCDBench, a set and benchmark method for LLM-based smart contract decompilation. The set holds 600 real-world Solidity contracts with paired bytecode, ground-truth source, and semantic checkpoints. Outputs pass four cumulative stages: format checks, compilability, ABI recovery, and semantic match via side-by-side replay. Frontier models often produce neat, compilable Solidity, but the best fully rebuilds only 42 of 600. Same-model build repair greatly lifts scores at modest extra cost.
arxiv-2605-29159: Emiliano Maria Glaviano studies how nonlocal form factors flow in 4D quantum gravity. Working at quadratic order in curvature, he shows the flow can be traced down to zero momentum scale. The running of Newton's coupling generates momentum-dependent corrections, with the Planck scale marking the divide. When the non-Gaussian fixed point sets the boundary, the result admits a finite limit free of the renormalization scale.
arxiv-2605-29259: Debopam Sanyal presents KLAS, a framework for stitching pretrained neural networks into better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Stitching maps activations from one model into another, yielding new networks that interpolate between the two. Existing methods pick stitch points by heuristics, which often gives suboptimal trade-offs. KLAS instead uses divergence between intermediate representations to pick the most promising stitches from a large pool of candidates. At the same fine-tuning cost as baselines, it raises top accuracy or holds accuracy while cutting compute by about one third.
arxiv-2605-29359: Robi Rahman asks whether scattered training weakens compute governance. Rule plans often assume frontier AI training needs large, visible machine clusters. Yet new methods for scattered training could let teams run frontier-scale training on scattered hardware instead of large data centers. Teams who wish to dodge rules may arrange their hardware to evade sign-up and watch. The paper weighs how doable such evasion is and lists defenses, including whistle-blowing, chip tracking, money-trail audits, and memory and compute thresholds for clusters.
arxiv-2605-29459: Rohan Shravan presents Kronecker Embeddings, a deterministic split by letter and place. Language models route every input through a vector table, using hundreds of millions to billions of learned weights. It swaps this table for a fixed encoder and a learned layer, cutting over nine tenths of input side learned weights. A probe of six language models shows vectors cluster type forms more than word kin, while it escapes this clumping. A test shows it reaching 2.5 percent lower loss than the BPE tied baseline, needing fewer steps.
arxiv-2605-29659: Ihor Stepanov and Aleksandr Smechov present Opir, encoder-based guardrail models for real-time safety filtering. Opir covers binary safe-or-unsafe calls, toxicity labels, jailbreak detection, and zero-shot prompt and response sorting, plus edge variants. Training data combine unsafe prompts, hard negatives, benign examples, generated responses, translations, and parts of two sets. The taxonomy holds 996 categories split into 16 top groups, 126 middle groups, and 854 leaves. Across 12 safety tasks and 17 category tasks against eight systems, Opir matches or beats the open-weight baselines on most datasets.
arxiv-2605-29759: Paulami Majumder studies how gyroscopes precess along timed paths in Kerr spacetime, the rotating black-hole geometry. Using the covariant Frenet-Serret frame, she tracks precession for forward and backward motion in two coordinate systems. Near the horizon, the precession rate blows up in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates yet stays finite in horizon-crossing Kerr-Schild coordinates. The finiteness, she shows, hinges on whether the path itself stays timelike, not on the horizon's presence. The apparent blow-up is thus a coordinate artefact, not an invariant mark of horizon structure.
arxiv-2605-30259: Yang Bai, Sida Lu and Nicholas Orlofsky test late-time quantum vacuum decay with cosmological observables. They construct models in which late tunneling shifts the vacuum energy and may convert dark matter into dark radiation. The conversion and domain-wall model eases ΛCDM tension, preferring a transition around redshift seven with a tenth of dark matter involved. For tunneling models, distance measurements still allow a halving of vacuum energy for a transition redshift below one. CMB constraints from bubble nucleation and the wall network restrict slow transitions.
arxiv-2605-30659: Murugaiyan and colleagues replace handmade viscosity formulas for 3D printing with a neural network trained on lab data. Carreau-Yasuda and power-law models capture shear behavior well, but each new material demands a derivation and solver rebuild. Their network serves as the viscosity closure inside a CHNS solver, with viscosity depending only on the local shear rate. Lipschitz regularization keeps predictions smooth, and the network ships in ONNX format for runtime queries. Benchmarks and silicone ink tests validate the workflow, with simulated speeds and droplet shapes matching observations.
arxiv-2605-30759: Kishimoto and colleagues develop a geometric frame of vertex operators in string theory based on whole forms. Starting from the built-in NS-NS vertex operator, they derive descent rules linking them with varied ghost and picture numbers. A key result links super objects and ghost superfields. A particular one-form and an even differential match the ghost superfield and its superderivative, giving a geometric superghost structure. The construction extends with inverse picture-changing operators, generating descent sequences. All are organized into a descent structure well-defined in BRST cohomology.
arxiv-2605-30959: Korsky improves a lower bound for the de Bruijn-Erdős gap problem, studying points placed on a unit circle. After n points are placed, the circle splits into n intervals, and largest and smallest r-interval totals are compared. A theorem gives a ratio of at least one plus one over r, sharp at one with factor two. Korsky proves a bound for r at least two: one plus r over r squared minus one. For two intervals, this gives five thirds, improving the classic three halves.
arxiv-2605-31159: Plyusov and colleagues warm up on-policy distillation, where a student learns from its own rollouts under a stronger teacher. Early student rollouts are weak, so their Trust-Region Behavior Blending swaps in the teacher-closest behaviour policy inside a shrinking KL budget, then fades back to pure student rollouts. Across two maths-reasoning settings, the blended warmup posts the strongest average among the methods compared.
arxiv-2605-31259: Cencillo and colleagues detect anomalies in high-voltage converter modulators at the Spallation Neutron Source, whose fourteen sensors are physically coupled. Faults can hide in how sensors move together while each signal looks normal, yet popular benchmarks mostly show single-channel faults. Holding the convolutional network fixed, the team varies only whether channels combine before or after temporal filtering. Combining channels first helps weakly separable fault families like flux faults most, and the best detector rivals published results at about half the parameters.
arxiv-2605-31359: Merino adds a matching result on Gaussian measures for a 3D periodic wave equation with defocusing nonlinearity. Earlier work showed such measures on smooth Sobolev spaces stay almost unchanged under this flow. For large enough settings, Merino proves dense sets of Sobolev spaces fail to keep their smoothness through the flow. That cuts against the way almost sure traits carry forward under the flow.
arxiv-2605-31559: Xiao and team present Functional Attention, a new way to learn mappings between function spaces, or operator learning. Transformer operators often use token-wise attention, treating continuous fields as discrete tokens and missing global structure. It reinterprets attention as a match between tuned bases, swapping softmax scores for set linear operators. The result is a compact representation that works at any resolution and captures global ties outright. Tests show it matches top performance on operator tasks, including solving PDEs and 3D segmentation.
arxiv-2606-00059:
Langschwert and co-authors teach a reinforcement learning agent to design experiments for pinning down a machine's parameters, in this 2026 arXiv paper. System identification builds math models of real hardware from test data, but it needs informative excitation signals, inputs that provoke useful behavior. Experts normally craft those signals by hand, juggling information yield against strict safety limits. The authors replace hand design with an agent that learns signals through trial and error, with safety enforced through reward shaping.

Their testbed is a Quanser Aero 2 dual-rotor device set for pitch motion, a standard mechatronics platform. Across 10 training runs, the agent achieved accuracy competitive across all three targets, beating classical baseline signals such as pseudorandom sequences and frequency sweeps. Safety breaches stayed low, under 1 percent in their aggregate. The work is presented as work in progress toward automating optimal test design for cyber-physical systems generally.
arxiv-2606-00159:
Woo and Lee test if fake patches that fool sky watchers on screen also work in print. Nets that spot cars from the air help track land and town growth. Printed cheat sheets could blind those nets in real life. The pair bridge screen tests and field use.

They tune patches to drop the top spot score a net gives. Rules on print range and smoothness keep the sheets real. Printed sheets are then placed on, off, and off to the side of cars. A YOLOv3 net is the test target. Off sheets win on screen, with top cuts in score. On sheets prove more tough in the field. Rain and sun tweaks in training do not help much.
arxiv-2606-00359:
Rawat and co-authors build an index for AI worth where most of the world lives. Top AI tests prize peak skill on clean tasks. They miss if a tool can last, adapt, and earn trust on thin ground. Their index, the Next Billion AI Index, fills that gap.

The index scores ten strands in three themes. Themes span thrift in use, ease of set-up, and fit with shared norms. Each strand holds marks for weak, mid, and strong runs. Talks with 11 pros who build for such markets test the frame. Pros found it keen on cost, ease, trust, and up-time marks. They asked for more scene notes and field proof per strand. The index is cast as a guide, not a world grade.
arxiv-2606-00459:
Saqib, Andrade Chavez, and Charbonneau cap a robot's energy by PD gains that adapt on the fly. Safe touch twixt folk and bots needs soft force or torque steers. Those steers lean on force or torque sense that not all bots have. Energy caps give a path that needs no such sense gear.

Their steer caps both move and stored energy past a set bar. Gain acts are shaped by dials that set the bar and its bite. Proof shows the steer holds firm in use. A bound for that firm hold is set in plain terms. Tests run on the TALOS bot in sims and on gear. Acts stay soft and caps hold as the proofs say.
arxiv-2606-00559:
Huang and co-authors enrich the code a net learns for step-wise rule tasks by a rebuild drill. Such tasks train nets to ape the steps of a classic rule set. State lines mark each step's end as the run goes. Most past work honed the step core and left the code tool plain.

Plain code tools may starve the step core of key traits. Their add-on asks the code to rebuild its input state from its own code. That drill forces the code to keep what counts in the state. A kin drill makes the code catch links twixt traits in one state. Tests on stock bench sets lift past net forms in score. The code learns richer traits for the same step core.
arxiv-2606-00759:
Yin studies games with shared limits and a learning task in this 2026 paper. Many AI problems are noncooperative games where rivals share constraints. These form Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problems. Most distributed solvers make agents swap Lagrange multipliers to agree and to find a special class of equilibria. That swap costs bandwidth and leaks private data.

Yin gives continuous-time algorithms that need no multiplier swap. Less data moves, and privacy improves. The study covers strongly monotone games with convex own limits and linear shared limits. Yin gives discrete versions of the flows. The methods reach general equilibria, not just the special class, and the result can turn on the start point. Tests cover multi-robot coordination and placement. A second part, done with Amazon scientists, uses contextual bandits to pick active learning strategies on the fly, since labels are costly and no one strategy wins on all data.
arxiv-2606-00959:
Fang and co-authors dissect how multimodal models mix their senses in this 2026 paper. A model that hears and sees may lean on one sense and slight the other. Partial Information Decomposition splits what each sense adds: unique, redundant, or synergistic parts. Their form, Sensory PID, conditions on language and splits video and audio shares at the decision level.

A bottleneck shows up across omni-modal models. Even on tasks built for audio-visual fusion, unique information rules the choice. Vision does most of that ruling. Shuffling tests back the asymmetry. Layer-by-layer views show a visual-first pattern of computation. Late fusion, in turn, bends to the language instruction. The team goes past diagnosis: reweighting samples by these local signals lifts reasoning and grounding scores in early tests. The work gives builders a gauge for sense balance inside a model.
arxiv-2606-01559:
Liu and Li prove stability of strong rarefaction waves in a chemotaxis system. The system is parabolic-hyperbolic and arises from chemotaxis models. They track long-time behavior toward rarefaction waves. The inviscid companion system supplies the Riemann problem. Its solutions admit rarefaction waves by assumption. Initial data are set as a small perturbation of an approximate wave. The Cauchy problem then has a unique global solution. That solution converges to the rarefaction wave over time.

The result holds regardless of wave strengths. Waves may be single or a composite of two. In the composite case, profile centers start far apart. This keeps their interaction error term small. Energy methods drive the proofs throughout. Monotonicity of the approximate waves is a key observation.
arxiv-2606-02059:
Liu and co-authors package tools for studies that use the ICC statistic. The intraclass correlation coefficient is a staple of reliability work. It is central in medical measurement and psychology. Behavioral science also leans on it a lot. Two obstacles complicate its practical use today.

ICC comes in many forms under one classic framework. Six standard forms and four design mixes exist. The right form depends on the study design at hand. Guidance is not always built into software menus. Tools for sample size, estimation, and evaluation are fragmented. Users must switch between separate R packages. Their ICCDesign package unites design and analysis in one place. It aims to cut errors from that tool switching.
arxiv-2606-02559:
Cunegatti and co-authors compress large language models at a finer grain than past work. Replacement methods swap whole components for fitted modules. Two design limits are standard. Selection works at full-layer granularity. Chosen parts must also sit in one contiguous block. Redundancy in real transformers breaks both assumptions. It scatters across depth and splits unevenly between Attention and FeedForward outputs.

Their method, SubFit, selects submodules instead of layers. Attention and FeedForward units are picked non-contiguously. Each gets its own lightweight fitted residual bypass. The method runs post-training and needs only calibration data. Tests cover ten models, five base and five instruction-tuned. Five sparsity levels run from 12.5 to 37.5 percent. Four replacement baselines compete. SubFit gives the best aggregate perplexity-accuracy trade-off. At 25 percent sparsity, it keeps 84.6 percent of dense downstream accuracy. Inference speed and KV-cache savings also improve.
arxiv-2606-02859:
Qi and co-authors ask how a group of AI agents can organize itself with no central control. Their answer borrows from Hayek's account of markets. Agents bid at auction for the right to act on each task. They pay each other and collect rewards from the environment.

Wealth then does the sorting. Agents that do well grow rich and are copied with small changes. Agents that fail go bankrupt and are replaced by fresh ones. The team built this economy with large language model agents that start out weak. The economy still produced multi-step reasoning plans on its own. It beat stronger single-system baselines on five tasks. Those tasks span math, finance research, science research, chip design, and system tuning. The authors argue that good incentives can yield coordination without anyone designing it directly.
arxiv-2606-02959:
Goehausen and Sousa build a stricter way to evaluate detectors that catch prompt injection and jailbreaks. Published evaluations suffer from two flaws. Thresholds are often tuned per dataset, and the operating point used for scoring is often undisclosed. Results then look better than they are.

Their harness scores one detector across 16 public benchmarks with 12,111 samples. It uses five-fold cross-validation with stratified splits by row. A parallel group-based split tracks leakage from near-duplicate prompts. One global threshold is chosen on held-out folds, with false positives capped at one percent. That single threshold is then applied to every dataset. A battery of diagnostics tests generalization, including leave-one-dataset-out runs, random-label controls, and permutation importance. For external comparisons, the threshold is retuned to each rival's published false-positive rate. Head-to-head values thus compare detectors at matched operating points.
arxiv-2606-03159:
Basant and a large NVIDIA team present OmniDreams, a generative world model for self-driving car tests. Safe checks of driving policies in rare, risky cases are a key bottleneck. In closed-loop tests the policy acts, the world state updates, and new sensor views must follow. Simulators built by rebuilding captured scenes look sharp but stay tied to their first data.

OmniDreams is mid- and post-trained from the Cosmos diffusion model. It makes action-conditioned video in real time, step by step. Training used 21,000 hours of driving scenes. It can show extreme weather and odd moves by other road users. It runs in a closed loop with a policy model and an orchestrator. Early results also show a world-action model built from it beating a larger vision-language-action policy with one fifth of the parameters.
arxiv-2606-03259:
Merx, Vylomova, and Cohn show that translation should fit its audience and purpose. The same source text can need unlike translations for unlike readers, tones, and intents. Machine translation still treats the task as a fixed map from source to target. Language models let users state purpose outright, but that skill had not been tested at scale.

Their study spans 50 languages, five model sizes, and eight text domains. Clear instructions raised adaptedness a lot, most on informal domains such as chat and social media. Gains grew with model size and with resource level of the language. Instructions beat matched few-shot examples and paragraph context. Standard metrics often fined good adapted translations, so they miss this quality. When no curated instructions exist, models can write their own from document context. That closed up to 80 percent of the gap to curated ones. The authors call for purpose-aware metrics.
arxiv-2606-03359:
Krasnoproshin and Vashkevich build a light network that reads emotion from speech. Speech emotion recognition is a core part of human-computer interaction. Top methods lean on large pretrained models with heavy compute and memory needs. That bars them from edge devices. The team's model, ResLSTM-SA, joins residual links with soft attention inside an LSTM frame.

The test set is RAVDESS, split with strict speaker independence, so no voice in training leaks into tests. The model beats standard attention LSTM baselines. It also tops several past CNN and hybrid CNN-LSTM designs on unweighted average recall. The best variant scores about 0.65 on that measure with just 46.8 thousand trainable parameters. That is three orders of magnitude fewer than large self-supervised rivals. The authors release the code. The design targets real-time voice assistants and edge hardware, where big models cannot run.
arxiv-2606-03459:
Pachet studies how to assign local keys to chord sequences with fewer needless changes. The task serves harmonic analysis, composition, and jazz improvisation. Standard dynamic programming cuts modulations but can spawn too many tonal centers. Pachet sets three goals side by side. One counts transitions only, one counts vocabulary only, and one blends both.

The blended goal, tonal parsimony, first cuts modulations, then cuts distinct keys. The joint task is hard in general, but the fixed set of 24 major and minor keys allows exact algorithms. On more than 31,000 sequences from the LMD Chords set, parsimony keeps the best transition count. It also trims the key vocabulary in over half of the cases. With jazz substitution rules added, both mean tonalities and mean modulations fall by clear margins. On annotated jazz standards, chord-scale agreement rises to 95.6 percent, supporting analysis at a professional scale.
arxiv-2606-04059:
R Ramakrishnan, with Sagardeep Talukdar, M Lakshmanan, and Avadh Saxena, studies in 2026 how a nonlinear wave equation mirrors the motion of a spinning system tied to a moving curve. The equation is the Fokas-Lenells equation, a known integrable model, meaning it admits exact methods of solution.

The authors apply a gauge transformation, a change of mathematical frame, and a zero-curvature condition to prove the two systems are equivalent. They also build the Lax pair, a pair of equations whose compatibility certifies integrability, for the generalized spin system. Mapping the spin system onto a curve in space, they show its bending and twisting laws reproduce the wave equation through a more intricate transformation than in classic cases.
arxiv-2606-04359:
Xinwei Song, Yizhe Huang, Dengji Zhao, and Xue Feng present COOPER in 2026. It is a multi-agent reinforcement learning method that learns two things at once: how to keep reputations, and how to act on them.

Reputation promotes cooperation in social dilemmas. But earlier work either fixed the scoring rules by hand or baked reputation in as a reward. That limited how well agents could adapt. COOPER's modules are built around reputation's own mechanics. They cope with the delayed, noisy feedback that tangles scoring and behavior. In donation and coin games, it adapted to varied reputation systems and partners. In self-play, reputation norms and cooperation emerged together. The results held across network shapes.
arxiv-2606-04759:
Christiansen, Mølmer, and Hubenschmid give an efficient analytical method for computing what a parametric amplifier does to a quantum light pulse. A single input pulse under parametric amplification feeds into at most two output pulses, but finding the output quantum state is normally a heavy computation. Their trick is to apply the amplification to the vacuum instead of the input state, and then apply a transformed version of the operator that creates the input state from vacuum.

Given the input and output pulse mode functions, the method is analytical and computationally very efficient. The authors demonstrate it on three inputs: a coherent state, a Schrödinger cat state, and a single photon. They use the method to obtain the state in one output mode conditioned on detecting vacuum in the other, less populated mode. The approach replaces numerical simulation with formulas wherever pulse shapes are known.
arxiv-2606-05259:
Lin Fu and colleagues introduce VideoKR in this 2026 arXiv paper, a large training corpus built to strengthen knowledge-intensive video understanding. Video models are usually trained on clips that reward surface description, so they falter when a question demands expert knowledge plus genuine reasoning over what happens on screen. VideoKR targets exactly that gap.

The corpus holds 315,000 video reasoning examples built over 145,000 newly collected, Creative Commons licensed videos from expert domains. A human-in-the-loop generation pipeline targets progressively deeper reasoning abilities while controlling the difficulty, diversity, and reliability of the questions and their rationales. The team also curated VideoKR-Eval, a benchmark whose questions require real video understanding rather than textual shortcuts. Models post-trained on VideoKR with supervised fine-tuning then reinforcement learning outperformed prior post-training approaches on such reasoning while staying competitive on general video reasoning. Ablations isolate which design choices drive the gains.
arxiv-2606-05659:
Hasegawa and colleagues report asteroids that blur a standard sorting line in a 2026 arXiv paper. Dark main-belt asteroids usually fall into the C or X classes. C-types show a shallow dip in reflected light near one micrometer. Dark X-types lack the dip and tilt the other way. Two asteroids, 1093 Freda and 1390 Abastumani, break the pattern: they tilt like X-types yet carry the dip.

A literature search turned up more asteroids with the same mixed traits. Together they form a smooth continuum between the two classes. That continuum hints the classes share a common origin rather than separate roots. The authors point to cronstedtite, an iron-rich layered mineral, as a surface material that fits the spectra. If confirmed, the finding would redraw part of the map of early solar system materials. It also warns classifiers against forcing every dark rock into two boxes.
arxiv-2606-05959:
Goetz and the LIGO detector characterization team hunt the thin noise lines that haunt gravitational-wave data in a 2026 arXiv paper, published in Classical and Quantum Gravity. Narrow spectral artifacts are steady instrumental tones, not astrophysical signals. They degrade searches for faint persistent waves from spinning neutron stars. The fourth observing run of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA network supplied the data under study.

Updated and new software tools sped up artifact investigations and monitoring. The paper presents several narrowband artifacts that were traced to their sources and successfully mitigated. Not every line can be removed, though. Searches still need precise lists of contaminated frequency bands to avoid false alarms. Minimizing those bands directly raises the chance of discovering a new signal class. The work is infrastructure science: unglamorous, essential, and shared across the collaboration. Clean spectra are the price of hearing the quietest sources in the universe.
arxiv-2606-06259:
Pedro Melo and co-authors check the thermodynamics of collapse models of quantum mechanics in this 2026 arXiv paper. Collapse models say wave functions shrink spontaneously, which would explain why measurements have definite outcomes. Standard versions also heat every system forever, an unphysical flaw. The dissipative Diósi Penrose model adds a friction like mechanism to stop the heating, but it distorts the system's statistics in complex ways.

Working in the Wigner phase space picture, the team goes far beyond the usual quadratic approximations. They built an exact pseudo spectral simulation to handle the strongly non Gaussian regime, where simpler methods fail. The system does not settle into ordinary thermal equilibrium. It reaches a non equilibrium steady state whose non Gaussian character grows as the third power of the dissipation strength. Entropy production computed from the Wigner function stays consistent, confirming the friction mechanism is thermodynamically sound.
arxiv-2606-06659:
Eric Wolf and Martin Zwierlein study how a cloud of ultracold atoms spreads when it is suddenly released into empty space. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a strongly interacting Fermi gas, a gas whose atoms collide so often that normal particle pictures fail. At unitarity, the point where the interaction strength is at its peak, the spreading cloud forms a rarefaction wave, a smooth fan of thinning gas.

The team found that this expansion matched Riemann's classic solution of the Euler flow equations at every temperature they probed. Moving away from unitarity raised the gas viscosity, meaning its resistance to flow, and the match slowly worsened. Even so, when sound damping grew twenty fold on one side of the range, the expansion kept its self similar shape, where the profile looks the same at each size.
arxiv-2606-07159:
Data centers increasingly pool memory across machines, but data that must survive crashes pays a toll. Hadi and co-authors move crash safety into the network switch itself in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is Compute Express Link, a fabric for sharing disaggregated memory. Persistence commands normally cross the whole fabric before reaching remote memory, and the latency caps scalability.

The team defines a Distributed Persistence Domain, persistence support spread across switches rather than centralized. Distributing it creates hazards: stale reads and writes can sneak in without careful coordination. Their Persistent CXL Switch design answers with read forwarding and write coalescing inside the switch. Correctness and crash consistency are argued formally from the new abstraction. Simulations on standard benchmark suites showed an average speedup of thirty three percent over volatile switches. Adaptive read forwarding pushed gains to thirty six percent. Persistent pooling becomes practical at fabric scale.
arxiv-2606-07259:
Systems that read speech from both sound and lip movements score near perfectly on the standard LRS3 benchmark. Zhaofeng Lin and colleagues ask whether those scores reflect genuine skill in this 2026 arXiv paper. They built a new test set carefully matched to LRS3 in sound quality, visual conditions, and speaker demographics. If models truly generalized, performance should hold on this matched but unseen material.

Instead, all five leading systems they evaluated suffered a universal performance collapse on the new set. Their attribute analysis across seven factors singled out clip duration as a major driver of failure. Models also showed strong lexical bias, favoring vocabulary typical of the old benchmark. Most surprisingly, adding video sometimes hurt accuracy compared with audio alone under matched conditions. The authors release their test set and urge the field to check future systems against this kind of controlled benchmark.
arxiv-2606-07459:
Steier bounds how much a network value drifts when a graph is thinned for speed, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spectral sparsification samples a graph's edges while keeping its Laplacian properties, which encode diffusion behavior, within a small error. But the adjacency spectral radius, the largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix, is not controlled, even though it sets epidemic thresholds in contagion models. Steier bounds its change in terms of the sparsification error and maximum degree.

For reweighting schemes a sharper bound follows from Perron-Frobenius theory, the mathematics of positive matrices. Under effective-resistance sampling, probabilistic bounds come from matrix concentration inequalities. Combining eigenvector delocalization with resolvent perturbation gives tighter results for graphs whose main vector spreads evenly and whose spectral gap is large. Corollaries cover random graphs, regular expanders, and community-structured block models, while matching lower bounds prove tightness for regular graphs.
arxiv-2606-07559:
Prakash and Dontabhaktuni investigate fine-tuning failures that hide behind improving loss curves, in this 2026 arXiv paper. When the correct completion has a near-synonym competitor, training loss can fall steadily while the correct token never overtakes its rival in ranking. The authors instrument this regime across 5 transformer architectures spanning a 5-fold size range, using 10 hand-picked contexts with embedding overlap between the answer and its competitor. Their order parameter splits the failure into signal, the model's commitment to the token, and drag from the vocabulary.

Two failure modes emerge: kinematic failure, where the signal never grows, and structural failure, where drag worsens as training proceeds. Sharp jumps in the order parameter look like transitions, but the authors prove they are phantoms. The jumps persist when embeddings are frozen, so no geometric transition can be occurring; the discontinuity lives in the softmax readout. Dimensionless quantities organize the behavior across architectures.
arxiv-2606-07859:
Colla builds a mathematical model of technical debt in agile software teams, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Technical debt is the future cost of shortcuts taken now. Colla focuses on involuntary debt, work started but left unfinished, separated carefully from defect backlogs and rework. Lost productivity is treated as the interest on that debt.

The model links backlog, debt, velocity, and economic value in one dynamic system. A first result is negative: the naive policy of always remediating maximally loses against decisions that weigh value over time. Colla instead proposes a dynamic policy balancing new development against remediation at each step, with decreasing marginal value for delivered work. The formulation extends to discrete, dissimilar items. Sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo simulation show behaviour matching the model's economic intuition. Its limits are stated plainly, including a macroscopic view and assumed intertemporal rationality.
arxiv-2606-07959:
Khai-Hoan Nguyen-Dang studies a simple sequence: for fixed whole numbers a and b, take the greatest common divisor of a-to-the-n minus one and b-to-the-n minus one, as n grows. This 2026 arXiv paper treats it as a divisibility sequence, each term dividing later ones, tied to the Ailon-Rudnick problem.

The main theorem is a clean dichotomy. The sequence obeys a fixed linear recurrence exactly when a and b are multiplicatively dependent. When they are independent, something stronger holds. Every integer divisibility sequence dividing both expressions term by term must be periodic. Nguyen-Dang also gives exact formulas for which n yield a divisor above one. In the normalised case that set is an explicit union of arithmetic progressions. He also gives the exact power of each odd prime dividing the terms, plus reductions toward the Ailon-Rudnick conjecture.
arxiv-2606-08059:
Zifan Wang and co-authors make humanoid robots watch the ground their human teachers never saw, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Behaviour foundation models learn reusable whole-body control from large collections of human motion. The catch is that a recorded motion assumes the performer's environment. It says nothing about the footholds, clearance, or contact timing the robot's terrain demands, so copied motion can stumble.

Their Perceptive Behavior Foundation Model keeps raw motion as the behavioural interface but adapts it with local terrain perception, adjusting contacts, posture, and timing. To train that adaptation they built terrain-conformal reference synthesis, converting locomotion clips into terrain-consistent references through contact-aware footholds, foot-aware swing planning, and collision checking. The premise: intent and terrain are separate inputs. The human supplies what to do; the robot's perception decides how the ground allows it.
arxiv-2606-08659:
Monroy reopens a basic assumption of classical mechanics in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hamilton's principle derives the equations of motion from an action functional, under an exact closure condition: allowed variations must vanish at the boundaries. That condition deletes the boundary term in the first variation and yields the Euler-Lagrange equation. Fixed edges are usually treated as a technicality. Monroy argues it is a physical closure hypothesis: the system is sealed off from its surroundings.

Monroy introduces variational openness: keep the boundary term in the balance instead of deleting it. The kept term defines a boundary-openness density. It must be projected onto allowed variations before it becomes a dynamical source. In this frame the classical equation returns as the exact-closure limit of an open balance. Openness to the surroundings becomes a built-in property of the theory, not an add-on bolted to the side of it.
arxiv-2606-08759:
Evan Aguirre and colleagues directly measure the ions inside an extreme plasma, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ion properties are basic to plasma applications. But in capacitively coupled discharges, a workhorse laboratory plasma, direct measurement of ion flow and temperature has been impossible for many years. The team shows laser induced fluorescence in such a discharge, reading ion motion from the light the ions emit.

The measurements overturn assumptions. Ion flow shows ions moving much faster than thermal motion would suggest, with reductions when dust is present. Ion temperatures also exceed room temperature, contrary to a common assumption that treats ions as cold. Because dusty plasma experiments model astrophysical and industrial processes, cold-ion assumptions propagate into many readings.
arxiv-2606-08859:
Baronett and colleagues build a faithful way to model how starlight heats the disks where planets form, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A protoplanetary disk is the rotating gas and dust around a young star. Its temperature structure steers disk dynamics and planet formation, yet many models simplify how dust absorbs light, using gray opacity, a single average value, and ignoring scattering. Real opacity varies strongly with the light's frequency, so ultraviolet starlight heats the disk's thin upper air while the thick midplane stays cooler.

Their framework extends the Athena++ code with multigroup radiation transport over many frequency bands, plus radial rays that track the stellar flux. Calibrated on hydrostatic disks, the models matched Monte Carlo benchmark temperatures within 2 to 5 percent on average using 64 bands. Cutting to 3 bands raised the average gap to 7 to 11 percent but cut computing cost at least tenfold. The calibration is groundwork for fully dynamical disk studies.
arxiv-2606-09059: Dated 2026 on arXiv, this preprint reports a new research result. Its title gives the subject as Stage-1 Controls the Entropy Regime, Not the Outcome. The study operates inside science and technology (careful study of how the natural and built world works). New findings are reported here for the research community.
arxiv-2606-09659:
Ang Li and a large team revisit a squeeze play for long texts fed to language models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Long inputs choke on memory, since the key-value cache grows with length. Past squeezes either hurt quality or took too long on a single prompt. An encoder-decoder route, which maps long text to a short latent code, looked good on paper but lagged in tests.

The team first ran a design search, training many small variants from scratch. Guided by the results, they then trained a family of models at length cuts of four, eight, and sixteen to one. Each pairs a small encoder with a four-billion-parameter decoder, over more than three hundred fifty billion tokens. The line, called Latent Context Language Models, pushed the frontier on quality, speed, and peak memory at once.
arxiv-2606-09859:
Yingxuan Zhuang and a large team tame made-up objects in image chat without bending the model's mind in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multimodal models often name things the photo lacks. The blame falls on language priors, habits from text that can swamp weak visual proof. Flat bans on those habits backfire, since the same habits help when they match the scene.

The team call the backfire manifold departure: the model's meaning space warps, and quality sags. Their fix, MGAP, works at decode time with no retraining. It first maps the prior subspace from blind runs, text with no image. Each live state is then split: its part inside that subspace is trimmed by a gate that checks the scene fit. The rest of the state passes clean. On POPE and CHAIR tests, MGAP beat past decode tricks. It cut fake objects more while it kept replies smooth.
arxiv-2606-10059:
Hulden and Ginn present a simpler way to compile linguistic rewrite rules into finite-state machines, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computational linguistics. Finite-state transducers are the standard tool for phonological and morphological rules, which rewrite sounds or word parts depending on context. Classic methods by Kaplan and Kay or Karttunen rely on intricate compositions with auxiliary markers.

Their scheme uses the worsening trick: generate all legal rewrite candidates for an input, then filter out any candidate that is worse than another candidate for the same input. Implemented as the built-in rewrite compiler in PyFoma, it supports multiple contexts, markup, directed and parallel rewriting, and weights. The formulas are short and uniform, and where semantics coincide they reproduce the same transducers as earlier approaches. Validation against the foma toolkit on many grammars and a regression suite found exact matches apart from state numbering.
arxiv-2606-10859:
Kaneda and colleagues propose a new sign of invisible mass in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stellar streams, the ribbons of stars torn from small galaxies, can betray dark matter subhalos and wandering intermediate-mass black holes that emit no light. The team shows, with analytic modeling and N-body simulations, that one such encounter can split a single stream into two parallel streams.

Splitting needs the perturber in a set mass and speed window. For a split like Andromeda's Streams C and D, about 15 kiloparsecs wide, the culprit weighs roughly five hundred million solar masses. Energy and angular momentum maps from Gaia data can test whether a given pair formed this way.
arxiv-2606-10959:
Candan and Servadio upgrade a Bayesian transport method in this 2026 arXiv paper. Physics-informed neural particle flow moves sample particles from a prior belief to a posterior one along a learned field that obeys the probability-evolution equation. The standard version steers each particle alone, blind to the rest of the cloud.

The population-aware version feeds every update a summary of the whole particle set, either of positions or of full physics features such as likelihoods and scores. On range tasks it cuts energy distance by about 78 percent against the original; on 100 time-difference-of-arrival tasks, by about 86 percent. Feature summaries beat position-only ones.
arxiv-2606-11159:
Adeleke and Leslie analyze flocking in a 2026 arXiv paper on the pressureless Euler alignment system. This system models collective motion, where agents move and align velocity through nonlocal communication, without pressure. They restrict to unidirectional flow, all motion along one axis, and recast the system as coupled scalar balance laws, one per horizontal slice of space.

Within such solutions they prove existence, uniqueness, and stability, under a bounded Lipschitz communication protocol. The solutions arise as limits of sticky particle Cucker-Smale dynamics, discretized first across the flow, then along it. Two stability estimates carry the argument, including a low-regularity one using only L1 and L-infinity control of flux differences, after Bouchut and Perthame. For long-time behavior, flocking can occur at a rate independent of the agent count even when communication vanishes in a cylinder around the flow axis. Direct communication along the motion is unnecessary for flocking.
arxiv-2606-11359:
Lei and seven co-authors map how neutral gas shapes polarized radio emission from our Galaxy in a 2026 arXiv paper. The interstellar medium is a multiphase medium, and sorting out its gas and magnetic field structure across phases is hard. Faraday tomography, from broadband radio observations, promises a probe of three-dimensional structure. But interpreting it needs knowing which components the distinct Faraday depth features probe.

The team compares Faraday-rotated synchrotron emission with hydrogen structures across the high-latitude sky, from about 300 megahertz to 23 gigahertz. Using measures of hydrogen structure along the line of sight, they observe enhanced depolarization in complex regions, where multiple velocity components sit. The first and second moments of the Faraday depth spectra link to the neutral gas structure. Regions dominated by neutral gas could contribute a large portion of the diffuse emission and Faraday rotation itself.
arxiv-2606-11859:
Nicola Baldoni, Michele Sparviero and Lorenzo Viola compare ways to simulate financial futures in this 2026 arXiv report from ARCA Fondi. Risk managers generate scenarios for asset prices and yield curves, the pattern of interest rates across maturities. A good generator must match history statistically while producing individual paths that remain economically plausible.

The standard tool is the stationary bootstrap, which resamples blocks of historical data. It preserves the overall distribution of returns best, as its low divergence scores confirm. But recombining history gives each single path little economic structure, so paths can look implausible. The authors test a VAR-bootstrap extension, which fits a vector autoregressive model, where each variable depends on recent values of all variables, then resamples its residuals. This builds in dependence on current levels, especially valuable for interest rates. The comparison frames a clear trade-off between distributional fidelity and path realism.
arxiv-2606-12059:
Fabio Pasqualetti and Taosha Guo replace a core AI operation with physics in this 2026 arXiv paper. Transformer attention usually uses softmax, which needs exponentiation and global sums, with no natural analogue in hardware. Coupled oscillators, however, synchronise in many substrates, from circuits to superconducting junctions. The authors show Kuramoto synchronisation dynamics, the maths of oscillators pulling into step, implement a well-defined attention step.

Queries become fixed anchor points on a sphere; free oscillators evolve until they settle, and where they settle gives the attention weights. The settling point is unique and attracts almost every start. At the smallest hardware setup, oscillator attention beats softmax on keyword spotting and hard subject-verb agreement tests, with no training failures. On language tasks softmax still leads, but the gap shrinks as oscillator dimension grows. Because synchronisation arises naturally in many materials, attention could run on physics itself.
arxiv-2606-12159:
Zhang and co-authors map the phases of atoms on a ladder pierced by a fake magnetic field, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The system holds bosons, particles that happily share states, on a two-leg ladder, two rails joined by rungs. An artificial flux, a twist in the atoms' motion, pushes currents around each ladder square. Depending on settings, the atoms flow freely as a superfluid or lock in place as a Mott insulator.

The team uses the cluster Gutzwiller method, a mean-field approach treating small clusters exactly and surroundings approximately. On a two-by-four cluster, it matches heavy simulations where they overlap. The authors then draw the first grand-canonical phase diagrams for this system, charts showing how flux tilts and reshapes the insulating lobes. At the flux of pi, the net swirling current vanishes, and a nonchiral Mott insulator holds instead of the expected chiral superfluid.
arxiv-2606-12259:
Ramkrishnan and co-authors fix a ten-year-old clash between cache security and data sharing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Partitioning splits the cache so an attacker's program cannot evict a victim's data and spy on the pattern, a side-channel leak. But strict partitioning breaks write-shared coherence, the mechanism keeping shared writable data consistent across cores. Their design, SCP, partitions only the tags, the index labels, while partitions share one data pool sized so cross-partition capacity evictions cannot happen.

In gem5 simulations, Prime+Probe and Flush+Reload, foundations of cache spying, perform no better than random guessing under SCP. An attack on shared writable lines is also blunted, since writes route through the last-level cache once a leakage threshold is crossed. The hardware cost is 2.8 percent more last-level cache memory. Speed matches the DAWG defense within 0.3 percent on SPEC CPU2017 tests.
arxiv-2606-12359:
Alamoudi and Alladi reveal a classic counting theorem as one floor of an endless tower, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Partition theorems equate two ways of splitting numbers into parts: Euler's and Lebesgue's are famous examples. Capparelli's theorem is a deeper identity of this kind. The authors previously built an infinite hierarchy of identities whose first levels recover Euler, Lebesgue, and Capparelli in order. Here they state new partition theorems at every even order beyond Capparelli's.

Bijective proofs, matchings between the counted objects, establish these higher theorems. Capparelli's result turns out to seed a fourfold infinite hierarchy. Two of the four generating functions agree at every order, odd and even alike. For the remaining two, a weighted-words framework, counting strings with assigned weights, covers all orders. It yields further hierarchies with different dilations and translations. What looked like an isolated identity is a base case of rich, structured infinity.
arxiv-2606-12459:
Boumali and co-authors rebuild a deformed version of relativity, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Fock-Lorentz transformations generalize Lorentz symmetry using projective coordinates: each spacetime point is rescaled by a factor involving a warp length and a warp vector. Ordinary Lorentz moves in the auxiliary coordinates then warp physical ones. The authors give a setup with a shared interval and a located singular surface where the chart breaks down.

Everything sorts into sectors by the warp vector's causal character: time-like, space-like, or null. The explicit formula for light's coordinate speed holds only in the time-like sector. The new dynamics appear in the space-like sector. There, an apparent mass breaks parity and adds a cubic anharmonicity to oscillators. Its first-order shift vanishes by parity. Combined corrections give a definite shift scaling as the inverse square of the warp length.
arxiv-2606-12559:
Chandravamsi and co-authors move a classic forecasting update into a learned latent space, so shock waves survive it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Data assimilation blends model forecasts with observations; the ensemble Kalman filter is its workhorse. But the filter assumes Gaussian statistics. In flows with shocks, members disagree about the shock's position, statistics turn multimodal, and the update smears in fake oscillations. Their latent-EnKF performs the update where features live smoothly instead.

An encoder compresses flow states to a low-dimensional latent space where shocks and contact discontinuities trace a smooth manifold. The ensemble update happens there, and a shared decoder maps members back to physical space. Sharp features move coherently rather than dissolving. It also drops tricks earlier approaches needed. On a Sod shock tube and a Mach 2 flow striking a cylinder, with sparse noisy observations, shocks and contacts are recovered, without spurious oscillations.
arxiv-2606-12859:
Sun and colleagues present AIR-VLA+, a vision-language-action architecture that decouples flight movement from arm manipulation for aerial robots, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Aerial manipulators combine a drone platform with a robotic arm, whose actions differ sharply in scale, dynamics, and objectives. End-to-end controllers suffer representation coupling, where the 2 control problems interfere with each other.

AIR-VLA+ uses cascaded dual-action decoders built on flow matching: the movement decoder observes the manipulator's intent one-way for workflow coordination, while arm control is shielded from movement backpropagation that would destabilise it. An input enhancement module gives the movement decoder a visual grasp projector, sensing gripper-object interaction state, plus compressed global semantic features. On the standardised AIR-VLA benchmark, the method surpasses all baselines with an overall average score of 48.0, and its task completion score improves by 80.2 percent over the single-head pi-0.5 policy.
arxiv-2606-12959:
Singh analyses one-nucleon matrix elements of current-current correlators using QCD sum rules, covering pseudoscalar, axial, and axial-anomaly currents, in this 2026 arXiv paper. These matrix elements at zero momentum transfer are the nucleon's axial and pseudoscalar coupling constants. They govern nucleon and hyperon decays and encode how the proton's spin is shared among its quarks and gluons. The singlet axial channel is special because the axial anomaly, a gluonic contribution to the current's divergence, enters it.

Using QCD sum rules, Singh expresses the coupling of the nucleon to each current in terms of nucleon matrix elements. The currents include the pseudoscalar octet, isovector and isoscalar currents, and the axial isovector and isoscalar currents. The matrix elements involve quark, gluon, and quark-gluon operators and moments of parton distribution functions. The paper highlights the nucleon matrix element of the axial anomaly, long ignored in the literature.
arxiv-2606-13159:
Formenti and Kamilya prove that the reversible second-order cellular automaton rule 115 is periodic on every finite initial configuration, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Second-order cellular automata update each cell using both its current state and its previous state, a memory that standard automata lack. The reversible elementary second-order class has puzzling dynamics, and rule 115 was singled out in explorations for its behaviour, raising the question of whether its orbits always return to their starting point.

The main theorem answers yes: started from any finite configuration, rule 115 repeats, so every orbit is periodic. What remains mysterious is the period as a function of the initial configuration, which appears complex and is not understood. Some families have simple, predictable periods, constructed using a merge construction that generates new periods from given configurations. One family seems to have a period function growing exponentially with the size of the initial configuration.
arxiv-2606-13259:
Verhoef and Kruizinga report a big speed-up for three-dimensional ultrasound in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ultrafast ultrasound captures living tissue thousands of times per second, but rebuilding a volume is heavy work. Each frame contains millions of voxels, the cubes that make up a three-dimensional image. The standard delay-and-sum rebuilding leaves graphics processors underused because its memory reads arrive in scattered pieces. The authors fix this with three changes to how data are stored and fetched.

They align memory access with the hardware's transfer size and store data at half precision to halve traffic. They reuse nearby data so specialised tensor cores can help. Together these steps reach kilohertz frame rates for volumes of 128 voxels per side, using arrays of about 1,000 elements. Image quality stays intact while beating implementations by a wide margin. The code is released as the ffdas library.
arxiv-2606-13359:
Galois and a large collaboration catalogue galaxy clusters in two deep survey fields in this 2026 arXiv paper. Galaxy clusters, the largest gravitationally bound structures, trace how cosmic structure formed and how galaxies evolve in environments. The team analyses the cluster content of fields observed by the VIDEO near-infrared survey, regions partly covered by the MOONRISE survey. Two cluster finders, both working from photometric redshifts, estimates of distance from galaxy colours, are run over about 4.5 square degrees of sky.

Keeping only candidates detected by both finders yields a sample of over 500 clusters spanning a redshift range, out to when the universe was young. 74 of them lie at high redshift, beyond 1.5, where clusters are rare and valuable. For every detection the team identifies the brightest central galaxy and characterises the system. The catalogue prepares the ground for MOONRISE spectroscopy in two well-studied fields.
arxiv-2606-13759:
Wilhelmi and colleagues tutorialise the Wi-Fi standard's multi-access-point coordination in this 2026 arXiv paper. The IEEE 802.11bn amendment, the basis of Wi-Fi 8, sets ultra-high-reliability targets for wireless local networks. The standard is expected to improve throughput, cut the tail of the latency distribution, and reduce packet loss, each by at least a quarter. Multi-access-point coordination, where neighbouring access points cooperate instead of competing, is one of its mechanisms. This tutorial walks from the standard to testing, explaining how the modes work and what they deliver.

Tutorials of this kind serve engineers who must implement a standard written in dense language. The authors span universities and industry laboratories across countries. Cooperation matters because dense deployments, offices, stadiums, apartment blocks, are where Wi-Fi struggles: uncoordinated access points interfere. If Wi-Fi 8's cooperation delivers its targets, the experience of crowded wireless networks changes.
arxiv-2606-14059:
Jin finds how fast a predator invades when its habitat itself is moving. The setting is a prey-predator reaction-diffusion system in a shifting environment, where favorable conditions drift at fixed speed, as under climate change. The coupled system has no direct comparison principle, the usual bounding tool. His 2026 arXiv paper proves a pointwise estimate: wherever predator density is small, prey density stays near its carrying capacity. That lets the system be compared with scalar Fisher-KPP equations.

The comparison yields an explicit formula for the predator's spreading speed. For the classic scalar case the speed is twice the square root of the growth rate; Jin's formula extends this logic to the coupled, shifting system. Nonmonotone environments produce richer behavior. Locking can occur, the front pinned to the shifting habitat edge. Nonlocal pulling can also occur, distant favorable regions dragging the front faster than local growth predicts.
arxiv-2606-14159:
Li and co-authors predict how tightly a drug molecule binds its protein target by measuring the curvature of the interaction geometry. Affinity prediction guides drug discovery, but models struggle to capture both local geometry and global cross-molecule coordination. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes RicciBind. Ollivier Ricci curvature, a measure of how neighborhoods overlap, captures local tightness within each molecule, organizing atoms into layered structures shaped by it. An optimal transport step then matches protein and ligand clusters across domains.

Experiments across benchmarks and virtual screening tasks showed top accuracy and strong transfer to new targets. Ablation studies, removing parts one at a time, confirmed its essential role. The authors argue the approach extends to tasks such as pocket detection and docking. It also highlights where binding is tight, giving chemists a readable signal alongside the score.
arxiv-2606-14259:
Zhang and colleagues put the leading explanations for why Adam beats SGD on trial together, and find none guilty alone. Prior work blamed data properties, architecture choices, or optimization quirks, studied in isolation. Their 2026 arXiv paper runs a controlled study across vision, language, genomics, and graph tasks, on Transformer and classical architectures, with learning rate and momentum tuned for both optimizers.

The gap refuses a single cause. Adam's advantage persisted under a uniform vocabulary distribution yet nearly vanished under a heavy-tailed one. It reversed for SGD in softmax-attention models, and grew when ReLU was swapped for GeLU. One pattern recurred everywhere: a crossover batch size where the advantage shifts from SGD to Adam as batches grow, set jointly by data and architecture. Their theoretical gap model predicts it. In genomics Adam won even at batch size one; on ResNet50 with ImageNet-21K, SGD stayed ahead at large batches.
arxiv-2606-14359:
Li and colleagues listen to stars ringing in a young cluster and read off core spin rates. Gravity-mode pulsators in open clusters are precious: the cluster supplies age and mass limits while pulsation period spacings reveal near-core rotation. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses TESS photometry for members of the open cluster NGC 3532, about 300 million years old. It measures their period spacings, and fits isochrones for NGC 3532 and the younger NGC 2516.

The instability region for its gamma Doradus pulsators runs from a blue edge near 7760 kelvin to a red edge near 7070 kelvin. Below 1.6 solar masses, near-core rotation rises with mass, as in NGC 2516; above it, the stars plateau near 2.8 cycles per day. Matching transport models requires the pulsators to have been born spinning above 55 percent of critical. Measured asymptotic period spacings also disagree with theory for some pulsators, as in NGC 2516, a cluster about one third as old.
arxiv-2606-14459:
Theresa Pekarek Rosin, Kerzel, and Wermter introduce MoDiCoL in a 2026 arXiv paper on speech recognition robustness. Modern systems score well on standard tests yet slip under real-world shifts in recording conditions, accents, speech impairments, and noise. Most benchmarks test each factor alone, missing how they combine in daily use.

MoDiCoL is a modular diagnostic dataset built for continual learning, where a model is updated step by step over time. It separates linguistic content, speaker traits, and acoustic environment so each can be varied in a controlled way. The authors add a realistic training sequence that mimics incremental updates and study how robustness is gained, transferred, and forgotten. They evaluate three continual learning strategies on it and report detailed findings about which conditions erode recognition accuracy most.
arxiv-2606-14559:
Grifó and Valenti analyze pattern formation in a plant-herbivore system in a 2026 arXiv paper. Plant toxins shape the system. Plants defend themselves chemically. Herbivores move toward or away from vegetation. Their two-compartment model has a toxin-based feeding response. It also has cross-diffusion. That is movement of one group driven by the other's gradient.

Two regimes appear. Under weak toxicity, at most one coexistence state is biologically feasible. That state can lose stability through a Hopf bifurcation. Small temporal oscillations then arise. Under strong toxicity, the feeding response turns non-monotonic. Several coexistence states become possible, with abrupt regime shifts. The authors find conditions for Turing instabilities and mixed patterns. They derive amplitude equations near the thresholds. Simulations confirm the predictions. Uniform states give way to oscillations and spatial patterns.
arxiv-2606-14659:
Ratnayaka and Fischer present a mesh partitioner for exascale simulations in a 2026 arXiv paper. Spectral element simulations split their computational mesh across thousands of processors, and the split's quality decides how much costly inter-processor communication occurs. Their tool, parRSB, partitions the mesh's dual graph using recursive spectral bisection.

The method repeatedly cuts the graph along its Fiedler vector, the eigenvector tied to the smallest nonzero eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian, which exposes natural divisions. They implemented two ways to compute that vector, a Lanczos method and inverse iteration with conjugate gradients. Results on the Summit and Frontier supercomputers at Oak Ridge show the partitions are high quality and the implementation scales, and the paper details optimizations that sped up the partitioning process itself.
arxiv-2606-14859:
Scali reviews and extends a way of building modified gravity theories in a 2026 arXiv paper. The theories are called f(R) gravity. They change Einstein's equations by letting the action depend on curvature in a freer way. In earlier work, a family of such theories was built inductively. Only Solar System physics was used as the guide. The modified equations were solved step by step around a normal black hole background.

Classical Solar System tests then pinned down the family's one length scale. That scale measures how far the theory strays from general relativity. Here Scali stresses how general the recipe is. It can serve other modified gravity frameworks too. He then derives the Newtonian potential of an extended source in this model. The Newtonian limit stays consistent. Galactic dynamics is named as a promising next use.
arxiv-2606-14959:
Jin and coauthors use the James Webb Space Telescope to probe which sources reionized the early universe in a 2026 study. They observe the field around a quasar at redshift six point five, deep in the reionization era. Earlier imaging had found eight oxygen-emitting galaxies there. The team adds new camera and spectrograph data to widen the census.

The new observations identify sixty-five more line-emitting galaxies at similar redshifts in the same field. Gas between galaxies transmits more light near these galaxies than average, hinting that star-forming regions boosted the local ionizing background. The pattern matches simulations with a mostly ionized medium and a modest escape fraction for galaxy light. Among forty-nine galaxies with spectra, four show broad hydrogen lines marking active galactic nuclei. Gas near those nuclei transmits still more light, suggesting their radiation escapes far more freely than galaxy light does.
arxiv-2606-15159:
Li proves every natural number is a sum of distinct semiprime unit fractions, in a 2026 number theory paper. A unit fraction has numerator one, and a semiprime is a product of two distinct primes. Erdős and Graham asked which restrictions allow Egyptian fraction expansions. Butler, Erdős, and Graham settled the three-prime case but conjectured the two-prime one. Fewer primes make the induction harder, since its feed of fractions thins. Li adapts the induction to survive that regime.

The induction step reduces to an onset inequality. Li proves it for cases using Olson's addition theorem and Chebyshev bounds. A base range is checked by computation. The engine extends the result to rational numbers above a threshold. It completes the proof of the rational three-prime statement. Every claim is verified in the Lean proof assistant. One conjecture on subset sums remains open below the threshold.
arxiv-2606-15259:
Li and coauthors date the polarity reversal of the Sun's polar magnetic fields in solar cycle 25, in a 2026 solar physics paper. Each cycle, the fields near the poles flip sign around sunspot maximum. Pinning down the flip dates tests dynamo theories and helps predict the next cycle. The team used magnetic field data from the Hinode satellite's spectropolarimeter. They stitched observations into composite maps of both polar caps.

The maps show the north cap fading from positive to negative polarity year by year. The south cap moved in the opposite direction over the same years. For caps above seventy degrees latitude, reversal likely came in October 2024 in the south. The northern reversal followed around November 2024. The northern flip lagged its hemisphere's sunspot maximum by about nineteen months. The southern flip coincided with its hemisphere's maximum. Lower latitude bands reversed earlier, matching cycle 24 behavior.
arxiv-2606-15359:
Giaretta and coauthors present DiRecT in a 2026 robotics paper, a method for making diffusion-based planners respect hard safety constraints. Diffusion models learn rich distributions over robot trajectories, but a generated plan might clip an obstacle. Existing fixes project every noisy intermediate step onto the feasible set, though the constraints concern only the final trajectory, and that over-restriction degrades plan quality. DiRecT instead enforces constraints only on the finished sample.

Borrowing receding-horizon control, which replans over a moving window, the authors turn the constrained sampling problem into a tractable surrogate steering samples toward feasibility. The method needs no retraining and can plug in domain optimizers, dynamics priors, and soft goals. On safe planning benchmarks it substantially improves both constraint satisfaction and task success over earlier diffusion planners. Splitting noise from the safety check preserves what the model learned while guaranteeing the plan obeys the rules.
arxiv-2606-15459:
Herreros and coauthor track the slowest debris from NASA's DART impact in a 2026 planetary science paper. In 2022 the DART spacecraft slammed into Dimorphos, a small asteroid moon, and nudged its orbit, the first full-scale deflection test. Most excavated mass left at speeds below escape velocity, yet earlier studies followed mainly the fast ejecta. The authors simulate the first twenty-two hours with a model coupling orbital motion to surface transport on terrain.

Re-accretion is fast and lopsided: nearly all returning mass lands back on Dimorphos within about five hours. The slowest particles settle near the crater and dominate the blanket, while faster ones travel and favor the opposite and trailing sides. Surface sliding and bouncing reshape the first-contact pattern, and rough terrain produces ray-like deposits ruled by local bumps. The predictions give ESA's Hera mission, now en route, patterns to check against the real blanket.
arxiv-2606-15559:
Weiß and colleagues present SDVDiag in 2026, an online diagnostic system for software-defined vehicles, where faults spread through software services. The visible symptom often sits several causal hops from the real defect, and existing tools usually read one data type and run offline by hand. SDVDiag fuses log-based and metric-based service representations into one shared embedding space before building its causal graph.

An anomaly-driven trigger turns the platform from a batch tool into a continuously running service. On an autonomous valet parking testbed, the multimodal pipeline builds sparser causal graphs than a metrics-only baseline, 134 edges on average against 182. It beats that baseline on edge-weighted reward against an expert knowledge graph at every stage of feedback refinement, reaching a 2.4-fold edge after sixty feedback queries. In a fault-injection test it recovered a root cause two hops upstream of the symptom, which the baseline missed.
arxiv-2606-15859:
Xia and colleagues present EPIC in 2026, a framework that makes always-on perception affordable on augmented-reality glasses. Perception-first glasses capture high-resolution egocentric video continuously, and the power and memory costs are brutal on such a device. EPIC instead infers what the user is attending to and keeps only the informative parts of the stream.

The framework fuses gaze, pose, and inertial signals to estimate user intent, then discards redundant video before it consumes memory and energy. Algorithm, hardware, and in-sensor processing are optimised together. Against a full-video baseline, EPIC cuts the memory footprint by a factor of about twenty-seven and energy consumption by a factor of about twenty-four on average. Accuracy on egocentric video understanding tasks, the key assistance scenario, is preserved. For embodied intelligence on glasses, the lesson is that perception should be selective by design: sense everything, store almost nothing.
arxiv-2606-15959:
Li and colleagues quantify how lossy compression of training data affects neural generative surrogates in 2026, learned stand-ins for expensive scientific simulations. High-fidelity surrogates need massive training sets, straining storage and input pipelines; lossy compression shrinks them, but its errors might quietly degrade the trained model. The key observation: training itself is noisy, identical setups yielding noticeably different models through random starts, shuffling, and optimisation noise.

Against that noise, a well-chosen compression level's error is smaller, often negligible. The team turns the observation into a method computing how much compression error a surrogate can tolerate without accuracy loss. On two simulations, training data compress by factors of about twenty-four and thirty-nine with negligible quality impact. Smaller data also loads faster, cutting training time by up to a factor of three. For simulation campaigns, the test tells users how hard they may compress before ever training.
arxiv-2606-16059:
Han surveys the Mojo programming language in 2026 as an answer to a long-standing split in financial computing. For thirty years, quant teams have prototyped models in Python, then rewritten them in C++ for production, a two-language tax that can introduce mismatches. Graphics-processor deep learning adds drift, because nondeterministic rounding can change long backtest results and threaten audit trails.

Mojo, a Python-like systems language from Modular, compiles through MLIR so one codebase can target scalar, vector, multicore, and graphics-processor execution. Han stresses its ability to build bit-exact deterministic kernels, kernels whose results repeat exactly on every run. Four workloads cover Monte Carlo option pricing, sentiment scoring, multi-asset backtesting, and portfolio Value at Risk. Reported speedups over pure Python range from 20 to 180 times on Apple Silicon. Han places Mojo at the compute-critical seams of the stack, not as a full replacement.
arxiv-2606-16259:
Bartholdi and co-authors prove in 2026 that a simple lamp-and-switch model relaxes at a super-Arrhenius pace, settling a conjecture from 1999. In the triangular plaquette model, a lamp sits at every vertex of a triangular lattice, and switches on the dual hexagonal lattice each toggle the three lamps of one face. Energy counts the lamps left on, and Glauber dynamics flips switches. The question is how the relaxation time grows as temperature falls.

For every dimension two and above, the authors bound the infinite-volume relaxation time between a lower bound scaling like the exponential of beta squared and a double-exponential upper bound. The exponential-of-beta-squared scaling matches what Newman and Moore conjectured in 1999. It also mirrors supercritical kinetically constrained models such as the East model, recovering fragile glass behavior with no kinetic constraints built in. A byproduct is that the Gibbs measure is unique.
arxiv-2606-16659:
Yanhan Zhou leads a large 2026 team benchmarking fraud detection that spans text messages and webpages. A scam text sends the victim to a page, and the real risk depends on whether the page matches the message claim. Older tests judge the message alone, or leak the web address so models can rely on reputation shortcuts.

Their benchmark, FraudSMSWalker, hides addresses, hosts and reputation data from the model under test. It holds bilingual chains of message plus cleaned webpage evidence, split between fraudulent and benign cases across ten service settings. Hard benign cases include normal login, payment and verification pages that resemble scam flows. Nine web agents are tested, plus trials where addresses are visible. Agents spot suspicious cues well, but they often misjudge benign flows and support fraud calls with weak evidence, a clear warning for automated fraud screening.
arxiv-2606-16859:
Malosso and colleagues teach machine learning models to simulate excited-state chemistry in a 2026 paper. Light-driven processes power solar conversion, vision and photosynthesis, but simulating atoms in excited electronic states is far too slow with standard quantum chemistry for big systems or long times.

Ground-state machine learning potentials work because energy grows with system size, so atomic contributions can be summed. Excitation energies break that rule: a gap is intensive, set by the most and least willing atoms, not by a sum. Their framework therefore pools predicted atomic orbital contributions with smooth maximum and minimum operations instead of adding them. Trained only on excitation energies and forces, the model learns where an excited electron localizes. Applied to a photoexcited electron in liquid water, it reproduces known reaction paths, including hydrogen release and proton-coupled electron transfer, in cells far larger than reference methods can reach.
arxiv-2606-17059:
Nair and Saini route language model requests across a peer-to-peer network in a 2026 systems paper. Serving is slowed by repeated prefill computation: requests sharing a prompt prefix rebuild identical key-value caches. Caching helps, but in a cluster the caches sit scattered across machines.
