Their scheme is decentralized and prefix-aware, with no coordinator and no cache transfers. Each node keeps a radix tree of its own cached prefixes and gossips estimates of peers' caches, refreshed by periodic anti-entropy exchange. A request goes to the node with the longest estimated prefix match. Stale estimates only cause cache misses, never wrong answers, so weak consistency suffices. Simulations on question-answering workloads show latency gains when network delay is low and prefix popularity is skewed, as routing concentrates hot prefixes. High latency and hotspot queueing erode the benefit. The design also removes the central router's single point of failure.
arxiv-2606-17159:
Schleith, Bril and Bultinck explain how a fractionalized metal becomes a superconductor in a 2026 theory paper. A fractionalized Fermi liquid is an exotic metal whose carriers coexist with spinons and chargons, fractional pieces of the electron. Doping it slightly is a route toward cuprate pairing symmetry.

Doped electrons enter as bound states of a spinon and a chargon, forming a small reconstructed Fermi surface. These composites are gauge-neutral, so they interact through a two-body dipolar potential. The interaction is repulsive, which sounds fatal for pairing. But translation symmetry acts projectively on the pieces, twisting the interaction so its components peak at the antiferromagnetic wave vector. A repulsion peaked there is exactly what favors d-wave pairing, where the order parameter changes sign across the zone. The pairing equation confirms it. Fractionalization, often seen as an obstacle, becomes the engine of superconductivity.
arxiv-2606-17459:
Dai and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper asking whether language models could do a chief executive's hardest job: moving money between business units under conflicting advice. Existing benchmarks test isolated reasoning or stylised economic choices, missing the clashing stakeholders and shifting constraints of real executive work. Their benchmark, CEO-Bench, casts the model as chief executive across many rounds in a constraint-rich simulated firm with four role-conditioned advisers.

The advisers, playing finance, technology, operations, and marketing chiefs, hold private signals and distinct priorities that often pull against each other. Plans are scored on role integration, conditional boldness, history-sensitive judgement, and plain validity of the allocation. Five frontier models all produced structurally valid plans but split sharply on strategic calibration, the hardest layer. Failure modes included capture by a single adviser, timid defaults under ambiguity, and forgetting the firm's own history.
arxiv-2606-17759:
Agdestein presents a 2026 arXiv paper extending a neat trick in turbulence simulation from space into time. Large-eddy simulation models the small scales a grid cannot see, and a recent exact approach rests on noticing that a coarse spatial difference is really a filtered exact derivative. Agdestein observes the forward-Euler time step has the same filtered character, one-sided in time. Repeating the construction across space and time yields an exact split of the discrete flux with just one extra term, a time-quadrature error.

That term grows with the time step size while the spatial terms stay put, as a Burgers test case confirms. Adding its leading form to a classic closure keeps accuracy at coarse time steps where space-only closures fall apart. The result folds time-integration error into the same exact bookkeeping as spatial error. Builders gain one honest ledger for both discretisations.
arxiv-2606-17859:
Landim and Maura compute a complete asymptotic expansion for the cost of rare behavior in a noisy one-dimensional system, in a 2026 probability paper. Their process is a diffusion on a ring, pushed by a drift and shaken by Brownian noise whose strength is a small temperature parameter. The drift need not be reversible, so the system can settle into a genuine non-equilibrium steady state with circulating currents.

The object of study is the level-two rate functional from large deviation theory. It prices how unlikely each long-run occupation pattern is. The authors derive its full Gamma expansion as the temperature vanishes, a leading term of order one over temperature, a constant term, and a ladder of corrections at intermediate scales. Each correction is an explicit functional built from the drift and diffusion coefficients. Such expansions sharpen predictions for metastable transitions in non-reversible dynamics.
arxiv-2606-18159:
Hosseini and Murata carry a classic theorem of geometry onto spaces with corners and seams, in a 2026 mathematics paper. The Hodge theorem says that on a compact smooth manifold, each class in cohomology has exactly one harmonic form. Their setting is the piecewise-algebraic spaces of Kontsevich and Soibelman, built by gluing real semialgebraic pieces. The class covers algebraic varieties and simplicial complexes alike.

First they prove a Poincaré lemma for these spaces, computing singular cohomology through a de Rham style variant built from the forms the spaces support. Then, with Sobolev space methods, they embed the cohomology into the harmonic forms. The embedding stands in for the isomorphism of the smooth theorem, which fails here, hence the weak form of the title. The work feeds a program that extends arithmetic intersection theory to singular spaces.
arxiv-2606-18559:
Molinero, Monsó, and Samaniego propose a new way to measure each player's power in a simple voting game, in a 2026 game theory paper. They show it is secretly a workhorse of data science in disguise. Power indices such as the Shapley-Shubik index quantify influence by counting how often a player turns a losing coalition into a winning one.

Their index is built from the game's winning coalitions, and they prove it coincides with quantities obtained from principal component analysis of a matrix representing the game, computed through singular value decomposition. That makes the index easy to calculate directly from the list of winning coalitions. They also characterize the index by four properties, placing it within the axiomatic tradition for power measures. The authors sketch extensions to richer classes of games and further indices built on the same principal component idea.
arxiv-2606-18659:
Godambe and colleagues at Krutrim in India evaluate whether large foundational speech recognition models can handle real telephone conversations in Hindi and Indian-accented English, in a 2026 speech technology paper. Call-center speech is narrow-band, spontaneous, and colloquial, while most training resources and models are built on wide-band read speech, leaving low-resource languages and accents badly served.

Testing open-source and commercial systems zero-shot, the team found performance suboptimal across the board. Fine-tuning open models on a limited set of real annotated recordings brought moderate improvements. The gains varied by language and accent and depended heavily on how much similar data the model saw in pretraining. Pseudo-labeling and domain-adaptive training reduced the need for costly manual annotation, and the paper weighs fine-tuned foundations against an in-house system trained entirely on domain data.
arxiv-2606-18859:
Bakkaoui constructs unconditional primality certificates for a family of numbers built from the centered hexagonal numbers, in a 2026 number theory paper. The Pocklington-Lehmer criterion proves primality from a split chunk of the number minus one, plus witnesses. For this family, that splitting comes free. That cuts the work to witnesses for the primes two and three, which folklore took to be fixed numbers.

Bakkaoui proves that folklore wrong, and gives conditions instead. The witness five works precisely when the exponents differ by one or two modulo four, by quadratic reciprocity. The witness seven works when a congruence modulo seven is avoided, by cubic reciprocity in the Eisenstein integers. Three filters discard most candidates at tiny cost. A run on home hardware produced four certificates. The largest was for a prime of under thirty thousand digits, which the author presents as a demo, not a record.
arxiv-2606-19159:
Cudennec and colleagues guide design choices for the wide-field integral field spectrograph of the planned Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope in 2026. The telescope will run both a high-multiplex multi-object spectrograph and a panoramic integral field spectrograph. The integral field design builds on MUSE at the Very Large Telescope, using field splitters and image slicers to reformat a large field into pseudo-slits feeding spectrographs with two spectral channels.

The trade study weighs pixel pitch, detector format, and camera design against throughput, image quality, error budgets, volume, and cost. It adds one unusual metric, the carbon footprint of building each spectrograph, to inform sustainable choices. Curved detectors are also explored as an option. Early results suggest many simpler spectrographs beat fewer complex units, both technically and economically. That replication-over-complexity lesson can steer the final design of this major survey instrument toward lower risk and cost.
arxiv-2606-19359:
Frank and colleagues prove extremal representations for functions of matrices in 2026, with applications to multivariate prediction. Two classic results motivate the work. Helson and Lowdenslager, and Wiener and Masani, founded multivariate prediction theory with theorems on optimal linear prediction of stationary vector processes. The authors extend those results to a wider class of matrix sets.

The main goal is computing the infimum of trace values over a set of matrices. The sets studied are norm-bounded unit spheres with forms of unitary invariance. That structure allows the theory of majorization to enter, ordering matrices by how spread their spectra are. From the extremal representations, the paper derives prediction-theoretic consequences for multivariate forecasting. It sketches how matricial inequalities follow. Exact infima sharpen what optimal prediction can promise. The work shows a classical mid-century theory still yields new matrix results when its geometry is pushed further.
arxiv-2606-19559:
Gregory Matsnev tackles a practical snag for language model agents in 2026: knowing when to ask a clarifying question. Agents fail quietly when a request is underspecified, leaving key choices unstated. Deployment limits rule out log-probability tricks, repeated sampling, and retraining, leaving prompt-based estimates as the workable route.

Matsnev splits uncertainty into two parts with a simple prompt design. Action confidence tracks how sure the agent is of its next step. Request uncertainty tracks how ambiguous the task itself remains. High request uncertainty triggers a clarifying question before the agent acts. Two new benchmarks, WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification, leave half of all tasks deliberately underspecified. Across five model backbones, the split beats ReAct with uncertainty estimation and an uncertainty-aware memory rival. Clarification scores rise by 73 percent over the ReAct rival on the ALFWorld variant.
arxiv-2606-19659:
Yuhang Zhou and seven colleagues refine on-policy distillation for multi-turn language agents in 2026. On-policy distillation trains a student on paths its own policy generates, curbing exposure bias. Most studies stay single-turn, while real agents act over many turns.

Early errors warp later observations and compound along the path. Dense token-level supervision can over-penalise valid alternatives and entrench repeated actions. SAGE-OPD intervenes selectively instead of supervising every turn alike. Environment feedback plus teacher judgment decide whether each student response needs intervention. Token weights scale with teacher confidence, muting shaky guidance on odd histories. Loss normalisation keeps the overall scale of standard distillation. On agent tasks, gains reach a 13.3 percent relative improvement in unseen ALFWorld success. Ablations credit turn selection, confidence weighting, and normalisation jointly.
arxiv-2606-20359:
Ali Asaria, Tony Salomone, and Deep Gandhi run a four-way contest to find what makes a language model cite the right law. Their 2026 paper uses Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act, a statute that self-represented tenants and landlords constantly need quoted correctly. Four arms compete on the same base model: zero-shot prompting, LoRA fine-tuning alone, retrieval alone, and a hybrid. Scoring is exact-match citation, down to section and subsection, on a small real evaluation set flagged as preliminary.

The base model cannot cite the Act at all, and fine-tuning alone mis-recalls sections. Retrieval proves essential and eliminates hallucinated citations by construction. The hybrid scores highest, at 0.481 exact match, because fine-tuning makes provision selection robust to the larger candidate sets that hurt zero-shot retrieval. Strikingly, the cheap hybrid matches pipelines with bigger specialized retrieval models, and more training data does not help.
arxiv-2606-20459:
Zahra Asghari Varzaneh and four colleagues model IVF lab conditions with context-aware features instead of raw sensor averages. Their 2026 paper notes that pregnancy-rate models usually rely on patient variables, while detailed data from the lab itself go unused. Incubator temperature and humidity swings may carry real signal.

The team engineers 55 time-based features, including rolling thermal stability, joint temperature-humidity adherence, peak stress duration, and recovery speed after stress. On 61 weeks of data from an Asian clinic, these features cut cross-checked forecast error to 1.27 percent, versus 3 to 5 percent for raw averages. A hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression then shares lab effects across the Asian clinic and a Northern European one. Lab microenvironment swings, it turns out, belong in IVF outcome models.
arxiv-2606-20559:
Wenhao Chi and four colleagues unify egocentric video representations by distilling many teachers into one encoder. Their 2026 paper argues that wearable-camera understanding is limited by a single viewpoint, a single modality, and a single model. A truly expressive representation must absorb complementary knowledge yet deploy from egocentric video alone.

UniEgo trains with nine teachers spanning ego and exo viewpoints, RGB, depth, and skeleton modalities, and four foundation models, organized in a hierarchical multi-teacher distillation framework. Proxy representations mediate between the teachers and the student encoder. At deployment, only the egocentric stream is needed. First-person video systems can thus carry third-person and multimodal knowledge in a single deployable model.
arxiv-2606-20659:
Boyin Tan and two colleagues propose skill coverage in 2026, a test adequacy metric for agent skills, which are written guides that give language model agents reusable steps for tasks. Judging only by final task success hides which parts of a skill were actually used or left untested. Skill coverage treats the skill document itself as the object under test, much as code coverage treats a program.

Tan and colleagues extract observable behavior constraints from skill documents, then check whether an agent run gives enough evidence that each constraint was exercised. The judgment is binary, covered or not covered, without adding a separate pass or fail label for the behavior. Applied to SkillsBench, current runs cover only about 40 to 44 percent of constraints. That gap shows many benchmark tasks leave large parts of documented guidance untouched, so a high task score may overstate how well a skill has really been tested.
arxiv-2606-20759:
A doctoral thesis hosted with template placeholders in place of its title and author pages investigates bulk viscous matter in cosmic evolution in 2026. Bulk viscosity acts like internal friction in the cosmic fluid. The thesis studies several forms of its coefficient inside modified gravity theories. Early chapters review general relativity, its teleparallel forms, the standard cosmic model, and system methods.

Later chapters apply power-law and linear gravity models with different viscosity laws. Analytic solutions are derived for the field equations. Data sets, including supernova and expansion data, constrain free parameters. Results often favor quintessence-like behavior for the faster expansion. Dynamical analysis traces how models behave at late times. Chapter five gathers results and future directions. The thesis tests whether cosmic friction, added to modified gravity, can explain faster expansion without a simple constant.
arxiv-2606-20859:
Johan Hallberg Szabadváry presents a family of conformal test martingales in a solo 2026 paper on online exchangeability testing. Exchangeability means data order carries no information. Online tests must detect when that assumption breaks. A martingale here is a betting score that should stay controlled under the null case. The work extends the Simple Jumper martingale using shifted Legendre polynomials.

Replacing a linear betting function with polynomials of any degree helps detect changes in variance, skewness, and higher moments. One variant combines several degrees, but its state space grows fast, a cost called the jumping tax. A variational variant factorizes adaptation to restore linear time. A composite variant mixes jumping rates and keeps a wealth floor. Tests on a real classification task show consistent gains. Sensitive online tests help monitor data streams where distribution shifts can silently ruin a deployed model.
arxiv-2606-20959:
Elias Hossain and three colleagues tackle outdated answers from language models in 2026, where a model knows a newer fact yet still gives the old one. Models can store both an outdated fact and its replacement. Standard prompting may still elicit the old answer. They formalize that failure as parametric temporal conflict. Their method, Temporal Attractor Steering, intervenes at test time without retraining.

Three stages detect likely conflicts, locate a critical layer, and steer hidden states toward the newer fact. A verified benchmark holds close to nine thousand records across five relation types from Wikidata. Four open-weight models from three families are tested. Single-layer patching flips answers at high rates. The full method recovers a large share of conflict cases. Accuracy on non-conflict questions stays mostly intact. Steering could offer a light fix for stale facts between model retraining cycles.
arxiv-2606-21059:
Zhen Wang and nine colleagues introduce DefenGraph in 2026, a knowledge graph enhanced assistant for blue team cyber defense, where defenders protect a live network. Language models can support security decisions. Their reliability in fast-changing, high-stakes settings is limited by hallucination, weak temporal reasoning, and shallow context. DefenGraph grounds model outputs in a dual-layer knowledge graph, split into static and dynamic layers.

Graph path retrieval, model-driven filtering, and reasoning-based re-ranking connect questions to graph evidence. Long-term domain knowledge joins evolving event context. Evaluation uses graphs built from security alerts, system topology, attacker behavior, and prior defensive actions. Data come from live red versus blue exercises on critical infrastructure. Temporally aware support could help defenders under time pressure, where a confident but invented recommendation can waste the minutes that decide an incident.
arxiv-2606-21259:
Victoria Bjelland, William Millar, Walter Wuensch, and Morten Kildemo study conditioning in 2026, the slow raising of voltage that trains high-field electrodes to hold stronger fields without arcing. In pulsed direct-current electrodes, spots exposed to higher surface fields break down more often, yet those same spots also condition faster. The team asks how this local interplay decides where breakdowns finally occur.

They pair Monte Carlo simulations with experiments on electrode pairs whose surface field varies with radius. A camera pair triangulated each breakdown spot during conditioning in a high-field pulsed DC system, and the recorded pattern is compared with the simulations. Matching the two supports their account of the competing effects. The findings matter for accelerator cavities and other high-voltage devices, where conditioning is slow and can damage parts.
arxiv-2606-21359:
Raia Abu Ahmad and five colleagues deliver an unwelcome finding in 2026: fine-tuning language models on scientific data makes their factual reliability worse, not better. The team built SciFactCheck, a benchmark of 2,500 prompts across five scientific domains, graded on three failure types: claims that cannot be verified, overclaims, and false attribution. Eighteen models were tested, each science-tuned model against its general-purpose base version.

Fine-tuned models degraded on every hallucination type and every domain. Internally they were less confident, yet their wording grew more assertive, a risky mix for readers. A human pilot study adds that current fact-checking tools agree only modestly with expert judges on scientific content. The results challenge standard domain fine-tuning and call for better verification tools.
arxiv-2606-21759:
Edward C. Waymire revisits a bridge between Markov processes and Gaussian random fields in 2026, and walks it from a new direction. Physicists and probabilists have long built Gaussian fields from Markov processes, using Green functions as covariances, in the work of Dynkin, Diaconis and Evans, and others. Waymire's note starts instead from a central limit theorem of Rabi Bhattacharya for additive integral functionals of a Markov process run under its ergodic invariant distribution.

The resulting universal Gaussian random fields are defined for processes that need not be transient or symmetric in the classical way. Under extra conditions on the generator, he connects these fields to the Dynkin and Diaconis-Evans constructions. The note shows how much of the classical theory is really fluctuation theory in disguise.
arxiv-2606-21959:
Jeong introduces OpenBioRQ in 2026, a benchmark of 12,553 unsolved biomedical research questions designed to test research agents on faithfulness. A citation that resolves can still point to the wrong paper, and Jeong finds current agents rarely fabricate citations yet link to the wrong source in about 15.9 percent of cases. Fixed answer keys cannot catch that failure, because a model can reproduce the expected source without verifying it supports the claim.

The questions span twelve domains, carry no answer key, and had their openness checked against real follow-up evidence. Difficulty was anchored empirically on questions that three open reference models failed. On the hardest subset, three frontier agents scored between twenty-nine and sixty percent, leaving the benchmark far from saturated. Jeong also observed agentic collapse, where agents stop using their tools on the hardest questions, and showed a frozen per-question checklist improved agreement between judges.
arxiv-2606-22059:
Choi, Kim, and Woo prove, in 2026, a cautionary result about parabolic Sobolev spaces, the function spaces used to solve heat-type equations with boundaries. For ordinary Sobolev spaces, extending a function by zero outside its domain stays inside the space, a fact analysts rely on constantly. Parabolic spaces mix time and space regularity, and the authors test whether the same comfort holds there.

It does not. For every integrability exponent, they construct a function on a half-space-time cylinder that belongs to the parabolic space with zero boundary values, yet whose zero extension falls outside the larger space. The obstruction appears even with a flat boundary. It comes from a self-similar boundary layer at the corner where initial time meets the boundary, creating a normal flux defect after extension. The paper also discusses which spaces remain suitable for parabolic equations.
arxiv-2606-22559:
Jing-Tong Xing and seven colleagues, including Jian-Min Wang, hunt for signs of hidden black holes in this 2026 astrophysics paper. Stellar-mass black holes may sit embedded in the disks of active galactic nuclei. As they migrate inward they pile up at migration traps, radii where the torque on them vanishes.

The team couple a one-dimensional population model with a model of disk variability from corona heating and reprocessing. At the traps, the holes trigger magnetic reconnection heating the disk atmosphere. The heating regulates itself: pile-ups raise the reconnection rate, while the gaps the holes open lower the gas density and suppress the power. The signatures are excess short-timescale variability in optical and ultraviolet light, flattened short-term structure functions, and departures from the lag-wavelength relation. Effects peak at low to moderate feeding rates, offering an indirect detection route.
arxiv-2606-22859:
Raul Jimenez and nine colleagues argue that AI systems are becoming scientists, in this 2026 position paper. Agentic systems already synthesize literature, generate code, analyze data, propose hypotheses, and criticize models. The authors contend this shift is qualitative, not incremental: well-designed multi-agent systems could expand the hypothesis-generating and checking capacity of science itself.

They illustrate the claim with Denario, a prototype framework whose agents traverse model spaces beyond human reach and speed up the discovery cycle. The paper then examines what such systems imply for authorship, peer review, and the enduring role of human scientists. Institutions, they argue, must be redesigned for verification, accountability, interpretability, and dual-use safety before AI scientists are deployed at scale. Their closing recommendations treat AI as an epistemic actor, an entity that produces knowledge claims, rather than a mere instrument.
arxiv-2606-23059:
Matthew McCormack, Gregory Chini, and Rich Kerswell build a weakly nonlinear theory for non-normal systems in a 2026 fluid mechanics paper. Non-normal operators can amplify disturbances hugely for a while even in stable systems. Whether that transient growth triggers lasting change depends on how non-normality meets nonlinearity, which lacked a systematic theory. Their framework studies stable non-normal systems under harmonic forcing. A small parameter is defined from the system's maximum linear amplification, and the method adapts to each system's structure to stay consistent.

McCormack and colleagues apply the theory to a forced channel flow and then to a two-dimensional model mimicking shear flow equations. Unlike classic theory near a bifurcation, the resulting amplitude equations are not universal. One amplified mode can excite a multi-mode, multi-frequency response at leading order, specific to each system. The equations still capture stable nonlinear states as forcing grows.
arxiv-2606-23359:
Duc Tien Nguyen and colleagues harden physics-informed neural networks against boundary errors in a 2026 paper. These networks solve partial differential equations by baking physical laws into training. The standard design imposes every constraint as a soft penalty inside one combined loss. That often converges slowly, reacts badly to loss weights, and enforces boundaries sloppily. Their framework, HSPINN, splits constraints by type. Some boundary conditions hold exactly by construction, enforced through lifting functions, masks, and periodic feature maps. The rest stay as soft terms.

Nguyen and colleagues add an adaptive weighting scheme that rebalances the loss parts during training. No manual penalty tuning is needed, and gradients stay steadier. On elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic test problems, the method converged faster and more robustly than the conventional design. Boundaries held exactly throughout training.
arxiv-2606-23559:
The MicroBooNE Collaboration reports the first measurement of a key neutrino interaction on argon using transverse kinematic imbalance, in a 2026 particle physics paper. Neutrinos are elusive particles. Future experiments such as DUNE must infer their energy from the debris they leave in a detector. That inference depends on modeling how the nucleus reshapes the outgoing particles, through effects called final-state interactions. Resonance-like events, where the neutrino excites a baryon state, dominate near the peak of the planned DUNE beam.

The team rebuilds the momenta of the muon, the leading proton, and the neutral pion from each event. Ten measured cross-section patterns are compared against several interaction models. Together they give a detailed portrait of the pion-proton final state. The sobering result is that no model considered can match all the measured patterns at once. That gap marks where interaction modeling must improve before precision oscillation studies.
arxiv-2606-24159:
Crenshaw, McQuinn, and Werk measure dust floating around other galaxies, using a sliver of early Rubin Observatory data. Galaxies are wrapped in circumgalactic gas. Its dust reddens the light of background galaxies passing behind. Working with just a few square degrees of ComCam Data Preview 1, the team stacks background galaxy colours around foreground positions sorted by photometric redshift.

A clear reddening profile emerges. It stretches from near the foreground galaxies out to a megaparsec away. Read through a Milky Way extinction curve, the dust column falls steeply with distance. The innermost bin reaches a level comparable to high-latitude extinction through our own galaxy. Amplitude and slope agree with earlier Sloan, KiDS, and DES results. That holds despite a far smaller survey area and a fainter foreground sample. The 2026 result previews what the full survey will map routinely.
arxiv-2606-24259:
Mohammad and Bayazıt re-engineer fine-tuned language encoders, so one model can serve many text tasks without each task corrupting the others. Mixed deployments face mismatched inductive biases per task. Class imbalance warps feature statistics. No channel exists for outside lexical knowledge. Their 2026 framework, SURGeLLM, answers each problem with a small light module inside a unified transformer.

A surgical feature gate learns a per-dimension weighting over chosen lexical indicators, collapsing to the identity when those features carry no signal. Task-conditioned prefix tokens announce the task and binned feature values at every input. Instance-Weighted Normalization strips class-prior bias from the gate's statistics. Across four tasks — sentiment, multi-hop retrieval, prompt attribution, and authorship detection — the full variant posts the best average scores, with the largest jump on authorship detection. A control using random vocabulary confirms the gains come from genuine lexical signal, not extra parameters.
arxiv-2606-24759:
Xiaowei Gao and six colleagues present UniDrive, a framework that explains driving risks in words and points at them on the image. Multimodal language models read driving scenes well, but two weaknesses persist. Models using single frames or low resolution miss small, distant, or partly hidden hazards. Language centred models often give explanations with little grounded evidence. UniDrive merges a temporal branch with a high resolution perception branch.

A gated cross attention module fuses the two branches. From the fused representation, UniDrive writes natural language risk descriptions. It also outputs bounding boxes around the risky objects. On the DRAMA Reasoning benchmark, it beats representative image and video baselines at both captioning and grounding. The validation split shows its best overall performance there. Gao and colleagues also report strengths in small object localisation. Zero shot transfer to NuScenes and BDD100K works well, and human raters trust its explanations.
arxiv-2606-24859:
Samuel Laliberte and Reiko Toriumi add new constraints to the tensor bootstrap, a method that bounds tensor integrals using positivity. Tensor models organise interacting degrees of freedom into higher rank tensors, serving quantum gravity hopes and SYK model variants. Recently suggested positivity constraints can bound arbitrary unitary tensor integrals. The authors explore two variants of those constraints. One variant is built from open bubbles, tensor like objects made by removing a tensor from a bubble invariant. The other uses colour matrices from removing a colour contraction.

With these constraints, Laliberte and Toriumi obtain sharp bounds on unitary tensor integrals at finite N. Finite N is the regime where large N simplifications fail. The bounds also probe how far the integrals stray from Gaussian behaviour. Universality would predict Gaussian like answers; the deviations measure what tensor structure adds. The work extends the bootstrap toolkit rather than closing the subject.
arxiv-2606-24959:
Stefan Haas, Luca Killmaier, Alireza Javanmardi, and Eyke Hüllermeier build a conformal prediction method for ordinal classification. Ordinal problems, where labels have a natural order, arise in medicine and finance, and mistakes differ in severity. The approach gives distribution free sets with coverage guarantees. The authors propose the ranked probability score, a proper scoring rule over cumulative forecasts, as the nonconformity function. The score reflects ordinal risk naturally, yet conformal work has neglected it.

Used as the nonconformity measure, the score yields median centred contiguous prediction sets. The method is model agnostic and handles assessed and grouped ordered outcomes. It also runs faster than greedy interval selection procedures. Across image and tabular datasets, the sets stay in one piece. The balance between set width and the size of ordinal miscoverage beats conformal methods. Haas and colleagues argue the score deserves to become the default choice.
arxiv-2606-25459: This paper probes in the wild: a case study of self-supervised speech representations on Mandarin sub-dialects. The probing probes. Their probing is in the wild. The representations are self-supervised speech. It is speech. The probing is Mandarin sub-dialects case study.
arxiv-2606-25559:
Decentralised software still evolves through centralised platforms, volunteer maintainers, and goodwill, a mismatch Stan Verlaan and Johan Pouwelse confront in 2026. Their prototype, TwoStepDemocracy, moves the whole evolution loop onto peer to peer rails. Costly cryptographic identities keep voting honest, users propose and vote on issues, developers submit solutions, and accepted work connects to voluntary Bitcoin funding campaigns held outside any custodian. Demand, approval, and payment are deliberately kept apart.

That separation is the point: money can back a solution but never buys extra voting weight. Storage, identity, and funding costs were measured across the prototype's moving parts. Results show the coordination layer is technically feasible as local, signed, peer to peer software. Whether real communities would actually govern themselves this way remains untested, and the authors say so plainly.
arxiv-2606-25859:
Thekla Hamm, Bart Jansen, and Faezeh Motiei study the computational hardness of designing power networks. A network is not one tree but several, each rooted at the same source, each serving a subset of terminals so no line is overloaded. Costs mix cable length with trench digging, and sharing a trench among cables can save money, which couples the placement choices tightly.

Variants split by voltage level. Low-voltage networks lose power over distance, so tree depth must stay bounded, while high-voltage networks face no such cap. With the terminal count as the parameter, the team shows many variants are W-one-hard, meaning no efficient algorithm tuned to that parameter is expected. One positive result survives: for planar low-voltage inputs they give an XP algorithm, powered by a nontrivial treewidth bound for solution subgraphs.
arxiv-2606-25959:
Jinming Zhang and colleagues merge two audio jobs that meeting software usually runs in sequence: speech enhancement, which cleans noise from voices, and automatic gain control, which evens out loudness. Running gain first can amplify the noise, while cleaning first can erase quiet speech. Their SE-AGCNet framework trains both tasks together in one network, designed for meetings where speakers vary widely in volume.

Synergy between the tasks is the point: enhancement that protects quiet speech gives the gain stage something to work with. A companion data pipeline, SE-AGC-DataGen, simulates training material, and scoring uses standard loudness measures including integrated loudness in LUFS and loudness range. Across their experiments the joint system reaches target loudness reliably while improving speech quality and speech-recognition accuracy over strong separate-module baselines.
arxiv-2606-26259:
F. Espinoza-Arancibia and colleagues characterize double Cepheids, rare binary systems where both stars pulse as Cepheids. Such pairs pin down Cepheid origins, evolution, and pulsation theory with unusual firmness. Ten systems are known, and only one had measured parameters before this work. Nine newly identified pairs, in the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds, get the full treatment here. A recently introduced method, extended for double Cepheids, does the measuring.

Periods stand in for the missing mass ratio. The team combines both components' pulsation periods with evolutionary and pulsation models, testing first-crossing, blue-loop, and mixed life-stage configurations. Eighteen Cepheids gain first estimates of age, mass, radius, temperature, and luminosity. One Galactic pair's measured mass ratio fits a first-crossing plus blue-loop pairing. Several systems show mass ratios below one, hinting at past interactions between the partners.
arxiv-2606-26459:
Ben Adcock, Simone Brugiapaglia, and Avi Gupta improve a key step in sparse approximation. Many functions are nearly sparse, meaning a few building blocks from a large dictionary describe them well. Compressed sensing recovers such functions from random point samples. First, though, the endless dictionary must be cut down to a finite list. That cut introduces a truncation error at the sample points.

Standard bounds treat that error in the worst case. They ignore the randomness of the sample points entirely. The dictionary must then stay unnecessarily large, which inflates computing cost. The authors exploit the random structure of the samples instead. Their new bound follows the faster-decaying average error rather than the worst case. Smaller truncation sets and cheaper recovery follow. Applications to two weighted function spaces show the gains in practice.
arxiv-2606-26759:
Hrishika P, Manpreet Kaur, Suneel Dutt, Harleen Dahiya, and Arvind Kumar compute how hot, dense, magnetised matter changes the magnetic moments of decuplet baryons. Baryons are three-quark particles. The decuplet family includes the Delta and Omega particles. Their setting is strange matter, rich in strange quarks, with unequal numbers of up and down quarks, inside a strong magnetic field.

Two quark models are chained together. A mean-field model first finds how the medium shifts quark and baryon masses. Those masses feed a second model that sums the magnetic contributions. Valence quarks, sea quarks, and their orbital motion all contribute. Landau quantisation, the bunching of charged-particle motion in a magnetic field, is included. The results map how extreme environments reshape these particles' magnetic properties.
arxiv-2606-27259:
Jiang and Holmes-Cerfon give coders a simple way to handle particles that stick. A sticky diffusion wanders like ordinary diffusion but can cling to a boundary point for random stretches before detaching. Capturing that change in code is the challenge. Their algorithm modifies the standard Euler-Maruyama scheme, the workhorse for simulating stochastic equations. In 2026, at each step it flips a weighted coin between a reflected update and a jump onto the sticky point.

The sticking chance is chosen to match the generator of the target dynamics, the operator encoding the process's rules. Weak convergence to the true sticky diffusion is proven with order one accuracy. Few moving parts keep the method easy to implement and analyse. Finance and physics models with lingering boundary behaviour gain a solid simulator. Sticky dynamics join the standard numerical toolkit.
arxiv-2606-27359:
Zenn and Geiping ask a deceptively simple question about large language models: when the model finds an answer likely, is it usually right? Decoding methods, from low-temperature sampling to best-of-N selection, shift probability toward likely outputs. Their success hinges on probability tracking correctness. The relationship is measured at four levels: across decoding methods, across settings within a method, across prompt-answer pairs, and across repeated answers to one prompt. Benchmarks and models vary widely, in a language model study published in 2026.

Within a fixed dataset, higher sequence probability does predict correctness across different prompts. That comfort ends there. Raising probability by changing decoding settings or methods does not reliably raise accuracy. For repeated answers to the same prompt, probability is a poor correctness signal. The findings draw a firm boundary around a popular intuition.
arxiv-2606-27559:
McKechnie, McDonald, and Macdonald build the missing test collection for search systems that must find information without leaking private details. Such search serves queries over collections, like internal email, that mix useful content with sensitive personal information. Developing such systems needs documents tagged for sensitivity, plus queries with relevance judgments, and the classic Enron email corpus had none. In 2026, the team crowdsources one hundred fifty query formulations across fifty topics and over eleven thousand relevance assessments for a sensitivity-labelled subset.

Language-model judgments then extend the collection with further relevance assessments and privacy labels, following current best practice for model-assisted evaluation. Baseline results are reported for relevance ranking, sensitivity tagging, and the combined task. The collection ships through standard dataset tooling with pre-built sparse and dense indices. Systems can be compared on helpfulness and discretion at once.
arxiv-2606-27659:
Generating a face from many viewpoints is easy to do badly. Each view may look real alone, yet the views disagree in shape. Yeji Choi and five colleagues present GeoFace in 2026 to enforce agreement. GeoFace is a diffusion framework with geometry built in. It starts from a single input image. It then generates many views that share one three-dimensional structure.

Two streams generate together. One stream makes the colour images. The other builds three-dimensional face geometry. Shared attention layers let the streams interact. A new alignment loss supervises that attention using three-dimensional correspondences. Geometry is stored as a canonical UV position map from a FLAME mesh fitted to the views. Tests on RenderMe-360 and NeRSemble show consistent wins. GeoFace beat existing methods on visual quality and cross-view consistency, with the largest gains under big pose changes.
arxiv-2606-27759:
Binary neural networks store weights and activations as single bits. They are cheap to run but hard to train from scratch. The standard straight-through estimator creates a mismatch that deepens with depth. Evan Gibson Smith and Bashima Islam study a different axis in 2026: when and where binarisation is enforced. Their method, StoMPP, binarises layer by layer from input to output. Stochastic partial masks with soft refresh manage the transition.

StoMPP works as a fully estimator-free training rule on its own. On a binary ResNet-50, it beat the standard estimator clearly. Gains grew with depth across CIFAR and ImageNet tests. Adding the estimator only on frozen entries improved results further. One mechanism explains both regimes. Progression order is decisive. Forward progression prevents depth collapse, while reverse progression falls to near-chance accuracy. Committed binary activations block gradient flow upstream, the authors show. Ordering controls when those blockades form.
arxiv-2606-28059:
E-commerce platforms rerank search results to raise revenue from paid promotions. Pure revenue maximisation can hurt relevance and raise fraud risk, though. Svetlana Shirokovskikh and five colleagues formulate reranking as constrained optimisation in 2026. An integer linear program maximises revenue under per-query limits on other metrics. Solving it exactly per query is too slow for production. Their algorithm, PermR, swaps neighbouring items step by step. Each swap either improves the objective or repairs a violated constraint.

Offline tests span several categories of a large classified platform. PermR achieves about sixty-three percent of the exact solver's revenue improvement, within production latency limits and preserving all constraints. A fourteen-day online A/B test over fifty-six million queries followed. Revenue rose by about two percent. Open-source solvers were too slow, and a genetic algorithm gave too little uplift.
arxiv-2606-28559:
H. Zou, presenting work for the DESI Collaboration, builds the fake universes that a real survey is graded against. The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument maps high-redshift galaxies to probe how structure grew. Emission-line galaxies and quasars serve as its tracers, and mock catalogs let the team test every analysis step on a universe whose true contents are known.

The mocks grow inside the Uchuu simulation, a vast N-body calculation, filled by a modified abundance-matching method that ties galaxies to dark matter halos. Quasars fill one redshift window, emission-line galaxies another, with satellites chosen for low relative speeds. Number densities and clustering patterns are matched across scales from one to one hundred megaparsecs. Large-scale clustering bias is measured in data and mocks alike, sharpening how lightcones are built and the galaxy-halo connection.
arxiv-2606-29159:
Hu, Liu and Fu audit how offline root-cause analysis benchmarks rank competing methods. Such benchmarks, used to judge systems that diagnose faults in software services, commonly pool scores across many subsystems into one leaderboard. Engineers then read the pooled winner as the best choice for their own subsystem, an inference the authors question.

Their audit covers three public benchmark families, eleven subsystems and 778 matched scoring units, with four methods compared on identical cases. All six pairwise comparisons showed subsystem-level effects in both directions: each method won somewhere and lost elsewhere. Every pooled prediction interval crossed zero, and interaction tests rejected the idea that cases are interchangeable in most pairs. Selecting on all but one subsystem often picked the loser for the held-out one, with regret reaching about twenty-five points in the worst case. The team release a compact audit module recomputing these stability checks.
arxiv-2606-29359:
Lu, Cheng and Huang propose a new place to hunt for a puzzling particle structure called G(3900). It was seen in electron-positron collisions producing pairs of D mesons, but its nature is unclear. It may be a genuine resonance, a real particle, or a fake peak from charmonium interference and threshold effects.

They propose producing it instead in a kaon-proton reaction that yields a strange D meson, a Lambda_c baryon and the neutral G(3900). In that channel the interference that muddies the original signal is absent. Using an effective Lagrangian approach, they model the reaction as central production through D meson exchanges, treating G(3900) as a molecular state of two heavier D mesons. They include initial-state interactions that substantially boost the rate. Measured cross sections and angular distributions, they argue, could reveal whether G(3900) is a genuine resonance.
arxiv-2606-29559:
Akeno proves results about Goldbach primes, the primes that appear in representations of even numbers as a sum of two primes. The Goldbach setting is classic number theory. His object is the set of primes p where both p and the complementary value are prime for a given even target. The key quantity is its level of distribution, a measure of how evenly that set spreads across arithmetic progressions.

He proves that for almost all even integers, this set of Goldbach primes has a stated level of distribution. Two applications follow. First, almost all even integers can be written as a sum of two primes whose difference plus one is an almost-prime with few prime factors. Second, a similar statement holds for almost all even integers divisible by six.
arxiv-2606-29759:
Qin and five co-authors present GoodDiffusion, a proactive copyright scheme for diffusion bridge models that transform inputs into images. 

GoodDiffusion instead builds authorization into its own process, borrowing from backdoor methods. Queries carrying valid signatures generate at high quality. Other inputs are refused. The authors show that naive static signatures are fragile: a surrogate can be recovered by gradient-based optimization. Their fix is a Learnable Signature Network that assigns a signature specific to each input. Experiments validate that unauthorized use is blocked while authorized quality stays strong. The code is released for other groups to test.
arxiv-2606-30659:
Dhiman Bhadra and Nicholas Polson study horseshoe priors for small area estimation, the task of estimating quantities for many small regions from thin survey data. Direct survey estimates per area are noisy, so statisticians borrow strength across areas. One tradition smooths each area toward its geographic neighbours. Another shrinks area effects globally with heavy-tailed priors, which pull weak signals hard but leave strong ones nearly alone.

The pair analyse the horseshoe version of the Fay-Herriot model with known, unequal sampling variances. They prove a tail-robustness result: the posterior mean leaves strongly signalled areas almost unshrunk, bounding outlier influence, unlike Gaussian models whose shrinkage grows without bound. They also transfer sharp contraction theory to this unequal-variance setting, and map when smoothing beats shrinkage and vice versa. On Scottish lip cancer data, smoothing predicted held-out districts best, while the horseshoe flagged the exceptional districts that smoothing hid.
arxiv-2606-30759:
Kun Cheng, Tao Han, Guanghui Li and Bin Yan work out how to read quantum information from pairs of photons produced at lepton colliders. Photon pairs have been a laboratory for entanglement and Bell inequality tests at low energy, but extending such tests to high-energy colliders had not been explored. Their trick is photon conversion: on-shell photons convert in detector material, leaving tracks from which the pair's quantum state can be reconstructed.

The team formulate a factorisation framework and an effective two-qubit description of the pair. Applying it to data from the Belle experiment, they estimate that a Bell inequality violation of seven point four standard deviations could be achieved. The framework could also measure quantum discord and nonstabilizerness, two quantum resources, to precisions of a few percent. Reconstructed results matched the kinematic approach for real photons, and the formalism extends to other spin-one systems.
arxiv-2606-30959:
Renato Campanini maps what existing data force any account of quarkonium suppression in small collision systems to look like. In busy proton-proton and proton-lead collisions, excited Upsilon states are suppressed in a hierarchy. In heavy-ion physics that pattern is a classic sign of deconfined matter. Campanini's work is a constraint analysis, not a new measurement or model. He gathers six tests from public CMS and LHCb data. They cover isolation, sectors around the beam, event shape, momentum ordering, long-range links and the forward-backward imbalance.

Together, the tests rule against mechanisms driven only by local track density or by total event activity. They fit an early pattern instead: global, linked across the event, and sensitive to its shape. The activity level where suppression switches on also matches a known change in soft-particle behaviour.
arxiv-2606-31059:
Lu, Jia, and Lee model wormlike micellar fluids, soapy solutions whose long, flexible molecular chains constantly break and rejoin. That breaking and recombination gives the fluids striking behavior, including shear banding, where flow splits into layers moving at different rates under nearly constant stress. Older two-species models track only long and short chains, which blurs intermediate structures and broad relaxation behavior.

The authors add a third species, a gel network, and build a cascade breakage model in which gel breaks into long chains and long chains into short ones. The extra pathway produces a three-mode viscoelastic response, a better match to high-frequency measurements, and a flow curve that flattens into a stress plateau with coexisting shear bands. The model also reproduces stress overshoot and multistep relaxation after shear stops.
arxiv-2606-31159:
Siddiq, Rahman, and Santos run the first large study of security calibration in code-writing language models. Calibration asks whether a model's confidence matches reality. A model that sounds sure about insecure code is dangerous, because developers may ship the flaw. The team calls that failure mode False Trust.

They tested GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, and Qwen3-Coder-Next at several temperature settings. Two benchmarks were used: self-contained security tasks and multi-language, repository-level contexts. Overconfidence was common across all three models. Models judged security outcomes more reliably than functional correctness, an interesting split. Calibration-guided repair of vulnerable code helped only a little, and often broke working functions. Gating strategies improved calibration on the controlled benchmark. In realistic repository settings, though, calibration got worse, raising the risk of confident but vulnerable output.
arxiv-2606-31259:
Mai and three colleagues present SwiftAudio, a fast text-to-audio generator that learns from captions alone. Diffusion text-to-audio models sound strong but need many denoising steps, which slows them down. Earlier one-step methods still required paired text and audio during distillation, the training stage where a student copies a teacher.

SwiftAudio adapts variational score distillation to audio and adds a temporal smoothness rule that keeps latent sound coherent over time. The student inherits the teacher's skill with no paired audio at all, training on roughly 45,000 captions only. On AudioCaps and Clotho it leads strict one-step methods and closes much of the gap to multi-step systems. The result shows caption-only training can make audio generation both quick and data-light.
arxiv-2606-31359:
Benning and three colleagues test a celebrated claim about a perovskite said to cut one photon into two. Ytterbium-doped CsPbCl3 was reported to emit with quantum yield above 100 percent, which would boost silicon solar cells. Many groups matched those yields, yet others could not, leaving the quantum cutting story in doubt.

Photon-correlation tests settle the question by looking for photon bunching, the paired arrival true cutting should cause. Nanocrystals and bulk samples show no bunching at all, and under focused excitation they show anti-bunching instead. An Auger quenching path, where extra energy is lost to another charge, explains the pattern at high power. High yields alone, the team conclude, do not prove cutting happened.
arxiv-2606-31459:
Peterzil settles a classification question for Fuchsian groups with torsion. These are discrete groups of motions of the hyperbolic plane, and torsion means some of their elements are rotations. Bergfalk and Smythe had shown that surfaces can be classified by concrete invariants, and they asked whether the same holds for orbifolds, where torsion appears.

Peterzil answers yes. In that setting too, the action on discrete subgroups that are finitely generated admits concrete classification. A second result follows: a nonsingular ergodic space for the group, with large finitely generated stabilizers, must be homogeneous. The proofs rest on Selberg's lemma and a Greenberg result on commensurators, the near-symmetries of a subgroup. Concrete classification is a strong form of order for a classification problem.
arxiv-2606-31659:
Shui and eight others report an experiment on quantum tunneling, the process by which particles cross barriers they classically could not surmount, when many particles act on each other at once. Single-particle tunneling is well understood, but many-body effects have stayed mostly unknown. The team built a hexagonal-triangular quantum simulator with cold atoms in laser-made lattices, controlling barrier height, temperature and interaction strength, each on its own.

In the weak-interaction regime, the critical tunneling coefficient grows with the square of temperature under varied setups, unlike the linear growth of the single-particle case. Pushing interactions beyond the mean-field regime lowers the scaling exponent, matching what quantum field theory predicts. The results show how interactions among particles reshape a basic quantum process, with relevance for correlated quantum materials and devices.
arxiv-2606-31859:
Kramer proposes Review Residuals, a change to how transformer layers accept their own updates. Standard residual connections add each sublayer's proposed update with a fixed weight of one. Nothing checks the update before committing it, an arrangement borrowed from no safety-critical field. Kramer borrows independent verification instead: check a proposed action before taking it.

A learned gate, conditioned on both the current state and the proposed update itself, scales each update before it joins the stream. A convex Highway-style gate revives vanishing gradients and fails past about 20 layers, while the additive form trains at all depths tested. Across five sizes from 60 million to one billion parameters, benefits appear only at scale, reaching significance at 590 million.
arxiv-2606-31959:
Hou and three colleagues present AnyBokeh, a framework for editing photographic bokeh from a single image taken under unknown settings. Depth of field shapes attention and depth cues, but most editors assume an all-in-focus input. Refocusing pipelines that first rebuild a sharp image throw away the source blur cues and let reconstruction errors leak into the edit.

AnyBokeh estimates the source blur state directly, using a signed circle-of-confusion map alongside a disparity map. A linear relation between the two yields a source-specific optical fingerprint, which is transferred to the target focus and aperture. A generative editor conditioned on both blur maps then synthesizes the result. A synthetic dataset with exact depth and full camera metadata supports the training.
arxiv-2608-00059:
Yin and Cardona build an automated method to infer neural circuit function. Connectome maps now exist, but reading circuits from them is the hard step. Their method, LLantia, uses language models for that reading. It first pulls cell-type functions from the literature. With the connectome, it then infers functions for all other cell types.

Results are ordered in a hierarchy of possible circuit functions. Each function sits under behavioural and physiological contexts. Subcircuit descriptions and linked cell types accompany each claim. That structure lets readers trace claims back to published work. The team applied it to the adult fruit fly brain. They also tested select broader circuits inside it. Checks against later literature backed their findings, they report.
arxiv-2608-00259:
Kamahori and co-authors present Themis, a software-defined approach to hardware prefetching. Cache misses eat a large share of stall cycles in datacenter work. Hardware prefetchers fetch data ahead to cut those stalls. Aggressive prefetching wastes memory bandwidth on wrong guesses. Bandwidth is scarce in multi-tenant datacenters, so waste hurts.

They observe that bad prefetches can be filtered at page granularity. Coverage need not fall in the process. Storing per-page usefulness data in hardware is costly, though. Themis lets software direct where hardware should prefetch. Page-level hints in page-table entries disable the prefetcher for set pages at runtime. No binary or ISA changes are needed. Useless prefetch requests fell by about 40 percent. All evaluated prefetchers sped up on datacenter workloads.
bunsen-egypts-place-universal-history-vo:
Christian Bunsen weighs his proofs in Vol. 3 of Egypt's Place in Universal History, out in English in 1859. Two tomes have told the tale and set the dates. This mid tome turns to the raw stuff: king lists, priest tales, and the writ stones from which all dates must be drawn and checked with care.

Bunsen shows his work here, scrap by scrap. Fans can see where each claim rests and where it shakes. Few read such store rooms for fun. Yet this is where his whole scheme stands or falls. Its worth is in its proofs.
calmet-dissertations-upon-apparitions-17:
Dom Augustin Calmet's Dissertations upon the Apparitions of Angels, Daemons, and Ghosts appeared in English in 1759, its first English translation. Calmet was a French Benedictine abbot and Bible scholar. He turned the same care he gave to scripture toward reports of spirits and the returning dead.

Calmet sorted cases of angels, demons, ghosts, and vampires, and asked what proof each report really had. He quoted witnesses, church writers, and tales from lands where vampire fears ran high. Often he left the verdict open, urging readers to doubt easy belief and easy scorn alike. The book set the terms for later debate on apparitions.
chambers-testimony-1859:
Robert Chambers asks science to hear proof fair in Testimony, his brief tract of 1859. Chambers was the hid hand back of a famed book on life's growth that shook his age. Here he turns to the dark room. His point is one of law: proof must be weighed by its weight, not spurned for its theme's strangeness.

He prints his own tests and tales from men he trusts. The tract is short, yet its plea is shrewd. It shows how the faith won men of mind, not just crowds. Its calm sets it past hot tracts.
charlotte-s-inheritance-pg9259:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon's novel is arranged as ten books, each with its own motto-like title. Book One, De Profundis, begins with Lenoble of Beaubocage in the Paris of the Bourbons. Cafés, law students, and an exile's household set the French foundation. Banishment follows despair in the opening chapters' own words.

Book Two traces Susan Lenoble downhill, forgiven too late. The Horatiad, Book Three, turns retrospective and epistolary. Captain Paget awakens to duty in Book Four, and takes a coadjutor. Normandy hosts Diana in Book Six, at Côtenoir. A cloud of fear, a fight against time, and a dread revelation drive the last books. Valentine's skeleton and Dr. Jedd's opinion are among the secrets forced into daylight.
cia-0000012259:
A reported attempt at provocation, with names and details blanked out, is the subject of a CIA operational item from November 1960. The file carries an attached routing slip and a record of decisions, the paper trail such incidents generated. In the Cold War's gray zones, staged incidents and false alarms were tools both sides understood well.

What survives is the outline: a provocation was reported, and officers recorded how it moved through the system. The blanks hide who acted and where, but the shape of the response remains. The item preserves one of those murky episodes that were never fully explained.
cia-0000012359:
Two names are blacked out in the title of a June 1962 note about a meeting at a Fourth of July reception. Somewhere in the Penkovsky file's social margins, a redacted person met another at the holiday party. Receptions were working ground in the secret world, where talk over drinks could move what memos could not.

The note captures that social side in a single line of record. Espionage ran amid fireworks and small talk as readily as in safe houses. For readers, the fragment is a festive footnote: proof that the case's business followed its people even into a celebration.
cia-0000013859: Hai Phong Province is where an American pilot was captured, in a CIA note dated June 4, 1967. Hai Phong was North Vietnam's main port and was ringed by guns and missiles. Pilots who fell there were deep inside enemy ground. The note adds one more airman to the list of men held in the north.
cia-0000014459: An updated report on a Soviet ground forces brigade in Cuba is dated August 2, 1979. The report revisits a unit whose presence on the island drew sharp U.S. attention. Soviet troops in Cuba had been a sore point since the missile crisis years. A fresh update in 1979 fed a public row in Washington over what the brigade meant.
cia-0000014659: Mexican sovereignty is an odd heading for a CIA file dated March 5, 1957, naming Morton Sobell. The file also names Luis Sanchez Ponton and Alfred Stern. Stern was a rich American tied by rumor to the Sobell case who had moved to Mexico. The mix of names shows how one spy case could cross borders and touch foreign pride.
cia-0000015359: An FCDA meeting is the clipped subject of a CIA file dated March 4, 1953. The civil defense agency met the day before its follow up file in this set. Two files on one meeting show the paper a single session could spawn. Saucers, panic, and public warning sat on that table together.
cia-0000015459: Meetings of the Office of Scientific Intelligence and its scientific advisers are reported in a CIA record dated in 1953. That office gave the agency its science staff, the people who first handled saucer claims. Meeting reports show the subject being worked through normal channels. The entry is a plain window on staff process during the first winter of official saucer study.
cia-0000022359: Soviet criminal law calls espionage the most dangerous of state crimes, a point kept in a CIA record dated in 1960. The heading quotes the law's spirit in the catalog's rough spelling. For Powers, that law set the frame of his Moscow trial. Filing the statute's claim helped American readers grasp the peril the pilot faced in a Soviet court.
cia-0000023359: More information on American prisoners reportedly held in North Vietnam fills a CIA record dated in 1979. Reportedly does the honest work in the title, marking the claim as unproven. Six years after the homecoming, reports like this still arrived and still were checked. The late date shows the prisoner question outliving the war by years, with no clean end.
cia-0000026759: The Arab-Israeli arms problem, with relative capabilities and the prospects for control, is weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1958. Israel and its Arab neighbors were arming hard a decade after the 1948 war. Comparing their strength, and asking whether arms could be curbed, were linked tasks. The paper forms part of the long effort to read that balance before it broke into war.
cia-0000037159:
Alleged sightings of Caucasian prisoners held in the Socialist Republic of Vietnam fill a CIA record dated April 1, 1983. The reports claimed that Western men were still jailed years after the war. Vietnam denied holding any such prisoners, which made each claim hard to settle.

Inside are the sightings as they reached the agency, kept for checking and comparison. Analysts set new reports beside old ones, looking for detail that held together. The file captures the uncertainty at the heart of the postwar POW and MIA debate. Reports of this kind arrived from travelers, traders, and refugees, each with a different story to tell.
cia-0000049059: El Salvador's minister of defense worried in 1983 about a possible reduction, the title cut off before saying of what. A CIA item from that year preserves his concern, kept with the Truth Commission records. Ministers in San Salvador lived by Washington's decisions, and even the hint of a cut could move policy.
cia-0000049159: The FMLN decided in 1990 to postpone a planned national offensive, in part because its front groups could not play their assigned role. A CIA item from that year preserves the decision, kept with the Truth Commission records. Postponements told watchers as much as attacks: about strain, timing, and a movement husbanding its strength.
cia-0000049259: The fourth update on the Jesuit killings is preserved in a CIA item from 1990, kept under the Truth Commission's eye. By the fourth installment, the case had settled into the pattern that defined it: pressure abroad, silence at home, and paper in between. The item adds its layer to that pattern's record.
cia-0000096659: The New Look in Chinese Communist Aid to Sub-Saharan Africa is the title of declassified CIA document 0000096659, dated August 1, 1968. The heading promises a changed pattern in Chinese aid to the region. Readers get a short declassified paper on that aid subject, part of the agency's wider tracking of Chinese activity abroad.
cia-0000102959:
Corrective labor camps located in Karaganda Oblast are listed in declassified CIA document 0000102959, dated June 3, 1987. The sample names camp offices under the Internal Affairs administration for that region of the USSR. It uses the terms corrective labor camp and corrective labor establishment as interchangeable names.

General regime prisoners got more parcels, more visitors, and somewhat better food and living terms than strict regime prisoners. Average general regime terms ran one to five years, while strict regime inmates usually served ten years or more. One strict camp held about four hundred prisoners, split into living and work zones behind barbed wire fences.
cia-0000109059: Bolsheviks and Heros: the USSR and Cuba is the heading, with heroes misspelled, on declassified CIA document 0000109059, dated October 2, 1967. The title pairs two revolutions in one short, literary line. Bolsheviks names the Soviet side, Cuba the other, in the heading itself. The brief record is a relations study item, filed in the autumn of 1967 as released.
cia-0000126859: An April 1966 CIA memorandum to the White House concerns Ramparts magazine, with its subject line deleted before release. Ramparts was the muckraking monthly that would soon expose agency funding of student groups. The memo preserves the agency's message to the president, minus its heading. Within a year Ramparts printed the exposure the agency feared, a sequence that makes this early memo read like the first move in a losing fight.
cia-0000126959: A November 1965 CIA document bears the single-word heading Venezuela. The country was then fighting a leftist insurgency while its young democracy held on. The paper preserves the entry under that plain label, part of the agency's standing file on the nation. One-word headings usually marked a standing country file being fed, and this entry's plain label hides whatever mixture of politics and insurgency its pages carried.
cia-0000132159: Iraq-Kuwait situation report 476, dated January 1991, notes Iraq widening its reserve call-up while the French join something the heading leaves unfinished. Saddam was calling up men as the coalition against him assembled. The report tracks that military buildup. Reserve call-ups were tracked as a readiness dial, since each widening told analysts how large a war Iraq was preparing its public and army to fight.
cia-0000132659: An aid pact signed by Communist China with Cuba fills a CIA paper dated November 4, 1960. The pact also promised more trade between the two states. Havana had now won backing from two communist giants in a single year. Beijing's pledge was formal and on paper at last. The short paper covers the pact and its main terms.
cia-0000132759: Cuba drawing its Soviet bloc ties tighter fills a CIA paper dated May 1, 1960. Each new tie made the break with Washington harder to undo later. The embrace between Havana and the bloc grew closer month by month that year. The short paper tracks the tightening in trade, arms, and public statements as analysts recorded it that spring.
cia-0000135859: A CIA meeting record from 1 July 1952, now declassified, deals with a conference with a person whose name is deleted, held in the summer of 1952. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136159: On 6 April 1954, the agency filed a cable, now declassified, on transmitting messages verbatim, word for word with no paraphrase, for PRINCEP and ONTRICH. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136259: Press file in the declassified files, dated 6 May 1954, covers a Guatemala press digest covering the fifteenth through the seventeenth of June, filed in May. Behind the paper stands PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA campaign against President Arbenz that closed with the 1954 coup in Guatemala. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136359: Messages numbered 17, 18, and 19 from the SECANT base are transmitted in this June 1954 LINCOLN cable, and they show confusion after the pact. One sender has learned of the pact but says the Zacapa road system is in danger and the troops are not aware of junta authority. Another reports the liberation army demoralized by the latest news, disgusted officers, and a request for a plane. Victory, on the ground, looked like disorder.
cia-0000136559: Filed in the Spanish texts of Brigade 2506, this document is dated 4 November 1960. That week produced a dense cluster of brigade records in this release. The brigade itself was a CIA-trained unit of Cuban exiles preparing to invade Cuba. The catalog assigns this item no subject heading. It survives in Spanish as released, and it is identified here by its date and its place in the brigade's papers.
cia-0000136759: A Spanish document dated 3 January 1961, filed with the 2506 Brigade papers in the CIA's declassified release. The brigade was training that week for the invasion of Cuba, still a secret plan. The catalog record gives this item no subject. It survives in the original Spanish, part of the early-January run of brigade records, and is identified here by its date and collection.
cia-0000136959: Prepare for the worst while PAGE is inside Guatemala, headquarters advises in May 1954. Frank Wisner signed the cable. LINCOLN made the correct decision in returning PAGE. A calculated risk can still win big results. His knowledge, ability, and relationships are the prize. Difficulties around the CALLIGERIS effort are growing. One step is urged. The station should plan embassy action now. The plan would cover PAGE's arrest or disappearance. His stay should be as short as possible.
cia-0000141159:
Declassified CIA cable traffic from November 1961 deals with two linked tasks after the failed Bay of Pigs landing in Cuba. Headquarters tells a station that a security officer and an associate will arrive on 4 November 1961, on Pan Am flight 551. The two men already hold rooms at the Gran Hotel, and the station is asked to meet them there.

The same cable turns to the crew of B-26 number 933, an armed bomber painted with Cuban markings. Its wreck had been found in jungle near the Bocay River in Nicaragua. The station is told to remove the remains, hold them under control at Managua, and wait for orders on final handling.
cia-03177759:
The Turkish-Syrian border opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 13 November 1957. Turkish manoeuvres, mostly ground forces with some air coordination, run until 15 November. Syria renews charges of an imminent attack. Afterwards the Turks are expected to pull back to permanent stations. One F-86 squadron near the border has already gone home.

Egypt deepens its military hold on Syria in the second item. Between one and fifteen hundred Egyptian troops are now there. Egyptian officers will command several Syrian armoured and parachute companies, and inspect logistics that week. Jordan's politics, a British move against Omani rebels set for 15 November, and Laos follow. Communists lead early returns in Indonesia's Jogjakarta elections, extending their Java gains. The USSR proposes exchanging scientists with Japan. Honduras is threatened by revolution.
cia-03179259:
Nepal opens a short Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 15 December 1959. Tibetans acting for Peiping have spent two months urging border tribes to owe allegiance to Tibet. A late-October clash with Khamba rebels suggests Chinese troops moving west along the undemarcated frontier. Katmandu sought written boundary guarantees in September and failed. Incursions into Nepalese territory look increasingly possible.

Ceylon is prepared to suspend its rice-rubber trade with Peiping for 1960. Colombo's terms for the next protocol must be accepted shortly, or it will buy rice elsewhere. Talks have run since late October. Ecuador now thinks the Inter-American Conference may slip to summer. A late item reports a new Soviet package proposal in the Geneva nuclear test talks. The issue is brief, and two of its three sections hold a single item each.
cia-06557559:
Terrorism Review dated 21 April 1988, numbered DI TR 88-009 and marked Secret, is a Directorate of Intelligence issue built around a chronology. The chronology lists noteworthy foreign and international terrorist events since the last issue. It warns that in some cases the actors and their motives may not be known.

Entries from February 1988 include bombs outside a court building in Dhaka, Bangladesh, injuring several people. Bombs at four district courts in the Punjab, India, killed at least eight, with Babbar Khalsa claiming responsibility. Three Red Brigades suspects were arrested in Barcelona, Spain. In Colombia, the ELN kidnapped two mayors of Huila Province, later released. Later entries cover an ETA rocket grenade attack on civil guard barracks at Llodio, Spain, and an ELN kidnapping of two journalists in Bucaramanga.
cia-06628559:
Research project progress report No. 3, dated March 1975 and marked Confidential, tests a model of political violence. The countries studied are Argentina, Ethiopia, and Thailand. The model adapts Ted Robert Gurr's frustration-aggression theory from his 1970 book Why Men Rebel, published by Princeton University Press.

The report explains that group frustration, joined with a belief that violence is justified and the means to act, drives political violence. Forms range from turmoil and insurgency to conspiracy and internal war, set by ties among groups in each country. An earlier test on Chile in mid-1973 is cited.
