Findings reported here judge actor groups in Ethiopia more than twice as frustrated as those in Argentina or Thailand. Coercive capability, though, stayed about the same across all three countries.
copyright-renewals-1959: Copyright Renewals 1959, issued by the Library of Congress Copyright Office, survives in this copy only as a placeholder note. The file states plainly that it is an unused, empty reservation, kept for an ebook in the United States Copyright Renewals series. The renewal records for 1959 were placed instead in two companion files, one covering January to June and one covering July to December. No entries, names, or listings appear here at all. A reader seeking the actual 1959 renewals must use those two companion volumes.
coriolanus-pg2259: Volumnia's plea breaks him in this edition: the proud warrior, marching on Rome with the Volscians, yields to his mother's kneeling. "O mother, mother! You have won a happy victory for Rome, but for your son a mortal one." Pride's tragedy, stark and Roman.
countess-kate-pg3259:
Charlotte M Yonge wrote Countess Kate, a novel for young readers reprinted by Macmillan in London in 1902. Kate and her sister Sylvia grow up in a clergyman's modest home, short on money and taught lessons by their older sister Mary. Early chapters show the girls dreaming of governesses, ponies, and pretty clothes they cannot have.

Then a lawyer brings startling news about a family title. Lawyers had assumed the earldom passed only to male heirs. Instead, Kate herself is Countess of Caergwent, ahead of Colonel Umfraville. Sudden rank brings money, duties, and hard lessons about pride and generosity. Yonge follows Kate as wealth tests the habits formed in a poor, loving home, in a story shaped by her strong Anglican faith.
cyril-commentary-luke-pusey-1859:
Cyril of Alexandria preached on the Gospel of Luke through a full church year at Alexandria, and 156 of his sermons survive. The Greek text is mostly lost, so the sermons come down in Syriac. R. Payne Smith translated them into English from a Syriac manuscript, and Oxford published his work in 1859.

Sermon by sermon, Cyril walks his flock through the parables, healings, and passion of Luke. He reads each scene for doctrine, above all for the unity of Christ, and then for the shaping of a Christian life. The set is one of the great sermon courses of the early church. It shows Cyril the pastor, not just Cyril the fighter.
darwin-origin-of-species-1st-ed-1859:
Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in London in 1859. The first edition states his case as he first made it, before six rounds of change. He argues that all life forms descend, with changes, from shared ancestors.

Darwin shows how breeders shape pigeons and stock by picking traits. Nature, he says, does the same work far more slowly. Species that fit their place live and breed, and the rest die out. Few books have changed science, or thought about life, our place in it, so much. He had stacked facts from farms, pigeons, and wild shores.
dee-true-faithful-relation-1659:
John Dee, Elizabeth's astrologer, spent years recording conversations with angels through the scryer Edward Kelley. Meric Casaubon printed those records in 1659 as A True and Faithful Relation. Casaubon meant the book to discredit the pair; instead he preserved the source text of Enochian magic for all later ages.

Day after day, the diaries log spirits speaking through Kelley's shew-stone. Letters, calls, and whole angelic languages arrive in session. Dee's patience and Kelley's performances make strange, gripping reading. The volume is Elizabethan England's oddest spiritual diary. Occultists still mine it as scripture, while historians read it as a window on two remarkable, entangled minds.
dickens-tale-of-two-cities-1859:
Charles Dickens published A Tale of Two Cities in 1859, set in London and Paris. Its first line, it was the best of times, is famed around the world. The French Revolution drives the plot, with the guillotine as its grim refrain throughout.

Lucie Manette frees her father from eighteen years in the Bastille in Paris. Charles Darnay, her husband, is twice tried for his life in both capitals. Sydney Carton, a wastrel lawyer, swaps places with Darnay at the scaffold in Paris. Madame Defarge knits names of the doomed into her cold register of hate. Sacrifice and resurrection give the swift tale its lasting moral weight and fire.
erckmann-chatrian-the-man-wolf-1859:
Erckmann-Chatrian tell of a lord cursed as a wolf in The Man-Wolf and Other Tales, in English from 1876. The pair were famed tale smiths of France. Their chief tale is set in a great house in the Black Forest. A guest hears of a white wolf that plagues the line, and of a wild dame of the woods whose fate is bound to the curse of the house.

Rich air and slow dread fill the tale. The mate tales deal with dreams, ghosts, and doom in the same grave tone. The book is the theme in fine dress. Its craft sets it past pulp.
europmc-pmc10088059:
Lee and co-workers report that contact points with the endoplasmic reticulum control the behavior of membraneless organelles, in a 2020 study. The endoplasmic reticulum is a membrane network inside cells that helps move ions and molecules. Membraneless organelles are droplets of proteins and RNA with no skin of their own.

The team found an unexpected interface between the network and these droplets. That contact shapes how droplets form, move, and break apart. The finding adds a new control layer to cell organization. That layer matters for health and disease alike.
europmc-pmc10838959:
Kumar and a large team review tiny cell-made sacs as tools for diagnosis and therapy in this 2024 paper. Extracellular vesicles are nano-sized sacs, meaning sacs a few billionths of a metre wide, that cells release into body fluids. They carry proteins, gene messages, and fats between cells. Blood holds many of them, though sorting them from other blood particles is hard.

Because their cargo mirrors the state of the cell that made them, these sacs can flag disease early, the authors say. In cancer, testing sacs in blood could spot tumours sooner and without surgery. Loaded with drugs, sacs could also deliver cargo to chosen cells. The review ranges over cancers, brain diseases, and diabetes. The authors see wide promise, paired with a need for better sorting methods.
europmc-pmc11153159:
Pirnay and a large multinational team report outcomes for 100 personalised virus treatments of stubborn infections in this 2024 study. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect and kill bacteria. Personalised phage therapy picks phages matched to a patient's own germ. Trials of off-the-shelf phage products had disappointed, so the team reviewed tailored cases instead.

The 100 cases ran from 2008 to 2022 across 35 hospitals in 12 countries, coordinated by a Belgian consortium. Lung, skin, and bone infections were most common. Treatment used 26 phages and six defined cocktails, sometimes pre-adapted to the target germ. Clinical improvement was reported for 77.2 percent of infections, and the target germ was cleared in 61.3 percent. Skipping antibiotics alongside phages cut the odds of clearance sharply, their analysis found.
europmc-pmc1247559:
Xia and co-authors tested which particle chemicals damage cell power stations in 2004. Diesel exhaust particles were split into chemical fractions. The question was whether particles or their cargo cause oxidative stress. Cell tests compared three fractions.

The quinone-rich polar fraction proved most potent. It generated more reactive oxygen and dropped membrane voltage. It also shrank mitochondrial mass and triggered cell death programs. In isolated mitochondria it pried open a leak pore directly. Redox-cycling quinones copied that pore effect. Xia pins ultrafine particle toxicity on specific chemicals. Mouse liver cells were used for the pore tests.
europmc-pmc1283159:
Aranzana and colleagues tested genome-wide association mapping in a model plant in 2005. The plant Arabidopsis thaliana mostly self-fertilizes. It exists as inbred lines that can be typed once and tested repeatedly. The team sampled 95 lines with genome-wide data.

Traits tested were flowering time and pathogen resistance. False positives ran extremely high due to population structure. Despite that noise, known major genes were found for every trait. Those recoveries prove the approach can work in this species. Aranzana also warns structure correction is essential for human studies. Linkage patterns in this selfing species run unusually long.
europmc-pmc1397859:
Does living near a burger joint make people heavier? Jeffery and co-authors asked that question in 2006, using a phone survey of 1,033 adults in Minnesota. They recorded height, weight, and how often each person ate out. They also mapped how close homes and jobs sat to fast food places.

Eating fast food often went with a high fat diet and a higher body mass index, a simple score of weight for height. Yet living or working near fast food places showed no link to weight or to eating there. Jeffery suggests weak measures may hide a link, or sheer spread of outlets may not drive obesity on its own.
europmc-pmc1475659:
A sensor that spots flu may also make flu worse. Le Goffic and co-authors tested that idea in mice in 2006. The sensor, TLR3, detects viral RNA in lung cells. Mice lacking it were infected with influenza A and compared with normal mice.

Mice without TLR3 made fewer swelling signals and drew fewer killer T cells into the airways. Oddly, their lungs held more virus, yet they survived better. Le Goffic concludes the sensor drives much of the harmful swelling that makes flu deadly. The work warns that a strong immune reply can harm the host more than the germ itself.
europmc-pmc1513259:
A vaccine made of short germ pieces only works if a person's immune tags can grab them. Bui and co-authors built a tool in 2006 to forecast who a vaccine would cover. Human immune tags, called HLA, come in over a thousand forms. Each form grips a unlike set of pieces.

Their algorithm uses HLA frequency data for each ethnic group. It computes the share of people who should respond to a given piece set. Builders can test designs before trials and widen coverage where it lags. Bui offers the tool free as a web application, aiming to curb ethnic bias in vaccine reach.
europmc-pmc1769359:
Parents' ratings of a child's quality of life must be trustworthy when children cannot answer. Varni, Limbers, and Burwinkle tested parent proxy reports in 2007 in 13,878 parents of children aged 2 to 16, using the PedsQL survey.

Missing answers ran at just 2.1 percent, showing the survey is feasible by proxy. Most scales in each age subgroup cleared the 0.70 reliability bar for group comparisons. Total scores neared or passed the higher bar. Varni concludes proxy reports are reliable and valid in each age band, backing recent FDA guidance that asks for such subgroup proof.
europmc-pmc1780059:
Doytchinova and Flower built VaxiJen in 2007, a free web server that predicts which proteins might work as vaccine parts. An antigen is a protein piece that the immune system can learn to attack. Older tools hunted antigens by lining up sequences, which misses new proteins with no close known match.

Their method skips alignment entirely. It turns each protein sequence into a fixed set of numbers based on the main traits of its amino acids, using a transform called auto cross covariance. Models trained on sets built from 100 antigens already known and an equal count of non-antigens covered bacteria, viruses, and tumors. In checks the models scored between 70 and 89 percent correct. VaxiJen was the first server of its kind.
europmc-pmc1794559:
Carpenter, Sabatini and colleagues introduced CellProfiler in 2006, free open-source software that measures cells in microscope images. Modern microscopes can gather thousands of cell images in a day from drug or gene screens. Scoring those images by eye had become the bottleneck that slowed whole experiments.

CellProfiler lets researchers build an analysis pipeline by chaining modules, each doing one step such as finding cell borders or measuring brightness. It counts and measures many features at once, including the size, shape, and location of labeled cell parts. Unlike a human scorer, it applies the same rules to every image and can run through large screens unattended. The authors describe it as the first free system of its kind built for flexible, high-throughput cell image analysis.
europmc-pmc1976759:
Hobson and Denekamp measured in 1984 how fast the lining of blood vessels grows inside tumors compared with normal tissues. Fast vessel growth feeds tumors, and earlier single-dose labeling hinted that tumor vessel cells divide far more often. Their method gave rats of labeled thymidine, a DNA building block, every eight hours for a week.

Five experimental mouse tumors were compared with placenta and with normal tissues. Continuous labeling confirmed the large gap: tumor vessel lining had potential doubling times between 2.4 and 13 days, and placenta was at least as fast. Normal vessel lining turned over vastly more slowly, an estimated 47 to 23,000 days. That slowness held even in gut and skin, whose surface cells renew quickly, so vessel growth is set by the tissue's tumor status, not by local cell turnover.
europmc-pmc2064959:
Vazeille and colleagues compared two chikungunya virus strains in mosquitoes in 2007. In 2005 and 2006 a major outbreak hit La Réunion island, spread by the mosquito Aedes albopictus. The team fed virus to eight mosquito collections from La Réunion and three from Mayotte. One strain carried alanine at position 226 of a surface protein. The later strain carried a valine change there, called A226V.

The later strain spread through mosquitoes at least twice as fast as the earlier one. It also produced nearly 100 times more viral RNA copies in infected females. Virus reached the salivary glands within two days, ready for transmission by biting. La Réunion mosquitoes proved as efficient as other known vector species. The findings support that a highly competent local mosquito drove the outbreak.
europmc-pmc2124559:
M. C. Winternitz and C. R. Meloy measured catalase in human tissues in 1908, asking how the enzyme's strength changes in disease. Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide, and they stress that a good test must allow several readings during one experiment. That way the speed of the reaction can be followed over time.

Disease patterns emerged. In nephritis the kidney always showed the sharpest drop in activity. Blood, lung, liver, and spleen also fell, in step with the kidney lesion's severity. Nephritic urine also blocked the reaction more than normal urine. In two cases of eclampsia, by contrast, blood activity was not reduced. If that holds, they note, a blood test could tell eclampsia from nephritis before death. In pneumonia the lung changed with its stage. Readers get an early attempt to turn an enzyme into a diagnostic sign.
europmc-pmc2124759:
M. C. Winternitz and J. P. Pratt, of the Johns Hopkins pathological laboratory, tied the blood's catalytic activity to its red cells in 1910. In healthy rabbits the activity varies almost directly with the volume and number of red blood cells.

Two tests then break the pattern apart. Heating a rabbit's brain by puncture raised its temperature without changing either blood activity or white cell count. In experimental peritonitis, by contrast, blood activity always rose. It rose independently of temperature and white cells, since either could rise, fall, or stand still while activity climbed. The authors look ahead to ward use: the test might flag the start of peritonitis in typhoid fever or a burst appendix. Readers get a careful effort to make one blood measurement mean one thing.
europmc-pmc2125159:
Paul F. Clark, Francis R. Fraser, and Harold L. Amoss asked in 1914 whether the poliomyelitis virus rides in the blood. Human blood taken during the paralytic stage, and after death, failed to infect rhesus monkeys. Monkey blood at many stages of the experimental disease failed as a rule too.

One exception stands among ten tests: blood drawn at the very start of paralysis, on the seventh day after a brain inoculation, did infect. Blood taken from one to forty-eight hours after cord material was injected also failed to paralyze. Only overwhelming quantities injected into the blood produce paralysis at all; moderate doses do not, though traces of virus may linger in a sample a day. Readers get the blood ruled out as the virus's ordinary road, with the exceptions carefully weighed.
europmc-pmc2125259:
R. Burton-Opitz and Daniel R. Lucas of Columbia's physiological laboratory took up the kidney's blood supply in 1911, fifth in their series: does the vagus nerve govern the left kidney's vessels? The splanchnic nerves plainly do, by direct flow measurement. For the vagus, opinion was split and methods indirect.

Cohnheim and Roy, and Bradford after them, denied the vagus any vessel-moving fibers to the kidney; Masius argued they exist. The authors' own records answer quietly. They read them as the kidney tonically holding its bed open against a rising general pressure, keeping its own supply normal. The kidney, they add, plays a very small part in the big pressure rises those stimulations cause. Readers get a nerve acquitted by the shape of a curve.
europmc-pmc2125359:
Carroll G. Bull of the Rockefeller Institute explained in 1915 how antipneumococcus serum cures. The serum clumps pneumococci in the dish and in the body. Read under the microscope rather than by eye, it clumps them at far greater dilution than the standard test suggests, a caution about how potency was being measured.

Injected into rabbits whose blood swarms with pneumococci, the serum clears the blood fast. One experiment films it in stills: before serum, heart blood shows many separate diplococci; thirty seconds after the injection, large clumps; crushed organs then show clumped germs inside phagocytes. An earlier paper had charted how untreated septicemia runs its course by dose and virulence. Readers get the cure of serum therapy reduced to clump, carry off, and devour.
europmc-pmc2128159:
Francis G. Blake and Russell L. Cecil gave monkeys a strain of Bacillus influenzae to see whether it alone could produce influenza-like disease. Their paper is the ninth in an experimental pneumonia series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1920. The strain came from a human empyema case and had been strengthened by animal passage. Twelve monkeys received it on the nose or nose and mouth membranes.

All twelve developed an acute respiratory disease lasting three to five days, with sudden onset, deep prostration, and inflamed nose and windpipe passages. Sneezing, cough, fever in varying degree, and a scanty mucoid discharge marked the course. Five cases developed pus-filled sinus infection, and three went on to bronchopneumonia. The bacillus was recovered from the lesions at autopsy. Of ten monkeys injected into the windpipe, seven developed bronchopneumonia. The germ alone, their results say, can start the disease.
europmc-pmc2128559:
H. E. Jordan and C. C. Speidel set growth and decay running at once in frog tadpole tails, then watched the white blood cells at work. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924. Thyroid feeding drove the tail toward metamorphosis and shrinkage, while cutting part of the tail off forced regrowth, and the timing of the two treatments was varied.

Regrowth ran fastest with no thyroid at all. Thyroid given two days after the cut slowed it less than thyroid given at the cut, and thyroid given two days before slowed it most. Among the cells, neutrophils pushed tissue breakdown forward, while lymphoid eating cells hauled the debris away. Lymphocytes were too few to matter much as growth promoters here, against Carrel's suggestion. Blood-forming cells joined in as part of the general thyroid reaction. The paper sorts the white cells into wreckers, cleaners, and bystanders.
europmc-pmc2131359:
Joseph Wearn, with the technical assistance of Louise Zschiesche, counted the capillaries of the heart in a 1928 paper from the Thorndike Memorial Laboratory in Boston. Capillaries are the finest blood vessels, where exchange with tissue takes place. By injecting the coronary arteries of beating hearts, he made the whole capillary bed visible and counted it in normal heart muscle.

The supply proved very rich. Ventricular walls and papillary muscles held on average about one capillary for each muscle fiber, roughly twice the count per area that Krogh found in skeletal muscle. The ear-like upper chambers and the Purkinje system held fewer. Heart valves, though, showed no constant capillary filling. The method also suits the study of diseased hearts, Wearn notes.
europmc-pmc2140859:
John Northrop studied the swelling of isoelectric gelatin in water in a 1927 paper, part one on equilibrium conditions. A dry gelatin block in water swells as water enters, then stops. Northrop asked what balance fixes that stopping point, and wrote an equation for it.

He models gelatin as a network of insoluble material holding a solution of a more soluble part. Water enters under the osmotic pressure of the dissolved part and stretches the network until its elastic pull equals that pressure. Warmth, or long swelling, slackens the network and lets more water in. In big blocks the second swelling overlaps the first, so no clean maximum shows. Small blocks and films follow the equation given.
europmc-pmc2362859:
Culig and co-authors built a new cell model of prostate cancer resistance in 1999. Advanced prostate cancer is treated by cutting male hormone supply or blocking its receptor. Tumors often escape, and the drug bicalutamide normally blocks that receptor, called the androgen receptor.

They grew hormone-sensitive prostate cells without androgen for 87 generations, creating a subline named LNCaP-abl. The new cells carried about four times more receptor, and their resting receptor activity ran 30 times higher than the parent cells. Bicalutamide flipped roles in them: instead of blocking, it stimulated growth and switched the receptor on. In mice, bicalutamide sped growth of the new tumors while testosterone slowed it. The receptor gene itself had not mutated, showing resistance can arise without new gene changes.
europmc-pmc2592359:
Coppé and colleagues discovered in 2008 that senescent cells, cells that have permanently stopped dividing, broadcast a rich cocktail of secreted signals. Senescence protects against cancer by halting damaged cells, but what those cells release was poorly mapped. Using antibody arrays, the team measured secretions from human cells driven into senescence by DNA-damaging stress.

The cocktail, named the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, built up over several days and mixed inflammation and malignancy signals. It appeared in normal and tumour cells alike, and in prostate tumours of patients treated with DNA-damaging chemotherapy. Fed to premalignant cells, the secretions pushed them toward invasion. Two factors, IL-6 and IL-8, drove most of that push. Cancer-causing RAS amplified the effect, while losing the p53 suppressor did the same, revealing how p53 guards neighbouring tissue.
europmc-pmc2635959:
Davies and co-authors tracked harmful drug effects in hospital patients in a 2009 study of twelve wards. They followed 3,695 patient stays over six months in 2005. Every suspected bad reaction to a medicine was logged and judged for cause, severity, and whether it could have been avoided.

In total, 545 stays, about one in seven, included at least one bad reaction. Half of the reactions were judged avoidable, fully or in part. In 147 patients the reaction itself kept them in hospital longer. The medicines linked most often were water pills, strong opioid painkillers, and blood thinners. In detailed checks, the one clear risk factor was simply how many medicines a patient took. Each added drug raised the risk further.
europmc-pmc2671559:
Kaufmann and colleagues mapped in 2009 the genes switched on by SEPALLATA3, a master flower-building protein in Arabidopsis. Flowers form through homeotic genes that tell each ring of organs what to become. SEPALLATA3, from the MADS family of switch proteins, is needed for every organ type, yet which genes it directly controls was largely unknown.

The team fished the protein off the genome in two ways, using sequencing and gene chips, and found it bound at thousands of sites. Most strong sites stayed bound even in a mutant lacking another master switch, which makes only sepals and petals. The target list tied SEPALLATA3 to many growth and hormone pathways, with repeated links to auxin, the plant growth hormone. Gene readings backed the picture. Plants with a jammed version of the switch responded differently. The protein, it seems, tunes auxin response so young flower organs can grow out.
europmc-pmc2688759:
Mann and colleagues showed in 2009 that Staphylococcus aureus, a germ behind many hard-to-treat device and wound infections, uses the DNA of its own dead as building glue. In the slimy cities these bacteria build, called biofilms, some cells burst and spill their DNA. That loose DNA, named eDNA, helps the film stick and stand.

Two gene systems pull in opposite directions. One, cid, promotes the bursting; another, lrg, restrains it. Mutants lacking the restraint stuck harder and held more DNA in their matrix. Mutants lacking the bursting system failed to mature into the film's tower shapes. A third player, the bacterium's own DNA-chewing enzyme, trims the glue back, and its loss made films thicker and richer in DNA. Timed self-destruction, the authors argue, is not waste but construction, and the trimming may later help the film shed cells to spread.
europmc-pmc2698859:
Bahadori and colleagues reviewed in 2009 the economic cost of asthma across 68 studies from four decades of literature. About 300 million people live with the disease, and its price tag ranks among the highest of all illnesses. The review separates direct costs, such as care and drugs, from indirect ones, such as lost work.

Hospital stays and medications were the twin engines of direct spending. On the indirect side, missed work and school days formed the largest share, ahead of lost future earnings from illness and early death. Total costs climbed with the patient's age, with other diseases present, and above all with severity: a few poorly controlled patients account for a huge slice of spending. Despite good preventive inhalers existing, costs keep rising. Better patient and doctor education plus regular follow-up, the authors argue, are the brakes available now.
europmc-pmc2732559:
Donlan reviewed in 2002 biofilms, communities of microbes that attach to surfaces and enclose themselves in a self-made polymer matrix, a slime-like scaffold. Most microbiology had treated microbes as free-floating cells grown in rich broth. Biofilm cells differ from floating kin in matrix production, slower growth, and distinct gene activity.

Formation involves attachment shaped by the medium, the surface, and the cell coat, then growth into a structured community that favors gene exchange between cells. Cells also signal each other through quorum sensing, which can trigger detachment. Biofilms matter for public health through infections on medical devices and in the body, so understanding their life cycle should guide new control strategies.
europmc-pmc2738459:
Lanciotti and co-authors reported in 2007 laboratory-confirmed chikungunya virus infections in travelers returning to the United States from India during 2006. Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne virus that causes acute joint pain, fever, and rash, and it is native to Africa and Asia. Huge epidemics hit Indian Ocean islands and southern India in 2005 and 2006, with over a million cases in India alone.

Among travelers tested, thirty-five infections were confirmed, thirty-three in people returning from India and two from Réunion Island. Diagnosis used antibody tests, virus isolation, and genetic tests on early blood samples, since virus circulates for only a few days. The cases show how explosive overseas epidemics reach United States clinics through travel.
europmc-pmc2790859:
Finn and co-authors tested a cell-cycle drug called PD 0332991 against forty-seven human breast cancer cell lines grown in the lab in 2009. The drug blocks two enzymes, CDK4 and CDK6, that push cells toward division by acting on a brake protein called Rb.

Cell lines of the luminal type, which respond to the hormone estrogen, were hit hardest, while basal-like lines resisted the drug. Sensitive lines carried more Rb and cyclin D1 protein and less of a blocker called p16, and their growth stalled in an early cell-cycle stage. The drug also worked well alongside tamoxifen and trastuzumab, and it restored tamoxifen response in resistant lines.
europmc-pmc2806359:
Stöver and Müller built TreeGraph 2 in 2010, a free editor for drawing family trees of species, called phylogenetic trees. Researchers now run several analyses on the same data, and the support values they produce often conflict. Comparing those values branch by branch by hand is slow and error prone.

The program merges support values from different analyses onto one tree and marks where they clash. Users can attach unlimited data to each node or branch, import values from spreadsheets, and let line width or color follow any chosen value. Whole branches can be copied between files, and finished trees export in formats ready for journals or slides.
europmc-pmc2811159:
Gilley and Coleman showed in 2010 that a fast-vanishing protein called Nmnat2 is what keeps healthy nerve fibers alive. Axons, the long fibers that carry nerve signals, wither quickly once cut off from the cell body. A rare mutant protein that slows this decay hinted that a natural survival factor must be shipped down the fiber nonstop.

Briefly blocking Nmnat2 production made uninjured axons break down on their own, the team found. The natural protein is short-lived and must be replaced constantly by fresh supply from the cell body. When supply stops, the fiber's self-destruct program wakes. Because raising Nmnat2 levels is a drug-friendly idea, the authors name it a target for diseases where axons die back.
europmc-pmc2814859:
Hollenbach and co-authors compared two look-alike leukemia drugs head to head in human cell lines in 2010. Azacitidine and decitabine are both used for blood disorders and are often treated as the same kind of drug, since both strip chemical tags from DNA. The team measured shared and split effects across several readouts.

Both drugs depleted the tagging enzyme and damaged DNA, but decitabine matched azacitidine at doses two to ten times lower. At higher doses azacitidine cut cell survival and protein building more, while decitabine mainly stalled cells late in their cycle. Gene activity patterns barely overlapped. The split fits chemistry: azacitidine slips into RNA as well as DNA, while decitabine enters DNA alone.
europmc-pmc2873959:
Noren Hooten and colleagues profiled in 2010 how tiny regulatory RNAs in blood cells change as people age. These microRNAs, short strands that tune gene activity, help set lifespan in worms and flies, but their human pattern was unclear. The team measured over eight hundred of them in blood immune cells from young and older adults.

Most microRNAs faded with age rather than rising. Nine dropped clearly in older people, and five of those nine are already tied to cancer growth. The genes those RNAs normally keep down, including a growth signal hub and a DNA repair protein, rose with age as expected. Lowering one RNA in cells was enough to lift its target, which supports a real cause link and a possible blood test for aging.
europmc-pmc2898859:
Liu and Wu estimated in 2010 how much of the world's liver cancer is caused by aflatoxin, a poison made by molds growing on maize and nuts. Liver cancer kills more people than almost any other cancer, and it strikes developing countries far harder. The team combined data on toxin levels in food, how much people eat, and rates of hepatitis B, a virus that multiplies the toxin's danger.

Of roughly six hundred thousand new liver cancers a year, they attribute between twenty-five thousand and one hundred fifty-five thousand to aflatoxin. That is up to about a quarter of all cases, with deep uncertainty in the range. Sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, and China carry most of the burden, where moldy food and hepatitis B overlap.
europmc-pmc2911859:
Häuser and co-authors pooled in 2010 the trials of aerobic exercise for fibromyalgia, a state of chronic widespread pain. Twenty-eight trials compared exercise with usual care, and seven compared types of exercise head to head. In all, the trials covered nearly twenty-five hundred patients. Outcomes were pain, fatigue, low mood, fitness, and quality of life.

Exercise beat usual care on every outcome. Pain, fatigue, and low mood each eased by a small but real amount. Limits on quality of life shrank, and fitness rose. Pool-based and land-based programs both worked, and no type won the head-to-head trials. Gains were clearest while the programs kept going. The pooled numbers give doctors firm effect sizes to cite when they prescribe exercise.
europmc-pmc2924359:
Estes and a large team produced in 2010 direct visual proof that gut microbes leak across the bowel wall in SIV infection, the monkey analogue of HIV. Chronic HIV keeps the immune system pathologically activated, and that activation predicts decline better than virus levels do. Leaked microbial products from the gut were the prime suspect, backed only by indirect blood evidence.

Examining tissues from chronically infected rhesus macaques, the team found microbial constituents deep in the gut lining, the draining lymph nodes, and the liver. The leaks mapped onto visible breaks in the epithelial barrier, with local immune responses gathered at the breach sites. Damaged gut integrity thus feeds the systemic activation that wears the immune system down, making barrier repair a legitimate treatment goal beside antivirals.
europmc-pmc2965659:
van Wijk, Stam, and Daffertshofer warned in 2010 that comparing brain networks of different sizes with graph theory can mislead. Graph measures offer a neat language for brain connections, yet they shift with node count and link density alone.

Fixing thresholds to equalise size can force weak links in or throw real ones out. Normalising against random look-alike networks can, counterintuitively, worsen bias for popular measures such as clustering. The authors survey fixes from network science and social research, and try estimating the size effect directly from data so genuine differences in brain wiring stand out.
europmc-pmc3037559:
Sullivan and coauthors compared in 2010 the genomes of ocean viruses that infect photosynthetic bacteria, set against their freshwater and land relatives. These viruses, among the most common genes found in seawater, carry tools for building new viruses and copying DNA. The team lined up twenty six full genomes from diverse hosts and waters.

All shared a core set of building and copying genes in the same order. The ocean set added its own shared genes, including some tied to light harvesting, nutrient stress, and nitrogen handling during infection. Genes for phosphorus use matched the waters the viruses came from, not the host they were grown on. No single gene cleanly split viruses by host type, suggesting the groups blur through cross infection. The maps give a yardstick for reading virus DNA gathered straight from the sea.
europmc-pmc3069059:
Lee, Lessler, and Stuart tested in 2011 whether trimming extreme weights improves a common technique for making compared groups fairly matched. The technique, propensity score weighting, reweights people so treated and untreated groups look alike on background traits. A few huge weights can dominate results, and cutting them down is a popular fix whose value was unclear.

In simulations, trimming clearly helped when the matching scores came from the usual regression model, cutting both bias and noise. With modern tree based methods, trimming added nothing, and those methods alone matched the best trimmed regression results. The catch is that the best trimming level is hard to know in advance. The authors advise analysts to invest in building the matching model well, rather than leaning on after the fact trimming to rescue a weak one.
europmc-pmc3087759:
Signorini, Segre, and Polgreen tested in 2011 whether chatter on Twitter could track flu during the 2009 swine flu pandemic in the United States. Twitter then carried tens of millions of short messages a day, and illness talk was buried in that stream. The team built methods to pull out tweets that signaled real sickness, public worry, or both, and to follow them over time.

Estimates of flu like illness built from the tweet stream matched official reported disease levels closely as the pandemic rose and fell. Separate measures captured surges of public concern that did not always move with case counts. The authors argue such streams can supplement slow official reporting, giving health officials a near real time sense of both spread and mood. Their study was an early proof that social media can serve as a public health sensor.
europmc-pmc3098059:
Zhu and coauthors released in 2010 a software package that explains, in bulk, the binding site lists produced by genome wide protein binding experiments. Such experiments, called ChIP-seq and ChIP-chip, return thousands of enriched DNA stretches with no labels attached. Working through them in a genome browser one by one is impractical at that scale.

Their package annotates whole lists at once inside the R statistics environment. It reports the nearest genes and their distances, draws summary charts, tests whether overlaps between experiments are larger than chance, and pulls the DNA sequences around sites for further study. Users can supply their own annotation sources, keeping the tool flexible across species and platforms. It also links each site to the known functions of neighboring genes. The package is free through the Bioconductor project, the standard home for such tools.
europmc-pmc3145159:
Jakob Zinsstag and colleagues traced the idea that human and animal health form one system in a 2011 paper in Preventive Veterinary Medicine. From early history through European universities to modern comparative medicine, healers have repeatedly noticed the bond. A twentieth-century thinker coined one medicine for it; practice later widened the frame to one health, adding social and ecological context.

Evidence now grows that joint approaches beat separate human and animal services, and training courses, ministries, and world bodies increasingly adopt them. Ecosystem thinking widens the lens further, treating health as a property of whole social and natural systems. The authors argue the remaining silos between professions are the main obstacle, and sketch what a modern systems theory of health needs.
europmc-pmc3154959:
Kirstin Mittelstrass and colleagues mapped sex differences in blood chemistry and their genes in a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Men and women differ in disease rates, symptoms, and drug responses, yet most studies pool the sexes. Using samples from more than three thousand adults, the team measured over a hundred blood metabolites and scanned genomes separately by sex.

Most metabolites differed significantly between men and women. Genetic control also differed: one gene region governing an amino acid breakdown product showed a strong effect pattern unique by sex. The results show cell regulation runs partly differently in male and female bodies, right down to single genes. The authors insist future studies should design and read results with sex split in mind.
europmc-pmc3378559:
Foulongne and colleagues took a census of viruses living on healthy human skin in 2012, using high-throughput DNA sequencing. Skin bacteria had been studied for years, but its viruses stayed largely unexplored. Samples came from the normal-looking skin of five healthy people and one patient with Merkel cell carcinoma.

The surface carried a rich viral mix, including many polyomaviruses, papillomaviruses, and circoviruses. The survey also turned up new papillomavirus and circovirus genomes. Within known skin polyomaviruses, variety proved very low. The results support a standing viral flora on healthy skin, not just passing germs, and raise questions about its role in skin growths.
europmc-pmc3397359:
Belouzard, Millet, Licitra, and Whittaker reviewed in 2012 how coronaviruses break into cells using their spike protein. These enveloped RNA viruses must merge their coat with a cell membrane to deliver their genome. The spike both grabs a receptor on the cell and drives that merger.

Different coronaviruses trip the spike's shape change in different ways: receptor binding, acidic surroundings, or cutting by enzymes. The review compares the spike with other viral fusion proteins and marks what is shared and what is special. Those special traits shape which species and tissues each virus can infect and how severe it becomes. The map helps anticipate how new coronaviruses might jump hosts.
europmc-pmc3420959:
Dahlem and co-workers laid out simple methods in 2012 for making targeted mutations in zebrafish with engineered cutting proteins called TALENs. Zebrafish are prized for studying gene function, but knocking out chosen genes had been hard. A TALEN can be built to cut DNA at almost any preselected spot, and sloppy repair of the cut leaves small mutations.

The team tested four such cutters against different genes. Nearly every injected embryo gained targeted mutations, sometimes in half its genome copies, and most adults passed them to offspring. A melting-based test detects the new mutations cheaply. Off-target damage stayed minimal. From design to mutant embryos takes about two weeks using free tools, they report.
europmc-pmc3427559:
Woolhouse, Scott, Hudson, Howey, and Chase-Topping took stock in 2012 of all virus species known to infect humans and how new ones keep emerging. The count stood at well over two hundred species, the first found in 1901, with three or four added each year. The team asked how much of the pool remains hidden.

Extending the discovery curve suggests plenty of human viruses await discovery, though a slowdown in new families hints at limits. More than two thirds of human viruses also infect other animals, mostly mammals and sometimes birds. Only about half of animal viruses that can jump into people can then spread between them, and fewer still cause major outbreaks. New emergences look inevitable, so the authors call for a global watch system.
europmc-pmc3443459:
Todd, Luzina, and Atamas reviewed in 2012 the molecular machinery behind pulmonary fibrosis, the slow scarring that stiffens lungs. Its idiopathic form is the most common and severe, with median survival around three years and no proven therapy. Thirty-five years of literature have piled up without pinning down the drivers, so the review organizes the suspects.

Three broad arenas get separate hearings: inflammation and immune mechanisms, oxidative stress and its signaling, and clotting-related pathways. Running through all three are transformed fibroblasts churning out matrix, dying air-sac lining cells, and the matrix piling up between them. The authors stress the pathways interlock in real patients even though they are reviewed apart. The map shows where a therapy might break the cycle.
europmc-pmc3516559:
Hepatitis C virus builds a membranous web inside infected cells to copy itself, and Ines Romero-Brey leads a fifteen-author team mapping that structure in three dimensions in 2012. Combining fluorescence and electron microscopy, they trace where the web's membranes come from and which viral proteins build each part.

The web derives mainly from the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's membrane factory, with markers from several other compartments mixed in. Double-membrane vesicles dominate, and their appearance tracks the pace of viral RNA replication. One viral protein, NS5A, mainly induces the double-membrane vesicles, while NS4B induces single-membrane ones. Building the web, the study shows, is a concerted viral construction project.
europmc-pmc3539359:
Mammalian life resets its DNA methylation twice, and Stefanie Seisenberger, Julian R. Peat, Timothy A. Hore, Fatima Santos, Wendy Dean, and Wolf Reik review that reprogramming in 2013. Methylation patterns define cell identity yet also fence in developmental potential, so they are wiped and rewritten at fertilization and again in primordial germ cells.

Each window uses its own machinery. In the new zygote, the TET3 enzyme, passive dilution, DNA repair, and the elongator complex all play parts. Germ cell reprogramming implicates the deaminase AID, repair pathways, and passive loss, though the full account stays incomplete. The review assembles the mechanisms and the open questions around these epigenetic barriers.
europmc-pmc3547959:
Extra weight tracks with bowel cancer risk in this 2013 systematic review and meta-analysis by Yanlei Ma and seven colleagues. Pooling prospective studies found through MEDLINE and EMBASE, the team covers some nine million participants across many countries, with 41 studies on general obesity and 13 on central obesity.

People in the obese body-mass category face a pooled relative risk of colorectal cancer of 1.334 against normal weight. For waist size, the highest category against the lowest gives 1.455. Both general and central obesity raise risk, and the analysis separates colon from rectal outcomes. The dose pattern strengthens the case that adiposity itself, not only diet, drives part of the burden.
europmc-pmc3610159:
Jean-Frederic Levesque, Mark Harris, and Grant Russell rebuilt the concept of health care access in the International Journal for Equity in Health in 2013. Access decides how well any health system performs, yet authors meant different things by the word, leaving measurement scattered. Their synthesis of the most-cited frameworks offers one definition: access as the opportunity to spot a health need, seek care, reach it, use it, and have the need actually met.

Five features of services carry the supply side: how approachable they are, how acceptable, how available, how affordable, and how appropriate to the need. Facing them stand five abilities in the population: to perceive a need, to seek care, to reach it, to pay, and to engage with treatment once inside. Access happens where the two sides meet, step by step along the care path. The frame gives equity researchers measurable joints where systems fail people.
europmc-pmc3629559:
William Razzell and colleagues found the first alarm signal of wound healing in Current Biology in 2013. Working in fruit fly embryos, they knew hydrogen peroxide is the earliest known call that summons immune cells to a wound, released within minutes by an enzyme called DUOX. What switches DUOX on was unknown. Laser wounds under the microscope gave them a live view.

Each wound fired an instant flash of calcium that rippled outward through gap junctions, the channels joining neighboring cells, reaching several cell rows back. Blocking the flash stopped peroxide release at the wound and cut the number of immune cells arriving. The calcium wave fits the enzyme's own calcium-sensing handle, completing the chain: damage, calcium flash, peroxide, immune cells. Calcium, they conclude, is the true first signal of injury.
europmc-pmc3647259:
A heart disease of old age is charted from first signs to outcome by Pinney and a large team in a 2013 study in the Journal of the American Heart Association. The disease, senile systemic amyloidosis, comes from a blood protein that folds wrong and clogs organs, above all the heart. It must be told apart from a kin heart form tied to blood cell faults, since care differs.

The study covers 102 patients with the age-linked form and 36 with the heart-only blood form, seen at the United Kingdom National Amyloidosis Centre from 2002 to 2011. Median survival from first symptoms ran 6.07 years in the age-linked group against 1.7 years in the other. A blood stress marker, a pacemaker and worse breathlessness marked poorer outlook. Age plus one blood test level helped tell the two forms apart at first visit.
europmc-pmc3686659:
Fratz and colleagues, writing for an expert consensus group of the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance, set out standard guidelines for heart MRI in children and adults with congenital heart disease. The document covers how to prepare and keep patients safe, the main imaging techniques, and protocols matched to specific conditions.

Cardiac MRI now plays a central part in assessing these patients and planning procedures, complementing ultrasound and avoiding the radiation of CT scans. Where trial evidence is thin, the recommendations rest on expert consensus. The aim is a shared, safer approach across centers. These centers scan patients whose heart anatomy varies enormously from person to person. A common protocol should also make results easier to compare between hospitals.
europmc-pmc3707059:
Romay and colleagues genotyped the United States national maize inbred seed bank, profiling 2,815 preserved lines drawn from breeding programmes worldwide. Genotyping by sequencing yielded more than six hundred eighty thousand variable sites spread across the genome, sensitive enough to catch rare variants reliably.

More than half of those variants proved rare. Most rare variants have found their way into public temperate breeding lines, but commercial seed lines hold only a modest share of the total diversity. Distance analyses showed the collection clusters around a few key founder lines, with moderate differences between the major maize groups. The authors demonstrate trait mapping on the panel and release the data for agriculture research.
europmc-pmc3718659:
Richard Osborne and four co-authors reported the building and first testing of the Health Literacy Questionnaire in BMC Public Health in 2013. Health literacy means the skills people need to find, grasp, and use health information. The team wanted a tool that could map the needs of both patients and health services.

They built the questions from workshops and interviews with the public, patients, workers, and policymakers. Early versions held 91 items, and testing in a group of 634 people cut the weak ones. A second group of 405 recent emergency patients helped refine the tool to nine scales with 44 items. The scales cover areas such as feeling supported by care providers, finding good information, and moving through the health system.
europmc-pmc3765959:
Gabriella Ficz and a large group of co-authors reported a study in Cell Stem Cell in 2013 on resetting the epigenetic state of mouse embryonic stem cells. Wiping DNA methylation clean happens naturally in germ cells and early embryos and is tied to pluripotency, the ability to become any cell type. A two-inhibitor treatment, called 2i, that blocks FGF signaling paths had been shown to lower methylation.

Sequencing the whole genome's methylation, the team found that 2i drives fast, genome-wide demethylation much like the natural process. Some regions resisted, including major satellites and imprinted genes. The wipe works by converting methyl marks to a form that is poorly maintained, while the enzymes that lay new marks are switched off. The authors map a control region in one such enzyme gene that answers to pluripotency factors.
europmc-pmc3785459:
Dominik Aschauer, Sebastian Kreuz, and Simon Rumpel reported a comparison study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on virus vectors for delivering genes to the mouse brain. Recombinant adeno-associated virus comes in many serotypes, natural variants that differ in which cells they enter. Researchers lacked a detailed side-by-side comparison for choosing among them.

The team tested six widely used serotypes across three brain regions: striatum, hippocampus, and neocortex. All could enter the major brain cell types, but reporter gene levels varied sharply by cell type and serotype. One serotype drove expression especially well in astrocytes, another suited cortical neurons. A further serotype travelled backwards along axons from one region to a connected one. Self-complementing versions of the vectors cut the wait for gene expression to begin.
europmc-pmc3799859:
Mori and colleagues reported in PLoS ONE in 2013 on the sigma-1 receptor, a chaperone protein that sits where the endoplasmic reticulum meets mitochondria. Chaperones help other proteins fold and stay in working shape. This contact zone, called the MAM, lets the two organelles trade signals and materials.

Working in CHO cells, the team showed that the sigma-1 receptor holds IRE1, a sensor of stress inside the endoplasmic reticulum, in a stable and active form. With IRE1 protected, stressed cells could send a survival signal through the mitochondrion and reticulum to the nucleus. The authors present this pathway as one way cells endure stress that would otherwise push them toward death.
europmc-pmc3820259:
Franziska Baenke, Barrie Peck, Heike Miess, and Almut Schulze review fat making in cancer in Disease Models & Mechanisms in 2013. Cancer cells build fats at a high rate, a fact known for years. The review asks what that fat building does for tumor growth and spread.

Fast growth needs new cell walls, and fats supply much of that stock. Fresh work links fat making to cell movement, to invasion of near tissue, and to the growth of new blood vessels that feed tumors. Those steps drive spread to new body sites, the main cause of cancer death. The review weighs how far fat pathways explain these steps, and where proof is still thin. That map helps labs pick the next tests.
europmc-pmc3857059:
Aude Munin and Florence Edwards-Lévy review packaging for plant polyphenols in Pharmaceutics, dated 2011 in the record. Polyphenols are plant compounds that mop up harmful oxygen forms and bind proteins. Those gifts suit them for drugs, skin care, and food supplements.

The same traits make them fragile. Light and heat break them down, many dissolve poorly in water, and their bitter taste limits food use. Wrapping them in tiny capsules can shield them and ease delivery. The review sorts wrapping methods into physical, mixed, and chemical routes, plus linked stability tricks. Each method is matched with real polyphenol cases. The survey helps makers pick a wrap that keeps the compounds active until they reach their target.
europmc-pmc3877259:
Jong-Kuen Lee and a team of co-authors study stem cell vesicles in breast cancer in PLoS One in 2013. Mesenchymal stem cells home to tumors and sway their growth in mixed ways. Their shed vesicles, exosomes, carry RNA and proteins to other cells, a route less explored.

Vesicles from the stem cells held a protein and RNA mix distinct from their parent cells. Breast cancer cells took the vesicles in. Treated cancer cells then made far less VEGF, a signal that calls in new blood vessels. With less of that signal, vessel growth eased in tests. The find suggests stem cell vesicles can calm a tumor's blood supply drive, a twist in the stem cell and cancer story.
europmc-pmc3909459:
G. Ekin Atilla-Gokcumen and seven colleagues report in Cell in 2014 that cells change their fats, called lipids, in a planned way as they divide. Membranes are rebuilt on a large scale during division, yet the role of specific lipids in that process was largely unknown when the study began.

Profiling lipids across the cell cycle, the group found eleven lipids with set structures that build up in dividing cells. Dividing cells and their lipids also felt mechanically different when probed with an atomic force microscope. Silencing lipid-making enzymes pointed to which enzymes division needs, and the team showed that certain lipids are sent to the midbody, the bridge where the two new cells finally part.
europmc-pmc3930559:
Philippe Lemey and colleagues combine virus family trees with human travel data to predict how flu spreads worldwide, in PLoS Pathogens in 2014. Knowing how people move is central to forecasting influenza, yet case counts alone cannot show which routes matter most. Gene sequences from viruses carry a record of where lineages have been, but earlier analyses rarely used mobility data directly.

Working with the H3N2 flu subtype, the team built a model that reconstructs the virus's migration history while testing candidate drivers, including air travel patterns, at the same time. The framework can weigh how well each factor explains the observed spread and can forecast spatial patterns for influenza A more broadly. It turns two separate data streams into one test of global transmission routes.
europmc-pmc3953959:
H. Susana Marinho and four colleagues review how hydrogen peroxide steers gene switches. Their paper appeared in Redox Biology in 2014. Hydrogen peroxide was long seen as mere cell damage. Cells also use it as a signal, though. The review follows its sensor proteins across life. Bacteria come first, then yeasts, then mammal cells. The control webs grow more complex along that line.

Peroxide can change a gene switch at four levels. Level one is how much of the switch is made. Level two is how long it survives before disposal. Level three is its trip from the cell body into the nucleus. Level four is how well it grips DNA once there. Partner proteins and repressors matter at that stage too. The authors catalog the switches under this control. They run from bacterial OxyR to human NF-kappaB and p53.
europmc-pmc3975359:
Piergiorgio Gentile and three colleagues review a biodegradable plastic for bone repair. Their paper appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2014. The plastic is PLGA. It is friendly to tissue. Its recipe can be tuned so it dissolves at a chosen rate. It is already approved for use in patients. It also avoids animal-derived implants, which some cultures reject. Those traits make it a favorite scaffold material. Bone tissue engineering is the main use in view.

The review surveys how PLGA scaffolds are made. It weighs the field's hard problems with care. One problem is matching strength to growing bone. The scaffold must fade as new bone firms up. Surface shaping is a second problem. Cells must attach well and thrive on the surface. Newer methods aim at scaffolds that mimic natural bone. Such scaffolds could guide cells to restore lost tissue.
europmc-pmc4007559:
John C. Castle and a large team of co-authors map a widely used mouse tumour line at gene and immune level, in BMC Genomics in 2014. The line, CT26, grows from mouse colon cancer and is a workhorse for testing cancer drugs in mice with working immune systems.

Sequencing found a double fault in a growth gene called Kras, no faults in two other classic cancer genes, and loss of a brake gene. Growth and stem-cell markers ran high, while markers of mature gut lining ran low. The cells display one class of immune ID tags but not the other. Of the many protein-changing variants, about one hundred and fifty sat in active genes and in bits predicted to be shown to immune cells, making them candidate targets for immune therapy. The profile matches aggressive human bowel cancers that resist standard drugs.
europmc-pmc4015559:
Cheryl L. Gibbons and ten co-authors compare ways to count the cases that disease reporting systems miss, in BMC Public Health in 2014. Watch systems track outbreaks, yet they lose cases at two steps. Some sick people never seek care, and some who do are never reported. Both gaps shrink the counts below the true toll.

Working within a European project on disease burden, the team reviewed studies that gauge these gaps for two food-borne infections, salmonellosis and campylobacteriosis. Each study yields a multiplier that scales reported cases up to an estimated true count. Multipliers ranged widely between diseases and countries, and even within one country. The best choice often depends on the disease, the country, and the age and sex of patients. The authors warn that raw reported counts can mislead choices on funding and on judging disease patterns, unless the gaps are measured and matched with care.
europmc-pmc4044159:
Angela Coulter and five colleagues set out how patient decision aids ought to be built, in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making in 2013. Decision aids help patients weigh treatment choices. A quality standard had long required that they be developed in a careful, documented way. The team checked whether that demand still fit practice.

They reviewed trial reports, papers on how aids were made, and methods from groups that build them often. Shared stages emerged: scoping and design, a prototype, early testing with patients and clinicians, field testing in real care, and production. The record was patchy. Only about half the aids had been field tested with patients. Fewer still had outside clinician review. Very few reports described how the medical evidence was gathered, and almost none planned distribution. The paper offers an expanded model and a checklist for future aids.
europmc-pmc4158559:
María Muriach, Miguel Flores-Bellver, Francisco J. Romero, and Jorge M. Barcia reviewed how diabetes harms the brain. Their review came out in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2014. Diabetes brings mild to fair faults of thought, with slow work pace and stiff thought, much like a brain that ages too fast.

One master switch for swelling, NF-kB, stands where oxygen stress and swelling cross, and it can sense both. Swelling tied to fuel use also sets off stress in the cell's power hubs and in its folding shop. It breaks the self-cleaning that clears worn parts. Blocked cleaning then feeds the swelling path by way of the same switch. The team uses this web to show how a whole-body fuel ill can age the brain in a quiet way.
europmc-pmc4237059:
Christoph D. Mathys, Klaas E. Stephan, and five co-authors generalized a brain computation model in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2014. Perception, in the Bayesian view, is the brain guessing the causes of its senses while tracking how uncertain those guesses are. The Hierarchical Gaussian Filter, or HGF, turns that idea into equations that can be fitted to a person's behaviour.

The paper extends the model's hierarchy to any number of levels and shows how different kinds of uncertainty enter its update rules. It also pairs the filter with decision models so choices, not just beliefs, can be predicted. Simulations compared four fitting methods across noise levels; all coped well, and variational Bayes gave the best mix of speed and information. The work aims to make the model a standard tool for studying perception gone wrong.
europmc-pmc4339959:
Elliot Marseille, Bruce Larson, Dhruv S Kazi, James G Kahn, and Sydney Rosen argue that world health cost thresholds do more harm than good. Their paper appeared in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2015. Many countries judge an intervention cost effective if each healthy year it buys costs less than one to three times national income per person, following World Health Organization guidance.

The authors call that rule theoretically empty: it skips the hard local ranking of what a health system should fund first and ignores whether the money exists. Blunt thresholds can bless wasteful programs and block cheap ones. They propose alternatives grounded in local budgets and opportunity cost. The debate matters wherever scarce funds meet long wish lists.
europmc-pmc4348559:
Joe W. McGreevy, Chady H. Hakim, Mark A. McIntosh, and Dongsheng Duan review animal models of Duchenne muscular dystrophy and the path to gene therapy. Their review appeared in Disease Models and Mechanisms in 2015. The disease, caused by loss of the dystrophin gene, wastes muscle progressively and has no cure, so replacing or repairing the gene is the leading hope.

Models range from worms and flies to the standard mdx mouse and large dogs that show symptoms much like boys with the disease. Thirty years of work in mice laid the groundwork for gene therapy. The review weighs each model's strengths and gaps. It charts how results are now being checked and scaled in the canine model before human trials.
europmc-pmc4349859:
Carrie Reed and eleven co-authors estimated the true burden of influenza in the United States for the seasons after the 2009 pandemic. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. Hospital surveillance counts only patients who are tested and test positive, and testing is uneven, so raw counts understate the disease.

Five surveillance sites measured how often patients were tested and how sensitive the tests were, yielding correction factors of roughly twofold or more. Applying those multipliers to national hospitalization and intensive care rates for 2010 to 2013, and a ratio for deaths, gave corrected burden estimates. Health officials use such numbers to size vaccine programs and judge their reach.
europmc-pmc4359359:
Piotr Ponikowski and the CONFIRM-HF team tested vein iron treatment for heart failure. The trial report ran in the European Heart Journal in 2015. Many people with heart failure lack iron. Low iron makes breathlessness worse and cuts stamina. The trial enrolled 304 outpatients with weak heart pumping and low iron. Half got ferric carboxymaltose into a vein. Half got salt water as a placebo. Neither side knew which was which. Treatment lasted 52 weeks.

By week 24, the iron group walked farther in six minutes than the placebo group. The gain was clear and it held to week 52. Heart class ratings improved in the iron group. So did quality of life and fatigue scores. These gains appeared from week 24 on. Hospital stays for worse heart failure fell sharply with iron. Deaths did not differ clearly between the groups.
europmc-pmc4383959:
James Robinson, Jason Halliwell, James Hayhurst, Paul Flicek, Peter Parham, and Steven Marsh described the immune polymorphism databases in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. Genes of the immune system, above all the HLA genes that govern tissue matching, vary enormously between people. The Immuno Polymorphism Database project gathers that variation into one curated platform. Specialist nomenclature committees check each section before it is published online.

The project holds five core databases, headed by the IMGT/HLA database, the main reference for HLA variants used in transplant matching. Partner groups include the HLA Informatics Group and the European Bioinformatics Institute. New tools respond to next-generation sequencing, which produces variant data at new scale, and to user requests. Regular updates push new and confirmed sequences out to immunogenetics and clinical users quickly.
europmc-pmc4468859:
Kang Liang and ten co-authors coated proteins and DNA in a protective crystal shell, reporting in Nature Communications in 2015. Useful biological molecules are fragile: heat, solvents, and storage break them down, limiting their use in drugs, industry, and stockpiles. Inspired by how organisms build mineral shells, the team grew metal-organic frameworks, porous lattices of metal and organic parts, directly around the molecules.

Proteins, enzymes, and DNA draw the framework's building blocks to themselves and speed crystal growth at body-like conditions, so a shell forms fast around them. Coated enzymes kept working after heating that would normally destroy them, and one survived boiling in a harsh solvent. The coating is stable under conditions that decompose many biological molecules. The authors present the cheap, quick process as a way to store and ship fragile biological products safely.
europmc-pmc4484459:
Valentina Minciacchi and a large team of co-authors characterized large oncosomes, oversized vesicles shed by cancer cells, in Oncotarget in 2015. Most studied tumor vesicles are tiny, but cancer cells also shed membrane blebs one to ten micrometers wide, called large oncosomes, which are linked to advanced disease. Whether they form a distinct class, with their own cargo and job, was untested.

Comparing large and nano-sized vesicles from prostate cancer cells, the team found a quarter of the proteins they measured differed between the two. Large vesicles were enriched for metabolic enzymes handling glucose, glutamine, and amino acids, and they altered glutamine use in receiving cells, an effect tiny vesicles did not have. One abundant protein, cytokeratin 18, let them build a test to detect these vesicles in blood and tissue. The authors argue large oncosomes are a functional class of their own, not merely big exosomes.
europmc-pmc4534859:
Angela Scanzano and Marco Cosentino review how the body's fight-or-flight nerves steer the first line of immune defense, in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2015. That nerve branch talks with immune cells all the time, using two chemical signals it sends to receptors on their surface. The review asks what those signals do to the cells that act first when germs invade.

In human blood cells called neutrophils, the signals rein in movement and blunt the burst of harsh chemicals used to kill germs. Natural killer cells are held back by the same route, and monocytes shift toward a calmer, less hostile stance. Brain support cells carry the same receptors, and faults in this control may help drive lasting brain inflammation. The authors say drugs long used for nerve and heart care deserve tests as immune treatments.
europmc-pmc4544059:
Makhsud I. Saidaminov leads a twelve-author team growing solar crystals in minutes, in Nature Communications in 2015. Single crystals of methylammonium lead halide perovskites carry charge well and trap it rarely, traits wanted for solar cells and lasers. Growing them in high quality, though, took days of slow work.

The trick exploits a quirk: in certain solvents these crystals dissolve less as the liquid heats up, the reverse of normal behavior. Heating therefore forces crystals out of solution fast. By tuning the setup, the team controlled crystal size and shape. The quick-grown crystals matched the best slow-grown ones in charge transport and trap counts. The authors present the method as a major step for perovskite crystal work.
europmc-pmc4558759:
Gerardo Chowell and six co-authors compare how MERS and SARS spread inside hospitals, in BMC Medicine in 2015. Both are coronavirus diseases that pass weakly in the community yet explode in care settings. SARS did so in 2003. MERS has done so since 2012, most recently in South Korea in 2015. The team asked how likely such hospital clusters are and what shapes them.

Using case-level data and infection trees from past hospital clusters, they simulated outbreaks with branching process models. A large share of MERS cases tied to care settings, ranging from 43.5 percent upward across clusters. The models gauge the odds and likely size of future big hospital outbreaks. They stress that infection control, not community spread, is the weak point.
europmc-pmc4669759:
A team led by Joel D. Leverson published a 2015 study presenting the first potent small-molecule blockers of MCL-1, a protein that keeps cancer cells alive. MCL-1 also causes resistance to other BCL-2 family drugs. Blocking it means breaking a tight protein grip, which had defeated earlier chemistry. Their lead compound is called A-1210477. The work appeared in Science Translational Medicine.

The compound bound MCL-1 selectively and broke its hold on the death protein BIM inside living cells. It triggered the classic signs of programmed cell death and killed myeloma and lung cancer lines that depend on MCL-1. Combined with the drug navitoclax, it killed a wider range of lines. The molecules give biologists a sharp tool and a possible new cancer therapy.
europmc-pmc4699359:
Anthony S. Zannas, Janine Arloth, Tania Carrillo-Roa, and a large team linked lifetime stress to faster epigenetic aging in Genome Biology in 2015. Chronic stress tracks with earlier disease, but the molecular path was unclear. The team used a DNA methylation clock, which guesses age from chemical tags on DNA, in an urban African American group of 392 people. They tested which kinds of stress moved the clock ahead.

Total stress across a lifetime predicted a clock running fast, while childhood maltreatment or current stress alone did not. Personal life stressors drove most of the effect. Stress hormones look like the messenger: many clock sites sit in DNA regions that answer to glucocorticoids, and a hormone drug shifted those very sites in a second sample. The work names a plausible chain from hard lives to faster molecular aging.
europmc-pmc4702859:
Paul Julian Kersey, James E. Allen, Irina Armean, and a large team updated Ensembl Genomes in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. While Ensembl covers vertebrates, Ensembl Genomes does the same job for the rest of life, through five kingdom-based sites. Its holdings grew sharply: over twenty-three thousand bacterial genomes, hundreds of fungal and protist genomes, plus plant and invertebrate sets. All share the same browsing and programming interfaces as the vertebrate resource.

A headline challenge is polyploid genomes, whose multiple chromosome sets strain standard displays; bread wheat is the test case for new views. Automation is the other theme, pulling archival sequence and variant data into reference context at scale. Gene models, expression data, and cross-species comparisons fill out each genome's page. The update shows comparative genomics stretching from single-celled life to the crops that feed the world.
europmc-pmc4706059:
Steven Wingett, Philip Ewels, Mayra Furlan-Magaril, and four colleagues released HiCUP in F1000Research in 2015. Hi-C experiments reveal how DNA folds in three dimensions by joining fragments that sat near each other in the cell. The raw output is messy, full of artefacts that can poison later analysis. HiCUP is a software pipeline that maps the data to a reference genome and strips those artefacts out.

Along the way it writes a detailed quality report that readers can actually interpret. Good reports matter because they show how to tune the wet-lab protocol for the next run. The pipeline also handles Capture Hi-C, a variant that zooms in on chosen genome regions. The software is free, and several published studies had already run on it at release. For labs entering chromosome-folding work, HiCUP offers a tested path from raw reads to clean maps.
europmc-pmc4717859:
Dimitry A. Chistiakov, Yuri V. Bobryshev, and Alexander N. Orekhov explained how macrophages handle cholesterol in atherosclerosis, in the Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine in 2016. The disease begins when white blood cells slip into an artery wall and turn into macrophages. There they swallow oxidized LDL, the damaged form of the main cholesterol carrier, through several scavenger receptors. Inside, enzymes free the cholesterol from its stored form, and repackage some of it into droplets.

A healthy macrophage can also ship cholesterol back out through dedicated transporter proteins. In atherosclerosis that balance breaks: intake outruns export, cholesterol piles up, and the cell swells into a foam cell, the hallmark of early plaque. The review walks the whole circuit, uptake, breakdown, storage, release, naming each enzyme and transporter. Knowing where the circuit jams points to where drugs might unjam it, a map the authors lay out step by step.
europmc-pmc4880559:
Ana M. Guzman Prieto and co-authors reviewed in 2016 how enterococci, gut bacteria once seen as harmless lodgers, became global hospital pathogens. Two species matter most in clinics, Enterococcus faecium and Enterococcus faecalis. Both live in the guts of people, animals, and insects and in soil and plants, yet both now headline hospital infection lists.

Hospital strains of E. faecium form a marked clan, rare outside hospitals, stocked with gained genes for surface slime, fuel use, and drug resistance. E. faecalis hospital strains blend more with community ones. Gene gain from other bacteria drives the shift. The review frames hospital spread as clone warfare, shaped by antibiotics and ward life.
europmc-pmc4885859:
Anna M. Kielak and co-authors reviewed the ecology of Acidobacteria in 2016, a bacterial phylum among the most widespread on Earth. Soil surveys find them nearly everywhere, yet their role in land ecosystems stayed sketchy, since they resist growth in lab dishes. Their family breadth rivals the well-known Proteobacteria, hinting at wide talents.

Fresh routes now open the group: new culture tricks, single genomes, and DNA read straight from soil. Joined, these show acidobacteria breaking down plant matter, cycling nutrients, and shifting with soil acidity. The review couples gene hints to field roles. A phylum long counted but not understood starts to take shape as a soil workforce.
europmc-pmc4896459:
Dana C. McCoy and co-authors estimated early childhood development gaps in low- and middle-income countries in 2016. Early thinking and social-emotional growth shape later health, yet past counts of unmet potential leaned on body growth or poverty as stand-ins. The team used direct caregiver reports for 99,222 children aged three and four in 35 countries, gathered from 2005 to 2015.

Models then extended the rates to countries without survey data. A large share of young children scored low on thinking, social-emotional growth, or both, with wide gaps between regions. Direct measures sharpen the target for aid: preschool access, caregiver support, and nutrition where delay clusters. The count gives policy a firmer base than proxy guesses.
europmc-pmc4910259:
Loris Mularoni and co-authors built OncodriveFML in Genome Biology in 2016, a framework to spot cancer driver mutations in coding and non-coding DNA alike. Tumors carry many mutations, and most are passengers. Drivers reveal themselves by clustering more than chance allows, a sign of positive selection. Non-coding drivers had lacked a general test.

The method scores any region by how oddly its mutations stack against a local background model. It recovered known driver genes and flagged promoters, untranslated regions, splice zones, and long non-coding RNA genes with driver signs in several cancers. Hidden drivers outside genes can now be hunted with the same lens as gene faults.
europmc-pmc4943559:
Jonathan M. Hazlehurst and four co-authors review how non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and type 2 diabetes drive each other. Their review appeared in Metabolism in 2016. Fatty liver unrelated to alcohol is now common, and it often occurs with diabetes. Each condition makes the other worse. Together they raise the risk of diabetes complications in vessels large and small, and of severe liver outcomes such as cirrhosis, liver cancer, and death.

Weight loss and good blood sugar control remain the core of care, the authors say. They slow the disease before scarring sets in. Once cirrhosis develops, screening for its complications becomes the priority. Drug evidence is thin, drawn mostly from case series rather than strong trials. The authors sort the published data on diabetes drugs that may also help the liver. They call for well designed randomized trials with firm end points.
europmc-pmc4974459:
