Katjana Tantale and a broad team of co-authors watch single RNA molecules being made and find polymerases travel in convoys. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. RNA polymerases are the enzymes that read genes into RNA. Using improved single molecule microscopy in living cells, the team studied the HIV-1 promoter. Instead of lone enzymes starting one by one, groups of closely spaced polymerases launched in quick succession, forming convoys along the gene.

A factor called Mediator drives the rapid restarts behind convoys. During the run, physical modeling suggests twisting stress in the DNA helps keep the enzymes spaced. The promoter also flickered on and off at two time scales, minutes and near an hour, each run by a different switch. A normal cell promoter showed the same convoy pattern. The authors propose the slow flicker helps create cell to cell variety in gene output.
europmc-pmc4982059:
Lorna McAusland and five co-authors study how the speed of stomatal response affects photosynthesis and water use in plants. Their study appeared in The New Phytologist in 2016. Stomata are leaf pores that trade carbon gain against water loss. Photosynthesis reacts to light shifts almost at once, while stomata lag far behind, so the two fall out of step under changing light. The team measured both responses to step changes in light across several species with gas exchange tools.

Species differed widely in strategy, some saving water and others chasing carbon. Guard cell shape mattered: dumbbell shaped cells opened and closed fast, while in oval celled species other traits set the pace. Slow stomata could cut carbon gain by about a tenth. The authors propose stomatal speed as a fresh breeding target. Faster pores, they argue, could lift crop yield and water efficiency together.
europmc-pmc4983759:
Jean-Louis Vincent, Amanda Quintairos e Silva, Lúcio Couto, and Fabio S. Taccone review the value of tracking blood lactate over time in critically ill patients. Their systematic review appeared in Critical Care in 2016. A single high lactate reading flags danger, but the trend may say more about whether treatment is working. The team searched major databases to February 2016 for studies that used serial lactate measures to predict outcome in acutely ill adults.

Ninety-six studies qualified, spanning general intensive care, surgery, trauma, cardiac surgery, and sepsis. One finding held throughout: falling lactate went with better prognosis. The pattern was not specific to sepsis; it applied across the common causes of high lactate. Changes were slow, though, and the review could not set a target speed of fall. The authors advise repeating measures at set intervals and reading the direction, not chasing a single number.
europmc-pmc4990459:
Amy R. Cameron leads a team showing that metformin, the first line diabetes drug, also calms inflammation without diabetes. Their study appeared in Circulation Research in 2016. Metformin users suffer fewer heart events than users of other diabetes drugs, and the advantage is unlikely to come from blood sugar control alone. In rodents the drug shrinks heart attack damage in diabetic and non-diabetic animals alike. The team probed the drug's anti-inflammatory action in liver cells, macrophages, plasma, and mice.

Metformin suppressed inflammatory signaling, including signals through the NF-kappaB pathway. That effect ran alongside, not downstream of, its known metabolic actions: blocking the inflammation path did not blunt glucose or fat gene effects. Adding back the suppressed cytokines did not cancel the drug's glucose action either. The authors define a dual action for metformin, likely triggered from one mitochondrial target. The split may explain its heart benefits.
europmc-pmc5012559:
B. Ian Hutchins, Xin Yuan, James M. Anderson, and George M. Santangelo, with a co-author, introduce a new citation measure in PLoS Biology in 2016. Judging a paper by its journal's impact factor is widely seen as flawed, yet hiring and grant panels still lean on rough numbers. Their Relative Citation Ratio instead rates each article against its own field.

The ratio divides a paper's citation rate by the rate expected for its field, where the field is drawn from the papers cited alongside it. Scores therefore compare fairly across unlike subjects. Tested on 88,835 articles from 2003 to 2010, the scores lined up well with expert judgments of influence, and grant holders held steady ranks across fields. A free web tool, iCite, lets anyone compute the ratio for papers listed in PubMed.
europmc-pmc5020059:
Samar M. Hatem and six co-authors review arm recovery after stroke in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2016. Stroke is a leading cause of disability, and loss of arm and hand movement limits daily life, work, and social life. Training is the best-proven way to regain movement. The team sifted 5,712 papers on stroke rehabilitation and kept 270 that met their quality rules for upper limb outcomes.

The review sorts methods into those strong enough to stand as the main therapy, those best used as add-ons, and newer tech-based options. Muscle strengthening, therapy that forces use of the weak arm, mirror therapy, and botulinum toxin earned main-therapy backing. Mental practice with movement imagery suited an add-on role. Brain stimulation, robot training, and virtual reality are weighed as rising choices. A decision tree ties the choices to each patient's state, aiming to fit treatment to the person.
europmc-pmc5031759:
Qing Zhao, Xiao-Ya Chen, and Cathie Martin review the medicinal plant Scutellaria baicalensis in Science Bulletin in 2016. Known in China as Huang-Qin, or the golden herb, its dried root has been used for more than 2,000 years against diarrhea, bleeding, sleeplessness, inflammation, and lung infections. The plant grows wild across East Asia and Russia and is now farmed in Europe as well.

The review centers on the root's flavones, above all baicalin and wogonoside and their active forms baicalein and wogonin. Studies credit these compounds with actions against cancer, bacteria, and viruses, plus protection for the liver and brain and calming of seizures. The authors also cover clinical uses and the lab and gene work that has traced how the plant builds its flavones. That pathway knowledge opens the door to breeding or engineering richer sources of the active compounds.
europmc-pmc5052459:
Neyssa M. Marina and a very large international team report the EURAMOS-1 trial in The Lancet Oncology in 2016. Osteosarcoma is a bone cancer of the young, treated with chemotherapy before and after surgery. Patients whose tumors respond poorly to the first chemotherapy face worse odds, so the trial asked whether adding two more drugs after surgery would help them. It enrolled patients aged forty or younger across 325 sites in 17 countries.

Of 2,260 registered patients, 618 poor responders were split at random between the standard three-drug plan, MAP, and the same plan plus ifosfamide and etoposide, MAPIE. After about five years of follow-up, event-free survival was essentially identical in the two groups, with a hazard ratio of 0.98. The added drugs brought extra burden without extra benefit. The trial, the largest of its kind in this rare cancer, supports staying with MAP for poor responders and looking elsewhere for gains.
europmc-pmc5088659:
Minghui Wang and a broad team of co-authors map gene activity across the Alzheimer's brain in Genome Medicine in 2016. Why the disease destroys some brain regions and spares others is unexplained. The team built an expression dataset from 1,053 postmortem samples across nineteen cortical regions of 125 people, spanning the range from no dementia to severe Alzheimer's pathology. They ranked genes, gene modules, and regions by their tie to illness.

The sifted signals pointed to actin structure, axon guidance, and nervous system development. Matching the abnormal signatures to cell types showed many belonged to oligodendrocytes, the myelin-making cells, alongside astrocytes and neurons. Strikingly, many changes, including the oligodendrocyte ones, appeared early in disease, marking them as possible treatment targets rather than late debris. More than half of the top gene modules were enriched for known Alzheimer's risk genes and replicated in an independent cohort, validating the network approach.
europmc-pmc5090659:
Jörg T. Regula and a large team of co-authors reported a drug study in EMBO Molecular Medicine in 2016. They built a single antibody, called a CrossMAb, that blocks two signals at once. One is VEGF-A, which drives leaky new blood vessels in the eye. The other is angiopoietin-2, a partner signal raised in diseased eyes.

In a mouse model of abnormal vessel growth under the retina, blocking both signals beat either one alone, with fewer lesions, less leakage and swelling, and less nerve cell loss. The antibody, named RG7716, also beat VEGF-A blockade alone in monkeys with laser-made vessel growth. Changes to its tail region sped removal from the blood but not the eye, a profile the team offers as a next step for treating wet macular degeneration and similar diseases.
europmc-pmc5094759:
Lukasz Aleksandrowicz, Rosemary Green, Edward J. M. Joy, Pete Smith, and Andy Haines systematically reviewed diet change studies in PLoS ONE in 2016, with Andrea S. Wiley also on the byline as printed in the text. They gathered research on how shifting what people eat affects greenhouse gas emissions, land use, water use, and health.

Across the studies they found 14 shared patterns of more sustainable eating. Adopting them could cut emissions and land use by as much as 70 to 80 percent in the strongest cases. Typical cuts ran near 20 to 30 percent. Water use could fall by up to half. Gains grew as animal foods were cut more deeply. The same shifts also brought modest drops in overall death risk, linking greener diets with healthier ones.
europmc-pmc5095159:
Simon P. Skinner, Rasmus H. Fogh, Wayne Boucher, Timothy J. Ragan, Luca G. Mureddu, and Geerten W. Vuister described a software release in the Journal of Biomolecular NMR in 2016. Their program, CcpNmr AnalysisAssign version 3, handles analysis of NMR data, a method that probes molecules in conditions close to those in living cells.

NMR is powerful but hard for non-specialists, so the new version aims for simple, flexible workflows built on modern graphics tools. The authors walk through assigning a protein's backbone signals as a worked example of how tasks are built in the program. The package covers liquid and solid-state NMR, can be downloaded from the project site, and is free for non-profit use.
europmc-pmc5122959:
Walid Mottawea and a large team of co-authors probed the roots of Crohn's disease in Nature Communications in 2016. Crohn's brings chronic gut inflammation, and gut microbe imbalance is linked to it, but cause and effect were unclear. They studied newly diagnosed children, before treatment could blur the picture.

The patients' gut proteins pointed to weakened mitochondria, the cells' power units, with proteins that detoxify hydrogen sulfide turned down while sulfide-making microbes rose. One microbe, Atopobium parvulum, sat at the center of the sulfide producers' network. In susceptible mice it triggered gut-wide inflammation that needed other microbes present, and a sulfide-scavenging drug eased it. The work ties a specific microbe and a toxic gas to Crohn's mechanism.
europmc-pmc5250659:
Clemens J. Sommer reviewed experimental models of ischemic stroke in Acta Neuropathologica in 2017, writing as a solo author. Most strokes come from a blocked brain blood vessel. The damage depends on how long and how badly flow stops, on backup vessels, blood pressure, age, sex, other diseases, medicines, and genes. No single model can hold all of that, Sommer argues.

The review walks through the main options. A thread passed into a rodent's middle cerebral artery gives repeatable damage and can be withdrawn to mimic clot-removal treatment. Direct vessel blocking needs skull surgery. A vessel-tightening drug can starve nearly any region, and light-activated dye makes neat cortical lesions but leaves almost no salvageable border zone. Clot-based and spontaneous models sit closest to human stroke, at the price of variable lesion size, place, and timing. The lesson is to pick the model that matches the question.
europmc-pmc5258859:
Jinrui Shi and eight colleagues used CRISPR-Cas9 to improve maize yield under drought in the Plant Biotechnology Journal in 2017. The maize gene ARGOS8 damps the plant's response to ethylene, a stress hormone, and plants engineered to overproduce it had already yielded better in dry conditions. The team wanted the same gain from editing the native gene rather than adding a foreign one.

Scanning over 400 inbred maize lines showed natural ARGOS8 levels were always far below the helpful engineered level. So the team inserted a moderate, always-on promoter from another maize gene into ARGOS8's control region, or swapped it in for the native promoter. The edited plants made more ARGOS8 in every tissue tested. In field trials under flowering-time drought, they out-yielded normal maize by five bushels per acre, with no yield penalty when water was plentiful.
europmc-pmc5282359:
W. J. Stuart, assistant surgeon at the Royal Infirmary in Edinburgh, collected cases of operative injury to the thoracic duct in the neck for the Edinburgh Medical Journal. The thoracic duct carries lymph up through the chest and empties it at the root of the neck, exactly where surgeons increasingly operated. Many practitioners still feared cutting it meant a grave, perhaps fatal, injury, yet few cases had ever been published.

Stuart argues the missing reports hide many accidents, and that good treatment can only be set by studying past cases, so surgeons have a duty to record theirs. His own case concerns a dressmaker of thirty-five. Her cancer ran from a breast tumour removed in 1903 to gland masses cleared from her armpit in 1905, then a fixed tumour below the collarbone in 1907. His collected list outnumbers those in French and German monographs.
europmc-pmc5333359:
Karsten Suhre led a large team in linking genes to blood proteins in Nature Communications in 2017. Gene scans have tied hundreds of gene variants to disease, yet the paths from variant to illness often stay dark. Protein levels in blood sit between genes and disease, so ties at that level can light the path. The team ran a gene scan against hundreds of blood proteins at once.

In a German study group, they found hundreds of firm links between gene variants and protein levels. More than half held up in a second group of Arab and Asian roots. The links overlapped with known gene risk spots for dozens of diseases. The team built a web tool and a network map that join genes, proteins, and disease ends. The map gives drug and test makers a base for new work.
europmc-pmc5381059:
Yoshiko Iwai, Junzo Hamanishi, Kenji Chamoto, and Tasuku Honjo reviewed PD-1 blockade cancer care in the Journal of Biomedical Science in 2017. Immune care now stands as a fourth pillar of cancer work, beside surgery, radiation, and drug care. The fresh wave does not whip the immune system on. It takes the brakes off, by blocking PD-1, a switch that tires killer T cells out.

Antibody drugs that block the switch won clear trials and gained first clearances for skin cancer in 2014 and lung cancer a year later, across the United States, Europe, and Japan. Since the drugs free the patient's own T cells, gains can last long and span many tumor types. Yet a large share of patients gain nothing. The review sums up the path of the care and the open work: drug pairs and marks that foretell who will gain.
europmc-pmc5456159:
Poletto and co-authors study how the structure of native cellulose shapes the heat resistance of natural fibers. Their research article appeared in Materials. Cellulose is the main building material of plants. Makers increasingly use plant fibers in composite products. A fiber's behavior under heat depends on its inner structure. Crystallinity, crystal size, and chemical makeup all matter. Knowing them in advance can guide better material choices.

The team examined ten natural fibers. Six came from plants such as sisal, jute, and ramie. Four came from Brazilian woods. They measured the fibers with infrared spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and heat-based weight tests. Fibers with more extractives and lower crystallinity broke down sooner. Smaller cellulose crystals also meant weaker heat stability. In contrast, larger crystals and higher crystallinity pushed breakdown to higher temperatures. The results let makers predict fiber performance before mixing composites.
europmc-pmc5571659:
Fang and co-authors report a genome-wide study of soybean traits in Genome Biology. Soybean is a major source of protein and oil. Traits such as yield and oil content tend to move together. That linkage makes breeding better varieties a hard puzzle.

The team grew 809 soybean lines from around the world. They scored 84 traits over two years at three sites. Genome scans found 245 significant gene regions. Among them, 95 interacted with other regions. Network analysis linked 51 traits through shared regions. Some regions shaped several traits at once. The team also pinned down 14 genes for fatty acid build-up. Readers get a map of how soybean traits share genetic roots.
europmc-pmc5579659:
Pullar, Carr, and Vissers review vitamin C in skin health for Nutrients. Skin is the body's barrier against the outside world. Healthy skin holds high levels of vitamin C. The vitamin drives collagen synthesis there. It also shields against ultraviolet damage.

Creams often add vitamin C on that logic. Whether smearing it on beats eating enough is murkier. The review weighs cell and animal studies against human ones. It compares dietary intake with topical application directly. Some skin traits likely gain most from better nutrition. Gaps in the evidence get named plainly. Scurvy shows the extreme case of deficiency. Fragile skin and slow healing follow when the vitamin runs out. Readers get a balanced brief on a popular skin ingredient.
europmc-pmc5662659:
Brooke and co-authors describe a national register in the European Journal of Epidemiology. The Swedish cause of death register covers all deaths in Sweden. Electronic records run from 1952 onward. Sweden's recording tradition reaches back to 1751. The clergy first gathered such data at population level. All causes have been included since 1911.

The register serves official statistics and medical research. It can link to other national registers on health and social factors. That linkage gives it much of its research value. The article sets out the register's origins and contents. It lists key strengths and weaknesses for users. Main causes of death are shown by age group and over time.
europmc-pmc5701259:
Du and co-authors report a cancer study in Nature Communications. It explains fat buildup in clear cell kidney tumors. These tumors are defined by lipid-rich clear cells. Loss of the VHL gene steadies hypoxia factors called HIFs. Why fat piles up was still undefined. The team pinned it on one transport enzyme. CPT1A gates fatty acid entry into mitochondria for burning. HIF1 and HIF2 directly repress that gene.

With the gate shut, fatty acids head to storage droplets. Droplet growth happened whatever the fat source was. Restoring CPT1A slowed tumor growth in tests. Human tumors showed lower CPT1A than healthy kidney. Low CPT1A also tracked with worse patient outcomes.
europmc-pmc5704459:
Hall and co-authors identify a gut bacterium strain group linked to bowel disease. Their research article appeared in Genome Medicine. Inflammatory bowel disease alters the gut microbiome. The team sequenced stool samples monthly. Twenty patients and twelve controls took part. The study gathered 266 samples in total.

Oxygen-tolerant bacteria were more common in patients. One species bloomed briefly during flares. That species is Ruminococcus gnavus. The team found two distinct strain groups. One group was enriched in patients. It carried 199 special genes. Those genes aid stress survival and mucus use. The authors say oxidative stress shapes the diseased gut. This strain group may thrive because of it.
europmc-pmc5730859:
Gassler and co-authors study how the genome folds just after fertilization. A mouse egg and sperm bring in two very unlike genomes. The team asked how loops and domains first form in the one cell embryo. They used single nucleus Hi-C on normal and altered embryos.

They report that loops and domains depend on cohesin, a ring shaped protein complex. A second protein, Wapl, sets loop size and how far loops reach. Maternal and paternal genomes respond in unlike ways. Computer models of loop extrusion match the data well. The work gives a clear model for early genome order.
europmc-pmc5741059:
Cameron and co-authors present GRIDSS, a software tool that finds large genome rearrangements. Finding such changes from short DNA reads is hard to do well. False calls plague cancer and medical work in particular. GRIDSS builds break ends first, using a positional de Bruijn graph.

The tool merges assembly, split read, and read pair proof into one score. On test and patient tumor data it stays both keen and precise. It halves the false call rate of rival methods on human cell line data. It also flags odd inserts, grades each call, and handles many samples at once.
europmc-pmc5750659:
Mohammed and co-authors review chitosan nanoparticles for drug delivery without needles. Chitosan is a safe, degradable polymer that breaks down in the body. Its particles carry a positive charge and stick to mucus. That makes them fit for mouth, nose, lung, and eye routes.

The review covers chitosan traits, chemical changes, and safety data. It also covers how the body handles these particles. Uses include cancer, gut and lung disease, brain delivery, and eye infection. Slow, sustained release is a key strength of the forms. Recent studies and early test work are summed up.
europmc-pmc5753159:
Bongomin and co-authors check how precise world estimates of serious fungal disease are. Fungal diseases kill over 1.5 million people a year and affect over a billion. Most of those deaths could be avoided with fast diagnosis. The LIFE portal has built country by country burden counts since 2013.

Those counts cover over 80% of the world's people. The team re-examined the 43 published country papers behind them. Burden differs sharply between countries and risk groups. Big case counts include lung aspergillosis, cryptococcal meningitis, and fungal asthma. The review tests where the numbers rest on firm ground.
europmc-pmc5796059:
Altmann and Schmidt review the role of microglia in diabetic retinopathy. This eye disease strikes about a third of people with diabetes and can blind. It was first seen as a vessel disease. Fresh work adds inflammation and nerve damage to the picture. Microglia, the retina's resident immune cells, sit at the center.

High blood sugar switches microglia on, the authors explain. The cells then release inflammatory signals and multiply and move more. Retinal neurons suffer, die back, and the nerve fiber layer thins. New treatments must act early, before eye changes can be diagnosed, they argue.
europmc-pmc5807059:
McWilliams and co-authors test whether routine cell cleanup needs PINK1. Cells clear worn-out mitochondria by a process called mitophagy. Faults in the PINK1 gene cause early Parkinson's disease. Lab work cast PINK1 as the master switch for that cleanup.

The team used reporter mice that make mitophagy visible in tissues. Busy tissues like brain showed high cleanup rates. Mice lacking PINK1 kept the same routine rates almost everywhere. Only pancreatic islets differed. The result implies other, unknown pathways run daily cleanup. Readers get a challenge to a tidy story about Parkinson's biology.
europmc-pmc5817859:
Liu and co-authors review how lung cancers escape EGFR-blocking drugs without using EGFR itself. The review appeared in Molecular Cancer. Drugs such as gefitinib and erlotinib help patients whose tumors carry EGFR mutations. Most tumors still adapt and resume growth.

Resistance splits into two broad routes. New EGFR mutations like T790M block the drug directly. The review centers on the second route, bypass signaling. Other receptor kinases, such as MET and HER2, switch on and revive the PI3K/Akt and MAPK pathways. Faulty downstream parts can do the same job. The authors map each bypass track and the trials testing paired drugs against it.
europmc-pmc5833859:
Petrova and co-authors review the oxygen-starved zones inside tumors and their hold on cancer's course. Their review appeared in Oncogenesis. Poor blood supply leaves many tumor regions hypoxic. Cells answer through HIF factors, which rewrite gene activity.

The review follows hypoxia through each neighbor of cancer. Fibroblasts reprogram into tumor helpers. The matrix stiffens and shifts. Blood and lymph vessels sprout in crooked patterns. Immune cells lose their fighting edge. Together these changes select harder clones and favor spread. The authors close by weighing where this knowledge could guide treatment.
europmc-pmc5848259:
Russell and co-authors map how often group B Streptococcus colonizes pregnant women worldwide. Their systematic review appeared in Clinical Infectious Diseases. The bacterium passes from mother to newborn during birth. It remains a leading cause of newborn sepsis.

The team pooled 390 studies covering nearly 300,000 women in 85 countries. Adjusted estimates put worldwide colonization near 18 percent. Rates run lower across southern and eastern Asia. Five serotypes account for almost all colonizing strains found. Serotype III, tied to invasive disease, makes up a quarter. The map guides vaccine and prevention planning. The series this paper belongs to aims to size the whole burden of the disease.
europmc-pmc5852359:
Vanderwalde and co-authors read microsatellite instability straight from sequencing panels. Their study appeared in Cancer Medicine. The marker flags tumors likely to answer immune checkpoint drugs. Their assay needs no matched normal tissue sample.

Across 2,189 cases, the sequencing call matched PCR testing closely. Mismatch repair status from tissue staining agreed as well. The team then scanned 11,348 patients spanning 26 cancer types. High instability turned up in 23 of those types. It overlapped only loosely with mutational burden and PD-L1. Few tumors carried all three markers at once. The authors argue each test adds its own signal.
europmc-pmc5929359:
Aragão and co-authors describe the MX2 beamline at the Australian Synchrotron. Their article appeared in the Journal of Synchrotron Radiation. MX2 is a microfocus beamline for crystallography. It serves both chemical and protein researchers. High flux helps with crystals that diffract poorly. A tiny beam suits micro-crystals and cuts background scatter.

User work began in late 2008, they report. Most time goes to structural biology users. Protein Data Bank deposits from the beamline pass 1,700. Chemical crystallography now takes about a tenth of time. Gear includes a robot, cryostream, and a large pixel detector. Readers get full specs of source, optics, and hutch.
europmc-pmc5999759:
Kumar and Trivedi review glutathione S-transferases and their role in plant stress defence, with focus on arsenic. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science. Arsenic in groundwater used for irrigation threatens crops and food chains. Inside plants it disrupts metabolism and sparks oxidative stress. These enzymes attach glutathione to harmful molecules. That quenching shields cells from oxidative damage. The enzyme family is large and responds to many stressors.

Past work ties these genes to arsenic handling in plants. Sulfur and glutathione are both needed for that detox path. The review updates evidence on uptake, metabolism, and cleansing. Genetic experiments that clarified enzyme functions are also covered.
europmc-pmc6032159:
Wang and Lo review diabetic retinopathy and its treatments. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. This eye disease is the most common complication of diabetes. It damages small blood vessels in the retina. It is a leading cause of vision loss in working-age adults.

Early disease brings leaky vessels and blocked capillaries. Later stages grow fragile new vessels that can bleed. Swelling of the macula is the main cause of sight loss. The review covers inflammation and nerve damage too. Both may start earlier than vessel changes suggest. Anti-VEGF drugs now lead treatment, with laser and surgery beside them. Many patients still gain little vision, though. New targets from lab work are discussed.
europmc-pmc6109259:
Kerpedjiev and co-authors present a software article in Genome Biology on HiGlass, a web tool for viewing genome interaction maps. Such maps show which parts of the genome touch each other inside the cell. The data are large and hard to inspect with static pictures.

HiGlass runs in a browser and lets users zoom across scales in two-dimensional maps. One-dimensional tracks can sit beside the maps. Views can be synced, mixed, and shared as snapshots with collaborators or the public. The team shows the tool at work comparing experimental conditions. It is free online and also runs as a container on any platform.
europmc-pmc6113859:
Salmaso and Moro wrote an overview in Frontiers in Pharmacology on computer methods for drug discovery. Drug design often starts by asking how a small molecule binds a protein. Early tools treated both partners as stiff shapes. That view missed much of how binding works in real life.

The overview traces the shift from static docking to molecular dynamics. Docking places a molecule into a protein pocket. Dynamics then lets both sides move and flex. New sampling methods capture rare poses and shifts. The authors show how the two steps now link up. Readers get a clear path from the old lock-and-key idea to modern moving models.
europmc-pmc6139259:
Global Research on Developmental Disabilities Collaborators report a study in The Lancet Global Health on developmental disabilities in young children. The work covers 195 countries and territories from 1990 to 2016. It counts children under five years with six conditions. They include epilepsy, intellectual disability, hearing loss, and vision loss.

About 52.9 million young children had such a disability in 2016. That is about 8.4 percent of that age group. Roughly 95 percent lived in low- and middle-income countries. Vision loss was the most common condition. Intellectual disability caused the most years lived with disability. Rates fell in nearly all countries over the study years.
europmc-pmc6158259:
Luu and co-authors present a research article in Scientific Reports on how a gut microbe product steers killer T cells. Gut microbes make short-chain fatty acids that affect energy balance and immune cells. Giving these acids by mouth is being explored as a therapy for inflammatory disease. Most past work looked at CD4 T cells.

The team focused on CD8 cytotoxic T cells, which kill infected and abnormal cells. Butyrate, and propionate to a lesser degree, changed gene activity in these cells. Treated cells made more interferon gamma and granzyme B, tools for killing targets. Butyrate also switched Tc17 cells toward the killer type. The effect worked by blocking histone deacetylases, not the usual receptors.
europmc-pmc6160559:
Cory and co-authors wrote a mini-review in Frontiers in Nutrition on polyphenols, plant compounds found in many foods. Polyphenols are widely studied for their effects on health. Much of the evidence comes from animal studies, feeding trials, and human cohort and case-control studies.

The review weighs claimed protective effects against major non-communicable diseases. These include obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and brain diseases of aging. Possible harms of some polyphenols are also considered, though evidence of harm is limited. Government rules on safety and health claims are discussed. The authors draw out what the evidence means for public health practice, policy, and future research.
europmc-pmc6204759:
Tan and co-authors reviewed antioxidants and stress in ageing. Ageing brings a slow loss of organ and tissue function. Oxidative stress harms cells when harmful species outnumber protective ones. The review appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. It covers diseases linked to old age.

The authors explain how free radicals form and cause harm. They set out how antioxidant molecules block that harm. Some stop radical chains from spreading. Others stop radicals from forming at all. The review links this work to arthritis, diabetes, dementia, and heart disease. The authors say a clearer view of these paths could aid healthy ageing. It could also guide new care options.
europmc-pmc6247459:
Suetens and co-authors report two large European surveys of infections caught in care settings. Their report appeared in Eurosurveillance. The surveys ran in 2016 and 2017. They covered more than 310,000 patients in acute care hospitals. They also covered more than 117,000 residents in long term care homes. Data came from twenty-eight and twenty-three countries in turn.

About six and a half percent of hospital patients had at least one such infection on survey days. In care homes the share was about four percent. The team estimates near nine million such infections per year across Europe. Drug resistance was common in both settings. Resistance markers appeared in about a third of hospital cases. Care home levels were nearly as high, a point the authors flag with concern.
europmc-pmc6320759:
Xue and co-authors review inducible nitric oxide synthase in immune cells and disease. The review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. This enzyme, called iNOS, makes nitric oxide after immune triggers. Nitric oxide can kill microbes and guard the host. It can also damage healthy tissue. Macrophages, T cells, and dendritic cells all express iNOS.

The authors trace how iNOS shapes each cell type. It steers T cell differentiation and macrophage behavior. Mature dendritic cells are also affected. Nitric oxide alters key molecules in signaling paths. The review draws on lab studies in animals and humans. It closes with prospects for new research. Targeting iNOS may help several inflammatory diseases.
europmc-pmc6348759:
Johns and co-authors report health risks among transgender high school students. Their report appeared in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. It uses the 2017 Youth Risk Behavior Survey. That survey covers grades 9 to 12 in the United States. Ten states and nine large urban districts took part. Students reported gender identity and health behaviors.

About 1.8 percent of students identified as transgender. Compared with cisgender peers, they faced far higher risks. Violence victimization was more common for them. Substance use and sexual risk behaviors were higher too. Suicide risk stood out as sharply raised. The authors present the numbers by risk area in detail. They frame the results as a call for safer schools. Supportive settings may blunt these stark disparities.
europmc-pmc6350359:
Greene and co-authors review claudin-5, a key seal protein of the blood-brain barrier. Their review appeared in Fluids and Barriers of the CNS. Tight junctions seal the gaps between vessel cells. Claudin-5 is the most enriched of those proteins in brain vessels. The seal keeps harmful material out of the brain.

That same seal blocks most small drug molecules. Over 95 percent of them cannot pass it. Claudin-5 faults appear in brain diseases. Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis are among them. Depression and schizophrenia also show links. Adjusting claudin-5 levels could treat disease, the authors argue. It might also open a door for medicines. The review weighs the risks of loosening the brain's gatekeeper.
europmc-pmc6357359:
Tellier and co-authors offer a commentary in BMC Infectious Diseases on how respiratory infections spread through air. They sort out terms that are often mixed up, such as droplets, aerosols, and airborne spread. The question matters because the answer decides which control steps a hospital must use.

Small particles can stay in the air and carry germs beyond short range, they argue. Large droplets fall fast and act at close range. Some diseases, like tuberculosis and measles, are widely accepted as airborne. For other germs the proof is less clear. Clear terms help staff choose masks, ventilation, and isolation steps that fit the real risk.
europmc-pmc6514059:
Barrow, Martin and Colonna review the natural cytotoxicity receptors in health and disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. These receptors, NKp46, NKp44 and NKp30, sit on natural killer cells. They were among the first activating NK receptors cloned. They help NK cells spot tumour and virus-infected cells.

Many ligands from host and pathogen can bind these receptors. Ligands may sit on cell surfaces or be secreted. They tune killing and cytokine release in distinct tissues. Other immune cells can also express the receptors under some conditions. That spreads NK-style recognition to those cells. The authors close with therapy ideas built on this biology.
europmc-pmc6517359:
Korbecki, Bobiński and Dutka review how PPAR receptors calm inflammation. Their review appeared in Inflammation Research. PPARs are nuclear receptors that act as transcription factors. The family has three members: alpha, beta/delta and gamma. Fatty acid derivatives and some prostaglandins switch them on.

Their main task in inflammation is to restrain NF-κB. PPARs can bind and inactivate its p65 part directly. They can also mark it for breakdown. Indirect routes add more control. PPARs raise antioxidant enzymes and cut reactive oxygen species. They boost IκBα, SIRT1 and PTEN as well. The review maps ligands, activation steps and each pathway in detail.
europmc-pmc6518059:
Baartscheer and co-authors test direct heart effects of empagliflozin. Their study appeared in Diabetologia. Empagliflozin blocks the kidney SGLT2 transporter. It lowers the risk of cardiovascular death in type 2 diabetes. Why it helps the heart was unknown.

The team measured ion levels in heart muscle cells from rats and rabbits. High glucose raised cell sodium and calcium. Empagliflozin cut sodium-hydrogen exchanger flux. Cell sodium and calcium then fell. Calcium inside mitochondria rose. A known exchanger blocker, cariporide, blunted these effects. The drug acted even without glucose present. The authors conclude the heart effect is direct and apart from SGLT2.
europmc-pmc6520659:
Dresselhaus and Meffert review cell-specific roles of NF-κB in the nervous system. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. NF-κB is a transcription factor found in nearly all cells. Its roles in immunity and cancer are well mapped. Its basic roles in the brain are less clear.

The brain holds many cell types, and each may use NF-κB in its own way. The authors separate cell-autonomous control from wider effects. They review work in neurons first. Then they turn to glial cells, astrocytes and microglia among them. Normal function and disease states both get covered. Subunit and cell-type detail runs through the piece.
europmc-pmc6582859:
Cañedo-Dorantes and Cañedo-Ayala review how skin heals an acute wound, writing in the International Journal of Inflammation. Repair runs in three overlapping phases, and the review assigns every player its entrance. Sensory nerves fire first, triggering pain signals, bleeding control and inflammation within seconds.

The inflammatory phase then sends in neutrophils, monocytes turned macrophages, and lymphocytes to kill germs and clear debris. The proliferative phase rebuilds: fibroblasts lay down new matrix, fresh skin creeps across the surface, new vessels sprout, and severed nerves regrow. Remodeling, which can run for months, reorganizes the scar and restores strength. Throughout, the authors track the cytokines, growth factors and matrix signals that keep the cast in step.
europmc-pmc6600059:
Dutta, Majzoub, and Agarwal offer a systematic review in the Arab Journal of Urology. Their subject is oxidative stress and sperm function. Reactive oxygen species help sperm mature at normal levels. In excess, they damage sperm and cut fertility. The review pulls the evidence together for clinicians who treat male infertility.

The authors searched PubMed, Medline, EMBASE, and Cochrane sources under PRISMA rules. Their search found 1,857 studies, and 66 met the rules for inclusion. Excess reactive oxygen species can drive lipid peroxidation and sperm DNA damage. The review covers lab tests that can measure oxidative stress in semen. Care usually pairs antioxidant supplements with removal of the cause. The authors argue that testing should guide treatment choices.
europmc-pmc6615259:
Arioz and co-authors test melatonin against infection-driven depressive behavior in mice. Their research article appears in Frontiers in Immunology. Inflammation helps drive major depressive disorder in many patients. A bacterial toxin, LPS, triggers depressive-like states in lab animals. The team asked whether melatonin could blunt that effect.

Mice given LPS got melatonin at 500 milligrams per kilogram. Behavior tests came 24 hours after the LPS dose. Treated mice stayed mobile longer in suspension and swim tests. Melatonin cut NLRP3 inflammasome activity in the hippocampus. It lowered IL-1β release from microglia in cell tests. It also curbed pyroptosis and reactive oxygen species. Blocking SIRT1 or Nrf2 erased the benefits, tying them to that pathway.
europmc-pmc6667459:
Chen and co-authors present pLink 2, a faster search engine for cross-linked peptides. Their paper appears in Nature Communications. Cross-linking mass spectrometry maps protein structures and interactions. Finding linked peptide pairs faces a squared search space. Existing tools were slow and hard to validate at scale. pLink 2 uses a two-stage open search. Fragment indexing trims the coarse scoring load sharply. The result runs about forty times faster than pLink 1. It also beats the rival Kojak by three to ten times.

The team designed four ways to judge credibility. Ten leading engines were compared on equal footing. pLink 2 led on precision and sensitivity overall. Re-analysis of published datasets found up to 27 percent more pairs.
europmc-pmc6702459:
Fernandez and co-authors present Intervention Mapping as a framework for health promotion planning. Their perspective appears in Frontiers in Public Health. Good planning must integrate theory and hard evidence. Stakeholder and community engagement matters equally. Knowing how and when to use each input is hard. Intervention Mapping answers with six careful steps. Problem analysis opens the sequence. Outcomes and change objectives follow. Theory-based methods are then picked and translated. Parts combine into a coherent program. Roll-out and evaluation planning complete it.

Over a thousand published articles use the framework. Uses span community and clinical settings worldwide. New directions include adapting existing programs. Roll-out strategy planning is another growth area. Methods for spotting key drivers keep improving.
europmc-pmc6710759:
Moldogazieva and co-authors review oxidative stress and aging. Oxidative stress builds up when harmful oxygen byproducts outpace the body's defenses. Over time, these byproducts damage fats and sugars, forming sticky end products called ALEs and AGEs. The review links this damage to aging and age-related disease.

The authors describe how these end products cross-link proteins and disturb cell signals. They also cover failing mitochondria, worn protein cleanup systems, and key control genes such as Nrf2 and NF-kB. The damage is tied to brain disease, artery disease, and chronic inflammation. Knowing these paths may point to ways to slow them.
europmc-pmc6711459:
Zeidman and co-authors wrote the first part of a guide to group brain connectivity analysis. It focuses on Dynamic Causal Modelling for fMRI, the main tool for inferring how brain areas influence each other. The guide walks through one full example analysis in detail. Data and instructions let readers repeat every step in the SPM software.

The method has grown over 15 years of use in brain research. Appendices lay out the theory and the prior assumptions built into the models. A companion paper then takes the results to group level. Together they show how to move from one person's scan to claims about a whole group.
europmc-pmc6744659:
Li and co-authors mapped the regulators of m6A, a chemical mark on RNA, across 33 cancer types. The mark helps run many cell processes. The team analyzed genetic changes and activity levels of its regulators in more than 10,000 subjects. They asked how these regulators tie to cancer traits and patient outlook.

Genetic alterations in m6A regulators proved widespread. Their activity levels tracked closely with the activity of classic cancer pathways. Regulator patterns could sort patients by likely prognosis. One reader protein, IGF2BP3, stood out as a possible cancer-promoting gene across many types. The results form a resource for studying how this RNA marking layer feeds cancer.
europmc-pmc6770259:
Dei Cas and Ghidoni examine dietary curcumin, linking how much the body absorbs to what it can do for health. Curcumin is the yellow pigment of turmeric. It is credited with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer, and many other effects. Its weakness is pharmacokinetics: the gut absorbs little, and the liver transforms most of what gets in.

In one food study, volunteers ate 3 grams of turmeric, about 100 milligrams of curcumin. The parent compound appeared in only one of four blood samples. Its breakdown products showed in everyone, at low levels. The review surveys fixes: metabolism blockers, and new solid and liquid carriers. Some raise solubility, blood levels, and cell uptake.
europmc-pmc6815659:
Paget and co-authors present new estimates of flu deaths in the Journal of Global Health. Seasonal influenza spreads every year, but its true death toll is hard to count. Many deaths are recorded as lung or heart disease instead. Older World Health Organization figures were widely seen as too low. The GLaMOR project set out to rebuild the count.

The team gathered flu-linked excess death estimates for 31 countries across five WHO regions, covering 2002 to 2011. They then extended those rates to the rest of the world. Their work weighs how age and region change the toll. It also tests which country traits best predict flu mortality where direct data are missing.
europmc-pmc6823959:
Taylor-Weiner and co-authors describe a faster way to run genome studies, in Genome Biology. Tools for genetics were built for hundreds or thousands of samples. Cheap sequencing now points toward millions. Standard computing would take too long and cost too much at that scale.

The team moved a common analysis, mapping links between DNA variants and traits, onto graphics processing units. They rebuilt the tool with machine learning libraries such as TensorFlow. Runs became more than 200 times faster than on normal processors. Costs fell roughly five to ten fold. The authors expect such chips to become routine in genomics as datasets keep growing.
europmc-pmc6835559:
Geyer and co-authors address a hidden flaw in blood biomarker studies, in EMBO Molecular Medicine. Blood plasma holds clues to health, and protein tests guide medical choices. Yet few new protein markers reach the clinic. One reason is handling. How a sample is drawn, stored, and processed can change its proteins, faking a disease signal.

The team built deep protein profiles of red cells, platelets, plasma, and whole blood from 20 people, covering over 6,000 proteins. Spike-in tests showed which proteins betray contamination or poor handling. From those they defined quality marker panels. Labs can use the panels to flag suspect samples before trusting a new biomarker.
europmc-pmc6893459:
Abenavoli and co-authors review gut microbes, obesity, and probiotics, in the journal Nutrients. Obesity research of the past 30 years blamed energy imbalance, lifestyle, and genes. Gut bacteria have since joined the list of suspects. Their mix differs between lean and obese people, starting in infancy. Whether that mix drives weight gain, and whether probiotics can fix it, is the question here.

The review first lays out what a healthy intestinal community looks like and does. Pregnancy studies illustrate the pattern: in one study of 50 women, overweight mothers carried more Staphylococcus and fewer Bifidobacterium. The authors then weigh trials of probiotic supplements. Evidence for real benefit, they find, remains suggestive rather than settled.
europmc-pmc6919559:
Caicedo and co-authors report the results of the 2018 Data Science Bowl. Their article appeared in Nature Methods. Finding cell nuclei in microscope images is the first step in most image-based biology studies. Existing tools work, but each new experiment tends to need fresh setup by hand.

The contest drew 3,891 teams from around the world. Their task was to segment nuclei in any two-dimensional light microscopy image, with no human adjustment. Leading teams built deep learning models that handled many image types and conditions. Their success marks a step toward analysis software that needs no configuration. Such tools could make quantitative image work faster and far easier to repeat.
europmc-pmc7005859:
Bekker-Jensen and co-authors report a faster way to profile protein phosphorylation at scale. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Phosphorylation switches proteins on and off and steers nearly all cell signalling. Measuring it across whole cells has been powerful but slow to scale.

Their method uses data-independent acquisition, scanning everything rather than cherry-picking signals. It beats the older approach on range, consistency, sensitivity, and accuracy. Dropping the usual need for prebuilt spectral libraries barely hurt results, still yielding over 20,000 phosphopeptides in a 15-minute run per sample. A scoring upgrade pins down exact modification sites, and a model estimates what fraction of each site is occupied. As a test, 30 kinase-blocking drugs were profiled under growth factor stimulation. Specific kinases emerged as the drivers of the response.
europmc-pmc7013859:
Mazgaeen and Gurung review how the immune system detects lipopolysaccharide, the bacterial toxin known as endotoxin. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The molecule coats Gram-negative bacteria and is vital to their survival. It is also the most studied alarm signal in immunology.

For years the receptor TLR4 was the known sensor, catching the toxin outside cells or in internal compartments. The past decade added two more systems. TRP channels in cell membranes sense it directly, including in pain neurons, where detection triggers firing and pain signals. Inside the cell, enzymes called caspase-4 and caspase-5 in humans, caspase-11 in mice, catch toxin that slips in. The review traces the toxin's discovery, then each sensor in turn. The layered defence, the authors show, guards every space the toxin can reach.
europmc-pmc7136959:
Schlepckow and co-authors developed an antibody that boosts the protective activity of TREM2, a protein on the brain's microglia cells, in EMBO Molecular Medicine. TREM2 helps microglia switch into a disease-fighting state, but enzymes constantly clip it off the cell surface. Their antibody, 4D9, binds near the cutting site.

The antibody worked two ways at once: it kept more full-length TREM2 on the surface and switched on its signalling. In cell tests, microglia survived better and cleared more myelin debris and amyloid protein. In an Alzheimer's-model mouse, 4D9 cut amyloid formation and pushed microglia toward the disease-associated state. The authors present it as a protective strategy worth developing.
europmc-pmc7190659:
Cang and Nie present a method that restores spatial information to single-cell gene data. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Single-cell sequencing reveals each cell's activity in fine detail. But the process destroys the cell's original location in the tissue. The method, called SpaOTsc, rebuilds that lost geography.

It uses spatial measurements of a small set of genes as an anchor. A mathematical transport approach then places each cell on the map. From those positions, the method infers which cells signal to each other. It also estimates how genes in different cells influence one another. Tests on four datasets checked the predictions. Work on fly embryos recovered known signaling patterns. Biologists gain a way to study tissue conversations in place.
europmc-pmc7235159:
Shelton and co-authors propose extending the RE-AIM framework so health programs last longer and serve people more fairly. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Public Health. RE-AIM is a popular tool for planning and judging health interventions. It handles short-term upkeep well. Long-term survival of programs, over years, gets less attention.

Programs live in settings that keep changing. Staff turn over, budgets shift, and guidelines evolve. Populations' needs move as well. The authors argue for planning adaptations in advance and recording why they happen. Equity belongs in the frame from the start, not as an afterthought. Repeated measurement over a program's life cycle is recommended. The piece speaks to researchers who want proven programs to endure. It reframes success as impact that persists.
europmc-pmc7239959:
Yu and co-authors review how nanoparticles can harm the body by generating reactive oxygen species. Their article appeared in Nanoscale Research Letters. Nanoparticles serve in imaging, drug delivery, and many other medical roles. Their tiny size and reactive surfaces also make them prone to produce these aggressive molecules. Excess reactive oxygen damages proteins, fats, and DNA inside cells.

The review explains the mechanisms by which particles spark that production. Consequences range from membrane destruction to cell death and mutation. Both worn-down organelles and broken DNA strands are documented. The authors sort the evidence by particle type and cell response. Safety testing needs to catch this chemistry early, they argue. Designers of medical nanoparticles gain a checklist of hazards to engineer around.
europmc-pmc7247559:
Bukowski and co-authors review why cancer cells stop responding to chemotherapy drugs. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Multidrug resistance is blamed for over 90% of deaths in patients given standard or targeted drugs. Cancer remains one of the main causes of death worldwide, and chemotherapy is still its main treatment.

Cancer cells resist in several ways. They pump drugs out, break them down faster, repair DNA damage more quickly, and change their genes or gene control. The authors sort the main drug classes and explain how each one fails. They also describe new antitumor drugs built to dodge or reverse these defenses, and argue that knowing the resistance routes should guide the search for better treatment plans.
europmc-pmc7251059:
Xie and co-authors review cell-penetrating peptides, short protein chains that can slip through cell membranes. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. These peptides have fewer than 30 amino acids. They can carry drugs and other cargo into cells that would normally block them, which makes them attractive for diagnosis and treatment.

Uses under study include cancer, inflammation, brain disorders, ear and eye problems, and diabetes. Most work so far is in the lab or early trials. No peptide of this kind has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration. The authors sort recent progress in delivery design and list the problems that must be solved before such peptides reach routine clinical use.
europmc-pmc7296259:
Kirk, Zanker and Duque review osteosarcopenia, the combined loss of bone and muscle in older people. Their review appeared in the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle. Having both osteoporosis and sarcopenia together is worse than either alone, and the authors call the syndrome an emerging geriatric giant.

Among community-dwelling older adults, prevalence ranges from 5% to 37% in those aged 65 years and over, and is highest after fractures. In one group of 2353 adults, rates climbed steeply with age and were tied to inactivity, low body mass index, and higher fat mass. People with the combined condition had poorer nutrition, balance, and function, and higher rates of falls, fractures, and earlier death. Aging, inactivity, obesity, and fat infiltrating muscle and bone are expected to grow the problem.
europmc-pmc7349059:
Colizzi and co-authors survey parents of children with autism spectrum disorder in Brain Sciences about life under COVID-19. Young people with autism are especially unsettled by sudden, unpredictable change. Parents answered a 40-question online survey, and data came in for 527 children.

The emergency was a challenging period for 93.9 percent of families. Managing free time and structured activities proved hardest. About a third of the children showed more intense behavior problems, and earlier behavior problems predicted worse outcomes. Support continued for many, yet needs stood out, above all more health care help and in-home support. Readers see the pandemic through families whose routines are lifelines.
europmc-pmc7395159:
Zhang and Zhang review the history and advances of cancer immunotherapy in Cellular and Molecular Immunology. Immunotherapy has revolutionized treatment, with cell transfers and checkpoint drugs winning durable responses. Yet only some patients benefit, and the tumor's immune neighborhood helps decide who.

Immune cells inside a tumor shape its growth and the patient's outcome. That neighborhood is mixed and ever-changing, which long blocked precise analysis. Single-cell sequencing and mass cytometry now let researchers interrogate it systematically, exposing how cancer evades immunity. The two authors outline progress cell type by cell type, and the treatment ideas that follow. Readers get both a history and a field guide to the tumor microenvironment.
europmc-pmc7468859:
Carroll and co-authors survey how COVID-19 changed daily life in Canadian families with young children. The families had middle to high incomes and were part of an ongoing study. Parents answered an online survey with fixed and open questions.

In all, 254 families took part, with 235 mothers and 126 fathers responding to the survey questions. More than half said eating and meal routines had changed. Snack foods rose, and home cooking time rose too. Screen time rose for 74% of mothers and 87% of children in the sample, while activity fell for most. Stress came from juggling work with childcare and schooling, plus money strain. Some healthier habits also emerged. The authors call for work on long-term effects and family support.
europmc-pmc7558959:
Castañeda-Babarro and co-authors measure physical activity change during COVID-19 confinement in Spain. Lockdown kept people at home for long periods. Daily movement and sitting habits were likely to shift.

A total of 3800 healthy adults aged 18–64 took part. They answered an activity questionnaire twice during confinement. Vigorous activity fell by 16.8% in the sample. Walking time fell by 58.2% over the period. Sitting time rose by 23.8% in contrast. Those most active before confinement dropped the most. Men cut vigorous activity more than women. The authors flag young people and students as groups of concern.
europmc-pmc7660659:
Leeb and co-authors track mental health visits to emergency rooms by US children during COVID-19. It uses data from the National Syndromic Surveillance Program. The span runs from January 1 to October 17, 2020, with the same span in 2019 as a base.

Total emergency visits fell sharply from mid-March 2020, and mental health visits fell 43% at first. Yet the share of visits tied to mental health rose. It rose 24% for children aged 5 to 11 years. It rose 31% for teens aged 12 to 17 years. The authors urge continued checks on child mental health. The data came from hospitals in 47 states, covering about 73% of all US emergency visits.
europmc-pmc7676259:
Bowerman and co-authors compare gut microbes in lung disease patients and healthy people. The disease is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a progressive lung illness with no cure. The lung microbe mix is known to matter, but the gut side was unclear.

Stool tests found 146 bacterial species that differed between patients and controls. Several species tracked with worse lung function. Chemical tests found a distinct patient signature, rich in lipid-related compounds. One microbe linked to a web of disease-tied chemicals. The authors say gut profiles may help in the search for markers of this disease.
europmc-pmc7703759:
Chaumeil and co-authors present a toolkit for classifying microbe genomes. The toolkit, GTDB-Tk, assigns bacterial and archaeal genomes to taxa in the Genome Taxonomy Database. Samples from nature now yield thousands of draft genomes. Hand placement of each in a family tree is slow and prone to bias.

The tool places genomes into reference trees built from joined proteins. It runs fast and can classify thousands of genomes in parallel. The team tested it on 10,156 genomes assembled from metagenomes. Its calls proved accurate across a wide range of groups. The software is free under an open license for all users.
europmc-pmc7721859:
Levin and co-authors estimate how COVID-19 death risk climbs with age. They sought age-specific infection fatality rates to guide policy. The search found 113 prevalence studies. Of these, 27 studies from 34 places met their rules and fed the pooled analysis.

The fatality rate rose in a steep curve with age. It was 0.002% at age 10 and 0.01% at age 25. It reached 0.4% at age 55, 1.4% at age 65, 4.6% at age 75, and 15% at age 85. Age mix explained about 90% of the gap in overall rates between places. The authors stress guarding older adults. The search took in published articles, preprints, and government reports shared before 18 September 2020.
europmc-pmc7755059:
Heinzerling and co-authors trace COVID-19 spread from one patient to hospital staff in California. The patient was the first US community case, confirmed on February 26, 2020. Staff cared for the patient for 4 days before COVID-19 was suspected. Care used standard precautions and no special protective gear.

Of 121 exposed staff, 43 fell ill in the next 14 days and were tested. Three tested positive, among the first known work-based cases in the nation. The ill staff had longer contact and more exposure during nebulizer care. The authors urge early spotting and isolation of possible cases, plus full protective gear.
europmc-pmc7759459:
The Zoonomia Consortium presents a mammal genome resource for science and conservation. The project studies traits shared and specialized across placental mammals. It gives genome assemblies for 131 species, all but 9 of them new. It also aligns whole genomes of 240 species, spanning more than 80% of mammal families.

Regions of low genetic diversity were more common in species at high risk of extinction. Fine-scale signals of natural selection stand out in the alignment. Single reference genomes add their own insights. By putting diverse species first and sharing data fast and free, the project aims to aid discovery, medicine, and protection of wild life.
europmc-pmc7816359:
Ocloo and co-authors review the evidence on patient and public involvement in care and safety work. Involvement in UK health care dates back to the 1970s. Campaigns by harmed patients renewed the push for it. Benefits for research are now widely noted. Power gaps and low diversity still limit it.

This is a systematic review of earlier reviews. The team gathered theory on how involvement should work. They sorted the barriers that block it in practice. Enablers that help it succeed were listed too. The scope spans health care, social care, and patient safety. The authors aim to give a shared base for stronger involvement.
europmc-pmc7823859:
Lin and co-authors rapidly review public confidence in COVID-19 vaccines. Vaccines were eagerly awaited as the virus raged. Hesitancy was widespread all the same. The team compared polls from the US and other countries. Sources included three academic databases plus news and official reports.

The team screened work published by October 20, 2020. They kept 126 studies and surveys. Acceptance fell from over 70% in March to under 50% in October. Gaps split along age, income, and party lines. Safety fears and doubt about fast approval drove much of the drop. Doctor advice and past flu shots raised acceptance. Many people preferred to wait and watch others first. The authors warn that mandates could backfire.
europmc-pmc7835259:
Kansra and co-authors review obesity in children and teens. Obesity weaves together body, growth, setting, behavior, and gene factors. It is a major public health problem. The usual cause is taking in more calories than the body uses.

Early fat rebound in childhood raises later risk. Rising youth obesity brings diseases once seen only in adults. Type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and fatty liver disease now appear in teens. Sleep apnea and poor blood fats join the list. Diet and exercise advice stays the standard care. Effects of lifestyle plans alone are modest. New drug trials with GLP-1 medicines show stronger weight loss. The authors also warn of eating disorders tied to body image pressure.
europmc-pmc7886759:
Geng and co-authors present a review of how fat build-up harms the liver in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Extra lipid in the liver is not caused by alcohol in this disease. The harm done by that lipid is called lipotoxicity. The review explains how a mild fatty liver can progress to the inflamed form known as NASH.

The authors focus on free fatty acids and where they end up in liver cells. An imbalance between fat coming in and fat being burned or shipped out shifts many lipid species. Those shifts strain cell parts such as the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria. Stress signals switch on, and cells can die. The review maps these steps in detail. It gives readers a clear account of how simple fat storage turns into active liver damage.
europmc-pmc8020059:
Starr and co-authors map every spike mutation that lets SARS-CoV-2 escape a leading antibody drug. The antibody LY-CoV555, also called bamlanivimab, targets the spike receptor-binding domain. It was used alone and in a cocktail with LY-CoV016. Viral evolution could, in time, defeat both. The team tested all single amino acid changes in the domain.

The authors report a complete escape map for each antibody and for the pair. E484K escapes LY-CoV555, while K417N/T escapes LY-CoV016. Both changes already circulate in the South African and Brazilian lineages. The L452R change in a Californian lineage also escapes LY-CoV555. A few single changes even beat the combined cocktail. The authors urge antibody designs that spread across more epitopes.
europmc-pmc8065159:
Ellabaan and co-authors forecast how antibiotic resistance genes will jump between bacterial genomes. Resistance spreads when genes move sideways between bacteria. The team built a statistical method to spot past transfers. They then asked which genes sit ready to move again. The raw material was tens of thousands of bacterial genomes.

The authors identify 152 gene exchange networks holding 22,963 genomes in total. Sequences around the resistance genes exposed the moving parts. Transposases and integrases turned up as likely engines of transfer. Some resistance genes ride many different mobile elements. The team mapped how far each element can reach across the family tree. A second database of 472,798 genomes confirmed 34 of 94 predicted moves. Host limits, they show, can still cage a gene in one bacterial group.
europmc-pmc8280459:
Colón-González and co-authors project mosquito-borne disease risk in a warmer, more crowded world. These diseases are spreading and returning to old haunts. How altitude and population density shape that spread was untested.

The study used several models and several climate scenarios together. It estimated how transmission seasons will lengthen. It also counted future populations at risk across altitude bands. Dense and sparse areas were compared. Malaria and dengue-type risks sit at the centre. Results help health systems plan for shifting disease maps. No single model carries the verdict alone. Altitude turned out to matter for season length changes.
europmc-pmc8369359:
Wang and co-authors report the China Osteoporosis Prevalence Study, a national survey of bone health in mainland China. The cross-sectional study covered adults aged 40 years or older. It measured how common osteoporosis and fractures are, by sex, age group, town or country residence, and other factors.

The team enrolled 20,416 participants aged 20 years or older from December 2017 to August 2018. They measured bone mineral density and recorded clinical and vertebral fractures. Earlier work had found vertebral fractures common in older women in Beijing, but no nationwide study had covered both men and women. The results give China a firm base for fracture prevention planning.
europmc-pmc8452859:
Gao and co-authors build ggVennDiagram, an R package that draws Venn diagrams with ease. Venn diagrams show how sets overlap in biomedical work. Older tools could be clumsy or hard to tailor. This package builds on the popular ggplot2 system.

The package can draw diagrams with two to seven sets on its own. Good results need only minimal setup. Its data objects store all values and plot parts. Users can reach intersection counts and each label, edge, or fill. That gives deep control to anyone who knows ggplot2. The package is free under the GPL-3 license through CRAN. Early uptake in papers and on GitHub looks strong.
europmc-pmc8466659:
Bouysset and Fiorucci present ProLIF, a Python library that turns molecular contacts into fingerprints. Such fingerprints sum up how molecules touch in three dimensions. Drug projects use them for screening and machine learning. Good tools to build them were still needed.

ProLIF reads complexes from simulations, lab structures, and docking runs. It handles mixes of ligand, protein, DNA, or RNA parts. Users can retune the built-in contact types or add their own. Tutorials cover the common use cases step by step. Code snippets show how to pair the library with other analysis tools. ProLIF is free to install from the team's GitHub repository.
europmc-pmc8491759:
Baxi and co-authors review digital pathology and artificial intelligence in medicine. Classic pathology gives diagnosis and grades protein levels by eye. Whole slide imaging now turns slides into data. AI tools can pull out detail beyond human sight.

In immuno-oncology, these methods aid drug development and lab research. They help decode complex disease biology and find new biomarkers and targets. They also sort patients for the right test and treatment. With more options per disease, such sorting grows in value. The review weighs the gains against the limits of current tools. It maps where digital methods fit in daily practice.
europmc-pmc8508759:
Belinskaia and co-authors review serum albumin in health and disease. Albumin is one of the body's main proteins. It ferries ions, drugs, nutrients, and toxins through the blood. It also keeps blood's osmotic pressure in balance. Nearly all known drugs bind to it.

Albumin is no passive carrier, though. It has enzyme-like action on many esters from inside and outside the body. A free thiol group lets it trap reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. Sugared albumin feeds into diabetes and other diseases. Albumin also talks with blood and vessel cells. The review covers these transport, signaling, and antioxidant jobs in turn.
europmc-pmc8512059:
Aranaz and co-authors give an overview of chitosan, its properties and applications. Interest in this natural polymer grows year by year. Papers and patents based on it keep climbing. Yet its weak solubility in neutral and basic settings limits use.

Chitosan is not one fixed polymer but a family of molecules. Members differ in mix, size, and monomer order. Those traits shape how it performs in the body and in technology. The review shows how chemistry can fix the solubility problem and boost traits. It links physical traits to biological effects. Green uses follow, from making metal nanoparticles to holding biocatalysts.
europmc-pmc8785459:
Bian and co-authors review mesenchymal stromal cells and their exosomes as tools to heal skin wounds. These cells can form skin cell types and calm inflammation at wound sites. They also spur new vessel growth and limit scarring. Most of their benefit comes from signals they release, not from the cells themselves.

Their exosomes carry those signals in tiny packages. Growth factors, cytokines, and small RNAs ride inside. Exosome therapy avoids some risks of live cell therapy, such as tumor formation. It also provokes less immune reaction. The review sums up animal studies of both routes. Skin repair with smaller scars is the shared goal.
europmc-pmc9023059:
Del Alamo and co-authors show how to coax AlphaFold2 into predicting membrane proteins in more than one shape. Transporters and receptors work by switching between states, yet the default program returns near-identical models. The team thinned the input sequence alignments at random, which pushed the program to sample other states. Benchmark models spanned the gap between two known structures, and the extreme models were among the most accurate.

The trick worked across diverse transporters and G-protein-coupled receptors. The authors offer the method as a simple route to native-like alternative states. They also urge that future predictors be built to output ensembles, not single shapes.
europmc-pmc9139759:
Smolarz and co-authors review breast cancer, covering its spread, types, causes, and treatment. Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed malignant tumor in women worldwide. It is also the leading cause of cancer death in women. Rates keep rising in all regions despite better detection and care.

Treatment rests on the molecular subtype of each tumor. Care mixes surgery and radiation with systemic therapy. Systemic options include hormone therapy, chemotherapy, anti-HER2 therapy, and newer immunotherapy. Triple negative disease forms over 15-20% of cases and is hard to treat. Future care aims to tailor dose and drugs to tumor biology. Readers get a compact survey of a major disease and its care.
europmc-pmc9268159:
Geers and co-authors test how new variants of concern escape immunity after infection or vaccination. They study blood from recovered donors and vaccine recipients. The focus is on spike-specific antibodies and T cells. The variants tested were those first found in the UK, South Africa, and Brazil, which carry many spike changes.

The team found that variants partly escape antibody responses. T-cell responses, by contrast, held up well against the variant spikes. Spike-specific CD4+ T cells did not care about the variant mutations. Breakthrough infections in immune people were mostly mild in past trials. The work suggests memory T cells guard against severe disease. It also frames why vaccines still help when antibodies wane.
europmc-pmc9329459:
Ferruz and co-authors present ProtGPT2, a language model that designs new proteins. The model trains on natural protein sequences without labels. Like text models, it learns the patterns of its alphabet, here amino acids. It then writes fresh sequences that follow natural rules.

Disorder checks suggest 88% of its proteins are globular, in line with nature. Database searches show the outputs are only distantly related to known proteins. Network maps show the model samples unexplored parts of protein space. Structure predictions give well-folded shapes with new topologies. Generation takes seconds per sequence. The tool is freely available. The authors say fast, natural-like design could help with medical and environmental problems now hard to reach.
europmc-pmc9508259:
Morris and co-authors give a mechanistic review of redox regulation in the immune response. Immune activity raises nitro-oxidative stress in the body. Redox shifts then steer how immune cells switch on and do their jobs. The review asks how deep that control runs.

Cell by cell, the authors trace redox control at work. Macrophages, dendritic cells, and neutrophils come first. T cells, B cells, and natural killer cells follow. Key players include reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. Cell antioxidants such as glutathione and thioredoxin push back. The HDL, ApoA1, and PON1 complex also guards the balance. Chronic stress breaks that guard down, they show. It harms mitochondria and cell metabolism over time. The result can be a suppressed immune state.
europmc-pmc9540059:
Fries and co-authors argue that the many molecular pathways of major depressive disorder converge on the synapse. The causes of depression at the molecular level stay poorly grasped. Studies point to a tangle of linked systems instead. No single pathway explains the disease.

The review tours each major system in turn. Monoamines, stress, and neurotrophins all feature. Excitation and inhibition balance gets its own look. Mitochondrial faults, epigenetics, and inflammation follow. The opioid system and the gut-brain axis are included too. Each system is checked for links to synaptic signaling. The authors treat synaptic activity as the closest physical echo of mood. Their closing model joins the pathways into one frame. Better models should guide better treatments, they argue.
europmc-pmc9816059:
Li and co-authors trace how the protein CST1 shields gastric cancer cells from ferroptosis and fuels their spread. Spread is a chief reason gastric cancer outcomes stay poor. How tumor cells gain that roaming power was unclear. The team suspected CST1 after sequencing pointed at it.

Metastatic tumors carried far more CST1 than quiet ones. High CST1 levels also tracked worse patient outlooks. Extra CST1 made cancer cells migrate and invade in dishes. In mice it boosted spread to liver, lung, and belly lining. The cells also took on a more mobile cell state. CST1 was found holding onto GPX4, the ferroptosis guard. It recruits a helper that strips GPX4's disposal tags. Stable GPX4 keeps cell rust low and death at bay. Blood and belly fluid CST1 rose in spread cases too. The authors name CST1 a marker and drug target.
europmc-pmc9825559:
Groza and co-authors present the International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium resource for knockout mouse data. The project knocks out genes one by one in mice. Each line gets broad, standard health screening. The portal shares the curated results with everyone.

The data set holds 85 million measured data points. Over 95,000 statistically strong phenotype hits are mapped. Those hits link mouse traits to human diseases.
