Data come from 9,000 mouse lines built so far. A library of 750,000 images supports the records. The lines have fed over 4,600 publications to date. Rare disease diagnosis draws on the gene trait links. Poorly known genes, the ignorome, are a prime target. Standard screens keep results comparable across centers. The consortium aims at genome wide coverage in time.
europmc-pmc9913659:
Nguyen and co-authors review why antibody-drug conjugates cause toxicity and how tolerability can improve. These drugs link an antibody to a potent cell-killing agent. Twelve such agents are in clinical use. Many others failed in trials due to excess toxicity.

Even approved drugs often force dose cuts, delays, or stopped treatment. Dose-limiting harms often match the payload, not the target antigen. Much toxicity hits cells that lack the target, an off-target effect. Such harm can cap doses below the best level for tumor control. The authors sort the main toxicity routes. They then discuss design and dosing tactics to widen the safe dose range.
frus-1861-d159:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 October 1861. The dispatch is document 159 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton's late October report is the last Paris paper in this run of the volume. The Trent crisis would soon seize the French file as well. His calm page stands at the edge of that storm, closing the autumn watch. The Trent crisis would test the Paris post as hard as it tested London. The storm, when it broke, found Dayton's post in good order to weather it.
frus-1861-d259:
James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 10 October 1861. It stands as Document 259 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter comes from the autumn of the war's first year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d59:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 July 1861. The dispatch is document 59 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams wrote nine days before Bull Run, in the last calm of the summer. His report covers the steady work of watching Britain for any lean toward the South. Read in sequence, his letters let readers feel how slowly a crisis can move, and how fast it can break. His reports often closed with a calm sum of the week, which Seward prized. A calm sum of the week, from a man Seward trusted, steadied the whole cabinet.
frus-1862-d159:
Seward sent more than one letter to London on 10 October 1862. And this one is printed as Document 159 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Its reader was Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, who dealt face to face with the British foreign secretary, Earl Russell.

Same-day batches of mail often split orders, news, and enclosures among several short letters. That clerical habit is why the wartime file holds so many brief dispatches. Together they let a modern reader follow, almost day by day, how the Union held its ground in London during a tense autumn. The legation's clerks copied each dispatch into bound letter books before the mail sailed.
frus-1862-d259:
On 19 March 1862 William L. Dayton sent another report to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 259 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Two reports on two days show the Paris legation working at a brisk pace.

Back-to-back reports usually mean talks were moving or papers had piled up for the mail. Dayton wrote as French forces pushed inland in Mexico and French sympathy for the South stayed warm in court circles. Reports like these gave Washington its running account of the power most tempted to change the war's course. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d359:
Marshal Pelissier, the French commander and governor in Algeria, wrote to Foreign Minister Edouard Thouvenel on 3 March 1862. The letter is printed as Document 359 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, within the French papers.

Papers from Algeria enter the American file because France's empire and the American war touched in trade, shipping, and the politics of cotton and ports. Pelissier was one of France's most famous soldiers, a marshal of the empire. His letter shows how far the paper trail of the American question reached into French councils. Seward tested what Mercier said against what Dayton reported from Paris, week by week.
frus-1862-d459:
John Lothrop Motley reported from Vienna to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 August 1862. The dispatch is Document 459 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department's printed record.

Late August 1862 was a grim season for the Union, with defeat looming again in Virginia. Motley's post in Austria gave him a clear view of how Europe's conservative courts read American weakness. His reports warned Washington where sympathy was cooling. Yet Austria never moved toward the Confederacy, and the steady presence of a respected minister helped keep it that way. The letter belongs to the summer file in which the Union's friends abroad mostly watched, waited, and held their breath.
frus-1862-d559:
Henry Shelton Sanford received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 October 1862. It is Document 559 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

October orders could speak from the new facts of Antietam and the emancipation order, and Sanford was quick to use both in Brussels. Belgium's court had channels into London and Paris that larger legations envied. Seward's instruction belongs to the autumn effort to convert military relief into diplomatic safety, post by post. The Belgian file that season is brisk and frequent, the mark of a minister who answered quickly and a secretary who kept him supplied.
frus-1862-d59:
Word from Charles Francis Adams reached Washington on 8 May 1862, in a letter to William H. Seward. It stands as Document 59 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d659:
Dated 20 December 1861, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to Robert H. Pruyn, the next American minister to Japan. It is document 659 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, one of a tight group Seward sent that month.

Back-to-back letters like these let a secretary fine-tune an envoy's orders as news changed. Pruyn had not yet reached Japan, so each fresh note could still shape his first steps there. The letter shows the hand-over of the Japan mission in slow motion, on paper, while the war at home grew worse by the week.
frus-1863p1-d159:
On 17 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 159 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the middle piece of three sent that day.

The middle of a three-sheet set often bore the day's fullest matter. Adams wrote in that shape by habit, and Seward read in it by habit too. This letter holds the center of the 17 April set. With its mates, it gives one day's whole view from the legation at the height of the ship spring, a small file in itself.
frus-1863p1-d259:
Washington's orders to London on 7 August 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 259 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d359: On 12 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 359 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d459:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State sent an official note to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 13 April 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d559:
8 June 1863 is the date on a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d59:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 January 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 59 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late January mail from London weighed the British scene as the war's new year opened. Adams reported on the cabinet's care and the public's mood after the freedom edict. His sheets were the State Department's chief source on the power most able to harm the Union from afar. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day, each holding its own part of the post's work.
frus-1863p1-d659:
From Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to Secretary of State William H. Seward: a letter dated 12 November 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late autumn of 1863.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Each crossing of the Atlantic took the better part of two weeks, so these letters also show leaders acting on news that was already old. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d159: The Joint Strategic Survey Committee, the senior planning body that advised the Joint Chiefs, filed a report dated October 22, 1943, and it is Document 159 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Placed by the editors in the Moscow Conference section, the report belongs to the season when strategy for 1944 was being fought over. The record gives the body's name and the date. The report is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d259:
A Chinese summary record, printed in translation, covers President Roosevelt's conversation with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek at Cairo on the evening of 23 November 1943. Since no American record of the talk survives, this account is the volume's main source for what the two leaders settled between themselves.

Roosevelt holds that China should stand as one of the Big Four, deciding world questions on an equal footing. On Japan's emperor, Chiang says the Japanese people should choose their own form of government after the war. The two agree that Manchuria, Taiwan, and the Pescadores must return to China, and Chiang proposes joint trusteeship for the Ryukyus. He declines the lead role in occupying Japan, offering Chinese support under American command instead.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d359: According to the President's Log, Soviet foreign minister Molotov called on President Roosevelt at Tehran on 28 November 1943, after Stalin had left. An editorial note in the volume records the call. No record has been found of the remarks the two men exchanged. The editors note that the call was probably short. It may have been limited to an exchange of courtesies. Roosevelt's talk with Stalin ended at four o'clock, when the next meeting began. Elliott Roosevelt's book mentions the call briefly.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d459: Where the wartime file runs thin, the editors step in at Document 459. Their editorial note forms part of the Cairo-Tehran volume. Notes in this series explain background and identify the people named nearby. They also tell readers where a related paper can be found. The summit record behind the note comes from Cairo and Tehran in 1943. Three Allied governments coordinated their war there. The note keeps their paper trail intelligible.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d559:
President Roosevelt wrote to Congressman Jan Mruk on March 6, 1944. A letter from a president to a single member of Congress belongs to the domestic side of wartime leadership, where foreign policy met voters and their letters. It appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Congressmen wrote to Roosevelt often on behalf of constituents with family, property, or roots in the war's path, and the President's replies carried policy into American homes. Mruk represented a New York district with deep Polish-American ties, at a moment when Poland's future, argued over at Tehran, weighed on many Americans. For readers, the letter shows summit diplomacy echoing into ordinary politics.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d59: Roosevelt answered Churchill on October 26, 1943, and the letter is Document 59 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Same-day replies kept the two capitals in step while their ministers finished in Moscow. The catalog record supplies the parties and the date only. In the published series the letter stands near the end of the Moscow sequence, with Cairo four weeks away and Tehran five.
frus-1944-quebec-d159:
H. Freeman Matthews recorded a delicate telephone exchange with the British Embassy on August 29, 1944. He first told Michael Wright that the president had deferred the French mission question until the forthcoming high-level meeting. Then Donald Maclean called back, brandishing a copy of the Joint Chiefs' letter suggesting no military objection to the British request.

Matthews checked with Admiral Leahy and held the line. The chiefs' letter conveyed views on the military aspect only, he told Maclean, and could not modify the president's decision to defer. The editors' note adds a quiet ending: despite the anticipation, the subject was in fact never raised at the Quebec Conference.
frus-1944-quebec-d259:
The secretaries' note in C.C.S. 520/6, dated September 14, 1944, transmits the approved directive on strategic bomber control. Executive responsibility for the bomber forces in Europe was vested jointly in the Chief of the Air Staff, RAF, and the Commanding General, United States Army Air Forces. Bottomley and Spaatz were designated their representatives on the spot, providing control and local coordination through consultation.

The directive states the bombers' over-all mission: the progressive destruction and dislocation of the German military, industrial, and economic systems, and direct support of land and naval forces. Attacks would follow the objective priorities Eisenhower had established unless the two commanders judged changes necessary. The German Air Force, its fighting effectiveness substantially reduced, was no longer a primary objective; Germany's war economy was.
frus-1944-quebec-d59:
H. Freeman Matthews of the State Department wrote to Ray Atherton, the American ambassador in Canada, on September 6, 1944. Matthews directed European affairs work at the department. The letter appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Writing to the ambassador in the host country six days before a conference meant arranging the department's part on the ground: staff, papers, and contact with the Canadians. Atherton's Ottawa embassy was the conference's local base. For readers, the letter shows the State Department planting its flag in Canada ahead of the leaders, in the practical way that makes diplomacy function.
frus-1945-50-intel-d159:
Minutes record the Sixth Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board on 28 June 1946. It stands as document 159 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The war had just ended, and the United States was keeping a central spy service in peace for the first time.

Minutes trade color for proof: they may skip the tone of a talk, but they pin down its outcome. Later fights over who agreed to what often end with a page like this one. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d259:
On 17 February 1948, the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan) sent a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett). The State Department prints it as document 259 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d359:
Dated 19 January 1949, this letter runs from Robert Blum of the Office of the Secretary of Defense to Allen W. Dulles. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 359 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Reform of the CIA was in the air, with the Dulles survey under way and each agency guarding its own role.

Letters between senior men often carried the real weight of a matter, since a signed letter put the writer's name and office behind the words. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d59:
General Malin Craig, chief of the War Department's operations division, wrote to the members of the Lovett Committee on 18 December 1945. An operations chief writing to an intelligence study group crosses staff lines. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Craig's view mattered because operations consumes intelligence: the men who plan campaigns know what they need to know. His memorandum brought the user's voice into the Lovett group's work at a late stage. Readers can watch the War Department still feeding views into the study even as the secretaries neared agreement. The overlap of committees, letters, and minutes in December is the volume's picture of a government deciding by accumulation.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d159:
Stettinius urged a fast reply to Stalin on 29 December 1944, before Moscow recognized the Lublin Committee. His memorandum to the President is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Stalin's answer of 27 December was the trigger.

In that answer, Stalin refused the President's request to hold off recognition of the Lublin body as Poland's provisional government. He went further, suggesting that Washington and the other allies do the same. Recognition is expected on 31 December, Stettinius warns. The answer should be in Stalin's hands before that date, even though the President returns only tomorrow. A draft reply is attached, drawn along the lines of the British stand in Churchill's telegram of 16 December.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d259:
Admiral King turned to the Kurile Islands in a Joint Chiefs paper of 11 December 1944. His memorandum, J. C. S. 1176/2, is titled “Operations in the Kuriles” and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. King commanded the fleet and served as chief of naval operations.

The paper grows out of the staff studies on Russian entry into the Pacific war. King agrees that the time has come for more concrete action in developing plans for the northwest Pacific. His own line is to broaden the base of operations and keep the Japanese spread out. Diversionary strokes, above all those that stop Japan from massing her air power, will help most. The Kuriles, the island chain running north from Japan toward Kamchatka, are weighed in that light.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d359:
Staging American bombers near Vienna and Budapest came before the Joint Chiefs at Yalta on February 7, 1945. Admiral Leahy laid out a staff paper on using the Fifteenth Air Force in that area. The planners advised asking the President to seek Stalin's agreement. Bases in the Budapest area would host elements of the force.

The chiefs found no objection and backed the paper. The item sits oddly at Yalta, where Germany's fate led the agenda. Yet it mattered: Soviet armies were overrunning the very ground American planes hoped to use. Even airfields needed the alliance's permission by February 1945.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d459:
Bohlen's note on the last plenary session, February 11, 1945, centers on credit for the voting plan. The communiqué was debated in detail, he records, and most talk dealt with language. The Soviet side suggested one change: the communiqué should not say the accepted proposal had been put forward by the President.

Stalin said he had no objection to the President, or any American official, stating publicly that the American proposal had been adopted. But such a reference, he felt, did not properly belong in a communiqué. The Soviet suggestion was adopted. The note, filed in the Bohlen Collection, shows vanity and diplomacy being balanced line by line.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d59:
President Roosevelt cabled Ambassador Harriman on 16 January 1945 with a personal request about food at Yalta. The short top secret message appears in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. It shows the President planning his daily routine weeks before the talks began.

Roosevelt wants his own mess set up ashore, with his own stewards and cooks. The point is to keep his usual diet during the conference. Supplies would come from the ship Catoctin. He asks Harriman to arrange it without offending the Russian hosts, a small detail that reveals how carefully the trip was stage-managed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d159:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded a conscience-clearing talk with the President in an extract dated June 18, 1945. The extract is document 159 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Grew had drafted a statement calling on Japan to surrender unconditionally, meant for release when Okinawa fell.

Truman liked the idea, Grew writes, but decided to hold it until the Big Three could discuss it. Grew says he spoke up so his conscience would be clear. He had left out no step that might save the lives of thousands of American fighting men. That held so long as Japan was still rendered powerless for the future. The President asked him to put the subject on the summit agenda. The debate fed into the surrender demand the Allies issued from Potsdam in July.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d259:
A briefing paper fixed the American line on Europe's borders, in extracts dated June 29, 1945. The paper is document 259 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It formed an annex to the State Department's agenda memorandum and covered territorial settlements across the continent.

The extract printed here covers Germany's northern edge. The United States is opposed, it says, to revising the Danish-German frontier, unless such a change proves necessary in connection with a possible internationalization of the Kiel Canal. Other extracts of the same paper appear elsewhere in the volume, dealing with the bigger questions, above all the German-Polish frontier. The Danish point is small, but it shows the care with which the briefing book settled even minor border questions before the leaders met.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d359:
Restitution of looted property is coordinated in a Washington cable to Pauley dated June 26, 1945. It passes on a message the Joint Chiefs had sent General Eisenhower at the President's request on June 23. The President had approved a recommendation of Pauley's about removals from land held by American forces in Germany and Austria.

Under the rule, any removal of property for restitution first needed approval from the American representative on the Reparations Commission. Such coordination was essential, the message says, because restitution touched broad reparations policy. Yet it was not to delay unduly the return of works of art to the countries they were taken from.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d459:
Revised strength figures for Bulgaria arrive in Kirk's cable from Caserta of July 3, 1945, reporting General Oxley once more. The Bulgarian Army, Oxley said, should now be read as thirteen infantry divisions, one cavalry division, one guards division at Sofia, and one armored division in process of formation. The Red Army's strength in Bulgaria he estimated at 250,000 men.

Most Soviet aircraft, the report adds, are in Bulgaria, and airfields north and south of the Balkan mountains will be taken into use. Kirk also notes a Bulgarian War Ministry bulletin giving British strength in Greece as nine motorized infantry divisions. The figures are false, he remarks, but Moscow may let them stand to justify its own buildup.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d559:
Alexander Kirk, the U.S. ambassador in Italy, reported from Caserta on June 19, 1945. His wire is document 559 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It follows talks between Allied and Yugoslav officers over Venezia Giulia, the land around Trieste.

Kirk passes on word from General Morgan at 13 Corps. Three Yugoslav envoys had gone to Belgrade to consult and were due back at noon on June 18. Talks would not restart until June 19. The point that most troubled the Yugoslavs was civil rule in the zone. They had set up committees on the Russian model, while the Allies meant to use their own military government system.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d59:
Only part of President Truman's June 14, 1945 message to Stalin is printed as document 59 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. One paragraph is left out and can be found in the published Stalin correspondence. What remains is Truman's warm closing, sent as the two leaders prepared to meet in person near Berlin.

Truman says he is confident that the friendly understanding and cooperation built during the war against the Nazis will go on to preserve peace and goodwill between their countries. He looks forward with much pleasure to meeting Stalin soon and talking over their shared problems in full. The friendly tone belongs to the last weeks before Potsdam, when open Allied friction over Europe was already growing beneath it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d659:
Ambassador Caffery sent the agreed text for notifying Moscow about Tangier from Paris on June 27, 1945. The secret wire is document 659 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The British ambassador in Moscow and the French charge would deliver it on June 30.

The message says the end of the war in Europe makes it timely to act. Spain should be called on to withdraw its troops and administration from the Tangier zone. Britain and France, with the United States, are preparing talks in Paris to concert that approach. The talks will also settle details for restoring an international regime on a provisional basis. A new Tangier convention would be negotiated later. The Soviet government, the message promises, will be kept informed of developments.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1059:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled the Secretary of State at Potsdam on July 17, 1945, about supervising the coming Greek elections. A British draft proposed that the four Allied governments share the task. Washington agrees in substance, but objects to framing the approach as an invitation to Moscow and Paris.

The cable offers substitute wording. It rests on Allied duties to Greece and the pledges made at Yalta. Greece's own government, a party to the Varkiza Agreement, has accepted supervision by the four Allies named. The draft voices earnest hope that the Soviet and French governments will agree to take part. Byrnes may settle timing and phrasing with the British at the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1159:
Winant cabled from London again on 19 July 1945, his second dispatch in two days. The pace shows how closely the embassy reported during the summit's first week. British politics were in suspense, with an election count due within the week.

Each dispatch layered fresh detail onto Washington's picture of its ally. The home office could weigh British stands at Potsdam against the mood Winant heard at home. This cable keeps that running account going. It is a small part of a large flow, but the flow itself is the story: a wartime embassy working at full stretch.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1259:
Sato cabled Togo on 28 July 1945, the day Tokyo's premier spoke to the press about the Allied terms. The Moscow envoy's reports kept arriving while Japan's leaders stalled in public. His channel was now the only live move Tokyo had left.

Sato could report only what Moscow gave him: courtesy, delay, and no firm word. Behind the delay, Soviet armies were massing in the east for their own entry into the war. The envoy sensed the trap more clearly than Tokyo did. This dispatch is his word from that day, part of the secret thread the Allies read in full.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1359:
J. Rives Childs reported again from the Tangier talks to the acting secretary of state on 26 July 1945. His first report in the volume is dated eight days earlier. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Talks about Tangier moved slowly, since several powers claimed a say in the port city's rule. A second report lets readers measure what changed across a week of negotiation. Childs wrote for a Washington audience that was watching Potsdam first and Tangier second, so his papers had to make a small city's case clearly. The pair of reports shows patient, detailed work on a question most histories pass over in a line.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-159: This editorial note appears unnumbered after document 710 in the second volume of the Potsdam papers. Written by the Foreign Relations editors, it guides readers at a point where the files grow dense. Such notes cite sources, explain links, and mark missing pieces. The note keeps the reader's footing sure near the conference's close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-59:
An editorial note in volume two of the Potsdam papers draws on Stimson's diary for July 22, 1945. No official record of the conversation has been found, the editors say. Stimson, Bundy, and Lord Cherwell talked with Churchill at British headquarters for over an hour that morning.

Stimson records that Churchill read Groves' report in full at the meeting. Churchill then told him what he had noticed at the Three's session the day before. Truman, Churchill said, was evidently much fortified by something that had happened. He stood up to the Russians in a most emphatic and decisive manner, Churchill said. He told them that on certain demands they absolutely could not have their way. Now I know what happened to Truman yesterday, Churchill added. Reading the report had made Truman a changed man, and Churchill felt the same lift himself.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d759:
The British delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 27, 1945, as document 759. It arrived just as Attlee returned with a new government behind him. British texts carried the alliance's second voice. This one joined the numbered papers of the second Potsdam volume.

A British proposal lets readers triangulate the talks. Where London's draft sits between Washington's and Moscow's, the deal's center comes clear. The document also shows a new government acting fast. Attlee's team had days, not months, to shape its line. The proposal stands as proof of how quickly the British machine reset itself mid-conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d859:
Document 859 is a draft of the Economic Subcommittee's report, dated July 18, 1945. Drafts preceded the report the conference later received. This early version shows the experts' first framing of the economic questions. It was kept with the conference files and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A draft report lets readers watch judgment form. Lines that later hardened appear here still soft. The document pairs with the subcommittee's finished report in this run. Between the two, the group's mind can be seen changing. Such pairs are the surest guide to how expert bodies actually work: slowly, in writing, toward a text all can sign.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d959:
Josiah DuBois, a member of the American reparations delegation, wrote this legal memorandum for Edwin Pauley, filed with the July 29, 1945 papers. The question is whether gold held by American forces at Frankfurt may be treated as war booty. That question stands even where the gold's source can be traced.

DuBois reviews the Allied pledge not to honor transfers of looted gold. He then cites the Hague rules, which let an occupier seize state property usable for war. The gold, he concludes, was plainly used on behalf of the German state. On strict law, apart from policy, it may be treated as booty.
frus-1952-54v10-d259: Editorial Note 259 in the Iran volume records a joint aid body. On December 27 and 30, William Warne and Prime Minister Mosadeq traded notes. Their deal set up a Joint United States-Iranian Economic and Social Development Commission. It was to start on January 1, 1953. Washington pledged up to $20 million in aid for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1953. Funds under the earlier technical pact of January 1952 were added to the pool.
frus-1961-63v11-d59: An editorial note in the Cuba volume gathers U Thant's appeal of October 24, 1962, and the replies. The Acting Secretary-General asked both leaders to shun any step that might raise the risk of war. He sought a pause for talks. President Kennedy answered on October 25 with his wish for a sound settlement. Khrushchev agreed the same day. U Thant then asked Soviet ships to skirt the quarantine zone, and Kennedy to keep his ships from a clash. The note marks the UN's brief hour at the crisis's center.
frus-1969-76v01-d59:
A memorandum from the President's Special Assistant, Patrick Buchanan, to President Nixon reports a leadership meeting of February 17, 1970. It is document 59 in Volume I of the 1969-1976 Foreign Relations series. The meeting dealt with Nixon's State of the World message. Kissinger outlined the message, some 40,000 words of policy, for about forty-five minutes. Nixon called it the most important statement of his time in office so far.

Buchanan's notes record Nixon's stress on Japan as a base for U.S. forces. They also record his view that allies must carry more of their own defense. The President framed the message as a way to stay engaged in the world, not to leave it.
gao-gaoreports-b-295959:
International Outsourcing Services protested its removal from a Defense Commissary Agency contest in GAO decision B-295959, dated May 25, 2005. The work was coupon redemption work for commissaries. The award went to NCH Marketing Services. The agency had judged the firm's price too low to trust.

GAO denied the protest. The price realism test in the rules let the agency weigh a very low price. GAO found that fear for good work was sound on this record. The firm lost its place for that reason. Readers can use the ruling to see when a low price can end a bid.
gao-gaoreports-b-297959:
NCR Government Systems protested a Defense award for a sales system in GAO decision B-297959, dated May 12, 2006. The winner was IBM Corporation. The system was the Commissary Advanced Resale Transaction System. It would run sales at commissaries. The firm hit a late bid fix, gear fit, tech marks, and the pick.

GAO denied the protest. The late fix was a shift to a bid that had won in the main. That take was sound. Gear fit was pledged by the winner with no facts to doubt it. Tech marks set the bids apart in a fair way. No harm from marks was shown. The best value pick thus stood on all points.
gao-gaoreports-b-298259:
Southwest Educational Development Laboratory protested an Education award in GAO decision B-298259, dated July 10, 2006. The winner was Edvance Research. The work was to run the Southwestern Regional Educational Laboratory. The deal ran for 5 years. Tests were price, past work, and tech merit. The firm hit how a small firm sub plan was scored.

GAO denied the protest. The claim rested on a wrong read of the call. When the call is read as writ, the score fits its terms. A protest built on a wrong read of the call will fail. Firms should weigh the whole scheme, not one line in a lone way.
gao-gaoreports-b-298759:
Symetrics Industries, LLC protested the rejection of its final proposal revision as late. The Air Force buy covered the AN/ALE-47 Countermeasures Dispensing System. Revisions could be sent to the contracting officer by email. GAO decided B-298759 on October 16, 2006.

The firm's revision reached a government server before the deadline. It reached the officer's mailbox after that time. The rule counts receipt at the stated office, not first entry to a server. The stated terms set a firm hour for receipt. A late revision cannot be taken under the rule. The plea for an exception failed. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298859:
Squires Timber Company protested the rejection of its high bid in a Forest Service timber sale. The sale was named the Devil's Club Timber Sale. Bids offered set rates for each type of timber. GAO ruled in B-298859 on December 1, 2006.

The firm's total bid of $184,051.68 topped the field. One rate, though, fell below the floor for white oak sawtimber. It bid $26.09 per unit against a $33.22 floor. GAO weighed the size of that gap in context. The shortfall was tiny next to the full bid. Such a small slip counts as a minor flaw. It can be fixed post-opening. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299859:
Alpha Genesis protested a Health and Human Services award to Charles River Laboratories. The contract covers upkeep of a free-range monkey breeding colony. The animals live on an island and ship to research sites. GAO decided B-299859 on September 12, 2007.

The firm had held the work for 27 years through its line of firms. It attacked the technical scoring of both bids. GAO found those marks sound on the record. It also claimed the winner's bid held deal-breaking conditions. Those points touched a lease the winner would get post-award. A letter of commitment backed that lease path. No bar to award was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310759:
Tiger Truck LLC lost its protest in GAO decision B-310759, dated February 7, 2008. The General Services Administration sought utility trucks and vans. The order went to Mag International, Inc. The call asked for trucks with set traits. Those traits were E-85 ethanol engines and self-shift gear boxes. Tiger said the winner's quote showed no such trucks.

GAO denied the protest. The winner's quote made the traits plain on its face. One more claim dealt with past-work names. The call asked for buyers of the same or like truck types. Like is not the same as the exact truck. Wider names were fair to send in.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-259:
Workforce Investment Act, GAO-05-259 of February 18, 2005, asks how well one-stop job centers serve the firms that hire. The U.S. economy rests on 8 million private firms. They employ 106 million of the nation's 137 million workers. One-stop centers aim to link those firms to trained staff in one place. Use by firms was the open point.

GAO asks how many firms know of and use the centers, small firms among them. It asks how glad user firms are, and what keeps the rest away. It asks what the Labor Department does to spread use, and how it grades its own reach. More data would help, the title says.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-459:
Small business subcontracting at Energy Department sites is the subject of GAO-05-459, a report GAO released on May 13, 2005. The department sends almost $20 billion a year to 34 facility management contractors. Of that, $3.3 billion went to small business subcontractors in fiscal year 2004. GAO judged whether the data used to track that share were sound and what the department had done about known flaws.

The reported figures overstate what small firms actually receive. Contractors left some large-business subcontracts out of their counts, which made the small business share look bigger. A firm could also subcontract very little overall and still report a high small business share. The department knew of these flaws as early as 2002. Because the numbers showed goals being met, officials did not press for fixes. GAO found the data unfit for judging whether small firms get the full chance the law intends.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-859:
The strengthened visa process gets a progress report in GAO-05-859, issued September 13, 2005. In October 2002, GAO urged that visas serve as an antiterrorism tool. It called for clear security policy, better screening guidance, a staffing review, and revamped training. This report grades progress since then. It covers policy, consular staff and training, and information sharing.

GAO found many steps taken. Consular officers got clear guidance that security comes first. Officers at eight posts told GAO security is their top priority, while legit travel still matters. Hiring rose, language skills were targeted, and training was rebuilt around counterterrorism. More data now flows to officers for name checks. Gaps remain: manuals lag policy changes, and guidance on Homeland Security staff roles is needed. Key posts also lack seasoned supervisors.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-259:
Fraud in immigration benefits and the weak net against it fill GAO-06-259, a report issued on March 10, 2006. In 2002 GAO called benefit fraud pervasive, with a scattered response. Fakes can let criminals, even terrorists, enter or stay in the country. GAO asked what the data show about the fraud's size and shape. It checked the steps the citizenship agency has taken to spot fraud. It also asked how the homeland security department punishes those it catches.

The full scale stays unknown, but the signs point to a serious problem. Staff denied about 20,000 applications for fraud in fiscal year 2005. The agency built a fraud office, a control plan, and risk checks. Core habits still lag, from steady monitoring to clear fraud goals. The department has no sanctions strategy at all. Most fraud draws no criminal case, and fines on hand go largely unused. GAO urged added controls and a real sanctions plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-59:
Therapy caps in Medicare raised a question: do some patients truly need more care? Report GAO-06-59, issued November 10, 2005, reviews outpatient therapy payments. The services are physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech-language pathology. In 1997 Congress set per-person spending limits for nonhospital therapy. Concern for patients needing extensive care led to repeated pauses on the caps. The current pause was set to end at the end of 2005. A 2003 law required this report.

GAO judged whether data justify lifting caps for certain conditions. It assessed work on a needs-based payment policy. Little progress has been made in targeting payments to needs, GAO found. Readers get the policy tension in full.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-659:
Computer security for Treasury debt auctions is assessed in GAO report GAO-06-659, released on August 30, 2006. Federal Reserve Banks act as agents of the government for the Treasury Department. They run the mainframe and distributed systems that support auctions of marketable Treasury securities. Those auctions are a core way the government borrows money. GAO tested the controls that guard the systems and their data.

GAO found that controls over the mainframe systems were generally effective. Those systems support Treasury financial reporting. But controls over the distributed systems and their support networks were not effective. Weak spots put sensitive data and computing resources at risk. GAO urged the Federal Reserve to address the gaps in the auction systems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-859:
Housing help for homeless veterans is reviewed in GAO-06-859, the GAO report of September 11, 2006. About one-third of the nation's homeless adults are veterans, the veterans department estimates. Many of them struggle with substance abuse or mental illness. The Grant and Per Diem Program funds community groups that give veterans transitional housing. The housing helps them prepare for a permanent home. The program faced reauthorization as GAO wrote.

GAO reported that about 194,000 veterans were homeless on a given night in fiscal year 2005. The department had changed its counting method in 2004 to a one-night snapshot. That method gives a cleaner figure than the old yearly totals. GAO judged the grant program itself as well. Better communication and follow-up with grantees, GAO said, could further enhance the program's reach.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-159:
The District of Columbia spends over $1.8 billion a year buying goods and services. GAO found its buying system deeply flawed in GAO-07-159, a report dated January 19, 2007. The District set up a central procurement office in 1997. Since then, its own watchdogs have flagged improper contracting. GAO tested the system against sound procurement principles drawn from model codes. It reviewed District audits and spoke with current and former officials.

The District's procurement law lacks key safeguards, GAO found. It does not cover several entities that spend tens of millions yearly. Many exemptions have been carved into it over time. Sole-source deals are allowed under broad exceptions. Agencies could even pay vendors with no valid contract, up to $217 million in fiscal year 2004. Five chief procurement officers had quit in 10 years. GAO urged the Mayor to send Congress a full reform plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-259:
More than 500,000 reservists have been called up since 2001, and many return to job disputes. GAO reviewed their employment protections in GAO-07-259, dated February 8, 2007. A federal law guards reservists' civilian jobs. The defense department tracks each member's employer. Four agencies handle complaints under the law. GAO checked the employer data and the complaint systems.

Employer reporting rose from 60 percent in August 2005 to about 77 percent a year later, GAO found. The main reserve reached 91 percent, short of its 95 percent goal. The ready reserve lagged at 30 percent. Records were often stale, since no rule forces yearly updates. About 24 percent of employer records could not be verified. That covered 108,125 of 453,596 reporting members. Agencies also file complaints under mismatched categories. Counts of disability-related cases, about 200 over 3 years, are likely low.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-559:
Start work now, set the price later: that habit is examined in GAO-07-559, a GAO report issued June 19, 2007. The Defense Department uses undefinitized contract actions to meet urgent needs. A contractor begins before final terms are set. In that open window, the firm has little reason to hold costs down. Rules say the deal must be locked once 40 percent of the work is done.

GAO sampled 77 contracts at seven sites. It found the department understates how much it uses the tool. Deadlines to lock terms were often missed, which weakens the government's hand in price talks. Files rarely showed whether profit rates fell as risk fell. GAO told the procurement policy office to fix the data fields that hide such orders. It also told the Secretary of Defense to issue clear guidance on the 40 percent rule.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-59:
Wheelchairs and oxygen gear billed to Medicare draw about $700 million in bad payments, and GAO-07-59, dated January 31, 2007, studies the guardrails. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) gave that estimate for gear and supplies from April 1, 2005 through March 31, 2006. Three safeguard contractors and four claims processors run the front-line checks for the agency.

GAO mined claims data for odd billing spikes by supplier and item. It read CMS files and spoke with agency and contractor staff. Prepayment computer checks were too weak to flag claims in a sudden surge or claims that made no medical sense. Regions also failed to share the checks that worked. CMS had begun a fix for the wildest claims, which GAO praised. Two recommendations ask CMS to set surge thresholds and require regions to swap their best screens.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-759:
Systems that shield Army vehicles from missiles are the topic of GAO-07-759, dated June 8, 2007. An Active Protection System spots incoming rounds and knocks them down before they hit. In 2005, the Army's Future Combat Systems program sought a builder for such a system. Raytheon won the job. At the same time, a Pentagon office tested near-term systems for use in Iraq. GAO reviewed how the Army ran the contest and the studies behind it.

The selection avoided conflicts of interest, GAO found. A trade study used one consistent method and backed Raytheon's vertical launch design. The Army and Boeing, the lead integrator, both played large roles in the process. The Pentagon's Office of Force Transformation took a more test-based path for near-term needs. It picked the Trophy system as the most mature of six candidates. In June 2006, defense officials deferred fielding that system.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-159:
Base closure costs that keep climbing are tracked in GAO report GAO-08-159, issued December 11, 2007. The 2005 closure round is the largest and costliest ever held. It aims to reshape bases for the next 20 years and save money over time. First, though, the Defense Department must spend billions to build and renovate.

GAO found that cost estimates have risen from $21 billion to $31 billion, a jump of 48 percent. Yearly savings estimates slipped from $4.2 billion to $4 billion. Payback will take longer than planned. GAO visited 25 sites and warns that the figures are likely to shift again.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-359:
Medicare Advantage plans are examined in GAO report GAO-08-359, dated February 22, 2008. In 2006, the federal government spent about $59 billion on these private plans, an alternative to original Medicare fee-for-service. GAO studied how plans used their payments and rebates in 2007.

Of an average rebate of $87 per member per month, plans projected about $61 would cut cost sharing. About $17 would cut premiums. Only about $10 would fund added benefits such as dental and vision care. On average, members faced lower cost sharing than under fee-for-service. But some plans set higher charges for care like home health and hospital stays. Heavy users of those services could end up paying more than under fee-for-service.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-59:
Free trade deals under Trade Promotion Authority are analyzed in GAO report GAO-08-59, dated November 7, 2007. Congress gave the President this fast-track authority in 2002, with set negotiating goals and duties to consult Congress and advisory groups. The authority lapsed in July 2007.

In 5 years, the United States pursued 17 agreements with 47 countries; 6 are approved and in force. These partners cover about 16 percent of U.S. trade and investment. The trade office held 1,605 consultations with congressional staff from August 2002 through April 2007. Nearly all staff called the briefings informative, but over half said they gave no real chance to shape the deals. Advisory chairs cited late papers and slow rechartering. GAO offered fixes for access and timing.
goncharov-oblomov-1859:
Ivan Goncharov published Oblomov in 1859, his comic-tragic monument to Russian inertia in one Petersburg flat. Ilya Oblomov cannot rise from his sofa, and his gown became shorthand for a whole social disease. Oblomovshchina, the word the novel coined, indicted the gentry's sloth for the rest of the century.

Oblomov plans to reform his estate, answer letters, and rise by noon, and fails at all three daily. His friend Stolz, half German and all energy, drags him into society and to Olga, who loves and tests him. Olga's love nearly wakes him, but the sofa, the gown, and Agafya's quiet kitchen win him back for good. He dies, stout and still, having chosen the peace of Oblomovka, his childhood paradise of sleep and food, over life. Goncharov's pity keeps the satire human, and Oblomov remains Russia's most loved failure.
greenmantle-pg559:
John Buchan's Greenmantle, his second Richard Hannay novel, sends the soldier-spy east in the middle of the First World War. A mission is proposed: Germany is stirring a holy war in the Muslim world, around a prophetic figure called Greenmantle. Hannay gathers his companions, including Boer scout Peter Pienaar and American Blenkiron.

The party crosses enemy Europe in disguise, rides the Essen barges, survives indiscretions and prison cells, and reaches Constantinople and beyond. Chapter titles trace the chase to the garden-house of Suliman the Red and the guns of the north. Buchan keeps the pace breathless while grounding the plot in wartime fears about Turkey, Persia, and empire. It remains one of his best-loved thrillers.
helvetius-de-lesprit-1759:
Claude Adrien Helvétius published De l'Esprit, On Mind, in Paris in 1758, and the London English translation of 1759 is the text here. The book, Englished as Essays on the Mind, and its Several Faculties, was burned by the hangman in France for its bold materialist psychology. Helvétius was forced to recant, and the scandal made his fame.

His doctrine holds that self-interest is the spring of all judgment and morals. Men call actions just or unjust as those actions help or harm them and theirs. Education and law, then, can shape virtue by shaping interest. The argument shocked its age and fed the radical thought of the next. It still bites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-josep:
Aaron ben Joseph, called the Elder, was a Karaite teacher, philosopher, physician, and liturgical poet in Constantinople. Born in Sulchat, Crimea, about 1260, he died about 1320. At nineteen he was already spiritual head of the Karaite community of his native town.

His "Mibḥar," written in 1294, is a commentary on the Pentateuch in the critical style of Ibn Ezra. It stresses the plain meaning of Scripture, free will, and the spirituality of God. His "Seder Tefillot" prayer book was adopted by most Karaite congregations as their standard. He also wrote on the Prophets and Psalms, plus a grammar, "Kelil Yofi," left unfinished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abracadabra-359:
Abracadabra is a magic word used in charms, above all against fever and swelling. A patient wore it on an amulet at the neck. The word was written in full, then with one letter less per line, down to a single letter.

Serenus Sammonicus, doctor to the emperor Caracalla, first names the practice. The shrinking lines were meant to shrink the disease spirit's hold. The entry doubts a Hebrew origin and doubts a link to Cabala. It finds a close match in Pesahim, where a like charm weakens the spirit Shabriri, linked with blindness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adam-book-of-75:
Book of Adam names a lost stock of tales about the first pair. The Talmud knows no such book. Zunz claimed it did, but the entry shows his proof text was misread. Still, a body of Adam lore stood ready at an early date. It may reach back before the fall of the Second Temple. The tales now live in changed form, not in their first tongue.

Works like the Apocalypsis Mosis and the Life of Adam and Eve keep much of the stock. Kindred forms in Slavonic, Syriac, Ethiopic, and Arabic keep more. Two angels guard the pair in Eden. Garden fruit feeds them and the beasts alike. Satan blames Adam for his own fall from heaven. He had refused God's order to bow before man. Cast out with his host, he chose the serpent as his tool.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahadboi-959: Ahadboi was a Babylonian amora of the sixth and seventh generations. Late in the life of the academy of Sura, he became its president. He held the office for only six months. An earthquake on the Day of Atonement then caused his death. The year was 822 of the Seleucidan era, which is 511. His name, the entry adds, is a contraction meaning "father's brother," and it matches the Biblical name Ahab.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-tiber:
Tiberius Julius Alexander was a Roman general of the first century. He was a son of the alabarch Alexander, and a nephew or cousin of Philo. Unlike his family, he gave up his ancestors' faith. Claudius made him procurator of Judea in 46. Nero made him a knight, then prefect of Egypt. In the Parthian war he served beside the general Corbulo.

His posting proved fatal to the Jews of Alexandria. When they fought to keep their rights, he sent out the legions. The soldiers wrecked the Jewish quarter and killed about fifty thousand Jews. On July 1, 69, he had Egypt's troops swear loyalty to Vespasian against Vitellius. As a reward he marched with Titus in the Jewish war, as general of the army. The entry calls it the highest army office a Jew ever reached. In the council before Jerusalem, he voted to spare the Temple.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-allemanno-johan:
Johanan Allemanno was a cabalist born in Constantinople. He worked in the second half of the fifteenth century. He moved to Italy and won fame there. He taught Pico della Mirandola in Hebrew and the Cabala. Through that teaching Jewish mystic thought reached Christian scholars. The entry lists his wide learning with care.

His chief work bears a title that means the delight of Solomon. Its preface ranks Solomon above Plato and his peers. Other works treat the Torah, long life, and stray thoughts. One book runs to about two hundred pages. Parts of his chief work came out at Leghorn in 1790.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amarillo-abraha: Abraham Amarillo was a rabbi at Salonica. He worked about the start of the nineteenth century. His sermons on the Pentateuch came out in print. The book bears a title that means the covenant of Abraham. It came out at Salonica in 1802. The hosted entry runs to three short lines. It gives no dates for his birth or his death. It names no work of his but that one book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anan-son-of-ana: Anan, son of Ananias, kept watch over the Temple. He held the post of governor of the Temple mount. In the year 52 he was sent to Rome. He had to answer for riots in Judea. Those riots grew from a clash with Samaritans. His father and a past high priest went with him. Agrippa II used his sway to clear them all. They came home to Jerusalem in peace. His brother held the same post from 63 to 66.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anointing-1559:
Anointing covers two Hebrew words in the Old Testament, the entry begins. One marks the private use of oils in daily grooming. The other marks their use as a sacred rite. In the fierce heat of Palestine, oil soothed the skin of the face.

Anointing went with bathing and with feasts, so mourners left it off as a sign of grief and took it up again when mourning ended. The entry traces the root word, first meaning to daub or smear. It then moves to sacred uses, such as oil poured on the altar and on holy furniture. Later sections treat the anointing of kings, priests, and prophets.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arias-montanus-:
Benedictus Arias Montanus was a Spanish priest and Orientalist born in 1527 at Freseenal in Estremadura, and dead at Seville in 1598. Philip II charged him with editing the Polyglot Bible printed at Antwerp in 1568-1572, in Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek, and Latin.

He was accused of Judaizing for putting into the Polyglot certain Aramaic paraphrases that seemed to back Jewish claims. A favorable report by the inquisitor Mariana in 1580 cleared him, the entry says. He turned Benjamin of Tudela's travels into Latin in 1575. His Antiquities of the Jews, with engravings, came out at Leyden in 1593, and many other works followed from his pen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-benja:
Benjamin Ashkenazi, a Russian communal worker and giver, was born in 1824 and died at Grodno in 1894. He was a son of Joshua Heschel Ashkenazi, rabbi of Lublin, and a descendant of Hakam Zebi. Settling at Grodno, he became the leading spirit in its Jewish affairs. On his initiative a hospital was built there, and later a home for the aged.

The government marked his service with hereditary honorary citizenship for him and his children. In 1882 he went as a delegate to the rabbinical convention at St. Petersburg. In 1883 he was one of the few Jewish representatives present in an official role at the coronation of Alexander III at Moscow. In 1884 he was made chairman of the committee on prisons for the government of Grodno.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avenel-georges-:
Georges Avenel was a French author. He was born at Chaumont-en-Vexin on Dec. 31, 1828, and died at Bougival on July 1, 1876. He was a brother of Paul Avenel. He gave most of his life to studying the French Revolution. His first book, on Anacharsis Clootz, came out in 1865.

Years of study then produced "Lundis Révolutionnaires" at Paris in 1875. He died with a second series unfinished. One chapter of the first was issued on its own in 1876, on the true Marie Antoinette. Avenel also edited a popular edition of Voltaire's full works, in nine volumes, in 1867-70.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baalath-2259: Baalath is the name of two cities in the Bible. One was a city of the tribe of Dan, listed in Joshua among the towns of Dan's portion. The other was a city built by Solomon. It is named together with Tadmor in the accounts of Solomon's building works, in Kings and in Chronicles. The entry adds one plain caveat. The site of that second city has not been fixed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bahiel-shortene:
Baḥiel ben Moses of Saragossa was a doctor of the thirteenth century. He served as court physician to King James I. of Aragon. At the conquest of Majorca he was of great use as a go-between, since he could speak with the Arabic-speaking Moors while the king knew only the Limousin dialect. In the fight over Maimonides' writings he led the philosopher's defenders.

In 1232 Baḥiel wrote an appeal asking the congregations of Aragon to uphold the ban on Solomon ben Abraham of Montpellier and his party. The entry then turns to his brother Solomon, also a doctor and interpreter with the king. Solomon wrote the Arabic proclamation that told the Moors of the conquest and called on them to submit. He died in 1264.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baptists-2459:
Baptists are a Christian body that rejects infant baptism and any baptism not preceded by a confession of faith. This entry reads their history for its Jewish ties. Baptists and their forerunners, the sixteenth-century Anabaptists, made liberty of conscience a chief doctrine. Balthasar Hubmaier argued in 1524 that Turks and Jews, like heretical Christians, were to be won by persuasion alone, never by fire or sword.

Two Anabaptist scholars, Hans Denck and Ludwig Hetzer, turned the Prophets into German from the Hebrew in 1527 and planned a mission to the Jews. Dutch Mennonites later gave large sums to relieve persecuted Jews. Seventh-Day Baptists kept the Jewish Sabbath as a lasting duty. Rhode Island, founded on liberty of conscience by men tied to the Baptists, drew Jewish citizens early. The entry ends with Baptist work for the bar on religious tests in the United States Constitution.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bartholomew-255: Bartholomew is one of the apostles, named only in the lists of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Acts. Some writers identify him with the Nathanael of John's Gospel, but on insufficient grounds. Eusebius mentions him as having preached the Gospel in India, a name that included Arabia Felix. Other legends have him suffer martyrdom. He is often mentioned in Coptic Gnostic literature. The entry is short and mostly points to the Bible dictionaries of Hastings and Cheyne for more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bath-sheba-2659:
Bath-Sheba was the wife of Uriah the Hittite who later became a wife of David and the mother of Solomon. Samuel calls her father Eliam, while Chronicles gives the name as Ammiel. The entry first tells the story from Samuel in full.

David saw her, took her while Uriah was at war, and had Uriah left to die in battle. Nathan then rebuked David with a parable, and the first child died. Later Bath-Sheba, aided by Nathan, won the throne for Solomon. Rabbinic and later views fill the second half. A closing note links her father to Ahithophel and to his later revolt against David.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beeth-lola-2759:
Lola Beeth was an Austrian opera singer born on Nov. 23, 1862, at Cracow, in Galicia. A merchant's daughter raised in comfort, she had to earn her living after her father failed in business. A princess patron spotted her gift for singing and acting.

After training in Vienna and a year in Paris, Beeth sang Elsa in Lohengrin at the Berlin Royal Opera in 1882. Success kept her in Berlin for six years and thirty-six roles. In 1888 she joined the Imperial Opera at Vienna. Wagner heroines became her favored parts. She also sang as a guest in Berlin, Leipsic, Paris, and New York with brilliant effect.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-azzai-2859:
Ben Azzai, whose full name was Simon ben Azzai, was a noted teacher of the first third of the second century. Though deeply learned, he never took the title of rabbi. He stayed all his life in the ranks of the pupils of the wise.

School tradition ranks Ben Azzai at the top of that pupil class, fit to judge law on his own. He handed down rulings from a famed day at Jabneh that fixed the canon of Scripture. The entry traces his ties to Akiba and to Joshua ben Hananiah. A late tradition lists him among ten martyrs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berg-3059:
Berg was a duchy of its own until 1815 and then became part of the Prussian Rhine province. Jews settled there at an early date. In 1298 its count shielded them from the bands led by Rindfleisch, but many died at the time of the Black Death in 1349.

The entry follows town by town, Deutz, Siegburg, and Mülheim on the Rhine. It tells of synagogues, burial grounds, protection money, and fresh attacks across the centuries. Jews of Siegburg were slain in 1287 on a charge of killing a boy, and later flights and fires mark the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berr-michel-315:
Michel Berr was the first Jew to practise as a barrister in France. He was born at Nancy in 1780. He died on July 4, 1843. His father was Isaac Berr de Turique. The elder Berr was a famed champion of emancipation. Michel was trained to continue that work.

The entry follows his protest against anti-Jewish laws. He later served as secretary of the Grand Sanhedrin. He held a senior post in Westphalia's Interior Ministry. His writings covered Job, Maimonides, and Hebrew literature. They also covered Jewish worship and religious teaching. From 1817 to 1823 he translated German papers. That work was for the Foreign Office.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blaustein-ozer-: Ozer Blaustein was a Russian teacher and writer. He was born at Dünaburg in 1840. He died in Warsaw on April 27, 1899. He wrote in Russian and Judæo-German. His Russian grammar won official recommendation. It served Jewish public schools by ministry approval. He also wrote a German method and a Hebrew manual. He translated the prayer-book into Russian. So too he translated the Maḥzor. His many novels appeared in Judæo-German. The entry names six of them. Most were printed at Wilna in the 1890s.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bodenheimer-lev: Levi Bodenheimer was consistorial rabbi at Krefeld, in the Rhine province. He was born on Dec. 13, 1807, at Carlsruhe and died on Aug. 25, 1867, at Krefeld. In 1837 he held a rabbi post at Hildesheim. The entry lists four works by him. They treat a will framed as a gift, Saadja Gaon's Arabic version, and the Blessing and Song of Moses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-booth-3559:
Booth renders the Hebrew word sukkah in English Bibles. It is also rendered pavilion or cottage at times. A booth was a hut of branches and foliage, apart from the nomad's cloth tent.

Leviticus ties dwelling in booths to the Feast of Tabernacles. The custom recalls the desert journey of the forefathers, the law says. Booths also sheltered cattle, field watchmen, and soldiers in camp. Jonah sat in one for shade before Nineveh. Leafy huts on housetops served the same purpose in harvest heat. The feast, the entry notes, is an old harvest thanksgiving.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bruck-solomon-b: Solomon Bruck, son of Hayyim, was an Austrian Hebraist born late in the eighteenth century. He died about 1846. His main work appeared at Altona in 1839, with a second edition at Vienna in 1842. That first edition held a sermon he had preached in England, in English, which the Austrian censor cut from the second edition. His other book came out after his death, published by his son Isaac Levi. It retells dream visits to the other world. In those dreams, the manners of certain classes are sharply criticized.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buttenwieser-la: Laemmlein Buttenwieser was a German Talmudist and linguist born in Wassertrüdingen, Bavaria, on Jan. 16, 1825. His father and grandfather were rabbis, and his family line held posts at Buttenwiesen. He studied Talmud at Aschaffenburg and went to the universities of Würzburg and Prague. Rabbinic diplomas came from teachers in both cities. In 1854 he emigrated to America. Not liking ministry work, he taught languages instead. Posts took him to Cincinnati, Philadelphia, and New York. From 1873 to 1886 he taught languages in New York public schools. He died there on Sept. 23, 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cancelation-of-:
Cancelation of documents covers the ways a written instrument loses its force. Marks across the page, burning, or tearing can all cancel a paper. In Jewish law, courts had their own method once a duty ended. They tore the document crosswise through its date, its witnesses' names, or other key parts. Any paper bearing those cuts counts as invalid.

Parties could also cancel a deed themselves, by knife cut or by tearing it in half. A paper only partly worn or stained stays valid while its words can still be read. The entry adds implied cancelation: a second deed on the same matter voids the first. A freed slave's grant, once ordered, can never be taken back.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caro-aryeh-lob-: Aryeh Löb ben Ḥayyim Caro preached at Posen in the second half of the eighteenth century. He wrote El ha-Millu'im, a homiletic commentary on the Pentateuch and the Song of Songs. His grandson, Abraham ben Isaac Zelig Caro, published the work at Krotoschin in 1845. That edition carried additions under the title Abne Ẓedeḳ. The brief entry names no other post or work for this preacher, and gives no dates for his birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castro-tartas-i:
Isaac de Castro Tartas, a Marano and martyr, was born at Tartas, in Gascony, about 1623. He died at Lisbon on Dec. 15, 1647. Trained in philosophy and classical languages, he lived for some years at Parahiba, in Brazil. He then moved to Bahia, where he was known as a Jew and arrested by the Inquisition.

Sent to Lisbon, Isaac told the tribunal at once that he held the Jewish faith and would stay true to it. Efforts to convert him failed. He was led to the stake with five fellow sufferers. In the flames he cried out the Shema, ending with the word for One as he died. Lisbon crowds repeated his last words for years. Amsterdam Jews mourned him with a memorial sermon and elegies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cavaillon-4159:
Cavaillon is a small town in the department of Vaucluse, in France. Jews lived there from an early period. A rabbinical source names Eliezer ben Judah of Cavaillon, a pupil of a teacher at Orleans in the late eleventh century. Rashi of Troyes may have corresponded with scholars of the town, though Gross held that the passage points to Châlons-sur-Saône.

A record of 1372 shows five Jews rendering homage to the bishop for the community. Jews paid a yearly rent for houses and lands in his territory. In 1453 Jews were shut into a special quarter. In 1485 Christians of the town attacked Jews and looted their property. Cavaillon was one of four communities with a special prayer rite, printed at Avignon in 1767. Scholars linked to the town include Todros, a physician, and Jacob Léon, for whom a calendar treatise was written in 1465.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chashkes-moses-: Moses Löb Chashkes, a Neo-Hebrew poet and Russian translator, was born in Wilna on Sept. 27, 1848. He later moved to Odessa. His first Hebrew song collection came out at Warsaw in 1869. More verse, often satirical, followed at Odessa and St. Petersburg. His Sefer ha-Yomi told in verse the life of a Jewish writer, and was partly his own story. A collected volume of his Hebrew poems appeared at Warsaw in 1896. He also wrote Yiddish songs and rendered works on Jewish suffering into Russian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-choynski-joseph: Joseph Choynski, an American heavyweight pugilist, was born at San Francisco on Nov. 8, 1868. His first time in the prize-ring came in 1884, when J. J. Corbett beat him in one round. He went on to face most of the leading fighters of his day. The entry names Dan Creedon, Kid McCoy, James Jeffries, T. Sharkey, and Steve O'Donnell among those he beat or held to drawn battles. In more than fifty battles, it says, he lost only seven.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-abraham-4: Abraham Cohen, chief rabbi of Djerba, an island near Tunis, died in 1870. Two works stand under his name. The first is Shir Hadash, a Hebrew poem on the 613 precepts of the Law. Israel Costa published it at Leghorn. The second is Kan Zippor, a Hebrew commentary on the Psalms. Israel Frumkin published it at Jerusalem in 1870, the year of Cohen's death. One bibliographic source, Cazes on Tunisian Jewish writing, supports the whole brief notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-colorni-colorno:
Abraham Colorni, also Colorno, an Italian engineer, was born at Mantua about 1530. His skill made him much sought after. By 1578 he held the engineer's post at the court of Alfonso d'Este, Duke of Ferrara. Alfonso sent him to Prague in 1588 and on to the Wurttemberg court in 1597.

Praise reached beyond engineering. Garzoni ranked him among the finest mathematicians and archaeologists of the age and praised his manners and even his dueling. Among his inventions stood a ten-chambered revolver, of which he is said to have made 2,000 for Alfonso. His writings include math tables, a rendering of the Hebrew Key of Solomon on magic, and a treatise on secret writing printed at Prague in 1593.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coriat-4659: Coriat is the name of a Jewish family of Morocco. The entry centers on one book. In 1812 a Hebrew work titled Zekut Abot appeared at Pisa. Three members of the family worked on it together. They were Judah, his son Abraham, and his grandson Judah. The book records the religious customs of the Jews of Morocco. It also lists their names and the places where Jews lived. The entry is short and cites a single source. It records the family through that one joint work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crespin-elias-4: Elias Crespin was a Rumanian rabbi, teacher, and journalist. He was born about 1850 at Eskee Sara, in eastern Rumelia. After the Turco-Russian war of 1878 he fled to Rumania. There he did a first in the East. He founded a Judæo-Spanish journal printed in Latin characters. The paper, El Luzero de la Paciencia, lasted two years, 1886-87. He edited it at Turn-Severin. The entry is short and rests on Franco's history of the Jews of Turkey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dama-son-of-net: Dama, son of Netina, was a non-Israelite of Ashkelon. The rabbis held him up as a model of love and piety toward parents. He held high office there, as head of the council. Once, grossly insulted by his mother before his colleagues, he kept his reverence and spoke no angry word. Another tale praises him more. Buyers came for a precious stone of his, needed for the high priest's breastplate. His father slept with the key under his pillow. Dama would not wake him for any price.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-abu-sulai:
Abu Sulaiman David al-Ḳumisi was a Karaite teacher of the tenth century, a native of the Persian province of Ḳumis. He died in Jerusalem in the year 945. His Biblical commentaries were written in Arabic, and they have been lost. Only two passages from his work are still known.

One passage concerns the Passover sacrifice. David held that it began only at twilight of the fifteenth of Nisan and, as a private offering, could not push aside the Sabbath. The other passage derives the Karaite ban on eating the fatty tail from Leviticus. Saadia refuted that proof, yet later Karaites kept repeating it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-delgado-juan-mo:
Juan Pinto Delgado, later Moses Pinto Delgado, was a Marano poet born at Tavira, Portugal, about 1530. He studied the humanities at Salamanca and befriended the poet Luis de Leon. His memory was so strong that he could repeat a speech heard only once, word for word. Pursued by the Inquisition, he left his wife and child and fled by way of Rome to France.

In France Delgado openly professed Judaism and took the name Moses. His poems won praise for grace, high style, and varied meters. His verse versions of Esther, the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and Ruth were printed at Rouen in 1627 and dedicated to Cardinal Richelieu. He died in 1591.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dhu-nuwas-zur-a:
