The PHQ-4 asks two questions about depression and two about anxiety. It takes under a minute to complete. Three hundred fifty-seven adults from one urban and two rural communities took part. Trained mental health professionals collected the data. The Bangla version's structure and reliability were then put through formal psychometric tests.

The results were about as clean as validation studies get. The expected two-factor structure fitted excellently. The scale worked the same across sex, age, and mental health state. Internal consistency was high. Scores correlated strongly with two longer established questionnaires and with rated mental health. For community health workers screening door to door, a validated one-minute tool in the local language is a practical breakthrough toward earlier help.
plos-pone-0352659:
Xu Zhu and four colleagues check whether a simple ratio from routine blood tests can forecast survival in cardiogenic shock, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. In this emergency the heart suddenly cannot pump enough blood, and many patients die within a year. The team pulled records for nearly twelve hundred intensive care patients from a large American database and divided a kidney-related measure, blood urea nitrogen, by the blood protein albumin.

Patients with higher ratios died more often in hospital and within a year, in a steady staircase across low, medium, and high groups. Adding the ratio improved existing risk scores slightly. A cheap, instant marker like this could help doctors triage the sickest hearts faster.
plos-pone-0352759:
Sunyoung Choi and five colleagues compare what faces show with what people say they feel. Their 2026 study recruited one hundred forty-eight healthy Korean adults. Participants watched video clips designed to stir joy, anxiety, sadness, or neutral calm. Cameras recorded their spontaneous facial expressions throughout. Software scored the expressions automatically. Afterwards, participants rated their own emotions on several scales.

The clips worked. Both self-reports and facial patterns reflected the intended emotions. Yet the two channels did not always move together. Women displayed stronger positive facial expressions than men during the joyful clips. Self-reported experience did not mirror that gap in the same way. Such mismatches matter for emotion research. A study trusting only questionnaires, or only faces, would draw different conclusions about the same viewers. Measuring both is the safer design this work demonstrates.
plos-pone-0352859:
Muhammad Jawad Ullah and five colleagues published this 2026 food safety study of Salmonella in shop-sold beef in Peshawar, Pakistan. From two hundred and fifty samples bought in city, village, and fringe markets, they cultured the bacteria, confirmed them by gene test, checked drug resistance, and profiled genetic variety.

Three in five samples carried Salmonella, with rural markets worst. Resistance to a common antibiotic was nearly universal, yet the strains were genetically diverse, pointing to many separate entry points along the supply chain. Ullah frames shop beef as a serious reservoir needing surveillance.
plos-pone-0353059:
Xinju Zhan and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One benchmark study testing fifteen leading language models on China's national nurse licensing examination across three years. Nearly ten thousand real exam questions were used, and models were only tested on exams released after the model itself, keeping the contest fair. Both Chinese and international models took part.

Performance climbed steeply: top accuracy rose from under half in 2022 to nearly four-fifths by 2025. Chinese-made models consistently beat international rivals, though the gap narrowed. Models handled knowledge questions better than applied clinical skills questions, and nearly half of the top models' remaining errors were failures of clinical judgment, like choosing the wrong nursing priority. The authors say passing an exam is not the same as thinking like a nurse.
plos-pone-0353159:
Maryam Kazemipoor, Shima Habibzadeh, and Fatemeh Keshmiri investigate unprofessional behaviour among dental students in Iran, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. One hundred and forty students at one medical university were rated by their clinical teachers, by nurses, and by themselves, using a multi-source feedback method. Interviews then explored why students said these behaviours happen.

Lapses clustered around responsibility and respect for others. Junior students and male students were rated worst. Students blamed personal pressures such as profit focus, but also pointed to poor role models and weak training structures above them. The authors recommend feedback systems like theirs, paired with early responsibility training and better examples from senior clinicians.
plos-pone-0353259:
Ling Sun led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of Shuangyu Granule, a traditional Chinese medicine used against influenza. Advanced instruments catalogued its ingredients in the dish and which of them reached the blood, while network analysis and single-cell data from flu patients predicted which immune genes the mixture might touch.

Key ingredients then calmed inflammatory gene activity and cut several inflammatory signals in cell tests. Sun suggests the granule cools excessive flu inflammation through many ingredients acting on many targets, a pattern typical of herbal formulas.
plos-pone-0353359:
Jang and colleagues linked blood pressure levels to hidden heart artery disease in a 2026 study. More than seven thousand adults without symptoms or known heart disease had heart scans during health checkups in Korea. Pressure was grouped from normal through two stages of hypertension under current American guidance.

Scans sorted arteries into normal, mildly narrowed, and seriously narrowed. Comparing groups shows how even modest pressure rises track with silent plaque before any symptoms appear. Such evidence matters because treatment thresholds are debated: if raised pressure already matches visible artery damage, earlier treatment gains support. The checkup setting also shows scanning can reveal risk that office numbers alone understate.
plos-pone-0353559:
Reuben S. Maghembe published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE testing whether gene-activity signatures that distinguish bacterial from viral infection survive the move to new patient data. Doctors need that distinction to use antibiotics wisely, but signatures often fail outside their discovery dataset. Maghembe fixed five whole-blood response modules in one public cohort, then applied them unchanged to two external cohorts, including one measured on a different technology, and stress-tested the results.

All five modules pointed the expected way in both cohorts. Four passed strict statistical correction comfortably, while the fifth stayed directionally right but borderline. Thousands of robustness checks, changing reference groups, case definitions, and deleting genes one or two at a time, almost never flipped a result. One alternative scoring method shifted support between two modules but changed no directions. These host-response modules, the author concludes, travel unusually well, a precondition for a clinical test.
plos-pone-0353759:
Louise de Palaminy led a team of six authors on this 2026 study of medieval Islamic gold coins and the trans-Saharan trade. Fatimid dinars were the era's global currency, supposedly struck from West African gold, but proof of origin was thin. The team combined trace element and three-isotope analysis on eleven coins.

Two distinct metal stocks appeared. Copper and iron signatures fit weathered West African ores, yet lead signatures pointed somewhere else, raising questions about where gold was processed and whether old metal was reused. The chemical detective work reopens a classic trade mystery.
plos-pone-0353859:
Divya Gumudavelly and seven colleagues interview HIV clinic staff in central Uganda about the mental health care they improvise for their patients, in this 2026 qualitative study. Mental illness is common among people living with HIV, and policy pushes integration, yet Uganda has almost no formal mental health infrastructure inside HIV services. Sixteen providers at two clinics described their routines, obstacles, and workarounds in semi-structured interviews.

Without formal integrated services, providers reported tension with their institutions and sometimes with patients. They bridged the gaps through adaptive habits the authors sum up as just trying to make it work. Those hidden efforts keep patients cared for but take a toll on the providers themselves. The authors argue integration plans should recognize, resource, and protect this invisible labor instead of assuming new protocols alone will do the job.
plos-pone-0354159:
Hanif Abdul Rahman and Hein Minn Tun use in 2026 computer learning methods to forecast how warming past set climate limits could raise disease worldwide. They modelled outcomes at three levels of warming above early industrial times. A first stage searched for curved patterns and sharp thresholds, and a second stage tried to explain the pathways behind them.

Even at the lowest level studied, deaths and years lost to heat rose by roughly two thirds from a recent baseline. At higher warming the rises grew much steeper, and heart disease burden climbed too. People in low resource places bore the heaviest load in the forecasts, the authors report.
plos-pone-0354259:
Zhao and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a review comparing cholesterol drugs in people with diabetes. Diabetes sharply raises the risk of clogged arteries and heart death, and the menu of lipid drugs keeps growing: statins, fibrates, absorption blockers, and newer injectable and oral classes. Which works best and safest for diabetic patients, head to head, is unsettled.

The planned network review will search the major trial databases with no language limits, keeping only randomized trials that compare these drugs alone or in combination. Two reviewers will screen and judge quality separately. Main outcomes are heart events; secondary outcomes include blood fat levels, heart biomarkers, risk scores, and side effects. Certainty will be graded with a network-specific framework, and results published for peer review. As a protocol, the paper promises a method, not an answer; the ranking of drugs awaits the review itself.
plos-pone-0354359: Naik and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on making a magnesium alloy resist rust. The alloy, AZ91, is light and prized for vehicles, but it corrodes easily. The team paired a severe shaping treatment called ECAP with heat treatments. The title reports that the pairing improved corrosion performance more than either alone. Lighter car parts save fuel only if they last.
plos-pone-0354459: Ansar and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on catching copied work that crosses languages. A student might translate a Persian text into English to hide copying. The team's deep learning system aims to spot such cross-language plagiarism between English and Persian. Tools like this help schools and journals guard honest work as translation software grows stronger.
plos-pone-0354959:
Koki Takeda and five colleagues published this 2026 safety study of a chemotherapy drug and a rare eye swelling. Scanning Japan's national side-effect database across two decades, including hundreds of thousands of reports. They checked whether paclitaxel and its albumin-bound form were reported with macular edema, fluid swelling at the center of the retina, more often than expected.

Both forms showed strong reporting signals, the albumin-bound one much stronger. Diabetes and certain glaucoma eye drops also flagged higher reporting. Takeda advises closer eye monitoring for patients on this chemotherapy with those extra risks.
plos-pone-0355059:
Chidera Ejike and colleagues set out in 2026 a review plan on studies that use photovoice to explore how green spaces affect community health. Photovoice lets people photograph and discuss their own surroundings, giving views that standard research often misses, especially in dry regions. The review will gather projects where taking photos was a core method with human participants.

Searches will cover databases and grey sources with no language limit, reaching back to when the method was first described. Screening and extraction will be done in duplicate, and trust in key findings will be rated with standard tools. Community actions that grew from projects are a central interest.
plos-pone-0355159:
Maha Atout and colleagues survey in 2026 what mothers in Jordan do at home when a young child has a fever related seizure. Mothers who attended clinics and wards at two public hospitals in the north answered a structured questionnaire. Most children were under six, and mothers were usually first on the scene.

More than two thirds acted in broadly proper ways, such as placing the child safely and watching how long the episode lasted. Many still panicked, and some used harmful steps such as chest massage. Better knowledge and a more positive outlook linked strongly to safer action, leading the authors to urge focused teaching by health staff.
plos-pone-0355259:
RETRACTED: The PLOS One Editors issued this 2026 retraction notice, withdrawing an earlier rat study that had claimed a food preservative compound eased early brain injury after bleeding around the brain. Readers should not rely on that study's findings. Concerns centred on several figures and on how the animals were treated.

Editors found a control image that appeared reused, a protein band size that raised doubt about identity, and overlapping panels that undermined related counts. Pain relief, humane endpoints, and approval details had not been reported, and anaesthetic and fluid choices raised welfare worries. Original data were missing, so the concerns could not be cleared.
plos-pone-0355359:
Qingmin Kong and co-authors studied how power plant production workers in China reinvent themselves as salespeople under electricity market reform. Selling used to be foreign to generation companies; reform made it a frontline job. Their 2026 dual-case study of two new-energy firms mixed grounded interviews with a supporting survey.

Beyond the expected blend of selling skill and service skill, a third capability stood out: digital capability, working with data platforms and online customers. Each capability stacked in two layers, foundation first, innovation second, with the first required before the second grows. Three growth paths appeared, led by analytics, by relationships, or by a third route. Kong and colleagues model the transition for other reforming utilities.
plos-pone-0355559:
Po-Yueh Chen and co-authors linked weather records with flu-like illness counts across Taiwan over five recent years. Flu timing follows weather in cooler climates, but the pattern is murkier in subtropical places. Their 2026 study used public health and weather data covering thousands of county-weeks in seventeen counties and cities.

Humidity showed the clearest pattern: more humid weeks came with fewer flu-like illness reports. Air pressure showed a weaker link in the same direction. Temperature and rainfall showed no reliable overall link. Patterns varied sharply by region, with humidity mattering most in the north. Chen and colleagues argue Taiwan's flu planning should treat weather effects as regional, not national.
plos-pone-0355659:
Retraction notice. The PLOS One editors formally withdrew a published study claiming antiviral effects for KIOM-C, a herbal medicine, across several viruses. This 2026 notice is the second retraction involving the same medicine and research group. It records why the journal concluded the antiviral findings could not stand.

Panels in the paper appear to match panels in another article while claiming to show different experiments. The statistics section named a test suited to two-group comparisons, yet many experiments used more groups and variables. The notice also records an undisclosed patent interest: the corresponding author was an inventor on a patent tied to the tested medicine. Readers should not rely on the retracted claims.
plos-pone-0355859:
Turgut Batuhan Baturalp and Selim Bozkurt built a simpler artificial left ventricle for testing heart devices and conditions. Bench circulation rigs often need complex controls, while animal work raises ethical concerns. Their 2026 study first compared actuation options with a structured decision method, then built the winner.

The chosen design squeezes a latex chamber with pneumatic artificial muscles, which contract when filled with air. The prototype beat at several resting and raised heart rates, healthy and diseased settings alike. It pushed flows above two litres per minute. Its tip twisted and shortened much like a real ventricle wall. The authors call it a promising early testbed for cardiac research.
plos-pone-0355959:
Xu Zhixin and co-authors built a fibre-optic listening system that can watch several points inside high-voltage switchgear at once. Loose metal particles inside gas-insulated gear spark partial discharges that precede failure. Standard sensors hear only one point at a time. Their 2026 method sweeps the light frequency to give each sensor its own channel on a single decoding box.

Bench tests on real switchgear fitted with four sensing units followed. The system picked up discharge signals and identified which cavity held the defect. Sensitivity matched conventional single-point interferometric sensors, the design's starting benchmark. Xu and colleagues present frequency-division fibre sensing as a practical route to distributed condition monitoring in modern power equipment.
plos-pone-0356059:
Jasper Mol and co-authors built a pipeline that fishes bacteria out of mixed communities by the sugars on their surfaces. Those sugars steer immune responses, but standard gene surveys cannot see them. Their 2026 method uses human immune sensor proteins as probes, sorting matching bacteria before gene sequencing identifies them.

Tests on a mock community recovered known interacting strains even at low abundance. Applied to stool samples from healthy donors, the pipeline named specific bacteria that bind each of two sensors. Follow-up cultures confirmed the matches. Mol and colleagues describe the platform as modular: other sensors and patient samples can be swapped in to map which microbes the immune system can actually taste.
plos-pone-0356359: An and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a protein that helps liver cancer hide from the immune system. The protein, FABP5, is the focus of their lab work. They report that it shapes a suppressive setting around the tumor through a chain involving NF-kB and PD-L1, both known immune switches. Blocking such chains is a major aim in modern cancer drug design.
plos-pone-0356759:
Haiwei Du, Runsen Lai, and Jianhua Zhu reconstructed a deadly kind of mountain disaster: the debris flow that races down steep gullies. A catchment in China's North Tianshan range served as their case. Their 2026 study combined field surveys and laboratory soil tests. It also used a validated flood simulation program. The program replayed a 2024 event and then tested how worse storms would behave.

The replay matched the real flood's depth and footprint closely. The recipe for disaster combined three things. Shattered rock supplied debris, steep slopes sped it up, and short intense rain pulled the trigger. Under a once-a-century storm, the simulated flow ran several meters deep at highway speeds. The danger zone swelled over downstream settlements. Such zonation gives engineers defensible lines for barriers and building bans.
plos-pone-0357159:
Yuri Fukai, Amane Fujiwara, and Kohei Matsuno test whether algae sleeping in Arctic seafloor mud can seed the autumn blooms now appearing on the Chukchi shelf. Stronger winds over open water stir sediments upward, and a recent field study suggested buried diatoms ride along. The team incubated natural water communities two ways, adding nutrients alone or nutrients plus microalgae-bearing sediment, and watched growth, species, and light use.

Both treatments bloomed, with diatoms leading. Sediment sped the start by adding ready cells, while growth rates and light efficiency stayed similar. Nutrient-only tanks favored open-water autumn species, while sediment tanks filled with species typical of the seafloor. Fukai and colleagues say resuspension shapes not just bloom timing but which community the Arctic gets.
plos-pone-0357259:
Ling Zong and Kexin Zhou published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on older adults in China who live with several chronic diseases at once. The study asks what family and social support do to their mental health. Using a nationally representative 2020 survey, they modeled how multimorbidity relates to mental health, and whether family or wider social support changes that link.

More diseases went with poorer mental health. Both supports were themselves linked to better mental health, but only family support changed the disease link, surprisingly: the mental health penalty of multimorbidity grew steeper where family support was higher. That effect weakened with age and vanished past eighty, while family support's direct benefit followed a U-shape across age groups. Close family involvement, they warn, is not automatically protective, and programs should work with families carefully rather than simply urging more of it.
plos-pone-0357459:
Siliang Guo, Yan Qu, and Youjia Liu published a 2026 economics study in PLOS ONE on whether education keeps Chinese families from sliding back into poverty. China has ended absolute poverty, but keeping families out is a different challenge. Using four waves of a national family panel survey from 2014 to 2020, the authors measured each household's stock of educational human capital and modeled relapse risk with several statistical approaches.

More education clearly lowered the chance of falling back into poverty. The protection ran through three channels: family members finding non-farm jobs, higher household income, and better family health. Households that themselves invested more in education got extra benefit, while heavy health spending diluted the effect. The protective impact grew stronger for families at highest relapse risk, and was larger in eastern and urban areas than elsewhere. The authors argue education budgets are anti-poverty insurance, especially where relapse risk concentrates.
plos-pone-0357759:
Ankit and coauthors published a 2026 materials paper in PLOS ONE on copper-graphite composites, blends prized for carrying current and resisting wear, made by pressing and baking metal powders. Three settings govern the result: how much graphite goes in, how hot the baking runs, and how long it lasts. Instead of trial and error, the team used response surface methodology to model how those settings jointly determine density and hardness.

A fitted quadratic model matched the measured values closely, with negligible error, and formal analysis confirmed which settings mattered. The best combination used a modest graphite share, a high sintering temperature, and a mid-length hold, giving the densest and hardest material in their tests. The model lets manufacturers dial in target density or hardness on paper first, cutting wasted runs, and gives powder metallurgy shops a template for other blends.
plos-pone-0357959:
Francisca Édla Santos Leite Gurgel and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE from Fortaleza, Brazil, on teaching pregnant women with diabetes how to care for themselves. Standard hospital handouts can be hard going for women with limited reading skills. So the team wrote the guidance as a cordel, a traditional Brazilian booklet of rhymed verse, working with health researchers and cordel poets, and tested it at two public maternity hospitals.

Hospitalized pregnant women rated every item of the booklet as fully valid, and forty expert judges nearly matched them, giving top or near-top clarity and relevance scores. Experts strongly agreed on the content overall, though they ranked individual items in quite different orders. The cordel, they say, is a culturally rooted format that makes discharge guidance easier to grasp and remember, and this early validation invites wider testing of whether it changes self-care.
plos-pone-0358259: Tang and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study that mines public data on stool fats and gene activity. Their combined computer analysis hints that the COX-2 pathway may be linked with one fat molecule, named CE(20:4). The link sits along the path from benign colon growths to cancer. A candidate link from free data can guide lab work on early colon cancer signs.
plos-pone-0358359:
Zongtao Li led a team of seven authors linking a common molecule to kidney damage in diabetes, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Lactate, known for the burn of hard exercise, may also signal renal trouble in diabetic kidney disease. The team combined animal experiments, clinical cohorts, and bioinformatics in one exploratory analysis.

Li's work ties higher serum lactate to worse kidney function across those sources. A cheap blood measure that warns early of failing kidneys would be valuable, since current markers lag behind damage. Triangulating across animals, patients, and gene data strengthens a claim that any one source could not carry. The analysis is exploratory by design, marking lactate as a lead worth testing in larger, focused studies.
plos-pone-0358459:
Braulio Tapia and colleagues studied in 2026 how fish communities differ from place to place on the rocky reefs of the Juan Fernández Archipelago. The islands, far off the coast of Chile in the southeastern Pacific, sit inside a marine protected area. The team examined demersal fish, those living near the reef floor, and asked how their groupings vary across the protected waters.

Understanding that spatial variety, called heterogeneity, is practical knowledge for conservation. A protected area drawn without it may guard plenty of water but miss the spots where particular communities thrive. The authors link their findings to the archipelago's conservation plans, showing where protection is well placed and where management may need adjusting.
plos-pone-0358659:
Muhammad Ali Ibrahim Kazi leads a team of eight studying heart outcomes in people who live with both inflammatory bowel disease and type 2 diabetes, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The pairing is dangerous, since gut inflammation and blood sugar problems feed each other's damage to blood vessels. The authors asked whether modern diabetes drugs in the GLP-1 family are linked to fewer heart events in this high risk group.

Using a large international health records network, they matched over sixteen thousand treated patients with similar untreated ones. Treated patients showed lower rates across the board: heart attack, heart failure, stroke, dangerous rhythms, and blood clots in veins and lungs. The authors caution that records based comparisons show association, not proof of cause, and that the study cannot separate the two drug types it pooled together.
plos-pone-0358759: Cui and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on hearing machine faults through noise. Bearings in spinning machines wear out, and their fault signals hide in loud, shifting conditions. The team's Wavelet-Mamba network mixes wave-based signal cleaning with a modern sequence model. Catching a failing bearing early can prevent a breakdown that stops a whole line.
plos-pone-0358959:
Rustam Akhmedov and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on exercise and women's health. It is an eight-week intervention study of indoor cycling, commonly called spinning. Outcomes cover body image, how the women see their own bodies, and anthropometric measurements, standard measures like weight and waist size.

Tracking body image alongside body measurements matters because the two do not always move together. A program can shrink a waist while leaving self-image untouched, or lift confidence before bodies change. Fitness practitioners designing women's cycling programs are the readers for evidence that joins the physical and the psychological.
plos-pone-0359559:
Joanna L'Heureux and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on the oral microbiome, the community of microbes living in the mouth. The authors look for signatures of ageing and of cognitive function in that community. Their cohorts come from distinct geographical regions, letting place enter the comparison.

Mouth microbes are easy to sample, so a signature tied to cognition would be a convenient window on brain health. Geography matters because diet and environment shape the microbiome strongly. Researchers of ageing and dementia screening are the readers for signatures that hold across places rather than reflecting one town's habits.
plos-pone-0359659: Shah, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on why muscles waste away. Using a tool called decoupleR, Shah compared the activity of transcription factors, the switches that turn genes on and off. Three causes of wasting were set side by side: space flight, old age, and lack of use. Seeing where the three match or split can point to shared targets for drugs or training plans.
plos-pone-0359859:
John Yinger published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies world-record envelopes in racing events: the outer limits that link how fast athletes can go and how far. The focus is the speed-distance trade-off, the way top speed falls as race distance grows.

An envelope here means the boundary formed by world records across distances, from sprints to marathons. Fitting that boundary shows the underlying rule connecting speed and endurance in human performance. Sports scientists use such limits to judge how close current athletes are to what bodies can do, and to spot records that break the pattern.
plos-pone-0359959:
Quang Toai Ton, Thanh Hien Vu, Thanh Nguyen Vu, and Tuong Le published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents HSCM-Lane, a computer vision system for lane segmentation, marking exactly which pixels in a road image belong to lane lines. The system is built on a ResNet encoder-decoder design.

Added to that base is context modeling that uses shifted windows at several levels, a way for the network to consider both fine line detail and the wider road scene. Lane marking detection is a core skill for driver assistance and self-driving cars. Engineers comparing segmentation architectures can judge whether this context modeling earns its extra complexity on road images.
plos-pone-0360059:
Ankit Singh, Varun Dutt, and Akash Rao studied in 2026 how mental effort and brain stimulation together shape the way people make decisions from experience. Their experiments vary cognitive load, how much a person's working memory is burdened, and apply prefrontal neuromodulation, gentle stimulation of the brain region behind the forehead that handles planning. They watch how these factors change exploration, risk taking, and the search for information.

Experience based decisions, learned by trying options and seeing outcomes, differ from choices made from written descriptions. Knowing how a loaded or stimulated brain explores helps explain everyday choices under pressure. The work speaks to psychology, to economics, and to the design of training for people whose risky decisions carry real costs.
pmc-10652459:
Debates over thyroid cancer screening after nuclear accidents have grown sharp, and this comment joins one side of them. Colin Soskolne writes in support of Tsuda and co-authors, who criticized a paper by Schüz and co-authors on radiation induced thyroid cancer in children. His target is a second group, Cléro and co-authors, whose reply defended recommendations from a European project published in 2021 without, in his view, answering the main criticisms.

Soskolne walks through the reply's paragraphs, arguing its recommendations rested on biased studies rather than objective evidence. He adds its claim about overdiagnosis in adults cannot be carried over to children. He says the defending paper deflected instead of engaging with the Chernobyl and Fukushima record. His conclusion mirrors the endorsed one for the other paper: flawed work of this kind should be withdrawn or retracted to protect public health policy.
pmc-10654159:
Segun Aroyehun and co-authors present LEIA, a language model that reads emotion in social media text, trained on labels people gave their own posts. Their study appeared in 2023. Emotion datasets are usually small, costly, and labeled by strangers guessing feelings, which adds noise. LEIA instead learned from over six million posts self-tagged for happiness, affection, sadness, anger, and fear. A word-masking trick during training pushed the model to learn emotion words deeply.

On three in-domain test sets, LEIA scored about 73 on a balanced accuracy measure, beating supervised and unsupervised rivals, and it held up across users and time. On five outside datasets it stayed robust, transferring anger, happiness, and sadness labels well. The authors say self-labels at scale beat careful labels in small sets.
pmc-10655259:
Jin Eun and co-authors published this 2023 study on cholesterol drugs and recovery after surgery for chronic subdural hematoma, a slow bleed on the brain common in older adults. Whether blood fat levels or the drugs that lower them change the odds of the bleed returning was unsettled. Five Korean hospitals pooled their recent cases.

The set held 462 patients treated from 2010 to 2021, most with the standard burr-hole operation. Seventy-five bleeds came back and sixty-two patients needed a second operation. Taking cholesterol drugs did not shift either rate in a meaningful way. One drug pairing did raise the protective HDL cholesterol level clearly. The authors conclude fat control, while good general care, is no lever on the outcome of this surgery.
pmc-10655459:
Daniela Gesell and co-authors present a 2023 study of the symptom burden carried by patients in specialist palliative home care in Germany. Such care aims to protect quality of life at home for people with advanced illness. Whether cancer and non-cancer patients suffer in the same patterns was little known, though it shapes how teams plan visits and drugs.

Working from a multi-centre study of care complexity, the team measured physical symptoms and psychosocial problems and searched for clusters with factor analysis. They compared cluster shapes between cancer and non-cancer patients. Distinct clusters would argue for diagnosis-aware care plans rather than one standard bundle for all home patients.
pmc-10688459:
Davide Genovese and co-authors test a heart scan measure in 2023 for people with a weak, stretched heart muscle. Doctors need to know the pressure in the left side of the heart to guide care. The standard test uses a tube threaded into the heart, which carries risk.

The team used magnetic resonance scans to measure how much the upper left chamber swells as it fills. They compared this index with the tube test in one hundred twenty-six patients. The scan index tracked the true pressure closely and flagged high pressure well. A simple formula from the scan gave close estimates in a check group. The authors say scans could spare some patients the tube test.
pmc-10692159:
Mary Kasten and colleagues follow COVID-19 in patients whose immune systems were blunted by a common drug class, in this study from twenty twenty-three. Anti-CD20 drugs wipe out B cells and are used for cancers and autoimmune disease. Plasma from recovered donors was widely tried as a treatment, but its value in such patients was disputed.

The team found one hundred forty-four adults at Mayo Clinic sites who caught COVID after recent anti-CD20 therapy. About a third were in hospital within two weeks, and nearly half within ninety days. Ninety-day mortality ran near fifteen percent. How long since the last drug dose made no difference. Neither did donor plasma: those who got it within two weeks fared no better on any outcome than those who did not. The authors call for trials of early antiviral mixes in this group, rather than more faith in plasma.
pmc-10692359:
Amy Milton reviews the science of drug memories in a 2023 paper. Addiction can be seen as a disorder of learning and memory. Cues tied to drug use can trigger strong urges years later. When a memory is recalled, it briefly becomes open to change. That window is called reconsolidation.

Milton traces the molecular steps that restabilize cue and drug memories. Work on habits of drug seeking shows much the same machinery. Blocking the window in animals weakens later drug seeking. Early human studies try to carry that trick into clinics. The review weighs what blocks the path, from timing to study design. It also marks chances for new treatments built on this science.
pmc-10696059:
Megat and colleagues published in twenty twenty-three an author correction to their genetic study of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The original article appeared in Nature Communications in January twenty twenty-three. It analyzed inherited risk for ALS and identified risk genes. The correction concerns errors in one table of that article. Columns listing variant location, DNA change, protein change, and database identifiers held mistakes. The notice prints the full corrected table in place of the old one.

Side-by-side corrected and original values let readers see each fix. Most entries change only in small details like prediction scores. A few change the named protein alteration itself. The correction does not alter the paper's stated conclusions as presented. Notices like this keep the scholarly record accurate for later researchers. Anyone using the variant table should use the corrected version.
pmc-10699559:
Xuanao Ma, Yang Liu, Yunhuai Zhang, and Yun Gong wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It builds a layered sodium titanate sheet whose crystal lattice matches sodium metal, easing the stubborn interface problem in solid-state sodium batteries.

Sodium batteries promise safety and cheap abundance, but ions struggle to cross between the solid electrolyte and the metal anode. The synthesized sheets are rich in oxygen vacancies and let sodium ions glide between quiet titanium-oxygen layers. The material conducts almost only sodium ions, with a very low energy barrier and a transference number of 0.91. Blended into a polymer electrolyte, it kept high conductivity. Test cells with sodium on both sides cycled stably through repeated stripping and plating. The authors credit the lattice match with the metal for the calm interface, a design rule for future electrolytes.
pmc-10701459:
Elsa Wilma Böhm and six co-authors review how oxidative stress harms the eye and feeds many eye diseases. Their review was published in twenty twenty-three. Oxidative stress arises when reactive oxygen outpaces the cell's defenses, and the eye is unusually exposed.

Light pours into the eye all day, and its front parts face ultraviolet rays while shielding the retina behind a layered defense. The back of the eye burns much oxygen, which makes more reactive waste. Inflammation, aging, genes, and pollution add to the load. A tipped redox balance shows up in diseases of both the front and back segments. The review sums up the mechanisms to give clinicians and researchers an updated picture of this shared pathway.
pmc-10702259:
Sumanta Saha and Sujata Saha set out a research plan in a protocol paper from 2023. The plan concerns women with polycystic ovary syndrome, a hormone condition often called PCOS. Women with the condition may gain weight and face blood sugar and heart risks. Many food and herbal products claim to help, but past trials tested them one at a time.

The protocol explains how the pair will search three databases and grade each trial for quality. A network method will then compare many products at once, even ones never tested head to head. Rankings will show which options look best for each outcome. The plan was logged in a public registry before the work began.
pmc-10703859:
Dongsheng Yu, Zifeng Liu, and three co-authors build a machine learning model to flag severe pain after wisdom tooth surgery. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, follows dental outpatients prospectively. One hundred eighty-five patients supply two hundred two extraction cases. High risk means peak pain of seven or more on a ten-point scale within a day.

Nine learning algorithms compete on the same data. A screening step narrows the inputs to five key variables. Checks run inside the sample and on later patients over time. Standard scores rate accuracy, sensitivity, and balance. A good flag lets dentists plan stronger pain control in advance. The model aims at routine clinic use.
pmc-10706259:
Jeon-Kyung Kim and co-authors published this study in 2023. It asks why red ginseng extract works unevenly from person to person. Gut microbes convert its ginsenosides into the active forms, so an antibiotic that disturbs the gut may blunt the extract's effect.

Mice given the antibiotic amoxicillin showed a poorer, less diverse gut community and absorbed far less of the key compound Rg3: blood exposure fell by nearly half. The microbes that perform the conversion step also lost much of their activity. In other words, the antibiotic cut both the workforce and its output. The authors suggest gut differences explain part of the extract's variable reputation. They also float a practical idea: tending the microbiome, by timing antibiotics or adding probiotics, could steady ginseng's benefits. Human studies would need to confirm the mouse findings before advice changes.
pmc-10708159:
Adrian Puițel and co-authors pull two products from corn stalks in this 2023 study. Hot alkaline cooking extracts hemicellulose, a plant sugar polymer, while the leftover pulp becomes papermaking fiber. The team tuned the cooking to keep both products good, since harsh treatment boosts extraction but weakens paper.

Extracted material ran 44 to 63 percent xylan, with recovery sensitive to conditions. The sweet spot used mild alkali at boiling for about half an hour, keeping paper strength while drawing a fair yield. A stronger second extraction proved the point in reverse: stripping more sugar polymer from pulp cut paper strength by a third to a half. The work shows farm waste can feed two product lines at once.
pmc-10709559:
Artem Smirnov and co-authors wrote a 2023 paper on a skin-only RNA and the switches that control it. Most gene studies focus on proteins, yet cells also make RNAs that never become proteins and still do work. Their RNA, called XP33, appears only in skin cells and rises as those cells mature.

Using public molecular data, the team show that two control proteins team up to build a switch for this RNA in skin cells. The switch loops through space to touch the RNA's start site, a contact found in skin cells but not others. Cutting the RNA lowered a late skin gene's activity. The work shows how a tissue builds private gene controls from shared parts.
pmc-10711459:
Yang and coauthors compare two biologic drugs for Crohn disease in China. Both drugs work well, yet no head-to-head trial exists. The team used real clinic data from six centers. Patients got one drug or the other for gut disease.

The pool held 536 patients treated from 2020 to 2023. Most, 386 in all, got the first drug. Scores tracked remission free of steroids at set weeks. Week 26 and week 52 gave the main check points. Weighting balanced traits between the two drug groups. After that fix, the first drug led on most marks.
pmc-10712159:
Yangmu Huang and co-authors published this scoping review in 2023 on artemisinin, the famed malaria drug drawn from a Chinese herb. Work hints the drug and its kin may also fight parasites, viruses, tumors, swelling, and skin ills. The team swept many data banks for clinical studies beyond malaria, in English and Chinese, up to late 2021. Seventy-seven studies made the cut.

Parasite studies led the count, with tumor, swelling, virus, and skin work behind. Most studies ran in Asia, then Africa. Virus work lagged, stuck mostly in early safety trials. Side effects were mild in nearly all reports, with one study noting a harsh event. Gains showed for most uses, though combo therapy for non-malaria parasites stayed in dispute. The authors map where proof is strong and where trials should go next.
pmc-10713759:
A J Morton, A Simpson, and D J Humes present a 2023 national study of unequal access to keyhole and robotic bowel surgery in England. The team mined linked health records for 93,735 adults who had planned colorectal surgery between 2006 and 2020, comparing open operations with the gentler minimally invasive routes.

Keyhole surgery passed open surgery in 2015, then leveled off; robotic operations grew fast from 2017. Uptake differed by up to twenty points between regions. Patients from the most deprived areas got invasive surgery far less often than the least deprived, and the gap widened for robotic cases. The authors call for national plans so the new methods spread fairly.
pmc-10716159:
Eleven researchers report a study from two thousand twenty-three on using AI to grade cataracts from video. A cataract clouds the lens of the eye, and the nuclear form sits at the lens center. Eye AI has grown fast for the back of the eye, but the front of the eye has lacked standard images to train on.

The team used a slit-lamp device that records video to gather a large, uniform set of frames. Eye doctors graded the cataracts on a World Health Organization scale. Those grades trained a learning system, which was then checked against the doctors. The system matched the scale well across the grades tested.
pmc-10719359:
Zhendong Chen, Xuefeng Feng, Li Liu, and Zhenhong Jia present a 2023 study on finding surface flaws on factory parts with computer vision. Tiny flaws can trigger serious safety risks if they slip through checks. Yet the flaws look much like the surface around them, so systems often miss them or raise false alarms.

The team improved a known detection model in three ways. They rebuilt one part to pull out features at many scales and blend them better. They merged that part into the model's backbone to widen its view. They also added a focus step that weighs where in the image to attend. The goal was sharper, more reliable flaw detection.
pmc-10719759:
Timothy Ohlsen and a large team examine primary care use and heart screening in adults who survived childhood cancer. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three. Heart disease is the leading non-cancer cause of early death in this group, and most are followed by general doctors, not specialists.

The study drew on a trial cohort enrolled from twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-one, all at high risk for heart artery disease or heart failure. Researchers gathered records from their own doctors covering two years before enrollment: cancer history, heart-straining treatments, and care plans. The team then judged how often heart screening and follow-up actually happened. The findings expose gaps between the screening these survivors need and what busy primary care delivers.
pmc-10719859:
Tiny RNA molecules from plants may survive digestion and speak to human genes. Ester Díez-Sainz and co-authors test that idea for inflammation. Sequencing found plant microRNAs in fruits, vegetables, cooked legumes, and oils. Two candidates, miR482f and miR482c-5p, were picked for their predicted targets. In human macrophage cells, copies of the two molecules lowered specific immune genes. One cut CLEC7A and NFAM1. The other cut a toll-like receptor gene. Inflammatory profiles shifted as a result.

Both molecules survived simulated digestion and turned up in human feces, though not in blood. The authors suggest food-borne microRNAs could help explain the anti-inflammatory effects of plant-rich diets.
pmc-10720159:
Kuang and co-authors test in 2023 stem cells boosted to make a calming signal protein as a treatment for allergic airway disease. Both stem cells and the protein calm immune responses, so pairing them may help more. Stem cells from reprogrammed cells were engineered with a virus to overproduce the protein.

The boosted cells cut inflammatory cell entry and mucus cell growth in the lungs of allergic mice. Tests on immune cells from patients with allergic rhinitis showed shifts in helper cell types and signals. Gene reads probed how the cells act on those immune cells. The work supports cell therapy tuned by one added protective protein.
pmc-10726559:
Alexandra Larsson and co-authors interviewed Swedish patients about life a year after severe COVID-19 in a 2023 study. All eleven participants had been hospitalized and were of working age when infected. The team asked how daily life and the return to work actually felt, beyond clinical measures.

Four themes emerged from the interviews. Managing health with or without professional support was hard, and low energy interfered with almost everything. People adapted by trial and error, bending familiar strategies to new limits. Returning to work went better when patients had their own tactics plus employer support. The study shows recovery as long practical work, and where health services could lighten it.
pmc-10729059:
Ulugbek Nurmatov and a large team of co-authors set out a 2023 plan to agree on shared definitions of child maltreatment. Europe lacks one common language for naming abuse and neglect of children. Without shared terms, countries record and track cases in clashing ways. The plan serves a project spanning thirty-four European countries.

The team will run an online Delphi study of up to three rounds. Experts from research, health, social care, police, law, and survivor groups will rate statements. About one hundred experts will be invited, with fifty to sixty expected to join. Each round narrows the wording toward consensus. Agreed definitions would help Europe record cases alike and compare across borders.
pmc-10730159:
Devesha Kulkarni and co-authors test whether gut microbes from obese donors alone can drive weight gain in a 2023 study. Obesity has many candidate causes, from genes and diet to immune quirks, and past microbe studies mixed several of them at once. This team used mice with normal genes, normal diet, and fully developed immune systems to isolate the microbes' own effect.

Mice receiving the obese human gut community gained weight and developed inflammation in the gut, fat tissue, and body at large. Their gut barrier did not leak, which separates this effect from some past claims. Gene activity in the mice shifted toward harvesting more calories from food. The authors conclude the obese microbiota by itself is sufficient to drive weight gain and inflammation.
pmc-10735559:
Walter Boot frames a symposium on telehealth for older adults, weighing its reach against its frictions. The overview appeared in 2023. Remote care can help elders age in place and manage health from home. Yet many face thin tech skills, physical or cognitive limits, and no one to call when the app fails. The session gathers five studies: veterans' troubles with pharmacist video visits, who ends up with in-person, remote, or hybrid care, and a short course teaching telehealth basics.

Two more present a tool that flags elder mistreatment and a study of what personal and home factors govern video visit success. Boot argues the technology will only pay off if it is designed and tested around older users' real capacities.
pmc-10735859:
American nursing homes have struggled for years to keep enough nurses on the floor, and the pandemic strained staffing further. Gregory Orewa and co-authors track staffing patterns in this 2023 study using federal payroll data from 2017 through 2022.

Registered nurse and practical nurse hours per resident held fairly steady, even rising slightly during the pandemic. Aide hours fell notably by 2022, though. Use of contract nurses climbed across all roles over the period and may have peaked during the pandemic years. The mix also shifted toward registered nurses. The trends frame the staffing squeeze homes still face.
pmc-10736059:
Adriana Hernandez, Laura Driscoll, Andrea Leverentz, and Jan Mutchler report a study from two thousand twenty-three on aging in jail. More older people are held in prisons and county jails, and facilities built for the young fit them poorly. The pandemic made the strains worse, from health care access to daily movement.

Researchers from a Boston university partnered with a local jail to learn what older men there need. They held focus groups with the men and interviewed staff by video call. The men described limited medical care, poor diets, few accommodations, and little chance to exercise, all raising chronic illness risk. Both men and staff welcomed a dedicated unit for older adults. The poster offers policy suggestions.
pmc-10736259:
Muraira and colleagues published in twenty twenty-three a survey study of young adults' ageism toward older adults. Ageism covers stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination based on age. The team surveyed four hundred fifty-nine adults aged eighteen to twenty-five online. Measures covered conservative values, aging knowledge, and two kinds of ageism. Negative ageism demeans older people's abilities. Positive ageism casts them as warm and reliable in a stereotyped way.

Conservatism linked to both kinds of ageism in the results. Aging knowledge linked only to lower negative ageism, not positive ageism. Even after accounting for conservatism, knowledge explained extra variation in negative ageism. The authors infer education about aging can counter negative stereotypes. Such education likely will not dent positive stereotypes, though. Programs should treat the two forms separately, the findings suggest.
pmc-10737059:
Rahma Ajja and co-authors report in 2023 how participants and leaders rate Walk On!, a community walking program. At the end of the course, attendees filled surveys on the place, timing, length, and changes in their walking. Leaders rated their training and their readiness to lead.

Clients were highly satisfied, with 80 to 100 percent marking the top score for program parts. Their comments told of walking more at home, new confidence, more energy, and valued fellowship. Leaders mostly felt well prepared, with all of them rating the materials clear and easy to use. The authors argue the warm response supports spreading the program to more communities.
pmc-10737259:
Pildoo Sung, Ad Maulod, Angelique Chan, and Rahul Malhotra study older learners in a 2023 paper. They ask which mix of resources helps older adults return for more courses. The data follow 515 learners aged 50 and above in Singapore, gathered in 2017 and 2018.

The team grouped learners by schooling, social ties, and inner resources such as drive and sense of control. Four groups emerged, from well schooled and resource-rich to less schooled and resource-poor. One group, well schooled but low in other resources, was less likely to take another course within six months. The results can help course planners target support where it counts.
pmc-10737959:
A steady daily rhythm may matter more for the aging mind than hours slept, suggests a 2023 study led by Katie Stone and co-authors. Wrist monitors tracked 820 older adults for a week, capturing sleep and the strength of their rest and activity cycles, alongside a battery of thinking tests.

A robust daily rhythm, with strong contrast between active days and restful nights, tracked with better scores on every test. Poor sleep efficiency tracked with weaker memory and global scores. Total sleep time, by contrast, showed no link at all. The authors argue that rhythm and sleep quality deserve the attention usually paid to duration.
pmc-10738659:
Yafei Wu, Maoni Jia, and Ya Fang build, in twenty twenty-three, a machine learning model to predict mild cognitive impairment, an early stage of memory loss. They used a major Alzheimer's database with four hundred forty-four people. Inputs included personal facts, brain tests, a gene tied to risk, and brain scans. Data were split into training and test sets. Six learning methods were built to predict risk at three and five years.

Two methods led, one for each time span, with high accuracy scores. A simple version that used only the top three brain test scores also did well. The gene, brain volume, and a dementia rating score were the top predictors for three-year risk. The authors also seek markers that could guide early action.
pmc-10738759:
Depression in old age is a web of symptoms that feed each other, and some symptoms hold the web together. Zhongfang Yang and co-authors mapped that web in 3,438 Chinese older adults, surveyed three times over four years. They looked for bridge symptoms: knots tying the cluster of low mood to the cluster of lost positive feeling.

One symptom stood out on the negative side: poor appetite. On the positive side, enjoying life carried the most traffic. The strongest single path ran from poor appetite toward lost enjoyment. In Chinese culture, where food carries deep social meaning, appetite may be more than a symptom. The authors suggest appetite could be a culturally tuned lever for intervention.
pmc-10740459:
Silpa Mullakkalparambil Velayudhan and co-authors scan cattle genomes for milk traits under tropical stress in a 2023 study. Two hundred forty cows from sixty-eight small farms around Bengaluru, India, were genotyped and measured. The team ran a genome-wide association study on test-day milk yield, solids, lactose, density, and mastitis, and hunted for selection signatures across Holstein, Jersey, and crossbred herds.

Two genetic markers tied significantly to milk yield. The other traits showed no marker passing the bar. Selection scans compared the breeds for regions swept clean by breeding or climate pressure. First-of-its-kind data from harsh smallholder conditions can guide breeding that keeps yield without losing hardiness.
pmc-10741559:
Karl Swann, Luigia Santella, and Nunzia Limatola published a 2023 review of how fertilization wakes a mammal egg. A sperm delivers a special enzyme into the egg. That enzyme triggers repeated calcium pulses. The pulses start embryo development. Details of the feedback loop fill the review.

The messenger chemical must arise inside the egg. Diffusion limits rule out simpler sources. Egg sensitivity to the sperm enzyme varies by species. One lab trick works in mice but not other mammals. Receptor sensitivity explains much of that difference. Understanding activation guides fertility treatment and embryo research.
pmc-10742559:
Izabela Kranjcec and co-authors review childhood iron deficiency anemia care in Croatia in this 2023 paper. Precise national data on the condition were lacking. Records of children referred to specialist centers over five years were analyzed. Four tertiary hospitals across the country took part.

The review covered 864 children, mostly of preschool age. Primary care doctors had usually run basic tests but started iron treatment in only half the cases before referral. About a third of the children had symptoms. Poor nutrition was the leading cause found. Specialists favored one iron formulation at a median dose reported in the study. Compliance ranged widely by center. Hospital admission was uncommon. The gaps point to clearer primary care guidance.
pmc-10743459:
Daniela Osorio-Rodriguez and co-authors wrote a 2023 paper on microbes that eat methane deep under the sea. Teams of microbes living without oxygen join to consume methane rising from the seabed. Rocks formed at such seeps can hold traces of this life for ages. Whether the microbes themselves can turn to stone was unknown.

In long lab cultures, the microbe teams grew in clean seawater without sediment. Tiny grains of silica, about two hundred nanometers wide, formed inside the sticky clusters the teams live in. That shows the microbes can trigger stone-making themselves, not just sit in passing minerals. The finding helps scientists read ancient rocks for signs of this hidden methane-eating life.
pmc-10743559:
Pablo Molina and co-authors study a drug's link to survival in kidney disease, in a 2023 paper. The drug, sevelamer, traps phosphate in the gut and is used when kidneys fail. Earlier work hinted it might beat calcium-based rivals on survival, but most data came from patients already on dialysis.

This study followed 966 people in Spain with advanced kidney disease who were not on dialysis. Over a median of about twenty-nine months, 181 participants died, more than half from heart causes. The analysis used models that account for drug use changing over time. The paper weighs whether starting sevelamer before dialysis is tied to lower death rates. The answer matters for a large group with few proven options.
pmc-10743659:
Deepa Bandi and co-authors test pigmented extracts from two bacteria against breast cancer, including its hardest triple-negative form. Their study appeared in 2023. Triple-negative cancers lack the hormone and growth targets that modern drugs hit, so new agents are badly needed. The extracts came from an Exiguobacterium strain and a Bacillus strain. Screening showed they block legumain, a protein that helps cancers grow and spread and that also marks tumor-supporting immune cells.

The extracts slowed cancer cell growth in dishes, curbed blood vessel growth in a chick membrane test, and shrank tumors in mice. The authors say microbial pigments deserve attention as a source of selective cancer agents. Their target, legumain, links the cancer cells and their support crew in one strike.
pmc-10743859:
Danielle Hicks and co-authors present a 2023 review of a pair of cell proteins that help end the stress response in cells. When a cell's protein folding falters, it slows new protein work by marking a key factor. The two proteins, GADD34 and CReP, guide a partner enzyme to erase that mark and restart work. The review gathers what is known about both.

The pair act as brakes on the stress loop, above all on one branch that can tip a cell toward life or death. Timing is all: a short stress pause saves the cell, a long one can kill it. The review covers kin in model animals, lessons from mice lacking the genes, and cases in human patients. It also weighs drugs that touch the pair. The topic matters for diseases where cell stress runs long.
pmc-10744259:
Yu-Jen Pan and co-authors tracked low-cost blood count ratios in arthritis patients taking newer, stronger drugs, in a study published in 2023. Standard blood markers of joint disease can read normal even when joints are inflamed, so ratio markers from plain blood counts draw interest. The team read records for 273 patients on the newer drug types and tracked their laboratory results for at least a year.

Four ratio markers fell after treatment began. High starting scores on two of them matched a bigger drop in a classic inflammation marker at three months. Two ratios tracked that marker fairly well at the three-month reading. The links shifted over time, and the shift split by drug type: two classes showed it, and one did not. The authors present the ratios as handy day-to-day gauges, to be read with care for timing and drug type.
pmc-10745359:
Dippong, Toloman, Lazar, and Petean made and tested these nanoparticles in twenty twenty-three. The particles are nickel ferrite, a magnetic oxide, partly swapped with the element lanthanum. They sit inside a silica glass matrix. The team baked the material at three temperatures and checked its structure and surface with standard tools.

All samples formed a single clean crystal phase. Adding lanthanum shrank the crystals, while heat grew them back. The powders had fine pores of even size throughout. Under visible light, the materials broke down a pink dye used as a test pollutant. More lanthanum improved that cleaning action. The authors suggest the powders could help treat dirty water.
pmc-10746559:
Xin Chen leads a seven-author team simulating how ultrasonic polishing accelerates abrasive particles, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Such methods polish engineering ceramics, no matter how hard the material is. Sound-driven vibration and cavitation bubbles both push the abrasive grains that do the cutting. The team asks how the two work as one.

Past work treated each effect on its own, in separate media. The contact zone in real polishing mixes abrasive, workpiece, vibration, and cavitation all at once. The team built a unified numerical model of that zone. It brings in free abrasive velocity and fixed abrasive indentation depth across scales. Contact theory from Hertz and the Greenwood-Williamson model backs the mechanics at its base. The run makes clear how the joint push of vibration and cavitation speeds the abrasives up.
pmc-10747359:
Alfredo Ambrosone and co-authors review tiny sacs shed by plant cells and what they carry, in a paper from 2023. Like animal cells, plant cells release membrane sacs loaded with proteins, RNA, fats, and other compounds. Pulling the sacs from whole plants is hard, so labs grow plant cells in dishes to harvest them. Those cultures include pollen, root, and single-cell lines.

The review gathers what is known about the cargo and jobs of plant sacs. They seem to aid growth, wall building, and talks between cells. They may also help plants fight off fungi, viruses, and bacteria. The field is young, and many roles are still guesses. The authors map the open questions and the lab sources used so far. Uses in farming and disease control may follow.
pmc-10747459:
Gao and three co-authors teach mixed robot teams to spot a place from far-off views in this twenty twenty-three paper. Two cams in one team must agree where they are to work as one crew. Looks-based tools fail when the view gap grows too wide for shared marks.

Inside, their tool draws a mark web from the shape links among known sights, not just their looks. That web holds firm when the view swings wide from one cam to the next. Real-world tests ran the tool live and beat top tools on both build and match speed. Place calls were best in class at low-to-mid catch rates in hard view tests. Pose error fell by a wide share next to looks tools.
pmc-10748059:
Revtovich and colleagues test in twenty twenty-three new ways to kill Candida, a yeast that causes mouth, blood, and deep-body infections. Drug resistance in this yeast is rising, so new treatments are needed. The team studied sulfur compounds of the kind found in garlic-like plants, both made in a lab and made on the spot by an enzyme system.

The enzyme system made the active compounds fast and in good amounts. In lab tests it killed the yeast at lower doses than the lab-made compounds alone. Mixed with standard antifungal drugs, the preparations added to each other's effect rather than cancelling out. The authors propose the system for targeted delivery, such as coatings on medical implants.
pmc-10750059:
Astuti and five co-authors shone infrared light on catfish in this study from twenty twenty-three. Siamese catfish breeding depends on ripe gonads, and farmers want faster maturation. The team aimed a low-power infrared diode laser at a point on the male fish tied to reproduction. Doses varied across four treatment groups, beside hormone and untreated controls.

Laser treatment changed maturity level and the gonad and liver weight indexes. The middle dose, at zero point four joules per square centimeter, performed best. Fish at that dose reached the ripest stage with the highest scores. The authors credit a light-driven boost to the maturation process. They name that dose the best setting for male broodstock.
pmc-10753459:
Liisa Korkalo, Georg Alfthan, Lourdes Fidalgo, and Riitta Freese report a study of vitamin E in teen girls in Central Mozambique, published in twenty twenty-three. The work asks how much of one form of vitamin E, called alpha-tocopherol, these girls eat, where it comes from, and how many have too little of it in their blood.

The season and whether a girl was nursing a baby were the main things linked to her levels. Mango and dark green leafy greens were key food sources in one season. The study shows low vitamin E is common in this group and points to diet and season as big factors.
pmc-10755559:
Katharina Zühlsdorff and nine co-workers took a fresh look at old test data from people with gambling or cocaine use ills. Both groups find it hard to bend when rules change. A chance based swap task gauges that bend skill in the lab. The 2023 study used math models of learn by reward on the old task data. Brain scan scores were checked next to the acts as well.

The team set 18 gamblers, 20 people with cocaine use ill, and 18 plain controls side by side. A tiered Bayes method drew out the hid learn steps behind each choice. The aim was to split the two ills by their inner steps, not just call both stiff. Split steps would point to split cures. pmc-10766959:
Minjun Son, Andrew Wang, Bijentimala Keisham, and Savaş Tay review how single cells read changing signals through the NF-κB network, in a review paper from 2023. New tools in fluid handling and image work now let labs watch single cells over time. Studies show the network sorts pulses, shifts, and mixes of signals into distinct gene responses. The review sums up those findings and models. It helps readers see how timing alone can carry meaning for a cell.
pmc-10776059:
Yuzhou Gong and co-authors sequence, in 2023, the complete mitochondrial genome of a small minnow found only on China's Hainan Island. The fish, Tanichthys flavianalis, was described only recently, and its family tree within its genus was unsettled. The team assembled and annotated the full molecule.

The genome runs about sixteen and a half thousand bases and holds the standard thirty-seven genes, with the usual fish arrangement, several overlaps, and a strong tilt toward A and T bases. Tree analyses placed the species beside another newly described relative, and confirmed that Chinese and Vietnamese members of the genus form separate branches. The sequence anchors future work on this group.
pmc-10806259:
Food emulsions, like dressings and creams, usually rely on chemical surfactants that raise health and environmental worries. Yachao Tian and co-authors review plant protein particles as a cleaner stand-in in a 2023 paper.

These particles settle at the border between oil and water and hold droplets apart, a trick called Pickering stabilization. The review explains how that holding works and how the particles are made from soy, pea, and other plant proteins. pmc-10810559: Jun-yi Zhu introduces his kidney disease research in a first-person interview from twenty twenty-three. The series profiles first authors alongside their journal papers. Zhu studies fruit flies as a model for human disease. His paper concerns a gene variant that speeds kidney cell death. People of African ancestry carry these risk variants more often. Zhu explains those findings in plain words for non-scientists.
pmc-10822959:
Alcina Nunes and four co-authors study emergency care in Portugal during the COVID-19 crisis, in work published in twenty twenty-three. Many expected hospital emergency rooms to overflow. Instead, visits fell sharply in much of the world, and the team asked what that meant for patients.

Visits dropped by up to two fifths during lockdowns, while care before hospital and some ward discharges rose. pmc-10828959:
Bridget Chalifour and co-authors link early feeding to the chemistry of infant stool, in a 2023 study. Breast milk is the standard best food for babies, yet many families mix it with formula. The team asked how that mix shapes gut chemistry and, in turn, early brain growth.

pmc-10926459:
Tonja Fisher, Joseph Munyaneza, and Judith Brown study, in a paper whose head is dated 2023, how off-ideal heat affects a potato pest and the bacterium it carries. Heat thus stresses the insect while also curbing its passenger. The work helps explain how seasons shape disease spread in the field.
pmc-11225459:
Emrah Gokay Ozgur and Sibel Balci ask whether a common fungus is a risk factor for autism in a 2023 analysis. Autism rates have risen, which sharpens interest in possible causes. Candida albicans, a yeast that lives in the gut, has been proposed as one candidate worth testing.

Children with autism showed much higher odds of testing positive for the fungus. The pooled odds were about seven times the control level. The authors present this as an association that needs care, since few studies exist and cause cannot be read from such data alone.
pmc-11532559:
Patricia Irisarri and co-authors chart the genetic range of Spanish pear collections and build a core set that keeps that range in fewer trees, in a study from 2024. Spain's pear banks guard old kinds vital for breeding, but their national picture was unknown. Seven collections sent more than twelve hundred samples for DNA checks. A shared set of markers let the teams compare across banks.

From those groups, the team built a core set of about a hundred kinds that keeps most of the variety. The core gives breeders and curators a compact, rich bank to guard and study.
pmc-11536959:
Perron and co-authors review how shared decision-making changes when patients have complex care needs, in a 2024 study. Such patients juggle several illnesses, mental health issues, and social hardship at once, and each factor shapes care choices. Shared decision-making, where patients and professionals decide together, is known to improve the quality of choices. The team searched four databases for studies from 1997 to 2023 and consulted experts on the results.

Twelve studies made the cut. Two features stood out: these patients often face several decisions at the same time, and their care spans many professions and sectors. Standard decision frameworks had to stretch to fit those facts. The authors say keeping the known benefits of shared decisions for this group means planning around both features from the start.
pmc-11538259:
Islam Bendary and five co-authors build germ-killing power into the putty dentists use for tooth impressions, in a 2024 study. Alginate impression material passes between mouths and labs, and disinfection is usually a separate, inconsistent step. Mixing the disinfectant into the material itself could close the gap.

Two recipes were tested: one with povidone-iodine, the familiar surgical antiseptic, and one with silver nanoparticles. Discs of each faced staph, Escherichia coli, and a yeast on culture plates, against a plain control. Both experimental recipes killed broadly. Mechanical testing then checked the properties dentists depend on: the material must record fine surface detail and spring back after removal, per an international standard. Elastic recovery held up. Self-disinfecting impressions could simplify infection control in every dental office.
pmc-11558659:
Aligning DNA sequences is a workhorse computation that long modern reads have made painfully slow. Peiyu Zong and co-authors speed it up in a 2024 paper with an algorithm that splits the work across processor cores and vector units at once.

The classic method fills a scoring grid cell by cell, which wastes effort on regions that cannot matter. Their trapezoidal variant narrows the computed region while leaning on thread parallelism and single-instruction tricks. It handles both pairwise alignment and the harder multiple-sequence version. The code is public, so labs can drop it into existing pipelines. Speed of this kind quietly decides how much sequencing a small team can afford to analyze.
pmc-11568259:
Hans Verbeeck and a large team argue that climate and forest models need a proper plant type for lianas, the woody vines of tropical forests. Their review was published in twenty twenty-four. Lianas strongly shape forest carbon, yet models barely represent them.

Defining one vine type is hard: species vary hugely in form and life strategy, and all lean on trees for support. The paper lists the traits a vine type must carry, from stem build to leaf habits. It then maps the key processes to model, such as climbing, shading hosts, and competing for water. Several build strategies are compared, from simple add-ons to full trait-based schemes. The authors chart a path to put vines into the models that project tropical carbon.
pmc-11572659:
Shaheera Shakeel and co-authors published a 2024 study on a kidney disease in adults treated at one center in Pakistan. Minimal change disease causes the kidneys to leak large amounts of protein into urine. It accounts for roughly a tenth to a sixth of such cases in adults. Data on its features and outcomes in Pakistani adults were thin.

The team reviewed all adults with biopsy-proven disease treated at a kidney institute between 2010 and 2020. Only twenty-three patients qualified, a sign of how uncommon the confirmed diagnosis is. Two-thirds were men, and the average age was about twenty-six. High blood pressure appeared in about three in ten. Blood in the urine, seen under a microscope, appeared in over four in ten. Kidney function at arrival was near normal on average. The paper records treatments given and how patients fared over the medium term, adding rare local data.
pmc-11579459:
Yuze Hu and co-authors report a 2024 experiment that creates a new kind of topological state for light. Topology in physics describes shapes of wave behavior that resist small disturbances. A non-Abelian version involves several wave bands at once and is richer than the standard kind. Past lab work on it in two dimensions kept time symmetry intact, which limited what could be done.
