Edge waves linked to the state changed direction with frequency, in ways the team could steer. The work opens fresh paths for guiding light in devices and for basic studies of this topology.
pmc-11583359:
John Martin and nine colleagues published a tumour methods study in two thousand twenty-four on how sample preparation skews drug transport research. Tiny drug carriers must cross tumour vessel walls to work. A recent study using chemically fixed tissue claimed cell-driven transport dominates, challenging older views.

The authors ran experiments and computer models that separate passive drift from active cell transport. They found that fixation, the chemical preserving step, cuts passive movement as well as active movement. So fixed tissue cannot cleanly show which route matters more. They call for new methods that can split the two contributions in living tissue.
pmc-11585559:
Eugene Rosenberg reviews bacteria in the human gut and their role in holobiont unity in a 2024 article. A holobiont is a host plus its microbes, acting as one unit. Gut composition has interested scientists since the dawn of microbiology, and modern methods keep expanding the known diversity.

Culture work showed hundreds of species in the colon, varying between people. Molecular methods now count thousands of species in fewer genera, so diversity concentrates at species and strain level. Rosenberg discusses how diversity can still yield unity, partly because different species can carry similar functional genes.
pmc-11587659:
Sook-Young Lee and co-authors check whether an invasive crane fly at Antarctic research stations carries human gut viruses. Their 2024 study concerns a winter crane fly that recently reached maritime Antarctica, where isolated ecosystems are fragile. The flies gather around sewage facilities, raising the question of mechanical virus spread on their bodies.

The team washed and ground flies from habitats and sewage plants at three stations, then applied sequencing, targeted tests, and culture attempts. Genetic fragments of a human adenovirus and of a dormant human retrovirus turned up in fly samples. Both viruses are common in human feces. Plant virus fragments appeared as well. pmc-11587759:
Min Kyu Kang led a large team testing an infection marker in severe alcoholic hepatitis in a 2024 study. This liver disease kills a large share of patients within a month, and bacterial infection worsens the outlook but is hard to spot fast. They compared two blood markers at admission across ten medical centers, checking which better flagged infection, a body-wide response, and sepsis.

Patients with infection had higher severity scores and higher levels of both markers. The newer marker scored somewhat better than the standard one for infection and clearly better for sepsis, though the infection gap was not firm. The authors see a trend favoring the newer marker for early detection.
pmc-11590259:
Muhammad Abdul Qadeer and co-authors pool the evidence on a hard surgical choice: which kind of artificial valve to use when the heart's tricuspid valve must be replaced. Mechanical valves last but can clot; tissue valves are gentler but wear out. Replacement itself is risky, since patients often carry complex illness.

pmc-11595459:
Hardfacing lays a wear-resistant metal skin on machine parts, and knowing how fast the metal builds up guides the whole job. They vary how fast the wire feeds and how far it sticks out, using a planned three-level test design.

Across their settings, the build-up rate ran from about 4.3 to 11.3 kilograms per hour. Wire feed speed and stick-out length both mattered strongly, along with the square of feed speed. pmc-11596059:
Baba and a large team of co-authors studied heart transplant patients in this paper from twenty twenty-four. A transplant is the best hope for end-stage heart failure, but early complications remain a threat. The team asked whether long-term heart drugs taken before surgery shape outcomes after it. Records covered fifty patients treated in Romania between twenty eleven and twenty twenty-three.

One drug, carvedilol, linked to lower death rates in the first two months. It also guarded against early kidney injury. Two other drugs tied to shorter hospital stays, and one of them to shorter intensive care time. One drug class raised the odds of graft trouble, while another lowered them. The authors urge larger prospective studies to confirm the links.
pmc-11598059:
Yang Meng, Yanping Jiang, Yuhui Chen, and Jiangyu Zhang study how wood traps heat-storing materials in its tiny pores, in a paper from 2024. These materials soak up heat as they melt and give it back as they harden. Wood is cheap, renewable, and full of fine channels that can hold them. The team used balsa wood stripped of its glue-like lignin, leaving pores just nanometers wide. They loaded the wood with several organic heat-storing compounds. Each one behaved in its own way, shaped by its chemical groups and chain length. Bonds with the wood walls and the tight space slowed the trapped molecules. Effects grew stronger from one compound to the next, and computer checks backed the pattern. The work guides better wood-based heat storage.
pmc-11598759:
Kun-Hsien Tsai and co-authors pilot, in 2024, wastewater monitoring for rodent-borne diseases in Taiwan. Sewage testing can warn of infections circulating nearby. The authors present the work as a One Health proof of concept for early warning.
pmc-11599159:

pmc-11599759:
Shuai Yan, Lijun Han, Lingdong Meng, and Weisheng Zhao wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It cooks up artificial Cretaceous mudstone in the lab, matching the natural rock's clay recipe, so engineers can study why the real thing crumbles in wet coal mine tunnels.

Their property ranges overlapped the natural rock's noticeably, validating the stand-in. Sensitivity analysis ranked which ingredients steer the imitation's behavior most. pmc-11601059:

The study maps each enzyme's share in the parasite's inner logistics.
pmc-11605659:

pmc-11608259:

pmc-11608459:

pmc-11610059:

pmc-11612159:

pmc-11612859:

pmc-11616359:

pmc-11617559:

pmc-11617759:

Their computer analysis points to one clear message: treatment remains the remedy for safe water. The model gives water managers a way to test control plans on paper before acting. It also shows how the two pollutant forms trade off against each other over time.
pmc-11617859:

The authors use the gap to argue for better training, since most patients meet the generalists first. Referral habits and treatment choices were surveyed alongside.
pmc-11618859:

pmc-11619459:
Amal Khalaf Alghamdi, Sabiha Parween, Heribert Hirt, and Maged Saad explore the microbes living with a salt-loving mangrove, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. pmc-11621859:

pmc-11622459:

Few shared-decision steps showed in the joint meetings. Comfort-care staff pushed hardest for patient voice and for clear word on each option's gains and harms. True patient say stayed rare in daily work. Stops to cancer care hinged more on body signs of the end than on shared choice.
pmc-11623259:

Trend math measured whether yearly case counts rose or fell in steady runs. Map methods checked whether high-case areas clustered next to each other. pmc-11624259:

pmc-11626459:

pmc-11627159:

pmc-11627559:

pmc-11628959:

pmc-11631259:

pmc-11632959:

pmc-11635159:

pmc-11635559:

pmc-11636259:

pmc-11637259:

pmc-11638559:

pmc-11640959:
Tshiembe Masibigiri and co-authors listen to women describe maternity care at a hospital in South Africa's Limpopo province, in this 2024 study. pmc-11641259:

The liver is a chief site where beta-carotene gets worked and acts. Pups of dams fed a West-style diet got the part or a sham. Doses ran each day through the suck span of pup life. New-weaned pups gave size marks and liver mark pools.

Dams' pups of the she sex showed the more wide mark shift. Aim reads flagged growth, clock, and sugar paths in the marks. Those paths split by sex in the aim reads as well.
pmc-11642559:
Magdalena Zemelka-Wiacek reviews 2024 work on sealed rooms that expose people to allergens in a set, controlled way. Illness from airborne allergens, such as hay fever and eye swelling, grows more common and strains care systems. pmc-11643459:

The authors urge tighter standards and greener materials that cost less to make.
pmc-11644559:

pmc-11644859: María-Luz Couce and Isidro Vitoria review the nutritional care of patients with inborn errors of metabolism in a 2024 article. These are a large family of single-gene disorders in which a faulty enzyme breaks a chemical pathway in the body. For many of them, careful control of diet is a core part of treatment, since the wrong food load can push a blocked pathway into crisis. The review covers how feeding is managed across this group of conditions.
pmc-11645459:
Jia Li and colleagues review nanomedicine for stopping acute kidney injury becoming chronic. Their review from twenty twenty-four maps a dangerous disease transition. Sudden kidney injury greatly raises later chronic disease risk. The pathways between the two stages are complex and untreated.

pmc-11646159:
Daniel McWilliams, Rohid Zamani, and Sameer Limaye audit in 2024 how well stroke wards use devices that prevent blood clots. Squeeze devices and small stimulators lower clot risk only if they are on the patient and running. The team checked beds on a Leeds stroke unit across three days.

pmc-11647059:
Kirsten Lynch, Courtney Voelker, and three co-authors chart how the hearing pathway matures from infancy to teen years. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, uses diffusion MRI fiber tracking. pmc-11647259:

pmc-11647359:

pmc-11648159:

pmc-11650859:

pmc-11651659:

pmc-11652659:

pmc-11653159:

pmc-11654959:

pmc-11665459:

pmc-11666659:

pmc-11671259:

pmc-11673159:

pmc-11674259:

pmc-11674659:

pmc-11674959:

pmc-11675259:

The work lays groundwork for the use of melatonin to improve bull fertility.
pmc-11675659:
Yingjun Zhou and co-authors compare three probiotic strains in fermented hempseed milk. Their 2024 study works with a plant-based milk made from hemp seeds. Each strain was used alone to ferment the milk, and the team compared the results for health traits and flavor.

Adding probiotics raised the drink's power to block two enzymes tied to sugar and fat uptake. A broad chemical analysis tied that power to a set of substances, including plant compounds, amino acids, and short peptides. Dozens of flavor compounds were also found, from aldehydes to esters. Each strain left a distinct flavor and function profile. The work guides makers who want a hempseed drink with a chosen taste and added health value.
pmc-11676059:
Rayan Sabra, Daniel Kirby, Vikram Chouk, and a wider team wrote this review paper, published in 2024. It looks at giving drugs through the inside of the cheek, focusing on a class of drugs that dissolve well in water but pass poorly through body tissues.

Drugs in this class are hard to get into the blood, so new delivery tricks matter. The review walks through several of them. Some chemicals loosen tissue barriers. Sticky polymers hold a dose in place. Other tricks tweak acidity, pair drugs with carrier molecules, or use prodrugs that change form in the body. For each trick, the authors explain how it should raise absorption. They argue that pairing these tricks with standard cheek dosage forms could lift how much drug reaches the blood.
pmc-11676159:
Alessandro Bonis and a large team ask whether blood cell patterns mirror immune activity inside lung tumors that were worse than scans suggested. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The tumor's immune setting reflects T cell action, and immune cells travel to the tumor through blood.

The single-center review covered Padua patients from twenty sixteen to twenty twenty-four whose small-looking lung adenocarcinomas were upstaged after removal. Tumors were classed as immune-active when they held infiltrating lymphocytes or a key immune marker, and silent otherwise. Blood counts taken around surgery were compared between the groups. A blood signature of the inner state would help judge risk without extra tissue tests. The study explores that cheap window.
pmc-11676659:
Antonio Lo Casto and co-authors present a case series on odd nasal masses in a 2024 paper. Lumps inside the nose and sinuses can spring from many causes. Some are harmless, others are cancers, and telling them apart is hard. Scans carry much of the early sorting work.

The review walks through cases imaged by CT and MRI. Plain stones and stray teeth appear among the non tumor cases. Benign growths range from blood vessel tangles to bone lumps. Cancers covered include gland tumors, nerve cell tumors, and lymphomas. Each entry pairs images with the traits that hint at its kind. Tissue study still settles the final call, the authors stress. Their survey helps radiologists narrow the field faster.
pmc-11676959:
Timo Meus and co-authors published a 2024 pilot trial of hard exercise training delivered by video link for people with lasting low back pain. High-intensity training can improve fitness and cut disability in this group. Keeping the gains after a clinic program ends is the hard part. A home program guided from afar could help patients stick with it.

Fifteen people joined the six-week trial. The first four sessions ran at a research center. The last eight ran at home through an exercise platform, with twelve sessions in all. Fourteen people finished with no harmful events. Fitness, pain-related measures, motivation, and ease of use were checked before, during, and after the program. Motivation stayed high throughout. The authors treat the trial as a feasibility test: the home-based format worked in practice. A larger trial would be needed to prove how well it eases pain and disability.
pmc-11677159: Xinghuan Chen and four co-authors wrote this 2024 editorial opening a special issue on semiconductor materials, devices, and systems. The editors note that the field is shifting as the limits of Moore's law come into view. The hosted text gives only the opening lines, so the issue's full contents cannot be judged from it.
pmc-11677359:
Besart Jashari and co-authors survey a food-poisoning germ found in foods sold in Kosovo, in a study from 2024. The germ, Listeria monocytogenes, can spread through the food chain and resist drugs. The team wanted to know which types of the germ circulate in Kosovo and how they respond to antibiotics.

The team typed 114 samples with a method that reads several genes, and found 21 types. One type group was most common in meat goods, and another led in dairy goods. Tests against 18 antibiotics showed the most resistance to a few named drugs, led by levofloxacin. Many samples resisted three or more drugs at once. The authors call for wider and ongoing checks to protect food safety and public health.
pmc-11677559:
Beatriz Carrion-Ruiz and co-authors teach dental first aid to nursing students in a 2024 study. Knocked and broken teeth need fast, correct handling, and nurses are often first on scene. Three hundred students at two Seville universities took a pre-test, then a dentist-led session. The class paired a lecture with hands-on splinting practice.

Only a quarter of students had any prior training in dental trauma. After the session, self-rated knowledge rose clearly. Confidence in replanting a tooth jumped as well. Average scores improved by a firm statistical margin. Students had begun with thin knowledge but a willing attitude. The authors argue dental trauma training belongs in nursing curricula. Better first aid at the bedside, they say, saves teeth and improves outcomes.
pmc-11678159:
Rosa Cárdaba-García and co-authors review breast ironing, a harmful practice applied to girls, through the lens of a nursing theory, in a 2024 paper. In parts of Cameroon and elsewhere, heated objects are pressed on developing breasts to slow their growth. Families believe it shields girls from abuse, early pregnancy, and forced marriage.

The harms are severe: gland damage, pain, infection, and lasting health risk. A transcultural nursing frame urges respect for local custom in care. The authors ask whether respect can stretch to cover a practice that violates bodily integrity. Their verdict puts human rights first, with education campaigns and stronger penalties proposed.
pmc-11678259:
Maria N. Romanenko and colleagues published a 2024 genome study of a soil bacterium from Dagestan, Russia. Farmers seek bacteria that protect crops without pesticides. The new strain was isolated from local soil. Its full genome was sequenced and analyzed. Computer tools searched for useful and harmful genes.

The genome held many clusters for making antimicrobial compounds. Some predicted products kill bacteria or fungi. Other loci resembled insect-killing toxin genes. No genes for human gut toxins were found. That absence supports safety in farm use. Mobile DNA elements suggested an adaptable genome. Field trials would be the next step.
pmc-11678759:
Dawei Shi, Lejia Zhao, Ruijia Zhang, and Qiaofeng Song review what is known about melatonin in plants. Melatonin is a natural chemical found in many living things. In plants it touches growth, seeding, and the making of fruit. It also helps plants cope with stress such as drought, salt, cold, and disease.

The review covers how plants make melatonin and how it links with other plant hormones. The authors note open questions in the field and suggest ways to solve them. They argue the chemical could help raise crop yields in a lasting way.
pmc-11678959:
Masoud Nateghi and co-authors build a way to read brain waves for automatic sleep staging. Knowing sleep stages is key to diagnosing sleep disorders and judging health. Cheap brain monitors now pour out data, yet scoring full multi-lead EEG by hand stays slow and costly. A core need is to catch the shifts between waking and sleep, which reveal sleep quality.

The team tracks the brain signal with a model that changes over time. A Kalman filter, built to shrug off noise, follows the model's shifts through the night. From it they draw features such as the signal's moment-to-moment frequency and power. These feed a classifier that sorts wake and sleep stages. If a compact set of tracked features can stage sleep well, cheap home devices could do work that now needs a lab and expert scoring.
pmc-11679459:
Sabina Umirzakova and co-authors present a 2024 paper on a captioning system for images and video that remembers what it has seen. Good captions need context: a video caption should flow from the frames before it. Noise in training data and the demand for live output make that hard.

Their framework has three parts. A cross modal memory bank stores prior frames and text, and retrieves what fits the current moment. A pruning step filters noisy training pairs so the model learns cleaner alignments. A streaming decoder writes captions piece by piece, enabling real time use. Tests on standard benchmarks put the system at the front of the field, the authors report.
pmc-11679759:
Pedro Lopez and three co-authors build a phone app that spots roof hazards in underground mines. Their 2024 paper presents HUMApp for geotechnical safety. Mining is among the most dangerous jobs, and falling roofs lead the risks. Early spotting of weak ground can prevent deadly collapses.

A convolutional neural network reads mine photos for danger signs. The app scored about ninety percent accuracy in tests. Recall and overall balance matched that mark. Expert judgments agreed strongly with the app's calls. The paper walks through data prep, training, scoring, and app design. The same recipe could adapt to other mines and hazards. Phone-based checks put expert-like eyes in every crew's pocket.
pmc-11680059:
Ziba Arjmandzadeh and co-authors present a path planning method in two thousand twenty-four for self-driving cars based on Lyapunov optimization. Choosing a safe, smooth local path is central to full autonomy, but strong planners can be slow. The team tested their method against model predictive control and a sampling-based planner.

A prototype vehicle gathered real driving data in Norman, Oklahoma, using cameras alone for object detection and bird's-eye coordinates. Each of the three planners then drew paths from the same data. The Lyapunov approach produced safe, smooth paths with at least twenty times less computation than the baselines. The authors argue the speed gain suits real-world deployment where cost and reaction time matter. Vision-only sensing kept the setup cheap and practical.
pmc-11680159:
Four authors present a study in two thousand twenty-four on filling the socket left after pulling a dog's tooth. Filling the socket with a bone-like mineral material is growing common in veterinary dentistry. Roots differ by the dog's size, yet reference data on root size and socket volume were missing.

The team measured root length and socket volume for front teeth and canines, upper and lower, across four weight bands from the smallest dogs to those over twenty kilograms. Length and volume tracked together within each band. They then reviewed commercial filler products and built a table for computing how much material a given socket needs.
pmc-11681859:
Stella Oberle and three colleagues published an energy policy study in two thousand twenty-four on Germany's gas distribution networks as demand shrinks. Climate pathways show gas use falling steeply, stranding pipes built for decades of service. Regulators already allow faster write-down of new assets, but old networks remain unresolved.

A long-term investment model tested decommissioning rules. Shortening write-down periods for existing assets is needed to avoid stranded costs, the results show. Partial shutdown, with decommissioning costs shared through network charges, proved most economical for operators and users alike. The authors say the framework must price the exit, not just the build-out.
pmc-11688759:
Seven authors present a study from two thousand twenty-four on a video game that trains health care providers. The game, called the Virtual Clinic, simulates visits with older patients. It teaches a care framework built on four themes for older adults, which front-line staff said they wanted to practice rather than just read about.

The first version was tested in two thousand twenty-one, then revised through three more pilot waves. Two hundred sixty-two providers took part in all. Their work was scored before, just after, and four weeks after playing. They were matched against similar providers who did not play, to judge whether the game lifted skill and confidence.
pmc-11689259:
Yan-Jhu Su, Elizabeth Dugan, and Jaqueline Avila study combined health behaviors and cognitive health in older adults in a 2024 paper. Smoking, drinking, and low activity each may harm thinking, and they often occur together. Their combined effect has been little studied.

Data came from a national retirement study in twenty eighteen, with more than seven thousand adults aged sixty five and older. Thinking was scored with a standard telephone test. The most common pattern was the healthy one: never smoking, no drinking, and high activity. Compared with that group, people with no activity had lower thinking scores even without smoking or drinking.
pmc-11689459:
Lillian Hung and co-authors test an AI service robot in a Canadian long-term care home in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Care staff there juggle complex needs, and a robot that serves residents could ease the load. How such robots land in real homes is still little studied.

The team placed a robot named Aether in one home and gathered staff views before and after, plus talks with residents and managers. Staff engagement and training helped the rollout. Room dynamics and tight resources hindered it. The authors say support is needed at the level of the worker, the home, and the wider system. Their findings aim to guide future robot use in care homes.
pmc-11689859:
Wei Yang, Xingtong Pei, and Mingming Xu measure whether long-term care insurance frees family carers in China to work. Their study appeared in 2024. The insurance pays for formal care, which should ease the load on relatives. Using a national aging survey across 2011 to 2018, the team compared regions as the policy rolled out at different times, matching similar households. The insurance cut spousal care time by about eight and a half hours a month.

Younger family members gained most in paid work, earning on average about 4,534 yuan more per year. Benefits concentrated among carers of low-income elders and those from farming or informal work. The authors urge extending the scheme to more regions and widening who it covers.
pmc-11690859:
Teaching doctors to care for older patients is a hard sell in crowded medical curricula. Alissa Cooney and Edmund Duthie present a 2024 symposium built on a four-part framework from geriatrics educators: stigma, speed, stealth, and sources.

Stigma tackles ageist attitudes by anchoring teaching in patient-centered care. Speed uses micro-learning, tiny focused lessons delivered through web tools and a fast-facts resource at the point of care. Stealth slips geriatric principles into courses owned by other specialties, using cases those learners already care about. Sources shows how to borrow materials and allies instead of building everything alone. Veteran educators share how persistence carried these tactics past years of resistance.
pmc-11691159:
Miquela Ibrao and co-authors ask what matters most in health care to older Native Hawaiians. Their paper appeared in 2024. Health systems usually ask about end-of-life forms, which can feel cold or alien to indigenous elders. The team reanalyzed 20 interviews with Native Hawaiian elders, working with a national resource center for those elders. They coded the interviews against a standard framework and also let new themes emerge.

Three themes stood out in the part of the results shown. Elders wanted cultural traditions woven into care routines. They treated family as part of medical decision making, not as visitors. Their wishes covered daily living, home, and relationships, not only treatment at the end of life. The authors argue that care plans should start from these values rather than from forms.
pmc-11691359:
Ganbat, Byambaa, and Meneilly test in 2024 whether bedside ultrasound of thigh muscle predicts hospital stay length. Better forecasts of stay and readmission could guide resource planning. They measured quadriceps thickness and echo intensity in patients lying in the emergency department of a Vancouver hospital.

The cohort held 120 patients with mean age near 77, and mean stay was 27.4 days. Muscle thickness averaged 20 millimeters and differed by sex. Thicker muscle tied to shorter stays in correlation and in adjusted models. One month follow up tracked readmission and death. The authors close that thickness is a significant predictor of stay duration.
pmc-11692059:
Chitchanok Benjasirisan and co-authors reported this care study in 2024. Older adults with many chronic ills face heavy symptom loads and much hospital use. The COORDINATE program was built with patients, families, and staff to join up care and ease symptoms. It runs five visits over six weeks, with a needs check, prompt lists, goal talks, and symptom reviews.

Twenty-five adults, aged fifty-five and up with at least two chronic ills, joined after leaving an intermediate care unit. Most set goals were met. At three months, energy levels had risen by a clear mark. Hospital stays and critical care entries both fell against the prior three months. The group was small and mostly retired Black adults. The authors call the results a strong hint and press for a full trial.
pmc-11692459:
Retirement can drift without purpose, and purpose in later life tracks with health, memory, and longer survival. Leacey Brown and Jane Strommen describe a book club built to plant that purpose, in a 2024 program report from the two Dakota land-grant universities. The club reads and discusses its way toward a purposeful retirement plan.

Piloted in 2020 and run five times since, it has reached eighty-one adults. The report shares evaluation results and lessons from the pilots, plus a facilitator guide any community group can pick up. The authors argue universities are natural hosts for such planning help.
pmc-11692759:
Stephanie Saunders and co-authors gather the world's systematic reviews on what makes older adults who live at home more likely to fall, in a 2024 umbrella review. Falls drive disability, mental strain, and early death in later life, and the research base has grown hard to navigate. The team searched seven databases and kept 57 reviews of prospective studies of adults aged 60 and over.

Risk factors appeared under every heading of the World Health Organization's function model, from body problems to home hazards. Weak mobility and poor balance raised risk again and again. Frailty raised risk in nearly every pooled analysis. Body mass index, by contrast, showed no link in any pooled test. Reviews split their focus between repeated falls and falls that cause injury. Because effect sizes varied so widely, the authors could not merge them into single numbers.
pmc-11696659:
Sonia Molina-Pinelo and co-authors build telomere based risk models for early lung cancer diagnosis in a 2024 study. Telomeres are DNA caps that shorten with age and cell division. Their length in blood cells might flag cancer risk during screening of high risk patients.

The prospective study ran at two Spanish hospitals. Patients undergoing diagnosis gave blood, and telomeres were measured with a high throughput imaging method. Cancer patients had a higher share of short telomeres than controls with lung disease or healthy controls. A random forest model using telomere variables was tested for its ability to separate cancer from non cancer.
pmc-11697559:
Lubet and co-authors built and tested a fully 3D-printed trainer for keyhole surgery in children. Trainees need cheap ways to practice fine skills before operating. Their trainer, printed on a standard printer, costs about five euros per unit. Assembly takes ten minutes, and a phone serves as the camera. Print time was about nine hours using 434 grams of plastic.

Surgeons and trainees tried two basic tasks on the new trainer and on a standard one. Tasks were peg transfer and precision cutting, scored with a standard skill scale and timing. Users also rated how real and useful each trainer felt. The study checks whether the cheap trainer teaches as well as costly gear.
pmc-11699059:
Zixuan Li and Chengli Wang study safety oversight of escape room venues with big data tools in two thousand twenty-four. Escape rooms have boomed as a leisure form, but weak oversight has brought piracy and theme copying. The authors frame venue management through responsive regulation, where watch strength flexes with risk.

Online product data tied to venues are first turned into a network of links. A clustering method then splits that network into groups by a set distance rule. The team also tunes and tests a fault-tolerant agreement algorithm used to keep network records in sync. At one distance setting, the tuned algorithm performed at its best, which the authors say lifts security for venue platforms.
pmc-11704859:
Yunsu Choi and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on people living with HIV in South Korea. The state cuts medical costs for these patients, but the size of the cut depends on how each patient registers and pays. The team used national insurance data to see who uses the system and who is missed.

They analyzed claims from 2002 to 2021 and selected about twenty-two thousand people for close study. Insurance data showed a lower share of women than official disease reports did. Women also registered for the cost relief at notably low rates. Counting patients through billing data, not just case reports, gives a fuller picture of the epidemic and of gaps in support.
pmc-11709559:
Brijendra Singh and five co-authors test a way to lower a blood protein called complement C3 in mice bred to build up amyloid in the brain. Their paper came out in twenty twenty-five. Past work found that mice born without C3 kept better thought and brain links with age, and this study asks if lowering C3 in adult mice helps too.

Treated mice had much less C3 in blood and brain. They did better on maze and object tests than mice given oil alone. Brain scans showed no change in total amyloid, but treated mice had less swelling near plaques and stronger links in one brain area. The team reads this as help for thought and brain links.
pmc-11709659:
Dayalan Sampath and co-authors study lasting thinking loss after stroke in female rats and a treatment that may blunt it, in a research paper from 2025. Stroke can wear down white matter and memory areas far from the blocked vessel, a process called secondary degeneration. The team tested a small RNA molecule, mir20a-3p, given after stroke.

Middle-aged female rats had a blocked brain artery, then got the RNA or a scrambled control at set times. Memory tests ran for up to 100 days, and brain scans and tissue stains followed. Untreated stroke rats lost volume in key white matter tracts and showed swollen ventricles, signs of cell loss. Treated rats kept those volumes even, and their memory held up better.
pmc-11709959:
Min Zhu and co-authors test whether a gene variant and high blood pressure together batter the aging brain more than either alone, in a 2025 study from China. The gene, CD33, steers immune activity and has been tied to thinking decline. Blood pressure strain is the other suspect. Their combined effect on thought, brain shrinkage, and blood flow had not been mapped in a general population.

The study drew 4,444 dementia-free adults aged sixty-five and older from the MIND-China project. Of these, 1,047 had brain volume scans and 85 had blood flow measures. Among people with one form of the gene, a history of high blood pressure, wide pulse pressure, or late-life hypertension linked with worse outcomes. The authors also traced paths among the factors, asking whether blood flow and shrinkage carry the harm from pressure and genes to thought.
pmc-11710759:
Junyi Liang and co-authors report a 2025 computer search for partners of variant forms of the TREM2 protein. TREM2 is one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease. The protein helps brain immune cells clear amyloid and switch on. It comes in three forms made by alternative splicing of its gene. Known partners include the amyloid protein itself and a carrier protein. Little is known about what each spliced form binds to.

The study predicts binding partners for all three forms by computer methods. It builds on the one known case where a partner protein is marked for disposal through this contact. Finding form-specific partners could explain why the variants matter for disease. The work is computational, a search for leads rather than lab proof. Those leads can guide bench tests on brain immune cells. The authors frame the results as a map for follow-up studies.
pmc-11712359:
Pranav Mishra and co-authors study the hormone estradiol in cell cultures in a 2025 report on Alzheimer's disease. Levels of this hormone fall with age, and its loss tracks higher disease risk. The hormone is known to guard nerve cells, calm inflammation, and support their power units. The team tested it on mouse cortical neurons grown in dishes.

The cultures were over ninety percent pure neurons. Estradiol raised two proteins that sense energy and build new power units. The treated cells also made more ATP, the cell fuel, and held more spare breathing capacity. A key inflammation switch stayed quieter under the hormone. Next, the team plans to challenge the cells with amyloid to test protection under disease-like stress.
pmc-11712459:
Ralph Kern and co-authors re-analyze a device trial in a 2025 report on Alzheimer's treatment effects. The OVERTURE trial tested a non-invasive home device, used one hour a day for six months, against a sham device. The new analysis asks how much time the active treatment saved, using combined scores of daily function and thinking.

Seventy-four people took part and fifty-three finished the trial, with no serious treatment-linked harms. The active group declined less on daily function and memory scores than the sham group. Converted to time, the gains equaled roughly four to five months saved over the six-month trial. The authors say a larger trial now under way will test the device further.
pmc-11712559:
Miray Budak and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on two gene variants tied to Alzheimer's disease risk in older African Americans. One variant is the well-known APOE risk form. The other sits in a gene called ABCA7 and matters most in this group. The team asked how each one affects a memory hub deep in the brain.

They scanned 175 older adults whose thinking was still sound and measured how flexibly that hub linked with other brain areas. Carriers of the ABCA7 risk form showed less flexible links than carriers of the APOE form. The finding hints that the two variants harm the brain in unlike ways. That split could shape how future treatments are aimed.
pmc-11712659:
Youssef Abd El-Satar and co-authors propose that wrecked body clocks at work may raise the risk of Alzheimer's disease in this 2025 hypothesis paper. Night and rotating shifts scramble the daily rhythm that light normally sets. Sleep and rhythm problems are known symptoms of Alzheimer's; the authors ask whether they can also be a cause.

Their chain runs through dopamine. Brain studies show the chemical messenger's firing peaks in the morning and early night and sags midday, so rhythm sets its daily tide. Alzheimer's patients run low on dopamine, and the messenger is tied to the disease's onset and course. Scrambling the rhythm through shift work could thus drag dopamine down over years. The authors present the idea as a testable hypothesis, calling for studies that follow shift workers and their brain health directly.
pmc-11713859:
Varinder Singh, Manjinder Singh, and Richa Shri test a plant compound in mice in a 2025 study. The compound is a flavone, a natural substance found in herbal drugs. Lead exposure harms memory, so the team used lead to model memory loss. They ask whether the compound protects the brain through more than one path, not just the usual signal-based route.

Mice got lead each day for twenty-eight days, and some also got the compound an hour before. The treated mice did better in a water maze test of memory. Their brains showed less of a memory-blocking enzyme and less amyloid buildup. Levels of a protective protein and its helper proteins also rose, which points to a defense switch being turned on.
pmc-11715059:
Maura Malpetti and co-authors linked blood signs of swelling to brain swelling across the Alzheimer's disease span. Swelling in the brain starts early in the disease and may speed decline. Drug trials that aim at swelling need signs they can track in the living brain and blood. The team paired blood samples with a scan that lights up active guard cells in the brain.

The sample held healthy adults and patients with mild thought loss or the full disease. A stats tool sorted thirty blood swelling signs into two broad themes. Both themes were rich in signs that drive swelling on. One theme ran higher in the disease group than in the other two groups. That theme also rose in step with the brain scan across wide zones. The blood theme may thus mirror swelling in the brain itself.
pmc-11715259:
Lucas Uglione Da Ros and co-authors study high blood pressure in late life and memory loss in a 2025 paper. Midlife high pressure is a known risk for Alzheimer disease. Whether late life pressure also matters, and how it interacts with amyloid protein buildup, was less clear.

The team followed hundreds of older adults without impairment at the start, using brain related fluid markers and thinking tests over up to six years. Findings were checked in a second cohort with brain scans for amyloid. The work tests whether pressure and amyloid together speed memory decline more than either alone.
pmc-11715359:
Mahsa Dadar and Olivier Parent asked whether scan tools can sort out what makes white spots in the aging brain. The spots, bright on some scans, grow common with age and with Alzheimer's disease. Under the lens they can mean lost nerve wrap, lost fibers, or swelling, in mixed degrees. The cause may differ by place: front spots lean toward vessel harm, back spots toward the disease itself.

New scan ways can read iron, nerve wrap, fiber health, and water in each spot while a person lives. The pair used two such ways on data from a huge UK health bank. They set spots near the brain's core, at the front, and at the back side by side. The plan is to give each kind of spot a clear profile, which could help judge new drugs that carry risks for vessel-weak brains.
pmc-11715459:
Safiyyah Okoye and Laura Gitlin describe the homes of older Americans with cognitive impairment, split by whether they live alone, with a spouse, or with others, in a 2025 study. Home is where daily life happens, and safety there guides care, yet basic facts about these households were scarce. Their data come from a national survey of 968 community-living older adults.

About 26 percent lived alone, 46 percent with a spouse, and 28 percent with others. The survey recorded building type, owning versus renting, home modifications, and subsidized housing. Interviewers also noted disorder and disrepair inside the home and on the street. The paper sets out how housing differs across the three living setups.
pmc-11715559:
Shusaku Hosono and co-authors measured neck movement directly in patients with atopic dermatitis and related it to their sleep problems, in a 2024 study. Poor sleep is common and distressing in this skin disease, and stiff neck movement had been suspected as one factor, though earlier work leaned on self-reports. The team enrolled 261 adults with the disease.

Neck range of motion was read from bending X-rays by an automatic system. Sleep disturbance and itch were scored on rating scales, and blood tests covered allergy and inflammation markers. Comparing groups, the authors explored how measured stiffness lines up with broken sleep and with the lab values.
pmc-11715959:
Lasya P Sreepada and five co-authors ask whether how old a person's body seems, measured from chemical marks on DNA, predicts unusual patterns of Alzheimer's damage, in this 2025 study. Odd presentations of the disease, with more damage in outer brain regions than in memory centers, usually start younger. The team wondered if biological age explains the pattern better than age in years.

Data came from 646 people in a national study who gave blood samples and brain scans. The authors computed an epigenetic age from the blood and flagged people aging faster or slower than their years. Patients with memory problems or disease showed thinner cortex than controls. Early results link faster biological aging with the atypical damage pattern. The work may help explain why the disease looks different in different people.
pmc-11716559:
Lukai Zheng and co-authors published a study in 2025 on whether inherited tendency toward white matter damage speeds up Alzheimer's proteins. Bright white matter spots are common in the disease, but whether they drive amyloid and tau growth is debated. Using genes as a stand-in for lifelong tendency avoids many traps of plain observation.

The team built a genetic score from a huge British study and applied it to more than six hundred adults in a national cohort. The score did predict more white matter damage, as expected. It did not, however, predict faster amyloid or tau growth on brain scans. That null result argues the spots accompany the disease rather than feed its core proteins.
pmc-11716859:
Diana Guzmán and fourteen co-authors published a study in 2025 on moderate drinking, the brain, and thinking in middle age. Past work has hinted that moderate drinking might help the brain, but results have been mixed. The team asked whether any link runs through brain shrinkage or damage to small blood vessels, and whether it differs by race, ethnicity, and sex.

They studied 451 adults in northern Manhattan with brain scans and thinking tests. In one group, Latinx men, more moderate drinking went with a thinner cortex and a smaller memory center. The mixed pattern warns against simple claims that moderate drinking protects the brain. Results split by group like these can guide health advice that fits local drinking patterns.
pmc-11716959:
Isaac Llorente Saguer and co-authors work, in a 2025 study, with lab-grown cells from families who carry inherited Alzheimer's disease. Gene changes in these families lead to longer, stickier forms of the amyloid protein, and people fall ill at different ages.

The team measured five forms of the protein in cell models, mixing their own data with published results. The simple ratio of two forms has long been used to sort patients and guess age of onset, but recent work doubts it. They tested mixes of the forms instead. Better mixes could sharpen diagnosis and help predict when symptoms may start for each gene change.
pmc-11727759:
Bales of loose fibers, from plant scraps to glass strands, do not flow like sand. Peng Wang, Jiawei Han, Siyuan Wang, and Yu Guo review in 2024 how such crowds behave when pressed, sheared, or blown through pipes. Fibers lock arms, clump, and let go in small slides, and they soak up push far faster than round grains. Rules built for sand and powders miss most of that.

The review sorts what is known about squeeze, drag flow, and air-blown flow of fiber crowds. Gaps stand out: no shared math yet bends to cover the lock and spring of long soft parts. The team sketch where new theory and shop craft might meet. Their call is for models born from fibers, not borrowed from grains. The catalog adds a fifth name the head byline lacks.
pmc-11728559:
Yichen Liu, Sunan Xu, Xuemei Li, and Lihong Zhang study how connected shoots help a clonal grass bear toxic stress, in two thousand twenty-four. Clonal plants can share resources between their linked shoots, which may aid shoots in poisoned patches. The team tested lead, a tar-like pollutant, and both together, with the links between shoots cut or intact.

Linked shoots kept up far better photosynthesis under each stress. Their light-use measures rose, water loss control shifted, and cell damage fell. Protective enzyme activity also held up better, and growth suffered less. The mixed stress weakened the benefit of linkage, showing a joint effect of the two pollutants. The study supports linkage as a survival tool.
pmc-11736359:
Edwin Muyulema and co-authors measured how common leptospirosis is in breeding-age female cattle in the Ecuadorian Amazon, in a 2024 study. The bacterial disease spreads to people and harms ruminant reproduction, yet parts of its pattern were unclarified. The team studied 213 cattle in the province of Zamora Chinchipe.

A standard clumping test checked for eight bacterial variants across two species. About 12 percent of the animals tested positive. A farm survey hunted risk factors by animal and herd, and blood work compared positive and negative animals on red cell, protein, and kidney measures. The results give a baseline for control in the region.
pmc-11740259:
Ketan Vagholkar and nine co-authors ran a clinical trial in two thousand twenty-four on healing diabetic foot ulcers. Such ulcers heal slowly because of poor blood flow, nerve damage, and infection. Growth factors can help by driving cell growth, movement, and new blood vessels.

Fifty-two adults with mild to moderate ulcers were split at random into two groups. One group got standard care plus a concentrate of their own growth factors, made with a therapy kit. The other got standard care alone, over seventy days. The main outcome was healthy granulation tissue over at least three quarters of the ulcer. Other outcomes included full closure, shrinkage of the ulcer, and safety events. Final efficacy analysis covered forty-nine patients.
pmc-11770359:
Fatih Uzer and co-authors study mood after COVID-19 in a paper published in 2024; the catalog lists 2025, but the journal record in the text gives 2024. Patients who left one Turkish hospital after the illness were checked for low mood, worry, and trauma stress. The checks came at least a month after discharge. The team looked for traits that lined up with worse scores.

In all, 215 patients took part, and most were men in their fifties. People who still had breathing trouble scored worse on every scale. Married patients scored lower on worry and sadness than single ones. Older patients reported slightly less trauma stress. The results argue for mood checks as part of follow-up care after severe infection.
pmc-11770859:
Puja Das and Suresh Jungari synthesize twenty years of Indian research on menstrual disorders, in a review from two thousand twenty-five. Menstrual problems feed into the wider burden of chronic disease. Yet no review had pulled India's evidence into one whole till now, across prevalence, risk factors, and care-seeking.

The pair followed systematic review guidelines. They searched five databases for studies from two thousand to twenty twenty-two and appraised the quality of what they found. Reported prevalence of any menstrual disorder ran from three to eighty-seven percent across the studies. Painful periods led the specific disorders. Wide spans like that point to inconsistent definitions and methods nationwide. The work gives policymakers a baseline and researchers a case for standardized measurement in Indian women's health.
pmc-11790559:
Boukaré Bonkoungou and a team of co-authors tell how online learning reshaped health worker training in Africa, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. COVID-19 travel limits pushed the WHO Africa office to team with Project ECHO for virtual teaching. From twenty twenty to twenty twenty-four they ran 287 sessions.

Attendance topped one hundred twenty-five thousand from 173 countries and regions. Before the shift, in-person training reached under two thousand people a year. Nearly all survey replies called the sessions useful for their work. Self-rated knowledge jumped from twenty-eight to seventy-four percent after sessions.
pmc-11792159:
Marottoli and four co-authors reported in twenty twenty-four on two man-made germs used to carry genes into the brain. The germs, named BR1 and BI30, are meant to reach the cells that line brain blood tubes. Such cells help keep the brain in balance.

The team gave each germ, with a glow tag, to mice through a vein and then checked where it went. BR1 reached brain nerve cells and wall cells, plus lung and liver. BI30 reached brain wall cells and some outer tissue. Their point is plain: labs should pick the germ that fits the task at hand.
pmc-11799559:
Shoji Taniguchi and ten co-authors present a rice study published in 2024, though the catalog lists 2025, on drone based measures that predict plant traits. Drones can track crop growth over time with color and light band images. Height measures drawn from such images had already predicted traits like heading date in one rice group.

The team asked whether those measures hold for other rice groups and other planting methods. They used a mixed parent rice population grown under different transplanting plans. Height and a green leaf index moved in different patterns under the different plans. The paper tests how well each measure predicts final plant traits.
pmc-11803859:
Beatriz Alonso-Cortés Fradejas and five colleagues evaluate a service-learning program pairing physiotherapy students with older adults for group cane-walking in the community. The intergenerational walks ran through one academic year, supervised by faculty and senior student fellows. The mixed-methods study tracked adherence, exercise motivation questionnaires, interviews, and feedback surveys.

Older adults adhered well, with about seventy-two percent sticking to the intervention. Seniors rated the program's intergenerational value at 9.5 out of ten, and all said it improved their health and well-being. Students also rated relationship-building highly, though skill-development ratings dipped among third-years. Interview themes covered perceptions of exercise, barriers, motivations, and suggestions for improving the program.
pmc-11807959:
Emmerson de Farias led a large team studying a severe post-COVID illness in children in a 2025 paper. The syndrome inflames many body systems and can kill. At one center, dozens of critically ill children had immune and oxidative markers measured on their first and third hospital days. The team tested which markers tracked with survival, using curves and risk models.

A large share of the children had other conditions, and many did not survive. Children with high levels of one immune signal on day one died sooner on average. That signal stayed linked to death after adjustment, with a usable cutoff value. Other markers showed no such link in the reported analysis.
pmc-11815659:
Mehdi Shabani and eleven co-authors track how Omicron sub-lineages of the coronavirus changed over a year of spread in Iran, and how well the immune system's targets survived those changes. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. The team sequenced forty-nine virus genomes at high coverage in the national influenza center. Family trees sorted the strains into eight known clades plus one recombinant.

They then checked three kinds of immune targets on the virus. Targets for antibody-style B cells were conserved least across the strains. That low score signals escape from the neutralizing arm of immunity. Targets for T cells held up far better, especially outside the spike protein. The pattern suggests vaccines keep much of their T cell protection even as antibodies fade. The work guides vaccine updates for the region.
pmc-11883259:
Mehmet Karabey and co-authors compare autoantibody rates before and during the COVID pandemic in a 2024 study. Autoantibodies, immune proteins that attack the body's own tissues, may shift after widespread viral infection. The team re-analyzed autoimmune test samples from more than eighty-nine thousand people taken between January 2017 and May 2022.

Overall, about eighteen percent of tests came back positive, and women showed higher rates than men for most antibody types. Against the pre-pandemic years, a few antibody levels ran higher before the pandemic, while antinuclear antibody ran higher during it. Rates for several types also shifted year by year. The large sample gives a population baseline for judging pandemic effects on autoimmunity.
pmc-11970159:
Veremunde Nikanor, Emma Maano Nghitanwa, and Monika Nakweenda published this study in 2024. It surveys how mothers in a Namibian district practice exclusive breastfeeding. Health guidance urges breast milk only for a baby's first six months. Two hundred mothers of infants in that age band answered questionnaires at three clinics in April 2022. Despite the paper's title calling the work qualitative, the methods are a counted survey.

Most mothers, about sixty percent, scored poor on exclusive breastfeeding practice. Practice level tied to the baby's age. The authors warn that weak practice can harm infant health. They recommend stronger health education on the benefits, plus reinforcement at clinic visits. They also ask Namibia's health ministry to set a policy that actively supports exclusive breastfeeding.
pmc-12089959:
Wanxue Wang and her team weigh change in genes and in form through long lab growth of kept-cold human egg-gland flesh. Their 2025 study checks risk of gene change in a way to keep the chance to bear young safe for sick folk with tumours.

Flesh was kept cold with two guard goods, then warmed, washed, and grown for seven days in a 3D gel kit. Small-scope views and RNA reads set flesh prior to growth next to flesh at the end of growth. Math checks on the data looked at gene use, at form shifts in gene goods, and at links twixt proteins. Once growth was done, DNA and RNA checks showed rises in gene joins and in fresh cuts of gene notes. Such shifts could sway gene use and how cells work. The finds shape checks on safety prior to its use in care.
pmc-12661759:
Aastha Aastha and seven colleagues benchmarked five laboratory workflows for studying proteins in spinal fluid. Cerebrospinal fluid offers a window into brain disease, but its complexity makes unbiased protein discovery hard. The twenty twenty-five comparison used samples from nineteen patients with central nervous system lymphoma. The five methods ranged from nanoparticle enrichment to vesicle isolation. Input volumes, hands-on time, and costs differed widely among them.

Across eighty-two mass spectrometry runs, the team detected over 38,000 unique peptides and more than 3,000 proteins. The nanoparticle enrichment method achieved the deepest coverage, around 17,000 unique peptides per run scale. Vesicle and membrane-based methods followed at lower depth. The results give laboratories a practical basis for choosing a workflow matched to their sample limits and research questions.
pmc-12672159:
Andrew Ly, Evan Harnick, Tanisha Jowsey, and Amy Jean Bannatyne map what patients and clinicians say about eye shots used for retinal disease. The shots are among the most done eye steps worldwide and treat swelling and vein blocks in the retina. The review came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team searched four databases for studies that used talk based methods with adult patients. Of hundreds of finds, a small set met the rules. Most told of fear of sight loss, made worse by the need for shot after shot, which fed worry and doubt. Pain and unease varied with how the clinician gave the shot. One study told the clinician side.
pmc-12685159:
Deborah Tembo and co-authors review cholera deaths in Zambia during the outbreaks that ran from January 2023 to July 2024, in a 2025 study. Cholera can kill within hours through severe fluid loss, yet it can be both prevented and treated. The team used national case records to study how fast the disease moved and who died. They tracked the time from first symptoms to care and to death.

More than three thousand six hundred cases had full records, and about four in one hundred patients died. The middle time from symptoms to death was just three days. Death rates ran higher in men and in adults aged fifty and older. Lab tests were rare, which left a gap in tracking. The authors urge fast fluids on arrival, closer watch on high-risk groups, and wider use of quick tests.
pmc-12693959:
Benedikt Schurr and co-authors build chains of tiny light traps whose protected end modes show up in experiment, in a 2025 paper. The chain follows a classic pattern of alternating strong and weak links. Theory says such chains host special states at their ends, shielded by topology.

The traps are nanoslits in a metal film, spaced with sub nanometer care so the link strengths alternate as designed. Light emission microscopy revealed the mid gap modes sitting at the chain ends, as predicted. Shielded states at room conditions could one day couple to single light emitters and quantum matter. The team points toward flat surfaces with richer protected modes.
pmc-12699259:
Cui and co-authors make a millet rice crust boosted with Astragalus root. The root is classed as both food and medicine in China. It holds flavonoids, polysaccharides, and saponins. Millet adds protein, amino acids, and vitamins. The team tested how root dose changed crust nutrition and texture.

The boosted crust held 8.87 grams of protein per 100 grams. Ash content rose to 0.69 grams per 100 grams as well. Taste, color, and bite stayed acceptable to testers. Scans showed a sound inner structure for the new crust. Active compounds ran higher than in the plain control crust.
pmc-12700859:
Forecasting time series usually means large neural networks. It can also mean models that need many data points. Mostafizur Rahaman Laskar and Richa Goel propose Quantum Time Series instead. Their framework loads normalized sequences into single-qubit rotations. Shallow entanglement layers link the qubits, so the circuit can remember recent steps. Among several loading schemes, a phase-based sparse pattern scaled best. Its depth grows only linearly as qubits are added.

On synthetic and geophysical data, the shallow circuits reproduced complex patterns from limited data. Runs on IBM Heron and Eagle processors held up to 100 qubits. The authors read this as a scalable route for near-term quantum forecasting.
pmc-12702259:
George Kafera and co-authors survey dental students in Malawi about the national oral health policy in this 2025 paper. Malawi adopted its first such policy in 2022. Future dentists must know it to carry it out. The country has one dental surgery degree program, at Kamuzu University of Health Sciences.

All willing clinical year students answered a structured questionnaire. Items covered policy knowledge, exposure during training, and views on curriculum coverage. The tool was piloted and refined with expert review first. Ethics approval came from the national college committee. Gaps in awareness would show where teaching must change. A policy only works when its future workforce has actually read it.
pmc-12705659:
Mohamed Gabr and others encrypted medical images with chaotic methods in 2025. Medical images cross cloud services every day as care moves online. Strong encryption protects that sensitive data. Several images merge into one first. Layered scrambling then hides the content. Keys and code boxes are generated specially.

New layers strengthen each round further. Hyperchaotic signals drive the scrambling here. Automaton rules and gold sequences combine. Speed reached practical levels in tests. Statistical checks confirmed strong resilience. Key space was very large indeed. Cloud transfer is the target setting. Healthcare privacy is the clear winner in the end.
pmc-12706059:
Sabine Britting and co-authors connect how older people walk with how much they fear falling in this 2025 study. Fear of falling is common in later life and predicts real falls. A cautious, shuffling gait goes with the fear, but which parts of gait matter most was unsettled.

The team merged two studies of community-dwelling adults over sixty-five, 261 people averaging eighty years old. An instrumented walkway measured their walking at normal and top speed, and a standard scale scored their concern. Higher concern went with weaker performance on nearly every measure. Normal speed alone explained a quarter of the differences in concern; adding top speed and stride pattern raised that to nearly a third. Four questions about balance in motion could screen for the cautious gait. The authors say walking speed is a quick window into this fear.
pmc-12709859:
Célia Bienassis and colleagues published a review in 2025 on NBTXR3, a nanoparticle treatment designed to make radiotherapy work harder against tumors. Radiotherapy is used in more than half of cancer cases, yet doctors must limit the dose to avoid harming healthy tissue nearby. The review explains how physics and biology meet in this approach.

Injected into a tumor, the nanoparticles amplify the effect of radiation inside the tumor without adding toxicity in surrounding healthy tissue. The authors describe better tumor control in early work and evidence from animal studies that the activated particles can also stir a wider immune response against cancer. Readers get a clear account of why the treatment might improve outcomes and support immunotherapy.
pmc-12714159:
Serpil Özcan and Gülcan Bahçecioğlu Turan examine, in 2025, how nurses' religious beliefs shape their view of a good workplace. Forty-one nurses at a university hospital in eastern Turkey were interviewed over a short period in May. The team used content analysis for the interviews and simple statistics for background data.

Three themes emerged, covering team relationships, coping with hard clinical moments, and the wider ward climate. Nurses also produced twenty-three metaphors linking their faith and their profession, grouped into three kinds. The authors say the study is the first to show how belief colors what nurses count as a positive clinical environment.
pmc-12714559:
Benjamin Bonenti and co-authors compare harms by age among men who use muscle steroids worldwide, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Over one thousand men who used the drugs in the past year split at age forty. Mind harms, body harms, and care access blocks were all tallied.

Younger men reported more anger and low mood than older men. They also flagged more hair loss and fertility worries. Care blocks hit the young harder too, above all at pharmacies and hospitals. Pattern plots showed harms stacking in the young group. The authors urge age-fit harm reduction and easier service entry. Readers get proof that youth is no shield here.
pmc-12717959:
Chuan Foo and four co-authors compared two advanced treatments at a severe asthma clinic in a 2025 paper. Biologic drugs and bronchial thermoplasty both help severe asthma, but no trial pits them against each other. The team reviewed 115 consecutive patients treated with one, the other, or both at an Australian tertiary center.

Control scores and steroid-requiring flare-ups both improved markedly by follow-up. Sixty percent of patients on daily steroids stopped them, and half of the rest cut their dose. Thermoplasty patients were the harder cases: most had already failed biologics, and the rest were ineligible. Even so, their control scores, flare-ups, and steroid doses all fell significantly. The authors offer real-world evidence that thermoplasty still earns its place.
pmc-12719259:
Bateman and a team of co-authors check proton therapy beams with a three-in-one detector instead of water tanks. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Patient-specific quality checks today are slow phantom measurements or unverified machine logs.

The readings feed simulations that rebuild the full three-dimensional dose for comparison with the plan. Energy matched plan values almost perfectly at a London hospital's tests. The pixel sensor saturated on big fields, a limit the authors report openly. Dose linearity was exact. Phantom-free checking could free hours per patient.
pmc-12720259:
Mahesh Shinde and co-authors ask how long drug treatment for tuberculosis of the spine should run, using MRI scans to judge when healing is done, in a 2025 study. Spinal TB is the most common bone form of the disease and can cripple if missed. Scan-guided care lets doctors stop drugs when the spine has truly healed rather than by the calendar alone.

The team followed 100 patients over three years, with an average age in the early twenties and seven in ten of them women. The chest-level spine was hit most often. Most patients healed on drugs alone, while 22 needed surgery, and nerve problems were present in most cases at the start. Biopsy gave the surest diagnosis. Twelve percent of cases resisted standard drugs and moved to second-line treatment. Therapy ran until scans showed healing, classed as complete, partial, or absent.
pmc-12722159:
Toshimitsu Irei and eleven co-authors report a risky operation in patients on dialysis, in this twenty twenty-five case series. The surgery removes part of the pancreas and gut and rebuilds the tract, one of the biggest operations in medicine. Doing it in people whose kidneys have failed adds grave risk.

Eight patients on dialysis had the operation. All had heavy health burdens, and the surgery ran long with notable blood loss. No one died in the first three months, yet half had major complications, and one died in hospital months later from a clot. Most died within eight years of other causes. The series gives rare guidance on when the operation is worth it.
pmc-12722959:
Tyler Pia and five colleagues published a psychiatry study in two thousand twenty-five on suicide risk in schizophrenia spectrum disorders. Suicide is common in these conditions. Acting rashly under strong negative emotion, called negative urgency, may help flag risk but is rarely studied with brain data.

Thirty adults classed as high or low risk were analysed with a sparse machine learning method. A first model using symptoms and traits found hostility, guilt, and negative urgency predicted high risk, while abstract thinking difficulty predicted lower risk. Adding brain measures kept hostility and brought in frontal region activity and cingulate thickness. The authors present the combined model as a step toward circuitry-based risk flags. The sample was small.
pmc-12729059:
Yang Zhang and co-authors published a 2025 review weighing virgin coconut oil against heart and metabolic risk factors. The authors gathered randomized trials in adults and pooled their results through August 2025.

Five databases were searched. Eligible trials reported body measures, blood lipids, blood sugar markers, or inflammation after coconut oil supplementation. Pooling many small trials can reveal effects no single study could settle, or show that the noise cancels out. The review weighs outcomes like cholesterol fractions separately, since the oil could plausibly move them in opposite directions. For shoppers and clinicians facing confident health claims, the paper offers the current balance of controlled evidence, with its gaps named.
pmc-12729159:
Scott Wilson, Yong Ah, and Michael Aidoo test how slip-ups in method bend malaria rapid test results in the lab. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such tests are the main malaria check in sub-Saharan Africa, run by staff with scant lab training. Kit swaps without fresh training breed drift from the maker's steps.

Six kits face cultured parasites at set loads, first by the book, then with changed blood or buffer amounts and wait times. Too much blood floods most kits into invalid runs. Short waits stray most from base; lean buffer also spoils runs, while extra buffer does not. High parasite loads read true in spite of most slips. Training and kit care still matter most at low loads.
pmc-12729659:
Zi Jia Ng and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on helping schools actually use the results of social and emotional learning assessments. Schools collect data on skills like self-control and empathy, but staff often cannot interpret or act on the reports. The team ran guided sessions where educators and students unpacked their own data together.

Twelve schools took part, with thirty-seven educators and eleven students across repeated sessions in spring 2024. Recordings showed a pattern: sessions opened by positioning the data, dug into details, and ended with concrete teaching actions. The authors turn the pattern into a protocol any school can run, with lessons for classroom practice.
pmc-12729859:
Tatiana Priputnevich leads a large team studying antibiotics and gut microbes in infants, in work from twenty twenty-five. Early gut microbes help train the immune system and shape metabolism. Birth type, feeding, early birth, and drugs can all shift how those microbes grow.

The team compared babies born at full term who got beta lactam antibiotics with babies who got none. Stool tests at six to eight months and nine to twelve months measured gut microbe types with a precise lab method. Clear gaps showed between groups. The study helps show how early drug use can leave a mark on infant gut health.
pmc-12730359:
Yimei Wei and six co-authors survey life in two neighboring rivers in a 2025 study. They used DNA traces shed into the water to identify plankton and fish without catching them. The two rivers differ in their conditions, which lets the team compare how each group responds. Such knowledge guides river care and repair.

Overall variety was similar in both rivers for each group, but the mix of species turned over sharply between them. Plankton patterns faded with distance more strongly and formed mostly by chance processes. Fish patterns were shaped more by local conditions. Both groups tracked water traits like temperature, oxygen, and acidity, while plankton also tracked nutrients.
pmc-12730659:
Nilofar Sherzad and six co-authors published a stroke study in twenty twenty-five that asks where speech breaks when a stroke hits the brain's right side. Textbooks put speech on the left. Yet near half the right-side cases in this set of four hundred ten patients had speech trouble in the first two days.

The team mapped each patient's brain damage from scans and lined the maps up with a standard speech score. Harm in deep and side zones on both sides tracked with speech loss. The right-side speech zones mirror the left-side speech web, the maps suggest. The authors say acute speech loss is not a left-side tale alone. Their result may change how stroke teams read early scans and plan speech therapy.
pmc-12732659:
Jiyue Zhang and co-authors catalogue a family of cell-wall genes in soybean and flag the members that answer to drought, in a 2025 paper. The genes, called FLA genes, build proteins that help plant cell walls grow and cope with stress. Soybean is a major food crop that suffers under dry spells, yet its FLA family had never been mapped in full. The team searched the soybean genome with two standard hunting methods.

They found 55 FLA genes and charted where each sits, how it is built, and how the family branches by kinship. Shared building blocks and control switches in the DNA were catalogued too. From public gene activity data, the authors picked members that react to drought, then confirmed their response in dry-stressed plants with a precise counting method. The shortlist gives breeders concrete targets for tougher soybeans.
pmc-12733559:
Mateusz Szczupak and co-authors test whether pain after surgery tracks with delirium in heart and brain surgery patients, in this 2025 pilot study. Both problems are common after major operations, but their interplay across mixed groups was unclear. The team reviewed records of 408 patients, about half from each surgery type. Pain was scored on a standard scale, and delirium was checked with bedside tools over the first two days.

Heart surgery patients reported more pain on day one. In that group, stronger pain went with worse delirium on both days. No such link appeared in the brain surgery group. Across all patients, day-one pain predicted later delirium severity. The authors stress the records-based design cannot prove cause. They call for planned studies and routine paired checks of pain and thinking.
pmc-12733859:

Seventy-nine players played a mobile sports game for ten minutes wearing eye-tracking glasses. Ad zones were marked in advance so gaze could be measured. Statistical models showed placement mattered more than gaze time. Brands built into task-relevant spots, such as the central net area, were recalled far better than side ads. Gaze patterns varied by gender and tennis interest. The authors advise advertisers to buy placement inside the action, not screen edges.
pmc-12734559:
Ghica and a team including Icleanu test an eco friendly way to recover metals from used batteries in twenty twenty-five. The batteries are nickel metal hydride cells from portable defibrillators. Their pastes hold nickel and rare earth metals worth recovering. Harsh chemical methods can harm the environment.

Workers took the cells apart by hand and analysed the parts with X-ray methods. An ultrasonic bath separated the pastes from their metal supports. Citric acid solution drew the rare earths fully out of the anode paste. Water alone cleaned the nickel mesh of cathode paste. The recovered pastes were checked by microscopy and X-ray tools. The authors say ultrasound in weak citric acid is a cheap, greener option for recycling.
pmc-12735559:
Monika Fekete and co-authors published a review in 2025 on diet and brain health. The review looks at the eating pattern common around the Mediterranean Sea. The authors focus on two plant compounds found in grapes and olives. They sum up studies on how the diet may slow decline in memory and movement diseases. The diet may act by cutting cell damage, swelling, and poor blood flow in the brain. Early trials show some gains, but the authors say longer and larger trials are still needed.
pmc-12736559:
Fu Li and co-authors present IFD-YOLO, a light detector that spots small drones in infrared images. Their twenty twenty-five article deals with a hard sensing task: targets are tiny, the signal is weak against noise, and the drone carrying the sensor has little computing power to spare.

A new loss function tightens box placement for small targets. On two data sets it beat the base model on accuracy while using about a quarter fewer parameters and a fifth less compute.
pmc-12738459:
A fluoride tracer can light up active bone on PET scans, but turning glow into a solid number takes care. pmc-12738559:

It focuses on carbon monoxide oxidation, a niche where framework catalysts are still little tested. The authors expect the synergy to yield stronger, steadier performance for environmental cleanup and industrial gas treatment.
pmc-12739459:

They expect gains in both groups, with larger body changes in the diabetes group.
pmc-12740859:

A month later, regeneration was assessed. The supportive gel improved growth factor release. Protected cells clearly outperformed unprotected expectations. Tissue engineers gain a workable delivery platform.
pmc-12745259: Yang, Pu, and Li published in twenty twenty-five a review of new treatments for thoracic tumors, which include lung cancer, breast cancer, and thymoma. The review sums up recent work on targeted therapy, which attacks specific molecular changes, and immunotherapy, which helps the immune system fight tumors. It also covers clinical uses, open challenges, and possible ways around them, aiming to give a basis for better patient outcomes and future research.
pmc-12748059:

pmc-13222359:

pmc-13223059:

pmc-13224059:

pmc-13224159:

pmc-13224759:

pmc-13225159:

pmc-13225559:

pmc-13225659:

pmc-13231059:

The hybrid bloomed earliest, which left it most open to frost harm. The readings show which varieties brace best against cold snaps. Growers in frost-prone areas can use the ranking when planting new orchards.
pmc-13232959:

Standard fixes need either an untreated unit or an instrument variable, and sometimes neither is available.

pmc-13233259:

pmc-13233459:

pmc-13233959:
Iasmyn Vitória Cavalcanti Galvão and colleagues published a 2026 year-long study of a feather mite that infests laying hens in Brazil. pmc-13235359:

pmc-13239259:
Wenwen Shi and colleagues built a prediction model in 2026 for repeat bone fractures in older patients who already broke a bone and live with type 2 diabetes. pmc-13239459:

pmc-13239659:
Xuerui Li and co-authors introduce a long-running health cohort from Tianjin, China, in a 2026 profile paper. The study, launched in 2022, follows adults over time to find risk factors and intervention targets for common chronic diseases in the city.

Baseline examinations between July 2022 and November 2023 covered more than fourteen thousand participants with an average age in the early fifties. Checks included body measures, heart tracings, ultrasound scans, chest imaging, and blood, urine, and stool tests, plus lifestyle questionnaires. pmc-13239959:

pmc-13240459:
