Repair using the patient's own tissue replaced mesh because of heavy contamination.
pmc-13240759:

pmc-13240859:

pmc-13240959:

pmc-13241559:

pmc-13241659:

pmc-13242459:

pmc-13242659:

pmc-13243159:

pmc-13243459:

pmc-13243759:

pmc-13244059:

pmc-13244259:

pmc-13245059:

pmc-13245759:

pmc-13246559:

pmc-13246759:

pmc-13249559:

pmc-13250459:

pmc-13250859:

pmc-13251759:

pmc-13252459:

pmc-13253759:

pmc-13253859:

pmc-13253959:

pmc-13254159:

pmc-13254259:

pmc-13254759:

pmc-13256559:

pmc-13256759:

pmc-13256859:

pmc-13257059:

pmc-13257959:

pmc-13258159:

pmc-13258559:

pmc-13259059:

pmc-13259159:

pmc-13259359:

pmc-13259859:

pmc-13259959:

pmc-13260959:

pmc-13261859: Longfei Gao and colleagues issued a 2026 correction to their 2017 paper on making human nerve cells from adult astrocytes with small molecules. Two image panels in an added figure had been placed under the wrong test group while files were stored and the figure was built. The authors apologize for the error.
pmc-13262159:

pmc-13262659:

pmc-13262859:

Big gaps remain for wildfires, volcanic eruptions, and several diseases.
pmc-13263259:

pmc-13263359:

pmc-13263559:

pmc-13263859:

pmc-13264259:

pmc-13268159:

pmc-13269059:

pmc-13269959:

pmc-13271059:

pmc-13271359:

pmc-13271959:

pmc-13272059:

pmc-13272159:

pmc-13272259:

pmc-13272359:

pmc-13272459:

pmc-13272859:
Ekrem Ozdemir leads a 2026 study comparing frailty scores for predicting problems after wrist fracture surgery in older adults. The fracture is the most common upper-limb break in this age group. The team compared a five-item frailty index, a clinical frailty scale, and a comorbidity index in 562 patients aged 65 or older.

Over about 18 months, 34.8 percent had at least one complication. Each score linked to complications and to recovery of grip and daily life, but alone each sorted risk only modestly. Machine learning models did far better, reaching an accuracy measure of 0.878 for gradient boosting. The authors suggest such models could improve counseling before surgery.
pmc-13273359:
Anna Such leads a 2026 study of how red blood cells lose their calming effect on neutrophils during sepsis, a life-threatening body-wide inflammation. Neutrophils are white blood cells that can release web-like traps to catch germs, but excess traps damage nearby tissue. Healthy red blood cells normally curb that release.

In sepsis, in both humans and mice, red blood cells lose sialic acid from their surface and lose this braking ability. The authors describe the causes of that change and show it can be reversed with drugs. Restoring the interaction sustained trap inhibition during inflammation and prevented adverse effects in their experiments.
pmc-13273759:
Yushuo Duan and co-authors reviewed RNA methylation in the immune surroundings of gastrointestinal tumors in a 2026 article. RNA methylation is a reversible chemical editing of RNA, run by writer, eraser, and reader proteins. It tunes gene activity and has been tied to cancer growth and immune control.

In gut tumors, the authors explain, this editing reshapes the immune microenvironment by changing how tumor and immune cells act and how they use energy. That reshaping helps cancers hide from immunity and alters how they respond to treatment. The review gathers the latest findings across liver, colorectal, stomach, pancreatic, and esophageal cancers. Its aim is to support strategies that pair methylation targeting drugs with immunotherapy for stronger effect.
pmc-13273859:
Gonçalo Pinto and co-authors used a large language model to generate a synthetic pregnancy dataset in a 2026 data article. Real obstetric records are hard to share because of privacy, which slows methods research. Synthetic patients can stand in for teaching and testing if they stay plausible.

Their dataset follows five thousand low risk pregnant women from before conception to after birth. It holds trimester measures such as weight, hemoglobin, glucose tests, and body mass, plus visit, delivery, and outcome variables. An expert panel in family medicine and data science reviewed early output, and repeated prompt revisions improved consistency. Rule checks then verified internal coherence. The authors stress the data suit simulation and machine learning practice, not clinical decisions.
pmc-13274159:
Hiroshi Kobayashi wrote a 2026 review article re-reading endometrial cancer through an evolutionary lens. This womb-lining cancer is rising worldwide, especially in younger women, alongside obesity and delayed childbirth. Standard gene studies list the faults, but not why this tissue collects them so readily.

His frame is antagonistic pleiotropy: traits that help early in life can harm later. One growth pathway is vital for reproduction and womb repair, yet modern overnutrition keeps it switched on, feeding abnormal growth. The guardian protein p53 protects fertility and the placenta, but age and inflammation warp its work toward cancer. The pathways reinforce each other, he argues.
pmc-13274559:
Sufia Athar and co-authors examined emotional skill and workplace wellbeing among nurses and midwives in Qatar in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Health work demands resilience and compassion under pressure, and emotional intelligence may protect both. Their setting was a secondary hospital with a multicultural workforce.

They surveyed 121 registered nurses and midwives, each with six months of experience or more, using an online questionnaire across seven skill domains. Scores were highest for awareness of others and lowest for emotional reasoning. Self-awareness correlated with every other domain, most strongly with emotional self-control. Links between emotional skill and job satisfaction were weak, though, and work-life balance predicted satisfaction best. Interviews echoed the survey, crediting emotional skill with easing stress and improving teamwork.
pmc-13274759:
Jiayin Sun and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on whether cheap blood-count ratios can flag heart trouble in young heart disease patients. Six inflammation indices, all built from routine blood counts, were tested in 986 patients aged eighteen to thirty-five who had coronary angiography at a Beijing hospital between 2013 and 2021.

All six indices rose with the share of patients having an acute coronary syndrome, an emergency such as a heart attack. Two indices, SIRI and PIV, predicted that emergency best, though only moderately. Three indices tracked the severity of artery narrowing on a standard score. Over a median eight years of follow-up, though, most indices failed to predict future major events, limiting their long-term value.
pmc-13275359:
ZiLong Guo and co-authors followed university music club members over one activity cycle in a 2026 exploratory study. Clubs may be more than hobbies: they can build belonging, identity, and a sense of agency. The team paid special attention to gender marginalized students, whose experience is often overlooked.

They tracked 288 undergraduates in nine music clubs at six universities across eight weeks, with surveys before and after plus interviews, observations, and organizer logs. Belonging, identity growth, agency, recognition, and expressive safety all rose, with small to moderate gains. Students who joined more often gained more, and feeling recognized and safe helped explain the gains. Gender marginalized students scored lower on average throughout, though the gaps were not statistically firm. The authors urge cautious, inclusive reading of the promise clubs hold.
pmc-13276159:
Xin Li and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on exosomes as a possible new route for treating brain and nerve diseases. Exosomes are tiny sacs that cells release, packed with active molecules that pass messages between cells. They rarely provoke the immune system and can cross the blood-brain barrier, a wall that blocks many drugs.

The review covers how exosomes form, what they carry, and how doctors might give them, from nose sprays to injections guided into the brain. It surveys their roles in multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and stroke. The authors warn that big hurdles remain before clinic use. Labs still lack standard ways to isolate and purify exosomes, their exact actions need clarifying, and safety rules for patients are not yet settled.
pmc-13276559:
Catherine Volgenant and co-authors present a 2026 population study of oral health on Sal, one of the Cape Verde islands off West Africa. Local reports suggested poor dental health, but no scientific survey existed. The team set out to measure disease, quality of life, and risk factors across the island.

Final-year dental students examined one thousand three hundred seventy-one residents with teeth, from toddlers to the very old. Tooth decay touched nearly nine in ten people. Over half showed the consequences of untreated decay, like abscesses. Almost two thirds of adults had serious gum disease scores. Toothbrush ownership was high, but toothpaste access and dental insurance lagged. Insurance holders had notably less decay. Worse disease tracked with worse self-rated oral quality of life. The authors urge better prevention and access to dental services on the island.
pmc-13276759:
Iram P Rodriguez-Sanchez and a large team measure head lice among schoolchildren in two Mexican cities, in a 2026 survey. Lice infestations disrupt comfort, schooling, and family life, yet city-level Mexican data are scarce. Trained staff inspected each child's scalp directly under a standard method.

More than six thousand children were checked across Monterrey and Mérida. Overall, five hundred ninety children carried lice, with rates notably higher in Monterrey than in Mérida. Girls and children with long hair were infested most often in both cities. Links with home and hygiene factors differed between cities, so the authors advise school and family programmes tailored to each local setting.
pmc-13277659:
Md Shakhawat Hossain, Md Sahilur Rahman, and Munim Ahmed release a 2026 dataset for outlining single cell nuclei in breast cancer slides. Grading the HER2 marker, which guides treatment, must use nuclei that sit intact and apart from neighbours. Earlier computer methods relied on private image collections, slowing progress.

Three expert pathologists independently annotated dual-stained tissue images at high magnification. The set holds thirty-nine patches from twenty-one patients, with more than eighteen hundred nuclei under the loose rule and fewer under full consensus. Both inclusive and strict consensus labels are supplied, along with several mask formats. Test runs with deep learning models validated the resource for automated HER2 grading research.
pmc-13277759:
Tae Hwa Kang and Sun Jae Park present a 2026 genetic study of how an invasive beetle spread across the Korean Peninsula. The ragweed leaf beetle, first reported in Korea in 2002, feeds on ragweed, an invasive plant that arrived after the Korean War. The team sampled beetles from twelve areas and compared two kinds of genetic markers.

One marker set pointed to two common ancestral types, while the other split the beetles into three groups and three invasion routes. The authors settle on at least two founding populations entering through several ports, then spreading inland by hitchhiking on transport. Beetles are drawn strongly to their host plant once they arrive. Port checks may be the best choke point for control.
pmc-13278859:
Chang-Sen Bai and co-authors report a hard-to-classify chest tumour in a 2026 case study. A 43-year-old male smoker had a SMARCA4-deficient undifferentiated thoracic tumour, a rare and aggressive cancer with no standard treatment. One tissue marker, synaptophysin, was present, which usually points toward neuroendocrine tumours instead.

Other neuroendocrine markers were negative, and the growth marker showed very rapid cell division. The team read the lone marker as partial lineage leakage rather than true neuroendocrine identity. Combined platinum chemotherapy and immunotherapy shrank the metastatic cancer, and the partial response held beyond twelve months. The authors suggest this marker pattern may flag patients who benefit from that combination.
pmc-13279259:
André Nascimento and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether a high-salt diet harms blood vessels by driving their lining cells into early aging. Salt is a known heart risk, yet the chain of harm was unclear. Mice ate a very salty diet for two or four weeks while the team checked vessel function and aging markers.

Four weeks of salt, but not two, dulled vessel relaxation and raised aging signs. A drug that clears aged cells reversed the harm, restoring vessel responses. Salt also stirred immune cells, raising a signal molecule that alone could age vessel lining in lab dishes. The authors argue the harm runs through immune-driven aging, which such drugs might block.
pmc-13279659:
Zeliha Turan and Derya Tuluece present a 2026 systematic review of Reiki in breast cancer care. Breast cancer and its care cause pain, fatigue and mood strain in women. Reiki, a hands on or near body energy practice, is used more and more next to chemo care. The review judges Reiki effects on symptoms through a nursing theory lens, the Science of Unitary Human Beings by Martha Rogers.

Searches in five databases ran to May 2026 under standard review rules. Trial and quasi trial studies of Reiki in breast cancer patients were kept. Two readers graded study quality and bias risk with standard tools. Just four studies fit, with three hundred thirty nine patients in all. Those studies hinted that Reiki may cut fatigue in patients. Small proof calls for larger, tighter trials before firm advice.
pmc-13279759:
Carl Llor and Niels Kristian Kjaer write a 2026 commentary on combined biomarker testing in primary care. Antibiotic overuse is a top world health worry, most in chest infections seen in family care. Most such infections are viral and self limited, yet antibiotics flow at high rates. One nation example looms large: China uses about one fourth of all human antibiotics in the world.

In Chinese primary care, more than half of cold type visits end with antibiotics, and many patients get more than one drug. For bronchitis, the rate nears seventy percent, though antibiotics do not cut grave side effects there. Overuse feeds antimicrobial resistance, where germs beat drugs. The pair ask if paired biomarker tests, which flag bacterial infection, can steer doctors to prescribe less. Sound point of care tests could cut waste while keeping patients safe.
pmc-13280159:
R. M. El Shazoly and colleagues report a 2026 study of seed priming to guard wheat from zinc oxide nanoparticles. Zinc oxide nanoparticles, tiny zinc grains from industry, build up in farm soils and threaten food security. At high doses they stunt wheat growth and bleach leaf green. Wheat seeds were primed, or pre soaked, with alpha lipoic acid and a nitric oxide donor, alone and in two orders back to back. Nitric oxide is a plant signal gas.

Successive priming, most the lipoic acid plus donor mix, eased the nanoparticle harm a lot. Seedling growth came back as a strong antioxidant shield formed. Four guard enzymes rose, and metal binding activity hit near ninety eight percent. Computer chemistry checks, called DFT, traced how the priming agents meet zinc oxide at molecule scale. Order of soaks mattered, which gives farmers a recipe lead.
pmc-13280459:
Joshua Kinzel and Roland Seifert present a 2026 survey of German dentists on preventive antibacterial drug use in risk groups. Dentists write a significant share of all antibacterial prescriptions in Germany, and the volume is controversial. Guidelines are often lacking, and stewardship calls for more caution. The survey asks under what indications and with what consistency dentists prescribe. Four groups anchor the questions: endocarditis risk, joint replacement, diabetes, and organ transplantation or immunosuppression.

Dentists rated how often they prescribe for diverse procedures and comorbidities in each group. Primary and secondary drug choices were logged as well. Responses were summarized in an overall picture and briefly compared with German language guidelines. Year of state examination and felt confidence in drug use were also recorded. The survey maps where dentist habits align with guidance and where habit fills the gaps guidance leaves.
pmc-13280559:
Parisa Mirzaei and team report a 2026 case of recurrent pneumothorax after spine fixation in a polytrauma patient. Pneumothorax is an air leak that collapses a lung. Its return after spine surgery is rare but life threatening. Their patient was a nineteen year old man in a high speed maritime accident. He had a T12 fracture and a right sided pulmonary contusion, a bruised lung. A first pneumothorax was managed with a chest tube.

The tube came out after scans showed the leak resolved. He then had posterior T10 to L2 fixation. Right after surgery, acute dyspnea and massive recurrent pneumothorax needed urgent reintervention. He recovered fully after referral to tertiary care. The authors advise retaining chest tubes till after spine fixation. Prone positioning and positive pressure ventilation can reactivate occult leaks in contused lungs.
pmc-13280659:
Rashad Sholan and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a man shot in both testicles. Gunshot wounds there are rare but can end the ability to father children. The patient was thirty-two years old. Surgeons removed part of the left testicle and repaired the right one. They kept living tissue in place without any grafts.

Scans after surgery showed blood still flowed to both testicles. His sperm quality was very poor at first, then got much better over two years. The authors say fast, careful surgery can save both the glands and future fertility. They urge repair over removal when living tissue remains.
pmc-13281259:
Fuqun Wei and four colleagues link high FGFR4 expression in liver cancer to immune responsiveness yet poorer drug-combination results, in a study from twenty twenty-six. A major trial had found adding immunotherapy to lenvatinib gave no clear gain. FGFR4 is one of lenvatinib's targets. Public databases and patient specimens supplied the test data.

High expression predicted favorable immunotherapy outcomes in database analyses. It correlated with immune checkpoint genes and fewer suppressive macrophages. Single-cell data placed FGFR4 mainly in cancer cells. Those cells signaled to macrophages through a specific chemokine axis. A growth pathway and its transcription factor tracked with the signal. Yet in treated patients, high expression was linked to reduced benefit from the combination. The receptor thus cuts both ways, the authors show.
pmc-13281559:
Jimena A Ibagon and colleagues fed mother pigs two protein plans in a 2026 study. Soybean meal is the main protein in pig feed, but makers often swap part of it for pure amino acids, the building blocks of protein. Pure forms are absorbed faster, which may leave gaps for growth. One group got a high-protein soy diet. The other got less soy, more corn, and pure amino acids. Both were tracked through pregnancy and nursing.

Pigs on high protein took in and kept more nitrogen, a sign of protein use, and passed more out. Birth counts, though, did not differ between the plans. First milk from high-protein mothers was richer in fat, protein, and immune factors. A cell-stress marker ran higher in the low-protein group. The authors say cutting feed protein did not hurt breeding results here, a finding that could trim feed costs and waste.
pmc-13281659:
Melissa Perry and co-authors test whether chemical exposures before birth and in childhood predict chromosome errors in the sperm of young men, in a study from 2026. The chemicals are long-lived organochlorines and perfluorinated compounds, which can disturb hormones. Sperm with wrong chromosome counts link to infertility and failed pregnancies.

The men came from a Faroe Islands birth cohort followed since the late nineteen eighties. Blood from birth, childhood, and adulthood was assayed for the chemicals. Sperm samples at ages twenty-two to twenty-four were checked for extra sex chromosomes, a sign of errors in cell division. Higher chemical levels at several ages tracked with more such errors. Mixture effects across the chemical families were also estimated.
pmc-13281759:
Ruihan Cheng and Baolong Li reviewed Chinese herbal care for liver scarring in a 2026 paper. Liver scarring, or fibrosis, builds when star-shaped liver cells switch on and lay down too much fiber. Those cells are the core drivers of the process. They can rest, rage, or stall in a worn state that resists death. Herbal formulas and their active parts are known for hitting many paths at once with a light load on the body.

The review gathers work on coaxing the switched-on cells to die or settle back down. Killing them through several death paths can unwind the scarring, studies suggest. Herbal care has made real headway in this lab work. But gaps remain. Teams still must pin down which parts act, map how they act, and build liver models that mimic the organ's many cell types. The authors frame herbs as a rich but unfinished lead.
pmc-13281859:
Kenan Şimşek and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter picking apart a study of anesthesia in severe brain injury. The study compared two drug plans during surgery in many patients. It reported a near doubling of good recovery with the paired plan. The letter raises seven points of method that, in their view, block that claim. The first is sheer size. A gain that large from the choice of sleep drug alone would rank among the biggest ever seen in this field.

Proven tools show outcome rests mostly on age, coma depth, and scan findings. Standard care wins gains of a few points, not tens. The letter also notes the study never says why each patient got a given plan. In records work, that gap can hide cherry picking by sickness. Even the lone drug label misleads, since both groups shared other drugs. The authors urge strong doubt here.
pmc-13282059:
Rutvij Tope and co-authors report a 2026 case of a bulging weak spot on an artery near the stomach that kept coming back. Such pseudoaneurysms, false swellings of an artery wall, are a rare side effect of pancreatitis, long-term inflammation of the pancreas. The left gastric artery is among the least often affected vessels. Doctors had sealed the spot by guiding coils and glue through an internal ultrasound scope.

Despite that success, the swelling returned three times. The patient needed four sealing procedures in total, three of them through the ultrasound scope and one through radiology methods. The case shows that a clean first result does not end the risk for this vessel. The authors urge regular checks after treatment so any return is caught early, before bleeding can threaten life.
pmc-13282259:
Leili Hafizi and co-authors present a 2026 randomised trial comparing acupuncture with a standard fertility drug in women with polycystic ovary syndrome. That syndrome disrupts hormone balance and can stop egg release, causing infertility. Seventy-seven infertile women in Mashhad, Iran, were split between true acupuncture with a dummy pill and the drug clomiphene with sham acupuncture, a pretend form of needling.

Egg release rates were about thirty-two percent with acupuncture and about forty-two percent with the drug. That gap was not firm by standard tests, so the authors judge the two broadly comparable for triggering egg release. Follicle growth, the ripening of egg sacs, was faster on the drug in two of three cycles. Side effects were similar overall, except headache, which was more common in the acupuncture group. The authors present acupuncture as a safe option worth considering when drug use is a concern.
pmc-13282559:
Kazuma Iimura and co-authors present a 2026 study on how catheter design affects heart mapping for ablation of accessory pathways. Accessory pathways are extra electrical connections in the heart that cause racing rhythms. A mapping method called open-window mapping locates them. The team reviewed forty-three patients whose pathways were ablated after mapping with either an eight-spline high-density catheter or a conventional five-spline catheter.

The eight-spline tool collected far more mapping points in less than half the time. It also showed a narrower target gap and needed lower display thresholds. Every patient in that group had the pathway eliminated on the first ablation pass, against about two thirds with the standard tool. Fewer energy applications were needed. X-ray time and complications were similar. The authors suggest catheter design itself shapes mapping quality and procedure success in this technique.
pmc-13282859:
Katrin Giglhuber and co-authors present a 2026 survey of unmet needs in caring for two rare autoimmune diseases in Germany. The diseases, shortened to NMOSD and MOGAD, attack the optic nerves, spinal cord, and brain. Their true frequency in Germany is unknown; a national registry holds only about one thousand three hundred patients from specialist centres. The team surveyed neurologists and child neurologists through professional networks in spring 2025.

One hundred four physicians replied, half from university hospitals. Most reported rising patient numbers. Gaps were plain: almost half did not know which antibody tests their referral laboratory used, and an older test type persisted despite guidance favouring cell-based assays. An off-label drug, rituximab, was the commonest first treatment. Most striking, about forty-two percent reported untreated NMOSD patients and about sixty-five percent untreated MOGAD patients. The authors say care outside specialist centres needs mapping and standardising.
pmc-13282959:
Five patients with a hormone-raising pituitary tumor anchor a tiny 2026 gut microbe pilot run by Jianing Yang and colleagues. Prolactinoma is the most common type of pituitary tumor and raises the hormone prolactin. Gut microbes may affect such tumors, but direct proof is still early.

Stool samples came from five patients with prolactinoma and five with nonfunctioning pituitary tumors. Gene and chemical tests profiled microbes and small molecules in the samples. The prolactinoma group showed more Bacteroides and Eubacterium and less Blautia and Clostridium. Chemical shifts pointed to sugar and fat pathways. The authors stress that the small sample makes all findings early and in need of larger studies.
pmc-13283759:
Henry Knox, Rachel Hemsath, and Saptarshi Biswas described in 2026 a rare chest artery injury after a bicycle fall. A 60-year-old man hurt the left internal mammary artery, a vessel running inside the chest wall. Such injuries from blunt force are rare, easy to miss, and can bleed fatally into the chest. His blood pressure slid from high to shock levels in the emergency department.

Scans showed a large blood collection over the chest muscle with a spot of active bleeding. Specialists threaded a catheter to the vessel and sealed the bleeding branch with coils. A check image showed the bleeding had stopped, his blood counts steadied, and he went home after therapy checks. Follow-up showed the swelling much improved with no complications.
pmc-13284159:
Sarubala Malayaperumal and co-authors built a scalable human cell model in 2026 for growing osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. Bone research needs these cells, yet donor-based systems vary and starting cells expand poorly. Their platform uses blood progenitor cells made expandable by five reprogramming factors, then steers them through a monocyte stage into osteoclasts with standard growth signals.

The grown cells came out large and many-nucleated, stained positive for a classic osteoclast enzyme, and formed the actin rings osteoclasts use to seal onto bone. They switched on key osteoclast genes and resorbed bone strongly in tests. Because the starting cells renew on demand, the authors present the system as a reproducible standard for bone and biomaterial studies.
pmc-13284559:
Dian-Jeng Li and a large team mined Taiwan's national health insurance database in 2026 to ask whether relatives of bowel cancer patients face higher risks of major mental disorders. Links between mental illness and colorectal cancer in the same person were known, but kinship patterns were not. The team identified nearly sixty-nine thousand first-degree relatives of cancer patients and matched them against about two hundred seventy-six thousand controls.

Relatives showed a higher risk of autism spectrum disorder, strongest among males whose fathers had the cancer. People with a son who had the cancer showed higher bipolar disorder risk, mainly in females. Males whose mother had the cancer showed higher risks of ADHD and generalised anxiety. The authors call for genetic studies of the tangled causes behind the pattern.
pmc-13285359:
Nadica Nikolova Nakev and co-authors present four women whose abdominal infections were traced to a slow-growing bacterium linked with contraceptive devices left in place too long. The 2026 case series explains why this infection, actinomycosis, is so often found late. Its symptoms are vague, and scans can make it look like cancer or bowel disease.

The women showed abscesses in different places, including the abdominal wall, pelvis, and liver. Laboratory tests and tissue examination supported the diagnosis. Treatment combined device removal with long courses of antibiotics, and one woman also needed surgery. The authors urge doctors to consider this infection in women who have used an intrauterine device for many years.
pmc-13285559:
Liver transplants, once barred for cancer patients, now cure some liver tumors outright, Ingrid Woelfel and co-authors review in a 2026 article. Transplant oncology treats chosen cases of liver cell cancer, bile duct cancers, bowel cancer spread only to the liver, and hormone tumors spread only to the liver. Picking the right patients makes or breaks results.

The review walks through who qualifies, who does not, and which tumor traits sway the call for each illness. Immune drugs and targeted pills have widened the pool, turning some comfort-only cases into cure-hopeful ones. The authors urge joint multi-center studies to grow proof safely, warn that organs stay scarce, and back slow, data-led growth of the field.
pmc-13285659:
Shuang Tian and a large team review tiny engineered particles designed to stress a compartment inside cancer cells called the endoplasmic reticulum. Their 2026 review explains that tumors already strain this compartment, which handles protein folding. Pushing that stress further can push cancer cells to die in a way that alerts the immune system.

Particles can be steered toward the compartment with added ligands, peptides, or membrane tricks. Once there, they disturb calcium, create reactive oxygen, or switch on stress signals, prompting dying cells to release alarm molecules. Dendritic cells then mature and killer T cells activate. Combining such particles with light-based or heat-based therapies showed stronger effects, though delivery and safety problems remain.
pmc-13286359:
Jonathan M Huie and Sandy M Kawano film four salamander species climbing surfaces tilted from flat to fully vertical. The 2026 study asks how animals without claws or sticky toe pads manage to climb. Lungless salamanders are famously diverse climbers, so the team suspected behavior does much of the work.

High-speed three-dimensional video showed every species reaching vertical or near vertical. All shortened their strides, kept more feet on the surface, and held their bodies closer to it as slopes steepened. Two tree-living species climbed fastest, helped by longer limbs and foot shapes that can grasp. Behavior alone seems enough for adequate climbing, while small body differences produce the best climbers.
pmc-13286959:
Jay Shah and co-authors review hyaluronan's part in stubborn scars in a 2026 narrative review. Keloids and hypertrophic scars grow from botched wound healing, disfiguring patients and resisting every standard treatment, with keloid recurrence after excision running as high as total. The authors searched two major databases across eighty years for work tying the sugar polymer hyaluronan to these scars, keeping 21 studies with hard evidence.

Cell models of both scar types held less hyaluronan than normal skin models did. The polymer also sat in the wrong places, a pattern traced to garbled expression of the genes that make, break, bind, and read it. Injecting or smearing hyaluronan on keloids improved looks and cut short-term recurrence in early reports. The reviewers back the molecule as both a clue to scar formation and a treatment lead needing stronger trials.
pmc-13287159:
Kyuri Park and co-authors wrote a 2026 tutorial introducing causalnet, an R package for testing how the direction of links in a network shapes behaviour over time. Readers start from a partly specified map, add limits from theory or time-based models, and generate the directed versions that remain possible.

Within the package, users can run either a nonlinear model or a simpler linear one on each candidate map. Outputs can then be compared on features such as how long effects persist or how a system recovers. The authors stress that the tool screens competing theories rather than proving one true network from a single snapshot of data.
pmc-13287659: Editors of Scientific Reports retracted a 2025 article in 2026 that claimed a soil improvement material made from cattail plant matter at micro, nano, and pico scales, by Yasaman Zeynali and colleagues. The editors said particles at the pico scale described in the work are not physically possible. The authors could not explain the term well and did not supply source data when asked. Confidence in the work was therefore withdrawn. One author gave no clear position on the retraction, and the others did not reply.
pmc-13287759:
Preethi Veerlapalli and co-authors built a layered learning system in 2026 for rare brain and nerve disorders. It classifies magnetic resonance scans at several levels at once, from broad families down to single diseases. Rare classes give models little data, and black-box answers worry clinicians, so the design stresses both sharing across levels and visual explanation.

A convolutional stage reads local detail while a transformer stage reads whole-image context, and a cross-attention step lets the two views question each other. Extra models vote together for stability, and heat maps show the regions behind each call. Tests on a public scan set gave stronger multi-label results than earlier tools, the authors report.
pmc-13288359:
Lily Gloria Tagoe and co-authors tracked side effects in 31 children starting treatment for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Care took place at a teaching hospital in Ghana, between August 2021 and January 2023. Ages ran from one to seventeen. The first treatment phase carries the highest risk, and support care is limited locally.

Every child had at least one side effect. Twenty-nine children, at 93.4%, had at least one severe effect. Low blood counts, infection, fever with low white cells, mouth sores, and high blood pressure led the list. Death during this phase reached 19.3%. No trait predicted severe harm. The authors urge better bedside watch, blood supply, and infection control.
pmc-13288459:
Mai O Soliman and colleagues build a glowing test for sugar-coated proteins entering cells, reported in 2026. Sugars on cell surface proteins help decide what gets pulled inside, yet they are hard to track. The team fed cells sugar building blocks carrying a chemical handle. A split glowing enzyme then latched onto those sugars through click chemistry. Only sugars still on the surface completed the enzyme and lit up.

The mix-and-read assay separated the behavior of four cell-penetrating peptides. Those peptides are short protein pieces known for ferrying cargo into cells. Peptides reported to engage sugars strongly gave different uptake signals from weak engagers, matching expectations. Because the glow comes only from the membrane, inner cell signals do not confuse the reading. The authors offer the method as a screen for delivery molecules that ride the sugar pathway inside.
pmc-13288559:
Deniz Ozman and colleagues compare e-bike and bike crashes in Germany in 2026. Records came from a national trauma register. It holds 9,170 badly hurt riders. All were aged sixteen or more. Years ran from 2020 to 2023. E-bike cases numbered 1,160.

E-bike riders were older than bike riders. Median age was 63 versus 57 years. They had more multi-area harm. Head, face, and chest harm were more common. ICU care was needed more often. Death risk rose steeply with age. It hit 18.6 percent at age eighty or more in their data. The authors urge age-focused safety work.
pmc-13288859:
Rosario Isabel Espinoza Jeraldo and co-authors gather trial proof on dementia prevention in 2026. By 2050, two-thirds of dementia cases will sit in poorer nations. Most programs were designed in rich ones. The team hunted trials run in poorer settings. Only randomized trials were kept.

Twenty-five trials came from six nations. Seventeen sat in China alone. In all, 1,304 people took part. All had mild impairment or felt decline. Pooled results favored the programs for thinking. Exercise and mixed programs each held support. Arts-based work lacked data to pool. Publication bias was clear. Local context must shape design from the start.
pmc-13288959:
Anna Karin Hedstrom, Tomas Olsson, and Lars Alfredsson study MS outcomes by birth origin. Two Swedish case-control sets supplied the data. It covers 4,008 people with new relapsing MS. Records ran from 2005 to 2019. Follow-up used national registers through 2022.

First-generation migrants faced faster decline. Their risk of set worsening ran higher. Swedish-born children of migrants showed no gap. Origin in the Middle East or North Africa stood out. That group had higher risks on most measures. Thinking tests and self-reports also worsened faster. Free care for all did not erase the gaps. Early checks and tailored care may help.
pmc-13289159:
Rohan Shah and colleagues draft a 2026 review plan on iron programs for Indian teens. Anemia is a major problem for teens there. Girls bear the worst of it. National plans give weekly iron and folic acid. Blocks in rollout still persist.

The team will search five databases. Grey sources and trial lists will also be checked. Work to September 2025 will count. School and community programs both qualify. Two reviewers will screen each study. Quality will be graded with a set tool. Counts will be summed without pooling. Themes will be drawn from word-based work. Findings should guide future program design.
pmc-13289259:
Dania Jaamour headed a 2026 mixed-methods study on why patients in Chicago often do not use community help after hospital screening for social needs. Hospitals now screen for needs tied to housing, food, and other daily factors, then refer people to local groups. Whether people actually use that help, and what blocks them, was poorly known.

Surveys and interviews covered discharged patients at high social risk and six community groups across three Northwestern Medicine hospitals. Only 30 patients and six sites took part, so results are early. Most patients said referrals fit their needs yet still did not use the services offered. Limited English, doubt about benefit, and hard access blocked use, while community groups cited low funds, short staffing, and poor tracking from hospitals.
pmc-13289359:
Qianwen Wu and coauthors share a 2026 single-center look at belimumab for lupus-linked pulmonary arterial hypertension. In this condition, high pressure in lung arteries strains the right heart alongside lupus activity. Standard immune drugs plus targeted pressure drugs remain the usual base, and the team tracked what adding belimumab did over a year.

Ten patients got intravenous belimumab from January 2022 to January 2025, matched with 30 similar patients on standard immune care without biologics. All received dual or triple targeted therapy for lung pressure as background care. The belimumab group showed gains in walking distance, function class, heart markers, and right heart measures over twelve months. Two ultrasound ratios improved more than in controls, though numbers stay small.
pmc-13289659:
Lin Tu, Yuming Lu, Xingde Liu, and Xiangchun Shen tested a 2026 plant compound, salvianic acid A, for heart injury when blood flow returns after a blockage. That return injury, called ischemia-reperfusion harm, involves ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death. The compound is known for heart protection, and the team traced whether it works through a chain involving EGFR, Nrf2, and GPX4 proteins.

Cell tests under low oxygen then reoxygenation measured reactive oxygen, iron, and defense molecules alongside ferroptosis signs. The compound lowered harmful oxidants and iron while raising protective GPX4 and related defenses. Blocking Nrf2 or silencing EGFR erased the benefit, proving the chain matters. Animal heart injury also eased with treatment.
pmc-13289759:
Muhammad Owais and coauthors recount a 2026 fatal case of desmoid-type fibromatosis hidden behind the uterus that mimicked a fibroid. This rare, locally aggressive growth makes up fewer than 0.03 percent of all tumors and can invade nearby organs silently. A 21-year-old woman with lower belly pain and a large pelvic mass on ultrasound was sent home with a fibroid label.

She came back two days later with an acute abdomen, and scans showed a 29 cm mass behind the womb lining with free air from a perforated colon. Emergency surgery removed part of the colon with a stoma, but full removal proved impossible. Tissue review fit the fibromatosis diagnosis, though confirmatory stains were not done. She died nine days after arrival.
pmc-13290659:
Teenagers in South Africa's Limpopo province are still learning what self-awareness means, T. C. Masutha and colleagues find in a qualitative study from 2026. Self-awareness underpins empathy, sound choices, and emotional resilience, so the team asked school learners how they understand and talk about it.

Forty-eight learners from six schools, evenly split between boys and girls across grades nine to eleven, took part during a nursing-model boot camp. Reflective writing and group discussion fed a thematic analysis that surfaced five themes, running from how learners define self-awareness to their strengths, weaknesses, career hopes, and ways of fixing weaknesses. The authors describe a grasp of self-awareness that is developing but uneven, tied to how committed learners feel at school and how they picture their futures. They argue teachers should build it deliberately.
pmc-13290759:
Two hippocampus circuits split memory from mood in mouse brains, Yanling Liang and colleagues show in a circuit study from 2026. The orbitofrontal cortex talks to both the dorsal and ventral ends of CA1, but how those conversations differ was unclear.

With viral tracing and targeted disconnection, the team mapped the wiring. The dorsal link runs one way and indirectly, from orbitofrontal cortex through the claustrum, with no return path found. The ventral link runs the other direction, with a direct line into the orbitofrontal cortex plus detours through thalamus, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex. Cutting the dorsal circuit hurt spatial memory only; cutting the ventral circuit produced anxiety- and depression-like behavior while memory stayed intact. Liang and colleagues read the split as a circuit-level explanation for how one region can govern both knowing and feeling.
pmc-13290959:
Stepping outside the self may be how moral injury heals, Wesley Fleming proposes in a theory paper from 2026. Moral injury leaves rigid shame and broken meaning after events that violate a person's moral code, and Fleming builds on Mindfulness-to-Meaning Theory to cast self-transcendence as the recovery mechanism.

Self-transcendence, a state of loosened self-focus, widened awareness, and prosocial meaning, is theorized to grow through mindfulness practices that train decentering and meta-awareness. In that state, attention broadens, reappraisal turns flexible, and shame-locked self-stories loosen, letting moral identity be repaired and meaning rebuilt. Fleming sketches interventions that cultivate the state directly or as modules inside other therapies. He also flags the weak spots: the state is hard to measure, readiness varies, and inducing it reliably remains unsolved.
pmc-13291159:
Shuai Wang and colleagues review the appendix and colon cancer risk in a 2026 short article. The appendix was once seen as useless. New work casts it as a home for gut microbes and immune tissue. That shift raises a fresh question about removing it.

Past studies gave mixed answers on cancer after appendix removal. Some found higher risk soon after surgery. Newer work blames early detection bias for much of that signal. Lab studies still show plausible paths through microbes and inflammation. Effects may also differ by tumor site. The authors call for care in reading old data. No simple claim that removal raises long-term risk holds up.
pmc-13291259:
A gut microbe product may shield the bowel wall. Sweta Ghosh leads a 2026 study of urolithin A in mice and human tissue. The compound switches on a gut sensor called AHR. How that switch guards the bowel was not clear.

In mouse gut cells, the compound woke a second alarm unit. That unit released one signal, IL-18, but not its close kin. IL-18 then drove mucus and defense proteins. Mice gained protection from bowel inflammation. Human bowel samples from patients showed the same signal rise. A chain from sensor to shield thus takes shape. The path may guide new bowel disease drugs.
pmc-13291359:
Listening along fiber cables can spot faults and events. Yangyang Wan leads a 2026 study of smarter sensing without real training data. Such systems need many labeled examples to learn. Real event data is scarce at most work sites.

Their method builds training data from physics itself. Models of events and of the sensing gear create fake data. A second network learns to strip background noise from signals. Tests covered public sensing data for event naming. A factory belt fault task was also tried. Fault calls hit high accuracy in a real plant. Scores matched networks trained on real data. Skills also carried across sites in one task type.
pmc-13292059:
Yang Wang and co-authors build a 2026 gene signature from lactylation-related genes to forecast outcomes and immunotherapy response in triple-negative breast cancer. Public tumor data were clustered by those genes, and a scoring model grew out of the genes separating the clusters. Lab assays then checked the model's key genes.

Patients with high scores lived better outcomes and answered immunotherapy more favorably, judging by checkpoint profiles and drug sensitivity patterns. Three genes stood out in validation: PD-L2, immunoglobulin J chain, and the CSF2 receptor beta chain. The authors present the signature as a dual-purpose tool, estimating both prognosis and likely benefit from immune treatment. They flag the three hub genes as candidates for future therapy research.
pmc-13292259:
Shynggys Nuraly and co-authors tell a 2026 case story with a rare diagnosis and a striking outcome: squamous cell carcinoma arising in the renal pelvis. Fewer than 1 percent of upper urinary tract tumors take this form. Their patient was a 58-year-old woman with anemia, and MRI showed an infiltrative mass blocking urine flow and invading the pancreatic tail.

Surgeons removed the kidney and ureter with a bladder cuff, cleared lymph nodes, and took the pancreatic segment in the same operation, achieving a complete resection despite the patient's morbid obesity. Pathology confirmed a well-differentiated keratinizing tumor with nerve invasion, staged pT4N0M0. She received no further therapy. Five years later, PET/CT showed no recurrence, a result the authors credit to thorough multivisceral surgery.
pmc-13292559:
Xunhe Huang, with co-authors, reports a 2026 genome-wide association study hunting resistance genes against avian leukosis virus in Wuhua yellow chickens, a hardy indigenous Chinese breed. The virus suppresses immunity and causes tumors across the poultry industry. Infection status came from p27 antigen testing at 46 weeks in 259 birds, of which only ten, 3.9 percent, tested positive.

Fifty-eight significant markers clustered inside one 1.03-megabase stretch of chromosome 12. The gene FHIT alone held 44 of them, and conditioning on its lead variant erased the neighboring signals, marking it the driver. Eleven candidate genes in the block mix tumor suppression, metabolism, and immune signaling themes, with the citrate cycle the top enriched pathway. The authors offer the haplotype as a breeding target for resistant lines.
pmc-13292659:
Komal Sai Pedaballe writes a 2026 letter applauding a brief report by Lin and colleagues. The report shows how rarely the kidney drug finerenone actually gets started in chronic kidney disease with type 2 diabetes. The original study used electronic health record prescriptions and found just 0.3 percent uptake, mostly in advanced, high-risk patients. The letter raises a measurement worry rather than disputing the direction.

A written prescription, Pedaballe notes, is not a filled one. Finerenone has no generic, and 77.3 percent of new users in the study sat on Medicare, where specialty copays, especially inside the coverage gap, can stall pickup. Linked pharmacy data for other cardiometabolic drugs show abandonment is common. True uptake may therefore be lower still. The letter asks the authors to cross-check orders against fills to separate doctor hesitation from patient cost barriers.
pmc-13292759:
Joshua M. Lyte joins a large expert group in a 2026 guide on best practice for gut microbe studies in poultry. The guide focuses on 16S rRNA gene sequencing, a common way to profile bacteria in the chicken gut.

Rather than force one fixed protocol, the authors set out shared steps for study design, DNA extraction, sequencing, analysis, and reporting. They stress proper positive and negative controls and fuller reporting so results can be compared across labs. Experts from universities, industry, and government wrote the guide together. It serves as a checklist meant to make poultry microbe findings more consistent and easier to repeat.
pmc-13293259:
Qiang Zhang and co-authors present scTumorDrug in 2026, a tool that predicts drug response for each cell type inside mixed tumors. Tumors contain many cell types, and precision medicine needs to know which types a drug will hit. Single-cell sequencing plus drug data make such prediction possible in principle.

The tool combines single-cell, bulk, and drug response data. It beat prior methods on cell line, mouse, and human sample data sets. A mouse bladder tumor model validated one prediction: a marker-positive cell group was sensitive to a test drug. That sensitivity helped explain the drug's effect on tumors.
pmc-13293559:
Subhas Chandra Debnath and co-authors present three children treated for a rare blood vessel tumor growing inside the lower jaw, in a 2026 case series. These intraosseous hemangiomas account for under one percent of bone tumors and are seldom seen in young patients. Because they mimic tooth-related cysts and tumors, they are often misread, and cutting into one unprepared can trigger dangerous bleeding.

The patients, aged nine to fourteen, each had painless jaw swelling and facial asymmetry. Imaging varied from a classic sunburst pattern to hollow or destructive lesions, so needle aspiration and angiographic scans were used to reveal the vascular nature of each growth. All three underwent removal of the affected jaw segment with vessel control and reconstruction, and tissue study confirmed the diagnosis in every case.
pmc-13293659:
Nicolò Ricciardi and colleagues track, in a 2026 rat study, how a high-fat diet over 20 weeks harms both body metabolism and behavior. How thinking and mood worsen as metabolic syndrome builds, and which body signals drive each change, was still unclear.

Rats on the diet developed steady metabolic strain plus worse anxiety-like behavior and memory, each on its own timeline. Statistical modeling tied behavior shifts to fat burden, oxidative stress, leptin signaling, and ketone control acting together. Leptin signals linked most to mood changes, while redox imbalance linked most to memory loss. Thinking problems thus sit inside the syndrome itself, the authors argue.
pmc-13293759:
Leyla Moghaddasi and seven co-authors build a step by step framework for validating the imaging panels that check radiation therapy plans before treatment, in this 2026 study. Guidelines from the American physics association ask centers to verify the measured and calculated parts of these electronic portal checks separately. The team commissioned their method on two machines with two panel generations, across beam types.

One older panel saturated under intense beams at short distances, under reading by up to five percent, a fault cured by moving it back. Independent checks of each dose component passed at high rates. Benchmarking over eight hundred clinical fields, plus planted error plans, showed the system spotting errors better than phantom based checks at strict settings. The framework gives clinics interpretable, component level answers.
pmc-13294159:
BKM Firmke and colleagues map an oxygen-sensing pathway in kidneys for a 2026 study. Beyond the classic hypoxia factor route, the ADO-RGS pathway tunes G-protein signals by oxygen level. Kidneys suffer easily from low oxygen, a driver of chronic disease, yet cell-by-cell maps were missing. Gene signals were charted in mouse kidneys under normal oxygen, low oxygen, and scarring, then compared with human biopsies.

The ADO enzyme stayed even across regions and states. Its RGS partners shifted sharply: Rgs4 rose in fibroblasts during anemia and scarring, Rgs5 rose in vessels and medullary fibroblasts under low oxygen, and Rgs16 marked interstitial cells in scarred tissue. Human samples echoed the split.
pmc-13294459:
Min Wei and a large team report a rare neck infection found by broad DNA sequencing in a 2026 case. A newly diagnosed person with HIV arrived with repeated pus-forming neck lymph node swelling as the first illness sign. Standard germ hunts often miss non-tuberculous mycobacteria, and Mycobacterium porcinum had almost never been tied to this picture in HIV care.

Metagenomic sequencing of pus named the germ quickly. The species was first known from pig jaw nodes and later from wounds, line infections, and lungs, mostly outside HIV care. Fast broad testing plus awareness of odd presentations can shorten the path to right treatment for hidden germs.
pmc-13295159:
Yu Gu and colleagues test a blood protein on airway cells in a 2026 laboratory study. Beta-2 microglobulin had already been tied by the team to emphysema through cell ageing. Whether it also disrupts the energy factories of bronchial cells, called mitochondria, was the open question.

Human bronchial cells were exposed for 48 hours to the protein or to cigarette smoke extract. Both treatments raised ageing markers, lowered mitochondrial voltage, and cut energy production while reactive oxygen climbed. Cells also grew more slowly and died more often. The pattern supports a role for the protein in airway ageing, pending animal and mechanism work.
pmc-13295759:
Jamini Bhagu and colleagues image stroke recovery by sex in a 2026 study. Stroke plays out differently in females and males, and stem cell vesicles grown in three-dimensional clusters may aid repair. Whether benefit differs by sex, tracked inside the living brain, needed testing with very strong scanners.

Labelled vesicles or salt water were delivered at vessel reopening in a temporary blockage model. Scans at extremely high field followed tissue, sodium, diffusion, and chemical changes over 21 days. Vesicle treatment trended toward smaller lesions, earlier sodium balance, and steadier brain chemicals, with females recovering somewhat better. Behaviour gaps stayed unclear.
pmc-13295959:
Ming Yi and colleagues reflect, in 2026, on a drug class that blocks PD-L1 while also trapping TGF-beta, a signal that shields tumours from immunity. An earlier drug of this kind gave mixed results, yet a newer one, retlirafusp alfa, won approval in China for stomach cancer.

The authors argue suppression by TGF-beta sits in pockets of tumour tissue and is not always the main barrier, even when PD-L1 is present. Success in one defined setting shows the approach can work when biology fits. They recommend patient selection by markers and trial measures that test the mechanism directly.
pmc-13296059:
Ultra-fast radiation in fruit flies is tested in 2026 by Marvin Kreuzer and co-authors as a stand-in for studying the FLASH effect, where rapid dosing spares healthy tissue. A clinical accelerator was adapted to deliver electron beams at thousands of times the usual rate to adult female flies.

Flies given single high ultra-fast doses lived longer than those given standard-rate doses, and split ultra-fast doses helped further. Standard dosing at a lower level caused climbing problems that ultra-fast dosing did not. Signs of a damaging cell process appeared in brains only after standard dosing. The authors promote flies as a handy model for this puzzle.
pmc-13296159:
Omar Alhumaidan, Ali Almajwal and Mohammed Alsaif update, in 2026, reference values for daily energy needs in Saudi Arabia. Older figures leaned on general equations and tended to overshoot, so the team rebuild estimates from Saudi body data, activity patterns and measured child energy use.

Infant needs rise across the first year, and children's needs climb steeply with age. For adults at current activity levels, the average requirement lands near 2,207 kilocalories daily for men and 1,708 kilocalories for women, rising sharply if activity grows. The authors offer the values as firmer ground for national food guidance.
pmc-13296859:
Lihong Shi and colleagues weave, in 2026, health communication tasks into basic medical courses for forty-two junior students in China. Students often undervalue pre-clinical science, so the team set structured talking tasks, collected written reflections and interviewed fifteen community members about the students' manner.

Reflections grouped into six themes, from clinical communication thinking to taking responsibility for public understanding. Community members rated the students clear and professional, and some planned to change health habits after talking with them. The authors suggest the blend boosts respect for basic science and speaking skills, while urging measured follow-up study.
pmc-13298859:
Maria Tziastoudi and colleagues study a gene variant's link to diabetic kidney disease through a Greek case-control study plus meta-analysis, in a 2026 genetics paper. The AKR1B1 gene has been tied to high-glucose kidney damage. Five variants were typed in patients with nephropathy, diabetic patients without it, and healthy controls.

The Greek cohort alone showed no significant association for any variant. Pooling published studies changed the picture: one promoter variant linked to nephropathy when compared against diabetic controls, and a repeat variant mattered in Asian and type 2 subgroups. The authors argue control choice shapes conclusions, and the gene may influence progression rather than diabetes itself.
pmc-13299059:
Blood and tumor tissue tell different microRNA stories in early ovarian cancer, yet the plots converge, find Shuya Cai and co-authors in a 2026 database study. Mining public gene expression collections, they compared microRNA profiles from serum and from tissue in early-stage disease.

No core microRNAs overlapped between the two compartments: serum signals mostly rose while tissue signals mostly fell. Still, their target genes funneled into the same machinery, chiefly the cell cycle and PI3K-Akt signaling. The authors argue serum microRNAs are not mere leakage from tumors but may be deliberately packaged into exosomes, which would make blood tests a faithful window for early detection.
pmc-13299459:
Hamid Mostafavi Abdolmaleky and others test whether lactate-driven acidity in the brain switches on a gene network seen in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, in a 2026 study. Postmortem brains in both states show lactate build-up, lower pH, and raised TGFB2 expression. Stem-cell-derived neurons, astrocytes, and brain organoids were exposed to acid or alkaline shifts.

Most dysregulated genes in the patient data moved opposite to brain pH alongside TGFB2. Lactic acid raised TGFB2 expression and loosened its promoter methylation in astrocytes and organoids, while alkaline treatments did the reverse. The authors propose targeting lactate build-up or excess TGFB2 as a therapeutic direction.
pmc-13299659:
Qing-Ming Shi and others measure insecticide resistance in dengue-carrying mosquitoes from five areas of Yunnan Province, China, using samples from 2015 and 2016, reported in 2026. Larval and adult tests confirmed middling to high resistance to beta-cypermethrin everywhere. Biochemical and gene assays hunted the mechanisms behind it.

A single target-site mutation in the sodium channel gene appeared, and its share rose with resistance levels. Amounts of a detoxifying enzyme family also ran high and tracked resistance. Jointly, mutation plus metabolic change explain the pyrethroid resistance. The authors offer the data as a baseline backing steady checks and smarter vector control.
pmc-13299859:
Yu Guo and colleagues compare gut microbes in eri silkworm larvae switched between two food plants, in a 2026 insect study. The silkworm is an economically important species that eats many plants, and gut bacteria may help it adjust. Larvae fed tree-of-heaven leaves grew worse than castor-fed larvae and showed lower digestive enzyme activity in the midgut.

Short-term diet switching significantly reshaped bacterial richness, diversity, community makeup, and predicted microbial functions. One bacterial genus tracked larval weight closely. The authors conclude quick diet change alters both growth and gut community together, which matters for rearing this commercial insect on alternative host plants.
pmc-13299959:
L Jung and colleagues measure stroke risk after new atrial fibrillation appears in dialysis patients, using nationwide Korean insurance claims, reported in 2026. More than one hundred fifty thousand adults starting maintenance haemodialysis were followed, and a matched comparison balanced patients who developed the rhythm disorder against those who did not. A landmark design reduced early event bias.

New fibrillation carried a significantly higher stroke risk after matching. Annual stroke risk among affected patients averaged in the mid single digits and climbed steeply with a standard risk score, reaching the highest band at top scores. The authors stress individual risk assessment and prevention in this fragile population.
pmc-13300059:
Six genes tied to inflammation may help flag osteoarthritis, according to a 2026 computational study led by Xueya Lv. The team merged three public cartilage gene-expression datasets and corrected for batch effects before hunting for genes that separate diseased from healthy tissue. Single-cell data then checked where the candidate genes are active.

Fifty-eight genes differed between groups, mostly turned down, and six hub genes formed a diagnostic model with fair accuracy. Virtual knockouts of five hubs disturbed IL-17, NF-κB, and chemokine pathways, pointing to a shared inflammatory core. Clustering also split patients into two subtypes with different stress-response activity. The signature could guide diagnosis and future drug studies.
pmc-13300559:
Fixed spray zones only work if biting midges keep returning to the same spots, and Aaron M. Lloyd and colleagues tested that hope on a Florida residential island in a 2026 study. Trap records for Culicoides furens were checked across seasons and years for stable hot spots that control crews could target.

Catches swung widely with season and site, but no hot spot stayed fixed across years. Numbers also fell steeply from 2005 to 2007. Weather and the time of year predicted abundance better than closeness to larval habitat. For area-wide programs, the authors conclude, chasing fixed target zones is a weak strategy under Florida's legal and budget limits.
pmc-13300859:
Masaaki Akai and co-authors review low dose chemotherapy before surgery for advanced stomach and junction cancers in a 2026 retrospective study. Their regimen paired the oral drug combination S-1 with a reduced oxaliplatin dose, aiming to shrink tumors enough for complete removal in mostly elderly patients. Thirty-four patients with a median age of seventy-four went on to stomach surgery with full lymph node clearance at one center.

Complete, margin free resection was achieved in about eighty-five percent of cases, and the cancer vanished entirely under the microscope in about twenty-one percent. Nerve damage in the limbs was the commonest side effect, yet no severe grade four toxicities appeared, and serious surgical complications stayed under nine percent with no treatment related deaths. Three-year survival figures were strong for this population. The authors call the gentler dosing promising and ask for prospective trials to refine it.
pmc-13300959:
Elite water polo builds different bodies for different jobs, Milivoj Dopsaj and colleagues confirm in a 2026 study of seventy-two national-team men. Players from Serbia, Croatia, Greece, and Italy, all veterans of Olympics or world and European championships, underwent multichannel bioimpedance scanning. Ten body-structure variables were compared across playing positions.

The analysis found clear positional differences, with an effect that explained about forty percent of the variation. Body mass and body fat drove the split most strongly, with body mass index close behind. Because fat aids buoyancy while muscle powers grappling and shooting, the authors advise selectors and coaches to match recruits to position-specific profiles and to plan food and training around them.
pmc-13301159:
Y Matsuda and co-authors report long term outcomes of subcutaneous defibrillators in patients with inherited rhythm diseases, in a 2026 retrospective study. The cohort held 201 patients implanted between 2009 and 2024 at one hospital, with a mean age of forty. It spanned hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, Brugada syndrome, long QT syndrome, and a DPP6 mutation group.

Across a median follow-up near eight years, device complications touched about twenty-one percent of patients at similar rates in every disease group. Dangerous ventricular rhythms appeared in about nineteen percent, yet freedom from them differed significantly by diagnosis. The DPP6 group fared best, while the two cardiomyopathy groups carried roughly double the risk in adjusted models. Inappropriate therapy hit about seventeen percent, also varying by disease, and a wider QRS at implant predicted it. Seven patients died. The authors argue disease type, not the device, drives the long term story.
pmc-13301459:
M Valek and co-authors read the rhythm recordings of patients who died with implanted heart devices in a 2026 forensic study. The series covered 296 people, ninety-four with defibrillators and 202 with pacemakers, who died outside hospital and came to autopsy at eight forensic departments. Emergency reports, autopsy protocols, and device interrogations were combined to reconstruct what the heart did at the end.

A ventricular rhythm showed up in 124 patients, about forty-two percent, and more often in defibrillator carriers than pacemaker carriers, fifty-three against thirty-nine percent. Judges rated the arrhythmia the primary cause of death in about three quarters of those cases. Among defibrillator patients whose devices fought the rhythm, half degenerated into pulseless activity or standstill, and half never achieved termination. The authors attribute those failures to end stage muscle failure with no reserve left, rather than device malfunction, a limit on what implants can prevent.
pmc-13301759:
Jie Yuan and co-authors present a 2026 pot experiment on sweet potato seedlings treated with a helpful root fungus called Glomus intraradices. Such fungi live inside plant roots and trade nutrients with their hosts. The team asked whether adding the fungus would change seedling growth, nutrient uptake, root chemistry, and the bacteria living around and inside roots.

Treated seedlings gained more fresh and dry weight, took up more potassium, and stored more starch and soluble sugars. Soil near the roots held more organic matter and showed lower salt conductivity, while root chemistry shifted across hundreds of measured compounds. Bacterial groups also shifted, with certain genera becoming more common inside roots. Growers interested in cutting fertilizer use may find the potassium results especially useful.
pmc-13303659:
Aline Miranda de Vasconcelos heads a 2026 systematic review of mild electrical stimulation of the scalp and its effects on recognizing faces. Face recognition underpins daily social life, but study results in this area have stayed scattered.

Following PRISMA guidance, the team screened 261 records and kept 28 studies covering many stimulation types and groups. Stimulating vision and face areas at the back and side of the head helped in some tasks, but results clashed across studies. Small, narrow samples and wide differences in settings, tasks, and measures blocked firm conclusions. Tighter designs and clearer reporting are urged.
pmc-13303759:
Lukas Lütje and colleagues study donor brain tissue in multiple sclerosis in a 2026 pathology report. The illness varies greatly between people in damage patterns, course, and severity, and inherited factors may explain part of that spread.

Tissue from 287 donors in the Netherlands Brain Bank cohort was scored for vessel cuffs, immune cell clusters, wide-rim lesions, and repair quality. Vessel cuffs and immune clusters appeared more often in carriers of a known risk gene variant. Wide-rim lesions tied to more active damage and higher severity scores. Poor repair linked to other clinical features, helping place each donor's disease in context.
pmc-13305159:
Wendi Xu and colleagues build a light-sensing security device from a tin telluride memory cell in a 2026 study. Hardware fingerprints based on built-in randomness resist copying, yet merging secrecy with brain-like recognition in one device is hard.

The layered cell switched resistance reliably and held states for a long span, while also mimicking learning-like memory behaviors. Under light it produced jittery currents that differ from device to device by nature. Those random values became encryption keys that scrambled images, and a matching memory network read the scrambled images with high accuracy after training.
pmc-13306159:
Mirta Milić compared two slimming diets for DNA damage in adults with severe obesity in a 2026 intervention study. Fifty-three people with body mass index at or above 35.0 kg/m2 took part over three weeks.

One group ate about 600 kcal per day under hospital watch, while the other followed 1500 kcal per day at home in the reported design. Blood cell tests before and after measured fresh, oxidative and lasting DNA harm using comet and cell-block methods. The study tests whether faster energy cuts protect the genome or add stress in the short term.
pmc-13306359:
Wei Pan moved two disease resistance genes from a wild wheat ancestor into bread wheat in a 2026 breeding study. Powdery mildew and stripe rust threaten harvests worldwide, and heavy reliance on few resistance genes invites breakdown.

Three wild accessions showed strong resistance to both diseases, carrying gene forms named Pm60, Pm60b and YrU1 in marker checks. Durum hybrids acted as bridges, and repeated crossing with marker guidance produced lines holding single genes or both together. Offspring patterns confirmed the genes still worked in the new background, widening the defence pool for growers.
pmc-13306559:
Tatiana-Maria Coman and colleagues describe in 2026 the staged treatment of a twenty-one-year-old woman with severe skeletal Class II malocclusion. Her problems combined a set-back lower jaw, excess upper jaw height, gum damage, missing back teeth, and jaw joint symptoms. Specialists from orthodontics, surgery, periodontics, and prosthetics sequenced the work.

Care began with a bite splint and orthodontic preparation, then two-jaw surgery using a three-piece upper jaw cut and a lower jaw split procedure. Aligners refined the bite afterwards, while gum grafting and guided bone growth prepared sites for implants. Four years on, root coverage was complete and the skeletal correction held. Implants had integrated well, with function and appearance maintained. The case illustrates how precise planning across specialties handles problems no single field could solve alone.
pmc-13306759:
Jiajun Chen retuned a YOLO detector for tiny objects seen from drones in a 2026 study. Top-down views shrink targets, pack them densely and hide them behind clutter, so standard detectors miss many and place boxes poorly.

The ADA-YOLO design keeps the YOLOv8 backbone but rebuilds the neck and head around a high-resolution P2 branch spanning four scales. A light dynamic upsampler replaces fixed steps, and adaptive fusion calms clashes between scales in reported design goals. The authors present the combined changes as a sharper tool for traffic, farming and rescue flights.
pmc-13307159:
Basma Mostafa routed safety data in battered industrial sensor networks with fuzzy federated learning in a 2026 study. Disaster settings need critical packets favoured without central control, even as edge nodes drop out.

A fuzzy system labels packet criticality in readable rules from sensor readings, while averaging counts only reachable nodes during training. Low-confidence answers fall back to the fuzzy classifier under an auditable rule that guards against under-ranking danger. Tests on grid networks to 200 nodes at fault rates to 50% reached 99.00% critical recall in reported results. The design keeps a clear audit trail, a key need when safety calls are later checked.
pmc-13308059:
Michal Babják and colleagues test on a goat farm in 2026 whether fasting can rescue a failing worm drug. Groups of goats received albendazole under different fasting and dose arrangements, including a twenty-four-hour fast after dosing.

The clearest gain appeared in goats fasted for a full day after receiving the drug. Slowing gut passage keeps the medicine available to the host longer, which raises its effective exposure. Raising the dose also formed part of the farm-level strategy the team examined. New drug classes are unavailable locally, so squeezing more from old ones matters commercially. The authors propose controlled fasting plus dose optimisation as a practical resistance management tool. Their findings come from real farm conditions rather than a laboratory model, which strengthens the advice.
pmc-13308459:

Pairs of reviewers will screen, extract, and grade each study, with a third voice to settle clashes on close calls. Outcomes span cure, failure, death, and harms, split by virus control, CD4 based immune state, and drug resistance in HIV care. Merged proof could guide joint care for people who carry both infections in high burden lands. No results are claimed yet, as the plan comes first.
pmc-13308859:
Andrea Lo Sasso and co-authors explore in 2026 whether breath tests plus explainable artificial intelligence can flag lung cancer and gut or lung ills early, with no needle or cut. They used open data from three sets, fixed skewed class counts, and checked which breath chemicals drove each best model.

Breath holds volatile chemicals that mirror body state, and pattern tools can sort sick from well on those traces in past work. Open scoring of each chemical weight lets doctors see why a model calls a case as it does. Sample swings, weak sensors, and loose standards still block clinic use today. The frame still gives a sound base for breath based test work ahead.
pmc-13308959:
Christian Werner and a large German team report in 2026 on a home exercise programme for older adults with cognitive impairment after hospital rehabilitation. It briefly improved real walking quality, but not walking quantity. One hundred four participants, averaging eighty-two years, were randomised after discharge. Half received exercise plus activity promotion; half received a placebo motor programme.

pmc-13309359:
Sameh Abolfotouh and co-authors survey in 2026 spine surgeons worldwide on nerve watch use during surgery, its pull, and its blocks. Their web poll of AO Spine members ran in April and May 2025.
