Outside firms supply the watch most often, at 59.5 percent, and techs read the traces in 63.6 percent of shops that replied. Most surgeons, 76.3 percent, run a set check list when a signal drops mid case. Cost blocks lead the complaints, at 38.2 percent, ahead of supply snags and thin training. Views ran warm overall in the poll.
pmc-13310559:
PengKun Yu and co-authors assess a modified overlapping stitch for frayed Achilles tendon tears in a 2026 study. Some tears split the tendon into strands like a horse tail, which standard repair handles poorly. The overlapping technique layers the strands before stitching to restore tendon length and strength.

Records for 57 patients treated between May 2020 and May 2024 were reviewed, with follow-up averaging within two years. Standard ankle scores rose sharply after surgery, and the top outcome grade rate reached 98.2 percent in the reported scoring. Complications stayed few: one slow wound healing, two re-tears after falls, and no nerve injury. The authors back the technique for this tear pattern.
pmc-13310659:
Emmanuel Asante-Asamani and co-authors test blood RNA markers to sharpen prostate cancer detection in a 2026 study. The standard PSA blood test flags many harmless cases and was weakly validated in men of African ancestry, who bear the highest disease burden. RNA pieces from the PVT1 gene run high in prostate tumors and may add signal.

Serum from 144 men with raised PSA who faced biopsy was tested for three PVT1 segments, alone and joined with PSA. Statistical models weighed added detection value and risk sorting, with cross-checks for overfitting. The study is the first serum test of these segments in this setting. The authors frame combined markers as a route to fewer needless biopsies, above all in high-burden groups.
pmc-13310759:
David Mhlanga reviews how artificial intelligence could improve public services and governance in Africa in a 2026 study. Many governments face weak systems, fast population growth, and split record keeping, which slow fair service delivery. Digital tools and growing data stores open new paths, but gains depend on strong oversight.

Work draws on a structured review of past studies across welfare, health care, tax, and city services. Smart tools can sharpen targeting, cut waste, and support choices made ahead of need. Gains hinge on data supply, tool skill, office capacity, and human checks. Weak systems can spread bias and exclusion, so plans must fit local needs.
pmc-13310859:
Eman A Mady led a 2026 mouse study on how mother pup separation changes breast milk and pup brain signals. Early life stress can shape later health, yet the paths that carry stress from mother to pup are unclear. Milk is a prime suspect, since it feeds both body and gut germs.

Separated mothers had higher levels of a milk fat called myristic acid. Their pups had fewer helpful gut germs, lower inosine in gut and blood, and lower serotonin gene activity in the front brain. Feeding pups the milk fat alone cut the helpful germ count. Links tie milk change to gut and brain shifts.
pmc-13310959:
Maria Cristina Robin and colleagues describe 19 patients with acid sphingomyelinase deficiency in Argentina in a 2026 case series. The rare storage disease stems from gene faults that block fat breakdown, so fat builds up in many organs. Signs vary by type and age, and diagnosis often comes late.

Cases came from seven centers for diagnoses made from 1988 to 2022. All patients had enlarged liver and spleen, and most had anemia, lung involvement, and low platelet counts. Mean delay from first signs to diagnosis was 7.5 years in length, and two patients were first misread as Gaucher disease. Broader awareness may cut delay.
pmc-13311459:
Kyle T Enriquez and co-authors describe a 2026 case study in which a generative AI tool helped draft a lung transplant infection prevention protocol. The team asked Microsoft Copilot to build a cytomegalovirus prophylaxis plan using only PubMed-indexed sources. They also had the tool model costs across four protocols, including its own. The cost models used simulated patients drawn from a real 165-patient cohort at Vanderbilt University Medical Center.

The AI-drafted protocol rested on genuine evidence with no invented sources. It leaned on older guidance, though, and raised expected cost by an average of 4,740 dollars per patient over current guideline-based plans. The tool also ran its own sensitivity analyses. Those pointed to the drug letermovir as a major cost driver in the model. The authors conclude that, with expert oversight, such tools can support the economic homework stewardship programs often lack staff to do.
pmc-13311659:
Nanuka Jalaghonia, Rumana Huque, and David Daniels wrote a 2026 commentary drawn from the eighth Global Symposium on Health Systems Research. Their question is whether new tools, digital ones and AI, can help health systems in disaster-prone places withstand shocks without leaving more people behind. Such places face repeated climate events, outbreaks, and waves of people forced from their homes, all of which interrupt care.

Talks described digital dashboards, linked data systems, AI decision aids, and local projects that improved detection and kept care going during crises. Such tools can make neglected groups visible to planners. Yet the authors warn that technology alone guarantees nothing. Tools built on data that miss whole groups, or run under weak rules, can widen exclusion instead. They argue new tools pay off only when agencies are ready, rules are clear, safeguards are real, and local people help design what gets built.
pmc-13311959:
Stefan Steiner and colleagues present their 2026 study on a new eye measure, retinal nerve fiber layer thickness slope, and its link to visual field sensitivity in early glaucoma. The slope reads how fast the fiber layer thins along its paths.

The study compared 50 early glaucoma eyes with 139 healthy eyes using wide-field scans that trace fiber routes to field test points. Glaucoma eyes showed lower sensitivity and shallower slopes in both halves of the field. Point-by-point links between slope and sensitivity reached moderate strength, strongest in the upper field near the center. The measure may sharpen early glaucoma detection.
pmc-13312159:
Akinbode Okunola, Elliott Dennis, and Matthew Hille build, in a 2026 paper, a One Health Score for judging how countries regulate medically important antimicrobials. Their framework merges the World Health Organization's importance rankings for human medicine with the animal health rankings of the World Organization for Animal Health. Human health gets the priority seat. Countries are then scored on whether their drug residue limits in food match international Codex standards.

Codex, the European Union, and the United States emerge as the reference points most other countries follow. Just over half of classified drug pairings joined the highly important human category with the top veterinary category. Among those pairings, 21 percent of countries set limits looser than Codex allows. Heavily used farm drugs are regulated most often. Some drugs vital for human care but rare on farms escape attention. The authors frame residue policy as a balance between farm economics and resistance control.
pmc-13312259:
Nadia L. Farag and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study testing phenothiazine dyes as the positive-side liquids, or catholytes, in aqueous organic redox flow batteries. Such batteries could store grid energy cheaply, but organic catholytes often dissolve poorly and break down, so the team screened dyes already sold commercially for a workable candidate.

Azure-A performed best, and adding nicotinamide as a helper compound raised both its solubility and cycle life. Even so, only about half the expected charge capacity could be reached. Spectroscopy showed the active molecules pair up into dimers above a low concentration, leaving the dye effectively able to move just one electron in practice. Impedance analysis pointed to a further loss route: material polymerizing and coating the electrode. The authors map both limits for future dye design.
pmc-13312359:
Ruixin Mao and co-authors study, in a 2026 cross-sectional survey, how problematic smartphone use relates to mental health among Chinese senior high school students. The team surveyed 34,831 students in grades 10 to 12 in Tianmen, measuring phone habits, emotional growth mindset, well-being, and depressive symptoms under a dual-factor view of mental health.

Latent profile analysis sorted students into four groups, from very low depression with high well-being to high depression with low well-being. Heavy phone use was tied directly to poorer mental health, and also indirectly through a weaker belief that emotions can change and be managed. Having been left behind by migrant parents strengthened the first link in that chain. The authors argue that cutting screen time alone will not fix the risk for such students.
pmc-13312459:
F.J. Bruning and colleagues track, in a 2026 longitudinal study, how everyday walking recovers after total knee replacement. Surgery aims to restore mobility in end-stage knee osteoarthritis, but most follow-up relies on self-report rather than measured walking. Thirty-one patients wore inertial sensors before surgery and one and two years afterward, and their walking was compared with 31 healthy participants without joint pain.

One year after surgery, the patients' daily-life gait speed still sat 0.10 meters per second below the healthy group's, though it had improved by the same margin from before the operation. Stride length and stride timing also improved, while the longest walking bouts did not, and nothing further changed by year two. The authors judge the remaining gap minor and the gains modest, partly because these patients were already fairly functional before surgery.
pmc-13312759:
Sara Henricsson and colleagues explore, in a 2026 qualitative study, how older adults judge the faces and teeth of people their own age. Faces and dental appearance steer first impressions at every age, yet how seniors read those features in their peers, rather than in the young, had barely been asked.

The team interviewed 20 adults aged 68 to 76 drawn from a Swedish aging study and analyzed the conversations thematically. Three themes emerged. Charisma and personality could overshadow appearance entirely, warmth and expression mattering more than any feature. At the same time, judging by looks came easily: missing teeth or visibly poor oral health triggered assumptions about lifestyle, vulnerability, and self-care. Participants also expected peers to follow age-appropriate norms. The authors show peer judgment balancing kindness against quiet social rules.
pmc-13312959:
Eleanor V Thomas and Devesh C Pant write a 2026 scientific commentary on a blood biomarker study in motor neuron disease, the family that includes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The disease is devastating, patchy in presentation, and slow to diagnose. Progress has been blocked by the lack of easy, trustworthy blood markers that mirror its biology, since most discovery work relied on spinal fluid.

The commented study used an ultrasensitive multiplex platform to profile serum from 48 patients in the Scottish register and 38 controls, checking findings against a second assay. Neurofilament light chain stayed the single best marker, with diagnostic accuracy near 0.92 on the reported scale, but the wider protein signature around it captured more of the disease's variety. The commentators argue such multidimensional blood panels could speed diagnosis, sort patients by biology, and sharpen trial monitoring.
pmc-13313259:
Salar Saadi Hussain and Zahra Abdulqader Amin present a 2026 gene study of endometrial cancer in Kurdish women. Cancer of the womb lining varies widely, with many gene and gene-control changes, and data from this group of women were thin.

The study drew on 70 confirmed cases and tested DNA from blood. Nine cases picked for young onset or a family pattern of cancer got full exome sequencing, built through capture with tagged probes. Five variants of note turned up in five genes: CHEK2, POLE, MUTYH, USF3, and PLA2G2A. They included a missing amino acid in CHEK2, a double copy change in MUTYH, and single changes in the other three genes. The finds give a first map of inherited risk in this group and hint at which women may gain from gene screening.
pmc-13313559:
Hideyoshi Kaga and colleagues pinpoint, in a 2026 imaging study, where in the brain insulin resistance lives in type 2 diabetes. Brain insulin helps regulate appetite and body-wide glucose, and the hypothalamus is its control hub, but which of its nuclei fail was unknown. Using high-resolution functional MRI while volunteers inhaled insulin through the nose, the team compared 21 Japanese men with diabetes against 20 healthy controls.

In healthy men, insulin quieted activity in the posterior hypothalamic nucleus within five minutes. In the men with diabetes, that early suppression simply did not happen, marking a local failure of insulin responsiveness. Structural scans in a separate older group found the same posterior region shrunken in diabetic participants. Two independent methods thus converge on one small brain area. The authors propose the posterior hypothalamus as a candidate seat of brain insulin resistance, to be tested in longer and interventional studies.
pmc-13313759:
Fangfang Wang, Fengmei Ge, and Xuebin Wang present a 2026 case report, with literature review, of organizing pneumonia that returned nine years after its appearance alongside rheumatoid arthritis. Their patient, a 65-year-old woman, arrived with painful joints and recurring fever. Lung imaging showed right-sided inflammation that antibiotics failed to touch. A lung biopsy established the condition, a pattern of lung injury that is an uncommon companion to rheumatoid arthritis.

Steroid treatment with a taper, combined with the arthritis drug iguratimod, settled her fever and cough. Follow-up scans improved while her arthritis stayed quiet on maintenance therapy. Nine years later, fever and cough returned with pneumonia in both lungs. A second biopsy through an airway scope confirmed the pattern had relapsed, even though arthritis activity remained low. The authors stress that tissue diagnosis is key in such cases, since infection treatment alone would have missed the process twice.
pmc-13314759:
Habib Md Ahashan and a large surveillance team chart, in a 2026 retrospective study, three years of acute watery diarrhea at Cumilla General Hospital in Bangladesh, from 2022 to 2024. The condition floods hospitals seasonally and can signal cholera, so the team mined routine surveillance records across all ages to find who arrives, when, and with what pre-treatment history.

The burden fell heaviest on children under five, who made up most cases. Only about five percent of tested cases proved positive for cholera on rapid tests, and limited culture capacity left the true cholera share uncertain. A striking practice pattern stood out: ninety percent of patients had already taken antibiotics before reaching the hospital, a habit that feeds resistance while rarely matching the actual cause. Case loads peaked in the monsoon and post-monsoon periods. The authors argue for stronger laboratory confirmation and tighter antibiotic discipline in diarrhea care.
pmc-13315659:

Severe rectus diastasis with ventral hernia is usually reinforced with mesh, but plastic material carries infection risk. Skin harvested during tummy surgery offers a biologic alternative. Their patient, a 36-year-old woman after three pregnancies, had a separation, 15 centimeters during surgery and 19 on CT, plus a navel hernia and skin excess.

She underwent tummy surgery with an own-tissue graft placed beneath the fascia to reinforce the repair. One week after surgery, navel necrosis required cleaning and local-flap repair, after which recovery went smoothly. At one year, no return of the defect showed on exam or ultrasound, and the patient reported functional and aesthetic satisfaction. The authors present the technique as durable even for large defects, and note the absent mesh proved advantageous when necrosis struck.
pmc-13315959:
Ruihao Lan and colleagues added polydopamine in stages in 2026 to help lab-grown lung alveolar organoids from human stem cells mature. Such organoids model lung growth and disease and speed drug hunting, yet full maturity is hard to reach, and the mussel-inspired material offers sticky, antioxidant help.

A polydopamine coating first produced more early foregut spheroids by strengthening contact between the gel and the surface, with gene data showing richer cell and matrix interaction. Later, polydopamine nanoparticles mixed into the gel at the lung progenitor stage cut harmful reactive oxygen. The timed, two-step use matched each growth stage.
pmc-13316159:
Wolfgang Trapp, Susanne Röder, and Franziska Wimmer ran a proof-of-concept study in 2026 on a playful phone app that helps people face phobias through inverted augmented reality. Exposure therapy works well for phobic disorders, yet access, acceptance, and transfer to daily life hold it back.

Twenty people with varied phobias followed a multiple-baseline plan. At a random start point they used a phone AR app, or sometimes a VR headset, to collect color-coded virtual objects while moving through places tied to their own fears. Mixed model checks showed a clear drop in self-reported situational fear after the game-like practice, with a large within-person effect.
pmc-13316459:
Simon Scheiter, Julia Brugger, and Thomas Hickler model, in a 2026 study, how stable the world's plant zones stayed through the Quaternary, the last 2.6 million years of ice age swings. They test whether long-stable zones explain why some places hold so many plant species today.

Tropical forests, deserts, and boreal and temperate woods stayed put over wide areas, while northern Europe and North America churned as ice came and went. Stable zones matched rich plant life in tropical rainforests, but the global link stayed weak. Fire and local variety, they suggest, must share the credit.
pmc-13316759:
Yuanxia Wang and a team of Chinese researchers compared, in a 2026 study, mulberry wine made from whole pulp against wine made from juice alone, tracking quality through brewing and storage. Mulberries spoil fast, so wine making is a key route to value, and the starting form may shape the result.

Sixty-three scent compounds were found, with pulp adding herbal notes thanks to stem pieces. pmc-13316859:
Diala Bani Mustafa and colleagues introduce, in 2026, a laser method for coating surgical mesh with an antibacterial carbon layer. Their one-step process uses a laser and a toner-like donor to lay porous carbon onto the mesh without melting it. Microscopy and Raman testing confirmed continuous coverage over fibres and knots, with thickness up to about forty micrometres. Tests with Escherichia coli gave a surprising pattern, where mid-range thickness near fifteen micrometres left the fewest living bacteria. The authors present the method as a programmable coating route for three-dimensional plastics.
pmc-13317359:
Ahmet Yesildag and Ece Ugurluoglu Aldogan studied hospital staff who go past their job lines in a 2026 paper. Hospitals run lean, so extra effort from staff, beyond the written role, keeps care afloat. What sparks that effort, and what chokes it, matters for every ward.

The pair traced how leader behavior flows into extra-role acts. Two middle steps were in view: how silent staff stay about problems, and how engaged they feel in the work. A leadership model with five named parts framed the leader side. Their chain model may help managers lift effort without burning staff out.
pmc-13318059:
Mohammad Ismail and Waleed Kattan evaluate, in 2026, whether practice resuscitation drills improved real emergency performance at a Saudi tertiary hospital. Mock code simulations are widely used to prepare teams, yet evidence from adult hospitals in Saudi Arabia, tied to actual Code Blue events rather than drill scores, was scarce.

The team compared 37 adult Code Blue records from 2025, before and after an in-situ simulation programme began. Return of circulation and 28-day mortality did not change significantly. Process measures improved sharply, including documentation of two-minute pulse checks, rhythm identification and giving epinephrine for non-shockable rhythms, which reached full compliance. The authors recommend keeping and expanding simulation training to strengthen team performance, while noting survival gains were not shown.
pmc-13318559:
Casey A Clarke and co-authors analyse, in 2026, video of knee ligament injuries in men's Major League Soccer in the United States and Canada. Anterior cruciate ligament tears often end seasons, yet how they happen in this league was little described. Prevention programmes need that detail.

Across five and a half seasons, 65 injuries were identified and footage existed for 33. Most injuries involved no direct contact with the knee. Defensive pressing and offensive driving were the commonest actions at injury. The knee was usually bent and collapsing inward under load. Indirect-contact injuries all involved force to the upper body. Injuries clustered in the second half or overtime, more often on grass, with two peaks across the season. Training to control knee position during pressing may help.
pmc-13318759:

The team tested a flow turbulence measure from vector flow imaging. They asked whether it can flag those inner vessels without invasive tests.

They analysed 108 plaques, of which 82 had inner vessels on sensitive microvascular imaging. Turbulence was measured before, at, and after each plaque. The downstream value at the end of the heartbeat cycle ran lower in plaques with inner vessels. A combined model reached an AUC of 0.830 in internal checks. After correction, the figure was 0.768 in their validation. The authors propose the measure as a possible noninvasive marker.
pmc-13318859:

The team produced the outer part of glycoprotein B from the HeN1 strain in CHO cells. Mice were immunised, and fused cells yielded an antibody named 1G4. Tests showed strong specificity and reactivity. The antibody recognised multiple virus strains broadly. Labelled with a fluorescent tag and paired with another antibody, it tracked virus entry into HeLa cells under the microscope. The authors offer it as a reagent for mechanism research and immune detection.
pmc-13319859:
Elsahoryi, Abu-Alhija, and Alhaj survey exercise addiction risk in hobby athletes in Jordan in twenty twenty-six. Compulsive exercise can harm mind and body, yet it is rarely studied in Arabic speaking groups. More than one thousand adults from gyms across Jordan filled surveys on exercise habits, mood, and food choices. Close to half screened as at risk on a standard inventory.

At risk athletes had far higher stress, low mood, and anxiety scores. They chose food for performance and weight control more than for taste or custom. Men, heavy exercisers, and the highly stressed were most apt to screen at risk. The authors warn the tool screens rather than diagnoses. Living alone and pleasure in food seemed protective.
pmc-13320259:

Mild heat plus immune priming before surgery may shrink the mass and wake body defenses at once.

Gene checks showed an immune alarm switch runs high in this cancer, so a particle was loaded with a switch trigger plus a light active dye. A coat made from tumor cell skin, rich in an eat me signal, steers the particle to tumors and to immune trainer cells. Near infrared light then adds mild heat and cell stress, which fires the alarm in both tumor and trainer cells.
pmc-13320459:
Basavanna C and co-authors present a large text set of classical Kannada verse for language software in a 2026 data article. Kannada is a major tongue of south India with a rich verse past, yet machine ready sets for its old works barely exist. Verses from three verse forms that span the eleventh to the twentieth century were digitized, checked by hand, and paired with scholar written readings.

The set holds 24746 verses plus 22369 readings in a shared structured form, each verse tagged by form, author, and source. Forms cover short moral songs, three line verses, and a famed twentieth century wisdom poem set. The set can train tools for meaning match, logic links, search, and text making in a low resource tongue.
pmc-13320659:
Yue Bao and co-authors describe an unusual heart tracing in a 2026 case report of a young child. After repair of a hole between the heart's lower chambers, the 3-year-old developed complete heart block plus a right bundle branch block. A pacemaker using left bundle branch pacing, a more natural method favoured in children, was fitted.

During fitting, the pacing lead touched only the surface of the wall between the chambers, without deep fixing. The tracing then showed a right bundle pattern, which the team calls rare and unlike the usual left bundle pattern seen with standard pacing. No matching cases were found in prior reports, so the note alerts pacing teams to the pattern.
pmc-13321159:
Chinedu Ogbonnia Egwu and co-authors test how mixed malaria infections respond to drugs in a 2026 laboratory study. Rising tolerance to malaria drugs threatens progress against the disease, yet natural infections often carry several parasite strains at once. The team asked whether resistant strains in a mix drive the whole response.

Fifteen Gambian field samples plus two lab strains were exposed to standard drugs at low doses, and survival and reinvasion were measured. Resistant types shifted drug response clearly, most sharply for chloroquine in mixed cultures. Field samples with resistant markers survived more and reinvaded red cells at high rates after low dose exposure. Mixed infections thus cannot be judged by their weakest strain.
pmc-13321459:
Heng Shao and colleagues study pathways from childhood trauma to self-injury in teenagers with depression in a 2026 survey. Non-suicidal self-injury is a known risk in this group, but the steps between early trauma and later self-harm were unclear. The team surveyed 2308 adolescents treated at 12 psychiatric hospitals in China.

Teenagers who self-injured scored higher on trauma, sleep disturbance, and anxiety measures than those who did not. Trauma scores tracked with self-injury severity, poor sleep, and anxiety. Mediation tests found indirect paths running through sleep disturbance and anxiety, alone and in sequence. Emotional abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, and physical neglect each stayed linked to self-injury severity in adjusted models.
pmc-13321559:
Pau Moreno-Martin and colleagues ask residents, relatives, staff, and directors of Catalan nursing homes how person-centered care fared across the pandemic, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Thirty homes and three hundred thirty-five respondents scored care retrospectively for before, during, and after COVID-19.

The scores trace the trauma: one hundred seventy-six before, a plunge to one hundred thirty-six during, and a partial recovery to one hundred seventy-one after. Bigger homes and those enduring more months under red-code restrictions lost most. Homes that transferred more residents out paradoxically lost less, and, oddly, a higher physician ratio accompanied deeper drops, perhaps marking harder-hit facilities. Homes that fell furthest rebounded most. The authors urge crisis plans that protect dignity and autonomy alongside safety.
pmc-13322559:
Julie Y. L. Chow and co-authors refine how learning models handle graded outcomes in a 2026 psychology study. Classic associative models simplify learning to yes or no outcomes, such as recovery or not, and can track only an average when real outcomes vary in size. The team built a distributed version that links cues to a spread of outcome sizes.

Across four contingency learning experiments, the distributed model fit human data better than a simple delta model for nearly every participant. Keeping the full range of experienced values, rather than a single mean, seems to match how people actually encode events. The result sharpens theories of causal learning in messy, real world settings.
pmc-13323159:
Shuai Jin and colleagues track, in 2026, how often malnutrition appears on American death records for a combined heart, kidney and metabolic syndrome. Deaths tied to that syndrome fell overall across recent decades, yet how often poor nutrition was documented among them was unclear. The team used national multiple-cause mortality files spanning 1999 to 2023.

The adjusted death rate followed a U shape, falling into the early 2010s and then climbing steeply by 2023. Malnutrition's share of these deaths roughly doubled even as the total declined. Adults over sixty-five accounted for most deaths, while documentation rose fastest among younger decedents. Rates stayed highest in Black adults, grew relatively faster in White adults, and accelerated most in the West. The authors urge routine nutritional assessment in high-burden groups.
pmc-13324259:
Nawaz and Asokan test ways to improve gulmohar biodiesel for engines. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with Delonix regia biodiesel. A B20 blend of diesel and this biodiesel is the base.

Two fixes were tried: partial hydrogenation and a cetane booster. Gas tests measured how the fat mix changed with hydrogenation. Engine tests compared plain diesel and three blend forms. Output and emissions were the key traits in those tests. A design tool helped tune for the best mix. Gains over the plain blend are reported in the work.
pmc-13324459:
Chang Hyun Nam and colleagues map the genome changes behind spread in uveal melanoma, the most common primary eye cancer in adults, in a 2026 analysis. Risk tools today lean on large copy number changes and miss finer details.

Whole-genome sequencing of 40 primary tumors and matched healthy tissue catalogued losses, gains, and structural breaks. Two fresh markers stood out: hidden BAP1 damage, including truncations older tests missed, and gains on chromosome 1q. Timing work showed many gains arose early in life, decades before diagnosis. Early 6p gain often excluded BAP1 damage and meant a better outlook. Spread risk may be set early, which aids detection and prognosis.
pmc-13325159:
Jin Hee Lee and co-authors tune the polarity of a silver-based interlayer for organic solar cells. The layer between electrode and active film can make or break a cell's efficiency. pmc-13325459:

pmc-13325859:
Lisa Schellenberg and co-authors chart land-made pollutants in the coastal waters of Curaçao in a 2026 study. Drugs, pesticides, and human waste products wash from shore to sea, yet their spread around an island was unmeasured.

pmc-13326459:
Kim San Lim, Htin Kyaw Khine, and Barbara Helen Rosario studied advance care planning in the severely frail in a 2026 paper. pmc-13327159:

pmc-13327659:

pmc-13327859:

pmc-13328259:
Zheng Sun and Fan Zhang construct a scoring system for volleyball coaches' pre-match decisions in a 2026 study. pmc-13328359:

pmc-13328459:
Süleyman Bodur and four co-authors shared a study in twenty twenty-six. They measured a herbicide residue called fenuron in carrot juice. They were blunt about measurement error. It got back nearly all the analyte. It had the tightest precision too. Detection limits landed in the hundredths of a milligram per kilogram. The authors make the methodological moral plain. pmc-13329359:
Maarten J. M. Christenhusz and many collaborators present the genome sequence of sheep's-bit, Jasione montana, in a 2026 report. pmc-13330659:

pmc-13331359:
Mehmet Tatlı and Selin Bulut report pufferfish poisoning far inland in eastern Turkey in a 2026 case series. Three men came to a Van hospital in December 2020 after eating a silver-cheeked toadfish that a seller mistook for an edible type. Van sits over 1000 km from the coast in the account given.

Despite intensive care with ventilation and strong blood pressure drugs, he died on day four from unstoppable cardiac arrest. The other two ate less and no liver, had mild signs, and recovered fully within 24 hours. Seller training and supply checks are urged.
pmc-13332359:

Transverse colon volvulus causes mechanical bowel blockage, but bedside and plain X-ray findings are often vague, making preoperative diagnosis hard. CT scanning can pinpoint the transition point, the swirling mesentery sign, added bowel involvement, and signs that bowel is in danger. The scan showed marked dilation of small bowel and right colon upstream from a left-sided mesenteric whirl. The twist involved the transverse colon in a bird-beak shape plus a nearby upper jejunal loop, with a displaced vein.
pmc-13332659:
Craig Basman and colleagues introduce a 2026 mini-focus issue on valvular heart disease in JACC: Case Reports. pmc-13333259:
Andi Ade Wijaya Ramlan and colleagues test a 2026 adapted healing protocol against standard care in child major gut surgery. Care around surgery in such cases often involves prolonged fasting, delayed movement, and invasive monitoring, which may raise stress responses and slow healing. Early movement was significantly faster in the healing group. pmc-13333359:
Rachel Sayko Adams and colleagues tracked recorded alcohol use disorder diagnoses in United States insurance claims from 2016 to 2023, split by disability, in a 2026 study. pmc-13333459:
Akihiro Maeda and co-authors recount a urethral cancer held in check for nearly three years in a 2026 case report. Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the urethra is an uncommon tumor, and with so few cases there is no playbook for advanced disease with lymph node spread.

pmc-13333859:
Shoemaker and nine co-authors track COVID infections and vaccine protection in dental workers during the Omicron surge, in a study from twenty twenty-six. pmc-13334159:

pmc-13334759:

pmc-13335559:

pmc-13336559:

pmc-13336959:

pmc-13337059:

pmc-13337659:

pmc-13337759:

pmc-13337859:

pmc-13338759:

pmc-13339159:

pmc-13339459:

pmc-13340659:

pmc-13341359:

pmc-13341759:

pmc-13341859:

pmc-13342059:

pmc-13342259:

pmc-13342559:

pmc-13343159:

pmc-13343859:

pmc-13343959:

pmc-13346059:

pmc-13347159:

pmc-13347659:

pmc-13347959:

pmc-13348459:

pmc-13349959:

Her legs showed the orange-peel texture and groove sign of eosinophilic fasciitis. The rare disorder thickens the deep tissue under skin. Blood work revealed an IgA-kappa monoclonal gammopathy and heavy protein in the urine. Nerve studies confirmed carpal tunnel syndrome in both wrists. The trio also raises the spectre of amyloidosis.

Steroids brought marked relief, fitting the fasciitis pattern. Marrow study settled on a benign precursor gammopathy, and kidney biopsy excluded amyloid and every monoclonal kidney injury pattern tested, arguing against kidney damage from the clone. Imaging, the authors note, can prove fascial involvement and steer biopsy choices when patients hesitate. The case shows how signature skin signs steered the diagnosis away from closer mimics.
pmc-13394259:
Giulia Maria Ruggeri leads an seventeen-author pig study testing whether donor lungs on an external perfusion circuit can be graded lobe by lobe instead of as a whole organ. Ex vivo lung perfusion lets centres assess and revive marginal donor lungs, but mixed blood sampling hides local failure. In five healthy pigs the team cannulated each lung vein separately on the circuit, then clamped first one lower bronchus and then an upper one to fake localised injury.

At baseline lobar and mixed samples matched. Clamping drove the affected lobe to near-total non-aeration with shunt approaching complete, and its oxygen measure collapsed, while the mixed sample stayed deceptively comfortable. Overall lung mechanics and pressures worsened, and tissue from the starved lower lobe showed congestion and bleeding. The authors say lobar sampling pinpoints injury and could sharpen transplant decisions.
pmc-13394559:
Feng Wang and colleagues trace a non-coding RNA pathway that promotes glioma growth in a 2026 study. Glioma, the most common primary malignant brain tumor, invades aggressively and recurs often, and new molecular targets are urgently needed.

The long non-coding RNA CROCCP2 was markedly raised in glioma tissues and cell lines, boosting proliferation, migration, and invasion. It acted by soaking up miR-5584-5p, freeing the gene HOXD11, which then suppressed autophagy as shown by lower LC3B-II and Beclin1 and higher p62. Blocking CROCCP2 or HOXD11 reversed these effects, nominating a new therapeutic axis.
pmc-13395259:
Yan Wang and co-authors study, in 2026, why women drift away from an online symptom program for ovarian cancer. The program, Nurse WRITE, pairs nurse guidance with web tools over eight weeks. The team re-read data from 68 women whose cancer had returned. They tracked board posts, site use, care plans, and symptom control.

Schooling level tracked with several forms of taking part, from word counts to finished care plans. Worse health, busy family life, and site troubles were the top blocks. Many low users quit at set stages, such as goal setting. Women who took part more also felt better symptom control. The authors urge extra help for women with less schooling.
pmc-13395559:
Sayaka Honda and co-authors recount, in 2026, a robot-aided heart valve swap in a man with a severely curved spine. The 61-year-old had bad breathlessness from a leaky aortic valve. His chest cavity was markedly narrow, with just a hand's breadth between breastbone and spine. Such tight space usually rules out robot work.

The team shifted one robot arm lower to gain a better angle and cut the aorta lengthwise for room. Retraction and suction from the bedside crew exposed the valve ring. A tissue valve went in without mishap, and the man left hospital on day twenty. The authors say careful planning opens robot care to bent chests.
pmc-13396359:
Fu and team make, in 2026, cellulose fibers with spider-silk-like toughness by copying the helical nanostructure of cherry bark. Cellulose from plant biomass is strong but brittle, with toughness usually below 50 megajoules per cubic meter. Using a scalable microfluidic spinning method, the team gave new cellulose fibers a two-way aligned internal structure, with molecular chains running along two directions instead of one.

The two-way structure spreads stress and suppresses crack growth as the fiber stretches, according to their experiments and molecular simulations. The resulting fibers reached a fracture strain of 41 percent alongside a tensile strength of 553 megapascals, a combination ordinary cellulose cannot achieve. Together these yielded a toughness of 184 megajoules per cubic meter, the same order of magnitude as natural spider silk. The improvement carried over from single fibers to woven fabrics, pointing toward greener textiles, car parts, and aerospace materials.
pmc-13396459:
Mantena and team build, in 2026, a multi-ethnic reference map of germline diversity in the genes for T cell receptors, the molecules that let T cells recognize targets. The receptor loci are repetitive and hard to sequence, so variation there has been little charted. Using long-read data from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium and the All of Us program, covering 2,719 donors, they assembled a catalog of alleles across the V, D, and J gene segments.

The map revealed amino acid changes at almost every position within the V genes, with allele frequencies differing by group. Statistical tests found evidence of natural selection on these genes, including balancing and positive selection concentrated in the alpha chain locus. That is unusual for receptors usually assumed to diversify only within each person. Allelic differences changed T cell traits, including thymic fate and surface receptor levels, linking variation to immune response.
pmc-13396559:
Nattasha A. Mattaka and co-authors studied thyroid changes in the sickest hospital patients at a referral center in northeastern Tanzania, in a 2026 cohort study. In severe illness the thyroid hormone pattern often shifts even though the gland itself is healthy, a state called non-thyroidal illness syndrome that may mark a worse outlook.

The team enrolled 120 adults admitted to the medical intensive care unit between October 2024 and March 2025, testing three thyroid measures within a day of arrival. They recorded how common the syndrome was and hunted for traits that predicted death. Data from sub-Saharan Africa on this question were scarce, which the authors set out to remedy.
pmc-13396759:
Choi and co-authors demonstrate, in 2026, SlAction, a contact-free system that detects obstructive sleep apnea from wall-mounted near-infrared video, with analysis running on the device itself. Sleep apnea affects nearly one billion people, yet over 80 percent of moderate-to-severe cases go undiagnosed because standard testing needs an overnight laboratory study. SlAction instead reads the body movements that accompany respiratory arousals as stand-ins for breathing disturbances.

The team trained and validated the system on 936 clinical recordings totaling more than 5,000 hours from three hospitals. Across internal and external test sets, it cut apnea-hypopnea index estimation error versus prior video approaches and improved classification of severity and positional apnea, while running faster on low-cost hardware. The comparison matters because home sleep tests carry a 39 percent diagnostic error rate in a recent 20-study meta-analysis. The authors position the system as privacy-preserving screening for home use.
pmc-13396859:
Wettersten and team test, in 2026, whether kidney tubule secretion markers can predict potassium problems and treatment response in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. They used data from the TOPCAT trial: 372 participants, mean age 70 years, of whom 179 were randomized to the drug spironolactone. A summary score combined urine-to-plasma ratios of nine endogenous secretion markers measured at baseline.

In adjusted models, the score showed no link with changes in serum potassium, the study's central safety question, nor with incident high potassium during follow-up. It also failed to predict symptom improvement, natriuretic peptide changes, or heart and kidney events in the cohort. The single significant finding was modest: higher capacity tracked with a 3.5-point lower heart failure questionnaire score at twelve months, of uncertain weight. The authors conclude these biomarkers should not guide spironolactone decisions or risk prediction in this group.
pmc-13397759:
Huili Zhu and others tie Toll-like receptor signals with Eimeria tenella harm power in chickens in a 2026 study. This fierce coccidiosis agent settles in the cecum and imposes major poultry losses, yet Toll-like roles during illness were poorly defined.

Sick specific-pathogen-free chickens were watched for cecal lesions, oocyst output, and clinic signs, while ten Toll-like sensors and linked immune genes were read in cecum and spleen over time. Link reads tied sensor levels to harm marks, with marked clinic signs but no deaths. Poultry scientists gain innate immune aims for gut parasite control.
pmc-13398959:
Tomofumi Takayoshi and co-authors present a young woman whose inherited diabetes carries two gene variants at once. Their 2026 case report concerns a 21-year-old with early-onset diabetes of the maturity-onset type, called MODY, which accounts for at least 1 to 5 percent of diabetes cases in the estimates cited. Single-gene causes are the rule, and dual-variant cases are rarely reported.

Whole-exome and Sanger sequencing found a disease-causing HNF1A variant (p.Arg159Trp) plus a second variant in NEUROD1, both genes steering insulin-producing cell development. The team modelled how each change alters its protein's surface charge and stability. Pinning the exact genetic mix matters, since MODY type steers drug choice and family screening.
pmc-13400159:
Katelyn Eisner and colleagues report that the obesity drug semaglutide weakens bones in obese mice, and that the harm lifts once the drug stops, in this 2026 study. The team treated obese male mice with semaglutide for four weeks, comparing them with mice fed the same reduced calories. They measured femur mass, stiffness, and strength. A second cohort was assessed six weeks after treatment ended.

Semaglutide-treated mice ended with lighter, weaker, less stiff femurs than controls, and the deficits exceeded those of the calorie-matched mice. Ordinary weight loss alone does not explain them. Blood markers of bone-building activity fell in parallel. Six weeks after the drug stopped, femur weight, strength, and stiffness were indistinguishable from vehicle-treated animals. That shows the effect depends on continued exposure rather than permanent damage. The authors stop short of clinical claims but call for human studies.
pmc-13401059:
Xuehua Ye and colleagues build, in 2026, machine learning models to predict Parkinson disease stage five years after a dopamine imaging scan, using routine real-world data. Parkinson progression varies hugely between patients, complicating care. Most earlier models used research cohorts whose data differ from everyday clinic records, and targeted less practical measures.

Records and imaging from 343 real-world patients were harmonized with 134 patients from a research cohort, yielding 83 shared features. Two ensemble methods were trained to forecast the standard Hoehn and Yahr stage. Models fed two years of follow-up data performed best, with early stage, gait severity and select imaging features carrying the most weight. The authors see prognostic value in ordinary data, within limits.
pmc-13401159:
Lan Li and colleagues report 2026 laboratory work on Gomisin G, a compound from the fruit of Schisandra chinensis, and its effect on pancreatic cancer cells. Pancreatic cancer kills most patients within five years, so new drug candidates are badly needed.

Using colony formation tests, flow cytometry, and protein analysis, the team found that Gomisin G slowed cell growth, paused cells in the G1 phase, and triggered apoptosis, which is programmed cell death. In mice carrying human PANC-1 tumors, the compound shrank tumor growth. Gene and imaging studies showed it pushed the growth protein YAP toward breakdown through LATS1, lowering YAP target genes such as CTGF and CYR61 in the Hippo pathway.
pmc-13401559:
Carlos A Rueda-Pérez and a large team of co-authors wrote a 2026 methods study on photographing fresh human brain specimens for three-dimensional reconstruction by photogrammetry. Fresh brains cannot be re-imaged at leisure, so the camera and software settings must be right the first time.

The team systematically varied alignment settings in the Metashape software, testing 12,600 configuration combinations and 63,000 alignments. Their recommended setup uses four photo sets: two with the brain in anatomical position, at specimen level and 30 centimetres above with a 30-degree camera tilt. Two matching sets with the underside facing up. Rotating the brain 3 degrees between shots yields 120 images per set. Processing starts without masks at medium precision; if alignment fails, one mask per image tracing the brain's outline is the fallback.
pmc-13401659:
Li Zou and co-authors published a 2026 study of peptidylprolyl isomerase A, a protein-folding enzyme called PPIA, in lung adenocarcinoma, combining data mining with laboratory validation. They asked whether the protein drives the cancer's behaviour and predicts patient outcomes.

PPIA was overexpressed in tumour tissue and tied to shorter overall and progression-free survival. Its levels tracked with copy number changes, DNA methylation, methylation-enzyme activity, and RNA modification genes. Higher PPIA went with lower immune cell infiltration and lower immune gene expression, hinting at an immune-dampening role, and drug sensitivity analyses suggested it could predict treatment response. Because PPIA levels also tracked with DNA damage repair genes, the team ran cell experiments, which showed that knocking PPIA down makes cancer cells more sensitive to radiation.
pmc-13402659:
Emna Ketata and colleagues evaluate ferrociphenol, an iron-bearing organometallic compound, as a candidate for slowing excess melanin production in skin. Melanin guards against ultraviolet light and mops up free radicals, yet overproduction drives disorders such as melasma and age spots, and current blockers suffer from weak stability or side effects. The enzyme tyrosinase runs the rate-limiting step of pigment making, which makes it the natural target.

Ferrociphenol, also called Fc-diOH, first drew notice for killing breast cancer cells in culture at low doses, though it lacks the chain that makes its cousin tamoxifen-like. The study pairs biological testing with molecular docking, computer fitting of the compound against its target, to judge antimelanogenic promise. Zebrafish, whose pigment cells mirror mammalian ones and show color change plainly, frame the biological side of the work described.
pmc-13402859:
Anita Walden and colleagues report lessons from turning school-based physical fitness testing into trustworthy real-world health evidence. School fitness data cover nearly all children, a rare inclusive source, yet messy formats keep it out of electronic health records. The team worked with the standards body HL7 to build a Domain Analysis Model, a formal map of the field agreed by the people who run, use, and study school testing.

Stakeholders spent long hours defining terms and critical data elements, with successes and friction the authors recount honestly. The model alone does not create a learning health system, but it lays the shared language such a system needs. Their vision points toward a youth fitness learning system that folds test data back into better practice. They also generalize the steps for other nontraditional data sources seeking a path into health research.
pmc-13403159:
The EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain updates the risk assessment for emerging and novel brominated flame retardants in food. Helle Katrine Knutsen leads the panel authorship. These chemicals make consumer goods resist fire, but they turn up in the environment, in food, and in people. Several older formulations are now banned. The European Commission asked EFSA to refresh its 2010 to 2012 assessments family by family.

Earlier opinions in the series covered four other flame retardant families. This fifth one revisits the novel group last assessed in 2012. It follows a targeted consultation in spring 2026, whose comments are answered in an annex. Because the families share chemistry and effects, the panel plans a further opinion on whether combined exposure should be judged as a mixture. That judgment would use EFSA combined-exposure guidance.
pmc-13403359:
Pernilla Alencar Siljehag and co-authors interview older Swedes about the slow, wavering decision to accept home care for the first time. Sweden funds home care for all after municipal assessment, yet many people wait until needs are extensive before applying. Fourteen men and women aged 67 to 94 who started home care in Stockholm in 2024 described the phase before that first application.

Reflexive thematic analysis produced the theme of coming to terms as a movement that ebbs and flows: acceptance rose and receded rather than settling once. Some handled the shift pragmatically; others had to redefine who they were, and family or friends often supplied the push that finally moved them. Some began services still ambivalent. The authors say services should expect hesitation and design first contact for people mid-negotiation with themselves.
pmc-13403459:
Hye Seong and co-authors used Korean health records in 2026 to test whether fatty liver types differ in sepsis risk. Their cohort held more than 4.3 million adults screened in 2012 and tracked for ten years. Liver types split by metabolic risk and by how much alcohol a person drank.

Every fatty liver type tied to more hospital stays for sepsis than no fatty liver. Alcohol-related disease carried the highest added risk, at about one and a half times the base rate. Mixed metabolic and alcohol types came next. The split suggests that infection watch plans should differ by liver type, not treat all cases alike.
pmc-13403559:
Carlos Solórzano Flores and co-authors told in 2026 of a woman whose low blood calcium after neck surgery would not lift. The 35-year-old had repeat surgery for thyroid cancer that had come back. Large calcium and vitamin D doses failed to fix her levels.

Her parathyroid hormone sat low, which first pointed to gland damage from surgery. Only on day six did a magnesium test run, held back by scarce lab means. Her magnesium was very low, and topping it up quickly raised calcium and partly restored hormone output. The lesson is to check magnesium early when calcium stays low.
pmc-13403759:
Iaron Leal Seabra and co-authors tracked syphilis rates in Brazil in 2026, covering cases in pregnant women and newborns from 2011 to 2022. Reports logged 586,855 cases in pregnancy and 272,491 cases passed to babies over that span. The team mapped yearly rates for the whole country and each region.

Rates in pregnancy rose across Brazil, though the yearly climb slowed over time. Newborn case rates leveled off nationally and in three regions, while two regions kept growing at a slower pace. Rates still sit high overall. Earlier care in pregnancy and treatment of both parents are the fixes the authors press.
pmc-13404159:
Jinze Li and co-authors ran a trial in 2026 on tailoring breathing machine pressure for older patients during long keyhole surgery. Seventy patients aged 65 to 75 had rectal cancer surgery while tilted head-down for over two hours. Half got pressure set by their own lung stretch measures, and half got a fixed setting.

Lung ultrasound scores after surgery ran about four points lower in the tailored group. Their lungs also stretched more easily, with lower driving pressure during the operation. A lung protein in blood rose more after surgery in that group. Gas exchange and blood pressure showed no clear gap. Hard outcome trials come next.
pmc-13404359:
Kevin Coutu and a six-author team screened cleanup steps in 2026 for pulling a common drug coating, mPEG, out of blood and liver samples. Coated nano-drugs ride longer in the body, yet labs must strip sample proteins away before measuring them. Many cleanup agents seemed fine on paper, since the coating dissolves under all of them.

Actual recovery swung widely by agent choice, their tests showed. One solvent, acetonitrile, stood alone as broadly reliable for both human serum and rat liver mash. It recovered the coating and whole coated systems cleanly and in full. Coating size and system makeup barely changed the outcome under that solvent.
pmc-13406559:
Yu-Hsiang Wang and colleagues measure how precisely surgeons must locate lung nodules before removal, in a 2026 study. Ground-glass nodules are hard to see or feel during keyhole surgery, so a needle marks them under cone-beam CT in a hybrid operating room. Too large a miss risks leaving cancer at the cut edge.

The team defined a distance from needle tip to tumour edge and tested it against the final margin quality after wedge removal. At about 4.9 millimetres in the reported analysis, inadequate margins rose sharply. They propose that value as a warning line prompting the surgeon to recheck the plan during the operation. Outside validation is required before routine use, they caution.
pmc-13407659:
A 2026 retraction notice from the journal Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine withdraws a 2016 rat study that claimed a citrus fruit, satkara, protects liver and kidneys against paracetamol poisoning. The publisher, John Wiley and Sons, agreed the retraction after concerns surfaced about the article's figures.

Investigators found repeated image areas within one figure's panels, matches between panels and figures in several other papers, and shared regions across three panels of another figure. The authors could not supply the original images when asked, so the results and conclusions could no longer be trusted. The notice stands as the journal's formal record that the 2016 findings are withdrawn, and the retraction itself, rather than new research, is the entire content here.
pmc-13407859:
Ahmed M. M. Heneash and co-authors assess, in 2026, a hard-working Egyptian canal across four seasons. Al-Mahmoudia Canal supplies two governorates yet receives heavy pollution, so the team sampled seven sites through the year for microbes, heavy metals, turbidity, nutrients, and the plankton communities that register water health.

Phytoplankton peaked in spring at one station, tracking temperature and nutrients, while zooplankton diversity shifted with the seasons. Turbidity and nutrient loads rose in summer and autumn under organic pollution pressure. Faecal coliform counts exceeded safety limits, and metal and microbial contamination fluctuated by season and site, marking clear pollution hotspots. The authors call for continuous monitoring and active management to keep the canal a sustainable water source for the Nile Delta region.
pmc-13408159:
Ahmed Serag and co-authors present a 2026 method for finding the drug valbenazine in water. Their tool is a set of glowing carbon dots, doped with nitrogen and phosphorus. A salting-out step pulls the drug from river and tap water first. The dots then dim as the drug binds, and that dimming gives the reading.

Both the dot recipe and the pull-out step were tuned step by step, with a stats design guiding the pull-out settings. The method found the drug down to a few nanograms per millilitre. It won back nearly all of the drug from spiked samples, and repeat runs agreed closely. Green scoring tools rated it well against heavier lab methods. For teams tracking drug traces in waterways, it offers a cheap, low-solvent test with solid numbers behind it.
pmc-13408359:
Ankita Tapkir and colleagues compared Papoose Board and Comfy Wrap restraints for pediatric dental care on parent views and child oxygen saturation. Their 2026 randomized crossover trial enrolls 40 children aged 3 to 7 needing protective stabilization, with each child experiencing both restraints in opposite orders. Physical restraint is sometimes necessary for uncooperative children, but the Papoose Board has drawn psychological and physiological concerns.

More parents in each group favored the Comfy Wrap, rating it less scary and more acceptable. Oxygen saturation changed significantly over time in the Papoose-first group, with no significant difference between restraint methods overall, while the Comfy Wrap showed greater physiological stability in the wrap-first group. The paper supports the Comfy Wrap as a more child-centered option, while small sample and order effects warrant larger trials.
pmc-13410959:
Laura Amelinck and colleagues test in 2026 whether flu protection from the virus's second surface protein reaches beyond matching strains. Seasonal vaccines target mainly the first protein, yet the second, neuraminidase, also trains the immune system. Earlier work sorted that protein from recent H3N2 viruses into four families.

Mice were immunized with the protein from each family, or given immune serum, then challenged with a mismatched flu virus. Protection stretched wider than the standard enzyme-blocking antibody measure suggested, tracking instead with cross-reactive antibodies. One pairing oddly sped illness at the start, in one direction only, a quirk the team flags. Results support adding neuraminidase to future vaccine design.
pmc-13411159:
Lu Zhang and colleagues review in 2026 how packaging traditional Chinese medicines into nanoparticles could treat kidney scarring. Scarring is the final common path of chronic kidney disease, and current drugs cannot undo it. Herbal medicines hit many targets at once yet dissolve poorly and rarely reach the kidney.

Nano carriers solve the delivery half, steering cargo through the kidney's filters and tubules. The review sorts five carrier families by build and fate in the body. Four classes of herbal ingredients, from flavonoids to glycosides, get matched with their anti-scarring actions and best carriers. Batch consistency, long-term safety, and a clear approval path remain the hurdles before clinic use.
pmc-13411959:
Ruiqiu Zhu and co-authors review in 2026 how tumours rewire their fat metabolism, and how that rewiring changes responses to radiotherapy. Radiation kills cancer cells partly through oxidative damage, and lipid pathways govern how much damage sticks. The review separates lipid traits a tumour already carries from changes that radiation itself triggers.

Topics include iron-driven lipid damage called ferroptosis, cholesterol shifts that alter cell membranes, and fat droplets that buffer stress during treatment. The authors also cover fat trading between cancer cells and their surroundings, which can shield a tumour. They close by grading possible drug strategies from early lab ideas to those nearing clinical testing.
pmc-13413459:
Jiao Feng and co-authors trace in 2026 how one letter of DNA variation helps tuberculosis bacteria survive inside human immune cells. Genome studies had flagged the gene DUSP14 in TB susceptibility, and a variant called rs1051838 sits inside it. Working in macrophage-like and other lab cell lines, the team measured how each variant version drives the gene and what that does during infection with a weakened TB strain.

The G version of the variant switched the gene on more strongly, yet carries a spot that chemical methylation can silence. Infection stripped that methylation away, raising DUSP14, which then dampened a key alarm pathway and let bacteria persist while inflammatory signals fell. Silencing the gene reversed the effect, cutting bacterial load. The authors nominate DUSP14 for host-directed therapy research.
pmc-13413559:
Georgios Mavraganis and co-authors weigh in 2026 how far guidelines for hypertensive heart failure with preserved ejection fraction outrun the trial evidence behind them. High blood pressure drives this stiff-heart syndrome, yet the recommended pressure targets and flagship drug class were never tested in dedicated trials for this exact population. The narrative review folds in recent European and Japanese meta-analyses plus post-hoc looks at two landmark drug trials.

Glucose-lowering SGLT2 drugs cut heart failure events consistently in those analyses, with a pooled hazard ratio of 0.79 across the studies cited. Pressure control evidence stays patchier: device therapy data are thin, and real-world adherence among older Europeans runs under fifty percent. Registry figures show frailty in 68 percent of patients over seventy-five, complicating aggressive targets.
pmc-13413659:
Jinxing Lyu and co-authors turn rice husks into reinforcement for eco-friendly mine backfill in 2026, blending them with coal gangue, fly ash, and desert sand. Mines need cheap fill that holds weight without cracking suddenly, and natural fibres might beat synthetic ones on cost and footprint. The team varied husk dose and cement replacement, then crushed and split specimens while acoustic sensors, imaging, and microscopy tracked how damage grew.

At five percent husk, the fill reached 5.6 megapascals in compression and 0.376 in splitting tension, an 83.4 percent tensile gain over the fibre-free mix in their tests. Husks delayed crack concentration, turning sudden brittle failure into gradual damage under load. Microscopy showed husks embedded in the cement matrix with mineral growth around them. Longer curing raised strength, heavier cement replacement lowered it.
pmc-13414059:
Yu Xie, Ziying Chen, and Zhen Chen construct in 2026 a risk score from fat-metabolism genes to forecast outcomes in oral squamous cell carcinoma. Lipid rewiring shapes how this cancer grows and answers immune therapy, yet no clinically ready model used it. Mining the TCGA tumour atlas, the team distilled a gene signature by penalized regression, then checked it against an independent public dataset of patient tumours.

High-risk patients died sooner in both the training group and the validation group, with clear statistical separation. A chart combining the score with clinical traits confirmed the signature as an independent prognostic factor in their models. Low-risk tumours hosted more killer T cells and answered immunotherapy better, while high-risk tumours carried more mutations and shrugged off most chemotherapy drugs tried.
pmc-13414559:
William J. Branchett leads a 2026 study of airway immunity in people recently exposed to tuberculosis at home. The team examined fluid washed from the lungs of household contacts who stayed healthy, contacts who later became ill, and patients with active disease. Lung imaging helped sort the contacts before sampling.

Single-cell gene sequencing showed strong neutrophil patterns in progressors and patients, tied in part to type I interferon signals. Where neutrophils dominated, T cells looked worn out and prone to die. Contacts who controlled the infection instead carried calmer, stem-like T cells. Those contrasts point to early airway signs that could guide vaccines or host-directed treatments.
pmc-13415559:
Shweta Singh and colleagues improved DNA recovery in 2026 from scarce preserved cancer tissue, the formalin-fixed blocks that fill hospital archives. Formalin crosslinks and fragments DNA, so standard kits often yield too little usable material for modern sequencing, blocking studies of rare tumors.

Tuning two commercial kits lifted DNA concentration two to three times, with the advanced kit ahead on yield and fragment quality, and libraries built from it sequenced better. Cancer researchers gain a practical protocol for unlocking archived tissue for genomic study. Archived blocks from small biopsies can now join larger genomic studies.
pmc-13415659:
Jingtang Ma, Haofei Wu, and H. Harry Zheng prove that iterative deep learning can solve a hard class of stochastic equations from finance, in 2026. The equations describe best investment choices when markets remember their past, a non-Markovian setting. Their value function obeys a fully nonlinear backward stochastic partial differential equation.

Error bounds are derived for three layers: splitting time into steps, iterating the policy, and training the neural network loop. Numerical tests cover a standard model with varying volatility and a rough volatility model that ignores history free assumptions. Results show the method converging with good accuracy in both cases, supporting its use for complex portfolio problems.
pmc-13416159:
Alberto J. Ruiz, Sophie A. Lyon, Ethan P. M. LaRochelle, and Kimberley S. Samkoe chart how the surgical dye indocyanine green glows under varied excitation light, in 2026. The dye guides fluorescence surgery worldwide, yet its spectrum shifts with surroundings. Full excitation and emission matrices were recorded in a solvent, in albumin solution, and in 3D printed resin.

In plain solvent the emission stayed fixed regardless of excitation, obeying a classic rule of fluorescence. In albumin and resin, emission slid with excitation wavelength, a red edge effect never documented for a surgical fluorophore. Resin spectra matched albumin bound dye closely, validating printed phantoms for system testing.
pmc-13416659:
Pranav S Garimella and colleagues report a letter on kidney function in the AASK trial, published in 2026. They ask whether a simple estimate of how much creatinine the kidney tubules secrete can stand in for a direct measure. The estimate comes from the gap between creatinine clearance and estimated filtration rate.

The analysis covers 999 trial participants who had measured filtration, estimated filtration, and urine creatinine clearance at baseline. Lower secretion had earlier been linked to kidney failure needing replacement therapy. Readers learn why the easier estimate could let large studies assess tubular health without hard isotope tests, and which outcomes the team tracked, including heart disease and death.
pmc-13416759:
Ceyda Dadalı and Yağmur Özcan bake gluten free cakes with locust powder as a protein source, in a 2026 food study. They replace part of the rice flour with plain or defatted locust powder at 10, 15, and 20 percent levels. Cakes were checked for nutrition, texture, colour, microbes, scent compounds, and taste.

Protein rose with the powder, reaching 8.68 grams per 100 grams in the strongest defatted cake. Phenolic content and antioxidant activity also rose, more so with defatted powder. Some mid level cakes scored higher on overall liking than the plain control. The work shows insect protein can improve gluten free baking while using fewer resources.
pmc-13417659:
Ting-Han Lin and colleagues anchor single platinum atoms on a warped carbon nitride sheet to turn microplastics into fuel with light, in a 2026 study. Plastic waste piles up, and using sunlight to reform it into hydrogen is attractive. The support's bent framework holds platinum in an unusual loose coordination that lets electrons move flexibly.

X ray measures confirmed the odd bonding and showed fast charge transfer to platinum under light. Among plastics tested, PET gave the highest hydrogen rate, helped by alkaline splitting of its ester bonds. Computer models showed platinum lowers the energy barrier for hydrogen release. The design may guide other plastic to fuel catalysts.
pmc-13418659:
Luis Puelles comments on the distinctive molecular profile of the limbic mesocortex, a transitional ring of cortex sitting between the main isocortex and the older allocortex in mammals. His 2026 commentary reviews gene markers that set this ring apart from both neighbours in the adult mouse brain.

A shared profile of 46 selective genes was reported earlier, and the count of known mesocortex markers has since risen to 83. These genes label specific layers of the ring, with boundaries matching its mapped shape exactly. Over forty percent code for membrane channels or receptors, while many others relate to neurotransmitter handling, myelination, or synaptic machinery. The region also has few parvalbumin neurons and the lightest myelin in the cortex, suggesting thinner, slower connections. Puelles argues this combined profile marks the mesocortex as a functionally distinct cortical type.
pmc-13418759:
Ihor Kendiukhov asks whether large computer models trained on single-cell data learn real gene control links or just echo shared activity. The 2026 study looks inside two well-known models, scGPT and Geneformer, at the hidden streams where cell data is processed. Older tools built on correlation or regression have had only modest luck at mapping which genes steer which others.

The cancer, hemangiosarcoma, grows from blood vessel cells and usually starts in the spleen, heart, or skin. Dogs given combined treatment, such as surgery plus chemotherapy, lived longer.
pmc-13419359:
Mücke and colleagues asked whether quantitative susceptibility mapping, an MRI method that measures how tissue distorts the magnetic field, can tell the five most common kidney stone types apart without surgery. They embedded 53 removed human stones in three gel phantoms and scanned them repeatedly at two field strengths.

pmc-13420259:
Fatemeh Jahanimoghadam and colleagues survey dentists in Kerman, southeastern Iran, on what they know and do about natural disaster management. Working in both public and private clinics predicted stronger knowledge, and age played a part as well. Such readiness is striking for a group rarely counted in disaster plans. The authors argue that dental teams deserve a formal place in city emergency rosters.
pmc-13420959:
Bec Jenkinson and co-authors argue that research priority setting in Australia is being wrongly treated as research itself. Their 2026 paper calls for institutions to classify it as involvement rather than research.

pmc-13421359:
Gerbren B. Spoelstra leads a thirteen-author team testing, in a 2026 study, imaging tracers that home in on bacteria infecting orthopaedic implants. Infections around joint replacements and fracture hardware are hard to confirm, since standard scans cannot tell infection apart from ordinary inflammation.

The mice numbered 72. Uptake at the implant site was counted against bacterial load. The study asks whether aiming tracers at bacteria makes the diagnostic call clearer.
pmc-13422359:
Xu and co-authors identify an antiviral defender in this 2026 study of goose astrovirus type 2. The pathogen causes fatal visceral gout in goslings just 3 to 15 days old. The authors nominate both viperin and its product as antiviral leads for the poultry industry.
pmc-13422859:
Zhu and co-authors track diagnostic shadows of the pandemic in a large United States insurance claims database, in this 2026 study. They ask what happened to new diagnoses of asthma, eczema, and multiple sclerosis when healthcare use collapsed in 2020. They built twenty seasonal cohorts from 2018 through 2022 and standardized incidence by age and sex.

Against spring 2018, spring 2020 incidence fell 14 percent for asthma, 28 percent for atopic dermatitis, and 23 percent for multiple sclerosis by the reported rate ratios. pmc-13423159:
Paul McCallion and colleagues explore whether patients with bronchiectasis and their physiotherapists would accept choosing airway clearance techniques together, rather than by prescription alone. Both groups found the approach acceptable, and the themes now guide design of a future decision-support tool.
pmc-13425159:
Maartje Cox and six co-authors compare tiredness and movement in people with rheumatoid arthritis and healthy peers, in this twenty twenty-six study. The joint disease often brings deep fatigue, which may keep patients from being active. Whether fatigue holds patients back more than it does healthy people was unknown.

Small groups of patients and controls wore ankle motion sensors for at least four days. The devices counted steps and active minutes across weekdays, weekends, and evenings. Fatigue was self-rated. Movement fell as fatigue rose in both groups to a like degree. The result suggests fatigue itself, not the disease alone, is a fair target for activity coaching.
pmc-13425459:
Kaisheng Sun and colleagues report a 2026 materials study on making zinc metal batteries last longer with an ionic liquid additive. They used 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium methanesulfonate, which forms a layered protective film on zinc during use. The inner layer is zinc sulfide from broken-down anions and conducts ions while blocking electrons, while the outer layer holds cations and anions that can rearrange under the electric field.

That responsive outer layer evens out zinc deposition and stripping, reshapes hydrogen bonding at the surface, and curbs side reactions. The design aims at ultra-stable cycling for rechargeable zinc batteries, a low-cost option for storing energy.
pmc-13425859:
Ying-Cheng Lin and colleagues set out a trial protocol for a Mediterranean diet reshaped for local tastes, aimed at fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. The diet helps liver fat in general, but sticking to it is hard where it is not a habit.

One arm gets the adapted diet with live video coaching and behaviour-change support, while the other gets standard care. As a protocol it reports no outcomes yet, but it gives clinics a testable plan for diet help that fits local food.
pmc-13425959:
Michele Bevere and colleagues paint an integrated picture of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, a mixed family that varies in look, markers, genes, and behaviour. Layering gene, RNA, and epigenetic data over tissue study and survival has sharpened the field.

Changes in DAXX and ATRX, a telomere-lengthening pathway, and BEND2 gene fusions mark distinct paths. pmc-13426159:
Shuai Qing, Jianfeng Wang, and Shiming Huang examined blood carotenoids and migraine in American adults in a 2026 retrospective NHANES study. Migraine affects over a billion people and ranks among the top causes of disability, with oxidative stress, nerve inflammation, and mitochondrial problems implicated in its biology. Lutein and zeaxanthin are dietary carotenoids with antioxidant activity that could, in principle, counter free radical damage.

The analysis found a negative association, meaning higher serum levels of these carotenoids tracked with less migraine in the survey data. Association alone cannot prove protection, yet the result supports controlled studies of antioxidant status and headache.
pmc-13426359:

pmc-13426959:

Its scores proved steady and largely valid, but fairness warning signs appeared across essay topics.
pmc-13427059:
Tsai and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how quantitative EEG behaves across the dialysis cycle in kidney failure patients. Quantitative EEG is computer analysis of brain-wave recordings, and the review asks what it would take to use it as a bedside brain monitor. Thinking problems are common on dialysis, and each session stresses the brain as blood flow dips. Brain-wave measures might catch that strain live, but studies vary widely in method.

Sixty-two studies were sorted into before, during, and after dialysis windows. Patients typically showed slowed brain rhythms even at rest. During sessions, brain blood flow fell by roughly a tenth, with matching shifts in wave ratios. The review lists the practical blockers: electrical noise, motion, loose electrodes, and unsynced data streams, plus the fixes needed before routine use.
pmc-13427259:
María Cristina Almazán and coauthors surveyed soil for intestinal parasites in rural northwestern Argentina in a 2026 molecular surveillance study. In total, 116 soil samples came from 28 sites. Most sites were homes in Solazuti village, twenty-seven in all, plus a single country school at El Cedral in Orán Department, Salta Province. Soil from yards, paths, and school grounds was in view, the spots where young kids play and where bare feet meet the ground each day at home.
pmc-13427359:
Merlin Engelke and coauthors systematically reviewed artificial intelligence forecasting of transfusion demand in a 2026 article. Predicting blood product needs helps blood banks hold enough supply without wasteful overstocking, and machine learning tools now target scales from single patients to regional supply chains. Following PRISMA 2020 guidance, the reviewers searched PubMed and Scopus for studies from January 2015 to December 2025 applying AI or machine learning to demand prediction.

Starting from 535 records plus a targeted top-up search, findings were sorted into a four-tier framework by prediction scope and clinical goal. Blood services gain a structured comparison of forecasting techniques before adopting them.
pmc-13427459:
Chi-Ya Yang and coauthors compared skin cancer risk across three chronic skin conditions in a 2026 multicenter retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX network. Hidradenitis suppurativa, a painful inflammatory disorder of skin folds, has been linked with cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, while burn scars are a classic risk factor. Anatomical distribution of cancers was also mapped across hidradenitis, psoriasis, and burn cohorts spanning 2005 to 2025.
