Large, matched groups drawn from a vast web of wards give the counts weight that a lone site count could not hope to match in this field.
pmc-13427559:
Zhijie Huan and colleagues review, in 2026, how tiny magnetic particles are made and used in medicine. The particles have a magnetic core, often a metal or a ceramic ferrite, set inside a material the body tolerates well. Size, stability, and surface features depend heavily on how they are built. Makers use both physical and chemical routes, each with trade-offs.

Uses covered include carrying drugs to a target, sensing disease signals, sorting cells, and supporting cell therapy. Magnets outside the body can guide or hold the particles where they are needed. The review ends with open problems in making uniform particles at scale and proving long-term safety. Engineers and clinicians get one map of a fast-moving field.
pmc-13427659:
B. Daniels and colleagues argue, in a 2026 perspective, that Australia's cancer registries could watch new cancer drugs far better after approval. Trials that win approval often involve narrow patient groups and stand-in outcomes, leaving real-world safety and value unclear. Registries cover the whole population and can link to dispensing and hospital records.

The authors list upgrades they see as priorities for a whole-population watch system. Policy readers get a frank audit of a data asset that other countries also rely on, and a sense of what linkage alone cannot fix.
pmc-13427759:
Chandra and colleagues upgraded in 2026 a deep learning model that reads DNA sequence to predict where the genome is open for business in immune cells. Learning several cell types together beat training each alone. The authors argue that resolution itself teaches the model a richer grammar of gene control.
pmc-13427959:

pmc-13428159:

pmc-13429259:

Today the center runs fitness classes, line dancing, bocce, and a dine-out club. Homebound meals reach members who cannot travel to the center at all. During the pandemic closure, staff offered drive-by meals and online classes instead. They even won approval for parking lot line dancing to keep members moving. Programs shift as members age, serving people from their sixties into their nineties.
pmc-13430059:

Forty-eight fusion cases were found across many sarcoma types. Pathologist-led and clinician-led testing found different case mixes. Treating passenger fusions as drivers could misdirect therapy. pmc-13430159:

Observation units attached to emergency departments hold patients who need a day or so of watching. The statistical design compared change over time at the converted hospital against change at the others. Chest pain led the diagnoses, and the average patient was near 60. pmc-13430259:

pmc-13430559:

The team tracked naloxone units given out, people starting and staying on buprenorphine, and high-risk prescribing rates. The exploratory design set these against overdose deaths. Such counting helps funders see which moves shift outcomes for whole areas, not just single people.
pmc-13430759:

pmc-13430859:

pmc-13431459:

Average scores showed poor knowledge, at under half of the possible points, and attitudes below the positive threshold, yet intended practice scored high. Women with junior high schooling or less knew less and held less positive views. Higher knowledge predicted more positive attitudes, and both predicted better intended practice, so the authors urge education aimed at women with lower schooling.
pmc-13431759:

pmc-13432159:

pmc-13432959:

pmc-13433959:

pmc-13434559:

pmc-13434659:

pmc-13435659:

Screening completion ran highest, at 88.7 percent, when both risks coexisted. Diabetes alone and pressure alone each reached about 77 percent, versus 63.8 percent for controls. pmc-13436259:

Most children arrived within a day, and scope removal succeeded within thirty minutes in over half, with two needing chest surgery. Emergency clinicians get a school-age profile that favors quick imaging and scope readiness, with pen caps as the prime suspect.
pmc-13436659:

Charts from November 2024 cover 372 patients with intensive or step down orders. The consult team managed eighteen percent of them after first assessment. Downgrade to a lower care level is the main outcome tracked. Stay lengths in ward, unit, and hospital form the second set. Flow gains are the hope behind the service.
pmc-13437359:

pmc-13438559:

pmc-13439259:

The authors treat function findings as early leads beside firmer structure results.
pmc-13439359:

Travelling wrinkles ferried objects uphill and along set paths. Heat-reversible bonding also let the sheet join and split dynamic polymers and haul small cargo. The authors offer the wrinkling sheet as a flexible base for reconfigurable smart surfaces.
pmc-13439559:

pmc-13515259:

pmc-13517159:

pmc-13518459:

pmc-13518859:

pmc-13518959:

pmc-13519459:

pmc-13520359:

pmc-13520459:

pmc-13520659:

pmc-13522459:

pmc-13523359:

pmc-13524459:

pmc-13524859:

pmc-13525059:

pmc-13525859:

pmc-13526059:

pmc-13526159:

pmc-13526259:

pmc-13526859:

pmc-13527959:

pmc-13528059:

pmc-13529659:

pmc-13530059:

pmc-13530159:

pmc-13531759:

pmc-13531959:

pmc-13532759:

pmc-13532859:

pmc-13535259:

pmc-13535759:

pmc-13536159:

pmc-13536459:

pmc-13536559:

pmc-13536759:

pmc-13536859:

pmc-13537459:

pmc-13538059:

pmc-13540959:

pmc-13541859:

pmc-13543259:

pmc-13543359:

pmc-13543559:

pmc-13546059:

pmc-13547359:
Gai Liu and colleagues read the genome of an alpine snow alga that darkens snow and speeds melting. Published in 2026, the study mapped Chloromonas typhlos, a globe-spanning snow alga whose blooms cut snow shine-back. Snow algae feed cold germs and shape melt, yet this genus lacked a strong genome model.

Long reads plus chromosome-linking data built a 200.86-million-letter genome across 31 chromosomes, with repeats at just over 11 percent. The team found 16,133 protein-coding genes and gave 82 percent a known role. The genome gives snow-alga workers a base for tracing cold coping and pigment-driven melt feedback. Readers get a model genome for a far-flung snow genus.
pmc-13547559:
Patrice Ngangue and colleagues interviewed in 2026 thirty-three English-speaking women displaced by Cameroon's Anglophone crisis into Douala, exploring how gender-based violence and mental health intertwine under displacement. The women, median age 34 and a median five years in the region, were reached through purposive and snowball sampling across city neighborhoods. Conversations were analyzed thematically through an intersectional lens.

Four themes emerged. Silence served as protection against stigma, while trauma showed up in the body and in mental shutdown. A constant anxiety about survival grew out of poverty and discrimination against English speakers. Resilience rested on informal peer networks, faith, and reframing hardship. The authors argue daily structural stressors outweigh single past events, so support must join violence prevention, livelihoods, and care in the women's own languages.
pmc-13548059:
Infant Thomas and seven colleagues present SURE-Pipe, a pipeline for comparing genomes and extracting shared and unique regions, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. Species-specific regions power diagnostic assays and sequence-based identification. An automated tool with modest computational needs could advance genome-driven research. Their pipeline works within and between species.

Benchmarks on simulated data showed high accuracy for shared and unique region identification. Pairwise comparison was demonstrated on six genome pairs from diverse microorganisms. The multigenome module then handled ninety-six genomes across twenty-four Bacillus species. Species-specific regions proved highly conserved within each species and nearly absent elsewhere. Primers designed for all twenty-four species showed no off-target amplification in simulated tests. The pipeline is publicly available for other laboratories.
pmc-13548259:
Bezie Kebede, Bereket Bahiru Tefera, and Bezuayehu Alemayehu lay out a plan to review the health toll and economic cost of bacterial meningitis in Africa, in a study protocol from 2026. The infection still burdens the continent heavily, in both lives and money. A combined clinical and cost picture is missing.

The review will search three databases plus citations for African studies from 2008 onward. Two reviewers will screen and extract data on their own, then merge findings. Quality will be scored with checklists matched to study type. Results will appear as tables, figures, and maps. No ethics approval is needed for published data.
pmc-13548559:
Hongjie He, Yuanyuan Yan, and Yanming Zhang weigh proton beam therapy against standard photon radiation for liver cancer, in a 2026 meta-analysis. Protons can stop inside a tumor and spare nearby healthy liver, which matters because radiation injury to the liver is a feared complication. The team searched four databases for studies comparing the two approaches in hepatocellular carcinoma and rated the strength of the combined findings.

Only four retrospective studies qualified. Proton patients showed a lower hazard of death, yet that result carried uneven data and signs of publication bias, so the authors rate its certainty as low. The safety findings were firmer: protons cut the odds of liver injury to about a quarter, with roughly five patients treated to prevent one injury. They advise choosing case by case on liver reserve and tumor features until prospective trials report.
pmc-13548659:
Jacie T. Cooper and colleagues model whether a biomarker-based kidney risk score pays for itself in American Medicare patients, in a 2026 cost-effectiveness analysis. Diabetic kidney disease drives nearly half of new kidney failure, and protective drugs stay underused because standard staging sorts patients crudely. The KidneyIntelX score blends biomarkers with artificial intelligence to predict rapid decline, steering drug treatment toward those likeliest to progress.

Simulating lifetimes for patients in early disease stages, score-guided care produced fewer kidney failures, heart events, dialysis starts, and transplants than staging-guided care. Patients spent less time in advanced stages, gained a small amount of quality-adjusted life, and cost Medicare roughly five hundred dollars less each. Adding a second drug class widened the savings slightly. The authors call wide deployment a dominant strategy: better and cheaper at once.
pmc-13549959:
Haijun Huang and colleagues shake rounded gravel under repeated subway-like loading in a large laboratory press, in a 2026 geotechnical study. Metro tunnels increasingly pass through round gravel layers in Chinese cities, and years of train vibration can settle the ground unevenly. Using saturated samples in a dynamic triaxial machine, the team varied packing density, confining pressure, and shaking strength to watch stiffness and permanent strain evolve.

Looser, shallow gravel under strong shaking accumulated deformation that could endanger shallow tunnels, while deeper burial looked safer. Packing the gravel denser and raising confining pressure stiffened it, cut permanent and elastic strain, lowered water pressure buildup, and strengthened resistance to liquefaction. Drawing on time-hardening theory, the authors fitted a prediction model joining all three factors, aimed at design checks and long-term settlement forecasts for subway foundations.
pmc-13550559:
Mohamed Abd El-Wahed and co-authors present a 2026 study hunting gold along a fault zone in the Saudi Arabian Shield. The Al Amar zone cuts remote desert where fieldwork is hard. The team merged satellite imagery, airborne magnetic data, and targeted field checks to map rock types, faults, and the altered zones that betray hot fluid flow.

Image methods separated the main rock units and thrust contacts. Alteration halos of several styles lined up with known gold sites. Faults trending north-northeast and northwest acted as the main channels for gold-bearing fluids. Areas where lineaments crowd and alteration runs strong matched real mineral finds. The integrated map gives exploration crews a shortlist of ground to test first.
pmc-13550659:
Pyae Linn Aung published a 2026 commentary on how generative artificial intelligence is changing what online survey answers mean in digital health research. Surveys assume that replies reflect a person's own knowledge, beliefs, or behavior, and they guide programs and policy. Phone and internet access have widened their reach, while AI chat tools have become part of everyday digital life.

A respondent facing a hard question can now ask an AI tool and paste a polished, plausible answer without holding that knowledge personally. Aung notes that even well-meant help, from predictive text to search, can make answers reflect outside generation rather than lived experience, and can make responses look more alike. The piece warns researchers to rethink how such findings should be interpreted.
pmc-13551159:
Evans F Kyei and colleagues listened to Ghana's mental health nurses on drug treatment blocks. Published in 2026, the interview-based study talked with 20 nurses in the Kumasi area from April to July 2024. Ghana's drug response leans on crime-first rules, yet how that climate shapes treatment care was little studied.

Four themes emerged: broken treatment paths, thin rehab space, and uneven funds. Money strain and family systems gated access, while stigma and harsh rules scared patients off as graft eased drug supply. Clever workarounds by carers and patients rounded out the set. The authors urge health-first drug rules, wider treatment buildings, and workforce growth. Readers get frontline voices for reform in Ghana and similar cash-strapped settings.
pmc-13551859:
Jian Jin, with seven colleagues, published a 2026 study of a blood score and kidney disease in diabetes. The score, called PIV, blends several blood cell counts. Its link to kidney harm in type 2 diabetes was untested. Data came from one hospital and 38 community centers, spanning 2014 to 2022. A snapshot study held 7,610 patients. A follow-up study held 1,494 patients free of kidney disease at the start.

Higher scores tied to more kidney disease in both studies. The top quarter showed far higher rates than the bottom quarter. The link held after many adjustments. Its shape bent like an inverse J in the follow-up data. The team proposes the cheap score for flagging diabetic patients at kidney risk.
pmc-13551959:
Wang and seven co-authors study why green tea drinks fade in light, in work from twenty twenty-six. Color is a key sign of quality for bottled tea. Browning gets much study, but fading from light has had little attention.

The team exposed plain green tea to shop shelf light and to fake sunlight. A vitamin called riboflavin broke down fast, losing most of its amount in days under shelf light and in hours under sunlight. Chlorophyll also fell, but by less. Tests that added compounds back confirmed the roles. Riboflavin proved the main driver of color loss, a useful clue for makers on packaging and storage.
pmc-13552059:
Ahmed Ben Rhaïem, Abdul Majeed Kikar, and Mario Ruben Sanguina report an eighty-eight-year-old man whose hip replacement hid a deep infection. The pocket beside his hip muscle, the iliopsoas, filled with pus, and the bursa there connects to the hip joint, so infection can travel either way. Scans first showed the abscess, but inflammation persisted despite strong antibiotics.

New imaging revealed growing collections around the implant and a loosened thigh component. A needle sample from the hip grew the bacterium Escherichia coli, confirming a chronic prosthetic joint infection. Given his frailty, surgeons removed the implant without a spacer. Infection control was achieved, but bleeding, wound breakdown, and decline followed, and he died about three months later. The authors urge checking the joint whenever such an abscess appears.
pmc-13552159:
Varun Mehta and three co-authors report a rare case in which liver cancer first showed itself in the jaw, in a 2026 case report. Liver cancer usually spreads to the lungs, nearby lymph nodes, long bones, or the brain. Spread to the mouth or jaw is extremely rare, occurring in under one percent of cases. Their patient arrived with a jaw tumor and no prior sign of liver disease.

Such growths look like common dental problems, so they are often misread as gum disease or healing trouble after an extraction. Tissue tests settled the case: clusters of liver-like cells and marker stains confirmed the cancer's origin. The report warns dentists and surgeons to keep this rare path in mind when a jaw growth behaves oddly.
pmc-13554159:
Panyi Shen leads a nine-author team tracing how exercise links to student mental health in a 2026 survey of 3,466 college students in China. Four standard scales measured activity, distress, phone addiction, and felt social support. More active students reported less depression, anxiety, and stress. Activity also tied to lighter phone addiction and slightly stronger felt support.

Phone addiction carried the largest share of the link between activity and distress. Students hooked on phones felt less supported and more distressed. Felt support carried a smaller share, yet still pointed the same way, toward lower distress. The team reads the chain as activity freeing students from phones, which lifts support and calms distress. Schools may gain by pairing sport with phone habits work.
pmc-13554659:
Bacchi and six co-authors profile metabolism across human atrial tissue in atrial fibrillation with imaging mass spectrometry, in a pilot study from twenty twenty-six. Fibrillation remodels atrial structure, but molecular maps of that change are incomplete. Spray ionization imaging reads metabolic patterns in place across tissue slices. Ten surgical patients supply samples, four with fibrillation and six controls.

Histology shows minimal scarring with no group difference. Metabolic imaging still separates fibrillation from control spectra in part. Arachidonic acid and a phosphatidylinositol species track myocardial architecture and drive separation. Lipid patterns differ most between groups overall. Authors stress the findings are exploratory and need larger matched validation.
pmc-13555859:
Maitane Barasoain leads a large European team launching a school trial of digital cancer prevention for teens in a 2026 protocol. Many cancer risks start as habits formed in adolescence. The SUNRISE programme will run in about eighty schools across eight countries, reaching roughly four thousand students. Classes are assigned mostly to a six-month digital life-skills course or to standard lessons.

The course mixes phone coaching, a chat assistant, games, media literacy clips from influencers, moderated social spaces, and teacher modules. Design follows a behaviour model covering capability, opportunity, and motivation, and students helped create the content. The chief aim is judging whether the programme fits real school routines and lasts. Behaviour changes are explored as a secondary goal.
pmc-13556059:
Jiawei An and eight colleagues used genetics in 2026 to ask whether gallstones actually cause other diseases of the liver, bile ducts, and pancreas, or merely travel with them. Their Mendelian randomization study treats inherited variants linked to gallstones as a natural experiment, comparing disease rates across several cohorts. Extra analyses checked the direction of any effect and whether body weight explained the links.

Inherited liability to gallstones raised the risk of acute pancreatitis and of bile duct cancer outside the liver, with a consistent direction across datasets. No causal link appeared for a clotting condition of the portal vein, and reverse analyses found no sign that those diseases cause gallstones instead. Adjusting for body mass index did not explain the effects away. The authors argue that gallstone disease reaches further than the gallbladder itself.
pmc-13558259:
Keisuke Yonezu, Hidekazu Kondo, and Naohiko Takahashi argued in 2026 that doctors should track the electrical behaviour of the heart in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy as carefully as they track pump function. New stabiliser and gene-silencing drugs have turned this once relentlessly progressive disease into a chronic condition people live with for years. Amyloid protein infiltrates the heart's conduction system as well as its muscle, producing rhythm and timing faults.

Those faults range from atrial rhythm disorders and a failing natural pacemaker to delayed signals between chambers and uneven ventricle activation. The authors gather them under one label, the electrical phenotype, and note that clinicians often notice them late, after fainting or dangerous slowing. Systematic electrical monitoring, they contend, should become a routine part of long-term care in the treatment era.
pmc-13558359:
Wang Mingjian, Wang Xiao, and Zhao Guijun reported in 2026 a single case in which an endoscopic stent became a lasting fix for an inflamed gallbladder instead of surgery. Their patient was an 82-year-old man whose gallstones had inflamed the organ and whose other illnesses, including rheumatoid arthritis, emphysema, and a hernia, made removing it extremely risky. A first drainage through the liver settled him only briefly before pain and fever returned.

Doctors then threaded a small double-pigtail stent through the bile duct and the gallbladder's own duct using an endoscope, draining the organ from inside. Inflammation markers fell within five days, and a month later scans showed a normal-sized gallbladder with the stent in place. Five years on, he had no symptom return and normal liver tests. The authors offer the case as proof of durability for high-risk patients.
pmc-13559359:
Yang and co-authors built a tool to flag which lung surgery patients are apt to get a chest infection. Their 2026 study used health records for 512 people who had keyhole surgery to remove part of a lung. All were treated at one hospital in Kunming, China, from 2020 to 2024. The team trained five types of machine learning model, which learn patterns from past cases. It then picked the one that worked best.

The best model sorted high-risk from low-risk cases well in tests on new patients. A second tool showed which facts drove each call, so staff could see the reasons. Length of surgery was the top clue, then a lung test score, age, and a white blood cell count. The team says the tool could help staff plan care for those at high risk. It could also guide steps that cut infection risk.
pmc-13559559:
Xiaoxue Chen and colleagues explore the role of stanniocalcin-1, a protein called STC1, in laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma, a throat cancer prone to recurrence and treatment resistance. Their 2026 analysis works from public data, combining bulk and single-cell gene sequencing with clinical records. They probe where STC1 appears, what it correlates with, and how it relates to the tumor's immune surroundings.

High STC1 tracked with cancer spread, later stage, and shorter survival in the datasets examined. It also aligned with gene programs for tissue remodeling and a cell-state shift linked to invasion. Tumors rich in STC1 showed a suppressive immune setting, with fewer killer T cells and more resting macrophages. Single-cell data placed STC1 chiefly in epithelial cells, which signaled heavily to T cells through calming pathways. The authors suggest that targeting STC1 might loosen immune suppression, a hypothesis their computational study raises rather than tests.
pmc-13559659:
Qiangzu Shao and three colleagues examine B7H4, an immune checkpoint protein, in HER2-positive gastric cancer and its effect on response to trastuzumab, the standard targeted drug for this subtype. Their 2026 study moves from cancer atlas data and tissue staining to knockdown experiments in a co-expressing cell line. Resistance to trastuzumab, both initial and acquired, is a central problem in this disease.

Staining showed B7H4 and HER2 appearing together in tumors, their levels positively correlated. B7H4 abundance also tracked with larger tumors, deeper invasion, and spread to nodes and distant sites. Silencing B7H4 in NCI-N87 cells curbed their growth, migration, and invasion to varying degrees. Gene sequencing after knockdown shifted programs for proliferation and movement, and the team tested whether drug sensitivity changed as well. The authors frame B7H4 as a resistance lever worth targeting alongside HER2 therapy.
pmc-13560259:
Giorgi Kanchelashvili and colleagues measure hepatitis B coinfection and awareness among tuberculosis patients in Georgia, where routine testing is not standard. Their 2026 cross-sectional study enrolled 110 people with active TB at the national center between September 2024 and February 2025. Blood tests sorted people by past or current infection and immunity, and a survey probed knowledge and vaccine views.

Four people, 3.6 percent of the group, tested positive for current hepatitis B infection. Fourteen showed past infection with immunity, seven carried an isolated core antibody pattern, and only seven had vaccine-induced immunity. The large majority, 74.5 percent, still lacked any protection in the breakdown. Awareness was patchy: half could not name how the virus spreads, and just 14.5 percent were willing to be vaccinated, with safety doubts leading the refusals. Younger ones knew more. The authors urge folding screening, teaching, and shots into TB care.
pmc-13561059:
Emre Kocazeybek and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-six on which broken elbows in children need open surgery. Supracondylar fractures above the elbow are common in childhood and are usually fixed through the skin. Some, though, require an open reduction, and predicting which helps planning.

The team reviewed two hundred ninety-four operated children from two thousand sixteen to two thousand twenty-five. One hundred twenty-eight needed open reduction and one hundred sixty-six were fixed closed. Children in the open group were older on average. Flexion-type fractures, backward-sideways displacement, rotational deformity, and off-axis alignment all appeared more often in the open group. A joint model kept age and flexion type as independent signals. The authors offer the X-ray and clinical signs as a planning aid.
pmc-13562459:
Zeming Lei and five colleagues study a gene regulator called KDM5C and its part in the bone loss that can loosen artificial joints. Tiny titanium particles shed by implants stir up immune cells named macrophages, which then drive bone-eating cells and eat away the bone holding the implant. The 2026 study found KDM5C levels rose in macrophages exposed to titanium particles in the dish. The team blocked the gene in cells and in a mouse skull model of the disease.

Blocking KDM5C calmed the inflammatory signals and cut the formation of bone-eating cells. The regulator works by stripping a chemical tag from DNA near a protective gene, NFE2L2, and switching that gene down. Silencing NFE2L2 erased the benefit, which pins down the pathway. Treated mice lost less bone. The authors propose KDM5C as a drug target for wear-particle bone loss.
pmc-13563759:
Muhammet Firat and four colleagues pin a carbon-processing enzyme onto magnetic nanoparticles so factories could use it to capture carbon dioxide. The enzyme, carbonic anhydrase, speeds the gas's conversion in living tissue. Their 2026 team purified it from cattle blood cells, drawn from a slaughterhouse, achieving an 83-fold concentration. Two magnetic supports were built, one of bare iron oxide with amine groups and one silica-coated, and the enzyme was bound covalently to each.

Binding widened the enzyme's comfort zone but lowered its peak speed, a normal trade. The payoff came in reuse: after twenty cycles, the plain support kept 86 percent of its activity and the coated one 73 percent, while free enzyme died after a single use. Cold storage for sixty days told the same story, with the coated support holding 60 percent against the free enzyme's 17. The authors present the magnetically recoverable enzyme as a reusable capture catalyst.
pmc-13563959:
RuoFeng Wang leads a 2026 review of USP14, a protein that removes ubiquitin tags and sits on the cell's protein-recycling machinery, and of its widening role in cancer. Once seen mainly as a helper that stabilizes cancer-promoting proteins, it now links to the tumor surroundings and to treatment resistance. It also has jobs that do not involve its cutting action at all.

The review maps how chemical changes switch USP14 on, how it helps tumors resist targeted drugs, chemotherapy, radiation, and immune therapy, and where it can surprisingly slow tumors instead. Readers working on new cancer drugs get a systems view of one regulator and the openings it may offer for treatment.
pmc-13564059:
Junzhou Su, Ying Wang, and Sijie Feng report a rare tumor case in a teenage boy, in a case report from 2026. The tumor, called a plexiform neurofibroma, grows along nerves and is a hallmark of a genetic condition. Finding it alone in the scrotum, with no other signs of that condition, is very rare.

The boy, aged sixteen, had a slowly growing mass on one side of the scrotum. He had none of the skin marks or family history tied to the genetic condition. A scan showed a classic target pattern for this tumor type. Surgeons removed the whole mass while saving the testicle. Lab tests confirmed the diagnosis. Six months later there was no sign of return.
pmc-13564459:
Czerwik and three co-authors present three dogs whose odd episodes turned out to be a quiet form of epileptic seizure. The dogs showed fear, restlessness, staring, lip licking, and drooling, with no shaking or collapse. Such episodes are easily mistaken for behavior problems.

Brain-wave recordings over several hours found epileptic discharges in the parietal and temporal regions of all three dogs. Brain scans and standard exams had looked normal. Seizure medicine cut the episodes in all three, and two dogs became fully seizure-free. The authors urge vets to consider this seizure type in dogs with strange behavior spells. Brain-wave testing, read beside the history, can supply the missing proof.
pmc-13564959:
Zhang and coauthors probe why some lung tumors respond well to immune care. A gene pair found in some lung tumors marks that good response. One gene, KRAS, drives tumor growth in these cases. The other gene, p53, is changed from its normal form.

The team traced the link to a protein called SPP1. Changed p53 works with a partner to shut SPP1 down. KRAS, by contrast, turns SPP1 up through a growth path. Low SPP1 means fewer suppressor cells reach the tumor. With fewer such cells, immune care can attack the tumor more freely. The work names SPP1 as a key switch in this response.
pmc-13565259:
Mohit Mohnani and Daniel A. Henk used computer distribution models in 2026 to test whether three very common fungi truly grow anywhere. The three species turn up in samples worldwide and are often called generalists with few limits. The team built models from global sighting records and climate data. Each model mapped where the climate suits a species and how strongly that place matches its known records.

All three models fit well, and suitable areas clustered mainly in temperate and subtropical zones. Each fungus had its own distinct map, though the maps overlapped a good deal. In other words, even these widespread species follow clear, non-random climate rules rather than living everywhere equally. The authors offer their approach as a base for later work that adds genetic and evolutionary evidence to the geography of hard-to-track fungi.
pmc-13565459:
Seven authors present a framework dated two thousand twenty-six for tailoring diabetes care to each patient. Diabetes is a long-term disorder of blood sugar control, and bodies and daily habits differ too much for one fixed plan. Guessing the right insulin dose for a given person is a daily challenge.

Their answer is a digital twin: a software copy of the patient's own sugar and insulin system. It joins math models of the body with machine learning and risk checks. Inputs include food, sleep, drugs, and activity, so the twin tracks real life. The goal is to test doses in the twin before the patient takes them.
pmc-13565659:
Trevor Parton and four co-authors review new ways to treat lung cancer without open surgery in this twenty twenty-six paper. Thin scopes passed through the airways, once used mainly to find disease, can now reach tumors with the help of robot arms, maps of the airway, and live scans during the procedure.

The review covers heat, cold, light, and electric pulse methods that kill tumors through the scope, plus drugs placed right into the tumor. These options matter most for patients who cannot face surgery or who need to keep as much lung as they can. The authors weigh the proof for each method and where the tools still fall short.
pmc-13566259:
Prados-Carmona and seven co-authors compared two builds of a three-zone eye lens in twenty twenty-six, the first head-to-head of lens builds in print. Forty-two folks got both eyes fit with one build or the new one. Sight was checked at three months for far, mid, and near zones.

The new build gave a clear edge in one-eye mid sight. More of its eyes hit the top mid mark in both one and two eye reads. Far and near sight matched the old build in the checks. Glass use, joy, and harms matched too, they report.
pmc-13566459:
Stojkovic, Junghanss, and Gehling review in 2026 the current care of alveolar echinococcosis, a wildlife borne disease that mimics liver cancer on scans. The parasite grows through the liver like a tumor, and the disease counts as a neglected tropical illness. Their aim is updated management plus wider awareness.

Reports suggest rising prevalence in some regions, from better surveillance, spread, or weaker control. New diagnostics and treatments advance very slowly for lack of research funds. Cure still needs early, limited liver disease removed with clear margins. Inoperable disease gets benzimidazole drugs that hold the parasite static. Outlook hinges on liver damage, and drug intolerance worsens it sharply.
pmc-13567559:
Lorenzo Cortesi and colleagues reviewed greener food packaging analysis in 2026. Packaging chemicals can migrate into food. That migration raises health concerns. Testing such materials is analytically hard. Both known and unknown chemicals matter. Sample preparation shapes any result.

Recent greener workflows are surveyed here. Coverage spans twenty twenty to twenty twenty-six. Solvent use drops under green methods. Waste generation also falls sharply. Speed and safety both improve together. Target and screening methods are covered. Instrument advances get equal attention. Laboratories can cut their footprint substantially. Food safety testing gains from these advances.
pmc-13570259:
Omar Alqaisi and co-authors map barriers to inclusive cancer care for sexual and gender minority patients in a review from two thousand twenty-six. Advances in cancer screening and treatment are not shared evenly. The review gathers studies on access, delivery, and patient experience for these adults.

Twenty studies met the criteria. Few health workers answered all knowledge questions about this group's health correctly, though most wanted training. Many patients were unsure of their screening needs or missed recommended vaccines. Barriers included poor communication, bias, and record systems lacking fields for identity data. Welcoming signals, inclusive talk, and routine data collection helped. The authors urge training and system change together.
pmc-13570859:
Masahiko Nakatsui and colleagues test, in a 2026 historical cohort study, whether free-text Japanese medical records gathered under a national data law can rebuild survival results from a major lung cancer trial. Seventy-five patients treated with the immune drug atezolizumab were identified, trial eligibility rules were applied, and trained reviewers extracted outcomes by hand from unstructured notes.

Median time before the cancer worsened came to three and a half months, close to the figure in the trial's Japanese subgroup. Patterns by disease stage and fitness matched clinical expectation. Median overall survival could not yet be calculated. The close match supports using such real-world records to check trial findings in everyday practice.
pmc-13571359:
Katharina M. Wörgötter and colleagues present, in a 2026 report of three cases, a mapping-guided way to biopsy heart muscle when cardiac sarcoidosis is suspected. This inflammatory disease scars the heart, yet standard blind biopsy often misses it. Electrical maps of the heart locate abnormal low-voltage tissue so samples can be taken where disease actually lives.

The pathway starts with magnetic resonance imaging, adds a metabolic scan when findings fit, and turns to guided biopsy when no easier tissue site exists. European guidelines in 2025 gave the method a formal recommendation for the first time. The cases show both the gains and the limits of the approach inside a wider diagnostic workup.
pmc-13571559:
Nguyen and Nguyen set out a design method in twenty twenty-six for a lab device that imitates a solar panel's electrical behavior. Real panels depend on the weather, which makes testing chargers and running student labs awkward and hard to repeat.

Their emulator pairs a real-time simulator with a power amplifier. The simulator computes how a panel should respond, and the amplifier is driven to copy that response exactly, so test gear sees a stand-in sun. The model handles steady light and heat, plus the tricky case of partly shaded panels where cells mismatch. The builders used a one-kilowatt amplifier and checked the setup with simple loads. The platform can measure panel traits for teaching labs and test solar chargers under controlled conditions. The authors present the method as simple and fast to build.
pmc-13572259:
Zhang and coauthors test an enzyme that breaks neutrophil traps in lung tissue. Activated white cells cast DNA traps that can harm lungs. Those traps link to clots and lung swelling in sick patients. The enzyme DNase1 chews up those traps in the lab.

Mouse lung tissue was kept alive outside the body. Human white cells, switched on in the lab, were added. The team then added DNase1 to half the tissue samples. Swelling marks around airways fell with the enzyme. A vessel growth signal stayed intact in treated tissue. The work backs enzyme care for lung injury.
pmc-13572359:
Chaopeng Mei and a large team study, in a 2026 set of mouse and cell experiments, a brake enzyme called DUSP10 in severe acute pancreatitis. This pancreatic emergency can fail several organs through body-wide inflammation. The enzyme fell in disease models, so the team removed it genetically, added it back with a virus carrier, and traced its binding partners.

Without the enzyme, pancreatic, lung, and kidney damage, inflammation, and a fiery form of cell death all worsened; with extra enzyme, they eased. The enzyme binds and switches off a signaling protein called TAK1, and blocking either that protein or the fiery death route rescued deficient animals. Restoring this brake looks like a plausible treatment direction for a disease with few options.
pmc-13572459:
B. Santhosh Reddy, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 design for neural networks that can repair themselves after damage. Networks in safety-linked systems can suffer broken inner parts or attacks that feed them crafted inputs. Full retraining is slow and costly, so the design aims for small, local fixes instead.

The model scans each layer for odd activity, finds the faulty layer, and retrains only a light patch for that spot. Tests ran on four image data sets, from hand digits to street-style photos. After parts were zeroed out, accuracy bounced back near the intact level, at 97.33 and 97.22 percent against a 97.76 percent base in one case. The repair adds little compute or memory load. The authors pitch it for systems that must keep running without a full rebuild.
pmc-13572559:
Shantha Sheela J and David Maxim Gururaj A present a 2026 math study of a special fluid that carries tiny particles and swimming microbes. The flow, called MHD bioconvective nanofluid flow, responds to a magnetic field, heat rays, and the fluid's own changing thickness. Such flows show up in micro devices, nutrient transport in water, and biofuel cells.

The team turned the governing equations into a coupled set of ordinary equations and solved them with a fourth-order Runge-Kutta method. A surface regression model then ranked which inputs move the outputs most. Inputs under study span particle drift effects, magnetic strength, heat radiation, and two microbe numbers. Outputs cover microbe density, heat, and concentration profiles, shown in graphs. The ranked list tells designers which knobs matter most for each output.
pmc-13573059:
Aleshia Seaton-Terry, with nine colleagues, reviews 2026 work on small cell molecules that can act as glue between proteins. The molecules, inositol phosphates and their lipid cousins, carry dense negative charge. Some sit in membranes and call proteins over; others float free and lock inside protein cores.

Recent structure studies show these molecules wedged at the seam where two proteins meet, holding the pair together. The review sorts cases by how firm the glue claim is, from proven seams to pairs that await sharp structural proof. Cases span signal proteins, gene control parts, and membrane receptors. The authors argue the glue role has been under-rated and call for a systematic structural hunt. Such a hunt could seed new drugs that work by sticking proteins together on purpose.
pmc-13573459:
Yaoming Liu, with 18 colleagues, presents a 2026 design for a two-in-one coronavirus vaccine built on ferritin cages. Ferritin, an iron-storing protein, forms tiny cages that can display virus parts on their surface. Past cages were unstable and uneven, which blocked large-scale making and long storage.

Guided by AI modelling, the team added a sulfur bond across cage subunits. Sharp imaging confirmed the bond, and the new cage held up better to heat and acid, with cleaner, more even particles. A glue system then fixed the binding tips of both SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV onto the cages. In mice, the paired vaccine raised stronger antibody and T cell responses than single versions. Two doses guarded engineered mice against live challenge with both viruses. No body-wide harm appeared.
pmc-13573559:
Philippe Rodrigues Benedetti, Leociley Rocha Alencar Menezes, and Guilherme Lanzi Sassaki present a 2026 journal article on why wine feels astringent, at the molecular level. Catechins from grapes bind mouth proteins and polysaccharides from the wine itself. The team used a magnetic resonance method to watch saliva's proline-rich proteins join the mix with two wine polysaccharides, mannan and pectin.

Both protein types loosened the mannan-catechin grip, acting as rivals. With pectin the story split: acidic proteins changed nothing, while basic proteins tightened binding through charge attraction. Binding maps confirmed catechin docks differently on each partner. The authors frame the dual pattern as a handle for tuning wine feel.
pmc-13574059:
Fabiana Grillo and twelve colleagues published a sensor study in two thousand twenty-six on plastic stand-ins for an antibody-grabbing protein. Protein A is the standard tool for catching antibodies in tests, but it is costly and fragile. Imprinted polymer nanoparticles can mimic its grip with better durability.

The team moulded nanoparticles to fit chosen patches on the antibody's tail region, so antibodies land in the right orientation. The particles sat on a gold-patterned surface that boosts a fluorescence signal. The sensor detected the target antibody at very low levels with no confusion from a sister antibody class. It beat natural protein A by about a fifth on both target patches. The authors pitch it for cheaper diagnostics.
pmc-13574659:
Thin air at altitude can dull a pilot's mind before the pilot notices anything wrong, a trap that makes self-awareness of low oxygen a safety skill in its own right. Lenka Hanakova and co-authors test that awareness in a 2026 study. Volunteers sat through a normal session and a low-oxygen session while rating how they felt, moment by moment.

Blood oxygen fell hard in the low-oxygen runs for every volunteer. Felt ratings of overall state, focus, and breathing all sank, and the breathing sense slid most over time. People spotted the low-oxygen state more often while in it than in the control run. Yet scores on thinking tests did not shift, a gap that warns how quietly the mind can be at risk. Breathing feel may be the cue to train.
pmc-13574759:
En-Shi Jiang, with two colleagues, reports a 2026 lab study of how blood taints dental cements used to seal tooth roots. Calcium silicate cements set by taking up water, and blood often seeps into the work zone during root procedures. The team asked whether a week in blood weakens the bond or stalls the setting chemistry.

Four shop products filled tooth samples, which then sat in distilled water or in blood for seven days at body heat. A push-out test gauged bond strength, and nuclear magnetic scans read the silicate chain growth inside. Blood cut bond strength for the classic product but raised it for one rival, with no clear change for two others. In all, blood raised the calcium-to-silicon ratio and shrank chain growth, signs of stalled setting. The authors urge dry fields before placement.
pmc-13574859:
Roberto Cannella and colleagues surveyed how liver cancer care differs around the world, and where it falls short. Hepatocellular carcinoma management spans surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment, but access varies sharply by continent. Their 2026 survey drew 408 responses from 67 countries among attendees of the European Society of Gastrointestinal and Abdominal Radiology's Global Abdominal Imaging Forum.

Surveillance tools were broadly similar, led by ultrasound and the blood marker alpha-fetoprotein. But access to contrast-enhanced ultrasound, MRI, and PET/CT lagged badly in Africa, and African respondents reported the thinnest treatment availability, including no liver transplantation. Multidisciplinary meetings were most common in North America and least in Africa. The authors urge global efforts to close these imaging and treatment gaps.
pmc-13575059:
Giandomenico Roviello leads a 2026 study of drug interactions in bladder cancer care, drawn from the MALVA study. Patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma often take many medicines at once, raising concern about harmful interactions. The group focused on people receiving avelumab, an immune therapy used as maintenance treatment.

Records for 115 patients were scored with Drug-PIN, a tool that rates interaction burden from a person's drug list and gene data. Scores varied widely between patients, yet adding avelumab did not shift them in a meaningful way. Survival and time without progression were similar across risk groups. The authors present the work as exploratory, noting that measured interaction burden showed no link to outcomes here.
pmc-13575159:
Gloria Palazzo leads a 2026 study of multi-drug infusions for very sick newborns in intensive care. These babies often receive several drugs and feeds through one thin line into a vein. Mixing in shared tubing can delay doses or change what reaches the baby, with safety risks.

The team built software that simulates how fluids travel through common line setups, predicting transit times and the strength profile of each solution on arrival. A graphical interface lets clinicians enter patient details and line settings, then watch the fluid behaviour in real time. Users can test setups before use and compare options side by side. The authors present the tool as a teaching and planning aid for safer neonatal care.
pmc-13575759:
Bashkim Jaha and co-authors present a 2026 Swiss study of drug use tied to sex among gay and bisexual men. The practice, often called chemsex, carries health risks and draws growing concern. The team joined data from two large Swiss cohorts, one of men with HIV and one of men taking preventive HIV drugs.

Records covered more than one hundred thousand visits by over thirteen thousand men from 2019 to 2024. About one in six reported use of the drugs tracked, with higher rates in the prevention group than in the HIV group. Age, sexual orientation, and region all shaped the odds of use. The study tracks how use changed over time, through the COVID and mpox periods as well.
pmc-13576259:
Po Liu and five colleagues report a case of a large abdominal desmoid tumour that vanished on a single drug, in a 2026 case report. Desmoid tumours are rare growths that invade locally yet never spread to distant sites. They often return after treatment, and this one could not be cut out.

The patient, a 27-year-old Australian man, had a mass measuring 23 by 12 by 21 centimetres. A hormone and anti-inflammatory pairing failed to stop growth, so care switched to imatinib, a targeted pill, at 400 milligrams daily. Scans at four months showed shrinkage, and over six years the tumour cleared completely on imaging, despite patchy pill taking. One mild sun-sensitivity episode was the only side effect noted. He stopped the drug himself after ten years and stayed disease-free at eleven years of follow-up.
pmc-13576359:
Tilahun Degu Tsega leads a 2026 systematic review of whether arriving at hospital outside normal hours raises the risk of dying there, across sub-Saharan Africa. Earlier studies disagreed, and no single summary existed. The team pooled studies found in six databases up to the end of 2025.

Fourteen studies were included. Death in hospital for off-hours admissions pooled at 12.39 percent overall. Night admissions showed 26.1 percent mortality and weekend admissions 31.5 percent in their pooled shares. Against weekday daytime care, weekend arrival raised the odds of death modestly, while night arrival more than doubled them. The authors urge caution in reading the pooled figures, since studies varied greatly and defined off-hours differently. They frame the pattern as a signal for staffing and cover reviews.
pmc-13577559:
Kuo and colleagues report a 2026 study of how chloride ions help the bladder wall muscle contract, using rat tissue. Bladder squeezing is usually explained through calcium and potassium, with chloride less studied. The team checked bladder tissue for two chloride-related proteins, then mounted muscle strips in organ baths and varied the chloride around them.

Both proteins, ClC-3 and CLCA4, were present in the bladder lining and muscle layers. Replacing chloride with other ions, lowering its level, or applying chloride transport blockers changed how strongly the strips contracted under potassium or noradrenaline stimulation. The pattern shows chloride handling is a working part of bladder contraction, not a bystander. Naming the channels involved gives drug research new handles for overactive bladder, a common condition with limited treatment options.
pmc-13577759:
Hamish Brown and co-authors join gene and growth measures to pin down what sets wheat flowering time, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Six wheat types with wide sensitivity were grown under mixed heat and day length. Tip growth, final leaf count, and three flowering gene levels were tracked over time.

Shifts in leaf count were neatly explained by shifts in tip change timing and gene swings. A wheat timing model took in the joined data for direct checks against real gene curves. Gaps between model and leaf gene reads stress that leaf and tip signals differ. A leaf-count test plan closes the work. Readers who breed wheat get cleaner traits tied to genes.
pmc-13578259:
Jie Shang and colleagues report a 2026 trial of a patented chest strap made for thyroid surgery done through a small cut near the armpit. After such surgery a strap or bandage presses on the chest to limit fluid buildup. The team enrolled adults at one center in China and assigned them to the new strap or to standard bandages.

Just over one hundred patients wore the strap, and a somewhat larger group wore bandages. Total fluid drained after surgery came out lower in the strap group, and strap users had fewer problems overall. Skin allergy stood out, striking far fewer strap users than bandage users. The authors read the results as a good first showing for the device, while the single center design limits how far the claim can stretch.
pmc-13578759:
Tueanjai Khunluck and colleagues pair a plant compound called brusatol with standard chemo drugs against bile duct cancer cells, in a 2026 lab study. This cancer resists the usual drug pair, cisplatin plus gemcitabine, so new helpers are prized. Cells of one human line were dosed with the compound alone and in mixes, then checked for survival, stress chemistry, and death signals.

Mixes pushed reactive oxygen inside the cells higher than the drugs alone. Death switch enzymes woke on both known routes, cell powerhouses lost their charge, and far more cells died the programmed way. Colonies shrank, and cell crawling and invasion both fell. The authors cast brusatol as a promising partner drug, with animal and safety work still ahead before any patient use.
pmc-13579959:
Li-Pang Chen and Grace Y Yi present a software package for survival studies where gene data form networks and carry measurement error, in a 2026 paper. Survival analysis asks how traits shape the time until an event, such as death or relapse. Gene readings break two comforts of classic tools: they link to each other in regulatory webs, and their values wobble with noise that can bias results.

Their R package, called SurvGME, handles both snags inside one frame. It wraps several common survival models with tools that respect the web structure and correct the wobble. A breast cancer data set walks through the package in action, showing how the output reads. The authors pitch it to analysts facing messy, high dimensional gene data who still need trustworthy survival claims.
pmc-13580359:
Maria Wolf and four co-authors published a 2026 study of the barriers general practitioners face in following up stroke patients in Sweden. Drug prevention after stroke works well, yet results vary widely between clinics in the Stockholm region. The team ran eight focus groups with 49 doctors, chosen to span high and low performing clinics, and analyzed the talks for shared themes.

Two themes emerged: a many-sided mission inside a poorly organized system, and the hard problem of patient adherence. Doctors named short visit times, weak handovers from hospitals, unclear ownership of prescription renewals, and few tools to support adherence. Suggested fixes included more doctors, better training, and cleaner referrals. The study shows the gap is structural, not a matter of individual effort.
pmc-13580459:
Nesreen Saadeh and nine co-authors published a cross-sectional study in twenty twenty-six on fatty liver in people with type 2 diabetes. The FIB-4 score, calculated from routine bloods, is the standard first filter for liver risk. The team tested whether it actually separates diabetic patients with fatty liver from those without.

One hundred eighty-six patients were scanned by ultrasound; one hundred had fatty liver. That group was heavier and showed higher liver enzymes and triglycerides. FIB-4, however, failed to distinguish the groups at all. The authors built a simplified clinical score from the true predictors instead. Their message: in diabetes clinics, the popular index can falsely reassure, and better bedside tools are needed.
pmc-13581659:
Jaap Munneke, Brian Anthony, and Jennifer Corbett argue that commercial videogames are ready-made laboratories for studying perception, in a 2026 paper. Lab tasks in cognitive science are tightly controlled but artificial, which raises doubts about how well results carry to real life. Games are the opposite: demanding by design, self-paced, and consistent across players, with outcomes that matter to the player. The authors urge researchers to treat them as testing grounds that already exist.

Only a small toolkit is needed: screen recording, eye tracking, and timing of behavior. The paper explains how to pick games, turn their features into testable predictions, and run within-subject designs without developer help. The pitch is cheap ecological validity for a field that usually pays dearly for it.
pmc-13582259:
Le Li leads a team on burnout in medical students in China. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with a hard versus soft skills split. Schools stress hard science over human skills, they note.

Students filled scales on value seen, blocks felt, and burnout. The value and block scales were checked for sound form first. A joint stats test then linked views to burnout scores. The group was drawn from one set of clinical students. How students judge their training may shape their strain. The work maps those links in detail.
pmc-13583559:
Amna Islam and five co-authors make a magnetic powder that pulls a common antibiotic out of water, in a study from 2026. Amoxicillin often survives wastewater treatment and builds up in rivers, where it can drive drug resistance. Their material joins manganese iron oxide particles, which are magnetic, with hydrochar, a carbon made by heating wet biomass.

Tests confirmed the mixed structure and its surface groups. In batch trials at neutral pH, the powder removed up to about ninety-five percent of the drug. A simple rate model fit the uptake best. Being magnetic, the spent powder can be pulled back out with a magnet.
pmc-13584359:
Cheng Yao and colleagues interview foreign medical students in China about why they came and what they feel they gained. China now hosts many overseas students in English-taught medicine degrees. The 2026 study held long interviews with 17 students at two public universities, most from Asian and African countries and spread across the years of the course.

Students pointed to blocked paths at home, such as few places and high fees, and to draws in China, such as lower cost, a recognized degree, and safety. Feelings about the payoff shifted over time. Some grew more confident and more set on being doctors than they had expected. Others felt let down by scarce hands-on practice, language strain with patients, and unsure career paths. The authors urge better clinical access, language help, and career guidance.
pmc-13584959:
Li, Guo, Jiang, Xie, and Yao published in twenty twenty-six a review of cancer therapy aimed at a common RNA mark called m6A. Cells add this chemical mark to RNA to control how genes are used. The mark affects RNA stability, protein making, and breakdown. In cancer, it can raise or lower key transcripts and help tumors grow. Blocking the machinery behind the mark is a rising treatment idea.

The review covers small drug blockers and RNA-based tools aimed at m6A regulators. It also covers tiny carriers that ferry drugs to tumors more safely. Lipid particles, polymers, and cell vesicles all feature as carriers. Early lab results look promising, but clinical use remains limited. Drug precision and delivery still need much work.
pmc-13585359:
Chukwudera Okolo, Melanie Lagomichos, and Courtney Shaver compare two uterus devices for stopping postpartum hemorrhage, in a study from twenty twenty-six. One is a balloon tamponade; the other a newer vacuum system. Charts covered two hundred thirty-two hemorrhage cases where a device was used. Outcomes were compared head to head.

No statistically significant differences emerged between the devices. Blood loss was similar in both groups. Transfusion needs also matched. Escalation to surgery occurred at similar rates. Intensive care admissions did not differ either. The authors judge the two modalities comparably effective in practice. Choice between them can rest on availability and clinician familiarity.
pmc-13585559:
Supreet Khanal and colleagues characterized the soluble factors that CAR-T cells release to activate bystander myeloid cells, a driver of inflammatory side effects. CAR-T therapy succeeds against blood cancers but often brings cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity, fueled by myeloid cells releasing interleukin-6 and interleukin-1 beta. Earlier work had implicated three factors individually, without a fuller picture.

Comparing cytokines across human T-cell subsets and blocking candidates with antibodies, the team found four dominant drivers: GM-CSF, interferon-gamma, tumor necrosis factor alpha, and GPIb alpha. Silencing these factors in CAR-T cells cut myeloid activation without weakening anti-tumor activity. GPIb alpha, previously unrecognized in this role, joins the list of targets for safer CAR-T therapy.
pmc-13586059:
Curisa Tucker and Jennifer Baumstark link midwife practice rules to maternal health across US states in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Certified nurse-midwives give proven maternity care, yet half the states deny them independent practice. Rules may act as a structural driver of health gaps.

The team classified all fifty states by practice authority and compared midwife density with a maternal vulnerability index. States with independent practice held far more midwives per capita. A mediation check found about a quarter of the rule effect ran through workforce supply, and the rest was direct. New federal funding now rewards states for looser rules. The authors urge both reform and workforce investment.
pmc-13586159:
Zhuangzhuang Li and colleagues built a generative model that maps how Alzheimer's advances in brain scans while keeping each patient's identity. Mapping future scans could help test early prevention trials, but generic models may invent plausible scans of a different person. Their 2026 model, IP-DDGAN, mixes diffusion and adversarial training, guided by patient facts and identity-keeping rules, to make one-person future scans from a first scan.

Made-up scans kept body and disease traits and looked lifelike enough for later use. They caught change over time and key shifts from normal thinking to mild trouble and from mild trouble to Alzheimer's. The authors present identity keeping as the advance that makes mapped scans worth trusting for research, rather than merely lifelike.
pmc-13587559:
Shiqi Huang and a large team read classroom dust for clues to children's allergic rhinitis in southern China. Children spend long hours in classrooms, and the bacteria and chemicals settled there may shape airway allergy. Their 2026 study covered 45 middle schools in Guangzhou with close to four thousand students. The team read bacterial genes and hundreds of small compounds in dust, then compared rooms where rhinitis ran high or low.

Bacterial mixes differed clearly between the two room types, with some environmental genera richer where rhinitis was rare and gut-type genera richer where it was common. Close to four hundred compounds also split the rooms. One bacterium's link with rhinitis even flipped direction depending on the level of a certain fatty compound beside it. The authors argue that allergy risk reads best when microbes and chemicals are judged together.
pmc-13588459:
Prashant B. Jadhav reports two cases of chemical leucoderma, acquired skin lightening from plant chemicals, affecting the lips and mouth. Unlike vitiligo, chemical leucoderma usually lacks an autoimmune basis and stays at the contact site. This 2026 letter links bael leaves in one patient and clove in another to progressive lip depigmentation, with patch testing supporting the bael case.

A 51-year-old woman chewing two to three bael leaves daily developed whitening of both lips, gums, and cheek linings over six weeks. Depigmentation also appeared at the bael patch-test site six weeks after testing. A 78-year-old woman holding crushed clove near a sensitive molar daily for a year developed similar lip and surrounding-skin whitening. The author presents plant phytochemicals as emerging causes of contact leucoderma.
pmc-13590159:
Su Ji Heo leads a 2026 policy study on how South Korea could build a national One Health plan. One Health treats human, animal, and farm and wild settings as one linked health system. The study starts from a joint plan drawn up by four world bodies for health, food, animal health, and the environment. Heo and the team focus on the two parts of that plan tied most closely to diseases that pass between animals and people.

Their advice moves Korea away from reacting after outbreaks strike. They call for shared watch systems that link human, animal, and field data, plus joint teams across ministries and local groups. Risk based steps, taken before cases surge, form the core of the plan they propose.
pmc-13590259:
Dongqing Jing and Hongshang Chu review a natural compound called micheliolide and its drug form ACT001 as treatments aimed at brain disorders. Their review came out in 2026. The compound binds permanently to its targets, a strategy called covalent modulation, and touches inflammation, oxidation balance, and metabolism at once.

Evidence is strongest for the inflammation axis, with direct binding shown and consistent results across brain injury, Parkinson's disease, nerve pain, and a brain tumor type. The oxidation axis looks plausible but rests mostly on studies outside the brain. The metabolism axis is newest, with one strong direct result in the tumor setting. The authors sort diseases by which axis dominates in each. They flag open questions on drug levels in the brain and the long-term safety of permanent binding.
pmc-13590559:
Yong Shao and three colleagues mine records from one hospital to weigh side effects of antipsychotic drugs used for schizophrenia. Their focus is high prolactin, a hormone shift that can harm sexual health, fertility, and bones and can push patients to quit their drugs. They also tracked shaking and stiffness, a second common side effect, plus related hormone levels.

Women with schizophrenia had the highest rate of high prolactin, near one in five of those tested. Risk climbed with certain drugs, notably risperidone and its kin, and fell with others. Stiffness and shaking grew more common as prolactin rose, yet one low prolactin drug still carried high shaking risk. Shao and the team built a receptor based score that tracked prolactin risk well, to guide drug choice.
pmc-13591159:
Edibe Gozde Basaran and four co-authors present a 2026 study of how the COVID-19 pandemic changed the way celiac disease showed up in children. Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that damages the small bowel. Care delays during the pandemic may have changed how sick children were at diagnosis.

The team looked back at 114 children whose disease was confirmed by biopsy between 2017 and 2021. Half were diagnosed during the pandemic and half before it. They compared age, symptoms, antibody levels, and bowel damage scores. Children diagnosed in the pandemic years were older on median, and the paper weighs what else differed between the groups.
pmc-13591259:
Michael Batie and six colleagues study KDM2B, a gene editing enzyme, and its grip on the cell's answer to low oxygen. Cells sense low oxygen through HIF proteins, which switch on survival genes. KDM2B itself is switched on by HIF, hinting at a loop. Working across several cell lines, the team cut or raised KDM2B and watched what HIF did in reply.

Effects split by cell type: cutting KDM2B weakened HIF in bone and breast cancer cells yet strengthened it in cervical cells. Where it weakened, HIF protein, its gene message, and its grip on target genes all fell. Two parts of KDM2B proved vital, its chemical editing core and its DNA binding tip. Batie and the team also found KDM2B helps recruit the gene reading machine, and that cells need it to grow under low oxygen.
pmc-13592359:
Junyu Zhu and co-authors use genetics to test whether worn spinal discs raise arthritis risk, and whether weight and muscle loss carry part of the effect, in work from twenty twenty-six. Disc degeneration and joint arthritis disable millions, but cause and effect between them was unproven. Genes offer a natural experiment.

Instruments from a Finnish gene bank linked inherited disc risk to hip and knee arthritis and to joint replacement. Related traits like slipped discs and sciatica pointed the same way. A two step analysis showed fat and metabolic traits carried a slice of the link, up to about a third for some pairs. Muscle loss traits carried a smaller slice. Prevention could target both paths, the authors suggest.
pmc-13593159:
Jiajing Chao and five colleagues hunt, in 2026, for estrogen linked marker genes in fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction. Women before menopause seem partly shielded from the disease, pointing at hormone pathways. Six public gene datasets supplied cases and controls. Genes that both shifted in disease and touched estrogen signaling were filtered by two machine learning methods, then checked in a fresh cohort and in single cell liver data.

Fourteen candidate genes narrowed to two markers, IGFBP2 and P4HA1, each scoring high on diagnostic accuracy. Both sat mainly in liver cells and split patients into two subtypes with distinct immune patterns. Cell talk networks around liver cells weakened in disease. Chao and the team propose the pair as tissue markers needing blood level proof.
pmc-13593559:
Atef Badreddine and co-authors argue for placing a soft occlusion balloon in the superior vena cava before trouble starts. The usual habit is to reach for it only after the vein tears during a lead procedure. Their 2026 report shifts the balloon, usually a rescue bridge to emergency surgery, into a preventive role for high-risk lead removals.

A torn superior vena cava is rare but can kill quickly, and it can happen even with gently fixed leads when unexpected resistance is met while advancing them. Any resistance, the authors insist, should stop the maneuver at once and trigger imaging checks from several angles plus a contrast injection. When a balloon must stay inflated for a long time, ultrasound monitoring through the esophagus helps weigh bleeding risk against clots forming in stagnant blood.
pmc-13593659:
Anna Maria Auricchio heads a large team that tested whether a blood protein called S100B can forecast how patients fare after a spontaneous bleed around the brain, usually from a burst aneurysm. Their prospective study followed 108 consecutive patients admitted between January 2022 and August 2024, measuring S100B at one day, three days, and seven days after admission.

Higher early S100B levels went together with worse function and higher death rates, even after other severity measures were taken into account. Machine learning analysis ranked the day-one and day-three values as the strongest predictors of functional outcome. A link with delayed cerebral ischemia, a later complication, appeared in simple analysis but faded once illness severity was included. The authors call S100B a promising early marker while asking for larger studies before it guides care.
pmc-13593959:
Gebreanenia Gebretsadik Gebremamas and three co-authors study why care for malaria in young children is often sought late in Samre District, Tigray. Late care is a major health risk in poor and post conflict areas. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

The team ran a case control study in health sites in twenty twenty-four, with equal groups of late and prompt care seekers among children under five. Late care meant waiting more than a day after fever began. Late care linked strongly to no formal schooling for the caregiver, poor views of malaria, self treatment, no past malaria in the child, and living far from a health site.
pmc-13594159:
Bowen Cui and a team of co-authors built a deep learning system that sorts B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia into its molecular subtypes from gene activity data alone. Subtype guides modern treatment, yet the growing list of subtypes and the need for complex multi-test workups make classification slow and costly, which their 2026 tool, BALL6, aims to relieve.

The system feeds rank-transformed gene readings into a recurrent neural network, a design that shrugs off differences between testing platforms and tolerates missing values. One model separates B-cell leukemia from its T-cell and myeloid counterparts with near-perfect accuracy on unseen data, while a second assigns twenty established B-cell subtypes with accuracy in the low nineties. It even copes with sparse single-cell data. The code is open and a web tool is provided for clinical and research use.
pmc-13594459:
Jared Pleash and colleagues compared a personalised heparin dosing algorithm with standard weight-based dosing during atrial fibrillation ablation. Steady blood thinning during ablation matters, since too little risks clots and too much risks bleeding. Their look-back study covered 238 ablations at one centre, 125 weight-based and 113 algorithm-guided, aiming for a clotting time of 350 seconds.

Algorithm dosing hit the target more often at every time point and cut variability sharply early on, with spread at 40 minutes of about 14 seconds versus about 43 seconds. Gains were largest in patients under 80 kilograms, where deviation fell by about 27 seconds at 10 minutes. The authors call for prospective trials to test whether steadier thinning improves patient outcomes.
pmc-13595359:
Risi Liyanage, Lei Jin, and Shi-Jie Chen review, in a 2026 paper, how machine learning is sharpening CRISPR gene editing. The CRISPR system is now a basic tool of genetic engineering, yet its parts still misfire often enough to limit wider use.

The review covers learning methods that improve each stage: reading the short motif the cutter needs, engineering better Cas proteins, and designing guide RNAs that hit the target and miss everything else. It extends to newer editing styles beyond simple cutting. The authors weigh model claims against lab results and stress biophysics, where tangled data most need learning methods. Gaps and next steps close the survey.
pmc-13595659:
Carla Canal and colleagues tested whether long-term brain interleukin-6 worsens Alzheimer's damage in mice. Interleukin-6, an immune signal, rises with amyloid burden in patients and mouse models, yet its full effect through its classic receptor route was unclear. Their 2026 study crossed Tg2576 amyloid mice with mice making interleukin-6 in astrocytes, tracking death, metabolism, behaviour, and brain inflammation.

Chronic interleukin-6 cut body fat in both sexes and body weight in females, and shifted behaviour by age and sex. Aged mice showed higher harmful-to-benign amyloid ratios plus more gliosis, though gliosis near plaques fell even as overall gliosis rose. Gene readouts showed wide immune, synaptic, and stress shifts, differing by sex. Canal and colleagues conclude central interleukin-6 actively drives Alzheimer's manifestations.
pmc-13596459:
A protein that trims the tails of gene messages turns out to help breast cancers hide from the immune system. Wang and co-authors study CSTF2, a factor in finishing RNA messages, which runs high in many cancers and marks a worse outlook. They raise and lower its levels in breast cancer cells and read the effects in large tumor datasets.

The factor destroys the message for a second protein, THSD1. Losing that message lifts the brake on PD-L1, the shield tumors raise against killer T cells. With more shield, the cancer cells resist immune attack and grow more aggressively. The authors map this chain link by link using gene data, cell experiments, and immune profiling. They propose the chain as a fresh target for making immunotherapy work better in breast cancer.
pmc-13597259:
A twenty twenty-six study by Rafail C. Christodoulou and six colleagues asked whether texture patterns in perfusion scans predict early death in glioblastoma. The study covered 322 patients with IDH-wildtype grade four tumors. The team extracted radiomic features from arterial spin labeling scans, a contrast-free way to image blood flow. They tested whether feature heterogeneity predicted death after accounting for tumor volume and clinical factors.

Greater scan heterogeneity was linked to death within a year of imaging, with a hazard ratio of 1.39. The link held when tumor volume was modeled several different ways. It also survived a much wider screen of candidate features. A measure of fluid movement along vessel spaces added little. The finding suggests scan texture carries prognostic information beyond tumor size.
pmc-13598259:
Linda Varghese and co-authors show that a nerve channel long tied to warmth also acts as a direct pain sensor, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The channel is TRPM2, found in both immune cells and feeling nerves. Past work held that the immune copy drove long pain by stoking swelling, while the nerve copy sensed mild warmth in few cells.

Mice without the nerve copy felt far less joint and nerve pain, while swelling stayed much the same. Blocking the channel eased pain fast in normal mice. Two pain triggers switched the channel on by direct paths, with no need for the usual signal chain. Readers see a fresh drug target for long pain.
pmc-13598359:
Rabindra Acharyya leads a team that tests a plant extract against allergy. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with Actinodaphne angustifolia leaves. The plant is used in tradition for swelling and allergy.

Safety tests first confirmed the leaf extract was non toxic. In a chemical driven allergy model in animals, it helped. Sneezing and nose scratching fell under treatment. White cell counts in blood and lung fluid normalized. A key allergy antibody in serum also dropped. Effects matched a standard allergy drug for compare. Docking tests tied compounds to allergy targets.
pmc-13598459:
Xiao-Tong Niu and co-authors reanalyze gut gene data from a puzzling syndrome that pairs obesity with diarrhea, in this 2026 paper. The condition carries the name Linghu's obesity-diarrhea syndrome. Earlier work profiled gene activity in the small intestine of patients. This team re-mined that data for genes tied to soaking up fat, carbohydrate, and protein.

Against expectation, most of those gene sets were switched up, not down, in the patients' intestinal lining. Fat handling, sugar uptake and transport, and protein breakdown genes all ran hotter. The authors name the state diarrhea-hyperabsorption: a gut that loses fluid yet absorbs nutrients eagerly. They discuss how that pairing might work and what it could mean for treatment. The piece is a hypothesis-building reanalysis.
pmc-13598559:
Yen and colleagues build a fast way to read fat molecule changes in liver cells exposed to drugs, aiming to flag liver injury earlier than animal tests can. Broad lipid scans are slow and thirsty for sample. Their 2026 workflow measures 148 lipids across eleven classes by liquid chromatography and tandem mass spectrometry, in a targeted mode. Liver cells from human, rat, monkey, and dog grow in 96 well plates and meet three drugs known for liver effects.

One drug, chlorpromazine, stirred lipids most in human, monkey, and rat cells, rising with dose, while dog cells barely reacted. Bosentan shifted lipids in all species, strongest in human cells. Fialuridine, a drug infamous for late liver failure in people, moved lipids least, a caution flag. Overall the lipid changes matched classic toxicity markers.
