That supports the panel as a screen that compares species side by side before animal or human exposure.
pmc-13599659:
Mahmoud Salah and co-authors published this 2026 food science study on a protective gel for chicken breast built from food-grade parts: curdlan gum, bovine serum albumin, and flavonoids extracted from orange peel. Spectroscopy and microscopy confirmed the citrus compounds locked into the gel network. One recipe, the ninth variant, stood out.

That gel scored highest on antioxidant tests and released its flavonoids slowly, about 73 percent over the trial window. It held back four food-poisoning bacteria and two molds, with the widest clear zones against Listeria. Spread on chicken, it suppressed microbes, held the pH of the meat near 6.5, and kept fat oxidation low. The authors offer the gel as an eco-friendly shield for fresher, safer poultry.
pmc-13600859:
Zhanyang He and co-authors link body shape to swim scores in forty-nine young provincial racers, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Boys and girls near twelve years old had size, fat, and hand and foot areas logged. Top points per swimmer stood for race worth.

For girls, points rose with age, body mass score, and hand and foot area after strict checks. Boys showed no such firm ties. In the tuned girl model, hand area alone kept its tie, and even that shook when odd cases were dropped. Cross-sex tests found no firm split. The authors label all of it a lead for bigger samples. Readers get a careful maybe, not a talent test.
pmc-13601059:
Jeroen Deckers leads a very large team mapping inflammation across the whole skeleton, because bone marrow does not respond to disease as one uniform organ. Cardiovascular disease is increasingly understood as marrow-driven inflammation, yet researchers usually sample one site and generalize. Their method, MarrowMet, injects a radioactive glucose tracer into mice, then measures uptake bone by bone against a whole-body atlas.

Tracer uptake tracked inflammatory activity closely. Applied across models of atherosclerosis, heart ischemia, lung injury, metabolic syndrome, and aging, the maps showed distinct marrow sites lighting up asymmetrically depending on the disease. The atlas then guided which marrow regions to harvest for deeper molecular study. Location, the authors argue, is a variable immunology can no longer average away.
pmc-13601359:
Suresh Yadav, Pranali Ahir, and Dinesh Singh Bhati survey lung symptoms in silicosis patients in Rajasthan, India, in this 2026 paper. Silicosis is a scarring lung disease caused by breathing silica dust. It is common among sandstone quarry workers in the region. The study focused on certified patients in the Balesar area.

The survey covered 355 men who had lived in the area for at least two years. A standard breathing questionnaire measured symptoms. About four in five patients had the combined symptom measure. Morning cough and morning phlegm were the most common complaints. Breathlessness was also widespread. The analysis links symptom load to work related risk factors, which can guide local prevention.
pmc-13602059:
Birch and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six a four-year natural history study of choroideremia, a rare inherited eye disease. The disease slowly destroys vision in males with a faulty CHM gene. Fifty-seven males aged fourteen to seventy took part at five centers in the United States and Canada. They were tested every six months with vision charts, visual field tests, and detailed eye imaging. The goal was to find which measures track decline best.

Letter vision barely changed over the study period. Visual field sensitivity and preserved retinal area fell steadily each year, near ten percent for the imaging measure. Patient ratings of vision also worsened in a meaningful way. Several field measures matched the imaging area closely. The authors favor that area as a clean trial endpoint.
pmc-13602259:
Reeder Vermaak, Meelan Roopa, and Sara Grobbelaar introduce a problem-solving method for chaotic situations, in two thousand twenty-six. In crises, cause and effect often become clear only after people act. Hard-won lessons from a crisis also fade fast if no one writes them down once calm returns.

Their method, named ACTIVE, treats action itself as the main sense-making tool. It starts by classifying the disorder to license fast experiments where analysis falls short. Next, a targeted intervention steadies the problem and yields rich experience data. The solution is then abstracted into a general model with stated limits. The aim is to bank crisis effort as lasting organizational skill.
pmc-13602859:
José Sandoval-Díaz and three co-authors map what is known about climate migration and health in Latin America and the Caribbean. Their 2026 mini review gathers a scattered literature. Storms, droughts, and floods push people to move across the region. What that movement does to health is barely charted.

Only eight publications met the screen. Six were qualitative field studies; none compared migrants with locals head-on. Hurricanes, floods, and shifting rains dominated the events covered. Acute health effects appeared in half the papers; chronic ones were thinner still. The map's blanks are its main message. Funders and journals, the authors imply, have a region-sized gap to fill.
pmc-13603159:
Shiyao Han, Li Zheng, and Xiaohe Xu study family violence and mood in a 2026 paper on urban Chinese women. Being hit by a parent, or seeing violence between parents, can shadow mental health for decades. The team asked whether frequent social contact softens that shadow for married women in Beijing and Chengdu.

Data came from a 2020 family and health survey of near nineteen hundred women. Both forms of childhood violence were tied to more depressive symptoms. Contact frequency alone showed no clear link, but it weakened the tie between each violence form and symptoms. When both forms were counted together, seeing violence between parents kept its own link, while the direct abuse link faded. The authors back social ties as a buffer against early harm.
pmc-13603559:
Emergency doctors must guess which antibiotic will work before lab results return, and local resistance data guides the guess. Peter Erdelyi and co-authors audited five years of samples from a Hungarian emergency department. The final set held 6,510 bacterial isolates. Escherichia coli alone made up over forty percent.

Among the notorious ESKAPE pathogens, about twenty-three percent resisted multiple drug classes. A few species were far worse, with resistance above seventy-five percent. Truly hard cases stayed rare: thirty-two isolates showed difficult-to-treat resistance and five were extensively resistant. Using the World Health Organization's drug tiers, the authors found room to spare the strongest antibiotics. Their antibiogram now feeds revised local guidelines.
pmc-13604059:
Candan Tamerler and three colleagues write an essay urging materials designers to embrace disorder. Classic biomaterials design copies nature's lock-and-key logic, where a protein's fixed shape fits one partner. Yet much of biology runs on intrinsically disordered proteins, stretches that never settle into a single fold and instead flex and bind briefly. The authors argue this repertoire is an untapped design library.

Disordered regions act as effectors that trigger signaling, as motion-directing elements, and as assemblers of dynamic complexes. Their sequences change faster in evolution, widening the design space further, and shape-shifting or moonlighting proteins pack several functions into one chain. The piece also surveys AI guidance for searching these vast design spaces. Meeting real-world needs, the authors contend, calls for materials that are adaptive, modular, and responsive, qualities disorder supplies naturally.
pmc-13604259:
Tao Chen, Xinyu Bai, and four co-authors review structures that copy nature to bear loads and soak up crashes. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, spans design from the nano scale to full parts. Living things spread stress through layered materials and clever shapes. Copying that logic takes a frame linking biology to buildable forms.

Four design routes are sorted by mechanical role. Inner architectures and outer arrangements share load and steady the whole. Layered and lattice-filled designs crush in stages, taming failure. Making methods range from mineral growth to 3D printing. Each is weighed for scale, materials, and shape freedom. The review stresses how layout and process interact.
pmc-13604659:
Gaoming He and colleagues built a tiny safety checker for pathogen microscopes in two thousand twenty-six. Field clinics use automated detectors to spot germs. Such detectors can fail quietly on unfamiliar samples. Their add-on flags samples outside the training range. It fits in under one kilobyte of memory. It runs on a small clinic-grade chip.

The checker matched a far larger system on accuracy tests. It added only a tiny time cost. The team also exposed a flaw in standard safety certificates. Samples grouped on one slide break those certificates' assumptions. A slide-level certificate fixed the problem. Field diagnostics gain a cheap honesty signal.
pmc-13604959:
Ruppin and Graf review five-year results for a tooth implant with a graded thread design in Germany. The implant mixes a cylinder and cone shape with a grit-blasted, acid-etched surface. It was placed under routine care at a specialist referral practice.

Of 112 patients treated from 2019 to 2020, 44 returned with 94 implants for the five-year check. All 94 implants were still in place, a 100 percent survival rate among those seen. A standard score averaged 7.6 of 10 for function and look. Checks covered bleeding, tissue health, and bone levels on X-rays.
pmc-13605659:
Daniel Resendiz-Ventura leads a team on a YOLO frame for lung nodule finds. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses CT scans of the chest. Early lung cancer finds hinge on sharp nodule detection.

Their frame trains on nodules plus nearby body structures. Those structures act as spatial guides during training. The nodule stays the sole disease class in the model. Models were trained on one data set of many slices. They were then tested on a second set sans retraining. A cut test compared context and no context forms. Context gave steady gains across all model types.
pmc-13606159:
Zhenzhen Liu and co-authors published this review in 2026 on agarose, a seaweed sugar long used as the jelly in laboratory gels. The review follows its second career as a medical material. Agarose melts and sets reversibly, forms tunable pores, and stays transparent. It also rarely provokes the immune system. Those traits suit it to tissue scaffolds, drug delivery, diagnostic chips, immune modulation, and cell preservation.

Highlights include test chips that detect cancer-related DNA fragments in plasma. Composite gels in the review release drugs on schedule and repair joint cartilage. A freezing mix keeps cells alive after thawing without the usual toxic solvent. Most medical uses are still preclinical. The material degrades poorly inside the body and gives cells little to grip. The authors call for defined breakdown routes, reproducible recipes, and proper clinical validation.
pmc-13607759:
Erin Jadallah, Natalie McConaghy, Min-Jeong Cho, and Albert Chao wrote this review paper, published in 2026. Written for plastic surgeons, it sums up today's breast cancer treatments and how each one changes the planning of breast reconstruction.

Rebuilding the breast after tumor surgery must weigh the patient's wishes, other health issues, the tumor itself, and the cancer drugs or radiation still to come. Therapies given before or after surgery can raise complication risks and shift long-term results. The review covers radiation after mastectomy, chemotherapy, immune therapy, hormone therapy, and other targeted drugs. For each, it explains when the therapy is used and how to time reconstruction around it. The authors stress that surgeons who understand the cancer plan can individualize timing and improve the odds of a good rebuild.
pmc-13608059:
Li, Tian, Chen, and Wang examine how self-regulated learning shapes AI use effects on higher-order thinking in Chinese students, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Generative AI is spreading fast through university education. Concerns grow about effects on critical, creative, and computational thinking. Self-regulation theory frames the survey analysis.

Among weak self-regulators, AI use links negatively to all three skills. Among strong self-regulators, it links positively to critical and computational thinking. Creative thinking shows no significant link in the strong group. Self-regulation itself predicts all three skills positively. Responsible AI use in education depends heavily on learner self-management.
pmc-13608659:
Ciren Wangdui and six co-authors strengthen green concrete by treating only its weakest seam. Their 2026 study targets high-volume fly ash concrete. The seam where paste meets stone, the interfacial transition zone, is porous and weak. Most fly ash there never reacts, so the seam stays fragile.

Instead of mixing silica fume through the whole batch, the team coats coarse stones first. A thin cement paste rich in silica fume wraps each stone. Five recipe knobs were tuned by response surface methods. The best mix used set ratios of water, fume, stone, and paste, plus short mixing. A five-hour drying step confirmed the gains. Targeted treatment spends the pricey fume only where it counts.
pmc-13608959:
Zhen-Huai Fan and colleagues compare soil life around healthy and root-rotted medicinal plants. Their study from twenty twenty-six covers Aucklandia lappa in Chongqing. Root rot slashes yield and quality in this valuable herb. Soil microbes and chemistry may set the stage for disease.

Samples came from healthy plants in two soil types. Diseased plants in loam soil supplied the third group. Nutrient levels and soil enzyme activities differed sharply by group. Diseased soils carried higher nutrient readings in the results. Microbe sequencing mapped community shifts around roots. Enzyme panels covered carbon and fibre breakdown activity. Growers may learn to spot risky soil before roots rot.
pmc-13609759:
Abdullah Idrees and Gil Markovich present a two thousand twenty-six study of amino acids sticking selectively to chiral nanocrystals. Life's molecules are one-handed, and how that bias began is a deep puzzle. Mineral surfaces that prefer one hand could be part of the answer.

Three amino acids were tested on left- and right-handed terbium phosphate crystals. Matching handed pairs bound about twice as strongly as mismatched ones. At low amounts, simple binding rules held; crowding changed the pattern. Selectivity peaked at low concentrations and faded as solutions strengthened. The shared behaviour across acids hints at a general recognition rule.
pmc-13609959:
Jiarui Liu and nine co-authors rate drought tolerance in young sugarcane hybrids in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Drought is a top limit on sugarcane yields. The plants studied are advanced backcross lines bred from sugarcane crossed with a hardy wild relative. One hundred lines were grown in pots and put through twenty days of mounting drought at the seven-leaf stage. The team measured sixteen traits.

The traits covered root shape, leaf water state, gas exchange, and stress chemistry. Drought cut root growth, water content, and photosynthesis, while stress markers rose. Twelve traits proved clear enough to rank the lines. Multi-trait scoring helps breeders pick parents for dry regions. The study shows which young traits best predict a plant that can cope with dry spells.
pmc-13610859:
Qingqing Feng and co-authors test a communication program that weaves reflection into nursing skills training. Communication teaching often loses out to procedure drills, leaving students little room to grow patient-centered habits. The program follows the CICARE sequence and adds role-play scenes, emotional cue training, videos, feedback, and reflective journals across eighteen weeks. Two classes received it; two matched classes trained as usual.

After adjusting for starting scores, the program group beat the control group on communication competence and empathy. Their clinical judgment scores were clearly higher, with gains in noticing, interpreting, and reflecting. Course performance also rose. Professional identity did not differ significantly between groups. In their journals, students described sharper awareness of patients' feelings and stronger drive to learn on their own. The authors recommend the blend for nursing programs, while calling for longer follow-up.
pmc-13610959:
Jeaneth Linki Matsimbi and Maditobane Robert Lekganyane interviewed primary caregivers of teenagers living with HIV in Gauteng Province, South Africa, in a study published in 2026. Teenagers with HIV face stigma and health setbacks that spill into school life. As minors, they lean on caregivers, who often support them under heavy strain.

Eight caregivers described their days in face-to-face interviews. Their burdens included watching over teens who are often sick, keeping treatment on track, and managing behavior. Money strain, stigma from others, poor food access, and school troubles added to the load. The authors call for joined-up help: money, counseling, and food support, with nurses playing a central part in backing treatment routines at home.
pmc-13612059:
Daniel Schidu and seven co-authors wrote a vet case note in 2026 on a dog with a pus sac in the gut web and septic peritonitis. A Cane Corso of fourteen months came in with three days of no wish to eat, throws up, and belly pain. Two weeks past, it had care for a tick-borne ill.

Scans hinted at stuff the dog had gulped down, then fixed on a pus sac in the mesentery with bad fluid in the belly. A cut took the sac out and washed the belly; flesh tests proved what it was. Grown germs were Escherichia coli and Enterococcus faecium, which steered the choice of drugs. Germ counts in the fluid fell at each of three checks as the dog got well. At sixty days, full health was sure.
pmc-13612259:
Ji Sun, Jun Zheng, and Ye Shen pool the trials of gut-directed add-ons for acute pancreatitis. Prebiotics, probiotics, and their combination, synbiotics, have all been proposed to calm this pancreatic inflammation, yet benefit and safety stayed uncertain. Their review searched five databases plus grey sources through mid-2026 and kept thirty studies, twenty-five entering meta-analyses of recovery and harm.

Patients receiving the add-ons left hospital sooner, by 4.68 days on average, though studies disagreed enormously. Total infections fell clearly. Mortality looked lower in the main analysis but lost significance when fragile studies were removed. Pancreatic necrosis infection, organ failure, surgery need, and systemic inflammation did not improve. Safety reporting was patchy, and one large trial warned against live probiotics in predicted severe disease. The authors advise against routine use, above all live preparations in severe disease.
pmc-13612459:
Zhengmeng Wang leads a five-author team asking why some teenagers step in when they witness cyberbullying while most scroll past. Online cruelty unfolds before an audience, so bystanders hold real power, yet earlier findings were scattered. The systematic review searched six databases plus citations for studies from 2018 to mid-2026 and synthesized forty-nine reports, anchoring conclusions in a core set of forty-two.

The steadiest predictors were psychological: empathy, defender confidence, and a constructive moral outlook. How a teen appraised the incident mattered too, as did family climate and school ecology. Demographic, cultural-norm, and platform-design factors produced mixed or thin results. Most studies were cross-sectional self-reports from a handful of countries, which limits causal claims. The authors arrange the findings as a staged path from noticing to choosing an action. Training empathy and defender confidence, plus safe reporting routes, top their recommendations.
pmc-13615059:
Deivide Oliveira-de-Souza leads a team tracking in 2026 how a packed match schedule strains the bodies of professional soccer players across a full season. Modern fixtures pile high-intensity games close together with little rest, taxing many body systems at once. The team followed players through one competitive season, drawing repeated blood samples for chemical, blood-cell, and metabolic markers.

To read the whole picture at once, they used a perturbation score that measures how far a player's combined markers drift from a healthy baseline. The drift grew steadily as the season's load piled up, showing strain that single tests would miss. Clubs could use such a score to spot players sliding toward breakdown and rest them before injury or illness strikes, rather than reacting after the fact.
pmc-13615559:
Jonathan Lansey and co-authors present a new eye test that swaps letters for patterned arrows hidden in noise. Their study appeared in 2026. The test, called POINT, asks viewers to tell an arrow shape from its background by fine pattern detail, with difficulty stepped across twenty-two levels. It was tried on twenty adults with induced blur and fifty patients with real vision loss, against the standard letter chart.

Scores fell with blur and disease just as letter scores did, and repeat testing matched the chart's reliability. The pattern losses also followed optical theory closely. Agreement between the two tests on the final number was limited, though. The authors suggest pattern-based acuity could serve patients who cannot read letters.
pmc-13616259:
Shixia Lan and colleagues present a smart glove that can feel a material and name it, built around a hydrogel whose stiffness and stickiness can be switched on demand. Sensors based on contact electricity promise cheap touch sensing for wearables, yet soft gels face a trade-off: sticky gels sense well but wear poorly, and firm gels lose contact. Their gel uses silver ions and a small two-ended molecule in a tug-of-war binding scheme borrowed from biology.

Adjusting the mix flips the gel between a soft, clingy state and a stiff, tough one, tuning grip, strength, and electric output together. A compact neural network reads the touch signals and sorts materials, holding up even under the messy conditions of real wear. Reconfigurable touch skins like this could serve robots and prosthetic hands that must handle varied objects.
pmc-13617059:
Vassiliy Lozovoy and co-authors use three dimensional scans to plan newborn throat surgery, in a 2026 report. Some babies are born with a gap in the food pipe and a stray link to the windpipe. The join made in repair often narrows later, which is the most common problem after this surgery.

The team scanned five newborns before surgery and measured the pipe ends from rebuilt images. A shape based formula set the best length and form for the cut on the lower end. The aim was a wider join from the start. At one week, dye tests showed a sound join width. One baby leaked and needed a second operation, and no stray links returned within a year.
pmc-13618259:
Fihr Chaudhary and his three co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how emergency departments can shave minutes off stroke treatment. For a blocked brain artery, clot-busting drugs work best fast. The benefit fades steeply with every delay, while the bleeding risk does not. The review tracks the interval from a patient's arrival to the drug bolus, called door-to-needle time.

The biology is stark: about 1.9 million neurons die per minute of untreated blockage. The review covers how to measure the interval honestly, and what slows it before and inside the hospital. A Helsinki protocol that runs imaging, assessment, and drug preparation in parallel cut the median delay to twenty minutes, and Melbourne copied it within months. Registry data show the gains scale nationally, with fewer deaths. The authors also weigh speed against diagnostic certainty.
pmc-13618859:
Tao Hu led a 2026 study of a molecular chain that drives iron-dependent cell death in the soft core cells of spinal discs. The process is tied to disc degeneration and chronic back pain. The team found the enzyme UCHL3 raised in degenerating discs, rising in step with disease severity and cell-death markers. UCHL3 strips a specific ubiquitin tag from the protein HMGB1. That stabilizes HMGB1 so it accumulates in the cell fluid, where it switches on ferritin breakdown through NCOA4 and triggers ferroptosis.

Silencing UCHL3 or NCOA4 eased those effects in cells. The team then built a polydopamine nanoparticle carrying silencing RNA against UCHL3. It both quieted the gene and mopped up reactive oxygen species and iron. It reduced cell death and eased disc degeneration in rats.
pmc-13618959:
Tuan Anh Nguyen and one colleague design a tougher controller for electromechanical stabilizer bars, the active anti-roll devices that resist tipping in hard steering. Earlier work simplified the actuator and car dynamics and ignored outside disturbances. Their framework starts from a coupled model of actuator and vehicle, then layers three techniques. A super-twisting sliding mode controller gives robust motor current tracking; a disturbance-rejection observer estimates and cancels disturbances; and fuzzy logic adapts control gains to driving conditions.

In simulations the full system beat benchmark controllers, cutting vertical tire-force swings and improving vehicle dynamics. In a J-turn maneuver at one hundred kilometers per hour, motor current tracking error peaked below an ampere. Overshoot stayed under four percent, with settling well under a fifth of a second. The authors offer the framework as a template for active control where model error and disturbances matter.
pmc-13619259:
Özcan and seven co-authors published a surgical study in twenty twenty-six on isolated limb perfusion for melanoma and sarcoma that has spread within a limb. In this procedure, doctors separate the limb's blood flow from the rest of the body and wash it with a strong dose of chemotherapy, sparing the rest of the patient.

The team reviewed forty-nine patients treated at one center between twenty fourteen and twenty twenty-four. About two thirds had some complication, most within the first three days, and about one in five had a severe one. Three patients died early. Low levels of the blood protein albumin, before surgery and after, lined up with severe problems, as did a marker of inflammation on later days. The authors suggest that checking nutrition and these blood markers can help flag risky cases early.
pmc-13619559:
Qiongxian Yan and five colleagues mined the goat gut for short peptides made by microbes, in a 2026 study. Such peptides, under fifty amino acid units long, can kill drug-resistant bacteria, yet microbe-made versions remain little explored. The team identified 1,147 new peptides from the goat gut microbiome, and most had no match in existing databases.

Which microbes produced these peptides shifted as goats grew older. A worm infection changed some peptide levels and linked certain peptides to a type of immune response, without reshaping the whole community. Two peptides stood out in lab tests, killing resistant staph bacteria and another pathogen while doing little harm to cells. The authors present the goat gut as a promising hunting ground for new antimicrobial and immune-calming compounds.
pmc-13619659:
Gustavo Perrone and eight colleagues tested whether large language models can grade surgical complications as reliably as doctors. The setting was percutaneous nephrolithotomy, a kidney stone operation done through the skin. Six chatbots, including ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek, were asked to define the Clavien-Dindo grading scale, grade complication descriptions, and grade case summaries, with and without example prompts.

Every model defined the scale correctly and agreed with the reference grades almost perfectly. Six attending urologists and fifteen residents grading the same cases agreed slightly less, and the fastest doctor still needed seventeen minutes while models finished in a few minutes at most. Agreement among the chatbots also beat agreement among physicians. The authors call the result promising for an artificial setting, and they ask for prospective tests on real records plus debate about legal and ethical limits.
pmc-13620059:
Zhineng Wu and eight colleagues review where mRNA vaccines carried in lipid nanoparticles stand now and what holds them back. The COVID-19 vaccines proved the platform can be designed fast, made at scale, and drive the body to produce a target protein in place. Tiny fat bubbles protect the fragile mRNA on its way into cells, which the authors call the key enabling step.

Chapters move through mRNA engineering, particle makeup and delivery, immune responses, and clinical progress to date. Standing problems include keeping formulas stable in storage, limiting side reactions, and making protection last longer. Newer ideas covered here include heat-stable recipes, particles aimed at specific tissues, fresh RNA formats, and computer-aided design of both RNA sequences and lipid materials. The authors frame these strands as one design problem rather than separate fixes.
pmc-13620259:
Yunlong Zhou and seven colleagues designed a jelly-like electrolyte meant to fix the two big failures of zinc-iodine batteries. These water-based batteries are cheap and safe, yet iodine compounds drift across the cell and waste the cathode, while zinc grows spiky dendrites that short the anode. Their gel blends two polymers with flakes of vermiculite, a clay mineral ground into two-dimensional sheets.

The network traps drifting iodine species both physically and by adsorption on the clay flakes. Water-friendly groups in the gel calm free water and steer zinc into smooth, even layers, while charged sites on the flakes ease zinc ions out of their water shells. Test cells ran over a thousand hours in symmetric form, and full batteries kept almost all their capacity after ten thousand cycles. A pouch version also lasted hundreds of cycles, pointing toward practical storage use.
pmc-13620859:
Mohammad Amin Mosayebi and four colleagues looked for a common gut parasite in bats from western and southwestern Iran, and found none. Blastocystis lives in the intestines of people and many animals and can cause belly pain and diarrhea, yet its presence in bats was barely known. The team collected droppings from 115 bats caught in five caves across three provinces and tested the DNA for the parasite's marker gene.

Four bat species dominated the catch, two of them making up most of the animals. Every single test came back negative. The authors suggest the bats' roosting life on cave walls and ceilings, away from contaminated water and food, may keep them clear of a parasite spread through dirty food and drink. They are careful to limit the claim to these regions and species, asking for wider surveys elsewhere in Iran before bats are cleared as hosts.
pmc-13621559:
Wenlong Zhu and four colleagues review, in 2026, how the immune neighborhood of liver cancer helps the tumor spread and how treatment might break that alliance. Hepatocellular carcinoma, the commonest liver cancer, metastasizes readily, and most patients are found too late for cure. Checkpoint inhibitor drugs that revive exhausted immune cells are now first-line therapy for advanced disease, yet the suppressive microenvironment often blunts them.

The review maps the two-way traffic between cancer cells and immune cells at every step of spread, from local invasion to seeding distant organs. Suppressive cell types shield tumors, remodel tissue, and coach immune attackers into tolerance, though some immune players fight on the patient's side. The authors catalog current strategies aimed at this microenvironment, from combination immunotherapies to cell-targeted drugs, and sketch where the field should head. Their aim is raising the share of metastatic patients who actually benefit from immunotherapy.
pmc-13622959:
Sarath Chandra Varma and three co-authors present a computer model, published in twenty twenty-six, of eye surgery for a torn, lifted retina. During the repair, surgeons fill the eye with a heavy liquid that presses the retina back into place. The team asked how that push moves the retina and the fluid trapped beneath it.

The model shows the heavy liquid shoves the trapped fluid forward, away from the bubble. That flow drags on the retina and stretches it, and the direct push stretches it more. Some stretch stays after the liquid comes out, and heavier liquids leave more. The authors say a lighter liquid may cut this shift and help plan safer repairs.
pmc-13623359:
Taylan Onat and colleagues test whether a blood marker of inflammation can help flag polycystic ovary syndrome, a common hormone disorder in women. The marker, shortened to sTREM-1, rises with immune activity, and the syndrome is thought to involve quiet, long-term inflammation. The case-control study compared women with the syndrome against healthy women of similar background.

Forty patients and forty controls gave blood measured with a standard lab test. Marker levels ran clearly higher in the syndrome group, and each small rise in the marker nudged the odds of having the syndrome upward. A chosen cut-off value caught most patients while mislabelling about a third of healthy women. Combined with insulin resistance and another hormone measure, the marker helped a model sort the groups with fair accuracy. The authors present it as a supporting marker that reflects inflammation, not a stand-alone diagnostic test.
pmc-13623859:
Ralph Piedmont, Klaudia Bochniarz, and four co-authors test whether a spiritual motivation scale works across cultures. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, samples Poland and Vietnam. The scale measures the numinous: drives for endlessness, meaning, and worth. Three hundred twenty-eight Poles and three hundred seven Vietnamese answer it.

pmc-13624359:

pmc-13624659:

pmc-13624859:

pmc-13625659:

pmc-13626659:

pmc-13627059:

pmc-13627359:

pmc-13627759:

pmc-13627859:

pmc-13627959:
Carmen Sapsed and eleven colleagues propose a new way to teach and grade reflective practice, a core skill for health workers, now that students can generate text with artificial intelligence. Nine educators answered a survey and four students joined a focus group. Feedback suggested that treating each moment of reflection as one data point in a longer record could support real skill growth, though more testing is advised.
pmc-13628559:
Lia Gander and co-authors extend a fast heart wave model so it can replay re-entrant rhythms. Digital heart twins need speed that full biophysical models cannot give. pmc-13629459:

The authors suggest the scores may still sharpen personal risk estimates and trial selection, and that adult and child genetics of this disease should not be assumed identical.
pmc-13630459:

pmc-13631259:

pmc-13632059:

pmc-13632159:

pmc-13633959:

Drawing on phenomenology, psychiatry, and brain science, they name the core problem ontological dissonance: the chatbot feels like a present partner, yet no mind stands behind it to sustain the relationship. pmc-13634059:

pmc-13637259:

pmc-13637359:

pmc-13639359:

pmc-13643659:

pmc-13645759:

pmc-13646059:

pmc-13649659:

pmc-13649759:

pmc-13649959:

pmc-13650359:

pmc-13650759:

pmc-13651559:

pmc-13651759:

pmc-13658659:

pmc-13660659:

pmc-13669359:

pmc-13673159:

pmc-13676559:

pmc-13677959:

pmc-13678559:

pmc-13678659:

pmc-13682659:

pmc-13686759:

pmc-13687559:

pmc-13689559:

pmc-1780059:

pmc-1794559:
Carpenter, Jones, Lamprecht, and co-authors describe CellProfiler, software for analysing pictures of cells. It was the first free, open system built for flexible, high-throughput work of this kind. Microscopes can capture thousands of images, far too many to score by hand.

CellProfiler finds cells in those images and measures their traits, such as shape, size, and brightness. Automated measures let labs run large screens for drugs or gene effects with steady, repeatable scoring. Making the tool free and open put large-scale cell screening within reach of ordinary labs, not only rich centres.
pmc-2592359:
Coppé, Patil, Rodier, and co-authors show that senescent cells send out signals that affect their neighbours. Senescence is a near-permanent stop in cell division that blocks cancer after damage or when cancer genes switch on. The team adapted antibody arrays to measure what such cells secrete.

Their measurements reveal a rich secretory pattern, which they link to the cancer gene RAS and to the tumour suppressor p53. Signals from stopped cells can shape nearby tissue for better or worse. Understanding that secreted mix opened new thinking about ageing, wound healing, and cancer growth.
pmc-2732559:
Donlan explains biofilms, the structured communities microbes build on surfaces. Microbes that settle and grow this way differ from their free-floating kin. They surround themselves with a self-made slime layer, grow more slowly, and switch whole sets of genes on or off.

Biofilms form on pipes, teeth, implants, and wounds, where their shelter makes them hard to kill. Antibiotics and immune cells that clear floating microbes often fail against the film form. Donlan's review gathered what was known about their growth and traits, and it remains a base text for infection control.
pmc-3610159:
Levesque, Harris, and Russell propose a patient-centred concept of access to health care. Access is central to how well health systems perform around the world. Yet access remains a complex notion, interpreted in widely different ways by different authors.

The authors aim to conceptualise access at the meeting point of health systems and populations. Their framing covers both what services supply and what patients need and can reach. A clearer concept helps researchers measure access honestly and helps planners find where people fall through gaps in care.  Rural and remote care planning draws on the framework in several countries.
pmc-4383959:
Robinson, Halliwell, Hayhurst, and their co-authors described allele variant databases in 2014. The Immuno Polymorphism Database, or IPD, was created as a central system for studying variation in immune system genes. These genes vary a great deal between people, which matters for transplants and disease.

Through IPD, the team built a shared platform to curate and publish databases for each key locus. One of them covers HLA genes, which must be matched between donors and patients. Central, expert-checked lists of variants keep naming consistent worldwide. Clinicians and labs rely on that order when they type tissue for transplantation.
pmc-5753159:
Felix Bongomin, Sara Gago, Rita Oladele, and David Denning reviewed the global reach of fungal diseases in 2017. Fungal infections kill large numbers of people each year and sicken many more. Even so, health authorities often give them little attention.

The authors gathered estimates for serious fungal diseases country by country and judged how firm each estimate is. Many infections strike people whose health is already weak from other illnesses. Most deaths could be avoided with timely tests and drugs. The review makes the case that better counting is the first step toward better care.
pmc-6109259:
Peter Kerpedjiev, Nezar Abdennur, Fritz Lekschas, and colleagues presented HiGlass in 2018. Genome interaction maps show which DNA regions touch each other inside the nucleus. Such maps are huge grids that are hard to inspect with static pictures.

HiGlass runs in a web browser and lets users zoom across scales, much like a street map. One-dimensional tracks can sit beside the two-dimensional maps and stay in sync. Several views can be locked together for fair comparison. The tool made complex chromosome contact data something any researcher could explore interactively. A public demo server lets anyone try the viewer on sample maps without installing anything.
pmc-7395159:
Yuanyuan Zhang and Zemin Zhang traced in 2020 how treating cancer by rallying the immune system grew from an old idea into a modern success. Their review explains the traits of immune cells found inside tumors, since those cells often decide whether an immune based treatment works. They cover the main treatment families, including immune checkpoint inhibitors and cell transfers grown from a patient's own immune cells.

Along the way the authors mark the turning points that made these treatments durable answers for some patients, and the reasons responses still vary so much. They close by looking at how profiling the immune cells inside a tumor could guide who gets which therapy. The result is a compact history and field guide in one.
pmc-7703759:
Pierre-Alain Chaumeil and co-authors described in 2020 a software toolkit that sorts newly sequenced genomes into their proper place on the tree of life. The toolkit, called GTDB-Tk, assigns bacterial and archaeal genomes to taxa using the Genome Taxonomy Database, a classification built from genome data itself. It is designed to handle thousands of draft genomes at once without losing accuracy.

The authors show how the toolkit performs on real collections of genomes and explain the steps it uses to place each one. Objective, repeatable classification matters because names guide how scientists compare microbes across studies. As sequencing pours out new genomes daily, tools like this keep the catalog of microbial life consistent and searchable.
pouchet-heterogenie-1859:
Felix-Archimede Pouchet, a French man of science at Rouen, brought the old claim of life from rot back to life in this huge French book of 1859. Its name, Heterogenie, was his term for birth with no parent. The book ran to a great length of proof.

Pouchet set out trials with hay infusions and claimed new life grew in them each time. His stand stung the French Academy to set a prize on the theme in the 1860s. Pasteur took up the prize test, and the clash that came is a famed page of science.
quotations-from-the-project-gutenberg-ed: Quotations of John Galsworthy is number two in the Widger's Quotations series, by David Widger. The pages shown are the Project Gutenberg header alone. It gives the series title. It warns that copyright laws are changing around the world. It pleads with readers to keep the file intact on their own disks. It prints the standard notes too. Those notes praise free plain texts, readable by humans and computers since 1971. Galsworthy's extracts themselves begin beyond these pages.
rubaiyat-fitzgerald-1st-ed-1859:
Edward FitzGerald published his Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam in 1859, a slim book of seventy-five quatrains. Omar was a Persian poet and star scholar of the 1100s. FitzGerald worked from Persian texts but shaped the verses freely as his own.

The quatrains praise wine, love, and the brief joy of life. Again and again they ask why we live, suffer, and die so soon. Doubt of heaven and fate runs through the bright, sad lines. The book sold slowly at first, then became a Victorian craze. Poets soon praised it, and clubs formed to read it aloud.
sterne-tristram-shandy-1759:
Laurence Sterne published The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman in nine books from 1759. The set here is complete in the Everyman's Library edition of Sterne's strangest and funniest novel in English. Many call it the most formally radical novel of the eighteenth century on both sides of the Channel.

Tristram tries to tell his life and cannot get himself born for two whole volumes of digressions. Uncle Toby's sieges, Dr. Slop's forceps, and a sermon read aloud crowd out the promised story at every turn. Blank pages, black pages, and a marbled leaf mock the very form of the printed book itself. Sterne plays a century before modernism with time, mind, and the reader's soft heart in fiction. Beneath the jokes runs a tender study of hobby-horses and the men who ride them.
stowe-ministers-wooing-1859:
Stowe issued The Minister's Wooing in London in September 1859, with pictures by Phiz. Chapter one opens at tea in the house of Mrs. Katy Scudder on June second, in old Newport. Stowe admits at once that a storyteller never knows which end to start from.

At the center, the saintly Dr. Hopkins courts young Mary Scudder, drawn from theologian Samuel Hopkins. Mary loves a sailor thought lost at sea, and the clash tests her faith and duty. Stowe paints a fading Calvinist world with warmth and wit. Many critics rank the book her finest work of art, finer even than Uncle Tom's Cabin.
the-family-as-expounded-by-physiology-an: The Family as Expounded by Physiology and Phrenology, 1859. The phrenological family. The library retains it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
No. 59 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated December 23, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead item returns to Austria. The troubles there have not closed with the fall of Count Badeni. Baron von Gautsch has been appointed in his place. Many thought harmony would follow his dismissal. Instead, serious rioting in Bohemia has followed.

The paper explains the empire's peoples. The Germans number about ten and a half million. The Slavs, of about nine distinct races, number about twenty million. The Magyars number about seven and a half million. Yet the government is vested in the Germans and Magyars. The Slavs must obey with a very bad grace. The Czechs would like to be as independent as the Hungarians. Between Austrians and Czechs there is an intense antipathy.
the-illustrated-self-instructor-in-phren: O. S. and L. N. Fowler published this self-instructor in 1859. Both men worked as practical phrenologists. Fowler and Wells of New York issued the book. It advertises more than one hundred engravings. A chart for marking character comes with it. The title page carries their mottoes. Self-knowledge is the essence of all knowledge, one says. Character matches organization, says the other. Only the title and copyright pages are present here. A fragment of the chart's scale also survives. The lessons themselves do not appear.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
The False Nun, part of To Paris and Prison in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, follows the 1894 London edition in Arthur Machen's translation, with chapters Arthur Symons discovered. Chapter Twenty-One arranges a supper at Casanova's casino with the nun M---- M---- and M. de Bernis, the French ambassador. Before the party, Casanova confesses the anxiety spoiling his pleasure. His fatal habit of gambling roots it, since living and playing feel identical to him.

He admits he plays although he wants for nothing, driven by avarice and a love of spending only money won at the tables. In four days he has lost all the gold M---- M---- won for him at the ridotto. At the casino, Bernis unmasks and tries to place him. The chapter promises a proposal from M---- M---- and consequences Casanova cannot complain of. Readers see appetite and shame sharing one man's evening.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's No. 396, dated Saturday, October 31, 1829, illustrates Blarney Castle near Cork. The description comes from T. Crofton Croker's Researches in the South of Ireland, published in 1824. Blarney, famous in Irish song and story, lies about four miles north-west of Cork. Within a few years it has fallen from a thriving manufacturing village to decay, Croker reports.

In 1815 he remembers a large square of neat cottages around a green shaded by fine old trees. Most cottages now stand roofless, the trees are cut down, and on his 1821 visit barley ripened in the square. Quoted verse gives the clamorous rooks asking in vain for their wonted seat. The castle grounds, though much timber is felled, remain beautiful in rock and water. Readers watch an Irish village's decline recorded between two visits, six years apart.

Saturday, September 26, 1829, brings the Mirror's No. 391, which reports Mr. Gurney's improved steam carriage. Gurney has followed Franklin's advice to tire and begin again over four years of perfecting the invention. Public prejudice against a large boiler's high-pressure danger drove his redesigns. He split the boiler into forty welded iron pipes, then finally detached engine and boiler from the carriage as a separate locomotive part.

The detached machine works as a steam-horse, fastened to the carriage, with no more danger than a restive animal. Fair trials have run on common roads, and the premier has declared the machine of great national importance after experiments at Hounslow Barracks. The coach is announced to start working journeys for travellers between London and Bath on the first of next month. An earlier Mirror report, in No. 287, tracked the inventor's first carriage. Readers watch steam road travel approach its first timetable.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-04:
Motley's fourth volume covers 1555 to 1558. Chapter two promises sketches of the main rulers first. Philip the Second and Mary Tudor receive portraits. Royal councils and ministerial rivalry follow in the summary. Ruy Gomez rivals Alva at the Spanish court. The Truce of Vaucelles and papal intrigues come next. France resolves on war against Spain in Italy.

An amicable siege of Rome appears in the list. Peace with the pontiff follows that strange episode. Hostilities open on the Flemish border afterward. Coligny is foiled at Douay and sacks Lens. Philip visits England, and Mary joins the war. His army gathers at Givet by the close. Court portraiture and campaign narrative alternate in the plan.
the-white-people-pg459:
Frances Hodgson Burnett dedicates The White People to Lionel, under a verse about stars, tides, and what cannot keep her own away from her. The narrator opens by wondering whether the things that happened could have happened to anyone else. She is secretly, strangely glad of them, and writes the account down despite never having been clever or quick at talking.

Her curious life began at Muircarrie Castle, in a wild, remote part of Scotland. The huge frowning castle on its battlemented rock was hers: she was a great heiress and, so to speak, chieftainess of the clan. Yet she was a plain, undersized child, frightened of the civilised children relations brought on duty visits, and dumb with shyness before them. Burnett's ghostly tale grows from that lonely, important childhood.
thoreau-plea-for-captain-john-brown-1859:
Henry David Thoreau gave A Plea for Captain John Brown as a speech in 1859, then in print. The thunderous defense of John Brown followed the raid on Harpers Ferry that same fall in Virginia. Many call it the most radical abolitionist address of the era in the North at the time.

Thoreau hails Brown as a man of principle, not a madman, in the first public defense. He scorns editors and churchmen who damned Brown while they tolerated slavery's daily violence in the South. Brown's gallows, he argues, will make the cross itself seem less sacred to coming generations of Americans. The plea dared a Concord audience to rank conscience above law, order, and union in 1859. It helped turn Brown from felon to martyr in the Northern mind before the war.
tob-0159:
Rudolf Steiner published The Philosophy of Freedom in 1894, before his fame as founder of Anthroposophy. The book asks how a person can act freely in a world science describes as ruled by causes. Steiner answers through the act of thinking itself.

When thought grasps its own nature, he argues, a person can choose deeds from insight rather than habit or command. Moral imagination then shapes free action. The work is his most rigorous piece of philosophy, argued step by step. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. Later Steiner schools still build on its account of freedom.
tob-4059:
Volume two of Isis Unveiled, devoted to theology, completes the 1877 work that brought Theosophy to the world. Blavatsky traces Christianity, Buddhism, and the mystery faiths back to one old wisdom tradition. Churches, she charges, buried that inheritance under dogma, priestcraft, and literal readings of symbols.

Learned and fierce, the volume quotes scripture and the church fathers against their custodians, a method guaranteed to make enemies, as it did. Read together with volume one's attack on science, the theology half shows Blavatsky's full strategy: reclaim a universal ancient religion from both the laboratory's materialism and the pulpit's orthodoxy. Few debuts in occult literature arrived louder.
tob-4159:
Beatrice M. Hinkle's translation of Jung's Psychology of the Unconscious, the 1916 English edition, launched analytical psychology in America. In Hinkle's rendering, Jung's break with Freud unfolds across a long interpretation of one patient's fantasies. Libido appears as creative life force, and myths and symbols as the unconscious speaking in its native tongue.

Dreams, fairy tales, hero myths, and religions are read as one great text of the psyche's transformations. Hinkle, a practicing analyst, faced the task of inventing English terms for Jung's new vocabulary. Readers comparing this duplicate record with its twin nearby will find the same landmark text; its influence justifies the repetition.
tob-4259:
Henrik Ibsen wrote Peer Gynt as a dramatic poem in 1867, and William and Charles Archer's translation carried it to English readers in the edition of 1876. Peer, a boastful Norwegian farmer's son, talks his way out of every duty life sets him. Trolls crown him; the Button-Moulder waits to melt him down.

Solveig, who loves him, waits in the hut through all his wandering years. The play swings between satire, fairy tale, and sharp judgment on a self that never commits. The Archers' verse keeps Ibsen's music and bite. Verified from the 1919 edition, Peer Gynt stands the most Norwegian of plays, and the most universal.
turgenev-house-of-gentlefolk-1859:
A House of Gentlefolk, Turgenev's novel of 1859, is given here in Constance Garnett's English. Fyodor Lavretsky returns to Russia after years abroad and a broken marriage. At the Kalitin house he meets Liza, a grave, devout girl, and falls in love with her.

News that Lavretsky's wife has died seems to clear their path at last. Then the wife herself appears, alive, and hope closes for both lovers. Liza withdraws to a convent, and Lavretsky accepts a life of quiet work. Turgenev writes the tale in his most lyrical manner. It became his most loved novel in Russia, an elegy for the gentry world that raised him.
un-ga-res-2159: Who speaks for China at the United Nations? Resolution 2159, adopted on 29 November 1966, deals with the rule for deciding, not the claim itself. A 1950 vote had said such fights should be judged by the Charter's aims and the facts of each case. A 1961 vote then classed any change in China's seat as an important question, needing a two-thirds majority. The 1966 text states, in full, that the 1961 ruling remains valid.
un-ga-res-a-69-59:
Keep your word: that is the blunt core of Resolution A/69/59, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. States care deeply, it says, that rights and duties from the pacts they sign are honored in full. Keeping faith with the Charter, and with arms and spread-control deals, is cast as a must for peace and calm at home and abroad.

A state that breaks its deals, the text warns, does more than harm itself. It puts at risk all states that lean on the curbs and pledges in those deals for their own safety. The trust that pacts are kept is treated as a shared shield, worth guarding for its own sake.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 2159 (XXI) was adopted on 29 November 1966. It concerned the representation of China in the United Nations. It recalled the Assembly's 1961 ruling, made under Article 18 of the Charter. Under that ruling, any proposal to change China's representation counts as an important question, needing a two-thirds vote. It also recalled the 1965 vote affirming that ruling. The resolution then states, in one line, that the 1961 decision remains valid.

Resolution 69/59 of the General Assembly is about compliance with non-proliferation, arms limitation, and disarmament agreements. The Assembly stresses that such agreements work only if they are fully complied with and enforced. It stresses that non-compliance endangers states that rely on the agreements' limits. It urges all states to meet their obligations in full. It calls on those out of compliance to decide to return to it. It asks member states to help build capacity. It asks them to hold violators accountable in line with the Charter.
un-sc-res-1359:
A draft framework for Western Sahara's future reached the parties in 2001. On 29 June 2001 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 30 November 2001. The Secretary-General's envoy had drawn up the draft Framework Agreement. The Council backed his plan to invite the parties to direct or proximity talks. They could debate the draft and suggest exact changes. Nothing would be agreed until everything was agreed.

The Polisario Front's own proposals would also be weighed during the talks. The Council restated the goal of a free and fair referendum. It also recalled the safety rules for United Nations staff. The extension kept the mission alive while a new political track opened. That track later gave way to the 2003 peace plan.
un-sc-res-1459: Readers meet Resolution 1459 here as a Security Council record, catalogued with a date of 2002. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1559:
Lebanon stood at the center of this decision on 2 September 2004. The Security Council backed the full sovereignty and independence of Lebanon. It noted with concern that foreign forces still remained on Lebanese soil. It also pointed to armed militias that blocked the government from ruling all its own land. A presidential election was near, and the Council wanted it free of outside pressure.

The resolution calls on all remaining foreign forces to withdraw from Lebanon. It demands the disbanding and disarmament of every militia, Lebanese or not. It supports a free and fair presidential vote under Lebanese rules alone. The Secretary-General had thirty days to report on compliance.
un-sc-res-1659:
Afghanistan's post-Bonn framework was endorsed by the Security Council on 15 February 2006. The Afghanistan Compact had been launched in London on 31 January 2006. Afghanistan's foreign minister wrote to the Secretary-General on 6 February with the news. The Council said security, governance, and development gains reinforce each other, and that the fight against terror and narcotics threats went on.

The Council endorsed the Compact and its annexes as the framework for partnership between Kabul and the international community. Both sides were called to carry out its promises in full. The United Nations was confirmed in its central, impartial role, including joint steering of the effort. A joint board to steer and track the work was welcomed. The Council noted the interim national growth strategy and NATO's continuing lead of the security force. It also flagged the danger of opium growing and trafficking to the whole project.
un-sc-res-1759: Resolution 1759 dates to 2007 in the Council's sequence, and the collection keeps its official text through English Wikisource. A resolution's preamble is its argument; its operative paragraphs are its orders. This entry contains both, in the order voted, making it a complete primary source for whatever question the members were deciding.
un-sc-res-1859:
The Council spoke on Iraq through Resolution 1859, adopted on 22 December 2008. Iraq had gained ground on security, politics, and the economy. It still needed outside support to advance further. Money from oil and gas sales flowed into the Development Fund for Iraq under international watch.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends those fund arrangements until 31 December 2009. The advisory board that watches the fund keeps its task for the same span. Legal shields on Iraqi oil and fund assets also stay in place. A review is due at Iraq's request or by 15 June 2009. The Council will also review every Iraq resolution since 1990, aiming to restore the country's old standing.
un-sc-res-2059:
Syria's observer mission received its last short lifeline in Resolution 2059, adopted in July 2012. UN observers had entered Syria to watch a ceasefire that never held. With fighting spreading, the Council renewed their mandate for a final thirty days.

The text ties any further extension to a real drop in violence and an end to heavy weapons use in towns. Those conditions were not met, and the mission soon closed. The resolution is a small document with a bleak weight: it records the moment a monitoring effort admitted the war had outgrown it.
un-sc-res-259:
Arab civilians under Israeli occupation were the concern of a Security Council decision of 27 September 1968. Resolution 237 (1967) had called on Israel to protect the welfare and safety of people in the areas taken in the June 1967 war. The Secretary-General had reported on his efforts. Israel kept setting conditions for receiving his special representative, and the Council deplored the delay.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to send a special representative urgently to the Arab territories held by Israel since 5 June 1967. The envoy would report on how resolution 237 (1967) was being applied. Israel was asked to receive the representative, cooperate with him, and ease his work. All concerned were urged to give the Secretary-General full cooperation in the effort. The text kept the welfare of the occupied population on the Council's agenda while access for its envoy remained blocked.
un-sc-res-359: The United Nations Security Council issued Resolution 359 as one of its formal decisions, and the catalog carries it under the year 1974. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them.
un-sc-res-459:
Lebanon's interim force was renewed amid strain on 19 December 1979. The Secretary-General's report on UNIFIL lay before the Council. Cease-fire breaches went on, the force faced attacks, and blocks stood in the way of its full deployment. Lebanon asked for the renewal, and its government was working to restore its authority in the south.

The Council restated the aims of resolutions 425 (1978) and 450 (1979). It backed the Secretary-General's work to firm up the cease-fire and called on all parties to stop acts that clashed with UNIFIL's aims. The force and its commander won high praise for their performance. Lebanon's plan to protect its archaeological and cultural sites was noted with support. The Council then renewed UNIFIL's mandate for six months, to 19 June 1980. Member states were urged to use their sway so the force could deploy in full.
un-sc-res-59:
The killing of the United Nations mediator in Palestine was taken up on 19 October 1948. Count Folke Bernadotte and observer Colonel André Sérot had been assassinated on 17 September 1948. The Acting Mediator reported on the murders and on the troubles facing truce supervision. Israel's provisional government had sent no account of its investigation into the killings.

The Council noted that silence with concern. It ordered Israel's government to report soon on the progress of the inquiry. The report had to state what steps had been taken over official negligence or other factors in the crime. Both sides were reminded that their duties under resolutions 54 and 56 (1948) stood in full. The Council ruled that observers and truce staff must get ready access to airfields, ports, truce lines, and key points. Their aircraft and transport needed safe conduct, and both sides had to aid inquiries into truce breaches.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Fresh plans for Western Sahara stirred the file in the summer of 2001. A draft deal would give the land wide self-rule for a time. The final call on its fate would come later, by vote. James Baker, the chief's envoy, drove the talks. Resolution 1359 passed with no dissent on 29 June 2001.

MINURSO, the UN team in the land, stayed to 30 November 2001. The Council backed Baker's bid to get all sides in one room. The Polisario Front's own plans would still get a fair look. One rule was stressed: no part was agreed till all was agreed. The text also pressed a grim point. Both sides had to free all those held since the war began. The fate of the missing had to be faced.

Rough diamonds get a world certification scheme, and the Council backs it on 28 January 2003. Illegal diamond sales from war zones had funded armed conflicts in several countries. Governments, the diamond industry, and civic groups had built the Kimberley Process together, and it was adopted at Interlaken in November 2002.

The scheme is strongly supported as a real blow against trade in conflict diamonds, and the industry's voluntary self-regulation alongside it is welcomed. The widest possible membership, the Council stresses, is essential for the system to work. All member states are urged to take an active part, so diamonds from war zones can be kept out of the legal world market.

Lebanon's sovereignty took center stage in the autumn of 2004. On 2 September, the Council adopted Resolution 1559. A contested presidential vote loomed in Beirut. Many saw Syria's hand behind it. The Council voiced grave concern at armed militias beyond Beirut's control.

The text calls on all foreign forces left in Lebanon to withdraw. That meant Syrian troops above all. It also calls for all militias, Lebanese or not, to disband and disarm. Beirut's control must extend over all its land. The coming vote must be free and fair, under Lebanese rules, with no foreign say. Syria pulled out within a year. The militia clause stayed unmet and disputed.

A republic born from a broken union took its seat in 1960. On 28 September, the Council adopted Resolution 159 without dissent. The Republic of Mali had formed weeks before. Senegal had walked out of the short-lived Federation of Mali in August. Mali then proclaimed its own republic in September.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit the Republic of Mali. The Assembly seated it the same day. The two-step path tells the story in paper form. A federation was backed in June, then a lone republic in September. West Africa's map was redrawn at speed that year. This text is one small proof of the pace.

Resolution 1659, adopted on 15 February 2006, puts the Council's weight behind the Afghanistan Compact. The compact had been launched in London on 31 January, setting shared goals between Afghanistan's government and its international backers after the Bonn process ended. Afghanistan's foreign minister wrote to tell the Secretary-General of the launch.

The Council endorsed the compact. The text around that endorsement pledges continued support as Afghans rebuild their country, strengthen constitutional democracy, and take their place among nations. It stresses that security, governance, and development reinforce one another, and that the fight against terrorism and narcotics remains central. Regional cooperation is named as a real tool for Afghan security and growth.

Six more months for the Golan Heights force are approved on 20 June 2007. UNDOF is renewed until 31 December 2007, still watching the separation between Israeli and Syrian forces. The parties are called on to carry out resolution 338 of 1973 at once. The force's work on the zero-tolerance policy against sexual exploitation and abuse is welcomed. The Secretary-General is asked to report at the end of the period.

Iraq's oil-money protections are extended by Resolution 1859, adopted on 22 December 2008. The multinational force mandate was ending on 31 December 2008, and security had improved. Iraq's government asked in an annexed letter for another year of the arrangements. The arrangements shielded oil revenues from old regime-era debts and claims while Iraq worked to settle them. A transition to Iraqi-run oversight was being prepared.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the deposit of oil and gas export proceeds into the Development Fund for Iraq until 31 December 2009. It extends the monitoring role of the International Advisory and Monitoring Board and the legal immunities of Resolution 1483 (2003). The deal is reviewable by 15 June 2009 at Iraq's request. The Council also starts a review of its Iraq resolutions back to 661 (1990), seeking the facts needed to restore Iraq's international standing from before that resolution.

Burundi's UN office is scaled down in Resolution 1959, adopted on 16 December 2010. Five elections held through 2010 had passed without large-scale violence, a milestone for peace and democracy, and the integrated office BINUB was credited for its recovery work. Reports of extrajudicial killings, torture, and curbs on opposition parties and civil society remained a serious concern.

The Council asks the Secretary-General to replace BINUB with a smaller United Nations Office in Burundi, BNUB, for 12 months from 1 January 2011. BNUB must strengthen judicial and parliamentary institutions, promote political dialogue, back the creation of transitional justice mechanisms, protect human rights, and help tie economic policy to peacebuilding and fair growth. The government is urged to investigate rights abuses, bring those responsible to justice, and set up an independent national human rights commission. Reports are due every six months.

Syria's civil war had made the work of United Nations observers almost impossible by the summer of 2012. Resolution 2059 concerns UNSMIS, the United Nations Supervision Mission in Syria. Its unarmed observers had been sent to watch a cease-fire that was failing. The security situation grew more dangerous week by week.

The Council renewed the mission's mandate for a final period of thirty days. Plans to reshape the mission would guide that last period. All sides had to keep the observers safe and let them move and work freely. The main duty for their safety lay with the Syrian authorities. Any further renewal would come only if heavy weapons fell silent. Violence also had to drop enough for the mission to do its job. A report was due within fifteen days.

Resolution 259 passed on 27 September 1968. Twelve members backed it, and three did not vote either way. It tries to send a UN envoy into the Arab lands Israel held after the June 1967 war. The Council feared for the safety of the Arabs who lived there. A 1967 text had set out their rights as wards of war. Israel kept naming terms for the envoy's visit, and the visit kept slipping.

The Council asked the UN chief to send the envoy at once. He was to report on how the 1967 rights text was being kept. Israel was asked to take him in, work with him, and ease his task. Other states were urged to help as well.

United Nations peacekeepers in Cyprus were killed and wounded during the fighting of the summer of 1974. The force stood on the island with the full consent of Cyprus, Turkey, and Greece. Resolution 359, adopted on 15 August 1974, speaks directly to the safety of that force.

The Council deeply deplored the deaths and injuries among the peacekeepers. All parties had to respect the international status of the United Nations force in full. Nothing could be done that put the lives of its members at risk. Full cooperation with the force was required in all its tasks. That included its humanitarian work across Cyprus. The text stressed a wider point: the safety of any United Nations peacekeeping force must be respected under all circumstances.

Lebanon's request keeps UNIFIL in the south in Resolution 459, adopted on 19 December 1979 by twelve votes to none with two abstentions. The Secretary-General's report on the force was before the Council. Members noted with concern that the ceasefire kept being violated, that UNIFIL itself was attacked, and that obstacles blocked the force from deploying fully and moving freely.

The Council renewed UNIFIL's mandate for a further period, into June 1980. It restated its call for strict respect for Lebanon's territorial integrity, unity, sovereignty, and political independence within its recognized borders. It also welcomed the Lebanese government's efforts to reassert its authority in the south, a goal the force existed to serve.

The assassination of the UN mediator in Palestine drives Resolution 59, adopted on 19 October 1948. Count Folke Bernadotte and French observer Colonel André Sérot had been murdered on 17 September. A month later, the Council noted with concern, Israel's provisional government had still sent no report on how the investigation was progressing.

The Council asked that government to report at an early date on the inquiry and on any negligence by officials that bore on the crime. It reminded all governments and authorities in Palestine that their duties under the summer's truce resolutions had to be carried out in full and honestly. It also pressed the acting mediator to spread UN observers fairly across both parties' territory.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4559:
Section 4559 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with debts owed by staff of the House. It sits in Chapter 45, on pay and gains for Congress, in a part on the House. When a staff man of the House comes to owe a sum to the House and does not pay it, a step is set. The chair of the panel, or the chosen officer, who has charge of the work in which the debt was run up may act. That man may certify the sum of the debt.

The note of the sum is to go to the Chief Administrative Officer of the House. That officer may hold back the sum so noted from any sum paid out by him.
